stories.title: Ready. Set. Reset: How the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre improved ready-to-treat to treatment wait times
stories.summary: October 26, 2026
stories.content:
Photo from left: Meghan Koczwara and Christine Rossi, radiation therapists in the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre preparing the Ethos linear accelerator (used to deliver radiation therapy) for a patient.

October 26, 2026

After only twelve weeks, beginning in March 2026, the Radiation Therapy team at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre improved radiation therapy wait times by 34 per cent.

Some key figures to keep in mind:

The target for patient wait times for this project is measured from when a patient is considered ready to treat to the start of radiation treatment.

This project also included the target for patient wait times at LHSC from first consultation to the CT simulation appointment, which is three days. The CT simulation appointment is often the first step in planning for radiation therapy treatment, is three days.

The provincial benchmark is for the patient to be treated within their urgency category wait time window. The target for most patients is to begin treatment within a wait time window of 14 days from being ready-to-treat. And within that, the aim is that at least 85 per cent of patients should be starting their treatment in that period.

After the Radiation Therapy team implemented RESET into their workflow in August 2026, they saw 90.7 per cent of patients meet their wait time target from ready-to-treat to receiving their treatment.

When leaders in Radiation Therapy closely examined patient wait times for radiation treatment and CT simulation appointments, they noted that the issue was not about individual performance.

“Everyone was working hard and following the processes available to them. The team initially expected the system to self-correct as pressures changed from day to day, but a deeper investigation revealed that was not happening. Instead, delays were occurring throughout the pathway, creating barriers that prevented patients from moving efficiently from consultation to treatment,” explains Carina Feuz, Manager, Radiation Planning in the Verspeeten.

There were six areas that the team needed to focus on to improve these wait times:

Demand and backlog management

CT simulation

Treatment planning

Treatment delivery

Stabilizing the roles of staff and ensuring their well-being

Accountability and reporting as the project progressed

The three main goals of the project were:

Reduce patient demand where appropriate

Increase capacity where needed

Improve patient flow through the treatment pathway

Dr. David D'Souza, Division Chair/Head of Radiation Oncology at the Verspeeten notes that there are multiple steps and collaborators that work in the cancer centre to get patients assessed and started on radiation.

"The 14-day target was set to ensure that across Ontario, there was equitable and timely access to radiation," D'Souza explains. "Our performance at the Verspeeten is measured and compared with other centres in the province. The rationale is that an adequately resourced system should be able to do the work required to get a patient started on treatment within that target. Longer waits can lead to poorer treatment outcomes. The importance of including the CT simulation appointment in this project is that it is the first step in getting patient to treatment. If a patient waits more than three days, it becomes challenging to “catch up” and get a patient started on time."

Feuz explains, “We recognized there were opportunities for improvement. It wasn’t about any one person or one team. It was about understanding how the entire pathway was functioning and where we could make changes together.”

The Radiation Efficiency Scheduling & Execution Transformation (RESET) launched in March 2026 in response to patient wait times that were longer than the provincial target for Urgency Three patients – which are patients that should receive their first treatment within 14 days from their ready-to-treat date.

The other categories are Urgency One patients, who should receive their first treatment within one day from consultation, and Urgency Two patients, who should receive their first treatment within seven days from their ready-to-treat date.

Working in partnership with LHSC’s Project Management Office, the initiative used data and insights from staff to identify practical changes using existing resources to reduce bottlenecks, restore timely access for patients, and create a more sustainable operating model of care.

“Rather than simply scheduling appointments as space became available, teams began focusing on whether patients moving through the system were truly ready for the next step in their treatment journey,” Feuz says. “And CT simulation booking was aligned more closely with treatment readiness, helping create a smoother and more predictable flow.”

Early indicators helped leaders and frontline staff understand when trends were emerging and what actions were required. If a change appeared to be part of a larger pattern, leaders determined whether they should stay the course, activate contingency plans, or take more direct action. This disciplined approach helped create a shared understanding across the pathway and increased clarity around decision-making.

The program established clear rules to review cases as the patient moved through each stage of care. These reviews helped identify barriers, adjust bookings when necessary, and ensure patients continued progressing through the system in a timely manner.

“If ready-to-treat performance started to decline or shift, that served as a signal for us to respond,” Feuz says. “Each threshold had a specific action associated with it, which meant we could monitor access delays and intervene before a backlog was established.”

Clerks, physicians, physicists, radiation therapists, dosimetrists, electronic technologists, and leaders all had a role in helping patients move more efficiently through the pathway.

“The numbers were important,” Feuz notes, “but what mattered most was how the plan was implemented across the program and the positive impact it had on patient access to timely care.”

"The impact of RESET has been huge," shares Dr. D'Souza. "Since many of our patients travel for over an hour to get to our centre, in addition to convenience, these changes have made it easier for a patient to access the resources needed in a timely manner in order for them to receive radiation treatment. There is more flexibility in getting patients booked into a time slot that works for them. It also means that those suffering with symptoms like pain are getting relief sooner."

There were honest conversations throughout the process, and staff feedback was sought before, during, and after implementation. Many of the improvements that contributed to the program’s success came directly from frontline teams.

“A lot of the changes were staff generated,” says Feuz. “The success of RESET was because of the team here in Radiation Therapy. It was a huge team effort. We would not have achieved this success without everyone’s commitment.”

The shared goal was never simply to improve a metric. It was to ensure patients received the care they needed without unnecessary delays.

“We wanted patients to remain at the forefront,” Feuz says. “That’s why we were doing this. We wanted them to receive the best care possible and to receive it in a timely way.”

It is important to recognize that growth continues across both patient volumes and in terms of complexity of the patients the Verspeeten sees. Planning for additional capacity remains a critical component of the cancer centre's strategy.

Today, the Radiation Therapy team continues to monitor trends, review indicators regularly, and escalate concerns before they become larger issues.

RESET has demonstrated that sustainable improvement comes not from any single metric or intervention, but from a shared commitment to keeping patients moving through their care journey and ensuring timely access to treatment when it matters most.

"While the data shows improvement in access times, the true success of RESET can be measured in the experience of patients”, Feuz shares. "By identifying issues earlier, responding to trends proactively, and working together across the entire radiation therapy pathway, the team has helped ensure more patients receive the care they need, when they need it. And that remains the goal moving forward."

stories.title: Replica firearms seized
stories.summary: London, ON (October 26, 2026) – Two suspects were arrested within minutes of a 9-1-1 call early Sunday morning after a witness reported a dispute in the south end of the city.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 26, 2026) – Two suspects were arrested within minutes of a 9-1-1 call early Sunday morning after a witness reported a dispute in the south end of the city.

At approximately 4:10 a.m., ON October 25, 2026, two males attended an address near Chiddington Avenue and Chiddington Gate and began to argue with a resident, prompting a witness to call police.

Additional information was received that the suspect males were in possession of firearms.

Officers responded, located, and arrested both suspects.

There were no reported injuries.

During a search incident to arrest, officers located two replica firearms.

As a result of the investigation, Hamza Al Said, 18, of Ottawa has been charged with the following offences:

Carry concealed weapon; and

Utter threats.

Mohamad Al Saleh, 21, of Ottawa, has been charged with the following offences:

Utter threats; and

Breach of recognizance.

Both accused have since been released and are expected to appear in London court on November 26, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Doerkson says he’ll prioritize B.C.’s finances, work toward West Coast pipeline as next premier
stories.summary: BC Conservative Leader won a large majority government in a snap election called two years early by Ndp’s Eby
stories.author: Jesse Winter, Ian Bailey
stories.content:
British Columbia ’s next premier, a former rodeo rider and newspaper publisher who many people hadn’t heard of five weeks ago, says his first priorities will be taking an in-depth look at the province’s deeply indebted finances, and working with Alberta and Prime Minister Mark Carney to jump-start the planned oil pipeline to the West Coast.

BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson won a large majority government Saturday in a snap election called two years early by NDP Leader David Eby.

“British Columbians voted for change last night and for whatever reason, they liked the platform that we put forward,” Mr. Doerkson said at a news conference Sunday. “I intend to get to work right away.”

The loss has the BC NDP bitterly regretting the high-stakes gamble of calling the election, the timing of which appeared aimed at taking advantage of the disarray in the Conservative caucus. The Conservatives had elected a deeply unpopular leader in the spring, but she resigned two days before Mr. Eby made the election call.

Mr. Doerkson was named interim leader and was soon thrown into a campaign, uniting a fractious caucus behind him.

NDP MLA and cabinet minister Adrian Dix, who was re-elected, called Saturday’s result one of the most disappointing nights in the modern history of the BC NDP. After nine years of government under the leadership of John Horgan and Mr. Eby, the party is heading into opposition.

“Clearly, given the results, it was a mistake to call the election,” Mr. Dix told reporters after the results came in.

Mike Farnworth, who has served as B.C. transportation minister and was also narrowly re-elected, agreed calling the snap election was a bad idea.

“In hindsight, I don’t think it’s rocket science to say we probably shouldn’t have,” he said in an interview Sunday.

He said the caucus and the party will have to take time to reflect on the outcome and what comes next.

Mr. Eby resigned as party leader in a somber speech Saturday night, accepting responsibility for the outcome of the vote. He said he would continue to represent his riding.

“This is obviously something I do with a very heavy heart,” he said to supporters at his party’s gathering in Vancouver. “But it is time for new leadership within our party.”

The results with 99 per cent of the polls reporting showed 64 Conservatives elected, 27 for the NDP and two for the Greens. The NDP lost 20 seats compared to the party’s result in the last election in 2024.

At his news conference Sunday, Mr. Doerkson listed some of his first priorities.

He said briefings with the public service will begin in coming days with “some urgency” so the government will be able to swiftly advance its agenda once it’s sworn in.

He said after being sworn in, he would immediately launch an independent review of the province’s finances, citing the record-high $14-billion deficit and the need to find a way to bring it to balance eventually.

Other initiatives include an expert commission on hospital emergency rooms and wait times, as well as a tax break aimed at returning $1,000 to every British Columbian.

He said he hopes to engage with Mr. Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith to get the Pacific Link pipeline, between Alberta and B.C., moving.

Without being specific, Mr. Doerkson said he has been “thrilled” about recent announcements by the Prime Minister. “We’ll work very closely with him, and of course, our neighbours.”

Mr. Doerkson said Sunday that he hopes to use a session of the B.C. legislature next spring to repeal an Indigenous rights law passed unanimously by the legislature in 2019, the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, or Dripa. Critics worry the province is at risk of many lawsuits if Indigenous groups believe the province’s laws are not in alignment with Dripa.

“I am still committed to the repeal of Dripa. It has not worked in this province, and, frankly, it has caused more problems to date than, I think, potentially anything else,” he said.

The premier-designate said he looks forward to working with First Nations communities in the province, noting that he has received complimentary messages from some of those communities.

He said he had not ruled out holding a session of the legislature this fall.

Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney said Mr. Doerkson’s win offers lessons that other Conservatives should take to heart.

“Yet another reminder to Conservative parties: ignore the crazy fringe of the hard populist right. Don’t let the tail wag the dog. Let them stay in their little fringe parties,” Mr. Kenney posted on social media Saturday night.

“Instead, propose bold, thoughtful policy reforms rooted in conservative principles that appeal to the broad mainstream,” Mr. Kenney wrote.

Manitoba NDP Premier Wab Kinew said the B.C. results should be a warning for other politicians and consultants looking to eke out tactical advantages without considering voters themselves.

Politics is not a game, he said.

“It is a serious responsibly that isn’t to be played with. There’s no partisanship in these comments, it’s all about reminding people that we have a serious obligation to take our democracy and our duties with the utmost of care.”

Voter turnout appears to have played a significant role in Saturday night’s outcome.

Elections B.C. reported Sunday afternoon only 48 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot, a record low.

While the Conservatives took nearly half of all the votes cast, they netted fewer actual votes than in the 2024 election, as did the NDP.

The Conservatives recorded about 5 per cent fewer votes than in 2024, while the Greens took home roughly 13 per cent more. But the NDP took by far the biggest hit, with 274,000 fewer votes, a drop of 29 per cent.

Stewart Prest, a political science lecturer at the University of B.C., said that trend suggests a big chunk of the Ndp’s base stayed home, and it cost the party the election.

Mr. Eby had tried at first to frame the election around the need to repudiate what he described as a Conservative Party too closely aligned with the U.S. politics of culture war issues and division, Mr. Prest said.

But “voters generally don’t like being told what to do,” Mr. Prest said. “Being told you have to show up two years after you cast a vote to do it again to prove a point, I think that was a difficult sell with NDP supporters.”

With a report from Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. election turnout slumps to new low as fewer than half of voters cast ballot
stories.summary: Voters did not seem persuaded that a snap election was necessary, despite Eby’s efforts to make it about winning a new mandate
stories.author: Joe Friesen
stories.content:
Voter turnout in B.C. hit a new low in Saturday’s provincial election as fewer than half of registered voters cast a ballot, an indication, observers say, that many voters rejected the rationale for the snap vote.

According to preliminary results from Elections BC, about 48 per cent of voters cast a ballot, which would be the lowest level recorded going back as far as 1928. In 2024, voter turnout was about 58.5 per cent, and in 2020, it was about 53.9 per cent.

The stunning electoral turnaround that saw the Conservatives, led by interim party leader and now premier-designate Lorne Doerkson, sweep the incumbent NDP government from office was a remarkable rebuke for outgoing Premier David Eby.

With two years left in his mandate and with an opposition party that was without a permanent leader and in disarray, Mr. Eby called the vote on Sept. 22 with his party leading in the polls. Voters, however, did not seem persuaded that an election was necessary, despite Mr. Eby’s efforts to make it about winning a new mandate to tackle the U.S. trade war.

On Saturday, they punished the government, electing a sizable Conservative majority and ending a nine-year run in charge for the NDP that began in 2017 under premier John Horgan, who died in 2024.

Geoff Meggs, who was chief of staff to Mr. Horgan, said it appears that many of the party’s voters simply stayed home.

“Dave Eby’s campaign angered them. They were never persuaded by his arguments in favour of an election,” Mr. Meggs said.

He said in some ways it’s not surprising that the party’s support took a hit. The NDP campaign, when it eventually pivoted away from the trade argument for the election, proposed complex policies focused on affordability, such as one to regulate grocery prices, that didn’t capture the imagination of voters.

And while Mr. Eby raised fears about what the Conservatives would do if they won power, he didn’t clearly underline what his government had accomplished, according to some political observers.

“He didn’t campaign on the very real achievements of the NDP over the years since 2017 and proposed things that didn’t resonate with British Columbians,” Mr. Meggs said.

The NDP received about 274,000 fewer votes than in the previous election, while the Conservatives got about 49,000 fewer. The Green Party increased its tally by about 23,000.

The low turnout for the provincial election is in contrast with relatively strong turnout during the recent municipal elections. In Vancouver, municipal voter turnout was up seven percentage points for the Oct. 17 vote at 43.4 per cent, compared with 36.3 per cent in 2022. Across the province, municipal-election turnout was 32.8 per cent, according to the Union of B.C. Municipalities, up by about three percentage points from four years ago.

Allan Tupper, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of British Columbia, said the timing of the two elections, just one week apart, was odd and May have had an impact on how many votes were cast. With two sets of signs on local lawns and campaigns competing for often overlapping pools of volunteers, citizens May have experienced some election fatigue.

“It just seemed there was no energy for this thing,” Prof. Tupper said. “I think Eby didn’t size it up right. The opposition organized itself very quickly.”

In the Quebec provincial election of Oct. 5, turnout was a relatively high 67 per cent, while the Alberta referendum of Oct. 19, which asked whether to hold a vote on separation, had preliminary turnout of more than 62 per cent.

Duff Conacher, co-founder of Democracy Watch, a non-profit that works on democratic reform, said studies show that voter turnout is high when voters believe something important is at stake, when the leaders appear viable and competent and the race appears close.

Turnout was above 70 per cent in B.C. in all the elections held from 1983 to 2001 and hasn’t been higher than about 62 per cent since.

Mr. Conacher said it’s a worrying sign that voter participation appears to have dipped below 50 per cent this time, but it’s not surprising given recent trends.

stories.title: London man charged in hate-motivated incident involving swastika symbol
stories.summary: A 56-year-old London man is facing a charge following an investigation into a hate-motivated incident in the city’s downtown.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A 56-year-old London man is facing a charge following an investigation into a hate-motivated incident in the city’s downtown.

London police say Gordon Botaitis was charged with one count of offence motivated by hatred after a symbol resembling a swastika was created in a gravel parking lot in the 0-100 block of St. George Street.

Police were made aware of the incident on Oct. 22. They say a man completing construction work at the property used equipment believed to be a pressure washer to create the symbol.

Nearby residents captured video and photographs of the incident and provided them to police. The property owner was notified and removed the symbol.

On Oct. 23, police identified and arrested the suspect. The investigation was reassigned to the London Police Service Hate Crime Unit, which determined the incident was motivated by hatred.

Botaitis was released from custody and is expected to appear in London court on Jan. 18, 2027.

stories.title: Shuffling of U.S. tariffs will offer little relief to Canada, experts say
stories.summary: Along with lifting some tariffs and adding others, Trump administration has said trade negotiations with Canada are ‘gathering steam’
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
The shifting front line in the U.S-Canada trade war will lessen the economic pain in border states while still targeting Canadian manufacturing capacity, experts say.

The lifting of 50-per-cent tariffs on 22 categories of goods by the United States and the addition of 100 new categories will have a roughly equivalent impact in terms of dollars – about $2.5-billion in goods were exempted with about $2.6-billion newly targeted – but will also shift some of the focus away from products U.S. businesses need for their own operations.

Senator Susan Collins of Maine has taken credit for lifting the tariffs on some packaging products, which she said had impacted Maine businesses such as apple and blueberry growers.

Alongside its tariff adjustments, the Trump administration has also said that it’s nearing a trade deal with Canada. Kevin Hassett, the top economic adviser in the White House, told Fox News on Sunday that negotiations are “gathering steam” and that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been speaking with Canadian officials “all week.”

According to Wolfgang Alschner, a law professor with a specialty in business and trade at the University of Ottawa, there are lots of examples of integrated cross-border supply chains where tariffs hurt U.S. businesses and consumers as much or more than they strike at Canada.

“With tighter North American integration, it made total sense for states like Maine to trade with Quebec for supplies for local industries. Now of course with the border being a harder border you really have to re-evaluate those relationships,” Mr. Alschner said.

He said some of the new tariffs are on finished retail products such as shampoo, which won’t have a strong localized impact in any particular geographic market – such as a border state with a tense and close Senate election battle raging.

“I think that makes perfect sense from a defensive point of view. You ideally want to spread out the pain,” Mr. Alschner said.

Some other new tariffs could turn up the pain on specific industries in Canada.

One example is in the hardwood flooring market, where U.S. tariffs against China and Vietnam have caused those countries to shift exports to more open nations such as Canada.

According to William Pellerin, partner with law firm McMillan LLP and co-leader of its international trade group, even before the new tariffs on Canadian hardwood, his group of eight flooring manufacturing clients based mainly in Quebec and Ontario were struggling to compete domestically against imports.

“[China and Vietnam] totally flooded the market at prices that are ludicrously low. The Canadian producers have been able to survive by selling products to the U.S.,” Mr. Pellerin said.

Many of the companies are benefiting from federal work-share programs to keep the lights on. “A lot of the companies had layoffs, a number are on work-share, with workers on maybe three days a week,” he said.

But in the longer term, Mr. Pellerin said restricting imports of overseas hardwood May be the only path forward.

Kyle Peacock, principal at Peacock Tariff Consulting, said he has identified another pattern in the types of industries that are being targeted: U.S. companies with Canadian manufacturing sites that could see production shifted back to America.

“We had that on lip balm,” Mr. Peacock said. Since the first round of tariffs, he said five of seven Canadian sites making the wax or other parts of lip balm have either stopped shipping to the U.S. or are planning to relocate. In New Brunswick, social media darling Eclair Lips announced in October it would no longer make its lip balm in Canada, moving production to Vermont.

But even trade relief doesn’t necessarily change the case for manufacturers “re-shoring” operations back to the U.S.

A week ago, Polyethics Industries in Orillia, Ont., announced 118 layoffs, which Mr. Peacock said is part of the company shifting capacity to its factory in Antwerp, Ohio. The company makes polyethylene plastic products such as garbage bags that are now subject to tariff relief, but while Mr. Peacock has consulted with them, he still expects the company to move the remaining production to the U.S. in the coming weeks.

According to him, the company faced other rising costs, such as soaring diesel prices and transportation costs thanks in part to the U.S. war with Iran. Tariff relief won’t be enough to move the needle.

“That’s one piece of a very big pie that’s making us move,” Mr. Peacock said he was told.

Some other new tariffs could turn up the pain on specific industries in Canada.
One example is in the hardwood flooring market, where U.S. tariffs against China and Vietnam have caused those countries to shift exports to more open nations such as Canada.

According to William Pellerin, partner with law firm McMillan LLP and co-leader of its international trade group, even before the new tariffs on Canadian hardwood, his group of eight flooring manufacturing clients based mainly in Quebec and Ontario were struggling to compete domestically against imports.
“[China and Vietnam] totally flooded the market at prices that are ludicrously low. The Canadian producers have been able to survive by selling products to the U.S.,” Mr. Pellerin said.

Many of the companies are benefiting from federal work-share programs to keep the lights on. “A lot of the companies had layoffs, a number are on work-share, with workers on maybe three days a week,” he said.
But in the longer term, Mr. Pellerin said restricting imports of overseas hardwood May be the only path forward.

Kyle Peacock, principal at Peacock Tariff Consulting, said he has identified another pattern in the types of industries that are being targeted: U.S. companies with Canadian manufacturing sites that could see production shifted back to America.

“We had that on lip balm,” Mr. Peacock said. Since the first round of tariffs, he said five of seven Canadian sites making the wax or other parts of lip balm have either stopped shipping to the U.S. or are planning to relocate. In New Brunswick, social media darling Eclair Lips announced in October it would no longer make its lip balm in Canada, moving production to Vermont.
But even trade relief doesn’t necessarily change the case for manufacturers “re-shoring” operations back to the U.S.

A week ago, Polyethics Industries in Orillia, Ont., announced 118 layoffs, which Mr. Peacock said is part of the company shifting capacity to its factory in Antwerp, Ohio. The company makes polyethylene plastic products such as garbage bags that are now subject to tariff relief, but while Mr. Peacock has consulted with them, he still expects the company to move the remaining production to the U.S. in the coming weeks.

According to him, the company faced other rising costs, such as soaring diesel prices and transportation costs thanks in part to the U.S. war with Iran. Tariff relief won’t be enough to move the needle.
“That’s one piece of a very big pie that’s making us move,” Mr. Peacock said he was told.

stories.title: B.C.'s premier designate plans to speak with Whitecaps about future in Vancouver
stories.summary: Vancouver - British Columbia's premier designate says he doesn't know what the plan is to keep the Whitecaps in Vancouver.
stories.author: Gemma Karstens-Smith The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - British Columbia’s premier designate says he doesn’t know what the plan is to keep the Whitecaps in Vancouver.

Lorne Doerkson spoke to media Sunday, hours after his B.C. Conservatives were elected in about two-thirds of the province’s 93 ridings.

“I love the Whitecaps and there’s a great amount of support for them here,” said the party’s interim leader. “But I’ll be straight up with you — I don’t know the plan going forward.

“But I do want to have a conversation with the Whitecaps because — trust me when I say this — British Columbia loves the Whitecaps.”

The team has been for sale since December 2024 and the current ownership group has repeatedly said they want it to stay in Vancouver.

Both the Whitecaps and Major League Soccer have said the team’s ability to generate revenue is limited, in part because it does not own its home stadium and that has made it difficult to attract buyers willing to keep the ‘Caps in the city.

The 55,000-seat venue is owned and operated by PavCo, a provincial Crown corporation.

Whitecaps sporting director and CEO Axel Schuster said last month the club had reached an agreement to extend its lease at BC Place through the 2027 “sprint season.”

The condensed campaign will run from February through May, with each of the league’s 30 teams playing a 14-game regular season before the single-elimination playoffs.

MLS will then move to a summer-to-spring calendar, starting in July 2027.

What happens to the Whitecaps after the sprint season remains unclear, Schuster said.

“People should know we’re here, we’re staying in the sprint season,” he said. “So the club is not going yet, and nothing is happening yet. … And the only way you can show us your support and help is buying tickets and come to the games.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Olivia Chow, Brad Bradford battle to the wire in Toronto’s mayoral election
stories.summary: As voters head to the polls Monday, Chow is at risk of becoming first incumbent to lose since the city amalgamated in 1998
stories.author: Jeff Gray
stories.content:
A hard-fought race to lead Toronto between incumbent Mayor Olivia Chow and her leading challenger, east-end city councillor Brad Bradford, comes to an end on Monday, as Torontonians vote in a municipal election that recently published opinion surveys have suggested is too close to call.

If Mr. Bradford – a former city planner who has sat on council since 2018 and only took 1.28 per cent of the vote in his first bid for mayor three years ago – were to win, Ms. Chow would become the first incumbent in the mayor’s chair to lose since the current city was created by amalgamation in 1998.

Pollster David Valentin of Liaison Strategies, who has been tracking the race closely, says whether Mr. Bradford can put it over the top will depend on turnout, and particularly on whether downtown residents show up. Those in many areas of the city’s centre, he says, have been more likely to vote in recent years – and are more likely to support Ms. Chow.

Mr. Valentin says the result could hinge on whether the Bradford campaign’s door knockers can outpace the NDP-backed Ms. Chow’s traditionally strong get-out-the-vote operation.

“For me, the question really is, does he have the machine? Does he have the people power to get this done?” Mr. Valentin said.

The rest of Ontario’s municipalities are also going to the polls on Monday, with several races some observers believe could be tight battles for incumbents.

In Mississauga, former mayor and former provincial Liberal leader Bonnie Crombie is among the candidates gunning for her old job, facing off with current Mayor Carolyn Parrish. Local councillor Alvin Tedjo is also running in what has been a bitterly contested race.

In Hamilton, Mayor Andrea Horwath, a former Ontario NDP leader, faces a battle against a field of candidates that includes local business advocate Keanin Loomis, whom she beat only narrowly in 2022, and councillor Rob Cooper.

Ms. Chow, 69 – a former MP and councillor, long-time NDP stalwart and widow of former party leader Jack Layton – rode into Toronto’s city hall three years ago on her trademark flower-festooned bike, after narrowly winning a by-election prompted by the sudden resignation of mayor John Tory over an affair with a staffer.

Facing an inherited $1.8-billion budget hole blamed partly on the aftermath of COVID-19, she brought in two large property-tax hikes in a row (after promising “modest” increases) and signed an unprecedented multibillion-dollar financial deal with Premier Doug Ford, which included $1.2-billion in operating cash over three years and the transfer of the expensive Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway to the province. The moves were among the reasons the city won a credit-rating upgrade to AA-plus from S&P Global Ratings.

In her campaign, she has pledged to reduce fares for frequent transit riders and provide free school lunches, while keeping future property-tax hikes “in and around” the rate of inflation. But she has faced flak for muting her criticism of Mr. Ford’s controversial plans for the province’s waterfront Ontario Place site. And while the city has cleared many of the homeless encampments in its parks on her watch, many in Toronto still complain about the number of drug users or mentally ill people on the streets and in the transit system.

The 40-year-old Mr. Bradford, who worked to appeal to conservatives and suburbanites despite having been a city planner in favour of bike lanes, has repeatedly charged the city was “stuck” under Ms. Chow’s status quo. He vows to freeze property taxes, commission an external “line-by-line” review of spending and eliminate the city’s land-transfer tax on sales of homes under $1.1-million. The tax has been a key revenue source for the perennially cash-strapped municipality since it was introduced 20 years ago.

He also pledged to hire 1,000 additional police officers, capitalizing on widespread fears of disorder and crime – fears that persist despite low overall crime rates. Last September, he appeared on the cover of the tabloid Toronto Sun, posing with the softball bat he said he keeps in his bedroom to protect his family from home invaders.

Ms. Chow has charged that Mr. Bradford’s cost-cutting plans would mean shutting libraries and raising transit fares, which he denies. She also told viewers of Thursday’s final televised debate that Mr. Bradford’s tax freeze would still leave the city’s annual 1.5-per-cent building levy untouched.

In recent weeks, the two campaigns have clashed as Ms. Chow and high-profile allies, including environmentalist David Suzuki and former mayor David Miller, have charged that Mr. Bradford’s promise to hive off the Toronto Water department into a separate, publicly owned company is a step toward privatization.

Mr. Bradford says his plan would allow Toronto to finance new water pipes with debt instead of higher rates, cutting water bills by 25 per cent – and vows that the new entity would remain publicly owned under the new provincial law that allows the change. In last week’s debate, Mr. Bradford told Ms. Chow the criticism was “misinformation” and “scare tactics.”

Looming over the campaign was the shadow of Mr. Ford, who has often intervened in Toronto affairs and is a former city councillor and the brother of the late mayor Rob Ford.

The Premier, whose bid to override Ms. Chow’s objections and allow jets at the city’s waterfront island airport was blocked by Ottawa this summer , has in recent days carried out his threat to unilaterally rip out a stretch of the city’s west-end bike lanes. Mr. Bradford, who now agrees with the removal of those lanes despite previously supporting their installation, accuses Ms. Chow of failing to stand up to Mr. Ford.

Despite Mr. Bradford’s conservative thrust and the presence of former Ford aides on his campaign, the Premier all but endorsed Ms. Chow in September, in remarks his office later tried to recant, saying the Premier was not endorsing anyone. Before she was elected, he had warned she would be “unmitigated disaster” but he has since then frequently sung her praises.

Meanwhile, in several of Toronto’s 25 wards, there are races that are expected to be competitive, including in some where incumbents have stepped down, throwing the composition of the next council into question. In addition to Mr. Bradford’s former seat in Beaches-East York, there are open races in Toronto-Danforth, University-Rosedale and Parkdale-High Park.

stories.title: U.K. won’t join Canada-led defence bank, but pledges cooperation
stories.summary: The two countries will "work in close partnership" on investment opportunities and challenges, according to a joint media statement.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
The British government has turned down Ottawa’s attempts to have it join the international Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, though London says it will work in lockstep with Canada to meet Nato spending targets.

The Dsrb is meant to reduce borrowing costs for military spending by pooling credit strength among allies.

Canada has tried for months to convince the U.K. to join the project, but London has instead been pursuing its own program called the Multilateral Defence Mechanism.

Both countries agreed Sunday to craft a framework for cooperation between both banks, “having mutually concluded that it is best to develop two distinct but complementary institutions.”

The two will “work in close partnership” on investment opportunities and challenges, according to a joint media statement.

The Dsrb will be based in Canada and has the support of countries such as Belgium, Turkey and Ukraine.

stories.title: Wainwright soldier remembered as dedicated brother, friend at funeral
stories.summary: Edmonton — Family, friends and Armed Forces members filled the pews of an Edmonton funeral home on Sunday as one of the soldiers killed in the devastating Canadian Forces Base Wainwright fire was laid to rest.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By The Canadian Press

Posted October 25, 2026 5:08 pm.

Last Updated October 25, 2026 5:25 pm.

Edmonton — Family, friends and Armed Forces members filled the pews of an Edmonton funeral home on Sunday as one of the soldiers killed in the devastating Canadian Forces Base Wainwright fire was laid to rest.

All rose as Sgt. Morgan Wong’s casket was carried in by pallbearers, draped in a Canadian flag that was then carefully folded and presented to one of Wong’s loved ones.

In a eulogy, Wong’s sister Megan remembered her brother as a loyal friend and problem-solver who dedicated himself to serving his community and country.

“Long before he was the fearless soldier many of you came to know, he was one of the bravest and funniest people I have ever met,” she said.

The 26-year-old reservist with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, was one of four killed when a fast-moving fire overwhelmed soldiers during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright. Thirty-nine more were injured.

Buddhist practitioners sang and prayed for Wong, whose photo sat on an altar alongside bowls of white rice and plates of oranges and apples.

Those gathered at the funeral heard how the soldier joined the Armed Forces at 17, advanced through the military ranks and volunteered in 2024 to be deployed to Latvia.

There, he would ultimately meet his wife.

“They were married last December,” Wong’s sister said. “He was so excited to (build) an incredible life and family with her.”

After Wong returned from Latvia, he trained and mentored new recruits and was preparing for a second deployment abroad when he was killed in the fire at Wainwright.

Lt.-Col. Bryn Wright, the commanding officer of Wong’s regiment, said Wong quit a civilian job earlier this year to be an instructor for the Armed Forces.

“Dedicated to service, reliable, willing to put the regiment ahead of himself. That was Morgan Wong,” he said.

Wright said the soldier’s cap badge and regimental coin, sometimes called a challenge coin, will be returned to his family.

“Soldiers often challenge one another by producing their coin, and if the other soldier doesn’t have theirs, they lose. If they do, they win. Morgan carried his coin with him right to the end. In classic fashion, it was still in his pocket,” Wright said.

Megan said she was proud to be Wong’s big sister and that she hopes his life serves as a reminder “to use the time we have to achieve a life we would be proud of.”

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said after the service that Wong had an impact on the city.

“(We) heard from so many of the people who had stories to share today that it’s not just his military service, it was his service to family, to loved ones, to friends, to community, that this is somebody who, no matter who you are, he was there to support you,” Knack said in an interview outside the funeral home, located in the city’s north end.

“It’s impossible to replace someone like that, who’s given so much. And yet I hope that we all take this opportunity as Edmontonians and as Canadians to live up to that legacy.”

While the exact cause of the fire at CFB Wainwright is unclear, Brig.-Gen. Vanessa Hanrahan, head of the military police, said it was sparked during a routine training event at an anti-grenade launcher range on the grounds.

The fire was considered sufficiently under control that training exercises were allowed to continue, before high winds caused it to spread, said Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division.

Military officials wouldn’t say why training continued during the fire. Hanrahan said it’s part of the military police investigation.

The City of Prince Albert said a vigil would be held Sunday afternoon in Memorial Square for Pte. Shaun Farrell, another soldier who died in the tragedy at Wainwright.

Police in the northern Saskatchewan city posted a video Saturday showing a procession of police and other emergency vehicles accompanying a hearse into the city, passing underneath a Maple Leaf flag that was hanging from the extended ladder of a fire truck.

“Today, Prince Albert showed up with love, compassion, and respect as we welcomed Private Shaun Farrell home,” a message with the post said.

“Behind every uniform is a person, a family, and a story. And today, we were reminded that when one of our own comes home, they do not come home alone.”

stories.title: Canada receives first F-35 jets from U.S. as full order still under review
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney has paused plans to proceed with a planned order for 88 of these stealth fighter jets, and it May instead have a mixed fleet.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Canada has received its first pair of new F-35 fighter jets, with Ottawa still deliberating on how many of the American planes it will buy.

The Royal Canadian Air Force announced receiving the two Lockheed Martin jets Friday on social media with a photo from Phoenix showing one plane with a maple-leaf roundel.

The air force could not immediately say when it will start training pilots with the new planes, which U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra recently hailed as “the best fighter in the world.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney has paused plans to proceed with a planned order for 88 of these stealth fighter jets, and it May instead have a mixed fleet that includes Gripen jets made by Saab.

Carney launched a review of the purchase amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s repeated trade and annexation threats, and the review was supposed to have concluded a year ago.

Last year, Trump mused about providing allies with jets that have limited capabilities in order to maintain American supremacy, and former foreign minister Lloyd Axworthy warns in a Saturday blog post that Washington controls software used by F-35 jets.

stories.title: Political hubris claims another victim – the Ndp’s David Eby
stories.summary: Former Ontario premier David Peterson has gained some new company in the realm of snap election cautionary tales
stories.author: Gary Mason
stories.content:
British Columbians took a huge political gamble this weekend, handing power to someone they barely know who leads a party that looked like it was imploding only a few weeks ago.

But such was the level of anger and disgust over NDP Leader David Eby’s move to call a snap election – amid provincewide municipal elections no less, and with two years left in his mandate – that the public decided B.C. Conservative Party Leader Lorne Doerkson sounded normal enough to trust.

It’s impossible to overstate the enormity of the challenge now confronting him and his party.

First, we must say a few words about the man they vanquished – Mr. Eby. Since first being elected as an MLA in 2013, knocking off then-Liberal premier Christy Clark, Mr. Eby was viewed as a rising political star. As attorney-general, he became the heir apparent to much-loved NDP premier John Horgan. When Mr. Horgan resigned in the fall of 2022 because of illness, Mr. Eby was virtually handed the job.

But governing never came easy to him. He was unquestionably bright, but lacked the natural charm and easygoing nature of his predecessor. Where Mr. Horgan was a delegator, Mr. Eby centralized decision-making. He also treated the treasury as an ATM, using it to pay for things his government couldn’t afford, including grossly irresponsible public sector contracts.

Provincial debt soared to historic levels under his watch. Meantime, emergency rooms across the province were halting services for short periods because of staffing shortages, while doctors and specialists were resigning because of workload issues.

And that only begins to scratch the surface of the many problems Mr. Eby left behind for Mr. Doerkson and his party to clean up.

Had Mr. Eby been paying more attention, he would have detected the public wasn’t in the mood for an early election and that calling one was likely to make people even more ornery.

Still, he couldn’t resist pouncing on the opportunity that an opposition party in disarray offered. The disastrous new leadership of the Conservatives’ Kerry-Lynne Findlay was too juicy a situation to pass up. But when she resigned unexpectedly and the party announced that the relatively unknown Lorne Doerkson was being named interim leader, Mr. Eby didn’t pause his plan to go to the polls.

A more savvy politician would have slammed the brakes on his election plan right then and there. But Mr. Eby, no doubt pushed by advisers who showed him public opinion polling in his favour, decided to push forward.

It was a fatal mistake.

He isn’t the first politician to be punished for his political hubris. The scrap bin of history is full of them. And there are some, like former Ontario premier David Peterson, who will doubtlessly be overjoyed by Saturday’s outcome in B.C. Now, Mr. Peterson is unlikely to be cited as frequently or as instantaneously as a cautionary tale of the hazards of snap elections. He called one in 1990 when his Liberal government had a healthy majority. So disgusted was the public over the cynical move, it gave the NDP a majority. Mr. Peterson lost his own seat.

There needs to be something said here about Mr. Doerkson’s leadership. In a short period of time, he united the Conservative Party caucus, bringing back to the fold many of those MLAs who had left it over Ms. Findlay’s extreme lurch to the right. The new leader was not interested in making culture wars his priority.

Mr. Doerkson showed people he is a “normal” Conservative, whose priority is the big issues facing the province – health care, the economy, education – and not trans athletes in women’s sports.

As long as he continues to act and lead as a regular, middle-of-the-road conservative, he should be just fine. The moment he caves to loud voices promoting fringe issues, he will get himself in trouble. The premier-designate needs to remember he is leading a centre -right coalition, one previously represented by the BC Liberal Party, and Social Credit Party before that.

Managed properly, this type of coalition has shown it can rule B.C. for long periods of time, in fact decades longer than any other political alliance in the province’s history.

As for the NDP, well, they know the position in which they find themselves all too well. While its caucus has been drastically reduced in size, the party will still have several experienced MLAs who will constitute what should be a formidable Opposition.

With Mr. Eby announcing his resignation as leader Saturday, the party will soon need to begin the process of replacing him.

The pollsters said the B.C. public was demanding change in this election. Well, they got it. We’ll soon find out what that means.

stories.title: BC premier-designate Doerkson says province ‘chose change’ in election
stories.summary: The man who was previously a relatively unknown backbench MLA took the reins of the party as an interim leader heading into the election.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
B.C. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson said he was “deeply humbled” by his party’s victory and vowed to earn the trust British Columbians have placed in him.

Doerkson’s BC Conservatives won a resounding victory on Saturday night, with Global News projecting a majority government less than an hour after polls closed.

“I’m very excited that yesterday British Columbians chose change and they chose that,” Doerkson said Sunday in his first official news conference after election day. “People in every corner of this province, from the Peace to the island, from the Kootenays to the Coast placed their trust in us … It was lent to us for purpose and it must be earned back every single day.”

The man who was previously a relatively unknown backbench MLA took the reins of the party as an interim leader heading into the election after Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned amid numerous departures.

On Sunday, his party was projected to win 64 seats, a total no party has surpassed since the BC Liberals won 77 seats in 2001.

Outgoing premier David Eby triggered the election less than two years into his mandate, initially saying it was necessary in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs, though he later shifted his focus to affordability issues, a key part of Doerkson’s campaign.

Doerkson stressed he was an ally of British Columbia when asked about Trump reposting about the Conservatives’ win on his Truth Social platform.

“I’m an ally to British Columbia and we should have taken the opportunity years ago to protect ourselves against these attacks,” Doerkson said. “My focus is going to be to supercharge our economy … It’s just about endless, where I believe we can support different industries that will protect us against these attacks.”

Work was already underway in forming government, with the premier-designate saying he’s spoken with Lt. Gov. Wendy Cocchia and named Kim Henderson as chair of the government’s transition team.

“When this party is sworn in, it will be ready on day one and it will hit the ground running,” he said.

He said his government will launch an independent review of the province’s finances on day one to “know where things stand,” promising residents would have a “full picture” before a budget is tabled.

He also reiterated campaign promises, stating within the first 100 days an expert commission would look into keeping emergency rooms open and cutting wait times.

But the first priority, Doerkson said, was raising the basic personal exemption to $32,000, amounting to about $1,000 a year “back in the pocket” of working British Columbians.

“These are serious times, people are stretched, the economy has stalled and too many British Columbians have stopped believing government can get anything done,” he said.

Though the BC Conservatives won a resounding victory, they also achieved a majority with the lowest voter turnout in decades. Preliminary figures from Elections BC show 48 per cent of those eligible voted. Prior to this year, no provincial election in recent history has seen turnout fall below 50 per cent.

Doerkson’s party was projected to win 64 seats with 48.05 per cent of the votes, with the NDP receiving 27 seats and 37.38 per cent. The Green Party won two seats and received 10.97 per cent.

During the campaign, Eby questioned if Doerkson would remain as premier going forward. As interim leader of the party, he is not currently permitted to run in an eventual leadership race.

Asked whether he would stay, Doerkson said that’s an “administrative detail” that will see information provided “imminently.”

“But I will remain leader of the party and I am thrilled to be the premier-elect of British Columbia right now,” he added.

The next premier also faced questions on his stance on repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (Dripa).

He stressed he was committed to working with First Nations as premier, but remained firm on his plan.

“It has not worked in this province, and frankly, it has caused more problems to date than I think potentially anything else,” Doerkson said, questioning what it has done to solve problems in the province.

Congratulations for the premier-designate have come in from across the province and country, with Doerkson adding he’s heard from “a number of First Nations,” including in his riding of Cariboo Chilcotin.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew congratulated Doerkson on his win and thanked Eby for his friendship over the past few years.

Kinew did have caution though when questioned about Doerkson’s policies on Dripa and Indigenous rights.

“I think the election results in BC should concern every elected politician and every consultant out there for this reason,” Kinew said. “It’s a reminder that what we’re doing is not a game. When you’re elected to serve the people of your province or of your country, it is a serious responsibility that isn’t to be played with.”

A date for when Doerkson’s government will be sworn in has yet to be announced and he did not say if there would be a fall session, though he didn’t rule it out.

— with files from Global News’ Amy Judd

stories.title: Britain will not join Canada-led defence bank, sources say
stories.summary: Two countries say they will develop framework for co-operation between defence-funding initiatives
stories.author: Reuters
stories.content:
Britain will not join the planned Canada-led multinational defence financing bank, opting instead to work toward a separate defence procurement entity after weeks of negotiations.

In a joint statement released Sunday, the two countries said they have “mutually concluded that it is best to develop two distinct but complementary institutions that work in partnership.”

A senior Canadian government official confirmed that Britain will not be joining the institution, known as the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (Dsrb). The official said the two sides determined that it would be better to have the Canadian-headquartered bank focused on providing low-cost capital and the British initiative focused on procurement issues.

Meanwhile, the Dsrb is working toward being operational by next year, with a charter-signing ceremony set to take place in the last week of this November, according to two other Canadian sources with knowledge of the situation.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the sources as they were not authorized to comment publicly on the matter.

The development adds to growing pains for the Dsrb, envisioned as a way for Nato members and other allies to work together on raising the capital needed for vast military buildouts as geopolitical dangers multiply.

The nascent institution so far consists of a small group of founding countries: Canada, Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine.

The bank’s creation was first proposed in 2024, and Canada was announced as the host country in April of this year.

Negotiations between Britain and Canada broke down after government officials spent much of the summer working on a potential merger of the two countries’ defence-finance and procurement mechanisms: the Dsrb and the Multilateral Defence Mechanism.

Britain’s MDM is not dissimilar to existing programs within the European Union and Nato. For example, there is the Security Action for Europe instrument, which Canada can also participate in.

The mechanism currently has four countries committed: Britain, the Netherlands, Finland and Poland. It is working toward being set up by 2027. However, little has been said publicly about it since early July, and few details have been made available about its structure.

Britain has been touch-and-go on joining the Dsrb since last year. In September, 2025, Britain’s Treasury told Reuters that it had ruled out joining the initiative. A year later, after a change in government, the door to Britain joining seemed to reopen . Prime Minister Mark Carney even headed to Britain to catch a soccer game with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to help seal the deal of the country’s decision.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne also met with his British counterpart, Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey, in London the same week to discuss the subject.

However, despite the concerted effort by Ottawa, the sources with knowledge of the negotiations said ultimately that Britain made Canada an offer it could not accept. This included moving the headquarters from Canada to Europe and changing the mandate of the Dsrb to focus more heavily on procurement, rather than financing.

At least nine countries will be present at the Dsrb signing ceremony planned for November, with the possibility for others to still join before then. After the signing of the charter, further details, such as the Canadian city where the bank will be headquartered as well as the name of its chief executive officer, will follow.

For now, Canada and Britain have agreed to continue working on their respective initiatives to improve defence financing and procurement, with the caveat that one does not compete with the other.

The rest of the countries participating in the Dsrb were informed of the breakdown of negotiations between Canada and Britain on Saturday, the sources say.

In the joint statement released Sunday by Canada and Britain, the two sides said they have been working closely to consider how the Canadian bank “can best advance our shared objectives.”

The statement said that as they are operationalized, the two institutions will be designed “to work in close partnership, so that they can support each other on emerging industrial priorities, investment opportunities and strategic financing challenges. Together, they will provide complementary tools to strengthen the defence-industrial base and enhance collective defence readiness.”

stories.title: $6-million gift to establish first national myeloma research biobank in London
stories.summary: An anonymous $6-million donation will help establish Canada’s first national biobank dedicated exclusively to multiple myeloma research at London Health Sciences Centre.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
An anonymous $6-million donation will help establish Canada’s first national biobank dedicated exclusively to multiple myeloma research at London Health Sciences Centre.

The Canadian Myeloma Research Biobank will be housed at the London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute and developed through a collaboration between the London Health Sciences Foundation and the Canadian Myeloma Research Group.

The gift is among the largest donations to multiple myeloma research in Canada and the largest known gift from a Canadian philanthropist dedicated to the disease, according to the organizations.

The biobank will collect, store and make biological samples available to approved researchers across the country, helping advance discoveries, improve diagnostics and develop new treatment options.

Multiple myeloma is a complex blood cancer that begins in plasma cells, a type of white blood cell that produces antibodies. The disease can damage bones, cause anemia and kidney problems, and weaken the immune system. An estimated 4,400 Canadians will be diagnosed with multiple myeloma in 2026. While treatments such as chemotherapy, stem cell transplants and immunotherapy can help control the disease, there is currently no cure.

The new biobank will bring together blood, bone marrow and other biological samples collected with patients’ consent. Researchers will be able to study samples taken at different stages of the disease, including diagnosis, after treatment and relapse. The goal is to better understand how the cancer develops, why some treatments work better for certain patients and how the disease becomes resistant to treatment.

The biobank will also complement the Canadian Myeloma Research Group’s national database, which contains disease-specific information on more than 12,000 Canadian patients.

The anonymous donor, who is living with multiple myeloma and received immunotherapy through a clinical trial in Boston, said the experience highlighted both advances in treatment and the barriers some Canadians face in accessing care.

“I also know the cost and frequent travel required to access these treatments can put them out of reach for many Canadians,” the donor said.

The donor said the gift is intended to strengthen research in Canada and support efforts to find a cure.

Engin Gul, chief executive officer of the Canadian Myeloma Research Group, said the biobank will expand access to high-quality samples and help researchers collaborate on more precise and effective treatments.

Dr. Chris McIntyre, interim vice-president of research and scientific director of the London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute, said studying patient samples could help explain why treatments produce different results and lead to improvements in care.

Planning and implementation are underway, with the biobank expected to become operational in 2027. Once established, it will support research collaborations across Canada and internationally, including studies into early detection, personalized treatments and ways to improve outcomes for people living with multiple myeloma.

stories.title: Old South church helps ‘Fill the Van’ for London Food Bank
stories.summary: For more than 20 years London Food Bank (LFB) co-executive directors Glen Pearson and Jane Roy have been members of Wesley-Knox United Church (Wkuc) in Old South.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
For more than 20 years London Food Bank (LFB) co-executive directors Glen Pearson and Jane Roy have been members of Wesley-Knox United Church (Wkuc) in Old South.

That means the congregation knows the dire straits Londoners are facing in 2026.

Wkuc held a rapid response food drive Sunday as they filled a van to help the LFB.

“They really pulled in this week for the food drive and so we really appreciate it.”

Organized by EJ Lamb, the chair of leadership at Wkuc, the drive pulled sponsors, businesses, church members and others to help.

“About a week and a half before the Thanksgiving program that the London Food Bank was doing, they were down 25 per cent compared to last year’s donations,” said Lamb.

“We decided to do the ‘Fill the Van’ event and it has been a really cool event for the community. The church is obviously involved, but we have renters as the Shout Sisters Choir. The Spiritualist Church also runs their business here as well, so they’ve helped contribute. We had a Halloween Bingo last night and they brought food and neighbours are bringing stuff in, and some of the local businesses were also involved.”

Throughout the afternoon people were consistently bringing bags of food and non-perishable items. Pearson believes most of the donated items will go to local agencies.

“One thing you know is all this food will be gone within 48 hours,” said Pearson.

“The food comes in the Food Bank, and it’s just gone. Sixty per cent of the food that came in during the (Thanksgiving) food drive goes out to other agencies, so it doesn’t even get to the Food Bank. It goes straight to them.”

Pearson says every week agencies are coming to the LFB asking for help as cutbacks are happening.

While they try to manage that, Wkuc is just trying to do anything they can to help.

“It’s very much a community event and the community is very passionate about it,” said Lamb.

“We all know we can help others, and this is a wonderful way to do it.”

stories.title: 'He's earned it': Conservatives want Doerkson as premier amid constitutional question
stories.summary: Vancouver - Voters gave Lorne Doerkson's B.C. Conservatives a two-thirds majority government on Saturday, now members of his party need to do the same to change their constitution to allow an interim leader to become permanent.
stories.author: Brieanna Charlebois The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Voters gave Lorne Doerkson’s B.C. Conservatives a two-thirds majority government on Saturday, now members of his party need to do the same to change their constitution to allow an interim leader to become permanent.

The party’s constitution prohibits an interim leader from seeking leadership in subsequent ballot, and change would require the support of two-thirds of the party’s members.

The party’s board said after the election was called that if Doerkson became the premier, he would remain leader and that it would pursue appropriate means “to give effect to this intention.”

Doerkson moved quickly on Sunday to disabuse people of the idea that he not be the party’s leader and become premier because of the constitutional clause.

“I am leader and that’s an administrative detail that there’ll be more information on that imminently,” he told reporters.

“But I will remain as leader of the party and I’m thrilled to be the premier-elect of British Columbia right now.”

He said his party is “united” and the election results “decisive.”

Conservatives celebrated the win Saturday, praising the premier-designate for uniting the party after a tumultuous few months under the leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay, who quit days before the election was called.

Caroline Elliott lost to Findlay for the leadership race by a few percentage points but she won the riding of West Vancouver-Capilano on Saturday.

She said that Doerkson was the “right person” to lead the party to victory as “things were splintering.”

“He’s earned it. He’s earned the trust of British Columbians. He has earned more votes in this general election than we could ever dream of in a leadership race, and so, for me, that’s mandate enough and I’ll support him for as long as he wants to stay on,” she said Saturday.

Findlay congratulated Doerkson in a post to social media on Saturday, calling the election a “historic victory.”

“I am hopeful that under his leadership British Columbians will see the changes to how our province is governed that I, and so many others, have long advocated for,” she said.

Doerkson became the party’s interim leader just days before the snap election was called Sept. 22 by outgoing New Democrat premier David Eby, and the victory ends nearly a decade of NDP government in the province.

But how the party’s board would ensure Doerkson will lead Conservatives remains unclear.

“A premier chosen by British Columbians deserves the certainty of leading his party. This amendment will provide it,” the board’s statement said in a social media post on Sept. 23.

Doerkson also has the support of former B.C. premier Gordon Campbell, who called him a “decent, honest, straightforward guy.”

“He gets people to understand how good they are and where we can be. We can be a province of possibility and promise again, and I think that’s what we’re going to get to,” Campbell said while attending the Conservative election-night celebration.

Hamish Telford, an associate professor in political science at the University of the Fraser Valley, said it’s an interesting situation because a large portion of the party’s base wanted to make sure there was no taint of the B.C. Liberals, as was made clear in the leadership results and Findlay’s win.

“And now they want to represent themselves as a reincarnation of the B.C. Liberals. How is the base going to react to this new direction of the party? This is now a mainstream business-oriented party, that’s not the party they wanted,” he said.

Doerkson was elected in 2020 as a B.C. Liberal, which became B.C. United, but he jumped to the Conservatives before the 2024 provincial election to win again in Cariboo-Chilcotin.

As recently as the 2020 election, the party received less than two per cent of the vote, but the collapse of BC United paved the way for its rise to official Opposition status and now government.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 25, 2026.

- With files from Brenna Owen and Wolfgang Depner

stories.title: Funeral for soldier killed in CFB Wainwright fire is held in Edmonton
stories.summary: Sgt. Morgan Wong remembered as dedicated brother, friend
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Family, friends and Armed Forces members filled the pews of an Edmonton funeral home on Sunday as one of the soldiers killed in the devastating Canadian Forces Base Wainwright fire was laid to rest.

All rose as Sgt. Morgan Wong’s casket was carried in by pallbearers, draped in a Canadian flag that was then carefully folded and presented to one of Wong’s loved ones.

In a eulogy, Wong’s sister Megan remembered her brother as a loyal friend and problem-solver who dedicated himself to serving his community and country.

“Long before he was the fearless soldier many of you came to know, he was one of the bravest and funniest people I have ever met,” she said.

The 26-year-old reservist with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, was one of four killed when a fast-moving fire overwhelmed soldiers during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright. Thirty-nine more were injured.

Buddhist practitioners sang and prayed for Wong, whose photo sat on an altar alongside bowls of white rice and plates of oranges and apples.

Those gathered at the funeral heard how the soldier joined the Armed Forces at 17, advanced through the military ranks and volunteered in 2024 to be deployed to Latvia.

There, he would ultimately meet his wife.

“They were married last December,” Wong’s sister said. “He was so excited to (build) an incredible life and family with her.”

After Wong returned from Latvia, he trained and mentored new recruits and was preparing for a second deployment abroad when he was killed in the fire at Wainwright.

Lt.-Col. Bryn Wright, the commanding officer of Wong’s regiment, said Wong quit a civilian job earlier this year to be an instructor for the Armed Forces.

“Dedicated to service, reliable, willing to put the regiment ahead of himself. That was Morgan Wong,” he said.

Wright said the soldier’s cap badge and regimental coin, sometimes called a challenge coin, will be returned to his family.

“Soldiers often challenge one another by producing their coin, and if the other soldier doesn’t have theirs, they lose. If they do, they win. Morgan carried his coin with him right to the end. In classic fashion, it was still in his pocket,” Wright said.

Megan said she was proud to be Wong’s big sister and that she hopes his life serves as a reminder “to use the time we have to achieve a life we would be proud of.”

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said after the service that Wong had an impact on the city.

“(We) heard from so many of the people who had stories to share today that it’s not just his military service, it was his service to family, to loved ones, to friends, to community, that this is somebody who, no matter who you are, he was there to support you,” Knack said in an interview outside the funeral home, located in the city’s north end.

“It’s impossible to replace someone like that, who’s given so much. And yet I hope that we all take this opportunity as Edmontonians and as Canadians to live up to that legacy.”

While the exact cause of the fire at CFB Wainwright is unclear, Brig.-Gen. Vanessa Hanrahan, head of the military police, said it was sparked during a routine training event at an anti-grenade launcher range on the grounds.

The fire was considered sufficiently under control that training exercises were allowed to continue, before high winds caused it to spread, said Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division.

Military officials wouldn’t say why training continued during the fire. Hanrahan said it’s part of the military police investigation.

The City of Prince Albert said a vigil would be held Sunday afternoon in Memorial Square for Pte. Shaun Farrell, another soldier who died in the tragedy at Wainwright.

Police in the northern Saskatchewan city posted a video Saturday showing a procession of police and other emergency vehicles accompanying a hearse into the city, passing underneath a Maple Leaf flag that was hanging from the extended ladder of a fire truck.

“Today, Prince Albert showed up with love, compassion, and respect as we welcomed Private Shaun Farrell home,” a message with the post said.

“Behind every uniform is a person, a family, and a story. And today, we were reminded that when one of our own comes home, they do not come home alone.”

stories.title: New Canadian procedure could revolutionize AFib treatment
stories.summary: Atrial fibrillation is the most common type of irregular heart rhythm in the world, but a new approach could change the game for patients.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
A new Canadian approach to treating a common heart rhythm condition could change the game for patients who deal with atrial fibrillation or AFib.

AFib is considered the most common arrhythmia and occurs in the upper chambers of the heart.

Affecting one to two per cent of the general population, the irregular heartbeat can cause symptoms such as shortness of breath and fatigue, but can lead to severe consequences such as stroke or heart failure.

Fatigue caused Jon Davies of Edmonton to suspect something was wrong.

“I used to go mountain hiking and played a lot of squash and then that sort of quickly went away as I got into my early 50s,” he told Global News in an interview. “I just figured it was old age and having a desk job and not enough exercise maybe.”

His wife, Nora, said he was often tired and would sleep a lot.

He was eventually diagnosed with atrial fibrillation, but when speaking about treatment options he was left in shock.

“They told me that my heart had enlarged so much that it wouldn’t make sense for them to treat it surgically, so that’s when they said you’re going to stay on blood thinners,” Davies said.

Until this year, he said he’s had to accept the “status quo,” adding he got a second opinion with the same result.

People with AFib often receive treatment either through medication or with what’s known as “catheter ablation.”

“Patients are usually sedated or put to sleep entirely and we put little tubes in the groins and we pass wires into the heart, cross over to the left side of the heart and what we try and do is kill the tissue around the pulmonary veins,” said Dr. Paul Angaran, cardiac arrhythmia director at St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto.

The process involves creating tiny scars in an area of the heart, according to the Mayo Clinic. During AFib, faulty signals can tell the heart to beat irregularly. The scars prevent those faulty signals from reaching their target.

“Typically we burn, so we use energy sources that overheat the tissue and sometimes we can use energy sources that freeze the tissue,” said Dr. Gianluigi Bisleri, the director of minimally invasive and robotic cardiac surgery at St. Michael’s Hospital. “But either way, we create these scars that become permanent and stop the irregular heart rate.”

But Angaran said not everyone with AFib will see such a treatment be effective.

Angaran joined with Bisleri to develop a new approach for helping people with AFib.

The result is a two-part robotic technique using ablations from outside the heart and then going inside using a catheter technique.

“It allows us to not only use the robotic technologies which give us more dexterity, more ability to reach and see the heart, but also to treat broader areas of the heart with the ablation,” Bisleri said.

Using both minimally invasive robotic surgery and catheter technology is a Canadian first, Bisleri said.

Patients interested in the procedure must be referred to Bisleri and Angaran, but the former told Global News while a referral is simple there isn’t enough awareness of their approach.

Patients need to wait a few weeks or months between each procedure, with Angaran noting doctors want patients’ scars on the outside to have healed before they proceed with the internal procedure.

One of their first patients was Davies, who learned about the procedure by searching online.

Davies had the first part of the procedure, the robotic technique, in September and is expected to return to Toronto in the coming weeks for the catheter ablation.

“It’s nice to be able to potentially, you know, take that diagnosis and direct it in a much more human, in a way that, you know, appreciate much more than the alternative,” he said.

Angaran told Global News that in patients with long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation, the long-term success rate through this approach could hit as high as 70 to 80 per cent.

— with files from Global News’ Katherine Ward
