stories.title: Canada's anti-immigrant sentiment softening, according to new poll
stories.summary: 45% of Canadians polled said we have too many immigrants, 31% indicated we have about the right number, and 13% said we don't have enough.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
Canadians in the Atlantic region and on the Prairies are most likely to think there are too many immigrants coming to this country while British Columbians and Quebecers are least likely to see it that way, according to a new poll.

When you look at all 10 provinces, 45 per cent of Canadians polled said we have too many immigrants, 31 per cent indicated we have about the right number, and 13 per cent said we don’t have enough, according to the poll conducted earlier this month by Ekos for the Association for Canadian Studies.

“We’re still seeing the large plurality of Canadians saying there are too many immigrants,” said Jack Jedwab, the association’s president.

“But clearly relative to the previous three years, we are seeing some change in feeling around that and some loosening of concern on the part of Canadians.”

Manitoba and Saskatchewan respondents were most likely to say Canada has too many immigrants (52 per cent), followed by Atlantic Canada (50 per cent), then Alberta and Ontario (both at 46 per cent).

British Columbians were least likely to say Canada has too many immigrants (39 per cent), followed closely by Quebecers (40 per cent).

The poll comes ahead of Mark Carney’s Liberal government announcing immigration levels for the next three years in the coming weeks before presenting a budget on Nov. 5.

British Columbians topped the list of those who said Canada has about the right number of immigrants (34 per cent), followed by Alberta and Quebec (both at 32 per cent). Those polled in Manitoba and Saskatchewan were least likely to say Canada has the right number of immigrants (26 per cent).

British Columbians were also the most likely to say Canada doesn’t have enough immigrants (18 per cent), followed by Quebec (16 per cent), Atlantic Canada (13 per cent), and Ontario (12 per cent).

Immigration concerns have declined across the board, but they’re still high in Atlantic Canada and lowest in B.C. and Quebec, according to the poll.

Quebecers were most likely to strongly agree with the need for a common set of values (42 per cent strongly agreed with that, and another 42 per cent somewhat agree).

Only 31 per cent of respondents in Manitoba and Saskatchewan strongly agreed with the need for a common set of values, while 42 per cent somewhat agreed.

But a near equal share believes cohesion requires people accepting others with different values, according to the poll.

In all 10 provinces, 40 per cent of respondents strongly agreed with that statement, while another 39 per cent somewhat agreed.

Those who indicated Canada has too many immigrants was down 13 percentage points from a separate Leger poll conducted in March 2025. Those who say we don’t have enough was up 10 percentage points over that same period.

In Atlantic Canada, the number of respondents indicating there are too many immigrants has dropped eight percentage points since March 2025, from 58 per cent to 50 per cent.

In B.C., that number dropped 17 percentage points from 56 per cent in March 2025 to 39 per cent. In Quebec it tumbled 18 percentage points to 40 per cent.

For all 10 provinces, immigration concerns have fallen 13 percentage points from March 2025 until this month, from 58 per cent to 45 per cent.

The new poll indicates a majority of Canadians believe that a cohesive society requires a common set of values. For all 10 provinces, 39 per cent of those polled strongly agreed with that sentiment, while 44 per cent somewhat agreed with it.

Among those who feel Canada has too many immigrants, 89 per cent say social cohesion requires shared common values. Sixty-four per cent of them say it requires accepting different values.

“The people who believe that we need shared common values for cohesion are far more inclined to say there are too many immigrants,” Jedwab said.

“On the other hand, those saying we need to accept different values are far more inclined to say that we’ve got about the right number or, in fact, not enough.”

We're still seeing the large plurality of Canadians saying there are too many immigrants

Among those who say Canada has too many immigrants, 51 per cent indicated they’re very attached to Canada.

“These people are saying, ‘I don’t feel as good about Canada because there are too many immigrants,'” Jedwab said.

That attachment jumps to 70 per cent for the folks who think we have the right number of newcomers.

Immigrants are less likely than non-immigrants to feel that there are too many immigrants, according to the poll.

When you look at all 10 provinces, 45 per cent of Canadians polled said we have too many immigrants, 31 per cent indicated we have about the right number, and 13 per cent said we don’t have enough, according to the poll conducted earlier this month by Ekos for the Association for Canadian Studies.
“We’re still seeing the large plurality of Canadians saying there are too many immigrants,” said Jack Jedwab, the association’s president.
“But clearly relative to the previous three years, we are seeing some change in feeling around that and some loosening of concern on the part of Canadians.”
Manitoba and Saskatchewan respondents were most likely to say Canada has too many immigrants (52 per cent), followed by Atlantic Canada (50 per cent), then Alberta and Ontario (both at 46 per cent).
British Columbians were least likely to say Canada has too many immigrants (39 per cent), followed closely by Quebecers (40 per cent).
The poll comes ahead of Mark Carney’s Liberal government announcing immigration levels for the next three years in the coming weeks before presenting a budget on Nov. 5.

British Columbians topped the list of those who said Canada has about the right number of immigrants (34 per cent), followed by Alberta and Quebec (both at 32 per cent). Those polled in Manitoba and Saskatchewan were least likely to say Canada has the right number of immigrants (26 per cent).
British Columbians were also the most likely to say Canada doesn’t have enough immigrants (18 per cent), followed by Quebec (16 per cent), Atlantic Canada (13 per cent), and Ontario (12 per cent).
Immigration concerns have declined across the board, but they’re still high in Atlantic Canada and lowest in B.C. and Quebec, according to the poll.
Quebecers were most likely to strongly agree with the need for a common set of values (42 per cent strongly agreed with that, and another 42 per cent somewhat agree).
Only 31 per cent of respondents in Manitoba and Saskatchewan strongly agreed with the need for a common set of values, while 42 per cent somewhat agreed.
But a near equal share believes cohesion requires people accepting others with different values, according to the poll.
In all 10 provinces, 40 per cent of respondents strongly agreed with that statement, while another 39 per cent somewhat agreed.

Those who indicated Canada has too many immigrants was down 13 percentage points from a separate Leger poll conducted in March 2025. Those who say we don’t have enough was up 10 percentage points over that same period.
In Atlantic Canada, the number of respondents indicating there are too many immigrants has dropped eight percentage points since March 2025, from 58 per cent to 50 per cent.
In B.C., that number dropped 17 percentage points from 56 per cent in March 2025 to 39 per cent. In Quebec it tumbled 18 percentage points to 40 per cent.
For all 10 provinces, immigration concerns have fallen 13 percentage points from March 2025 until this month, from 58 per cent to 45 per cent.

The new poll indicates a majority of Canadians believe that a cohesive society requires a common set of values. For all 10 provinces, 39 per cent of those polled strongly agreed with that sentiment, while 44 per cent somewhat agreed with it.
Among those who feel Canada has too many immigrants, 89 per cent say social cohesion requires shared common values. Sixty-four per cent of them say it requires accepting different values.
“The people who believe that we need shared common values for cohesion are far more inclined to say there are too many immigrants,” Jedwab said.
“On the other hand, those saying we need to accept different values are far more inclined to say that we’ve got about the right number or, in fact, not enough.”

stories.title: The housing crisis is no longer shaping big-city politics. Why not?
stories.summary: In both Vancouver and Toronto, debates about planning and housing have been blunted by a lull in the market and rising housing supply. But experts say that is a temporary reprieve
stories.author: Alex Bozikovic
stories.content:
In 2019, the City of Toronto announced that it was going to create Housing Now. Then-mayor John Tory launched a program by that name to urgently build mixed-income housing on city land. Seven years later, not one of those homes has been completed.

Yet, despite housing costs and availability dominating local politics for years, it has not been a defining issue in Toronto’s municipal election campaign ahead of the vote on Monday. Nor has it been in Vancouver, where the Green Party’s Pete Fry defeated incumbent mayor Ken Sim on Oct. 17 to end ABC Vancouver’s hold on the mayor’s office. This year, candidates have devoted more attention to other issues, principally taxes and municipal spending, perceptions of public safety, homelessness and transit.

Part of the explanation is that, as the housing market has softened, elected officials no longer see planning reform and housing construction as an urgent priority. The current drop in rents and prices May be weakening the political resolve for change – even as a recent slowdown in construction points to another shortage in the near future.

“New people are likely coming to our cities whether we want them to or not,” says Mark Richardson, a housing advocate with the Toronto group HousingNowTO. (The group’s name refers to the city program.) “We will be ill-prepared for it. Rents will start climbing again, bidding wars will return to some neighbourhoods, and people will act surprised that this has happened again – even though it’s predictable.”

In the Vancouver region, “People feel the crisis is easing,” says Alexandra Flynn, a housing policy expert and associate professor at the University of British Columbia’s Peter A. Allard School of Law. “Asking rents in Vancouver are down from their 2023 peak and condo prices are still falling, so for some voters, the sense of emergency isn’t what it was.”

In Depth: The population is shrinking in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we put more housing there?

The market in both cities has been influenced by two trends: A high number of newly completed homes has coincided with a sharp decline in demand owing to decreased immigration.

At Vancouver City Hall, these changing conditions have altered the conversation. Mr. Sim and his ABC party came to power in 2022 promising to address housing affordability, including through zoning reform. The province has also weighed in: David Eby’s NDP government in 2023 passed a bill mandating higher-density housing near mass transit, and another bill widely permitting “small-scale multiunit housing.”

However, in Vancouver, specific city planning changes that would make it easier to build housing have sputtered. This summer, responding to vocal opposition from some residents’ groups, council voted to reject the proposed Villages Plan, which would have allowed new low-rise housing in 17 neighbourhoods. That set back the city’s effort to accommodate more homes across established residential areas, a centrepiece of the recently revised Official Development Plan .

Although housing May not be a primary election issue, it nevertheless remains a major source of concern among voters. A recent Ipsos poll of British Columbians found that housing affordability and availability is the third most pressing issue .

“It is strange how little politicians are speaking to housing affordability,” says Daniel Oleksiuk, director of the advocacy group Abundant Housing Vancouver. “Politicians don’t seem to want to address this in 2026, but they will have to face the facts eventually.”

He added that Mr. Fry has not set a clear direction on housing policy, and the new councillors – a majority, including several from the left-wing Cope party – do not have clear records on housing. “There is an opportunity for those people to see whether they want to open up more of the city’s neighbourhoods or not.”

In Toronto, “This has not been a housing election,” says Matti Siemiatycki, director of the Infrastructure Institute at the University of Toronto. “In the last few years, housing was the top issue – it’s really a good reminder of how quickly the winds can shift.”

This marks a change from the period between 2020 and 2024, when all three levels of government were actively trying to accelerate housing construction. The federal Housing Accelerator Fund tied funding to municipal commitments to reform planning and increase housing supply.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow has focused her re-election campaign on a property-tax freeze, capping transit fares and school food programs. Her principal opponent, Brad Bradford, has emphasized public safety, traffic congestion and “cost of living.”

On housing, Ms. Chow has emphasized protections for existing tenants, overseen the creation of Toronto’s public builder, and has emphasized the role of government in building social housing and partnering with private builders, as in the Housing Now program. She has set a broader target of 65,000 new rent-controlled homes approved – not built – by 2030.

Mr. Bradford, a professional urban planner who worked at City Hall before running for office, has taken a different tack. While promising tenant protections and financial supports for non-profit builders, he has also proposed eliminating the city’s land transfer tax on a first home purchase up to $1.1-million, a savings for homebuyers that his campaign estimates at $18,000 that will cost the city around $300-million annually.

Mr. Richardson, the housing advocate, argues that the current downturn is a missed opportunity for governments to invest in affordable rental housing.

“Construction materials, construction labour and land are never going to be cheaper than they are now in Toronto,” he says. “This is a Boxing Day sale on housing, and the fact that our governments at all three levels are mostly twiddling their thumbs, not exploiting this opportunity to greatly invest in affordable rental housing, is just sad.”

Housing starts in both Toronto and Vancouver have fallen sharply in recent years. In the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, condominium housing starts are down 90 per cent from their 2021 peak, according to the research group Urbanation. The number of apartment units under construction, including condominiums and purpose-built rentals, has fallen 45 per cent in three years.

In the Vancouver region, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. notes that overall housing starts and condominium housing starts remain low, which presents a longer-term risk to affordability, as buyers face increased competition for fewer homes.

The lack of building today will mean fewer new homes in two to five years. Shaun Hildebrand, president of the Toronto real estate research group Urbanation, expects completions to fall more than 60 per cent to 2029 from their current levels.

“The housing crisis is not easing – it is changing shape,” Mr. Hildebrand says. “While renters and buyers have seen some relief, it is short-term. The underlying problem of a structural shortage of supply remains, and it is getting worse because we have largely stopped building. We are already seeing rents find their floor and rental vacancy start to come back down.”

Rising rents could prompt a new sense of political urgency about housing, Mr. Richardson suggests, once middle- and upper-income people are feeling the pinch again. “A couple of years ago, this was an emergency and a wartime effort,” he says. “Now that the pressure on wealthier people has softened, it is no longer a wartime effort. Now it’s just inconvenience.”

stories.title: Wainwright fire a wake-up call for country unprepared for mass casualties, experts say
stories.summary: Experts warn health care system has limited capacity to handle multiple mass-casualty events, particularly those involving burn injuries
stories.author: Pippa Norman
stories.content:
Dr. Damian Paton-Gay raced through the halls of the Wainwright Health Centre on Saturday night as chaos swirled around him. Nearly every corner of the 100-bed Alberta hospital was crammed with gurneys holding patients suffering from severely scorched skin and in need of intensive care.

His job was to take stock of the condition of the 39 injured soldiers arriving from the nearby military base where they had been engulfed by flames during a training exercise. Calmly but swiftly, he determined which needed to go elsewhere for specialized treatment, and how soon first responders could get them there.

For Dr. Paton-Gay, this was a first – a scene of mayhem that he said would prompt someone watching a medical drama to say, “Well, this TV show is taking a bit of artistic license.”

But this scenario is precisely the type of mass casualty event that senior leadership in both the civilian and military health care systems in Canada have been simulating – and warning that the country is woefully unprepared for.

A domestic producer is an organization that processes and sometimes recovers skin from sources within Canada. Donor recovery operations only recover, but do not process skin.

For two years now, this group of experts have run war games involving the repatriation of hundreds of war zone casualties arriving from overseas for a sustained period to determine how Canadian health care systems would fare. Burns have featured heavily in the exercises.

What played out on Saturday night in Wainwright, a town about 200 kilometres east of Edmonton, is just a glimpse of how the capacity of Canada’s health care system can be challenged in an instant, said Adalsteinn Brown, dean at the University of Toronto’s Dalla Lana School of Public Health, and one of the experts involved in these planning simulations.

If the Wainwright fire and another tragedy elsewhere in Canada occurred around the same time, the system would falter, Dr. Brown said.

“If we continually run the systems as close as we can to the bone, we don’t focus on resilience, we don’t build in that capacity, and we don’t practice being ready to deal with not just one but many. Then we’ll find ourselves in real fundamental existential difficulties with the health system,” Dr. Brown said.

The Canadian Armed Forces relies on the country’s civilian, public health care system, which is often operating at maximum capacity, for specialized care. Canada also depends heavily upon imports for critical supplies such as skin and blood bags, leaving its supply chains vulnerable in the event of war or another large-scale mass casualty event. Those involved in the simulations are campaigning for better co-ordination of health care preparedness at a national level, especially between the civilian and military systems, to ensure Canada emerges resilient in the face of a crisis much larger than Wainwright.

In December, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned in a speech in Berlin that, “Conflict is at our door.” He added, “Russia has brought war back to Europe, and we must be prepared for the scale of war our grandparents or great-grandparents endured.”

For Canada, this call to action doesn’t mean only investing into arms and soldiers, but also, health care: “You really can’t talk about the defence of Canada without investing in a resilient civilian health care system,” Major-General Scott Malcolm, surgeon-general of the Canadian Armed Forces and a participant in the Canadian war games, said.

Similar disasters in the past have done little to spark change, said Gen. Malcolm. He referenced Quebec’s Lac-Mégantic disaster in 2013, during which a fiery explosion killed 47 people. That prompted calls to be better equipped for burn care in Canada, he said. But little changed.

Being prepared for an influx of burn patients is top of mind for Gen. Malcolm because of the types of injuries being documented in Ukraine, which are different than wars past.

“We’re seeing burns and a greater volume of patients in general,” he said. This has raised flags at home for the surgeon-general, where the Armed Forces often rely on the civilian health care system and lack burn surgeons among their ranks.

Modelling shows that capacity, supplies and specialized personnel in the civilian system are limited in terms of surge capacity.

When Dr. Paton-Gay was making calls from the Wainwright Health Centre on Saturday night, one of the things he asked was how much space hospitals could open up for the incoming burn victims. Were there existing patients who could be moved around to open up room in intensive and emergency care? How many?

Seven of the injured soldiers landed in his own intensive care unit at the Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton where he works full-time as a physician.

Dr. Paton-Gay walked into his Edmonton home on Sunday morning roughly 12 hours after receiving the call for aid in Wainwright. By Monday morning at 7 a.m., he was back at work in the ICU to begin his first shift of a seven-day stretch.

“There is some fatigue,” he said. “But no one’s going to shy away from caring for people who volunteered their service to protect our country.”

Many of his waking hours this week, as well as those of his colleagues, have been spent caring for the burn patients.

“It’s minute by minute for the nurses at the bedside,” he said.

The care includes painful dressing changes that often require painkillers or sedation, ensuring the patients’ airways remain open, frequent surgical procedures, and keeping their bodies free of infection and at the right temperature. It’s precise work and critical, until they are ready for the intensive surgeries necessary to replace their damaged skin.

This aspect of their recovery underscores another feature of the Canadian health care system that mass casualty experts say is deficient – a steady supply of tissues, such as skin, cornea and tendon. In the U.S., there are more than 100 establishments accredited by the Association for Advancing Tissue and Biologics whose members’ work includes tissue recovery, distribution and storage. In Canada, there are 15 organizations dedicated to supplying tissue to those in need.

Canada imports the majority of its tissues from the U.S., said Dr. Graham Sher, chief executive of Canadian Blood Services. The country has long been self-sufficient in blood, but tissues have been left behind owing to a lack of federal investment, he said.

That vulnerability is why, more than a year ago, Gen. Malcolm approached the national organization to increase the country’s sovereign supply of skin. This request was backed in June by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, who announced a $75-million investment into Canadian Blood Services to support its work with the Armed Forces.

“If we ran into a circumstance, where needs arose at the same time in our neighbours to the south or in Europe, we would be challenged,” Gen. Malcolm said.

“We simply don’t produce enough tissue in Canada, right now, in peacetime, to meet our demands.”

The Globe and Mail asked the provincial health agency Acute Care Alberta about how much skin will be required to treat victims of the Wainwright fire, and where it will be sourced from.

Acute Care Alberta declined to provide specifics about individual patients’ treatment requirements. Spokesperson Jennifer Vanderlaan wrote in an e-mail: “When donor skin is required, Give Life Alberta tissue banks in Edmonton and Calgary maintain supplies from deceased donors. If local demand exceeds supply, hospitals can also request donor skin from tissue banks in other provinces.”

It’s difficult to say how much skin Canada needs to be better prepared. With the caveat that there’s “not a lot of science to it,” Gen. Malcolm said he’s calling for an expansion of tissue banks across the country, with each location housing about 1.5-million square centimetres, roughly the area of 11 standard parking spaces.

“You never know truly how many casualties you’re going to have,” he said.

For now, planning to bolster Canada’s national skin supply chain is still in early stages, said Jody Faught, vice-president of supply chain at Canadian Blood Services.

In Quebec, where the province operates its own blood and tissue supply separate from the rest of the country, Héma-Québec spokesperson Josée Larivée confirmed the organization has been co-ordinating with the armed forces and Ottawa.

Quebec has previously been reliant on the U.S. for tissues. Today, it’s closing in on an agreement with the federal government, Ms. Larivée wrote in an e-mail, to have 1.5-million square centimetres of skin, or enough to “simultaneously treat approximately 75 to 150 severely burned patients.”

Wainwright is proof for Dr. Paton-Gay that the system and supplies supporting a country’s health care workers matter. “We can trust that people will do remarkable things, if they’re provided a system that supports them,” he said.

stories.title: Canada spent second most out of 32 countries on health care with little to show for it': Fraser report
stories.summary: Fraser report puts Canada second in spending among comparable nations, but near last in most measures of medical availability of resources.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
A new report from the Fraser Institute notes that, of the 32 high-income countries offering universal health care, Canada ranks among the highest for spending but falls consistently at the bottom when it comes to results.

The report , “Comparing Performance of Universal Health Care Countries,” by Mackenzie Moir and Nadeem Esmail, is the latest annual look at the topic by the Fraser Institute.

It examined countries that were members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (Oecd), offered universal or near-universal and had a gross national income per capita of more than US$13,935. Of the 38 Oecd countries, four — Mexico, Costa Rica, Estonia and the United States — do not have universal health care and two others — Türkiye and Colombia — did not meet the income cutoff.

Of the remaining 32 countries, Canada ranked second highest for spending as a percentage of GDP in 2024, the most recent year of comparable data. Only Chile spent more.

However, across 13 indictors of the availability of medical resources and timely access to medical services, Canada was generally below average among Oecd countries.

Notably, it ranked 30th out of 32 countries for the availability of doctors, 26th out of 31 for hospital beds dedicated to physical care, 28th out of 31 for the availability of MRI machines, and 28th out of 31 for CT scanners.

More specifically, Canada was found to have 2.8 doctors per thousand people. The average was 4.1, and the top countries in the category — Greece, Austria, Iceland and Norway — had more than five per thousand people.

Canada fared better on availability of nurses, with 10.5 per thousand people where the average was 10.1. However, this put our country in 14th place for this measurement, with top countries Switzerland, Iceland, Luxembourg and Ireland all recording more than 16 nurses per thousand people.

Canada’s MRI machine tally was 10.7 per million residents, barely more than half the Oecd average of 20.6 per million. CT and PET scanners were similarly near or below half the average in other countries. Canada had a better ranking for a type of scanner known as a gamma camera, placing third with 14.3 per million people. It also had 17.2 mammographs per million people, putting it in 13th place, though still below the average of 23.4.

Meanwhile, among the nine countries for which comparable wait times measures are available, Canada ranked dead last for the percentage of patients reporting they were able to make a same- or next-day appointment when sick, at 22 per cent.

When it came to timely access, our country also placed eighth out of nine for patients who waited more than one month to see a specialist (65 per cent) and had the highest percentage of patients (58 per cent) who waited two months or more for non-emergency surgery.

“There’s a clear imbalance between the high cost of Canada’s health-care system and the actual care Canadians receive,” said Nadeem Esmail, director of health policy studies at the Fraser Institute and co-author of the report.

The report did not make specific recommendations, but noted: “To improve health care for Canadians, our policymakers should learn from other countries around the world that also provide universal health care, often at lower costs to taxpayers and with significantly better access and shorter wait times.”

The methodology used in the report is based on that used in previous reports published between 2016 and 2025, the Institute said. It looked at 13 indicators, representing two broad categories: availability of resources, and access to resources.

It also noted that the population age profiles in the 32 countries vary significantly, and that older populations require higher levels of health-care spending. “For this reason, this study presents indicators measuring health-care expenditures and the availability of resources adjusted according to the age-profile of the country,” it added.

stories.title: Don't look now, but Canada is officially becoming a partisan issue in the U.S.
stories.summary: A new survey finds older Republicans are driving a decline in American warmth toward Canada, but will that divide outlast Trump?
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — “Canada treats us very badly.”

“They are one of the worst countries in the world to deal with.”

“(Canada’s leaders) are nasty people.”

President Donald Trump has said plenty of negative things about Canada in recent years, especially on trade, yet Americans remain largely positive toward Canada.

A new Pew Research Center survey of American views of G20 countries had Canada topping the list alongside Australia. But the figures still reflect a decline: Americans’ average rating of Canada on a “feeling thermometer” ranging from zero to 100 fell from 71 in 2018 to 67 in 2026.

So why the four-point drop in America’s warm feelings toward its northern neighbour? In a word: Republicans.

Since 2018, the share of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents with warm views of Canada fell from 59 to 50 per cent. Older Republicans were largely responsible for the decline, as those aged 50-plus saw their warm views drop from 61 to 47 per cent, while younger Republicans’ views had not significantly changed.

American Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, meanwhile, rated Canada 19 points higher than their Republican counterparts — one of the largest partisan gaps in the survey.

So is it fair to say that Canada is becoming a partisan issue in the United States?

“Yes,” said Laura Silver, associate director at Pew and an expert in international survey research. “That would be absolutely fair.”

“We did not see large partisan gaps when it came to views of Canada or perceptions of trade with Canada prior to recent years. But at this point, we’ve seen shifting views among Republicans, and as of now … the gap between partisans’ views of Canada is among the largest of any of the countries that we asked about.”

But does that widening divide mean Canada is increasingly being seen as aligned with the Democrats?

The Trump administration has portrayed some Canadian activities in explicitly partisan terms. This week, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released a “fact sheet” alleging potential election interference, highlighting Canadian officials’ meetings with Democrats and efforts to put economic pressure on Republican states. And last month, Peter Navarro, an adviser to President Donald Trump, warned Canadians that “if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan you will pay even more dearly.”

But not everyone thinks Americans increasingly see Canada as being aligned with the Democrats.

Chris Kirkey, director of the Center for the Study of Canada and Institute on Quebec Studies at State University of New York at Plattsburgh, sees similarities between some Canadian policies and Democratic priorities, but he does not think Americans largely regard Canada through a party-political lens.

“Canada has always been highly non-political in this country,” he said.

Brian Rathbun, professor at the Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy at the University of Toronto, sees the cooling of Republican views as voters taking cues from their party’s leader or “cueing,” rather than anything specific about Canada. He sees Republicans downgrading Canada because of Trump’s negative comments about the country, not because of a substantive change in their own relationship with Canada.

“I don’t think it has anything to do with Canada per se,” he said, adding that he expects views to become more positive after Trump leaves office.

Silver noted that about half of Republicans said in 2023 that trade between the two countries benefited both equally. By March 2025, shortly after Trump returned to office and began verbally attacking Canada over trade, the share saying Canada benefited more had risen sharply. The findings are consistent with a “cueing” explanation, but cannot establish cause and effect, she said.

“We have cross-sectional data, not causal data,” she explained.

Speaking before the Pew survey’s release, Christopher Sands, director of the Center for Canadian Studies at Johns Hopkins, warned that blaming Canada for potential Republican midterm losses could make it harder for Ottawa to work with the party.

“It carries a certain risk that if Democrats do well but are nonetheless seen as the enemy and Canada is associated with just one party, then it becomes harder to have conversations with Republicans who you’ll need unless the Republicans are completely wiped out,” he said.

But Rathbun remains optimistic “that Canada is not going to become part of American polarization,” noting that while Canada is currently associated more with Democrats, he doubts this will last.

“I’m not worried about this becoming … part of Maga lore … that Canadians are the enemy,” he said.

I don’t think it has anything to do with Canada per se

Silver suggested that negative feelings could fade if Canada becomes less prominent in Americans’ minds.

“When something is not particularly salient for the public, when they’re not thinking about it often, we can see kind of a reversion almost to the mean,” she said. But negative views could persist if the relationship remains economically consequential to Americans, she cautioned.

Even if American goodwill toward Canada rebounds, as he and other experts expect, Rathbun says the damage on the Canadian side is likely to last longer.

A Pew survey earlier this year showed that just 33 per cent of Canadians view the United States favourably, down 21 percentage points since 2024.

“Canadian attitudes towards Americans will probably be more negative for a longer period of time,” said Rathbun, noting that the confrontation and trade tensions are more consequential for Canadians.

“It affects them more; they think about it more.”

stories.title: ‘Always try to buy Canadian’: Are Canadians planning to ‘buy Canadian’ ahead of Halloween?
stories.summary: Every time Suzie Wisniewski grocery shops, she looks for Canadian products. For her and many Canadians that sentiment is no different when it comes to buying sweet treats for Halloween.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Winnipeg – Every time Suzie Wisniewski grocery shops, she looks for Canadian products. For her and many Canadians that sentiment is no different when it comes to buying sweet treats for Halloween.

“I always like to try to buy Canadian where I can,” she said, while shopping for candy at Winnipeg’s Food Fare grocery store.

“It’s important for me to support the country.”

A recent online survey conducted by Angus Reid for NextDoor Canada shows a majority of Canadians are on the same page as Wisniewski.

The survey shows 59 per cent of Canadians say it’s a priority to support local or Canadian businesses when shopping for or celebrating Halloween, from pumpkins picked at nearby farms to costumes from neighbourhood shops and treats from local bakeries.

That number is higher in Saskatchewan and Manitoba at 68 per cent, and 69 per cent in Atlantic Canada.

“My neighbours next door are not very nice,” Wisniewski said, referring to the United States. “(They) don’t have very nice leaders, so I choose not to support them if at all possible.”

The push to “buy Canadian” has resurfaced over the last several months, in light of tariff tensions between Canada and the United States.

Food Fare owner, Ramsey Zeid, has placed “Made in Canada” stickers all along his store’s shelves, to help consumers identify which products are Canadian.

Halloween revives buy Canadian sentiment

But he says it’s a little challenging when it comes to Halloween candy and treats.

“I haven’t seen any Canadian-made Halloween candies but certainly see a lot of candies that say prepared in Canada,” he said.

“You’re kind of limited to your choices, right? You got your Coffee Crisps, Aeros, your Oh Henry, your Twizzlers, Nerds, that kind of stuff, and little bags of chips.”

Zeid says sourcing local products and stocking them for Halloween can also be difficult, particularly because the store doesn’t put a significant focus on seasonal candy.

“Halloween comes around once a year. It’s hard for a business to start up and prepare all these candies and invest all this money for one day a year,” he said.

“So, unless you have a consistent supply of other candies for the rest of the year, it’s hard to do it for just the one day of the year.”

Sylvain Charlebois is director of the Agri-Food Analytics Lab at Dalhousie University. He says that while many familiar Halloween treats are manufactured in Canada, their ingredients and ownership May be foreign.

“There are very Canadian options out there, but they’re typically more expensive, but most candies that’ll be given out are manufactured in Canada, but most of them are foreign companies, and many of them are American companies,” Charlebois said.

“If I am a Canadian-focused shopper for Halloween, I would look around because sometimes some of these products are great, even healthy, but they’re not advertised.”

“You need to work a little harder to find them, and sometimes they’re in a pharmacy or in independent stores as well,” he said.

As Canadians fill their bowls for trick-or-treaters, the challenge facing shoppers is finding options that are both Canadian-made and budget-friendly.

The same online survey conducted for NextDoor Canada found that 88 per cent of Canadians plan to spend less than $100 on Halloween this year and about 65 per cent of Canadians set their Halloween budget at less than $50.

stories.title: Amid acrimony at Pickering City Hall, voters mull calming the waters
stories.summary: Conflict at the municipal level has caused ripples in a number of communities
stories.author: Joe Friesen, Photography by Shay Conroy
stories.content:
About this series

The Globe is reporting from cities and towns in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia to hear from residents about the issues affecting their communities and their votes in the municipal elections. Explore the entire series here .

Oakwood Drive is a long residential street that cars, e-bikes and scooters treat like a raceway, annoying residents and making it a treacherous place to walk or stand by the roadside.

It’s the kind of thing that Abdullah Mir, a candidate for the Ward 1 city council seat in Monday’s municipal election, describes as an ordinary, “unsexy” problem that city governments deal with all the time.

But in Pickering the basics of local government have lately taken a back seat. Over the last four years city council has been a raucous arena where divisive hot-button issues have sucked the air out of civic governance. Misconduct has become an issue of growing concern for local government in a number of cities and towns and people are looking for solutions.

In Pickering, the seven-member council has been wrapped up in the controversy surrounding outgoing Ward 1 city councillor, Lisa Robinson, first elected in 2022. Ms. Robinson is running for mayor this time in an attempt to unseat incumbent Kevin Ashe. She was a Conservative candidate in the 2021 federal election, but was dumped by the party after inflammatory and Islamophobic tweets surfaced, which at the time she denied writing.

Ms. Robinson, who did not respond to messages from The Globe and Mail, was the subject of nine reports by the city’s integrity commissioner during the last council term and was docked 90-days pay several times for actions that included maligning staff.

She has defended herself in the past by saying she is neither racist nor homophobic and that she is fighting an establishment at City Hall that’s protecting its own interests. She says government should be open, councillors shouldn’t be expected to fall in line and residents shouldn’t be dismissed as interruptions.

“They call me disruptive. I am disruptive because City Hall needs disrupting,” Ms. Robinson says on her campaign website. “Every sanction, every statement, every attempt to isolate me has made one thing clear: I cannot be controlled by the current establishment.”

She attracted a loyal following to council meetings who cheered her on as she opposed things like Pride flags and gender neutral washrooms, railed against what she called attempts to silence her and even accused colleagues of corruption. The atmosphere deteriorated to the point that council stopped holding meetings in person, due to “unruly, disruptive, and intimidating behaviours from visitors,” according to a 2024 city bulletin.

How a level of government normally preoccupied with potholes and parks became a vicious battleground is bewildering to many residents, Mr. Mir included.

“The last four years have been a massive distraction because of all the nonsense,” Mr. Mir says. “I’m looking to put all that behind us.”

Between Pickering and Rouge National Urban Park is the Duffins Rouge Agricultural Preserve, which Mr. Mir fought to preserve when the Ford government carved out pieces of the Greenbelt in 2022. The province reinstated protections after pressure from Stop Sprawl Durham, which Mr. Mir belongs to.

Pickering is a bedroom community of more than 100,000 people at Toronto’s eastern edge.

With a waterfront to the south, forests and farmlands to the north and a short commute to the country’s largest economic hub, the province’s growth plan calls for it to double in size in the next 25 years.

Mr. Mir, 33, lives in the community with his parents, who came to Canada from Pakistan. He saved up two years of holidays at his federal civil service job, managing a team at the Department of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, to run for office.

He says he’s running because he wants to see the area grow in a productive and responsible way.

“A lot of the things that people want here are similar across political lines,” Mr. Mir says. “A good city is one where we have good parks and good roads and good libraries and good snow clearing.”

He’s delighted to talk about his time leading an organization that opposes sprawl in Pickering, and how it kept parts of the Greenbelt out of the hands of developers, or his time on the library board, where he pushed for a local bookmobile. He does not want to talk much about Ms. Robinson.

On the campaign trail, Mr. Mir encounters voters who want reassurance that, if elected, he would be a different kind of councillor.

Nancy Ronchin, a volunteer canvasser for Mr. Mir, comes down Oakwood Drive for a debrief with the candidate. She tells him that residents are complaining about drivers acting as though this is Highway 407 and many have mentioned Ms. Robinson.

As one resident puts it, he wants a local representative who can disagree without descending to hostility.

Ms. Ronchin says she has never been involved in politics and didn’t know Mr. Mir until recently, but she made up her mind that she had to do something.

She was particularly upset about a fight over a gender-neutral washroom at a local recreation centre, which she says is useful but that Ms. Robinson opposes.

“I can’t just complain about it from my couch,” Ms. Ronchin says.

Conflict that extends to incivility has affected other local governments and put pressure on provinces to step in.

In neighbouring Whitby, Ont., which borders Pickering to the east, a councillor was docked pay earlier this year for maligning city staff and eroding public trust. In Sarnia, Ont., a local councillor has been investigated by the integrity commissioner and banned from attending council meetings in person. And in Kamloops, there have been lawsuits and investigations spawning from a dispute between the mayor and city council.

Partly in response to these concerns, Ontario passed a Municipal Accountability Act in May that gives councils the ability to remove from office those who’ve committed serious transgressions. B.C. introduced a bill in April to standardize codes of conduct that wasn’t passed before the provincial election was called.

Back in Pickering, Mara Nagy, councillor for Ward 2, says the last term on council has been difficult. She describes herself as one of many who opposed Ms. Robinson’s ideas and rhetoric. She felt frustrated by chaotic meetings that sometimes went on for five or six hours, she says.

“There were a couple meetings where we actually had to pause to leave the chambers because it was ready to turn into a riot.”

“If you tell the whole story, it sounds unbelievable that something like this could happen in what is, for all intents and purposes, a suburb.”

As he ends his day of campaigning, Mr. Mir ushers a reporter away from the roadside for safety. He says Pickering can be the best of both worlds, a place close to nature and the waterfront, that is near the city but offers something different. It can grow into something great over the next generation, he says. But someone needs to mind the parks and potholes and scrutinize the planning.

Looking at the stretch of road as another vehicle speeds past, he’s hit with a burst of enthusiasm for traffic controls. Maybe there should be a speed bump, or a chicane – he’d consult with residents, of course, but something can be done.

“This is what we need to be fixing. Not arguing about who’s using what bathroom,” Mr. Mir says.

stories.title: Why Toronto’s election is suddenly a horse race
stories.summary: With frustrations bubbling, a promise of change has transformed Monday’s faceoff
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
Incumbents have a big advantage in municipal elections.

With voter interest and turnout lower than at other levels of politics, they profit simply from having names that most people recognize. Olivia Chow is one of the best-known political figures in Toronto, with years of service as a city councillor, then an MP, behind her before she became mayor in 2023.

History and precedent say she should win. No sitting mayor of Toronto since the creation of a single, unitary city in 1998 has stood for re-election and failed.

Yet, with Monday’s vote just around the corner, the polls are suggesting Ms. Chow could be the first. Brad Bradford, a 40-year-old councillor who came in eighth in the last election for mayor, is nipping at her heels – even pulling ahead, some surveys suggest.

That is less surprising than it might look. Ms. Chow first entered politics when she won a seat on the school board way back in 1985. Her very familiarity is an impediment in a city that is bubbling with frustration.

Its discontent is manifold. Housing is hard to afford. Traffic is a famous mess. Transit projects go billions over budget and open years behind schedule. Disorder on the streets and the streetcars has many residents wondering what the city is coming to.

Mr. Bradford has seized on these frustrations like a bull terrier. Toronto, he says, is “stuck.” Stuck in traffic, stuck waiting for the bus, stuck paying higher taxes under Ms. Chow with little to show for it. This election, he says, comes down to the three Cs: “Crime, congestion and cost.” In a vigorous, focused attack, he has managed to paint Ms. Chow as a stand-pat candidate who is “very comfortable with the status quo.”

Until recently, the mayor failed to muster much of a counterattack. Instead, she stood on her record – freezing transit fares, delivering a school snack program, opening libraries seven days a week – while promising more relief for renters, transit riders and jobless youth.

Only in the last while, with Mr. Bradford whittling away at her incumbent edge, has she started to fight back in earnest, and even then, it has often looked panicky.

One of her posts seemed to suggest that Mr. Bradford would “go back to closing libraries,” but he denies any such intention. Earlier this week, she even trotted out the Yoda of Canadian environmentalism, David Suzuki, to back her dubious claim that Mr. Bradford’s plan to turn Toronto’s water department into a separate public utility was a plot to privatize it.

You never know. It might work. Her promises to crack down on slumlords and stop supposed price gouging by big grocery chains could help rally her base: left-of-centre voters in the city core.

Other voters might take a closer look at some of Mr. Bradford’s claims and start scratching their heads. It is just silly for him to say Ms. Chow has failed to stand up to Ontario Premier Doug Ford when he has stuck his nose into city affairs. She pushed back hard over things like the provincial government’s decision to rip out some bike lanes and remove speed cameras.

Ultimately, Ontario cities are subordinate to Queen’s Park. Every mayor chafes under that reality. Ms. Chow built a good relationship with Mr. Ford despite their political differences and got some big wins. Most notably, she secured a big funding deal that uploaded responsibility for two major highways, the Gardiner Expressway and the Don Valley Parkway, to the province.

More head scratching could ensue over Mr. Bradford’s campaign promises. They include hiring 1,000 new police officers over four years and hurrying ahead with a proposed light-rail transit line into the suburb of Scarborough. They also include some big concessions to taxpayers, such as freezing property taxes in his first year and getting rid of the land-transfer tax on homes valued at less than $1.1-million.

It doesn’t add up. Promising tax cuts and spending increases all at once is not change at all. It is just run-of-the-mill, have-your-cake-and-eat-it politics. Mr. Bradford is hardly reassuring when he asserts he can pay for all of this by changing the city’s accounting practices, cutting the amount of money that the city puts aside for long-term projects and borrowing more instead.

Even if Ms. Chow does prevail in the end, Mr. Bradford has picked up on something. Toronto is a successful city by most measures, but it has some big, complex problems. Its residents are losing confidence that city leaders are capable of grappling with them. Toronto’s mayor has to change that, whichever candidate wins Monday.

Toronto, he says, is “stuck.” Stuck in traffic, stuck waiting for the bus, stuck paying higher taxes under Ms. Chow with little to show for it. This election, he says, comes down to the three Cs: “Crime, congestion and cost.” In a vigorous, focused attack, he has managed to paint Ms. Chow as a stand-pat candidate who is “very comfortable with the status quo.”

Until recently, the mayor failed to muster much of a counterattack. Instead, she stood on her record – freezing transit fares, delivering a school snack program, opening libraries seven days a week – while promising more relief for renters, transit riders and jobless youth.
Only in the last while, with Mr. Bradford whittling away at her incumbent edge, has she started to fight back in earnest, and even then, it has often looked panicky.

One of her posts seemed to suggest that Mr. Bradford would “go back to closing libraries,” but he denies any such intention. Earlier this week, she even trotted out the Yoda of Canadian environmentalism, David Suzuki, to back her dubious claim that Mr. Bradford’s plan to turn Toronto’s water department into a separate public utility was a plot to privatize it.
You never know. It might work. Her promises to crack down on slumlords and stop supposed price gouging by big grocery chains could help rally her base: left-of-centre voters in the city core.

Other voters might take a closer look at some of Mr. Bradford’s claims and start scratching their heads. It is just silly for him to say Ms. Chow has failed to stand up to Ontario Premier Doug Ford when he has stuck his nose into city affairs. She pushed back hard over things like the provincial government’s decision to rip out some bike lanes and remove speed cameras.

Ultimately, Ontario cities are subordinate to Queen’s Park. Every mayor chafes under that reality. Ms. Chow built a good relationship with Mr. Ford despite their political differences and got some big wins. Most notably, she secured a big funding deal that uploaded responsibility for two major highways, the Gardiner Expressway and the Don Valley Parkway, to the province.

More head scratching could ensue over Mr. Bradford’s campaign promises. They include hiring 1,000 new police officers over four years and hurrying ahead with a proposed light-rail transit line into the suburb of Scarborough. They also include some big concessions to taxpayers, such as freezing property taxes in his first year and getting rid of the land-transfer tax on homes valued at less than $1.1-million.

It doesn’t add up. Promising tax cuts and spending increases all at once is not change at all. It is just run-of-the-mill, have-your-cake-and-eat-it politics. Mr. Bradford is hardly reassuring when he asserts he can pay for all of this by changing the city’s accounting practices, cutting the amount of money that the city puts aside for long-term projects and borrowing more instead.

Even if Ms. Chow does prevail in the end, Mr. Bradford has picked up on something. Toronto is a successful city by most measures, but it has some big, complex problems. Its residents are losing confidence that city leaders are capable of grappling with them. Toronto’s mayor has to change that, whichever candidate wins Monday.

stories.title: Toronto-bound Afghan woman deported to Africa after ICE detention
stories.summary: Former Médecins Sans Frontières nurse says she was sent to Central African Republic after Ottawa failed to respond to ICE request to release her to Canada
stories.author: Sara Mojtehedzadeh
stories.content:
An Afghan woman who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement while travelling to Toronto to reunite with her family says she was deported to the Central African Republic after Ottawa failed to respond to Ice’s request to release her to Canada, according to legal submissions made to the federal government.

The woman, who is a former nurse for Médecins Sans Frontières, was detained by ICE in Texas, December, 2024, and deported in June of this year. She fled Afghanistan alleging persecution for being Hazara, a minority Muslim community that is persecuted by the Taliban, as well as her family’s history working for Western organizations in Helmand province.

The Globe and Mail is not naming the woman because of the risk she would face in Afghanistan if the Central African Republic forcibly repatriates her, which her lawyer says remains a possibility. The former nurse has a temporary visa to remain in the conflict-ridden African country, but it expires at the end of the year.

In an interview with The Globe last week, the woman said she is terrified for her safety. The Central African Republic, located between Cameroon and South Sudan, is described by the World Bank as “one of the poorest and most fragile countries in the world.” Canada has temporarily paused deportations to the country owing to concerns over the humanitarian crisis there.

In the United States, the practice of removing people to countries they have no connection with has become a key part of President Donald Trump ’s immigration crackdown, according to the American Immigration Council, a non-profit that advocates for immigrant rights. The measure is used to deport individuals who cannot be legally returned to their home country owing to a credible risk of persecution.

The Afghan woman has now filed an application from the Central African Republic to obtain a Canadian temporary resident permit that would allow her join her sister and other family members, who have already been granted refugee status in Canada. These permits are granted on a case-by-case basis when someone is otherwise inadmissible.

Legal submissions made as part of the application say there is “reason to believe” that ICE unsuccessfully sought to send the woman to Canada, prior to deporting her to another country.

“Canada has a responsibility here,” said the woman’s lawyer, Adam Sadinsky. “We’re not talking about opening the floodgates. We’re talking about doing right by one family.”

In a statement Monday,a spokesperson for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (Ircc) said the department could not comment on individual cases for privacy reasons. The statement said Ircc “remains committed to the principle of family reunification in the context of its immigration programs.”

When the woman fled Afghanistan, she was unable to fly directly to Canada because she did not qualify for a visitor visa, according to immigration submissions made to the federal government.

However, she was eligible to claim refugee protection in Canada at its border with the U.S., according to Mr. Sadinsky. While the Safe Third Country Agreement prevents most asylum seekers from travelling by land through the U.S. to claim asylum in Canada, the treaty contains an exception for those with close relatives legally residing here.

The reunification plan was derailed after the woman, who fled to Brazil with her brother and father after being granted a temporary visa by the Brazilian government, travelled by land to the U.S. and was detained after crossing the border in Texas.

In submissions to Ircc, lawyers for the family described what unfolded next as a “ legal trap ”: U.S. authorities were willing to release the family if they could travel to Canada by air, but this required Ottawa to grant them temporary resident permits. Ottawa rejected the woman’s application for one in October, 2025, according to documentation reviewed by The Globe.

Earlier this year, an ICE officer told the Afghan woman that the U.S. immigration agency had made requests to remove her to the Dominican Republic, Panama, or Canada, according to a statutory declaration that she made as part of her immigration case. The officer told her that the first two countries refused the request, while Canada did not respond, she states.

Court filings show her father, who was held at a different detention facility and filed a habeas corpus application to be released, experienced a similar issue.

In deciding his case, a New Mexico district judge cited evidence from deportation officer Juaquin Quevedo, who said ICE had made four requests to Ottawa to remove the man to Canada – most recently in February, 2026 – but did not receive a response.

The New Mexico court ordered that the Afghan woman’s father, as well as her brother, be released from detention. Both were able to travel to the Canadian border, where they were granted entry to claim asylum.

However, the former nurse was deported by ICE before her family had the chance to complete a similar habeas corpus application for her, the woman’s sister said. The sister, who is based near Toronto, told The Globe last week that she realized something was amiss when her sister’s contact details disappeared from an ICE-monitored app that allows detainees to call family members.

“I kept calling the detention centre,” she said. “They sent no information.”

The former nurse’s statutory declaration says she was taken without prior notice from the Texas detention facility and driven to a Louisiana airport in early June. On June 11, she was handcuffed at the feet and hands, put on an airplane, and told that she was headed for the Central African Republic, the declaration says.

The woman now shares an apartment provided by the UN’s International Organization for Migration with 11 other asylum seekers, she told The Globe in an interview. She said the organization has imposed a strict curfew on residents, and said she only leaves her apartment if absolutely necessary.

The Central African Republic has struggled for years with sectarian violence between its Muslim and Christian populations. Last year, the United Nations released a report documenting “grave human rights violations” by armed groups targeting Muslim communities including summary executions, sexual violence and torture.

“There is simply no way I can remain here safely as a Muslim woman from Afghanistan with no ties to the country,” the woman’s declaration says.

The woman is now the sole member of her family who is not in Canada, submissions in her immigration case say. She has been unable to access the medication she was previously taking to treat the anxiety and depression she developed while in ICE detention, her declaration says. It also states that her eyesight declined significantly owing to repeated eye infections developed in detention, but she has been unable to obtain new prescription glasses in the Central African Republic.

Her declaration says she has limited access to clean water and electricity.

The woman’s sister told The Globe she feared for her sibling’s well-being.

“Her mental health is collapsing. She gets worse every single day . . . and I can’t do anything.” she said.

“It is affecting my entire family,” she added. “We are suffering. We are exhausted.”

The former nurse is seeking a temporary resident permit because of the long processing times for Canada’s other refugee resettlement streams, her immigration application says.

“[She] needs to be rescued from her current situation,” her lawyer, Mr. Sadinsky, said. “The government of Canada can do that with the stroke of a pen.”

stories.title: Alberta’s vote has softened the rhetoric, but peace and quiet are not guaranteed
stories.summary: Danielle Smith emerges into a fractious fight to keep her position, as Carney seeks ways to move his agenda forward
stories.author: Nathan VanderKlippe, Carrie Tait
stories.content:
For anyone looking, it was right there in bold text: white on blue, a message affixed to the front of the lectern Alberta Premier Danielle Smith used to speak two days after her province overwhelmingly rejected the pursuit of separatism.

“Stronger Alberta within a United Canada,” the text read. It was a new formulation of a familiar refrain for Ms. Smith, who has spent years agitating about Alberta’s place in Canada. Her government passed an “Alberta Sovereignty Within a United Canada Act.” The ranks of her United Conservative Party swelled with separatists. She lowered the signature threshold for citizens to petition lawmakers to consider a proposed referendum question, clearing the way for a campaign that ushered those separatists into a bright international spotlight.

But when Ms. Smith spoke this week, the word “sovereignty” was gone from the lectern, and with it – perhaps, if she can navigate the stormy political waters she herself had a hand in creating – the turmoil of a lengthy chapter in which some in Alberta loudly threatened the breakup of Confederation, until Albertans themselves made clear they had no interest.

“That was quite notable. She was sending a clear signal,” said Monte Solberg, the former Conservative cabinet minister who now leads New West Public Affairs, an influential government relations firm in Calgary. A restive Alberta moment, one in which Ms. Smith had sought to appease both separatists and federalists in her own party, “was over,” he said. “Albertans want to move on. They want some optimism. They want to work with the federal government.”

Out with the strident language, in with co-operative federalism. Out with demands to rip apart and remake the constitution, in with the slow business of talking out change and building new things, Edmonton and Ottawa together with other provinces. Out with “sovereign,” in with “stronger.”

That, at least, is one hope.

But none of this presages peace and quiet. Ms. Smith has found, like generations of Western leaders before her, that stoking anger at Ottawa is a potent political tool. Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, must find a way to calm the political headwinds while showing he is willing to work with Ms. Smith and wrest productive gains from a province where loud voices continue to advocate rupture – all while this country’s largest trading partner continues to inflict economic damage.

Even so, with millions marking ballots this week – in Alberta’s referendum and, on Saturday, in a British Columbia provincial election – the landscape of Western politics could be remade.

Mr. Carney has shown himself eager to spur economic growth, abandoning his predecessor’s desire to cap Alberta’s petroleum production; some Albertans, meanwhile, have taken to calling themselves “Carney conservatives.” British Columbians are choosing a new government, making choices that could alter tensions over the export of energy resources through the province. And three-quarters of Albertans said they wish to remain in Canada, raising a new possibility of snuffing the destructive flame of separatism in the province.

None of this, however, is a foregone conclusion.

Inside Ms. Smith’s United Conservative Party, separatist sentiment remains strong. In late November, the party will hold an annual general meeting in which members will elect nearly half the provincial board – and leading independence advocates are gunning for control of the seats.

Ms. Smith said this week that she expects, from this moment on, that party representatives must be committed to Canada. But separatists, beaten in the referendum, are girding to continue their fight for independence by exerting more control over the party, from the provincial executive to its most grassroots level, the constituency associations. If they act in sufficient numbers, they can force a review of Ms. Smith’s leadership.

“It will be a pitched battle,” Mr. Solberg said.

Alberta may have chosen Canada. But it’s no longer clear Ms. Smith’s United Conservative Party will continue to choose her. The premier has emerged from the referendum into a fractious fight to hold onto her position.

It is fight for federalism, and for Ms. Smith’s political life. It is a fight for the future of the united conservative movement. And it is a fight to wrestle into submission the fervid forces of separatism as they change course, pursuing a political path to splitting apart the country.

“There’s lots of things that could go wrong,” Mr. Solberg said.

After months of organizing from Edmonton to small-town Alberta, separatists held their referendum night watch party at the Alt Hotel in Calgary. They did not get the result they hoped for. Leah Hennel/The Globe and Mail

Two generations ago, Jacques Parizeau brought the country to within a breath of cracking apart. Mr. Parizeau was a scion of family wealth, an economist who interned at the Bank of Canada, then worked to foment Quebec’s Quiet Revolution from behind the scenes.

As a younger man, though, he “didn’t like politics. He found it difficult, he found it tough,” recalled Jean Royer, who served as Mr. Parizeau’s influential chief of staff.

But the secessionist leader who would rise to become premier came early to a realization that he could not succeed outside the halls of the legislature. To achieve sovereignty, he had to accept “the rules of the game. And the rules of the game are to participate in parliamentary debate,” Mr. Royer said in an interview this week.

It was under Mr. Parizeau that Quebec nearly said yes to secession during its 1995 referendum.

Three decades later, his example has taken on new relevance in Canada’s west.

“In my opinion,” Mr. Royer said, “the best way to demonstrate legitimacy is running in an election with a platform.”

Alberta’s separatists, led by a competing collection of lawyers, podcasters, a farmer and a guns-and-sports shop owner, lost in this week’s referendum, garnering roughly 25 per cent of valid votes. Now some want to capture their province’s governing party, to force it to advance their cause.

To have a shot at getting independence-minded candidates on the ballot under the UCP banner, let alone elected, the separatists have to control the party’s internal machinery. Succeed in that, and they can once again make secession an Alberta priority.

Podcasters Jason Lavigne and Chris Scott hopscotched the province ahead of Monday’s referendum, urging Albertans to vote in favour of instigating the legal process necessary to hold a binding vote on secession.

Now, both intend to compete for seats on the UCP’s provincial board, in races party members will vote on next month at the party’s annual general meeting.

Attendance at the annual convention has swelled in recent years after conservative activists on the party’s right flank recognized they could exert greater control over government if they elected board members who shared their worldview. Ms. Smith last week said roughly 6,900 UCP members already purchased early-bird tickets.

For the Premier, the imperative is to outflank the separatists. She began this week by withdrawing the welcome mat.

“A strong Alberta within a united Canada is the position of our party and our government,” Ms. Smith said in a video released Wednesday, striking the word “sovereign” from her catchphrase to align with the message furnishing her lectern that same day.

UCP candidates, MLAs, provincial board members and constituency association representatives must uphold this position, she said. “If they want to be in a position of representing our party in an official role,” Ms. Smith told reporters, “there has to be a commitment that they also accept the result of the mandate that Albertans gave us.”

Ms. Smith wants to align her party’s values with the outcome of the province-wide referendum, shielding the UCP from being associated with separatism, particularly as it looks toward a provincial election in 2027. The premier refused to say whether she or the party would disqualify those who do not comply. For now, she said she is asking people to use “self-reflection” to determine their future in the party.

Her call for loyalty, if followed, would force out prominent independence advocates with sizable influence in the party. Mitch Sylvestre, who spearheaded a petition to get a separation question on the referendum ballot, is the president of a UCP constituency association in northeast Alberta and one of the party’s most valuable fundraisers. Tanya Clemens co-chaired Let Alberta Decide, a prominent separatist organization, and is one of the party’s local directors in the Highwood constituency, which in September voted in favour of reviewing Ms. Smith’s leadership.

The Premier’s instructions will almost certainly inflame the battle for control of the UCP’s provincial board.

Wrestling separatism into submission, in other words, is unlikely to prove easy.

Mr. Sylvestre, in an online meeting Thursday evening, showed no sign of retreat. He painted Ms. Smith’s loyalty test as a “direct attack” on him and blamed her for the widening the fissures in the already fractured organization.

“She’s telling us to pick between her and Alberta independence,” Mr. Sylvestre said, noting Ms. Smith said there would not be another secession referendum as long as she is Premier. “I am not splitting this party up. Who split this party up? Danielle Smith split this party up. Period. End of conversation.”

He urged followers to flock to the UCP’s annual meeting, support the slate of board candidates he intends to endorse, and agitate to force a review to oust Ms. Smith.

“You have to be in the room with power to address power, and if you want to get your way, there’s no other path here, unless we get into government,” he said.

As Alberta lurches from referendum to an internal party clash, Ms. Smith’s task in enforcing her new federalist decree will also be complicated by something she may not have anticipated.

In this new contest for Alberta, language suddenly matters. Sorting conservative activists into tidy piles will be difficult. Separatists, said Mr. Lavigne, the podcaster, believe secession is the only way to resolve Alberta’s beef with Ottawa, while sovereigntists believe independence is one of many potential solutions. “I really don’t know how you would be able to determine where the line would be between sovereigntist and separatist,” he said.

Sorting friend from foe by preferred labels stands to amplify the UCP’s raging identity crisis, an internal fight with implications for the party, province and rest of the country.

Both Mr. Lavigne and Mr. Scott use the word “sovereignty” the way Ms. Smith once did, to describe a province determining its own future, free from Ottawa’s overreach. “I’m not a separatist. I’m not a federalist,” Mr. Scott said in an interview this week. “I believe in a sovereign Alberta.”

Mr. Scott, who rose to prominence when he refused to shutter his rural café during the COVID-19 pandemic and founded Let’s Talk Alberta, said his preference is for the province to stay in Canada, consistent with Ms. Smith’s vision. However, Mr. Scott thinks independence is the only clear path for Alberta to achieve sovereignty.

He thinks the Premier is making a mistake by trying to dissuade separatists from vying for power inside the party. If she wants party unity, he said, she could get there by returning to her sovereigntist roots, by revving up the effort to extract Alberta from the Canada Pension Plan and taking control over immigration into the province, for example.

“If they block somebody like me because of my views on sovereignty, that would make them disingenuous,” he said. “Because you can’t, out of one side of your mouth, say you believe in Alberta sovereignty, and from the other side say: ‘Hey, you believe in Alberta sovereignty, so you need to get out of our party.’”

Rural communities such as Mossleigh, Airdrie and Okotoks were more likely to see votes for Option 2 than the bigger cities, but over all, the remain side won handily across the province. Todd Korol/Reuters

What, exactly, does 75 per cent mean? Was the Alberta referendum an expression of unalloyed patriotism? A message to Edmonton and Ottawa that Albertans are content?

Or was it something else?

Albertans said yes to Canada. They may not answer the same about Ottawa, warns Gary Mar, a former Alberta Cabinet minister who is now president of the Canada West Foundation, a think tank. “There’s a whole host of issues where Albertans would say, ‘I don’t like the status quo, but I don’t think that separation is the solution, either.’”

In other words: “I don’t think the Prime Minister can rest easy.”

Mr. Carney has the power to bring change without opening messy constitutional debate, like giving provinces greater say in naming judges or rethinking the French language requirement for western civil servants, Mr. Mar said.

In Alberta, meanwhile, this moment represents opportunity for those who have long sought greater autonomy for Alberta. The industrial backbone of Central and Eastern Canada is under acute pressure from the U.S., whose tariffs have hurt the auto sector, steelmakers and others. Alberta’s economy and resources offer a counterweight, and Ottawa has already begun to respond with proposals like a new Pacific pipeline.

“What a great time for us to say, ‘absolutely. We’re here to make a stronger Canada, too. And part of that is to make sure we’re making a stronger Alberta,’” said Michael Binnion, an Alberta energy executive who has sketched proposals for how the province could wrest greater power for itself. Asserting provincial control over pensions and immigration are two areas he advocates. “For Albertans upset by the result, a constructive thing they can do is get involved in building the institutions to responsibly govern ourselves.”

Because, warned Reform Party founder Preston Manning, more trouble for Confederation lies ahead. On Wednesday, Quebec swore in Paul St-Pierre Plamondon as leader of a new government that has pledged another referendum on Quebec independence.

“The West is going to be watching,” Mr. Manning said, adding: “Will there be a double standard on how the federal government treats these two provinces?”

Both Quebec and Alberta, he said, share a desire for a more decentralized federation, Quebec for cultural, social and linguistic reasons, Alberta on economic grounds. If Ottawa were to act on Western priorities, he said, it might mollify at least some of those so frustrated they have agitated to leave.

“The overall high level of support to remain begs a question: remain and do what?”

Still, for a country that has had no shortage of dim self-reflection in recent years, Alberta’s referendum vote was “a refreshing moment,” said Calgary oil and gas pioneer Jim Gray, who spent the past year raising hundreds of thousands of dollars for Forever Canadian, the advocacy group that rallied for federalism. Now 93 years old, he collected signatures for a remain in Canada petition and personally delivered dozens of Forever Canadian lawn signs to people across Calgary.

“I’m glad that we had that referendum. Because it was really a moment to celebrate and to think rather deeply about how lucky we are,” he said this week.

“Canada isn’t perfect. Nobody is perfect,” he added.

But “Canada is not broken.”

At the very least, said former Alberta Lieutenant-Governor Lois Mitchell, the referendum should prompt a change in tone.

“We’re always kind of whining about things. And we shouldn’t be doing that,” she said.

“Ask yourself: Could you actually do something and make it better?”
