paragraphs: Ottawa — Global Affairs Canada would not have Googled or done an open-source search before granting security clearance to someone like the Canadian woman charged with spying at Nato headquarters.
That’s according to David Morrison, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s senior diplomatic and international affairs advisor and the former top bureaucrat at Global Affairs Canada (GAC).

“I agree… that the use of open-source, Google, however you want to characterize it, I think that should be a standard part of our vetting process. I also agree… that personnel information that speaks to someone’s integrity should be part of the system,” Morrison told MPs on the Public Safety committee Wednesday.
“It was not part of the system at the time, and that has now been rectified, according to my colleagues at GAC,” he added.

Morrison was testifying as part of the committee’s study into the the federal government’s security clearance process after Belgian authorities charged a Canadian intern at Nato with espionage in late July.

The Canadian woman of Chinese descent is suspected of “spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organization.” She was denied bail in August and remains imprisoned in Belgium.
The suspect was later identified by media as 33-year-old Biwei Zhang, who also went by Claire Zhang. Belgian and Canadian officials have neither confirmed nor denied her identity.

Government officials have since acknowledged that Global Affairs Canada (GAC) issued the security clearance necessary for her to intern at Nato’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (Shape) headquarters in Mons, Belgium.
At the time Zhang was granted her clearance by GAC, Morrison was the head of the department.

MPs on the committee have spent much of their time trying to understand how Zhang received “at least” a “secret” level clearance to go work at Nato when there was a trail of public red flags in her career.
A public Federal Court decision in early 2024 revealed that Zhang had been denied employment at the Canadian Border Services Agency after it was discovered she committed fraud in her job application.

Morrison’s testimony confirmed that GAC would not have looked for such a document, or even searched public sources for information about Zhang. But the senior public servant also noted that the RCMP and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis) have a role in the background check as well.

“If Global Affairs had been aware of anyone that has derogatory information that would speak to that person’s suitability and reliability to protect Canada’s secrets or Nato’s secrets, I have every confidence that they would have acted on that information,” Morrison said.
Morrison’s blunt admission that there were no open-source searches for a secret-level clearance at GAC at the time stunned Conservative and Bloc Québécois MPs.

Conservative MP Rhonda Kirkland described it as a “system failure”, while her colleague Frank Caputo highlighted that even a two-week intern in his office found the Zhang decision after media reported on her identity.

“As she pointed out to me, people research people for a first date, and they would Google this type of information, and I think find it. So I will say it again: when the information is publicly available, and we nonetheless give a security clearance — and a high one at that — that is a failure in intelligence,” Caputo said.
In his opening statement, Morrison told the committee that the government needed to tighten up its security vetting process in the wake of the affair.

He issued four recommendations, including a “government-wide repository” of information on employees’ security clearance and more consistent use of open-source verifications for all levels of security clearances in governments.
He also emphasized that government should be better and continuously assessing employees’ security clearances after they receive them.

“A robust personnel security program should extend throughout employment, through insider risk programs, continuous personnel security assurance, recurring screening, reporting obligations, and security awareness,” he said.
“These would help identify emerging risks, ensure clearance holders remain reliable and loyal, and ensure clearances reflect current information.”
In response, Bloc MP Claude DeBellefeuille wondered why all his recommendations weren’t already in place before the Zhang affair.
“I am pretty floored by your responses,” she said.
Last month, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree admitted there were gaps in the government’s security clearance process that were being addressed in the wake of the Nato intern’s arrest.

stories.title: Credibility challenged in retired teacher’s sexual assault trial
stories.summary: Only two witnesses were called during the sexual assault trial of Murray MacDonald: the female complainant and the accused.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Only two witnesses were called during the sexual assault trial of Murray MacDonald: the female complainant and the accused.

During the trial, which got underway Monday, the court heard that MacDonald, 69, was a teacher at Central Secondary School in downtown London in 1985-86. He came across the Grade 11 student one night at The Bavarian, a former bar located in Cherryhill Village Mall on Oxford Street West.

Both testified they had drinks together and, when the bar was closing, he drove her home. The two then began hugging and kissing in his car.

The complainant, now in her 50s, testified that MacDonald initiated a sex act, while the accused said it was the female who started it.

In his closing submissions, defence lawyer Lakin Afolabi told Justice Kelly Gorman that his client’s testimony was more reliable, saying, “His evidence can raise reasonable doubt therefore you should acquit.”

Afolabi said, “He knew he shouldn’t be making out with a student...he got scared and he backed out.”

He went on to say, “It was a situation he didn’t plan or thought was going to happen.”

Afolabi added that even though it was 40 years ago, “He (MacDonald) testified in an honest and consistent way...I submit she’s playing games... I think she’s just making this stuff up.”

At the start of the trial, MacDonald pleaded not guilty to a single count of sexual assault.

Later in the day, Crown attorney Jeremy Carnegie gave his closing submissions and attacked the credibility of the accused, saying he had a selective memory.

Carnegie said, “When you assess the credibility of Mr. MacDonald there are issues.”

The Crown said the accused was wrong about the female being 19 years old at the time, saying, “He made that up, he didn’t want to paint himself as recklessly engaging in sexual activity with a child.”

Speaking about the complainant, Carnegie argued, “This was a sexual assault...she says she was forced to do something.”

He said that despite the 40 years that have passed, “The things she remembered, she was very clear.”

Carnegie wrapped up by saying, “You shouldn’t accept his version of events and you should find him guilty.”

Justice Gorman is expected to hand down her decision in the case on Dec. 14.

stories.title: Recently-released repeat Ontario sex offender back in custody: police
stories.summary: For the fourth year in a row, repeat Ontario sexual offender Keith Constantin has been re-arrested shortly after his release.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Barely a week after his release, an Ontario man with a history of sexual violence against women and children and a track record of aggresive behaviour behind bars is back in custody after allegedly breaching court-ordered conditions of his release.

Keith Theodore Constantin, a high-risk repeat-offender whose rap sheet is peppered with convictions for sexual assault, assault with a weapon, robbery and possession of explosives, among others, was re-arrested after he allegedly breached his curfew on Oct. 19th, the Durham Regional Police Service (Drps) said Wednesday.

The Hamilton native is now being held in custody pending a bail hearing.

His re-incarceration comes nine days after a public safety alert about the 48-year-old’s statutory release to the region was issued on Oct. 11.

Constantin is not currently serving a federal sentence, the Parole Board of Canada (PBC) told National Post in a statement and, as such, is “no longer under” its authority, as the warrant for his last federal sentence expired in August 2023.

While details about the precise nature of his most recent federal sentence of two years, four months and two days are unclear, a July 2023 PBC decision to revoke his statutory release obtained by National Post shows he was serving time for four counts of uttering threats to cause death or harm, threatening to burn a property, assaulting a police officer, a mischief charge and failing to comply with probation orders.

During that stint of freedom in an undisclosed location (May wish to explain what this means?), the PBC noted Constantin showed up at a local hospital talking about self-harm and “thinking about children again.”

The board also said he “misused a media device… to take over 40 pictures of a young male who appeared to be a young female” and that he made statements “about having deviant fantasies of children.”

A subsequent “medication audit” showed he’d reverted to a “concerning pattern” of overusing mental health drugs to “calm” himself.

Constantin’s most current psychological risk assessment at the time placed him in the very high range for sexual recidivism and the high-moderate range for general and violent recidivism.

“You have no insight into your risk,” the PBC wrote. “While in custody and in the community you required close supervision because of your use of aggression, threats, self-injurious behaviour, and suicidal thoughts.”

Constantin was re-imprisoned that summer, but was released again in 2024 under Canada’s statutory release laws, as reported by the Toronto Sun at the time. He was re-arrested at some point thereafter because another warning came from Durham police in March 2025 that he was being released to live in the area. Two days later, they issued a press release noting Constantin had been arrested for breaching conditions of his release.

His most recent release, his fourth in as many years, follows that incarceration.

National Post has asked PBC for additional clarity on all of Constantin’s three federal sentences and his statutory release.

His first sentence came in 2000 when he was sentenced for two armed robberies and two sexual assaults — one against a seven-year-old boy he’d lured to a park and another on a 45-year-old blind woman who lived in the same building as him.

Again, it’s not clear how much time he served, but he was free in fall 2007, as he was later convicted of sexually assaulting an epileptic woman in the basement apartment of his parents’ home as she was recovering from a seizure that September, according to a 2014 story in The Hamilton Spectator .

Because of stress-induced seizures and fears of suicide in his 27-year-old victim, that case never went to trial. Instead, Constantin made a plea deal in 2009, was sentenced to eight years and received four years’ credit for time served. It also earned him a spot on the national sex-offender registry for life.

His 2014 release was met with considerable pushback in the Hamilton neighbourhoods where he was set to reside when York Regional Police (YRP) warned of it, National Post reported at the time. It led him to break curfew and ask to be imprisoned again.

YRP issued another warning in December 2015 when he was released again after serving 18 months for the breach.

The Pbc’s 2023 release revocation decision also shows that Constantin has been anything but an ideal inmate while incarcerated.

“While in provincial custody serving a sentence, you flooded your cell and wiped feces on the cell window. You threatened to throw feces at a correctional officer and also threatened to kill him. You later threatened to sexually assault another female officer’s children,” they wrote.

He was equally problematic while living in a “group home environment” between June 2020 and January 2021 where he “threatened staff and damaged property.”

“In February 2021, while at a hospital for treatment for banging your head on the walls, you threatened to kill two police officers and throw feces at them,” the Board wrote.

Meanwhile, previous PBC documents obtained by the Spectator indicate Constantin’s behaviour earned him a great deal of time in segregation. He was also diagnosed with alcohol and drug addiction, paranoid schizophrenia, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, depression, an “extremely low range of intellectual ability,” and “character features associated with psychopathy.”

His first sentence came in 2000 when he was sentenced for two armed robberies and two sexual assaults — one against a seven-year-old boy he’d lured to a park and another on a 45-year-old blind woman who lived in the same building as him.

Again, it’s not clear how much time he served, but he was free in fall 2007, as he was later convicted of sexually assaulting an epileptic woman in the basement apartment of his parents’ home as she was recovering from a seizure that September, according to a 2014 story in The Hamilton Spectator .

stories.title: Deadly CFB Wainwright brush fire was caused by training on grenade launcher range, officials say
stories.summary: The Canadian Armed Forces will provide an update on the Wainwright fire that resulted in the deaths of four soldiers and injured 39 others.
stories.author: Liam Newbigging
stories.content:
Officials provided an update Thursday afternoon about the incident that resulted in the deaths of four soldiers and injured 39 others.

Brig.-Gen. Vanessa Hanrahan, deputy Canadian Forces provost marshal, revealed new information about the fire, telling reporters that it was caused by regular training exercises on the automatic grenade range that day.

From there, the blaze initially remained in Permanent Dangerous Area 2, which restricted firefighters’ ability to suppress it. Then a sudden change in wind velocity and direction grew the fire and pushed it towards an area where soldiers were training and overtook their position.

Hanrahan said there is no indication natural gas was a factor or damaged as a result of the fire.

“The investigative team is still out there determining all of the decision-making that happened once the fire started, up to and including when they responded to the incident involving the tragedies of today,” Hanrahan said.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, also corrected the record on two points from the weekend. He initially said that an investigation into the incident would take around a month, but clarified Thursday that the formal board of inquiry investigation “will take as long as it takes.”

He also clarified that the injured soldiers weren’t conducting a section attack range — they were setting up for a pairs range.

“This is where two soldiers attack a target, taking turns covering and firing for one another,” Rutland said.

Officials clarified on Thursday that there are now three parallel investigations underway.

Twenty-seven soldiers injured in CFB Wainwright fire remain in hospital: Premier Smith

'Bright light': Friends and family remember Edmonton soldier killed at CFB Wainwright

The military police are investigating whether or not a possible criminal offence took place, while the chief medical examiner’s office is investigating the cause and nature of the fatalities. At the same time, there is a board of inquiry investigation being done by the army.

“The involvement of the military police should not be interpreted as an indication that an offence has taken place,” Hanrahan said Thursday.

Those killed in the incident were Pte. Aidan Goulding, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark with the Third Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Infantry and Sgt. Morgan Wong with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment.

General Jennie Carignan, chief of defence staff, said Thursday she was heartbroken by the loss, and thanked first responders and those who helped care for those caught in the fire.

“Last weekend’s tragedy in Wainwright has had devastating impacts for our members and their families, and they are being felt across our military community.”

The press conference marks the second formal news conference from CAF officials in the five days since a deadly fire broke out at the military base around 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

The training was prepping soldiers for two roles — the Global Response Task Force and for a deployment to Latvia in the spring. It was the Charlie Company, comprised of around 84 soldiers, that was impacted.

stories.title: Why do daycare costs vary so much between Vancouver, Toronto and Calgary?
stories.summary: One reason is provincial governments employ different methods to structure their child care subsidies
stories.author: Kristy Shen
stories.content:
When we moved to Vancouver from Toronto, we expected to pay more for housing, transportation and food. According to Numbeo, grocery prices are 17.9 per cent higher , gas is 13.2 per cent higher and transit tickets are 4.5 per cent higher in Vancouver than Toronto. But one higher expense caught us off guard: daycare.

Wasn’t the Canada-wide Early Learning and Child Care system designed to cut the cost of daycare to an average of $10 a day across the country?

My first instinct was to blame Vancouver’s notoriously unaffordable real estate, but Toronto’s wasn’t exactly cheap either. So why do subsidized daycare costs vary so much?

I decided to look at three big cities: Vancouver, Toronto and Calgary.

According to the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives , in Vancouver the median cost of daycare for an infant is $40 a day. In Toronto, it’s $22 a day, and in Calgary, it’s $15 a day.

In Vancouver, the range of daycare costs is especially jarring because according to the Ccpa, 45 per cent of preschool spaces only cost $10 a day while 25 per cent of them cost nearly five times as much, at more than $46 a day.

This means that one family could be paying $11,960 a year per child, while another pays just $2,600, despite living in the same city.

It’s tempting to blame the price difference on the cost of real estate. After all, renting or buying a space as a daycare operator in Vancouver won’t cost the same as in Calgary, and wages and other expenses also play a role. But that’s only part of the reason and it doesn’t explain why two Vancouver families can face such different bills.

A main reason for these price discrepancies is the method in which provincial governments have chosen to structure their child care subsidies.

B.C., for example, provides a subsidy toward the daycare provider’s market price. This means unless that daycare is one of the ones that participate in the $10 a day option, the cost could vary widely, since it’s a discount from its market value. But if you’re one of the lucky ones who manages to find $10 a day, you’re sitting pretty.

Ontario, ON the other hand, sets capped fees at subsidized centres at $22 a day. If the centre doesn’t apply or isn’t eligible, they charge market rates. So unless you live or work near one of the subsidized centres, you’re paying higher market rates.

Alberta sets a flat rate of $326.25 a month, the equivalent of $15 a day, at participating centres, and there are no separate $10-a-day daycares.

Eligibility differs across provinces. Not all daycares apply and daycares must be approved to participate in the government-subsidized programs. Not all do.

For parents, it’s not as straightforward as just putting yourself on the waiting list of a subsidized daycare and getting a spot.

Unlike choosing a data plan or clothing store, there are special restrictions, such as distance to home and work, or hours that fit your work schedule, among many other factors.

Even if you are lucky enough to snag a coveted $10-a-day daycare spot, you May have to weigh that against the extra cost and time, if the daycare is far from work and home, or you need to supplement with additional child care arrangements if the hours don’t fit your work hours.

The national daycare program has provided significant savings to parents all over the country, and it’s a vast improvement over the fees parents had to shoulder before. But the massive difference in daycare costs means that depending on where you live, some parents May have to work longer to afford daycare.

Assuming full-time daycare of five days a week for 52 weeks a year, it would cost parents $10,400 a year in Vancouver, $5,720 a year in Toronto and $3,900 a year in Calgary, based on the reported median daily fee.

Let’s translate that into hours worked. According to StatsCan, the median hourly wage for Canadian employees in 2025 was $30.77 , before tax. For simplicity, using before-tax wages across cities, this means the Vancouver parent would need to work 211 extra hours a year, compared to the Calgary parent. That’s the equivalent of five extra weeks of work.

I’m not saying parents should pack up and move to Calgary to cut daycare costs. There are many reasons a family might pick a city, outside of daycare. Nor am I saying that national daycare isn’t helpful.

Still, it’s ironic that the Canada-wide Early Learning and Child Care system, which was designed to help parents across the country afford daycare, has inadvertently resulted in costs varying wildly depending on your postal code, because of how provincial governments have chosen to structure the subsidies.

If you’re curious about how daycare costs in your city stack up against other cities, this daycare explorer lets you find out.

Kristy Shen and Bryce Leung are early retirees and co-authors of Parent Like a Millionaire (Without Being One) .”

stories.title: Ontario sending 28 burn-care workers to help with soldiers critically injured in CFB Wainwright fire
stories.summary: Toronto burn surgeon says the soldier-patients are going through “one of the most painful experiences one can endure."
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Ontario is sending 28 health-care professionals to help care for the soldiers severely injured in a deadly fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta last Saturday.

Thirty-nine soldiers were injured in the fire, 19 critically.

Premier Doug Ford announced that the assistance will include surgeons and nurses with burn care expertise.

“As Alberta hospitals continue to respond to the devastating fire that took place at CFB Wainwright last week, Ontario’s heroic health-care workers are stepping up to help,” Ford said in an X post on Wednesday.

“We’re also providing additional equipment to support their work as they care for those who were injured in last week’s fire,” added Ford, commenting that times of crisis are when Canadians come together, “(we) have each others’ backs. That’s exactly what we’re doing.”

“Some of the burns are 30 per cent to 80 per cent of their entire body — and sometimes changing those dressings can take up to two hours per patient,” Smith said.

Smith, noting three of the soldiers in “very dire health” are Ontarians, thanked Ford and welcomed the 19 burn-unit and five operating room nurses, additional resources she said will help ease pressures on Alberta health-care staff.

Toronto surgeon Dr. Alan Rogers is one of two surgeons on standby to go out to Alberta. He is a surgeon with the Ross Tilley Burn Centre at Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, as well as an associate professor of plastic, reconstructive and aesthetic surgery at the University of Toronto.

He told the CBC that the soldier-patients are going through “one of the most painful experiences one can endure.” He said the number of patients would put an “incredible strain” on existing resources in any province.

The complex care for extensive burns can involve weeks, even months, in hospital, while going through multiple surgeries. Rehab is also a “long and arduous” process, he said.

Sunnybrook has been in contact with the burn teams in Edmonton and Calgary, Rogers said.

“When something like this happens (in large) numbers, it overwhelms the system and it does make it very challenging to manage because ordinarily we’re actually close to or near or even often over capacity in our burn centres.”

As previously reported by National Post , the Canadian Armed Forces said four people were killed in the CFB Wainwright fire. The soldiers killed were later identified as Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.

Premier Smith confirmed the four deaths in an X post earlier this week.

“Many more are injured and in recovery across our hospitals,” she wrote. “Every part of the response is being coordinated, from first responders through to the hospitals treating the injured and the critical care teams working right now. Alberta stands with our Canadian Armed Forces and will provide whatever support is requested.”

Speaking on Sunday, Maj. Gen. L.W. Rutland explained that the soldiers were involved in “high intensity combat training with live munitions.” The purpose of the exercises was to prepare them to be a global response task force that could be quickly deployed anywhere in the world. Soldiers were also getting ready to serve in Latvia in April and May in support of a brigade already in the Baltic country.

Some soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range, said Rutland. A group of 10 soldiers were also conducting an attack exercise on a simulated enemy. The deadly “grass fire ignited in the training area,” said Rutland.

“Uncommonly strong winds cause the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range,” he said.

stories.title: Ottawa ‘not responsible’ for regulating AI data centre power use: minister
stories.summary: AI Minister Evan Solomon spoke to the Senate Committee on Social Affairs, Science and Technology on Thursday, where he was asked about power usage by data centres Canada.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
The federal government is “not responsible” for power regulation and cannot regulate power usage by AI data centres, Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon told a Senate committee on Thursday.

Solomon spoke to the Senate Committee on Social Affairs, Science and Technology on Thursday, where he was asked about power usage by data centres in Canada.

“The federal government is not responsible for power. That is the purvey of provincial regulators. So, we can’t put federal obligations on the power regulation,” he said, adding that provinces like Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia are in the process of creating their own data centre laws.

At the same time, however, both information technology and electricity grids are considered critical infrastructure by the federal government, giving Public Safety Canada the ability to “manage risks and reduce vulnerabilities,” according to the National Strategy for Critical Infrastructure.

Doubling the capacity of Canada’s energy grid was “absolutely critical” to rolling out Canada’s AI strategy, Solomon said.

“We work very closely with best practices around the world to develop very high standards on water use, energy use, investment in the community, strategic importance, consultation, and most importantly, transparency on the promises so you can actually hold them to account,” he said.

The federal government’s recently released ‘Responsible Data Centre Development Principles’ require that companies building new data centre projects “do not shift electricity costs onto Canadians” and “minimize water use and environmental impacts.”

Solomon was also asked how many data centres Canada was looking to build.

“We received proposals for… over 160,” he said.

While large data centre projects will require around 100 megawatts of power per building, there “May be some smaller ones” as well, he added.

“We have MOUs with about four (data center companies) so far,” he said.

Ottawa is “supporting the building of Canadian data that are Canadian-owned,” Solomon said, however, some major projects in Canada are being helmed by U.S. tech giants.

A company pursuing a wind and hydrogen development in Nova Scotia says it has plans for a $10-billion AI data centre in Cape Breton that it describes as the largest private investment in provincial history.

EverWind Fuels announced last week that U.S. AI company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for a 18,600-square metre data centre in Point Tupper, N.S., that would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase.

The data centre is scheduled to come online late next year. A 325-megawatt expansion is expected in mid-2028, which would bring the development’s total energy demand to 420 megawatts, the company said.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said the data centre project was a major vote of confidence in the rural area about 200 kilometres east of Halifax. He said Canada does not have enough secure data infrastructure to meet the requirements of its businesses, governments and health-care institutions.

Data centres are typically massive operations that require immense amounts of electricity to run and cool off computer servers.

Water from nearby Landrie Lake will be used to cool the Point Tupper data centre’s servers, and the company stressed it will safeguard the water supply.

EverWind said the cooling system will be closed-loop, similar to a car’s radiator, with cooling fluid recycled or disposed of off site, not in local waterways. The system will use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in the first phase, which EverWind said is about the same as a large shopping mall.

That will expand to an average draw of 500,000 litre per day when the expansion is complete, about one per cent of the lake’s safe daily yield of 34 million litres.

–with files from Canadian Press

A company pursuing a wind and hydrogen development in Nova Scotia says it has plans for a $10-billion AI data centre in Cape Breton that it describes as the largest private investment in provincial history.

EverWind Fuels announced last week that U.S. AI company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for a 18,600-square metre data centre in Point Tupper, N.S., that would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase.

The data centre is scheduled to come online late next year. A 325-megawatt expansion is expected in mid-2028, which would bring the development’s total energy demand to 420 megawatts, the company said.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said the data centre project was a major vote of confidence in the rural area about 200 kilometres east of Halifax. He said Canada does not have enough secure data infrastructure to meet the requirements of its businesses, governments and health-care institutions.
Data centres are typically massive operations that require immense amounts of electricity to run and cool off computer servers.
Water from nearby Landrie Lake will be used to cool the Point Tupper data centre’s servers, and the company stressed it will safeguard the water supply.

EverWind said the cooling system will be closed-loop, similar to a car’s radiator, with cooling fluid recycled or disposed of off site, not in local waterways. The system will use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in the first phase, which EverWind said is about the same as a large shopping mall.
That will expand to an average draw of 500,000 litre per day when the expansion is complete, about one per cent of the lake’s safe daily yield of 34 million litres.

stories.title: Five suspects receive warning in Tillsonburg weapons incident
stories.summary: Five suspects have been let off with warnings after a weapons incident in Tillsonburg.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Five suspects have been let off with warnings after a weapons incident in Tillsonburg.

Oxford OPP said they were called on Wednesday with a report of people in a vehicle pulling weapons on Broadway.

The vehicle was found around 10:30 p.m. and the suspects were arrested. The weapons were identified as toy guns, leading to the suspects, ranging from 16 to 20 years old, being let off with warnings.

OPP reminds that displaying anything that looks like a weapon in public is likely to lead to a call for police and it causes unnecessary stress for officers responding and the community.

stories.title: Joly gives Stelco 15 days to comply with job commitments or face court action
stories.summary: Stelco's American owner Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. intends to lay off 500 workers
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Canada

Canadian Politics

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called the layoffs a 'betrayal' to Stelco workers

Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly arrives to a Liberal caucus meeting on Parliament Hill October 21, 2026.Photo by Blair Gable /Postmedia

Ottawa – Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has sent a second letter to Stelco, demanding the steelmaker reverse its layoffs or provide detailed responses that justify its non-compliance under the Investment Canada Act.

Joly gave Stelco’s president Paul Simon 15 days to comply or face legal action.

Stelco is owned by Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., which signed several undertakings when the acquisition was approved in 2024 under the ICA, which included a commitment to maintain the same number of unionized employees for a period of five years.

Last month, the company confirmed it intended to lay off 500 workers at its Hamilton plant and Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont. Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves has cited U.S. tariffs as the reason for the “temporary” job cuts.

“In the event Cliffs fails to comply with this demand, the Minister May, pursuant to section 40 of the Act, make an application to the superior court,” the letter read.

The letter also took aim at several instances where Goncalves has endorsed U.S. President Donald Trump’s Section 232 tariffs, which amount to 50 per cent on Canadian steel and aluminum.

In an interview with CBC News earlier this month, Goncalves disputed the government’s claims.

“There is no provision in the contract that I have to keep employment at a certain level every single day of the five years,” he said. “If that was an imposition of the Canadian government, I would not have accepted.”

Joly’s letter demands that if the company would like to contest or justify non-compliance, it must provide monthly employment numbers for unionized and salaried employees from Nov. 1, 2023, to October 2026.

The letter outlined possible outcomes of court action including Cliffs’ divestiture from Stelco, a directive to comply with the undertakings, a penalty of $10,000 each day Cliffs is not in compliance or suspending Cliffs’ voting rights in the company.

This is the second letter Joly has sent to the company, after receiving a response on Oct. 9.

Joly’s letter on Wednesday also disputed that Cliffs was unaware of the possibility of U.S. tariffs when it acquired Stelco and signed onto to its commitments.

“The possibility of tariffs on Canadian steel was foreseeable in October 2024, and the Undertakings specifically reflect that possibility,” the letter said. “However, Cliffs’ Chief Executive Officer subsequently advocated for the very tariffs that Cliffs is now relying on as a basis for non-compliance with the Undertakings.”

When asked on Wednesday why his government hasn’t taken Cliffs to court yet, Carney said they are following the legal process.

“There’s also an opportunity, of course, for the company to respect their commitments, and of course we’re happy to sit down and work with them,” he said.

stories.title: N.S. NDP party whip removed over social media post calling for 'France-style riots'
stories.summary: "I want to be clear that I did not intend to encourage or condone violence in any way," says MLA Paul Wozney, after he deleted the post.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Nova Scotia NDP MLA Paul Wozney, who was the party’s caucus whip, has been removed from that role after the PC party condemned a social media post he shared that called for “France-style riots in Nova Scotia and Canada.”

“The riots in France have led to a curfew being issued in Paris and French police have estimated that 3,000 businesses and public buildings have been damaged or looted. Residents described the aftermath like they just had a war,” the province’s PC party wrote in a statement on Wednesday, in reference to Wozney’s post.

The PCs urged NDP leader and Dartmouth South MLA Claudia Chender to take action. In a statement shared with National Post, she confirmed Wozney was removed as party whip, adding that the party “unequivocally denounces violence or the suggestion of violence in civic life.”

The removal was sparked by a since-deleted Facebook post on Wozney’s personal account that concluded: “Don’t leave it to the courts. Learn from France. Own the streets. Shut government down. Grind the province/country to a halt… It’s the only ‘direct’ line to worker justice.”

The post was a critical response to the $470 million settlement stemming from Bill 148. The bill was imposed in 2015 by the Liberal government and “ directly interfered with workers’ right to full and free collective bargaining,” according to Canada’s largest private sector union, Unifor.

Wozney called it a “symbolic win” but said the remedy means that more than 80,000 Nova Scotian workers affected by the bill “are diminished financially for a lifetime, including every single day of their lives in retirement. That doesn’t look or feel like justice for them.”

As party whip , Wozney was charged with keeping party members informed about House business and ensuring attendance in the House or in committee.

Wozney, who is MLA for Sackville-Cobequid, is also the party’s critic for Ethics and Accountability, Labour, Education, Advanced Education, and the Public Service Commission.

“I understand that as an elected official my words really matter and that’s why I’ve removed the post,” said Wozney in a statement.

“I want to be clear that I did not intend to encourage or condone violence in any way — that is never acceptable.”

Damian Stoilov, a PC MLA for Bedford South, called the post “outrageous” and said that Wozney was saying “if Nova Scotians disagree on something, they should mimic riots in France where thousands of shops were looted and buildings burned to the ground.”

Protests in France were sparked by students upset over the horrible conditions of schools, lack of resources and no consistency when it came to teachers. Hundreds of thousands of people have joined in on the protests across the country since September.

They have taken a turn from peaceful to chaotic , with additional groups taking part, including those who are angry about the cost of living, the environment and other causes.

Schools have been ransacked and burned, cars have been set on fire, and riot police have taken to the streets to disperse crowds that have been looting from stores . There have been more than a thousand arrests and hundreds injured, including a teen who had his hand blown off after grabbing a stun grenade thrown by officers.

Chender said that Wozney apologized and “acknowledges the harm that he has caused.”

“In the last year, we’ve seen the government forced to walk back some of their cruellest cuts when Nova Scotians spoke up, protested responsibly and treated one another with respect,” said Wozney in his statement.

“These are the actions I support and wanted to encourage but my comments were careless and I apologize for the harm and distress they have caused.”

stories.title: Cleveland-Cliffs CEO’s Stelco stance is rife with contradictions
stories.summary: Executive advocated for imposing the tariffs he now cites as the reason for laying off hundreds of Canadian steelworkers
stories.author: Marty Warren
stories.content:
Marty Warren, the Canadian national director of the United Steelworkers union

As I write, more workers at Hamilton’s Stelco steel mill are being laid off. In all, the plant’s U.S. owner, Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., will cut up to 500 jobs. This, not two years after making legally binding assurances under the Canada Investment Act that it would maintain the number of unionized jobs for five years.

When seeking approval to purchase Stelco, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves couldn’t say enough about what a “net benefit” a takeover would be to Canada. Not to mention to Cleveland-Cliffs itself, acquiring one of the newest and most efficient mills going. Among the “lowest-cost steelmaking facilities in North America,” the company called it.

And how would U.S. ownership produce a “net benefit” to Canada? In part, through exports to the United States. After all, as Mr. Goncalves once said, “not all [American] imports were created equal … Canada follows the rules and does things the right way,” claiming “this is a large part of the rationale behind Cleveland-Cliffs acquiring Stelco.”

That’s Mr. Goncalves before Donald Trump was elected in 2024. How things have changed since – to the detriment of Stelco workers, the Canadian economy, and indeed to our national interest.

Not a year after investing US$2.5-billion in Stelco precisely because of its competitive advantage in the North American market and despite acknowledging that “Canada follows the rules,” Mr. Goncalves cheered on Mr. Trump’s tariffs.

“We at Cleveland-Cliffs appreciate the recently announced 25 per cent tariffs on steel imports from all countries,” he said. “We thank the Trump administration for having the courage to implement [them].” Without missing a beat, he explained American orders would henceforth be filled by American mills. And that if Canadian companies wanted to buy “more sophisticated grades” of steel, American mills would supply these higher-value orders, too.

In other words, Canadian operations would be pared back – and now stripped down – not to the net benefit of Canada as promised, but instead to benefit Cleveland-Cliffs as a whole. In effect, Mr. Goncalves paid $2.5-billion to prevent Stelco exporting into the American market. Why, after all, allow more efficient Canadian steel to compete with Cleveland-Cliffs’s pricier American steel when it can just pay to restrict supply?

Don’t just take the Steelworkers’ word for it.

As Mr. Goncalves told investors, “With Stelco’s favourable cost structure … [it] was a major disruptor here in the Midwest of the United States. The strategic repositioning of Stelco as a Canadian supplier of steel to the Canadian market has given our U.S. mills more business opportunities.” (My italics.)

He went on to say that his commitments to the federal government notwithstanding, “we acquired Stelco with the decision already made in our minds that we would take [it] out of the American domestic market as a disruptor … tariffs on steel were just a consolidation of what we were already doing.”

And when those tariffs were doubled, Mr. Goncalves doubled down: “We understand why the U.S. has a 50 per cent tariff on imported steel from Canada and that’s fine. We are keeping all Stelco steel in Canada, and we are doing that by design since we acquired Stelco in November [2024] and not now as a result of the tariffs being implemented in 2025.”

Yet in explaining Cleveland-Cliffs’s decision to gut operations in Hamilton and lay workers off at a separate plant in Nanticoke, Ont., Mr. Goncalves invoked changing market conditions and U.S. trade policy. But these were not simply imposed upon the company. They were, rather, created and advocated for by the company itself. Tariffs merely confirmed Cleveland Cliffs’s own, de facto export ban on Stelco.

Again, don’t take the Steelworkers’ word for it. Here’s Mr. Goncalves himself: “Prior to our acquisition, Stelco was a low-price exporter into the U.S. and a highly disruptive one, by the way. When you look at the big picture, what our acquisition has done to transform the U.S. marketplace more than justifies a return on our $2.5-billion purchase price of Stelco.”

These are the words that matter, not empty commitments made to Ottawa when seeking to purchase Stelco. An acquisition, it is increasingly clear, that has nothing to do with Canada’s benefit, but the monopolistic benefit of Cleveland-Cliffs for which Canadian workers are paying the price.

stories.title: Ottawa to announce funding for 60 national sport organizations
stories.summary: Ottawa - The federal government is set to announce funding for more than 60 national sport organizations today.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - More than 60 national sports organizations will share $60 million in additional federal funding as the government moves to shore up a national sport system that has been described as chronically underfunded.

At a news conference in Ottawa on Thursday, Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said the money will help elite athletes compete on the world stage and advance safe sport measures.

stories.title: Toronto Crime Stoppers temporarily stops accepting tips after data breach
stories.summary: More than 175,000 tips were stolen by hackers earlier this year, alongside nearly 15,000 names
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto Crime Stoppers has temporarily stopped accepting tips after it says more than 175,000 of them were stolen by hackers earlier this year, alongside nearly 15,000 names.

The organization, which allows people to submit confidential crime tips to law enforcement, says in a statement that the tip software it has used since 2018 was hit by a data breach in March.

It says the company that owns the software reported that 176,859 Toronto tips submitted between January 2022 and last November were included in the stolen data, as well as 14,973 names.

Toronto Crime Stoppers says the company, Navigate360, has not disclosed whether the names are of people who submitted tips, are named in them, or both, nor has it provided the text of the stolen tips, despite repeated requests.

Regional police in Halton, west of Toronto, also say they are suspending their use of Crime Stoppers after learning some data related to Halton was included in the breach, although they are still awaiting more information.

The pauses come after CBC reported that 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years were exposed in a massive data breach.

Toronto Crime Stoppers says it didn’t stop accepting tips sooner because Navigate360 initially said in April that Toronto data had not been taken, and when the company later said Toronto data was affected, it did not say what information was exposed.

It says it is working on a “safer way” to take tips and will share details in the coming days.

Toronto police say they are aware of new information regarding the breach, which they say “raises serious concerns regarding the protection of confidential information provided through the Crime Stoppers program.”

The force says it has suspended its use of the program while it reviews the new information and assesses the additional measures being put in place at the organization.

Halton regional police say they are looking into the potential impact of the data breach on their operations, and in the meantime urge people to still report crimes or public safety concerns directly to the force.

stories.title: One person killed after house fire: London Fire Department
stories.summary: Police and fire officials are investigating after a person was killed in a house fire in northeast London, fir...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Police and fire officials are investigating after a person was killed in a house fire in northeast London, fire officials say.

This was one of two blazes crews fought Wednesday morning.

“Both fires are around $500,000 in damages,” said Platoon Chief Colin Shewell.

London Fire Investigation van(Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM News)

Fire crews first responded to a house fire on Lyman Street, just before 7 a.m. They made an “aggressive offensive attack” on the blaze and saved one person and a dog, they said.

Unfortunately one person died.

Paramedics treated and transported the surviving person to hospital, said Shewell.

The investigation is still in it’s early stages as London Police, Fire Prevention, and the Ontario fire marshal (OFM) are on scene coordinating the investigation because it’s a fatal fire Shewell explained.

Around 9:30 a.m., firefighters responded to a garage fire on Avenue Road south of Dingman Drive.

“We were meant with heavy smoke and fire again from a garage area connected to the house,” said Shewell.

Emergency workers arrived to find two people outside of the house. Paramedics transported both to hospital with unknown injuries, said.

Crews had to hook up to a water hydrant far away from the garage, however crews put the blaze out quickly, although being very smokey Shewell stated.

While in an offensive attack the garage was determined to be unsafe forcing the fire crews out and to go on a defensive attack.

Fire Crews at Avenue Road (Credit London Fire Department/X)

“Our crews did a great job while in the offensive attack making sure the fire didn’t spread to the residents, however the residents did sustained major smoke and water damage,” said Shewell.

After the fight fire investigators on scene stating there’s no indication the fire was suspicious.

“Fire investigators are on scene waiting for a structural investigator to deem it safe to go in, as the garage roof did collapse,” said Shewell.

The investigation is still on-going in the early stages.

Shewell determined that in both fires smoke detectors were working, saying that it alerted the one individual on Lyman Street to self rescue with crews assistants. The two people on Avenue Road were already out of the house, but crews did find working smoke and CO alarms.

“I know smoke alarms seem expensive, but they’re the cheapest life safety to protect your family”

stories.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator pleads not guilty in U.S. court
stories.summary: James Bryant entered the plea after a grand jury indicted the 30-year-old Washington resident for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country
stories.author: Brenna Owen
stories.content:
The alleged co-conspirator in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., has pleaded not guilty in a U.S. court and is set to go on trial in December, accused of aiding one of the deadliest school attacks in Canadian history.

James Bryant entered the plea in a brief arraignment appearance in Seattle on Thursday, after a grand jury last week indicted the 30-year-old Bellingham, Wash., resident for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

Shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight last February, including five students and an educational assistant at the local secondary school, before she fatally shot herself as police closed in.

The criminal complaint against Bryant, who uses female pronouns and goes by the name Melody, alleges she colluded with Van Rootselaar online, helping set up an attempted livestream of the murders.

Bryant, who appeared in a tan prison jumpsuit and dark-framed glasses with her hair down to her waist, has been denied bail.

Her trial is scheduled to begin before U.S. District Judge Kymberly K. Evanson in Seattle on Dec. 21.

Bryant smiled at two people who sat in the gallery of the courtroom during the arraignment, which lasted only minutes. The pair then walked out of the courthouse with Bryant’s public defender, Greg Murphy, speaking with him briefly before they parted ways.

Bryant also allegedly advised 18-year-old Van Rootselaar on where to carry out the attack and sent the shooter money to buy a lighter for an explosive device.

The accusations against Bryant remain unproven.

Magistrate Judge Michelle Peterson presided over Thursday’s arraignment hearing, where Bryant was told she faces penalties of up to life in prison and US$250,000 in fines.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation’s complaint against Bryant says that on Feb. 10, Van Rootselaar told Bryant she had dressed for the mass shooting.

The document shows a photo of someone from their shoulders down, holding a rifle and wearing black fishnet stockings and a black miniskirt.

“A few moments later, Van Rootselaar told Bryant that she went live with the stream and had just killed her family members at their residence,” the complaint said.

Rootselaar allegedly told Bryant, “I’m going now. (for real). Live. I shot them,” after killing her mother and brother at their home.

Bryant is alleged to have helped Van Rootselaar start the family car – she did not know how to drive – before she headed to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

In arguing against Bryant’s detention last week, Murphy and fellow public defender Dennis Carroll said there was no evidence that their client “has ever communicated with any other person as deeply disturbed as Van Rootselaar.”

They also pointed to the delay between Bryant being interviewed by the FBI in February and March, then arrested on Oct. 6, saying that “if that danger were real, the government would not have left Ms. Bryant in the community for seven months.”

“As horrible as Van Rootselaar’s crimes were, and as cold as many of Ms. Bryant’s chats appear, there is no evidence – much less clear and convincing evidence – that she would pose an unmitigable danger to the community,” they said in a court filing.

The arguments were unsuccessful and Bryant was denied bail.

stories.title: Canadian diplomats banned from being in the same room as U.S. midterm candidates: sources
stories.summary: Canadian officials are barred from meeting with or even being in the same room as midterm candidates unless given special permission.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Canadian diplomats working in the US have been directed to stay away from candidates running in the midterm elections, and to keep a low profile to avoid allegations by the Trump administration of political interference, people familiar with the matter said.

Under written guidance distributed Tuesday, Canadian officials are barred from meeting with or even being in the same room as midterm candidates — all House candidates and a third of the Senate — unless given special permission.

Canadian officials are still allowed to conduct other business and meetings with elected US representatives who are not up for reelection, if necessary. But they’ve been told to ensure they don’t appear in photographs alongside any elected US officials, according to people who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe the internal memo, which called the measures a “very risk-averse approach.”

Nearly 500 Canadian diplomatic staff work in the US, including at its embassy in Washington and across 12 consulate offices in cities such as Detroit, Los Angeles, Dallas and Atlanta. The measures apply until the midterm vote on Nov. 3.

The guidance is a sign of the highly charged atmosphere as President Donald Trump’s party faces the prospect of a resounding midterm defeat. The House is seen as virtually certain to swing to Democrats, while the Senate — once seen as a firewall of sorts for Republicans — looks to essentially be a tossup.

With Trump’s approval ratings hovering near a record low, Republicans are being forced to actively campaign in what would otherwise be safe Senate seats, such as Kansas and South Carolina. Voting is already under way in many key states.

Canada’s foreign affairs department didn’t immediately provide a comment in response to a request from Bloomberg.

Trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed two months ago, even after Trump had announced a preliminary deal, and formal negotiations have not yet resumed. Trump has since threatened to hike tariffs on Canadian autos to 50%, up from 25%, ON Jan. 1, a deadline that May prompt a renewed round of discussions later this year. Those would occur at the same time as the so-called lame-duck session of the current, departing Congress.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and other Canadian officials have frequently made the case that US tariffs punish American consumers and businesses — but Trump administration officials have been aggressively pushing back, warning Canadians not to speak out.

On Wednesday, Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford rejected the idea that their advocacy against US tariffs was inappropriate.

“I have no interest at all in interfering in American elections,” Ford said, adding that he lived in the US for 20 years and “loves the American people.”

Carney said the White House initiated the trade war and Canada is simply responding. “All of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy,” he said.

The guidance to diplomats came shortly before the US embassy in Canada posted a “fact sheet” on Wednesday alleging a concerted effort by Canada to sway the American election toward a friendly outcome.

The document outlined a series of comments by Canadian politicians — particularly Industry Minister Melanie Joly — that suggested Canada targeted Republican-held states with pressure tactics, including counter-tariffs that hit exporters in those regions.

“All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence US elections in any way. Americans decide America’s elections,” the embassy said.

The fact sheet also pointed to last year’s TV ad campaign by the Ontario government. The ad, which ran on US broadcasts of baseball’s World Series, quoted former President making the case for free trade. It infuriated Trump, leading him to terminate trade talks with Canada.

Republican candidates in the US have been under siege over affordability concerns during the midterm campaign, and Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods have been an election issue in key battleground states such as Maine and Michigan.

Although most US-Canada trade remains tariff-free, certain sectors in Canada have been badly hurt by Trump’s tariffs — particularly the aluminum, steel, auto manufacturing and lumber industries.

Over the summer, Canadian and US officials spent weeks in intensive trade negotiations that would have lowered some of those tariffs, but the talks fell apart on Aug. 21 when Carney pulled his negotiators away from the table.

Trump then placed new tariffs of 50% on about $20 billion worth of Canadian items. He later imposed further measures that included banning the import of some Canadian alcohol and restricting Canadian firms from bidding on US government contracts.

Canada responded with its own set of 50% counter-tariffs on some categories of US-made goods.

Officials on both sides have remained in contact since then, and Carney said he and Trump had a lengthy phone call on Wednesday morning that included a discussion of trade. But there’s no sign yet of a resumption of formal negotiations.

Over the summer, Canadian and US officials spent weeks in intensive trade negotiations that would have lowered some of those tariffs, but the talks fell apart on Aug. 21 when Carney pulled his negotiators away from the table.

Trump then placed new tariffs of 50% on about $20 billion worth of Canadian items. He later imposed further measures that included banning the import of some Canadian alcohol and restricting Canadian firms from bidding on US government contracts.
Canada responded with its own set of 50% counter-tariffs on some categories of US-made goods.

Officials on both sides have remained in contact since then, and Carney said he and Trump had a lengthy phone call on Wednesday morning that included a discussion of trade. But there’s no sign yet of a resumption of formal negotiations.

content_blocks.text: Canadian diplomats working in the US have been directed to stay away from candidates running in the midterm elections, and to keep a low profile to avoid allegations by the Trump administration of political interference, people familiar with the matter said.

Under written guidance distributed Tuesday, Canadian officials are barred from meeting with or even being in the same room as midterm candidates — all House candidates and a third of the Senate — unless given special permission.

Canadian officials are still allowed to conduct other business and meetings with elected US representatives who are not up for reelection, if necessary. But they’ve been told to ensure they don’t appear in photographs alongside any elected US officials, according to people who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe the internal memo, which called the measures a “very risk-averse approach.”

Nearly 500 Canadian diplomatic staff work in the US, including at its embassy in Washington and across 12 consulate offices in cities such as Detroit, Los Angeles, Dallas and Atlanta. The measures apply until the midterm vote on Nov. 3.

content_blocks.text: The guidance is a sign of the highly charged atmosphere as President Donald Trump’s party faces the prospect of a resounding midterm defeat. The House is seen as virtually certain to swing to Democrats, while the Senate — once seen as a firewall of sorts for Republicans — looks to essentially be a tossup.

With Trump’s approval ratings hovering near a record low, Republicans are being forced to actively campaign in what would otherwise be safe Senate seats, such as Kansas and South Carolina. Voting is already under way in many key states.
Canada’s foreign affairs department didn’t immediately provide a comment in response to a request from Bloomberg.

Trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed two months ago, even after Trump had announced a preliminary deal, and formal negotiations have not yet resumed. Trump has since threatened to hike tariffs on Canadian autos to 50%, up from 25%, ON Jan. 1, a deadline that May prompt a renewed round of discussions later this year. Those would occur at the same time as the so-called lame-duck session of the current, departing Congress.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and other Canadian officials have frequently made the case that US tariffs punish American consumers and businesses — but Trump administration officials have been aggressively pushing back, warning Canadians not to speak out.
On Wednesday, Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford rejected the idea that their advocacy against US tariffs was inappropriate.

stories.title: 3 arrested after Toronto marketplace sellers targeted in violent robberies: police
stories.summary: Toronto police believe there May be more victims of a series of violent robberies targeting people who advertised high-value items on online marketplaces.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto police believe there May be more victims of a series of violent robberies targeting people who advertised high-value items on online marketplaces.

Supt. Paul Krawczyk of 43 Division told reporters Thursday the investigation began in July when someone selling a luxury watch was assaulted and robbed during an in-person transaction.

An individual using the name “Omar Clarkson” had expressed interest in buying the watch. The seller arranged to meet the buyer near Ellesmere and Bellamy roads. Police allege multiple suspects who were armed with crowbars arrived in a vehicle and ambushed the seller.

Krawczyk said investigators believe a group was targeting people who advertised high-value items online. After learning the suspects arranged to meet another watch seller on Oct. 9, police set up near the planned meeting location around Highway 401 and Weston Road.

When the suspects allegedly arrived in a stolen vehicle displaying stolen licence plates, officers moved in and arrested two 17-year-olds. A third suspect fled the area but was arrested a day later.

“One of the youths was found in possession of a firearm equipped with a prohibited extended magazine,” Krawczyk said.

The two youths face more than 30 charges combined, including robbery and multiple firearms offences. Krawczyk said both were already subject to conditions prohibiting them from possessing firearms. One had prior convictions while the other one was on a peace bond, Krawczyk added.

Desmond Okuonhae, 18, was charged with robbery with an offensive weapon, possession of property obtained by crime under $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence.

Police allege Okuonhae was also involved in a laptop theft in March and the robbery of a rare Pokémon trading card collection worth $80,000 in April.

He was charged with robbery and theft under $5,000 in connection to those incidents.

Police believe there May be additional victims who arranged online marketplace transactions with Okuonhae. Investigators allege he used the names “Oscar Morkil,” “Max Smith” and “Omar Clarkson.”

The investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Korchinski-Paquet's mother makes new allegation against police at coroner's inquest
stories.summary: Toronto - A coroner's inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet is scrambling to find a way forward after the Toronto woman's mother unexpectedly made a new allegation against police officers during her testimony this morning.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A coroner’s inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet was scrambling to find a way forward Thursday after the Toronto woman’s mother unexpectedly made a new allegation against police officers during her testimony.

Korchinski-Paquet fell from her 24th-floor balcony in the late afternoon of May 27, 2020, while police officers were in the west-end apartment she shared with several family members.

As she described her memories of that day on Thursday, Claudette Beals told the inquest that she saw officers push her daughter toward the balcony, then shortly afterward, heard the 29-year-old woman call out to her for help.

“That’s your belief?” inquest counsel Roger Shallow asked Beals after she summarized the sequence of events leading up to her daughter’s death.

“That’s my belief,” Beals replied.

“I think it’s important that you’re able to speak your belief. I want to focus in on what you actually saw with your eyes versus what your belief is,” Shallow said.

“I saw them pushing Regis towards the balcony. That’s all I saw, but I saw that myself,” Beals said.

Her comments prompted lawyers for several of the parties to raise concerns in the absence of the jury and witness about previously undisclosed evidence.

Among them were lawyers representing the officers at the scene, who said their clients weren’t given a chance to respond to the allegation when they testified earlier this week.

Two officers, Const. Shane Beaudoin and then-Const. Adam Vandenbrink, testified Korchinski-Paquet moved quickly to the balcony after she was asked to speak to a paramedic. She had been allowed into the apartment because she needed to use the bathroom, they said.

The presiding coroner called a recess Thursday morning so that counsel could discuss how to proceed, which was then extended to the early afternoon. When the inquest reconvened, however, Dr. David Cameron said it would be adjourned until Friday morning.

The inquest had done well so far in exploring issues related to epilepsy, postictal delirium and their “intersection with police encounters,” and plans to continue that exploration, Cameron told jurors.

“Exploring the circumstances of a death in terms of facts is also an important part of an inquest ... We’re strategizing currently in how to best do that in the name of fairness and transparency and the parties to the inquest are working collaboratively to bring you that information in a clear and fair manner.”

That process is “taking a little bit of time,” he said.

The inquest has heard Korchinski-Paquet had a history of seizures from epilepsy, often followed by erratic and aggressive behaviour.

A neurologist who did not treat her but reviewed her records said that on multiple occasions, she showed symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium, an altered mental state that can follow seizures.

Korchinski-Paquet had experienced two seizures earlier in the day before police were called over a violent disturbance involving knives.

One of the province’s police watchdogs later cleared the officers of wrongdoing in the fatal fall, which it said happened as she was trying to move from her apartment’s balcony to a neighbour’s.

The inquest’s scope includes how first responders are informed and trained about epilepsy but is not meant to examine the various watchdog investigations into the case.

Jurors in a coroner’s inquest do not assign legal responsibility but can issue recommendations meant to prevent similar deaths in the future. Those recommendations are not binding, however.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Supreme Court to hear federal appeal of Emergencies Act use
stories.summary: Government invoked extraordinary powers in 2022 during convoy protests in Ottawa, lost case twice in lower courts
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
A reckoning of the Trudeau government’s use of the Emergencies Act in 2022 to quell weeks-long trucker protests in the country’s capital is heading to the Supreme Court of Canada.

The top court on Thursday said it has agreed to hear Ottawa’s appeal of the case. A hearing has not been scheduled and likely wouldn’t happen before next spring or possibly next fall.

The federal government has twice lost in the lower courts, after legal challenges to its 2022 invocation of the Emergencies Act. In January, the Federal Court of Appeal concluded that Ottawa’s use of the emergency powers was not legally justified and violated the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the protection of freedom of expression and the prohibition against unreasonable search or seizure.

By invoking the Emergencies Act, Ottawa had tapped extraordinary temporary powers, including prohibiting citizens from assembling in public and freezing bank assets.

In March, Ottawa asked the Supreme Court to hear the case and argued in a legal filing it had acted reasonably in extraordinary circumstances to conclude there was a public-order emergency. Ottawa further argued that the lower court rulings had effectively neutered the Emergencies Act by restricting “governments’ ability to respond effectively to future crises.”

The Federal Court of Appeal decision in January, led by Chief Justice Yves de Montigny and signed by “The Court,” was a major judgment that clarified the limits of executive power during intense moments when the political-decision making of the prime minister and cabinet have the potential to overstep the boundaries of the law.

The stakes will be the same at the Supreme Court, as the nine judges look to delineate the boundary between what is reasonable and unreasonable in government decisions made during heated and challenging episodes.

The Supreme Court’s move to take on the Emergencies Act case comes during a year in which judges of the top court are saying yes to twice as many appeal applications as they previously had during the early 2020s. The Emergencies Act appeal was one of four on Thursday the court agreed to hear, increasing the total of new cases this year to 52 – the most since 2013.

The Emergencies Act story started in winter of 2022, when hundreds of protesters driving semi-trailer trucks and other vehicles gridlocked the centre of Ottawa near Parliament. They had been angered over pandemic vaccine mandates and felt generally aggrieved with the federal government. There were also several protests across the country at the border with the United States.

On Feb. 14, 2022, the federal government cited a threat to the security of Canada as it invoked the Emergencies Act. The act had become law in 1988, and it was used for the first time in 2022. The law had been tailored to include a high bar for its use, as it replaced the previous War Measures Act.

Both the Federal Court in 2024 and the Federal Court of Appeal this year ruled that former prime minister Justin Trudeau and his Liberal government failed to meet that strict legal test. In the appeal court’s judgment, it said the government had not shown there were reasonable grounds to believe there was a national emergency or that it couldn’t be resolved with other laws.

Ottawa had scored one initial victory outside of court. There was a public inquiry in fall 2022, which is required by the act after the invocation of the emergency powers. In a report in February, 2023, Justice Paul Rouleau concluded that the use of the act was appropriate but also said it could have been avoided.

The two leading civil society groups, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and the Canadian Constitution Foundation, are the primary challengers in court against the federal government.

As the Supreme Court considered whether to hear Ottawa’s appeal, the groups in their legal filings argued there was no reason for yet another court to scrutinize the events of 2022. They both argued Ottawa was only trying to relitigate arguments it had already lost.

The Civil Liberties Association on Thursday said the case wasn’t about the trucker protests but instead focused on the need for governments to adhere to the rule of law in times of crisis, and that emergency powers aren’t arbitrarily invoked.

The Constitution Foundation on Thursday said the Trudeau government had “used emergency measures meant for a genuine crisis to silence political opposition it found inconvenient.”

The office of federal Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree, in a statement, said Ottawa “remains steadfast in its commitment to ensuring the safety and security of Canadians in the face of threats to public safety and national security.”

There have also been questions among some in the legal community about Supreme Court Chief Justice Richard Wagner around allegations of bias and whether he should recuse himself. After the protests ended, he twice commented on the Ottawa protests. In one, an interview with Montreal newspaper Le Devoir, he likened the protests to the initial stages of anarchy: “c’est un petit debut d’anarchie,” he was quoted as saying.

Neither the Civil Liberties Association or the Constitution Foundation made this claim about bias and recusal but it was put forth during the Supreme Court appeal application process by a small group, Canadian Frontline Nurses, that had been involved in the case.

On April 29, Supreme Court Registrar Chantal Carbonneau sent a letter to lawyers in the case noting Chief Justice Wagner had considered the issue and “concluded that there is no actual or reasonable apprehension of bias that would require his recusal under the applicable legal test.”

stories.title: Supreme Court to hear final appeal of Trudeau government's invocation of Emergencies Act
stories.summary: Canada's top court will decide if the government's invocation of the Emergencies Act during the 2022 Freedom Convoy was constitutional.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada’s top court will decide once and for all if the federal government’s invocation of the extraordinary powers of the Emergencies Act during the 2022 Freedom Convoy was constitutional.

On Thursday, the Supreme Court Canada (SCC) announced it would hear the final appeal of two lower court decisions ruling that the invocation by former prime minister Justin Trudeau was unjustified as a way to stop the protests.

In its filing, the federal government argued that the Federal Court and Federal Court of Appeal applied the “wrong principles” and a “flawed approach” when they ruled that the government’s unprecedented decision to invoke the Emergencies Act on Feb. 12, 2022 was unconstitutional.

In January, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld a lower court decision that the Liberal government’s invocation of the Act to deal with lingering Freedom Convoy protests was unreasonable, unjustified and violated the Charter.

The challenge to the use of the act was brought forward by civil liberties groups such as the Canadian Civil Liberties Association (Ccla) and the Canadian Constitutional Foundation (CCF) as well as the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta.

In a statement Thursday morning, the Ccla vowed to defend its “historic victory” in both lower courts.

“For the Ccla, this case is not about the ‘Freedom Convoy’ protests,” the Ccla’s Anaïs Bussières McNicoll said in a statement. “It is about sending a clear message to this and future governments: even in times of crisis, no government is above the law.”

The 2022 Freedom Convoy protest had lasted for weeks across Canada but particularly in Ottawa, with many large trucks parked on streets to protest the government’s pandemic lockdowns and vaccine mandates. At the time, the government argued it needed the exceptional powers granted by the act to freeze some convoy participants’ bank accounts, compel tow truck companies to co-operate with local police clearing out the trucks, and mark parts of downtown Ottawa as a no-go zone.

Within one week of the act’s invocation, police forces from across Canada had assembled in Ottawa to push out protesters.

But in 2024, the Federal Court ruled that the powers were unnecessary to deal with the Ottawa protest as well as sympathetic blockades at two border crossings in Coutts, Alta. and the Ambassador Bridge in Windsor, Ont.

In his ruling, Federal Court Justice Richard Mosley determined that existing provincial and municipal powers were sufficient to address the disruptive protests.

In January of this year, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld Mosley’s decision, also finding that Trudeau’s cabinet did not have reasonable grounds to believe that the convoy created a national emergency.

“We are of the view that Cabinet did not have reasonable grounds to believe that a national emergency existed, taking into account the wording of the Act, its constitutional underpinning and the record that was before it at the time the decision was made,” wrote the court’s Chief Justice Yves de Montigny.
