stories.title: Recount flips Quebec riding to the Parti Québécois, Liberals refuse to concede
stories.summary: Liberal candidate Affine Lwalalika had initially been declared the winner of the Vachon riding by a margin of ten votes.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL - A judicial recount has flipped a riding in the Montérégie region of Quebec from the Liberal Party to the Parti Québécois by a three-vote margin.

However, the Quebec Liberal Party is refusing to concede victory to its rival for now.

Liberal candidate Affine Lwalalika had initially been declared the winner of the Vachon riding by a margin of ten votes.

A recount was triggered and ended on Wednesday.

Quebec’s election authority says the recount gave the upper hand to PQ candidate Stephan Fogaing by three votes.

The Liberal Party says it acknowledges the results of the recount but that its lawyers are reviewing the situation.

“All options are on the table, and we will make a decision quickly on how to proceed,” the party wrote on its social media accounts.

Data from the election authority, Élections Québec, shows more ballots were rejected in the recount than on election day, going from 588 to 730 rejected ballots.

The incumbent for Vachon, former Coalition Avenir Québec cabinet minister Ian Lafrenière, congratulated Fogaing.

“The judicial recount declared him the winner by three votes in Vachon. The phrase ‘every vote counts’ takes on its full meaning,” wrote the former domestic security minister on X.

Lafrenière had finished third with just under 21 per cent of the vote on election day.

The PQ has also requested a judicial recount in Champlain, in the Mauricie region, where its candidate lost by 191 votes to Conservative candidate Adriana Szalontai.

The Court of Quebec confirmed the recount on Tuesday. It is set to begin Thursday at the Trois-Rivières courthouse.

In its press release, the election authority says there have been seven judicial recounts after a provincial election since 2000. Recounts in 2003 and 1994 led to ties, which triggered byelections.

— With files from Frédéric Lacroix-Couture

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Toronto Crime Stoppers pauses tips after cyber breach affects 176K submissions
stories.summary: Toronto Crime Stoppers has paused tip intake after a cybersecurity breach potentially exposed identifying information included in some submissions.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto Crime Stoppers has paused tip intake after a cybersecurity breach potentially exposed identifying information included in some submissions.

The organization is asking people not to submit tips while work happens to establish safer reporting options. Anyone facing an immediate emergency should call 911.

Chair Sean Sportun said Wednesday that 176,859 Toronto Crime Stoppers tips were affected by a breach involving its software provider. The organization was given a list of nearly 15,000 names that were found in the breach.

“Until we have a safer way to protect you, please do not send us tips by phone, online or through the app,” he said in a statement.

“Pausing our program means that option isn’t available now, and we did not make this decision lightly. We are pausing because those people deserve a system we can fully stand behind.”

In March, hackers stole data from P3 – the tip software Toronto Crime Stoppers has used since 2018, Sportun said.

Navigate360, which provides the P3 platform, “repeatedly” assured Toronto Crime Stoppers the system was secure, Sportun said. A month after the attack, the provider said some Canadian data had been stolen but that Toronto submissions were not affected, he added.

Sportun said the organization was told in June tips submitted to the platform from January 2022 and November 2025 were affected. A month later, it pegged the figure at 176,859, adding 12,392 of them May contain personal information.

“We never ask for your name, and we don’t want it. But people sometimes include details to explain what they saw,” Sportun said.

“Before a tip goes to investigators, our practice is to remove those details. It has come to light that some of those original tips containing potentially identifying information were stolen from P3.”

In September and October, Navigate360 gave Toronto Crime Stoppers a list of 14,973 names found in the breach. However, Sportun said the list “lacks detail necessary to measure the risk involved” because it did not identify who the names belong to.

Navigate360 did not immediately return Global News’ request for comment.

“Despite numerous requests through our legal counsel, Navigate360 has not provided us with the text of the stolen tips, so we cannot see what each one says,” Sportun said.

He added “anonymously sourced information” on the breach being reported this week hasn’t been shared with Toronto Crime Stoppers. An investigation by CBC published Wednesday reported that more than 1.5 million Canadian Crime Stoppers tips were affected.

Toronto police said Wednesday the service is temporarily suspending its use of Crime Stoppers while it assesses new safeguards and other measures.

Police said members of the public can submit information through existing police reporting channels. Those methods are not anonymous, but the information will go directly to investigators, it added.

Sportun said Toronto Crime Stoppers has removed the “Tip Submit” feature from its website, has advised Navigate360 to suspend the intake function for the organization on its platform and has asked the National Anonymous Call Centre to stop processing new information intended for Toronto Crime Stoppers.

The organization continues to press Navigate360 for the text of the stolen tips, he added.

“We know waiting is hard, especially for anyone worried about their safety,” Sportun said.

“We will keep pressing for answers, and we will share what we learn as soon as we can.”

stories.title: Statistics Canada website down as internet hit by millions of hack attempts
stories.summary: Several government websites were still down Thursday morning at the same time a worldwide coding vulnerability has opened the door to millions of reported hack attempts.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Several government websites, including Statistics Canada, were still down Thursday morning at the same time a coding vulnerability seen worldwide has opened the door to millions of reported hack attempts.

“We’re sorry! The website is currently unavailable. We apologize for any inconvenience,” a bulletin on Statistics Canada’s website said as of publication.

That comes after other outages including the website for the Canadian Intellectual Property Office, which handles trademark and copyright information, was also taken offline on Wednesday.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said Wednesday in a social media post that websites went dark to protect government systems and Canadians’ information following guidance from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security.

He said it is being done in response to a vulnerability identified in PHP, a widely used programming language that underwrites roughly 70 per cent of the world’s websites.

“This is a global issue, and other governments and organizations are also taking protective measures,” he said.

The British Columbia government posted Wednesday on social media that it had taken some of its webpages offline “as a precaution following a new global cybersecurity vulnerability.”

The B.C. government said teams were working to restore services as soon as possible.

PHP developers released urgent fixes on Wednesday for vulnerabilities that had lurked in the software for years until they were uncovered using AI, urging users to “update immediately.”

“Details of these flaws became public before fixes were ready, and attacks have since been reported,” said Madeline Lawrence, co-founder of Belgian cybersecurity firm Aikido Security speaking to Reuters.

“So companies are racing to update against attackers who can use AI to exploit them. That’s the whole race.”

As companies and governments deployed patches and suspended websites as a precaution, hacking attempts surged into the millions, according to cloud services firm Cloudflare NET.N.

“In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it,” Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said in a post on X late on Wednesday.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now.”

The Fbi’s cyber division said the vulnerability could allow malicious actors to remotely execute code in the programming language, potentially compromising sensitive data and networks.

The PHP Foundation, which includes developers who work on securing the programming language, said it has released fixes for the vulnerabilities, along with instructions on how to update systems.

Governments in Europe and elsewhere took websites offline as a precaution on Wednesday while website operators scrambled to secure systems running the software.

The website of the Finnish government was only partly available Wednesday. A message to visitors said Finnish government websites were experiencing a temporary disruption and were fully or partially unavailable while the issue was being resolved.

The emergency shutdowns of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services from Tokyo to Helsinki showed how much public and corporate systems rely on the software, and how hard it is to fix such flaws quickly once they are made public.

“It was a long day and a long night, I know for all the IT and security folks … I’ve not seen anything like this in a long, long time,” Microsoft Msft.O CEO Satya Nadella said at a company event in Cologne, Germany, ON Thursday.

He said the episode underscored the importance of building digital systems that can be maintained securely.

– with files from The Canadian Press and Reuters

stories.title: Supreme Court to hear federal appeal over use of Emergencies Act
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada will hear federal arguments about the government’s legal justification for using the Emergencies Act to quell protests in the nation’s capital and at key border points four years ago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa -- The Supreme Court of Canada will hear federal arguments about the government’s legal justification for using the Emergencies Act to quell protests in the national capital and at key border points four years ago.

For about three weeks in January and February 2022, downtown Ottawa was filled with protesters, including many in large trucks that blocked streets around Parliament Hill.

While many of the protesters were demonstrating against COVID-19 health restrictions, the protest attracted some with a variety of grievances against then-prime minister Justin Trudeau and his government.

On Feb. 14, 2022, the government invoked the Emergencies Act, which allowed for temporary measures, including regulation and prohibition of public assemblies, the designation of secure places, direction to banks to freeze assets and a ban on support for protest participants.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association and others successfully argued in Federal Court that Ottawa lacked sound statutory grounds to usher in the emergency measures.

In January, a three-judge panel of the Federal Court of Appeal unanimously upheld the ruling, prompting the federal government to seek a hearing at the Supreme Court.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Ottawa gives Stelco 15 days to reverse Hamilton layoffs or face lawsuit
stories.summary: If the company does not reverse the layoffs, Joly warns she will proceed with court action that could see the company be forced to sell their Canadian operations.
stories.author: Mackenzie Gray
stories.content:
Industry Minister Melanie Joly has written to Canadian steel maker Stelco warning if they do not reverse the layoffs of up to 500 workers at their Hamilton steel plant within 15 days, the federal government will start legal action against the company, according to a letter obtained by Global News.

The government maintains Stelco’s U.S. parent company, Cleveland-Cliffs, has broken a 2024 agreement with Ottawa that stated they would not lay off anyone in Canada until 2029.

The text of that agreement had not been made public until Joly’s letter, which states the company agreed that “the average aggregate annual employment” of unionized employees in Canada would be “no lower than 1,766, representing 100% of the average aggregate annual full-time equivalent employment of the 12 months ending June 30, 2024.”

Stelco has maintained that they have not broken that agreement, writing to the minister saying Stelco does not need to maintain the same employment level for each day of the agreement with Ottawa.

If the company does not reverse the layoffs, which they have said publicly said multiple times they will will not, Joly warns she will proceed with court action that could see the company be forced to sell their Canadian operations.

A senior government source has told Global News that while legal action is an option, the Carney government recognizes the legal process will take too long to save the jobs in Hamilton and keep the plant fully functioning, leaving Ottawa looking for a faster solution.

stories.title: Canada, Turkey announce strategic partnership to deepen energy, defence and trade ties
stories.summary: Ankara is the latest stop in Carney’s drive to reduce reliance on the increasingly protectionist and unpredictable U.S. under Trump
stories.author: Steven Chase
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a strategic partnership with Turkey that will deepen co-operation in defence, energy and joint ventures with the country of 87 million.

Mr. Carney stood with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan at the Bestepe Presidential Complex in Ankara to unveil a three-year action plan the two leaders said will “fundamentally deepen and elevate” relations between Canada and Turkey, including “expanding political dialogue,” trade, technological development and common security.

Turkey is the latest stop in the Prime Minister’s drive to reduce reliance on the increasingly protectionist and unpredictable United States under Donald Trump – a challenge Mr. Carney indirectly referenced Thursday when he said Canada these days is seeking “reliable partners.”

Mr. Erdogan said Mr. Carney’s visit turns a page in Turkey-Canada relations, which entered a deep freeze more than five years ago when Ottawa restricted arms exports to Turkey.

“We had some kind of disconnect for a period, but today we put an end to it,” the President said.

The Canadian pact provides legitimacy to Mr. Erdogan, who critics say is responsible for Turkey’s democratic backsliding into an autocracy. The U.S. watchdog Freedom House scores Turkey as 32/100 on its civil liberties index, or “not free,” saying the President and his party “have become increasingly authoritarian in recent years, consolidating significant power through constitutional changes and by imprisoning opponents and critics.”

The Prime Minister announced that Export Development Canada, which helps finance and insure Canadian exporters, will sign an agreement with counterpart Turk Eximbank to help companies in both countries undertake joint ventures in foreign markets. The focus will be on energy, mining and critical minerals, infrastructure and transportation, Mr. Carney said.

The two leaders said an air transport agreement being finalized will raise the allowable volume of weekly passenger flights between Canada and Turkey to 21 from 12, with no limit on cargo flights.

Mr. Carney and Mr. Erdogan said negotiations toward a free-trade agreement, first announced in July, will begin next month.

The Prime Minister announced International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu will lead a trade mission to Turkey in 2027.

Mr. Carney is the first prime minister to make a bilateral trip to Turkey purely to advance Turkey-Canada relations.

Mr. Carney arrived Thursday afternoon at the Turkish presidential complex, where he was greeted with the firing of military cannons. The Prime Minister was welcomed by Mr. Erdogan, then stopped at a microphone to address members of a military band, saying “ merhaba asker ,” which loosely translates to “hello, soldiers.”

The Prime Minister, accompanied by Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson, spoke of his desire to sell Candu nuclear reactors, critical minerals and liquefied natural gas to Turkey. Mr. Carney said Mr. Hodgson and his Turkish counterpart have agreed to work together to advance collaboration across the energy sector, including liquefied natural gas, civil nuclear energy, renewable energy and critical energy infrastructure.

“Canada is on its way to becoming an energy superpower. Turkey’s economy is growing rapidly and needs a secure and reliable energy supply. We have much to offer: from LNG and civilian nuclear technology to clean energy and the critical minerals that will be at the heart of tomorrow’s economy,” Mr. Carney said.

He lauded a recent defence industry partnership deal with Turkey that will “connect Canadian and Turkish companies to work together, creating good jobs at home, export opportunities abroad and a stronger Nato alliance.”

Turkey’s ambassador to Canada, Can Dizdar, has said Turkey and Canada could deepen co-operation in drone technology, aerospace, naval systems, shipbuilding parts, munitions production and vehicles.

Canada is forming a 'strategic partnership' with Turkey aimed in part at securing a free-trade agreement, Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

The Canadian Press

Canada has high hopes for defence co-operation with Turkey, which was ranked the 11th-largest arms exporter in the 2021-25 period by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. It wants to benefit from Turkey’s expertise as Canada undertakes the sharpest hike in military spending since the Korean War.

Two senior officials said this could include tapping Turkey’s military drone prowess, and technology transfers or joint ventures. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the officials because they are not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.

Turkish officials have repeatedly said more than 80 per cent of the country’s defence industry’s content is now domestic, which reduces dependence on foreign suppliers.

Trade between the two countries has grown steadily in the past 15 years, but with gains mostly in Turkey’s favour. Ankara remains a minor trading partner, however. In 2010, two-way trade was about $1.6-billion, with Canada exporting $841.7-million to Turkey and importing $714.2-million, according to Statistics Canada. By 2025, that had grown to $4.3-billion, with Canada exporting $1.1-billion to Turkey and importing $3.2-billion.

In his own remarks, Mr. Erdogan said he hopes trade between the two countries will roughly double to $10-billion and said he plans on visiting Canada.

Before meeting with Mr. Erdogan, the Prime Minister on Thursday morning laid a wreath at the mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, a massive stone commemoration of the founder of modern Turkey. Ataturk is remembered in part for transforming Turkey into a secular, pro-Western country and laying the foundations for its transition to democracy.

Critics say that Mr. Erdogan, in contrast, introduced religion back into public life, and while he has brought great prosperity to Turkey over his more than two decades in power, is also responsible for the country’s illiberal turn in recent years.

In recent months, Turkey has taken over a pro-opposition media outlet, raided Lgbtq groups and convicted a stand-up comic of insulting the country’s President.

Asked whether the Canadian delegation raised human rights with Turkey, the Prime Minister‘s Office said that in a meeting between Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and her Turkish counterpart, the minister “raised the importance of the respect for human rights.”

This four-day trip is another demonstration of Mr. Carney’s pivot to what he has called “values-based realism” foreign policy – which the Prime Minister has explained means no more “lecturing from afar” if Canada disagrees with another country’s conduct.

“Engagement does not mean endorsement,” is Mr. Carney’s maxim.

With a report from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Joly demands Stelco owner comply with job commitments in new letter, gives 15-day deadline to respond
stories.summary: Ottawa has clashed with Cliffs boss Goncalves over his backing of Trump’s tariffs, decision to cut jobs in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont.
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has sent Stelco Inc. a new letter demanding it comply with its Investment Canada Act undertakings after it announced hundreds of job cuts last month, and criticized Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CLF-N boss Lourenco Goncalves for repeatedly backing U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steelmakers.

The letter sent to Stelco president Paul Simon on Thursday stated that the U.S. steelmaker has 15 days to respond or possibly face legal action by Ottawa that would seek to enforce the terms of the agreement.

Ms. Joly detailed in the letter multiple examples of the company allegedly violating its legally binding commitments and demanding it comply.

Cliffs has “failed to comply with its employment undertakings,” she wrote, “and/or has made decisions that will inevitably result in the breach of these undertakings.”

Ms. Joly pointed to a commitment Cliffs made when it acquired Stelco in 2024 to ensure the average annual unionized work force at the company be no smaller than 1,766 and its salaried work force be no smaller than 603, which was the size of the work force at the time of the acquisition.

On Sept. 28, Cliffs subsidiary Stelco announced that it was laying off up to 500 workers at its plants in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont.

The federal government has said that by proceeding with layoffs, Ohio-based Cliffs is in breach of a promise to maintain at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada for five years.

Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sept. 29 said Cliffs had “betrayed” its Canadian work force, and Ms. Joly has repeatedly demanded it comply with its undertakings or possibly face legal action.

Ms. Joly sent Stelco an earlier letter on Oct. 5 urging it to comply with its employment guarantees under The Investment Canada Act, and warning it that risked legal action including financial penalties, or the forced divestiture of assets.

In her latest letter, Ms. Joly is giving the company several options, including complying with its undertakings, providing proof that it isn’t in contravention of them, or in the case that the company is offside, taking steps to address the situation.

Ms. Joly also said in her Thursday letter that Cliffs had promised to be “a strong advocate for policies that benefit both the U.S. and Canadian steel industries,” including defending Canada’s exemption to U.S. steel tariffs in 2024.

She pointed to multiple examples of Mr. Goncalves advocating against Canada after the U.S. imposed tariffs on Canadian steel imports last year, including several times he publicly backed Mr. Trump’s trade policies.

Cleveland-Cliffs had not responded to a request for comment by late Thursday afternoon.

In an October, 2025, interview with Politico , the Cliffs CEO said that he was “very happy” with the 50-per-cent tariffs on steel, and in fact took credit for them.

“I have my fingerprints on that 50 per cent. In other words, I influenced that,” Mr. Goncalves told Politico.

Cliffs has said that it was forced to issue the layoffs in Canada in large part because of the trade war. It said the 50-per-cent tariffs have made it too hard for it to compete in galvanized steel in the U.S.

Mr. Goncalves has also argued that the trade war is an event that was out of its control and gives it leeway to not honour its commitments.

“Throughout the history of the Investment Canada Act and its predecessor foreign investment acts, it has consistently been understood that changes in circumstances May necessitate the non-enforcement or renegotiation of undertakings,” Mr. Simon wrote in a Oct. 9 letter to Ms. Joly.

But Ottawa disputes this reasoning. Ms. Joly in her Thursday letter said that when Cliffs acquired Stelco, the prospect of U.S. trade action against Canada existed.

“The possibility of tariffs on Canadian steel was foreseeable in October, 2024, and the undertakings specifically reflect that possibility,” she wrote.

She also pointed out that Mr. Goncalves “subsequently advocated for the very tariffs that Cliffs is now relying on as a basis for non-compliance with the undertakings.”

stories.title: St. Thomas fire chief to retire after more than 30 years of service
stories.summary: The city said recruitment efforts to find a successor will begin in the coming months.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
David Gregory, chief of the St. Thomas Fire Department, will retire in May following more than three decades of service.

Gregory served as a firefighter for 20 years before being promoted to captain. He was appointed fire chief in March 2022.

“It’s been like winning the lottery,” Gregory said in a media release. “I grew up in the courthouse district, not far from the original fire station, and to spend my entire career serving the community where I was born and raised has been incredibly rewarding.”

The city said recruitment efforts to find Gregory’s successor will begin in the coming months.

stories.title: François Carrier named Western’s first executive director of Global Engagement
stories.summary: François Carrier has been named Western University’s first executive director of global engagement to advance international priorities.
stories.author: Keri Ferguson
stories.content:
François Carrier has been named Western’s first executive director of global engagement, effective Nov. 9.

Carrier will lead Western’s newly created Global Engagement group within the Office of the President, working closely with the provost, vice-president (research), deans and other senior leaders to advance the priorities in Western in the World, the university’s global engagement plan.

“We are delighted to welcome François to the Western community,” said President Alan Shepard. “His strategic leadership and support will be invaluable as we continue to expand our international partnerships and strengthen Western’s global reputation and impact.”

Carrier brings more than 20 years of experience in higher education and expertise in international research collaborations. He currently serves as director of international research and experiential learning at the University of Ottawa, where he has developed and implemented global research collaborations, expanded institutional partnerships and created more international learning opportunities for students.

He was previously executive director of programs at Polar Knowledge Canada, a federal agency focused on Arctic research, where he led a multidisciplinary team of scientists and professional staff. Prior to that, Carrier was director of the Office of International Research at McGill University, where he oversaw a portfolio of international projects and partnerships.

Western’s global engagement plan seeks to prepare students, staff and faculty for success around the world and drive impact through international research and partnerships.

“Western is a university with a great reputation for both its academic programming and the excellence of its research,” Carrier said. “I look forward to building its global ties, deepening and diversifying those connections, while always maintaining a personal connection.”

The Montreal native believes successful global engagement is rooted in the one-to-one relationships that foster meaningful partnerships, collaborations and international initiatives.

“It ultimately comes down to people and those one-to-one interactions,” Carrier said.

It’s a perspective shaped early in his career as a civil engineer leading international development projects across Africa, Asia and the Caribbean, and as a master’s student working on solar water pumping projects in developing countries.

Collaborating with communities, researchers and organizations taught him technical solutions alone are not enough.

“Technology is not an end in itself,” he said. “As an engineer, you have to be aware of its impact on society. I learned early on to pay attention, listen to the anthropologists, the sociologists and community members to ensure the technology we brought would be well received, maintained and durable over time.”

Seeking to better understand the organizational and leadership aspects behind complex global challenges, Carrier pursued an MBA and eventually a career in higher education administration, where he identified opportunities to link research, education and international collaboration.

Despite a shift in his career, Carrier’s engineering background continues to influence his working philosophy.

“I’m practical, hands-on and focused on finding solutions,” he said. “I enjoy bringing people together around a shared objective. Taking a bottom-up approach helps to meet institutional priorities at what I call the ‘sweet middle,’ where interests and resources coincide.”

Carrier describes his new role at Western as “very entrepreneurial” and an opportunity to help others turn their ideas into reality. He sees faculty and students in the same light.

“Faculty members are very entrepreneurial. They have their own networks, and sometimes they just need a little help from central administration to realize their ambitions,” he said.

“Students are also very ambitious, with a lot of ideas, and there’s a sea of untapped opportunities through which to engage them.”

That includes access to more global learning experiences.

“International engagement should not be the privilege of a few,” he said. “It has to be made accessible to all.”

Through his new unit, he plans to work with university leaders to establish “a lasting model” across faculties and divisions, a system to build research partnerships that position Western as a globally connected, research-intensive institution with meaningful international impact.

“I want to add value to existing efforts and come up with original ideas that May not have been considered,” he said. “This role offers a really unique opportunity, where you have a chance to build something lasting.”

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

stories.title: Sarnia man charged with manslaughter months after death of 18-year-old woman
stories.summary: Sarnia police say officers were called to a residence in the 400 block of Nelson Street on June 16 after receiving a report of a sudden death
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A Sarnia man is facing charges in connection with the death of an 18-year-old woman earlier this year.

Sarnia police say officers were called to a residence in the 400 block of Nelson Street on June 16 after receiving a report of a sudden death.

When officers arrived, they located 18-year-old Leia Cooper deceased inside the home. Police launched an investigation and requested a post-mortem examination to determine the cause of death.

Earlier this month, the Office of the Chief Coroner determined Cooper’s cause of death. Based on those findings and the ongoing investigation, Sarnia police used a search warrant on Wednesday and arrested a 21-year-old Sarnia man.

The accused has been charged with manslaughter and trafficking a controlled substance.

Police said no further information, including the cause of death, will be released as the matter is now before the courts.

Sarnia police say officers were called to a residence in the 400 block of Nelson Street on June 16 after receiving a report of a sudden death.
When officers arrived, they located 18-year-old Leia Cooper deceased inside the home. Police launched an investigation and requested a post-mortem examination to determine the cause of death.

Earlier this month, the Office of the Chief Coroner determined Cooper’s cause of death. Based on those findings and the ongoing investigation, Sarnia police used a search warrant on Wednesday and arrested a 21-year-old Sarnia man.
The accused has been charged with manslaughter and trafficking a controlled substance.
Police said no further information, including the cause of death, will be released as the matter is now before the courts.

stories.title: Federal union says 120,000 public servants will participate in strike votes starting next month
stories.summary: If vote passes, the union would be in a legal strike position for 60 days
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Canada’s largest federal public service union says 120,000 workers will take part in nationwide strike votes starting next month after contract talks with the federal government broke down.

The Public Service Alliance of Canada says voting will take place from Nov. 16 to Jan. 22.

The union and Treasury Board have been in contract negotiations for a year and a half, and Psac in May called a government wage offer of less than one per cent per year “insulting.”

Psac says the government has refused to negotiate on key issues such as wages, job security, remote work and protections against artificial intelligence.

“The government has left us no other choice,” said Psac national president Sharon DeSousa. “This is a wake-up call for the government to stop playing games and put a fair offer on the table.”

Workers to take part in strike votes include wildland firefighters, passport and benefit officers, fishery officers, federal teachers, librarians and administrative staff.

If the vote passes, the union would be in a legal strike position for 60 days. But DeSousa says a strike is the last resort option.

“Our goal is to get a good collective agreement, and it doesn’t have to lead to a strike, but we will if required to do so,” she said.

In 2023, 155,000 federal public servants spent almost two weeks on picket lines across the country before winning wage increases amounting to 12.6 per cent over the agreement’s term, which ran from 2021 to 2024.

Since then, federal public servants have faced both job cuts and an increase in their required office presence.

The Liberals’ 2025 budget outlined a plan to slash the public service by 10 per cent by the end of the 2028-29 fiscal year as part of an effort to reduce spending.

The federal public service has shed more than 23,000 staffers over the last two years, says Canada’s parliamentary spending watchdog.

An online tool released by the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer last month estimates there were 344,970 federal employees in the second quarter of this year, down 6.5 per cent from two years ago.

At the same time, federal government departments and agencies are set to spend more than $18-million to get their employees to work in the office more often.

Thousands of federal public servants started a new work schedule in July requiring them to be on-site in the office four days a week. Executive public servants returned to the office full-time in May.

In response to an order paper question from NDP MP Heather McPherson, 13 federal organizations said they plan to spend a combined $18,720,150 to reconfigure or acquire office space to accommodate the increased frequency of in-person work.

stories.title: Some Alberta referendum questions flip to ‘no’ as count continues
stories.summary: In questions such as choosing their own judges and senators and changing the Constitution to boost provincial rights, the ‘no’ side pulls ahead
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
More of the constitutional questions in Alberta’s historic referendum have flipped to “no” with votes still being counted.

Alberta voters went to the polls on Monday and were asked 10 different questions.

The key question was on separation and roughly 75 per cent of votes backed staying in Canada, but it has taken longer to count votes on the nine other questions.

Early results showed Albertans were in favour of proposals such as choosing their own judges, abolishing the Senate and changing the Constitution to boost provincial rights.

But the “no” side pulled ahead Thursday as the counting continued.

The “yes” side continued to lead on questions dealing with immigration, but the margins were tight.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith had already claimed victory on the immigration questions, saying it appeared she was going to be given clear direction from voters to move ahead, although she hinted it could take some time for her government to act.

She acknowledged the immigration questions were set to pass with small margins, with urban ridings in Calgary and Edmonton largely voting “no.”

“I think that’s something we have to be mindful of,” Smith said at a news conference Wednesday, adding that the government would proceed with caution.

She said she spoke with Prime Minister Mark Carney and that he was accepting of the idea that Albertans want to see more collaboration between the two levels of government on immigration. She said she was putting together a proposal to submit to Ottawa.

Smith, speaking to reporters before the count was finished, conceded that the constitutional matters seem to be less important to Albertans, adding there’s valid skepticism as constitutional amendments can be lengthy exercises.

“Albertans would just rather that we spend our time focusing on things where we can make some meaningful change,” Smith said.

“And I think that’s a message we’ll take away. We have to focus on the things that Albertans want us focusing on.”

Question 1: Do you support the government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?

Question 2: Do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?

Question 3: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially funded social support programs?

Question 4: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family’s use of the health care and education systems?

Question 5: Do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate, or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?

Question 6: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King’s Bench and Appeal courts?

Question 7: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

Question 8: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?

Question 9: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province’s laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province’s laws and federal laws conflict?

Question 10: Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

Elections Alberta says it will publish final results on Oct. 29 and that the results reported so far will be subject to robust verification.

stories.title: Sports, stats and politics: Intersecting interests fuel grad’s PhD
stories.summary: Western PhD grad Noah Vanderhoeven studies how sports, identity and political psychology influence political behaviour.
stories.author: Keri Ferguson
stories.content:
When Noah Vanderhoeven began graduate studies at Western, he was unfamiliar with the field of political psychology. By his final year, he was teaching a course on it.

Now, as an active researcher in his field, Vanderhoeven is a frequent media commentator on how sports teams, athletes and fans May influence our political behaviour and decisions.

He’s one of 2,561 Western graduates crossing the stage during fall convocation.

Looking back, it’s a journey he could not have imagined.

“I never felt fully comfortable committing to a PhD without knowing what topic I wanted to study,” Vanderhoeven said.

He found one in political psychology, which examines how people’s thoughts, emotions, identities and experiences influence their political beliefs, behaviour and decisions.

For Vanderhoeven, that includes the passion people feel for their favourite sports teams.

He first learned about the field as a master’s student in political science, taking a seminar taught by professor Amanda Friesen, Canada Research Chair in Political Psychology.

The material captured his interest. Friesen unlocked possibilities.

“She put a belief in us that we could study the kinds of topics we found interesting in our life outside of school,” Vanderhoeven said.

“For me, that was sports and politics.”

Friesen encouraged Vanderhoeven to write his final master’s paper on where those two interests intersect. The assignment showed how he could build a research agenda around both. It was proof that pushed him to pursue his PhD in Friesen’s Body Politics Lab, where her team studies how people’s bodies and minds react to politics.

Vanderhoeven developed his passion for sports, and the numbers behind them, as a child growing up in London, Ont., where both his parents worked for the London Free Press.

“I always liked looking at newspapers, but the sports section really drew my attention,” he said. “Apparently, I liked to look at the stats every morning and was always obsessed with that.”

His fascination proved fitting for a future researcher whose work would one day include complex data analyses of Brexit voting patterns, immigration attitudes and local football club metrics – and be published in the International Journal of Sport Policy and Politics.

As Vanderhoeven grew older, his interests broadened to include economics and politics.

“I gravitated toward the kind of discussions and communicative aspects of political science,” he said.

Amanda Friesen, CRC in Political Psychology (Western Communications)

Friesen said Vanderhoeven made his mark in her lab by developing research that was rich in theory and methodology and by successfully distilling this knowledge for the public.

Inspired by the growing backlash against athlete activism, he wrote his first paper about a professional baseball team holding a Pride night, which later became a chapter in his PhD dissertation. It was also the basis of his first of 13 (and counting) articles written for The Conversation, a global, independent source of analysis, commentary and research from academics, intended for a public audience.

“Since that first paper, Noah has fully engaged in how sports teams, leagues, athletes and fans May engage with and influence politics,” Friesen said. “This is exciting, cutting-edge work that can advance our understanding of how individuals approach politics as part of their wider worldview, as well as how sports institutions can influence society.”

“Sport is a very important part of our national identity and reflective of how people think about themselves in the world,” he said.

His doctoral studies also corresponded with significant sporting events that fuelled public conversations about nationalism and identity, from the 2026 Winter Olympics and Canada’s hockey rivalry with the U.S. to the Canadian men’s performance at the 2026 Fifa World Cup and the Toronto Blue Jays’ 2025 World Series run.

Because of his ability to apply his knowledge of sport and nationalism to current events, Vanderhoeven’s expertise continues to be in demand across national media outlets.

Beyond his research, Vanderhoeven took on leadership roles throughout his PhD, serving as co-chair of the Graduate Association of Political Science and a member of the department’s equity committee, while also teaching undergraduate courses in research methods, Canadian politics and political psychology.

Public engagement will remain a central part of his academic work.

“It’s important to have these conversations,” he said. “More people pay attention to sports than they do to politics, so sports can be a valuable way to connect people with broader discussions about public issues.”

stories.title: Some referendum questions flip to 'no' as the count continues in Alberta
stories.summary: Edmonton - More of the constitutional questions in Alberta's historic referendum have flipped to "no" with votes still being counted.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - More of the constitutional questions in Alberta’s historic referendum have flipped to “no” with votes still being counted.

Alberta voters went to the polls on Monday and were asked 10 different questions.

The key question was on separation and roughly 75 per cent of votes backed staying in Canada, but it has taken longer to count votes on the nine other questions.

Early results showed Albertans were in favour of proposals such as choosing their own judges, abolishing the Senate and changing the Constitution to boost provincial rights.

But the “no” side pulled ahead Thursday as the counting continued.

The “yes” side continued to lead on questions dealing with immigration, but the margins were tight.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith had already claimed victory on the immigration questions, saying it appeared she was going to be given clear direction from voters to move ahead, although she hinted it could take some time for her government to act.

She acknowledged the immigration questions were set to pass with small margins, with urban ridings in Calgary and Edmonton largely voting “no.”

“I think that’s something we have to be mindful of,” Smith said at a news conference Wednesday, adding that the government would proceed with caution.

She said she spoke with Prime Minister Mark Carney and that he was accepting of the idea that Albertans want to see more collaboration between the two levels of government on immigration. She said she was putting together a proposal to submit to Ottawa.

Smith, speaking to reporters before the count was finished, conceded that the constitutional matters seem to be less important to Albertans, adding there’s valid skepticism as constitutional amendments can be lengthy exercises.

“Albertans would just rather that we spend our time focusing on things where we can make some meaningful change,” Smith said.

“And I think that’s a message we’ll take away. We have to focus on the things that Albertans want us focusing on.”

Here are the questions:

Question 1: Do you support the government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?

Question 2: Do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?

Question 3: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially funded social support programs?

Question 4: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family’s use of the health care and education systems?

Question 5: Do you support the government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate, or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?

Question 6: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King’s Bench and Appeal courts?

Question 7: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

Question 8: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?

Question 9: Do you support the government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province’s laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province’s laws and federal laws conflict?

Question 10: Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

Elections Alberta says it will publish final results on Oct. 29 and that the results reported so far will be subject to robust verification.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Fall for Dance North’s Landslide explores the ‘call to parenthood’
stories.summary: Landslide premieres at Fall for Dance North on Oct. 24 at Toronto’s Bluma Appel Theatre
stories.author: Martha Schabas
stories.content:
Rock Bottom Movement is known for weird and wily choreography that aims to challenge stuffy attitudes toward contemporary dance. Led by choreographer Alyssa Martin, its repertoire includes Sex Dalmatian’s Hot Holiday Spectacular and Manicpixiedreamgirls, titles that give a sense of the Toronto company’s trademark tone.

But earlier this year, all jokes were put on hold when one of Rock Bottom’s original members announced she was pregnant. The other dancers, women and non-binary people of reproductive age, began to ruminate on their own family planning. These ruminations became the foundation of Landslide, a full-length work set to an original score by Jacobi Vanderham and Britta Johnson.

Landslide premieres at Fall for Dance North on Oct. 24 at Toronto’s Bluma Appel Theatre and continues until Oct. 25. The Globe and Mail caught up with Martin, who is Fall for Dance North’s artist-in-residence and an artistic producer at the National Ballet of Canada, between rehearsals earlier this month.

You’ve described Landslide as “a call to parenthood.” What does that mean?

The dancer who had a baby was the first in our group to become a parent, and it felt like a huge change for all of us. We all have our own perspectives on parenthood – we have every window into the topic across the group. But the thing that I’m most interested in, more than the decision itself, is what it means to be right in the centre of the deliberation, in a sort of time pressure-cooker with yourself, your body and your community.

I’m curious now as to what this actually looks like. What is the movement quality and the movement language you’ve created to explore this deliberation.

I love that the question about parenthood sits so deeply in the body. And so it lends itself really well to the absurdity and the surrealism that I love playing with in everything that I make. Placing that into the pelvis, or the way the body tilts and shifts – it creates something really idiosyncratic. There’s this buoyancy that’s shown up in the movement. There’s more jumping than we’ve ever done.

What can dance tell us about parenthood that another medium can’t?

Dance is so deeply personal. As I mature in my career, I’m realizing that the way an audience member interprets a piece is so revealing of who they are as a person. And the way a dancer dances a piece is equally revealing. And parenthood is so deeply personal – and the choice is so deeply personal. That’s what I came to realize while creating this work; there’s no universally sweeping comment we could have possibly made. It’s been more interesting to invest in the topography of the personal.

How can we make contemporary dance appeal to a broader audience?

I think this is so important for the survival of the form. We can consider catering to different attention spans; we can consider offering more variety within the work so that people have more cues and clues and things to bite on. There’s also something about trusting the audience as interpreters – there needs to be a trust built around a diverse range of interpretations of the form, and that needs to be celebrated in order for people to feel included and on the inside of the bit.

You work with ballet dancers at the National Ballet of Canada, contemporary ones in your company and even actors these days. Do you cater your choreography to the individual or is your choreography a consistent language spoken by different bodies?

I think a little bit of both. I think my priorities are always the same. I prioritize a dynamic body and a brave, brazen, sharp-toothed punk energy. And then I will consider the movement history of the individual I’m working with. I’m trying to intuit their pathways so they feel both challenged and really good about where we’re going.

Tell me about the early days of Rock Bottom – how did you get to the place where you are the artist-in-residence at Ffdn and an artistic producer at the National Ballet of Canada?

We busked outside of the theatres where we aspired to perform. There were five of us, sometimes we had live musicians, and we danced in the park across from the Bluma Appel and in David Pecaut Square across from the Royal Alex. I thought maybe someone from these theatres would walk by and we’d have a big break and, somehow, it would all work out. And it did. . .it just took a decade longer!

This interview has been edited and condensed.

stories.title: Ontario to table fall fiscal update, Finance Minister warns of future deficits amid tariff and oil turmoil
stories.summary: Peter Bethlenfalvy says deficits are necessary as the province faces U.S. tariffs targeting its steel, auto and manufacturing sectors
stories.author: Jeff Gray
stories.content:
Ontario’s Finance Minister says he will release a fall economic update next Thursday, while warning that his province will continue to run deficits as it reels from a slower economy strained by U.S. tariffs and rising energy prices largely caused by the Iran war.

In a speech on Thursday morning before the Canadian Club in Toronto, Peter Bethlenfalvy also said his government is planning a new multibillion-dollar tax break for businesses.

The move is expected to match Ottawa’s proposed “productivity mega deduction,” which is meant to spur investment in new machinery and factories.

In his remarks, Mr. Bethlenfalvy said budget deficits were needed as Ontario faces tariffs that have hit its steel, auto and manufacturing industries hard.

He pointed to the $30-billion that the province has pledged to support businesses and workers affected by the trade war – although much of that money has yet to be spent. And he mentioned Wednesday’s announcement, with Prime Minister Mark Carney, of nearly $9-billion in joint federal-provincial support for the steel, auto and mining sectors.

But he also argued that Ontario has the fiscal room to manage the strain.

“Ontario has weathered the impact of tariffs better than economists had thought, but the slower economy has impacted our deficit, which was $13-billion last year and is predicted to be higher this year,” Mr. Bethlenfalvy said. “And while deficits are not desirable in the long term, they are necessary in the current environment.”

Mr. Bethlenfalvy also said the province is “planning to lower the cost of capital investments for Ontario businesses by providing over $8-billion in additional relief.”

He said this new move, combined with the accelerated write-offs Ontario announced earlier this year for businesses that invest in things such as new equipment, will amount to more than $12-billion in tax relief over the next five years.

At the federal level, the Prime Minister has announced a proposed “productivity mega deduction” that would allow companies to immediately write off the cost of a wide range of new capital investments.

Federal Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said this week that he would unveil his government’s budget on Nov. 5.

Ontario ran a $13-billion deficit in 2025-26 and has previously projected a $13.8-billion deficit for the current year, 2026-27, as a weakening economy slows the growth of the revenues Ontario takes in from corporate and income taxes.

Mr. Bethlenfalvy did not provide an updated figure on Thursday for the current year’s deficit. His government’s plan to balance its books has already been pushed back several times, with its most-recent projections showing a small surplus by 2028-29.

Provincial governments across the country projected large deficits earlier this year in the face of economic uncertainty. B.C. projected a record $13.3-billion budget hole and Quebec warned that it would be $8.6-billion in the red.

But Mr. Bethlenfalvy argues that his province, even with its large net debt – last projected at $485-billion – is in better fiscal shape than its peers.

He said Ontario benefits from borrowing costs that are low compared with previous decades and, he said, the lowest in Canada, thanks in part to the province’s practice of issuing long-term 30-year bonds and borrowing in advance.

He also said that credit-rating agencies have rewarded the province’s handling of its books with two upgrades. He pointed to Ontario’s net-debt-to-GDP ratio (last projected at 37.7 per cent) and the percentage of its revenue that it pays in interest costs (6.7 per cent, but projected to rise, in the 2026 budget), saying they were at their lowest levels in more than a decade.

In his remarks, he ruled out balancing the books by either raising taxes or cutting health care. However, he vowed that the province “will continue to root out wasteful spending, review agencies and ministries for efficiencies, curtail our headcounts and take actions to save taxpayer dollars and enhance value for money.”

He acknowledged that the pandemic and the tariffs had “pushed out the time frame to balance” but said “it remains a goal of our government.”

Echoing comments from both Mr. Carney and Mr. Ford, Mr. Bethlenfalvy started off his speech on Thursday by warning that the world had changed: “We are living in a post-free-trade, protectionist mercantilist world.”

stories.title: Ontario man convicted in U.S. terror plot gets 50 more years for stabbing prison staff
stories.summary: Officials also say a note in El Bahnasawy's sock made reference to a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
An Ontario man convicted of plotting a terrorist attack in the U.S. has been handed an additional 50-year sentence for stabbing two American prison staff.

The U.S. Department of Justice says Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy was an inmate at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood in Pennsylvania when he stabbed two correctional officers in December 2020.

It says the weapon, made from part of a steel desk in his cell, was used to stab one guard’s hand and the other guard’s head and face, causing the latter to lose his right eye.

Officials also say a note in El Bahnasawy’s sock made reference to a terrorist attack for the Islamic State, and a pledge of allegiance to the group was found in his cell.

He has been serving a sentence for plotting bombings and shootings on behalf of Isis in New York City.

The 28-year-old pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to Isis, a designated foreign terrorist organization. The additional sentence will be served consecutive to his previous 40-year conviction.

stories.title: Why has B.C.’s snap election caught both main parties unprepared?
stories.summary: The NDP has meanwhile pivoted its messaging from focusing on U.S. President Donald Trump, to affordability, to the need for a stable majority.
stories.author: Nono Shen
stories.content:
When a snap election is called, at least one side would normally be prepared.

But that hasn’t been the case in British Columbia, resulting in a provincial election campaign like no other, political watchers say.

The campaign has seen interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson going without media availabilities on several days, including on Tuesday and Wednesday in the home stretch, ahead of Saturday’s final voting day.

The NDP has meanwhile pivoted its messaging from focusing on U.S. President Donald Trump, to affordability, to the need for a stable majority.

And campaigning has also been notably muted with relatively few large-scale rallies, although both major parties have events scheduled this week.

Even the NDP campaign bus, which was adorned with Eby’s smiling face in 2024, is an anonymous-looking coach, devoid of slogans.

Hamish Telford, an associate professor of political science at the University of the Fraser Valley, said he had noticed the “lack of preparation.”

“This is especially surprising since the NDP called this election. You would think, if they were going to call a snap election, that they at least would be prepared, and that they would obviously catch the Conservatives off guard,” said Telford.

“This was an election of their making, and they are not entirely ready for it,” he added.

Telford said the NDP had initially been anticipating Eby running against Kerry-Lynne Findlay, a divisive and unpopular leader of the Conservatoves. But Findlay resigned and was replaced by Doerkson.

Eby called the snap election anyway.

Telford said he would have advised the NDP not to go through with it.

“They should have called the election off, but evidently things were too late, or they had built up too much momentum and couldn’t stop themselves.” said Telford.

Angelo Isidorou, who is chief strategist for the Conservatives, said snap elections can be messy compared with fixed-date polls.

“In this case, this is what makes this very unique … not only is it a snap election, but it was an election that took place at the same time as municipal elections, which never happens. So, it was all very chaotic,” said Isidorou of the Oct. 17 municipal polls across B.C.

He said the “biggest difference” between a snap election and a fixed-date election is the “predictability.”

“It’s difficult being in Opposition because you don’t know when the election is going to come, and when an election is called, you only have maybe over a week to recruit candidates and get them on the ballot because there’s a deadline. When there’s a fixed election, you can predict all of this,” said Isidorou.

“In this case, it wasn’t, and I think what surprised me the most is really how not prepared the NDP was,” said Isidorou, adding that otherwise, the NDP would have fielded a full slate of 93 candidates in every riding.

Elections BC said the NPD was one short of a full slate, after failing to nominate a representative in Peace River North.

But vetting May have suffered in the rush to field candidates.

While the Conservatives managed to fill their 93-riding slate, two candidates have since been disavowed by the party.

Jordan McIntosh, the 18-year-old former Conservative candidate for Vancouver-Strathcona, was dumped last Thursday over online posts that included saying Hitler killed “lots of Jews” not because he “hated them specifically” but because there were so many of them.

Another candidate, Joachim Agou, was ejected from the party earlier this month for online comments saying the driver of a car that rammed a pro-Palestinian protest group in Switzerland should have “reversed too.”

Political scientist Michael Prince said the election has “elements of some really unusual features.”

He said it was puzzling to see parties still fall into the trap of recruiting inappropriate candidates.

“They haven’t really thoroughly vetted their history of social media posts,” said Prince, the Lansdowne professor emeritus of social policy at the University of Victoria.

“We’ve seen, particularly on the Conservative side, candidates that have been removed by the leader or have stepped down very quickly,” he said. “So, that’s kind of the new unusual, but it’s been something that’s unfortunately pretty typical over the last several elections.”

stories.title: B.C. NDP Leader Eby campaigns in Vancouver, while Tories heads to Surrey
stories.summary: British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby campaigns in Vancouver and Richmond Thursday after wrapping his swing through the vote-rich city of Surrey with a rally.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby campaigns in Vancouver and Richmond Thursday after wrapping his swing through the vote-rich city of Surrey with a rally.

Hundreds of people attended the gathering near City Hall on Wednesday.

Eby made six stops in the Surrey-Delta area throughout the day to meet with seniors and visit a trucking company.

Meanwhile, interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson is set to make an announcement in B.C.’s second-largest city, where 10 ridings are up for grabs.

He’s also expected to hold a rally in Surrey later tonight.

Advance voting also wrapped up on Wednesday, ahead of Saturday’s election.

stories.title: Ontario to table fall fiscal update next week with 'disciplined' spending approach
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's finance minister says he will table his government's fall economic statement next week, ON Oct. 29.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Peter Bethlenfalvy announced in a breakfast speech to the Canadian Club today that the document will provide an update on the province’s finances and outline the next phase of his plan.

He did not divulge any details, but says it will continue with a “focused, disciplined and responsible approach” to spending.

Article continues below

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Ontario closed out the 2025-26 fiscal year with a $13-billion deficit, and Bethlenfalvy says today that this year’s is projected to be higher, which would be in line with the spring budget forecast of $13.8 billion.

Bethlenfalvy in the 2026 budget delayed the province’s path to balance, projecting it will be in the black in 2028-29.

He says today that Ontario has weathered the impacts of American tariffs better than economists had thought, but the slower economy is having an impact and leading to deficits as a necessity.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge mass shooting conspirator set to enter plea in U.S. court
stories.summary: The alleged co-conspirator in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., is expected to enter a plea at an arraignment in a Seattle courthouse Thursday.
stories.author: Brenna Owen
stories.content:
The alleged co-conspirator in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge , B.C., is expected to enter a plea at an arraignment in a Seattle courthouse Thursday.

A grand jury in Washington state last week indicted 30-year-old James Bryant for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

The criminal complaint against Bryant, who uses female pronouns and goes by the name Melody, alleges she colluded with shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar online, helping set up an attempted livestream of the murders.

The complaint says Bryant also advised 18-year-old Van Rootselaar on where to carry out the attack and sent the shooter money to buy a lighter for an explosive device.

Van Rootselaar killed eight victims last February, including five students and an educational assistant at the local secondary school, before she fatally shot herself as police closed in.

Bryant has been denied bail.

A statement from the U.S. Justice Department says conspiracy to murder in a foreign country is punishable by up to life in prison.

It cautions that the accusations against Bryant remain unproven.

stories.title: Carney lands in Turkey for meetings with Erdogan, business leaders
stories.summary: Joining Prime Minister Mark Carney on the trip are Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Turkey on Thursday to kick off a three-day trip aimed at deepening political and economic ties with the Nato ally.

Carney is set to meet with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara, in what the Prime Minister’s Office says will be the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey.

Shortly after landing on Thursday, Carney laid a wreath at the mausoleum of Turkish founding father Mustafa Kemal Ataturk.

Joining Carney on the trip are Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson.

Senior government officials told reporters ahead of the trip that Hodgson’s presence on the trip speaks to the importance of energy projects in talks between the nations.

Canada and Turkey do about $4 billion in trade annually and formally launched talks to pursue a free-trade pact on the sidelines of the Nato summit in Ankara earlier this year.

Carney is in Turkey for a three-day trip that experts say should show how his approach to international diplomacy differs from that of the previous Liberal government. Carney’s office says this is the first official bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey.

Carney’s bid to diversify trade beyond the United States and find new global investors for Canadian infrastructure projects is well-suited to deeper ties with Turkey, said Kerim Uras, the former Turkish ambassador to Canada.

Both the Canadian and Turkish economies need alternatives to the increasingly protectionist U.S. market, Uras said.

While neither country can replace the United States with any one partner, forging connections between middle powers should be part of the path forward, he said.

“One can summarize it like the Carney doctrine meets Turkish pragmatism,” said Uras, now a senior fellow at Carleton University’s Centre in Modern Turkish Studies.

After meeting Erdogan in Ankara, Carney will head to Istanbul for meetings with Turkish business leaders on Friday before heading back to Canada on Saturday.

stories.title: Riverdale home ticks all the boxes, sells $326,000 over asking
stories.summary: Marketing video boosts in-person visits to three-bedroom house near Withrow Park
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
22 Cavell Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $1,589,000 (September, 2026)

Selling price: $1,915,000 (September, 2026)

Previous selling price: Not available

Taxes: $9,292 (2026)

Days on the market: Seven

Listing agent: Suzanne Lewis, Bosley Real Estate Ltd.

Agent Suzanne Lewis created a minute-long marketing video about this three-bedroom house near Withrow Park for sale in September. The reel got lots of hits on Instagram, which Ms. Lewis says boosted in-person visits. One of those visitors mentioned the video when submitting their purchase offer.

“That one post got 120,000 views,” said Ms. Lewis. “Usually, we have about 1,000 to 4,000 views.

“At the open house, people were coming in, saying they wanted to see it because they saw it on Instagram.”

Five buyers ultimately made offers for the detached property. Even without parking, its turnkey condition and family-friendly location led to a sale $326,000 over the asking price.

“There wasn’t a lot on the market in Riverdale, and this was a really beautiful property,” Ms. Lewis said.

“A house that doesn’t need a full reno, is in a good school district, is on a good street, and has decent features, like three bedrooms – there’s always buyers for it.”

This three-storey house, ON a 20- by 120-foot lot, has 2,138 square feet of living space, including a primary bedroom with a balcony and a deck. It also has a fireplace, skylights and a bathroom.

There is a principal room with a fireplace, and a family room off the kitchen with skylights and French doors to the patio.

There are two more bathrooms and a sauna in the basement.

“My client finished the sauna as an authentic Finnish sauna. There are two working, wood-burning fireplaces, and the backyard has a koi pond.”

stories.title: Officials to provide update on fatal fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta
stories.summary: Officials are set to provide an update Thursday about a devastating fire at a Canadian military base in Alberta that left four soldiers dead and dozens more injured.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Officials are set to provide an update Thursday about a devastating fire at a Canadian military base in Alberta that left four soldiers dead and dozens more injured.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland of the 1st Canadian Division has said Saturday’s blaze began as a grass fire, but a violent windstorm sent flames racing toward soldiers training at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.

The fire initially sent 39 wounded to various hospitals, and officials said Wednesday that number was down to 27, with 13 in critical condition.

Roughly 150 people attended a vigil late Wednesday at a church in the nearby town of Wainwright, Alta., southeast of Edmonton.

Prayers were said, songs were sung and the names of those killed were read aloud, followed by a moment of silence.

Mayor Bruce Pugh says the last few days have been tough, but activities at the base have started to return to normal.

stories.title: Canadian convicted in U.S. terror plot gets 50 more years for stabbing prison staff
stories.summary: An Ontario man convicted of plotting a terrorist attack in the U.S. has been handed an additional 50-year sentence for stabbing two American prison staff.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
An Ontario man convicted of plotting a terrorist attack in the U.S. has been handed an additional 50-year sentence for stabbing two American prison staff.

The U.S. Department of Justice says Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy was an inmate at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood in Pennsylvania when he stabbed two correctional officers in December 2020.

It says the weapon, made from part of a steel desk in his cell, was used to stab one guard’s hand and the other guard’s head and face, causing the latter to lose his right eye.

Officials also say a note in El Bahnasawy’s sock made reference to a terrorist attack for the Islamic State, and a pledge of allegiance to the group was found in his cell.

He has been serving a sentence for plotting bombings and shootings on behalf of Isis in New York City.

The 28-year-old pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to Isis, a designated foreign terrorist organization. The additional sentence will be served consecutive to his previous 40-year conviction.
