Feds investing $1 billion for road to Ring of Fire in Ontario: Carney

stories.title: Feds investing $1 billion for road to Ring of Fire in Ontario: Carney
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government is putting down $1 billion to help build the road to the mineral-rich Ring of Fire region in northern Ontario.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The federal government will put down $1 billion to help build a controversial road to the Ring of Fire region in northern Ontario, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday.

The region is said to be rich in nickel, chromite, copper and gold and Carney said its development will secure Canada’s critical mineral supply chain.

“Canada is matching Ontario’s $1-billion investment to build road infrastructure to reach the Ring of Fire,” Carney said as he and Premier Doug Ford announced in Ottawa an $8.7-billion joint plan to help Ontario’s tariff-affected industries, including steel and automotive sectors.

The Ring of Fire sits partially in the James Bay lowlands, part of North America’s largest wetland, and is home to a number of remote, fly-in First Nations. Its mineral development has been a major focus for Ford since he took office in 2018.

“We can secure a sovereign supply chain and bolster Canada’s position as a critical minerals leader,” Carney said. “Now, to build those mines, we need roads.”

Earlier this year, Ford announced construction had begun on two of the roads that will eventually connect the provincial highway system to the mining area some 500 kilometres north of Thunder Bay, Ont.

Ford had long called for the federal government to match the province’s $1-billion investment in the road project. Ontario’s previous Liberal government had also asked Ottawa to match that money.

“Last December, I joined the prime minister here in Ottawa to sign an agreement that would eliminate federal duplication for the roads to the Ring of Fire,” Ford said Wednesday.

“Thanks to that agreement, we got shovels in the ground on the roads to the Ring of Fire this summer and are well on our way to unlocking, as the prime minister mentioned, 70,000 jobs and $22 billion in economic activity that will be powered by the Ring of Fire’s critical minerals.”

The province has signed partnerships with three First Nations who want the road, while many others are decidedly against it.

Webequie First Nation and Marten Falls First Nation, both remote fly-in communities, want a road to connect to the provincial highway system as well as the economic opportunities in mining the Ring of Fire. They both say it will lift their communities out of poverty.

Aroland First Nation sits further south and its road will be upgraded to handle greater traffic.

Australian mining giant Wyloo and Juno Corp, a Canadian junior mining company, own the vast majority of stakes claimed in the Ring of Fire. Wyloo has proposed to build several mines up north if the road gets built, including a large underground nickel mine.

However, many other First Nations in northern Ontario are against the proposed road and mines. They say they haven’t been consulted and the development will change their way of life.

Neskantaga First Nation and Attawapiskat First Nation have built a settlement where the proposed road will cross the Attawapiskat River. The Canadian Press visited the region last year, including the settlement, where community members plan to block the road whenever construction crews arrive, years from now.

Sol Mamakwa, the provincial New Democrat who represents the riding of Kiiwetinoong, where the Ring of Fire sits, said he was dismayed by the latest news.

He said First Nations are livid at several pieces of provincial and federal legislation, some that have become law, which propose to speed up approvals of large projects, including mines.

“I’ve talked to enough people on the ground that live on these lands for a long time, they’ll be there to protect them and I stand with the rights holders,” Mamakwa said. “Without the proper, free, prior informed consent ... I think that’s going to become an issue.”

Carney said speeding up mine approvals will be imperative, framing it as a way to counter U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods.

But the prime minister said Canada and Ontario are creating “a working group to engage with local Indigenous communities so together we’ll identify opportunities for economic development, conservation and Indigenous protected areas.”

Mamakwa said those words are meaningless.

“It’s just two white men in Ottawa deciding what’s going to happen with our lands,” he said.

“That project will not happen.”

By Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press

OTTAWA - Some government websites have been taken down temporarily as a precaution against a security risk, says Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon.

In a social media post, Solomon says the websites went dark to protect government systems and Canadians’ information following guidance from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security.

He says this is being done in response to a vulnerability identified in PHP, a widely used programming language.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Solomon says this is a global issue and governments and organizations around the world are also taking protective measures.

The FBI’s cyber division says the vulnerability could allow malicious actors to remotely execute code in the programming language, potentially compromising sensitive data and networks.

The PHP Foundation, which includes developers who work on securing the programming language, says it has released fixes for the vulnerabilities, along with instructions on how to update systems.

With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Some Canadian government websites taken offline due to vulnerability: Solomon
stories.summary: Some Government of Canada websites have been taken offline due to a vulnerability identified in the software, Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Evan Solomon says.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
Some Government of Canada websites have been taken offline due to a vulnerability identified in the software, Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Evan Solomon says.

In a social media post, Solomon said this response is temporary and is only a precaution to protect government systems and Canadians’ information.

The guidance came from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security.

“We take this situation extremely seriously. Thank you to the cyber security teams working to protect the services Canadians rely on. Affected websites will be restored once patches are applied,” said Solomon.

He added this is a global issue and other governments and organizations are also taking protective measures.

Among the websites that appear to be offline are Statistics Canada and Measurement Canada, which is a regulatory agency of Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada.

The Fbi’s cyber division says the vulnerability could allow malicious actors to remotely execute code in the programming language, potentially compromising sensitive data and networks.

The PHP Foundation, which includes developers who work on securing the programming language, says it has released fixes for the vulnerabilities, along with instructions on how to update systems.

With files from the Canadian Press

stories.title: Life-threatening injuries reported after Middlesex County collision
stories.summary: In a post on social media, OPP said at least one person appeared to have sustained life-threatening injuries and was expected to be transported for treatment.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A serious two-vehicle collision has closed a rural intersection in Middlesex County, according to Ontario Provincial Police.

Middlesex OPP, along with Middlesex-London Paramedic Service, Ornge air ambulance and local fire crews, responded to the crash at the intersection of Nairn Road and Centre Road on Wednesday.

In a post on social media, OPP said at least one person appeared to have sustained life-threatening injuries and was expected to be transported for treatment.

No further information on the extent of injuries or the number of people involved was immediately available.

Motorists are being asked to avoid the area and seek alternate routes.

stories.title: Man dead in ‘chaotic’ Richmond Hill fire that resulted in homes, vehicles ablaze
stories.summary: It was a “chaotic scene” with three cars fully engulfed in flames between the two houses that were also ablaze, fire crews told reporters Wednesday.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A man is dead after a fire ripped through two homes and several vehicles in Richmond Hill Wednesday morning.

It was a “chaotic scene” with three cars fully engulfed in flames between the two houses that were also ablaze, fire crews told reporters Wednesday.

The fire began on Crosby Avenue between Newkirk Road and Bayview Avenue around 3 a.m., York Regional Police said. A man was found unresponsive and was transported to hospital where he was later pronounced dead, police said.

The chaos of the environment made it challenging for fire crews to tackle the blaze, said Richmond Hill Fire Chief Tom Raeburn at a morning news conference.

Crews were still putting out hot spots on one of the homes when a man was pulled from the basement window, said Raeburn. Several other residents were able to escape on their own.

It was challenging to access the entrances to the houses, as some of the vehicles on fire were blocking the path, he said. The cause of the fire is unknown, and it is too early to determine if the incident is suspicious, said Raeburn.

David West, the mayor of Richmond Hill said Wednesday that “this is a heartbreaking morning for our community.”

“The hearts of the community of Richmond Hill are with the family and everyone affected by this tragedy,” he said in a statement published to social media.

The Office of the Fire Marshal has been called and is working alongside investigators to determine the origin of the blaze.

The fire began on Crosby Avenue between Newkirk Road and Bayview Avenue around 3 a.m., York Regional Police said. A man was found unresponsive and was transported to hospital where he was later pronounced dead, police said.
content_blocks.html: The fire began on Crosby Avenue between Newkirk Road and Bayview Avenue around 3 a.m., York Regional Police said. A man was found unresponsive and was transported to hospital where he was later pronounced dead, police said.

content_blocks.text: The chaos of the environment made it challenging for fire crews to tackle the blaze, said Richmond Hill Fire Chief Tom Raeburn at a morning news conference.
Crews were still putting out hot spots on one of the homes when a man was pulled from the basement window, said Raeburn. Several other residents were able to escape on their own.

It was challenging to access the entrances to the houses, as some of the vehicles on fire were blocking the path, he said. The cause of the fire is unknown, and it is too early to determine if the incident is suspicious, said Raeburn.
David West, the mayor of Richmond Hill said Wednesday that “this is a heartbreaking morning for our community.”
“The hearts of the community of Richmond Hill are with the family and everyone affected by this tragedy,” he said in a statement published to social media.
The Office of the Fire Marshal has been called and is working alongside investigators to determine the origin of the blaze.

stories.title: Smith tells UCP separatists to move on from referendum or find a new party
stories.summary: Alberta Premier says her party can’t afford to be split over the issue and risk losing next year’s provincial election to the NDP
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is urging separatists to accept the results of Monday’s referendum or leave her United Conservative Party in an effort to stave off an internal civil war that she says would sink the party in next year’s provincial election.

Ms. Smith, in a video posted to social media on Wednesday, stressed the need for unity within the province’s conservative movement and warned that infighting would hand the general election scheduled for next October to the Alberta NDP.

But Ms. Smith was not clear about what measures she’s willing to take to smother separatist leanings inside her party. She said she expects MLAs, UCP nominees and members of her party’s board and constituency associations to be committed to “a strong Alberta within a united Canada.”

“As a party, we cannot permit the next year to be one of internal division and endless debates about separation, when Albertans have spoken so clearly against it,” Ms. Smith said in the video.

Until now, Ms. Smith had not shared how she planned to address the large segment of her coalition that supports separation – particularly after the possibility of a future referendum was soundly defeated on Monday night.

Albertans rejected the prospect of separation, with roughly 75 per cent of voters preferring to remain in Canada rather than hold a second, binding secession vote.

Ms. Smith has pledged not to hold another separation referendum as long as she’s Premier, while pointing to her plan to carve out more autonomy from the federal government. She decided in May to put the question to electors after a separatist petition trying to force a binding vote ran into a legal roadblock.

The Premier was explicit in her Wednesday video about the party’s position on separation: “The United Conservative Party is not an independence party.”

“And for those few who cannot reconcile this fact and remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement, I would respectfully invite them to join a different party.”

She indicated on Wednesday that her party is turning its focus to the next provincial election. Her popularity has suffered in public opinion polls over recent months, underlined by a shocking by-election loss for her party last month in Calgary’s conservative heartland.

Leading up to the referendum, the Alberta NDP under Leader Naheed Nenshi attempted to paint Ms. Smith as a separatist. Ms. Smith said she voted for Alberta to remain in Canada, and she campaigned for the remain side last week with Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Ms. Smith has been facing frustration from many of those in her party who felled former premier Jason Kenney and subsequently hoisted her to the Premier’s Office in 2022, largely on the back of frustration over COVID-19 restrictions. Many of those people now harbour separatist sentiment.

In the days since the referendum, the same group has set its sights on electing allies to the party board at the Ucp’s annual meeting in November and as party nominees for the next provincial election. Some have vocally agitated to oust Ms. Smith from office while others have quietly supported her leadership.

The separation issue has, at times this year, pitted her against party brass.

In May, UCP President Rob Smith said he believed a majority of party members would vote to leave Canada, and that the party wouldn’t take a position on the referendum.

Last week, Mr. Smith, who holds no relation to the Premier, wrote on social media that there would be no purity test for party members. He did not respond to an interview request on Wednesday.

“No one will be ‘banned’ or disqualified from membership,” Mr. Smith wrote. “Under no circumstances will that happen. No way. Never.”

The video was Ms. Smith’s first public attempt at stifling separatist rumblings in her party. But she refused to clarify whether she would take steps to limit secessionists from running in party board or nomination races.

”I think a lot of people, when they do their own self-reflection, they make their own decisions about what their pathway would be," she told reporters.

“I’m asking people to do some self-reflection, and if they are able to accept the results and the mandate that Albertans gave us through a free and democratic process, then we can have a reset.”

Ms. Smith’s message didn’t sit well with leading separatists.

Keith Wilson, a lawyer and co-chair of Let Alberta Decide, said in an interview that he thought the Premier was implicitly shutting the door on a key segment of the party.

“It felt like what the Premier was saying today is that if you’re a separatist, you’re not welcome in the UCP,” Mr. Wilson said. “I don’t think she said that expressly, but I know that’s how it’s being felt by many members.”

He added: “Rather than trying to correct the split and unify the party, she might have inadvertently driven a bigger wedge into it.”

Mitch Sylvestre, chief executive of the Alberta Prosperity Project, said this week that he’s continuing to try getting like-minded members elected to the party board, while his separatist colleague Jeffrey Rath has continued his calls for the party membership to oust Ms. Smith.

Mr. Sylvestre said on Wednesday in an interview that he’s not leaving the party and argued the blame would be on Ms. Smith if the UCP loses the next election.

“We put them there to do a job. They have not done the job,” he said.

Mr. Sylvestre said Ms. Smith has failed on three issues that he believes would give Alberta greater autonomy: withdrawing from the Canada Pension Plan, creating a provincial police force and taking strong action on immigration.

Mr. Wilson, however, encouraged Ms. Smith to ignore Mr. Sylvestre’s agitating, adding that he supports her desire to pursue greater autonomy within Confederation.

The Alberta NDP declined to comment on the Ucp’s internal party politics.

Elections Alberta was still counting ballots on Wednesday evening on the other nine questions Ms. Smith put to voters in Monday’s referendum.

With 96 per cent of polls reporting, most of those proposals on immigration and constitutional issues had received support ranging between 50 per cent and 55 per cent. Two constitutional proposals on judicial appointments and federal funding had dropped below 50 per cent and one proposing proof-of-citizenship at provincial election polls had earned 60-per-cent support.

Ms. Smith said the results provide her a mandate to work with Ottawa to give Alberta more say over immigration.

But she hedged on whether she would move forward with the other proposals, such as limiting some non-permanent residents’ access to social services and charging them premiums for using Alberta’s education and health care systems.

“I would say that the results that I saw suggest we proceed with caution,” she said.

stories.title: Mother of Isis terrorist from Ontario running for school board trustee in Milton
stories.summary: Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy was sentenced to 40 years in US prison in 2018. This week he received 50 more years for attacking two guards.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
The mother of a convicted Isis terrorist from Ontario — whose sentence was recently extended by 50 years for another crime — is running to be a Halton District School Board trustee in Milton, just west of Toronto.

Dr. Khdiga Metwally is a candidate for Milton Wards 1 and 2 in the Oct. 26 election. She says she has experience as a life skills teacher, a university department chair, author, speaker and human development instructor, according to her campaign website.

Her son, 28-year-old Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, was convicted in the United States for plotting to carry out 9/11-style attacks in New York City in 2016 on behalf of Isis. The group is listed as a terrorist entity in Canada, and in the U.S. is designated as a foreign terrorist organization. El Bahnasawy was sentenced to 40 years in prison in 2018.

According to the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), El Bahnasawy conspired with others online, using encrypted electronic messaging applications. He then travelled to the U.S. to “to conduct bombings and shootings in heavily populated areas of New York City.”

This week, he was sentenced to an additional 50 years for attacking two correctional officers in 2020. The DOJ said he used a weapon made out of a steel desk in his cell and stabbed one officer in the head and face. He then stabbed another officer in the hand.

“My son has a documented history of severe mental illness. Before the prison incident, we repeatedly pleaded with prison authorities to provide his treatment. We sent his medical records, explained which medications helped him and which harmed him, and offered to put them in contact with his psychiatrist,” Metwally told National Post in an emailed statement.

“We warned that his condition would worsen without proper treatment and also asked the Canadian Embassy to intervene. Our pleas went unanswered, and he did not receive the care he needed.”

Canadian teen convicted of Manhattan terror plot takes on Omar Khadr's legal team

She said he was experiencing a psychotic episode at the time of the prison incident.

In a 2020 U.S. government report about terrorism in Canada, it said that El Bahnasawy’s parents “have alleged the RCMP knew of their son’s medical conditions and should have sought treatment for him.”

Metwally said the “painful experience” has strengthened her “determination, as a school board trustee candidate, to work so that no child or family goes through a similar tragedy.”

“I am committed to early mental health support, strong family–school communication, high academic achievement, and safe schools that protect students from drugs and other dangers. These are the priorities guiding my campaign to serve Milton families,” she said.

“It is about learning from what happened, protecting my son from his current situation and ensuring that he receives the appropriate and humane mental health care he needs.”

“My son has a documented history of severe mental illness. Before the prison incident, we repeatedly pleaded with prison authorities to provide his treatment. We sent his medical records, explained which medications helped him and which harmed him, and offered to put them in contact with his psychiatrist,” Metwally told National Post in an emailed statement.
“We warned that his condition would worsen without proper treatment and also asked the Canadian Embassy to intervene. Our pleas went unanswered, and he did not receive the care he needed.”

She said he was experiencing a psychotic episode at the time of the prison incident.

In a 2020 U.S. government report about terrorism in Canada, it said that El Bahnasawy’s parents “have alleged the RCMP knew of their son’s medical conditions and should have sought treatment for him.”
Metwally said the “painful experience” has strengthened her “determination, as a school board trustee candidate, to work so that no child or family goes through a similar tragedy.”

“I am committed to early mental health support, strong family–school communication, high academic achievement, and safe schools that protect students from drugs and other dangers. These are the priorities guiding my campaign to serve Milton families,” she said.
“It is about learning from what happened, protecting my son from his current situation and ensuring that he receives the appropriate and humane mental health care he needs.”

stories.title: Career college students worry about impact of Osap pause, extended to 2027
stories.summary: Toronto - Now that the Ontario government has confirmed that a provincewide pause on student financial assistance payments to career colleges will last for months, some students say they're worried it will prevent them from graduating.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A provincewide pause on student financial assistance payments to Ontario career colleges will last for months, the government has confirmed, leaving some students worried it will prevent them from graduating.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced late Tuesday afternoon that the pause won’t be lifted until the government establishes a new process for approving private post-secondary institutions under the Ontario Student Assistance Program.

That work isn’t expected to be finished until the new year, he said, and the government is also still working to secure third-party loans for students through banks.

Quinn enacted the pause after he said preliminary findings from an audit into Osap usage at career colleges highlighted serious concerns.

Ministry investigators launched in-person inspections last week at eight career colleges, he said. That is on top of six institutions the government cut off from Osap eligibility earlier this year.

Career Colleges Ontario also said that as part of its own review processes, it has removed seven schools and ownership groups representing 21 campuses from membership in its association.

Many students say they feel unfairly penalized for the allegedly suspicious activity of others. They and the industry association are calling for more of a targeted approach to weed out any bad actors.

“We are disappointed that yesterday’s announcement means students and compliant institutions will continue to face uncertainty until at least the new year,” Career Colleges Ontario wrote in a statement Wednesday.

“While we support stronger oversight measures and proposed legislation to protect Osap’s integrity, many students are struggling to pay rent, support their families, and continue their studies.”

The promise of a resolution months away is cold comfort for students like Jennifer Koster, who is in the law clerk program at Trillium College and was expecting to finish school in February.

“The only way that I could describe it was a bomb being dropped on me,” she said of the news earlier this month that Osap payments were paused for all career college students.

Further complicating matters for Trillium College students is a move late last week by the school to suspend classes at its various campuses due to the uncertainty around Osap. Several students say the college wanted to put them on payment plans with monthly instalments around $1,500, but they couldn’t afford that without Osap.

Koster is on the Ontario Disability Support Program and she would have to put almost her whole monthly disability payment toward tuition at that payment level, she said.

“I went to college to better my future, and now ... it feels like it’s leaving my entire future in jeopardy,” Koster said.

Scott Daley, a massage therapy student at the CTS Canadian Career College campus in Barrie, said the Osap pause and its extension into the new year is a major stressor.

“We’ve had times where we weren’t sure where we were going to be able to get groceries,” Daley said.

“We have to kind of rob Peter just to pay Paul. It’s kind of over the top right now. ... I’ve lost sleep. I’m not eating properly right now because of it.”

Deanna Hutten, a second-year master’s student in McMaster Divinity College’s counselling and spiritual care program, is dropping down to a partial course load and working more hours so she can afford to stay in school.

“This is (because of) something that I didn’t do,” she said. “It’s something that the government mismanaged.”

Quinn said in his statement Tuesday that he knows the pause is affecting students.

“While necessary to protect the integrity of Osap and to protect Ontario taxpayers from abuse, we understand the impact that this work is having on students and families across the province,” he wrote.

“This impact is not lost on us as we work to restore integrity to the system and provide students with greater certainty and stability as quickly as possible.”

Marina Whitehead, a Trillium College student in the community developmental service worker program, said she too is supposed to finish in February and now doesn’t know if that will happen.

She is frustrated both with the government’s sweeping Osap pause and Trillium’s handling of it.

“The government, they get to finish their day at five, go home to their families, and not have to worry about where their next meal is going to come from,” Whitehead said.

“They’re not going to have to worry about an eviction notice in the mail. They’re not going to have to worry about putting in so much hard work just to throw it down the drain. ... I would love for them to walk a mile in us, the students’ shoes.”

Students at various colleges and campuses are organizing protests and rallies against the Osap pause, including Saturday in St. Catharines and Tuesday in North Bay.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: NDP focuses on Surrey, B.C., battleground as election enters home stretch
stories.summary: Surrey - Health remains a top item on the British Columbia election agenda as the campaign enters its final days.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Surrey - NDP Leader David Eby says the B.C. Conservatives are behaving “as if they’ve won” the provincial election by focusing on fundraising instead of taking questions from the media in the last days of the campaign.

Final voting day is on Saturday, but interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson did not take questions from reporters on Tuesday and had no media availability scheduled Wednesday.

Instead, he had two fundraising events on his agenda, after five others in the past week, as the Conservatives push for donations to counter what they call NDP attack ads.

Eby said at a campaign stop in the election battleground of Surrey that Doerkson had “gone into hiding.”

“The Conservatives are conducting themselves as if they’ve won the election, but they do not deserve anybody’s vote,” he said.

The Conservatives said Doerkson would return to public campaigning on Thursday with an announcement and media availability in Metro Vancouver, followed by a rally in Surrey.

The party also said Doerkson would not take questions from media on election night.

“Should the Conservative Party of B.C. be in a position to form government, a media availability with the leader will be arranged for Sunday, Oct. 25,” the party told media outlets on Wednesday.

Surrey, with its 10 seats, will likely be crucial in the election.

Voting in the election is already well underway.

Advance voting was to close at 8 p.m. Wednesday, and Elections BC said about 711,000 people had voted in the first five days of early polling, down by about 9 per cent compared with the first five days of advance voting in 2024.

Eby said Conservatives would roll back projects important to the region, including a new tunnel under the Fraser River. The Conservatives say they will build a bridge instead.

“We are building the Massey Tunnel, not cancelling and sending people home, driving up costs and waits for drivers,” Eby said.

He said every seat in Surrey is crucial, calling it “a city that has been underappreciated and neglected by previous governments.”

During remarks at a Surrey seniors’ care home, Eby warned of health care cuts should the Conservatives come to power.

“They have committed to spending a lot of money, but they have also committed to paying for it with health care cuts, millions of dollars in health care cuts, which will make things so much more challenging,” he said.

The Conservatives have not said exactly what they would cut to achieve savings that they outline in their platform.

The party’s platform says they would fix health care in B.C. with policies including a pledge to keep rural emergency rooms and maternity wards open, via flexible staffing and a $50-million “rural health emergency fund.”

The B.C. Green Party made two announcements on Vancouver Island Wednesday.

Leader Emily Lowan said the Greens would bring in new protections for those living in housing subject to long-term leases that aren’t protected under law.

Andrew Appleton, the Green candidate in Oak Bay-Gordon Head, announced a tuition freeze and a funding overhaul for post-secondary institutions if the Greens were to form government.

Eby had appealed to Green voters on the weekend to vote New Democrat, saying a vote for the Greens could make the difference between an NDP and Conservative government.

The leader of another minor party, CentreBC’s Elenore Sturko, was asked Wednesday about strategic voting and if it could have an impact on the election.

But Sturko said her party doesn’t mesh with either the NDP or the Conservatives.

“We are fiscally responsible,” Sturko said as she referred to the Ndp’s $14-billion deficit.

She said her party is socially progressive, unlike the B.C. Conservatives, who have dumped two candidates during the campaign for online remarks. One said a car that drove through a pro-Palestine protest “should have reversed” over them too, while another said Hitler killed “lots of Jews” not because he “hated them specifically” but because there were so many of them.

“We are a party that is inclusive, a party for everyone, and we’re willing to stand up for British Columbians no matter who they love, who they pray to, or where they come from,” Sturko said.

“And so, I think the choice is clear if you’re looking for a true centre party with liberal values.”

Eby said at a campaign stop in the election battleground of Surrey that Doerkson had “gone into hiding.”
“The Conservatives are conducting themselves as if they’ve won the election, but they do not deserve anybody’s vote,” he said.
The Conservatives said Doerkson would return to public campaigning on Thursday with an announcement and media availability in Metro Vancouver, followed by a rally in Surrey.
The party also said Doerkson would not take questions from media on election night.
“Should the Conservative Party of B.C. be in a position to form government, a media availability with the leader will be arranged for Sunday, Oct. 25,” the party told media outlets on Wednesday.
Surrey, with its 10 seats, will likely be crucial in the election.
Voting in the election is already well underway.

Advance voting was to close at 8 p.m. Wednesday, and Elections BC said about 711,000 people had voted in the first five days of early polling, down by about 9 per cent compared with the first five days of advance voting in 2024.
Eby said Conservatives would roll back projects important to the region, including a new tunnel under the Fraser River. The Conservatives say they will build a bridge instead.
“We are building the Massey Tunnel, not cancelling and sending people home, driving up costs and waits for drivers,” Eby said.
He said every seat in Surrey is crucial, calling it “a city that has been underappreciated and neglected by previous governments.”
During remarks at a Surrey seniors’ care home, Eby warned of health care cuts should the Conservatives come to power.

“They have committed to spending a lot of money, but they have also committed to paying for it with health care cuts, millions of dollars in health care cuts, which will make things so much more challenging,” he said.
The Conservatives have not said exactly what they would cut to achieve savings that they outline in their platform.

The party’s platform says they would fix health care in B.C. with policies including a pledge to keep rural emergency rooms and maternity wards open, via flexible staffing and a $50-million “rural health emergency fund.”
The B.C. Green Party made two announcements on Vancouver Island Wednesday.
Leader Emily Lowan said the Greens would bring in new protections for those living in housing subject to long-term leases that aren’t protected under law.
Andrew Appleton, the Green candidate in Oak Bay-Gordon Head, announced a tuition freeze and a funding overhaul for post-secondary institutions if the Greens were to form government.
Eby had appealed to Green voters on the weekend to vote New Democrat, saying a vote for the Greens could make the difference between an NDP and Conservative government.
The leader of another minor party, CentreBC’s Elenore Sturko, was asked Wednesday about strategic voting and if it could have an impact on the election.
But Sturko said her party doesn’t mesh with either the NDP or the Conservatives.
“We are fiscally responsible,” Sturko said as she referred to the Ndp’s $14-billion deficit.

She said her party is socially progressive, unlike the B.C. Conservatives, who have dumped two candidates during the campaign for online remarks. One said a car that drove through a pro-Palestine protest “should have reversed” over them too, while another said Hitler killed “lots of Jews” not because he “hated them specifically” but because there were so many of them.
“We are a party that is inclusive, a party for everyone, and we’re willing to stand up for British Columbians no matter who they love, who they pray to, or where they come from,” Sturko said.
“And so, I think the choice is clear if you’re looking for a true centre party with liberal values.”

stories.title: The Legion is launching its poppy campaign early. Here's what to know
stories.summary: The Royal Canadian Legion is launching its annual national poppy campaign early in part to give Canadians more time to support veterans.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Well before last week’s tragedy at CFB Wainwright in Alberta, the Royal Canadian Legion had already decided this year’s national poppy campaign would begin earlier than it traditionally has.

But now, with four more brave soldiers killed during training exercises at the Canadian Armed Forces base, Canadians should have even more reason to wear a poppy in honour of the country’s fallen service members this Remembrance Day.

Monday morning in Ottawa, attendees at the presentation of the first official poppy to Governor General Louise Arbour held a moment of silence for the four men and their scores of injured comrades.

“As we prepare to enter this year’s Poppy Campaign, this moment was a powerful reminder of the sacrifices made by those who serve our country,” the Legion wrote on its social media channels.

“Our hearts are with the families, loved ones and military community affected by this tragedy. We Will Remember Them.”

Here’s what to know about the 2026 poppy campaign.

Before this year, the Legion adhered to a Canadian Armed Forces dress protocol that the poppy be affixed to uniforms starting the last Friday in October.

It was moved to Oct. 24 to “give more Canadians the opportunity to wear a Poppy, provide more time to raise funds in support of Veterans and their families, and make it easier for businesses, schools and community organizations to plan their participation,” the Legion wrote on social media last month.

The Canadian Armed Forces, meanwhile, announced last week that it would follow the Legion’s lead and require members to start wearing poppies on their uniforms as of Saturday.

“The October 24 start date will provide a consistent national period for remembrance activities in support of Veterans and their families,” the CAF wrote on Oct. 14 .

Aligning with the campaign’s Saturday start, the Legion will also launch the Don’t Forget to Remember initiative to mark its centenary this year.

It will include “the unveiling of a signature stand-alone display in Toronto’s Union Station, with other billboard and vertical versions circulating nationwide.”

“That same day, the Legion will unveil new technology in Canada — the first of its kind in a national fundraising campaign — which will facilitate a revolutionary and extremely convenient donation method.”

National Post has contacted the Legion for additional comment.

While poppies are technically free, donations are welcomed and valued.

The money goes to a trust fund for the Legion in the area where the donation was made. That fund supports veterans, CAF and RCMP members and their families through financial aid, housing, healthcare, transition programs, education, accessibility, community services, disaster relief and Remembrance activities.

“Branch executives are accountable for Poppy Fund expenditures and are required to inform the public through local media of the results of their campaign, including contributions received and disposition of funds,” the Legion explains online.

Canadians can also donate to the National Poppy Fund online to help fund national programs and supports for veterans and their families.

The Legion says the national campaign generates close to $20 million annually.

Like any year, it won’t be hard to find a poppy in Canada.

The Legion identified 29 major companies — mostly retailers and banks — collectively hosting thousands of poppy boxes, including Starbucks, which “will again collect local donations through point-of-sale systems,” and TD Bank, which will distribute poppies at all its Canadian branches.

RBC is also bringing back more than 2,000 of its Pay Tribute tap-enabled boxes “that enable Canadians to donate $5 with a simple tap of a payment card (credit or debit), or through their digital wallet on their mobile and wearable devices.”

Last year, those boxes alone brought in a record-setting $855,000 , the Legion said.

Of course, poppies are also available at almost 1,400 Legion branches throughout Canada.

You can also get your poppy — and other Remembrance-related merchandise — at the Legion’s Poppy Store or its Amazon storefront.

This marks the third year the Legion has partnered with the tech giant’s Canadian arm to sell poppies, with all proceeds supporting trust funds throughout Canada.

“People across our vast country can fulfill their wish to wear a Poppy, including where there are no Legion branches or it is more difficult to find one,” the Legion said.

Last year, more than 50,000 poppies were distributed this wa y, about double the amount in the inaugural year.

Shoppers can donate $5, $10 or $20 for a traditional poppy , or pick up a more permanent 24K gold-plated poppy pin for about $22 after taxes. (Shipping is extra if you’re not an Amazon Prime member.)

They also sell a variety of Remembrance Day lapel pins, magnets and lawn signs , along with scarves, headwear, cross-body bags, mugs, and tote bags bearing the iconic flower . Also on offer are poppy-shaped LED lights and 1,000-piece puzzles marking the Legion’s centenary.

All of the products are also available at The Poppy Store.

If you don’t mind spending a few more dollars at the Legion’s storefront, you can get a 10-pack of black butterfly pin centres for about $23 after taxes that prevent the poppy from falling off.

For those seeking a more frugal approach, there are other ways to secure the poppy.

As reported by National Post in 2019 , some people have been known to stick a piece of pencil eraser or duct tape on the pointed end of the pin to keep it from falling out — and keep from getting stabbed by it. You can also bend the pin with a pair of pliers once inserted or better weave it into the fabric.

Some people swap the original pin for a safety pin, while others use a Canadian flag pin in the centre.

As for where the poppy is worn, the CAF has its own dress instructions on placement, but the Legion advises regular Canadians to wear it as close to the heart as possible on the left side of the chest.

You can also get your poppy — and other Remembrance-related merchandise — at the Legion’s Poppy Store or its Amazon storefront.

content_blocks.text: The Royal Canadian Legion is on Amazon?
This marks the third year the Legion has partnered with the tech giant’s Canadian arm to sell poppies, with all proceeds supporting trust funds throughout Canada.
“People across our vast country can fulfill their wish to wear a Poppy, including where there are no Legion branches or it is more difficult to find one,” the Legion said.
Last year, more than 50,000 poppies were distributed this wa y, about double the amount in the inaugural year.

content_blocks.text: They also sell a variety of Remembrance Day lapel pins, magnets and lawn signs , along with scarves, headwear, cross-body bags, mugs, and tote bags bearing the iconic flower . Also on offer are poppy-shaped LED lights and 1,000-piece puzzles marking the Legion’s centenary.

content_blocks.text: All of the products are also available at The Poppy Store.
My poppy keeps falling off — how can I keep it on?
If you don’t mind spending a few more dollars at the Legion’s storefront, you can get a 10-pack of black butterfly pin centres for about $23 after taxes that prevent the poppy from falling off.
For those seeking a more frugal approach, there are other ways to secure the poppy.

As reported by National Post in 2019 , some people have been known to stick a piece of pencil eraser or duct tape on the pointed end of the pin to keep it from falling out — and keep from getting stabbed by it. You can also bend the pin with a pair of pliers once inserted or better weave it into the fabric.

stories.title: Cyber security awareness: how to spot a scam
stories.summary: Artificial Intelligence has made it easier and faster than ever for scammers to trick people into giving up pe...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Artificial Intelligence has made it easier and faster than ever for scammers to trick people into giving up personal information and money, say police and technology experts.

One technology expert says he uses a password with his family to prevent scams.

“I’ve seen people lose everything in one day,” said Carmi Levy a technology analyst and journalist in London.

“As technology gets better scammers have better tools to make it look less like a scam, and cover more ground all at the same time,” Levy said

Carmi Levy (Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM News)

As AI becomes more advanced scammers have the tools to make it look or sound more realistic.

“With all social media all it takes is one video or photo you post for scammers to use against people you know,” Levy said

The ‘grandfather scam’ is one of the more common scams used among people of all ages especially people over 60, said Levy. It’s becoming more common as scammers are able to use AI to make their voice sound almost identical to a loved one. They would act like someone you care about saying they have been in an accident saying they need money to pay for damages.

Since 2022 over $2.4 billion has been reported stolen through scams.

“It is used to get inside our circle of trust, if you think it’s someone close to you and it’s a tragedy, you will get emotional and make decisions you normally wouldn’t make,”

Levy and his family use a code word if any of these incidents happen. If they get any call suspected to be a relative he ask for “what’s our code word” if the person doesn’t know it is a scammer.

“It’s a rule I taught my kids and I think every family should do is sit at the table, create a word that everyone will know and that’s how we identify a scammer,”

Levy also stated no one is safe as even young people who think they know a scam when they see one still can fall for it. As scammers also use AI videos trying to target all age levels.

The most common scam people face are ‘imposter scams’ where scammers pose as a bank employee, a member of the school, or government agencies demanding or asking for money.

Screenshot of an import charge scam (Credit: Daniel Thuss XFM news)

“Your bank, never calls you out of the blue, same thing with your school, and government agencies. sometimes it’s ok to be rude to stop the interaction and do your own research. Because nine out ten times it is a scam,” said Levy

Cafc fraud numbers (Credit: The Global Statstics)

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (Cafc) received over 122 thousand fraud reports through 2025 and it was estimated that it counted for only 5-10% of nation wide frauds.

Investment fraud in 2025 reached a record high of over $351 million lost to scams, which totals around 50% of the total fraud lost in 2025. In 2024 it was reported by Cafc that almost a quarter of seniors in Canada lost money to scams with an average lost of over $21 thousand. For more information London Police Service has an Elderly Safety page.

If you or know someone that has been scammed you can contact the Cafc or your local police fraud services.

stories.summary: Oshawa - Durham regional police say a two-year-old girl was critically injured when a car struck a group of young children and a daycare worker in Oshawa.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Oshawa - Durham regional police say a two-year-old girl was critically injured when a car struck a group of young children and a daycare worker in Oshawa.

Acting Sgt. Nicholas Gluckstein says the daycare worker was on her daily walk with five children through a residential neighbourhood this morning when they were all struck by a car while crossing the street.

stories.title: The number of people using food banks continues to rise in Quebec
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - A new report says the demand at Quebec food banks is continuing to break records.
stories.author: Stéphane Rolland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTRÉAL - A new report says the demand at Quebec food banks is continuing to break records.

The 2026 Hunger Count report was published by Food Banks of Quebec.

It says the food banks are now fulfilling 3.27 million requests each month.

But close to 14 per cent of the network’s 1,400 community organizations say they had to turn people away because of food shortages.

The report adds that 70 per cent of organizations say they faced a shortage in the last year.

The report says the situation has been deteriorating since the pandemic.

“Needs remain at a historically high level,” Food Banks of Quebec Executive Director Alexandre Lebel told The Canadian Press. “There are far too many people who still have to rely on food assistance.”

Among the households assisted in 2026, nearly a quarter derive most of their income from a job, shows the report.

“Having a job doesn’t necessarily protect you from food insecurity,” says Lebel.

Chantal Vézina, executive director of Moisson Montréal, says that inflation is making it harder for households to get out of difficult financial situations.

“Unfortunately, food is a discretionary expense, and people will do whatever it takes, of course, to avoid ending up on the street,” she says.

Children account for around one-third of recipients in food banks, says Lebel.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Toddler in critical condition after group of children struck by vehicle in Oshawa
stories.summary: Police said the children were walking in the area of Ryerson Crescent and Sheridan Way with a daycare worker when they were all struck.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A two-year-old girl is in critical condition and four other children are also in hospital with minor injuries after they were struck by a vehicle in Oshawa, Ont.

Durham police said the incident happened at around 9:30 a.m. Wednesday.

Police announced at an afternoon news conference that the children were walking in the area of Ryerson Crescent and Sheridan Way with a daycare worker when they were all struck. The daycare worker, a woman, has also been taken to hospital with serious, but non-life threatening injuries.

The two-year-old was airlifted by Ornge ambulance to a Toronto-area trauma centre.

Investigators are at the scene looking into the cause of the incident, said Acting Sgt. Nicolas Gluckstein at the collision scene.

“We’ll look at any kind of distracted driving, whether it was cell phones or eating or anything of that nature. We’ll look at impairments, whether that’s a factor,” he said.

The driver has also been taken to hospital with minor injuries, and police suggested that it May be related to the emotional impact of the incident. Gluckstein said the driver remained on scene and is cooperating with investigators.

The intersection is shut down while police investigate.

stories.title: Alberta will take inspiration from Quebec on immigration issues, Danielle Smith says
stories.summary: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says the provincial government will seek inspiration from Quebec on strengthening its grip on immigration.
stories.author: Hiren Mansukhani
stories.content:
Premier Danielle Smith says the provincial government will seek inspiration from Quebec on strengthening its grip on immigration and wresting more control over the issue from Ottawa.

“If you have a good-paying job, then that allows you to start putting down roots and making a decision if you want to go on a pathway to permanent residency and ultimately citizenship,” Smith said at a news conference Wednesday.

“With this mandate, (we have) begun the conversations with the federal government about how we can move in that direction.”

The announcement comes as the referendum results show a majority of Albertans support the province taking greater control of immigration policy.

More than 53 per cent of voters said they wanted Alberta to have more control to decrease “immigration to more sustainable levels,” and a similar majority favoured a fee for temporary residents to access basic services, including education and health care.

“Quebec has the ability to select about 65,000 migrants that will suit the needs of their economy. In recent years, they’ve reduced that to about 45,000, and they have different categorizations for economic migrants versus family reunification versus a couple of others,” Smith said.

“That’s the framework of the kind of agreement we would like to negotiate with the federal government to make sure that we’re matching newcomers with the jobs that are here.”

Quebec’s unique immigration rules stem from the Canada-Quebec Accord in 1991, which leveraged Section 95 of the Constitution Act in 1867 that establishes shared legislative power between the provinces and Ottawa over immigration.

Those powers allow Quebec to choose all of its temporary economic immigrants, although final admission can only be approved by Ottawa.

The province sets targets for economic permanent residents, generally assigning lower thresholds than the rest of the country. It also requires students and temporary workers to apply for a certificate issued by the province.

In contrast, Alberta can only select a fraction of its total economic immigrants through its provincial nomination program. It is also unable to have caps on immigration as Quebec does, although Ottawa’s power trumps other forms of immigration, such as family reunification, which has been legally contested.

While roots of Quebec’s policy are cultural — the rules were put in place for immigrants to align with social and cultural norms — Alberta’s motivation is economic.

“Is it the same as French identity in Quebec? I don’t think so,” said Jatin Shory, Calgary-based immigration and refugee lawyer and past chair of the Canadian Bar Association’s National Immigration Section.

“I wouldn’t say (Alberta) is so unique compared to other provinces that it needs to, in the same way as Quebec, have its own kind of parameters around immigration.”

Meanwhile, Quebec’s policies have been prone to sudden shifts that have created more uncertainty for thousands of people .

In 2024, the province paused new applications for both the PEQ Graduates stream and the Regular Skilled Worker Program, leaving thousands of temporary residents in limbo as their work and study permits were due to expire before the pathways opened in July of this year.

“There was so much backlash from employers, from the economic community, from Chambers of Commerce, because the change in policy was so radical and had such a huge impact on the labour force that the government, subsequent to all of these pressures, actually went back on its own policy and they reopened the program because employers were telling the government we need people,” said Christine Beltempo, Montreal-based legal counsel at McCarthy Tetault and a chair of the Canadian Bar Association’s National Immigration Section.

That same year, the province declared a six-month freeze on applications from temporary foreign workers for low-wage jobs in the Montreal region, while pausing Labour Market Impact Assessments for job offers in Montreal paying below the province’s median hourly wage of $27.47.

“That created a huge climate of instability in the province for newcomers,” Beltempo said. It has also led to frustrating delays for immigrants who have to navigate additional layers of bureaucracy that push the timeline of their applications by several years.

Emulating Quebec, Shory said, could have other unintended consequences, such as significantly raising spending on immigration.

“I think putting in place infrastructure officers, understanding that immigration at a federal level is highly litigious right now — look at federal courts and how backlogged they are,” Shory said. “I imagine judicial review applications around immigration could skyrocket in the province.”

Smith said the referendum results simply demonstrate the need for such talks.

“We know that the success of newcomers is hinged almost entirely on being able to have a good-paying job,” she said.

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: Publisher cuts ties with Quebec author after finding evidence of AI use
stories.summary: Montreal - A Quebec publishing house is cutting ties with author Thélyson Orélien after saying it found evidence he used artificial intelligence to write his debut novel.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A Quebec publishing house is cutting ties with author Thélyson Orélien after saying it found evidence he used artificial intelligence to write his debut novel.

Les Éditions du Boréal said in a press release that analysis of some documents’ metadata indicated AI was used while writing the book.

The publisher said it will not reprint the book or publish more books by Orélien.

Orélien did not respond to The Canadian Press’ request for comment.

The allegations of AI use in his book, “C’était ça ou mourir” (“It was either that or dying”), emerged on social media in September. An account using the name “Balance ton Claude” alleged that, according to the Pangram software, excerpts of Orélien’s novel had been written “almost entirely by artificial intelligence.”

The novel explores a Haitian refugee’s journey to Quebec. The story is based on Orélien’s own experience leaving Haiti after the 2010 earthquake, the author has said.

Initially, the publisher and Orélien said they were working on gathering a detailed record to prove the book had not been written using AI. But a few weeks later, the publisher said the author had decided to end the process.

“While we do not, now or in the future, accept to play the role of investigator in relation to our authors, this extraordinary situation made it clear we could not simply leave matters as they were,” the publisher wrote Wednesday in its press release.

It decided to lead its own investigation and order an external analysis of the different versions of the manuscript, which revealed traces of “AI markers,” said the publisher.

“We still do not know to what extent AI was used in the creation of ‘C’était ça ou mourir,’ and we will likely never have a definitive answer,” it wrote.

The publisher said this case raises a fundamental question on the trust between authors and publishers.

“We chose this book because it moved us deeply, long before its success in bookstores and awards. We understand the disappointment felt by some, and we share it,” it wrote.

The book was set for a new printing this week.

The author has denied using AI to write the book, saying he started working on it in 2017 and finished the first draft in 2019. He said he had used AI for research.

“What I am going through is cruel,” he wrote in an Oct. 13 press release. “By attributing a text, one that is mine ... to a machine, they have not only called into question my status as a writer but also my humanity.”

Separately, he admitted plagiarism in some of his early work after media reported resemblances — or, in some cases, near-identical paragraphs — between some of Orélien’s texts and other books or news reports. The author apologized for what he described as unacceptable mistakes of his youth, while maintaining that no sentence in his novel was generated by a machine.

Before the controversy, the novel won the Prix du Roman Fnac and earned nominations for several major French literary awards. Since the allegations emerged, it has been removed from the running for France’s prestigious Prix Goncourt.

Boréal suspended promotional activities surrounding the novel in September, citing concerns for the author’s well-being.

Floriane Claveau, spokesperson for the major Quebec bookstore chain Renaud-Bray, told The Canadian Press Boréal’s decision to cut ties with the author would not make a big difference for the bookstores — until his book runs out.

“If a book is available and there is demand, we simply keep it available. We don’t position ourselves as judges or censors of content,” she said.

She said the book sold out in several Renaud-Bray libraries.

Pierre-Yves Villeneuve, president of the Quebec writers’ union, praised the publisher’s decision.

“We’ve just declared clearly that this type of work doesn’t have its place on our shelves,” he said in an interview.

He denounced how the publisher’s previously ambiguous information on possible AI use in Orélien’s book put the burden on readers to decide whether to buy the book.

“It’s a situation that was completely unfair, because the reader didn’t have any information to know whether this book was really written by Thélyson (Orélien),” said Villeneuve.

While he is happy with the publisher’s decision, he called on Boréal to release more details on the evidence they found indicating AI use. This information could help readers better understand the situation and provide a possible road map for industry professionals in similar situations.

“They had promised us a detailed record, and they did not deliver,” said Villeneuve.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Carney taps astronaut Jeremy Hansen as space strategy adviser
stories.summary: Hansen will work with Carney, Joly to expand industrial innovation and get more Canadians into space
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has appointed Jeremy Hansen as a special adviser on space – just as the United States takes note of Canada’s efforts to shift its space partnerships toward Europe.

“I’m just super excited to serve Canada in that role,” Hansen said in a video he posted Tuesday on social media.

“There’s so much opportunity to leverage this position that we’re already in, to do more to provide for our sovereignty, our security, our quality of life on the planet, and at the same time make significant contributions on the global stage.”

The role involves advising Carney and Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, Hansen said.

In April, as part of the Artemis II mission, Hansen and three other astronauts travelled around the moon and further out into space than any humans before them.

Joly said Hansen proposed helping the government “develop a new space strategy” when he left the Canadian Space Agency.

“We had a conversation of how he could continue to have an impact, to contribute, to serve,” she said at an event Tuesday.

Joly said she’s getting feedback from other Canadian astronauts and people in the aerospace sector on the strategy “in order to accelerate innovation and reinforce our international partnerships.”

The offices of Carney and Joly did not respond when asked for details of Hansen’s role, such as its end date and compensation.

On Wednesday, Defence Minister David McGuinty announced a $20 million agreement on the use of a space launch complex in southern Newfoundland, which builds on a March agreement involving a complex in Nova Scotia.

“Reliable and independent launch access will enable Canada to place critical satellites into orbit even during global uncertainty, geopolitical tensions, or disruptions in foreign launch markets,” McGuinty’s department wrote in a news release.

“With military, emergency response, and government services increasingly dependent on space-based systems, sovereign launch (capacity) protects national interests and enables continuity of operations.”

Hansen’s appointment comes as Canada looks to expand co-operation with European countries in space – and as Washington warns it could seek partners other than Canada for its space missions.

Joly spoke Tuesday at the SpaceBound 2026 Conference. U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra told that same conference that Canada has decided to “move away” from the American firm SpaceX.

“Canada has said that, ‘We’re going to take a look at the European Space Agency, we’re going do more with them,’” he said.

Hoekstra said it was helpful to know that Canada is not interested in partnering with the firm founded by billionaire Elon Musk, who has close ties to U.S. President Donald Trump.

“It’s kind of like, wow, Canada is really saying for all the investment, all the innovation, all the excellence that is being driven by Elon, we don’t want to be a part of it? OK. That’s fine,” he said.

Hoekstra said the United States will always have a “bias” toward the private sector.

“Competition breeds excellence,” he said.

“What we fight in the United States all the time is to make sure that we never come in and over-regulate it. We’ve had to fight that, in the digital world … We’ll probably have to fight this in the space realm.”

Hoekstra added that the F-35 jet is “the best fighter in the world.” He did not directly mention Ottawa’s decision to pause a planned purchase of F-35s after Trump launched his trade war and repeatedly threatened Canada’s sovereignty.

“We also recognize that Canada’s going through a re-evaluation of how they want to move forward on defence,” he said.

Hoekstra said Washington is waiting to see whether Canada wants to continue decades of airspace co-operation through Norad. He said Trump’s recent security deal with Greenland – which also followed his repeated threats to annex the island – is meant to shore up U.S. security in the North.

“We’re waiting to see exactly where Canada wants to go on this,” he said. “We’d love to do it with Canada. It would be very, very helpful. But at the same time, and I’ve said this for the past year and a half, we are not standing still.”

stories.title: In some Ontario municipalities, acclamations mean no elections next week
stories.summary: Ontarians in hundreds of municipalities will head to the polls next Monday, but in Kapuskasing it will be a day just like any other.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontarians in hundreds of municipalities will head to the polls next Monday, but in Kapuskasing it will be a day just like any other.

The northern Ontario town of roughly 8,100 is one of several communities essentially bypassing the municipal vote after only one candidate stepped forward for each elected position, from school board trustee to mayor.

“I’m so happy,” Kapuskasing Mayor David Plourde, who first won the job in 2018 and ran unopposed in the last election in 2022, said in a recent interview.

After a brief bid for a provincial seat last year, Plourde said he’s “completely content” not to take on another campaign so soon. “I was knocking on doors a year and a half ago in -35, -40 degree weather. To have to do it again, it would just suck,” he said.

Four of the six council spots are going to the incumbents, and the other two will be filled by people Plourde has worked with in the past “in some way, shape or form,” he said, adding he sees the acclamations as a sign that residents support the current leadership and its work.

“I think everything’s going to go smoothly. I think we’re going to take the opportunity to onboard everybody early so ... when the bell rings, we’ll hit the ground running, and hopefully we’ll be able to come up with a budget real early and get right to work,” he said.

Meanwhile, he noted, “the municipality saves themselves 60 grand for elections.”

Fewer candidates have been acclaimed in these elections than in the last ballot — 400 compared with 548 in 2022, bringing the tally more in line with historical numbers, according to data compiled by the Association of Municipalities of Ontario.

Similarly, fewer municipalities have seen their entire councils acclaimed this time around, the association reported. Nineteen municipalities, or five per cent of those holding elections, have been fully acclaimed, down from 32 municipalities in 2022 and 26 in 2018.

Acclamations are more common in smaller municipalities, and Kapuskasing is the largest to be fully acclaimed, the association said. The smallest is the Township of Brethour, a northern community of just over 100 along the Ontario-Quebec border.

As well, more than half the municipal governments subject to voting this fall experienced low candidature, which the association defines as a situation where one or more candidates are acclaimed or positions have no more than two candidates competing.

In Fauquier-Strickland, a cash-strapped township just east of Kapuskasing that received a provincial bailout last year, no one stepped forward to run for mayor or council before the August registration deadline.

The cutoff date was pushed back so that residents could throw their hat in the ring, and a handful of people will now vie for four council seats. Pierre Lamontagne, a current councillor, has been acclaimed as mayor.

The association, which had voiced concerns about low participation ahead of the nominations deadline, said the total number of candidates has increased in these elections, “enough that it’s moving in the right direction.”

The drop in acclamations is also a good sign, said Lindsay Jones, the association’s executive director.

“There’s nothing inherently wrong with acclamations. A lot of the time, it can mean that the population is generally happy with the job that folks are doing,” she said in a recent interview.

“But we do like to have a balance and we like for voters to be able to have choice. So, you know, ideally a mix of folks who have that experience in municipal government and understand the issues and are familiar with the process, mixed with folks who are bringing new ideas and perspectives, is what we’re aiming for.”

The association has been offering free workshops to those potentially interested in running for office to help them get familiar with the process and the job itself, Jones said. And while there’s an ebb and flow to participation and acclamations over time, she said AMO is interpreting this year’s numbers as “folks understanding the value and importance of participating in the process and wanting to be a part of those conversations and decisions going forward.”

There’s debate among researchers regarding the reasons that lead to acclamations, said Joe Lyons, the director of Western University’s Local Government Program. One possible cause is apathy, but some researchers say it could be related to satisfaction, he said.

For potential candidates, there are several possible deterrents and hurdles to running for office, Lyons said, one of them being the lack of political infrastructure to recruit and foster future contenders.

“It’s like low pay, long hours, little recognition ... especially with the sort of decline in civility, both on council and then in terms of like the public towards members of council,” he said in an interview.

“And so, you know, it’s a tough sell to get people to want to run. I definitely think the nature of being a councillor has changed right now that we’re so connected, so it’s not as though you can go and attend a meeting a month kind of thing and that’s the job, right?” he said.

“You’re answering emails, you’re responding to comments on social media (and) some of them might be very negative.”

If we want local democracy to function, we May need to rethink what’s being asked of both municipalities and their governments, Lyons said.

“Maybe it’s too much,” he said. “Especially in Ontario, the push is towards larger municipalities doing more things on behalf of the province, and so that expands the scope of issues that councils have to deal with.”

As they face big-picture issues such as housing and economic uncertainty, several local acclaimed politicians say skipping the campaign won’t affect how they approach the job or engage with constituents.

“An acclamation does not reduce the responsibility to listen, respond and remain accountable,” Nancy Peckford posted on Facebook shortly after being acclaimed as mayor of North Grenville, a township of approximately 18,000 people south of Ottawa, a few months ago.

“The next council will continue to face important decisions about affordability, growth, infrastructure, community services and how we care for one another,” she wrote, promising to seek residents’ input regarding their priorities over the weeks that followed.

Christa Lowry, who has been acclaimed for a second consecutive time as mayor of Mississippi Mills, said she feels “an even greater responsibility to reach out.”

Lowry and her colleagues on council — four of whom have also been acclaimed, along with a fifth candidate — have worked to establish ongoing communication with the Ottawa-area municipality’s roughly 15,000 residents who, in return, respond in droves to budget surveys and show up to information sessions, she said in a recent interview.

“It’s a four-year conversation. It’s not, you know, having a couple months’ worth of conversations just before an election,” she said.

A key priority for the next four years will be tackling the pressures of growth as more people move to Mississippi Mills from Ottawa, she said.

Though Nicole Fortier Levesque will be one of two newcomers acclaimed to Kapuskasing’s town council, she is no stranger to municipal politics or the issues at play in the region. The retired teacher spent a decade as the mayor of nearby Moonbeam before moving to Kapuskasing, a bilingual, predominantly francophone community, and making an unsuccessful run for the federal New Democrats last year.

In an interview earlier this month, she listed affordable housing, infrastructure and support for a financially fragile local paper mill as top concerns for the next four years, but lamented the lack of opportunity to petition residents directly about what matters to them.

“I’ve always had to work hard to get elected and I have to admit that deep down I’m disappointed (not to have to campaign) because I like going out to meet people, I liked seeing exactly what’s on their mind,” she said in French.

“And now, I get the impression that I’m missing something very, very important.”

Aside from the financial savings, Fortier Levesque said she doesn’t see any advantages to acclamation, though it won’t change her attitude toward the community or what she wants to achieve. “It’s just that I find it’s up to people to choose the representation they want on municipal council,” she said.

Plourde, Kapuskasing’s mayor, said people in a small community will always find a way to share their concerns with officials.

“If you go into the grocery store or you go wherever you go, there’s always a conversation to be had,” he said.
