paragraphs: Ontarians in hundreds of municipalities will head to the polls next Monday, but in Kapuskasing it will be a day just like any other.

The northern Ontario town of roughly 8,100 is one of several communities essentially bypassing the municipal vote after only one candidate stepped forward for each elected position, from school board trustee to mayor.
“I’m so happy,” Kapuskasing Mayor David Plourde, who first won the job in 2018 and ran unopposed in the last election in 2022, said in a recent interview.

After a brief bid for a provincial seat last year, Plourde said he’s “completely content” not to take on another campaign so soon. “I was knocking on doors a year and a half ago in -35, -40 degree weather. To have to do it again, it would just suck,” he said.

Four of the six council spots are going to the incumbents, and the other two will be filled by people Plourde has worked with in the past “in some way, shape or form,” he said, adding he sees the acclamations as a sign that residents support the current leadership and its work.

“I think everything’s going to go smoothly. I think we’re going to take the opportunity to onboard everybody early so ... when the bell rings, we’ll hit the ground running, and hopefully we’ll be able to come up with a budget real early and get right to work,” he said.
Meanwhile, he noted, “the municipality saves themselves 60 grand for elections.”

Fewer candidates have been acclaimed in these elections than in the last ballot — 400 compared with 548 in 2022, bringing the tally more in line with historical numbers, according to data compiled by the Association of Municipalities of Ontario.

Similarly, fewer municipalities have seen their entire councils acclaimed this time around, the association reported. Nineteen municipalities, or five per cent of those holding elections, have been fully acclaimed, down from 32 municipalities in 2022 and 26 in 2018.

Acclamations are more common in smaller municipalities, and Kapuskasing is the largest to be fully acclaimed, the association said. The smallest is the Township of Brethour, a northern community of just over 100 along the Ontario-Quebec border.

As well, more than half the municipal governments subject to voting this fall experienced low candidature, which the association defines as a situation where one or more candidates are acclaimed or positions have no more than two candidates competing.

In Fauquier-Strickland, a cash-strapped township just east of Kapuskasing that received a provincial bailout last year, no one stepped forward to run for mayor or council before the August registration deadline.

The cutoff date was pushed back so that residents could throw their hat in the ring, and a handful of people will now vie for four council seats. Pierre Lamontagne, a current councillor, has been acclaimed as mayor.

The association, which had voiced concerns about low participation ahead of the nominations deadline, said the total number of candidates has increased in these elections, “enough that it’s moving in the right direction.”
The drop in acclamations is also a good sign, said Lindsay Jones, the association’s executive director.
“There’s nothing inherently wrong with acclamations. A lot of the time, it can mean that the population is generally happy with the job that folks are doing,” she said in a recent interview.

“But we do like to have a balance and we like for voters to be able to have choice. So, you know, ideally a mix of folks who have that experience in municipal government and understand the issues and are familiar with the process, mixed with folks who are bringing new ideas and perspectives, is what we’re aiming for.”

The association has been offering free workshops to those potentially interested in running for office to help them get familiar with the process and the job itself, Jones said. And while there’s an ebb and flow to participation and acclamations over time, she said AMO is interpreting this year’s numbers as “folks understanding the value and importance of participating in the process and wanting to be a part of those conversations and decisions going forward.”

There’s debate among researchers regarding the reasons that lead to acclamations, said Joe Lyons, the director of Western University’s Local Government Program. One possible cause is apathy, but some researchers say it could be related to satisfaction, he said.

For potential candidates, there are several possible deterrents and hurdles to running for office, Lyons said, one of them being the lack of political infrastructure to recruit and foster future contenders.

“It’s like low pay, long hours, little recognition ... especially with the sort of decline in civility, both on council and then in terms of like the public towards members of council,” he said in an interview.

“And so, you know, it’s a tough sell to get people to want to run. I definitely think the nature of being a councillor has changed right now that we’re so connected, so it’s not as though you can go and attend a meeting a month kind of thing and that’s the job, right?” he said.
“You’re answering emails, you’re responding to comments on social media (and) some of them might be very negative.”
If we want local democracy to function, we May need to rethink what’s being asked of both municipalities and their governments, Lyons said.

“Maybe it’s too much,” he said. “Especially in Ontario, the push is towards larger municipalities doing more things on behalf of the province, and so that expands the scope of issues that councils have to deal with.”

As they face big-picture issues such as housing and economic uncertainty, several local acclaimed politicians say skipping the campaign won’t affect how they approach the job or engage with constituents.

“An acclamation does not reduce the responsibility to listen, respond and remain accountable,” Nancy Peckford posted on Facebook shortly after being acclaimed as mayor of North Grenville, a township of approximately 18,000 people south of Ottawa, a few months ago.

“The next council will continue to face important decisions about affordability, growth, infrastructure, community services and how we care for one another,” she wrote, promising to seek residents’ input regarding their priorities over the weeks that followed.
Christa Lowry, who has been acclaimed for a second consecutive time as mayor of Mississippi Mills, said she feels “an even greater responsibility to reach out.”

Lowry and her colleagues on council — four of whom have also been acclaimed, along with a fifth candidate — have worked to establish ongoing communication with the Ottawa-area municipality’s roughly 15,000 residents who, in return, respond in droves to budget surveys and show up to information sessions, she said in a recent interview.
“It’s a four-year conversation. It’s not, you know, having a couple months’ worth of conversations just before an election,” she said.
A key priority for the next four years will be tackling the pressures of growth as more people move to Mississippi Mills from Ottawa, she said.

Though Nicole Fortier Levesque will be one of two newcomers acclaimed to Kapuskasing’s town council, she is no stranger to municipal politics or the issues at play in the region. “And now, I get the impression that I’m missing something very, very important.”

Aside from the financial savings, Fortier Levesque said she doesn’t see any advantages to acclamation, though it won’t change her attitude toward the community or what she wants to achieve. “It’s just that I find it’s up to people to choose the representation they want on municipal council,” she said.
Plourde, Kapuskasing’s mayor, said people in a small community will always find a way to share their concerns with officials.
“If you go into the grocery store or you go wherever you go, there’s always a conversation to be had,” he said.

stories.title: Angine de Poitrine announce 2027 world tour
stories.summary: Among the eight Canadian dates are stops in Calgary, Ottawa and Winnipeg, as well as a performance at Toronto's RBC Amphitheatre — their largest headlining show in the city so far.
stories.author: Alex Nino Gheciu
stories.content:
Angine de Poitrine is taking its alien invasion global.

Quebec’s polka-dotted, self-proclaimed extraterrestrial duo has announced it will embark on a world tour in 2027.

It kicks off March 4 in Melbourne, Australia before touching down in South America, North America and Europe.

Among the eight Canadian dates are stops in Calgary, Ottawa and Winnipeg, as well as a performance at Toronto’s RBC Amphitheatre — marking their largest headlining show in the city so far.

The tour comes to a close in their hometown of Saguenay, Que.

In September, Angine de Poitrine won the $30,000 Polaris Music Prize for their second album, “Vol. II,” and the $10,000 Socan Polaris Song Prize for their track “Fabienk.”

They’re the first act to claim both prizes at the ceremony.

stories.title: Quebec police investigating after man in 40s killed in Sorel-Tracy, Que.
stories.summary: Quebec provincial police are investigating after a man in his 40s was killed Tuesday evening in Sorel-Tracy, Que., northeast of Montreal.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Quebec provincial police are investigating after a man in his 40s was killed Tuesday evening in Sorel-Tracy, Que., northeast of Montreal.

Police say emergency services were called around 9:30 p.m. to Chemin des Patriotes, where a man had been shot.

A Quebec provincial police logo is seen in Ottawa, ON Sunday, Sept. 28, 2025.

stories.title: New southern resident killer whale calf spotted in waters near B.C.
stories.summary: Friday Harbor - The endangered southern resident killer whale population has increased by one after a calf was spotted in waters near British Columbia.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Center for Whale Research says in an email statement that the new calf was first spotted on Monday with its mother, designated J35 by researchers.

The centre’s researchers then spotted the mother and calf again on Tuesday and determined the “very young” whale is a male likely less than a week old.

Article continues below

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

The calf has been designated J65 and is J35’s sixth documented calf, her first being born in 2010.

The centre says J35 previously lost calves, and was seen carrying a dead calf for 17 days in 2018, while another calf born in 2024 did not survive.

Researchers say J65 shows no health issues and is “moving well, socializing, and nursing,” but only about half of all calves survive their first year.

Another southern resident, J31, was spotted with a dead calf earlier this month near Sombro Point on Vancouver Island.

The centre says that as of July, the population of Southern Residents was 76.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Federal union announces strike votes for 120,000 federal public servants
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canada's largest federal public service union says 120,000 workers will take part in nationwide strike votes starting next month after contract talks with the federal government broke down.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada’s largest federal public service union says 120,000 workers will take part in nationwide strike votes starting next month after contract talks with the federal government broke down.

The Public Service Alliance of Canada says voting will take place from Nov. 16 to Jan. 22.

The union and Treasury Board have been in contract negotiations for a year and a half, and Psac in May called a government wage offer of less than one per cent per year “insulting.”

Psac says the government has refused to negotiate on key issues such as wages, job security, remote work and protections against artificial intelligence.

“The government has left us no other choice,” said Psac national president Sharon DeSousa. “This is a wake-up call for the government to stop playing games and put a fair offer on the table.”

Workers to take part in strike votes include wildland firefighters, passport and benefit officers, fishery officers, federal teachers, librarians and administrative staff.

If the vote passes, the union would be in a legal strike position for 60 days. But DeSousa says a strike is the last resort option.

“Our goal is to get a good collective agreement, and it doesn’t have to lead to a strike, but we will if required to do so,” she said.

In 2023, 155,000 federal public servants spent almost two weeks on picket lines across the country before winning wage increases amounting to 12.6 per cent over the agreement’s term, which ran from 2021 to 2024.

Since then, federal public servants have faced both job cuts and an increase in their required office presence.

The Liberals’ 2025 budget outlined a plan to slash the public service by 10 per cent by the end of the 2028-29 fiscal year as part of an effort to reduce spending.

The federal public service has shed more than 23,000 staffers over the last two years, says Canada’s parliamentary spending watchdog.

An online tool released by the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer last month estimates there were 344,970 federal employees in the second quarter of this year, down 6.5 per cent from two years ago.

At the same time, federal government departments and agencies are set to spend more than $18 million to get their employees to work in the office more often.

Thousands of federal public servants started a new work schedule in July requiring them to be on-site in the office four days a week. Executive public servants returned to the office full-time in May.

In response to an order paper question from NDP MP Heather McPherson, 13 federal organizations said they plan to spend a combined $18,720,150 to reconfigure or acquire office space to accommodate the increased frequency of in-person work.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Booking your Air Canada flight by phone? That’ll be $30 extra — per passenger
stories.summary: Montreal — Air Canada says customers who book their flights by phone are now paying $30 per passenger for the privilege.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Montreal — Air Canada customers who book their flights by phone are now paying $30 per passenger for the privilege.

The country’s largest airline says the policy came into force on Oct. 15, placing it alongside WestJet, United Airlines and the numerous low-cost carriers that charge non-refundable phone booking fees.

Other competitors such as Delta Air Lines and Southwest Airlines still offer tickets by telephone without the surcharge.

For a family of four who books their Air Canada trip the old-fashioned way, the bill will run an extra $120.

The move marks an attempt to steer customers to the company’s website or app and to cut call centre costs, or at least compensate for them.

“It’s expensive. But then again, it’s expensive to hire an employee, train them and have them answer the phone,” said Andrew D’Amours, co-founder of flight deal site Flytrippers.

The change could disproportionately hit seniors who rely on phone reservations, he said.

“A lot of people, probably older folks, don’t really like booking on the app or on the internet. So I get the argument that it’s kind of unfair for them.”

The move also highlights yet another area that airlines have found to charge for services, part of a decade-long trend of “unbundling,” where airline customers pay for perks that were once bundled into a standard flight. Passengers now routinely pay extra for checked bags, pre-selected seats, priority boarding and onboard snacks.

Airlines have argued that unbundling allows customers to know precisely what they are paying for, with the cost of a particular service borne more by those who use it.

D’Amours served up a pungent analogy. “If you buy cheese, you can buy the brick and it’s much cheaper. Or you can buy it shredded,” he said.

“It’s more expensive, but you choose that for the convenience. If you don’t want to book online, you can pay someone to do it.”

Customers who require specialized support, including those with accessibility needs, are exempt from the fee, Air Canada said.

“It does not apply to services that cannot be completed online,” added spokesperson Sean Davidson, who stressed the benefits of booking online.

“Using these digital tools for everyday travel needs helps reduce wait times and allows our contact centre agents to focus their expertise on situations that require personalized support.”

stories.title: First Nations say Elections Alberta unprepared for referendum turnout
stories.summary: First Nations in Alberta are celebrating the win for the pro-Canada side in Monday's referendum but also raising concerns about a shortage of ballots in their communities.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume
stories.content:
First Nations in Alberta are celebrating the win for the pro-Canada side in Monday’s referendum — but they’re also raising concerns about a shortage of ballots in their communities.

About three in four Albertans said yes to Confederation on Monday, while about one in four said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving.

Siksika Nation says that while it’s pleased with the outcome, the polling station in their community was understaffed and didn’t receive enough ballots from Elections Alberta, leading to long wait times and “unnecessary obstacles.”

Tania Cameron, who helped boost First Nations turnout in the vote, says she was proud to learn several First Nations polling stations had to request more ballots.

She also says Elections Alberta should have been more prepared.

She says not having enough ballots is a slap in the face to community members who wanted their voices heard.

stories.title: Most Canadian actors earn less than $20K per year from screen work, survey finds
stories.summary: Toronto - Seven in 10 film and TV actors earn less than $20,000 per year from their on-screen work, according to a survey conducted on behalf of the Canada Media Fund.
stories.author: Nicole Thompson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Most Canadian actors can’t pay the bills through onscreen work alone, according to a survey from the Canada Media Fund that found seven in 10 respondents earned less than $20,000 a year from their work on film and TV.

The poll of nearly a thousand screen performers also found only six per cent of respondents earned more than $75,000 per year, and just 13 per cent earned all their income from performing.

Two-thirds of respondents made less than half their money through acting, the Canada Media Fund said. The survey was conducted at the end of 2025 by Abacus Data, and asked performers to reflect on their earnings the year prior.

“People have to find other jobs, and really make ends meet in different ways ... to make their careers sustainable,” said Diego Briceño, senior manager of data equity at the Canada Media Fund, who presented the report on Tuesday at the Reelworld Summit in downtown Toronto.

“So (it’s) really a difficult situation in terms of economics and stability for them.”

The respondents suggested much of the work comes from international productions shot in Canada, including the filming hubs of Toronto and Vancouver.

Asked to reflect on their 2024 earnings, 47 per cent of said they worked on international or U.S. productions filmed north of the border, while 40 per cent worked on Canadian scripted TV and 35 per cent worked in Canadian film.

One possible solution the report presents is building up a more robust “star system” in Canada — one that promotes the visibility of homegrown actors.

The survey found only three per cent of English performers said there’s a “strong and consistent” star system in Canada, compared to 21 per cent of French-speaking performers.

That topic was also up for discussion at Reelworld on Tuesday, which included a panel on English Canada’s lack of infrastructure that boosts actors’ name recognition.

Among the participants was K.C. Collins, who stars as deputy Crown attorney Theo Forrester on “Law & Order Toronto: Criminal Intent.” He said that show does a great job getting its stars out there — which, in his estimation, helps explain why it’s such a success.

But he said his experience hasn’t always been so positive.

“I was crafted in Canada, but I was not promoted by Canada,” he said.

Collins said that whenever he finishes a project in Canada, it’s like he’s starting his career from zero. When he works in the United States, he said, producers and directors remember working with him and want to cast him again.

Actress and producer Tonya Williams, who founded the Reelworld Screen Institute in 2000, said the Canadian system generally doesn’t celebrate stars until they “make it” in the United States.

She said she’s noticed a reticence to build up Canadians’ star power at home.

“In my 50 years working in this industry, 50 years of listening to producers and people behind the scenes say they do not want a star system in Canada: silly excuses like, ‘Oh, they’ll start charging us more for their fees. They’ll go international,’” she said during the panel.

“Yes, you want the stars you built here to go international, that’s how it works. And what do you care if they charge more, they’re gonna make you more money. So I don’t really understand the mentality around it, but we have built an infrastructure that really supports the directors and the producers and a lot of other people within the industry, but it’s very little support for the actors.”

The Canada Media Fund is a public-private partnership that finances Canadian content and promotes the country’s screen industry. Its survey was conducted online in the last two months of 2025, and results were not weighted to reflect the broader Canadian population.

The report notes that 2024 May have been an “atypical” year because the American actors’ union, SAG-Aftra, went on strike in 2023, pausing some U.S. productions.

The strike ended that same fall and production picked up soon after, but a report from production intelligence company ProdPro found that in 2024 the U.S. industry still lagged behind 2022’s pre-strike activity by about 11 per cent.

Even in the United States, where actors are generally more celebrated, it can be tough to find steady work.

The actor Asia Kate Dillon, whose credits include “John Wick 3,” “Orange is the New Black” and “Billions,” recently announced they were looking for work in the service industry.

In an Instagram post, Dillon said they’d acted full-time since 2015, but work has dried up for them — along with “many, many other” non-binary and gender non-conforming actors.

Other performers, including Heather Matarazzo and Jack Haven, have publicly appealed for acting work so they could make the minimum US$28,090 needed to qualify for SAG-Aftra health insurance.
paragraphs: Toronto - Most Canadian actors can’t pay the bills through onscreen work alone, according to a survey from the Canada Media Fund that found seven in 10 respondents earned less than $20,000 a year from their work on film and TV.
The poll of nearly a thousand screen performers also found only six per cent of respondents earned more than $75,000 per year, and just 13 per cent earned all their income from performing.

Two-thirds of respondents made less than half their money through acting, the Canada Media Fund said. The survey was conducted at the end of 2025 by Abacus Data, and asked performers to reflect on their earnings the year prior.

“So (it’s) really a difficult situation in terms of economics and stability for them.”
The respondents suggested much of the work comes from international productions shot in Canada, including the filming hubs of Toronto and Vancouver.

stories.title: Social media ban for under-16s consistent with Charter, government says
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Liberal government says while its proposed digital safety legislation might affect freedom of expression, the bill itself is consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The Liberal government says while its proposed digital safety legislation might affect freedom of expression, the bill itself is consistent with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Bill C-34 would ban kids under 16 from accessing social media. Experts have warned it is likely to face a constitutional challenge.

The government included the analysis in a Charter statement, a document issued by the justice minister that looks at whether a bill is consistent with the Charter.

“As this measure would affect the ability of users to post and consume content, it has the potential to engage freedom of expression protected by section 2(b) of the Charter,” the statement says.

It says the bill might also affect equality rights and section 8 of the Charter, which deals with privacy.

But it maintains the social media ban is consistent with the Charter for a number of reasons, including the fact that age-based restrictions already apply to activities like voting and driving.

It also says there is considerable evidence about the risks social media use poses for young people.

“These include risks relating to privacy, problematic use, and exposure to harmful content, and can result both from the consumption of content on social media, as well as the posting of content,” it says.

“For example, information posted by young persons on social media May be effectively impossible to remove from the internet, May spread virally, May feed algorithms that encourage problematic use, and May make the poster a target for grooming and cyberbullying.”

The statement adds young people will still be able to browse sites anonymously, without an account.

The statement said this approach reflects “the increased risks to young people that stem from the collection and use of data in feeding algorithms that determine content to be served, as well as risks that stem from the ability to post content.”

The government also noted that a planned new regulator, which will be established once the bill passes, will be able to exempt social media platforms that implement adequate safeguards.

This summer, France’s top court struck down that country’s social media ban for kids under 15, saying the ban was too broad and infringed on freedom of expression.

Tamir Israel, a director at the Canadian Civil Liberties Association, said at the time Bill C-34 shares many of the same features as the French bill. Dalhousie University associate law professor Michael Karanicolas said a Charter challenge to Canada’s law is almost inevitable.

Bill C-34 was introduced in June and is up for second reading in the House of Commons on Wednesday. If it passes second reading, it must make its way through a House of Commons committee study and through the Senate before it can become law.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Bank of Canada expected to raise rates next week, some economists say
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada has held its key interest rate unchanged for about a year, but some economists expect rates to begin increasing again as early as next week.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The Bank of Canada has held its key interest rate unchanged for about a year, but some economists expect rates to begin increasing again as early as next week — which would be the first hike in more than three years.

This comes after a recent warning from the central bank that inflation is expected to keep rising as a ripple effect of the Iran war and other factors.

This comes after the U.S. Federal Reserve hiked its key policy rate last month for the first time in three years, and after U.S. inflation in August topped 3.4 per cent.

Tamping down red-hot inflation is key to making life more affordable for Canadians amid the heightened cost of living — along with increasing wages and salaries — but in order to achieve this, it May mean some will end up paying more to borrow money.

Central banks usually increase their benchmark borrowing rate to help cool down inflation, which can raise costs for Canadians and businesses with products like variable rate mortgages, and some loans for cars, tuition and business.

The Bank of Canada has a mandate to “promote the economic and financial welfare of Canada,” and this includes ensuring prices for goods and services remain relatively stable, while also keeping borrowing rates low enough to allow the economy to expand.

Its target range for inflation is between one and three per cent, with a target of two per cent, and its benchmark interest rate has been 2.25 per cent since October 2025.

Governor Tiff Macklem at the Bank of Canada spoke to reporters on Saturday in a press conference from the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, and said he expects the outlook for inflation will be “quite a bit higher” than it was in the central bank’s last forecast in July. That projection had inflation cooling to around 2.5 per cent in the second half of this year.

Consumer price inflation in September was measured at 3.1 per cent , which was mainly because of higher gas prices , and the consumer price index has been at or above three per cent for three straight months.

Although inflation has been hovering on the higher end of the central bank’s target range, it hasn’t necessarily spiked out of control. Elevated gas prices amid the Iran war have been mostly isolated, which has somewhat clouded the underlying price growth, known as core inflation, which has remained closer to two per cent for several months.

But over the long term, higher oil and gas prices can lead to higher prices for just about everything else, including food .

Macklem has said on several occasions that rising oil and gas prices are a risk to inflation, but there has been little evidence of broader spillover into consumer prices. This means that the recent higher inflation readings are being taken with a grain of salt.

However, Macklem warned that the longer oil and gas prices remain elevated, the more likely it is that it will lead to inflation becoming entrenched and rates will need to rise.

“If energy prices go higher, and particularly if they stay higher for longer, there could well be a need to increase the policy rate to get inflation back to two per cent,” Macklem said in August.

Speaking in Bangkok over the weekend, Macklem said, “The question we’re going to be asking ourselves is, is inflation likely to come back down towards our target on its own, or are we going to have to raise interest rates to influence the path?”

It was those comments that led some economists to change their own outlooks for interest rates in Canada, expecting the Bank of Canada to raise rates next week to get ahead of rising inflation.

“That is really what flipped the script for us a little bit and put us in the camp of expecting a Bank of Canada rate hike in October,” said Randall Bartlett, deputy chief economist at Desjardins.

“The Bank of Canada is really trying to get ahead of higher inflation, higher underlying inflation, which we haven’t materially seen yet, but to prevent it from happening.”

After the pandemic, when inflation peaked at over eight per cent, some economists felt the central bank waited too long to raise rates to get inflation under control. This comes after a recent warning from the central bank that inflation is expected to keep rising as a ripple effect of the Iran war and other factors.
This comes after the U.S. Federal Reserve hiked its key policy rate last month for the first time in three years, and after U.S. inflation in August topped 3.4 per cent.

Tamping down red-hot inflation is key to making life more affordable for Canadians amid the heightened cost of living — along with increasing wages and salaries — but in order to achieve this, it May mean some will end up paying more to borrow money.

Central banks usually increase their benchmark borrowing rate to help cool down inflation, which can raise costs for Canadians and businesses with products like variable rate mortgages, and some loans for cars, tuition and business.

The Bank of Canada has a mandate to “promote the economic and financial welfare of Canada,” and this includes ensuring prices for goods and services remain relatively stable, while also keeping borrowing rates low enough to allow the economy to expand.
Its target range for inflation is between one and three per cent, with a target of two per cent, and its benchmark interest rate has been 2.25 per cent since October 2025.

Governor Tiff Macklem at the Bank of Canada spoke to reporters on Saturday in a press conference from the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, and said he expects the outlook for inflation will be “quite a bit higher” than it was in the central bank’s last forecast in July. That projection had inflation cooling to around 2.5 per cent in the second half of this year.

Consumer price inflation in September was measured at 3.1 per cent , which was mainly because of higher gas prices , and the consumer price index has been at or above three per cent for three straight months.

Although inflation has been hovering on the higher end of the central bank’s target range, it hasn’t necessarily spiked out of control. Elevated gas prices amid the Iran war have been mostly isolated, which has somewhat clouded the underlying price growth, known as core inflation, which has remained closer to two per cent for several months.
But over the long term, higher oil and gas prices can lead to higher prices for just about everything else, including food .

Macklem has said on several occasions that rising oil and gas prices are a risk to inflation, but there has been little evidence of broader spillover into consumer prices. This means that the recent higher inflation readings are being taken with a grain of salt.
However, Macklem warned that the longer oil and gas prices remain elevated, the more likely it is that it will lead to inflation becoming entrenched and rates will need to rise.

stories.title: Musical about genetic discovery conceived as way to process 'life-changing' family secret
stories.summary: Toronto - After Noam Tomaschoff's parents revealed to him that his dad — the man who raised him from birth — was not his biological father, his gut instinct wasn't to keep harbouring the secret they had kept for 31 years: It was to share it, and share it widely.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - After Noam Tomaschoff’s parents revealed to him that his dad — the man who raised him from birth — was not his biological father, his gut instinct wasn’t to keep harbouring the secret they had kept for 31 years: It was to share it, and share it widely.

“My brain automatically told me, like, you need to make something out of this,” he said of his reaction in the summer of 2022.

That intuition led the writer-actor to process the news through penning a one-man musical with his two childhood friends based on his real-life extraordinary genetic discovery.

Another aspect of the personal bombshell was the fact that the only child actually had more than 35 half-siblings.

“I’ve met people who have had similar experiences and when they don’t have an outlet, whatever it May be, to wrangle it and make sense of it and own it, it can remain a big obstacle, something you never get past,” he said. “I think it was my way of getting through it.”

After successful runs at the Toronto and Edinburgh Fringe Festivals, a showcase in New York, and performances in other Canadian cities, “Our Little Secret: A True New Musical” is heading to the Off-Mirvish stage, giving the Toronto-born performer a special homecoming.

“It’s everything. It’s like the Olympics,” he said of the show hitting the CAA Theatre for a nearly three-week run, beginning Nov. 3.

For Tomaschoff, the last four years have been a whirlwind.

He had a typical childhood and said he never had any reason to suspect his parents were keeping anything — let alone an identity-shaking secret — from him. But as detailed in a lengthy 2023 Toronto Life feature, when he was 31, a woman he was dating, who is now his fiancée, told him about direct-to-consumer genetic test kits. On a whim, he ordered one. When he told his mom about the impending DNA test, the series of life-shifting events unfolded.

Unable to conceive naturally, Tomaschoff’s parents turned to sperm donation and decided to tell only a few family members. Tomaschoff said it wasn’t in his nature to lash out at his parents. Intellectually, he said, he understood their reasons for not telling him.

“That was the general guidance at the time; it made sense,” he said. “There wasn’t as much of a support structure. There’s a lot of shame around this type of thing, so I was never there being like, ‘How could you do this?’ I know why they did it.”

After taking the DNA test, Tomaschoff connected with other people who were conceived via the same sperm donor. The man died before Tomaschoff learned of their relation, but he has since grown close to some of his half-siblings, he said.

While his parents wanted their son to keep the truth under wraps, Tomaschoff refused. Before learning about his true backstory, the 35-year-old artist had been living in Los Angeles, struggling to land auditions and feeling “creatively adrift” after wrapping up an independent feature film project, he said.

“I had never had such a stroke of inspiration about any other project I’ve done in my life” he said.

After receiving a slot in the 2023 Toronto Fringe Festival, Tomaschoff wrote the show with his best friends, composer Ryan Peters and producer Russell Citron, whom he had met in high school and, fittingly, bonded with over a love of musical theatre.

The show, then called “Our Little Secret: The 23andMe Musical,” sold out all its performances and earned awards, including the Patron’s Pick and Best of Fringe.

Tomaschoff has since performed it at the Edinburgh Fringe in 2024 and later in Montreal. The show is currently playing at Edmonton’s Citadel Theatre until Oct. 25. Ahead of its return to the Toronto stage, Tomaschoff said the show’s rise has been “very amazing and humbling.”

“Our Little Secret” has evolved since its original conception. Initially, Tomaschoff said, it focused on the fun, joyful and wow moments, but after receiving constructive feedback that it lacked emotional, vulnerable notes, he said the show now better balances the highs and lows of that time period.

“It would be unsatisfying for the general audience to see a show that’s just kind of all happy. It certainly wouldn’t be true if it was all sad,” he said. “It’s trying to have everything in there that was a key step along the way, whether it was a difficult moment or overcoming that.”

The new production is directed by veteran stage performer Adam Pascal, best known for his role in the original Broadway and West End productions of “Rent.” In “Our Little Secret,” Tomaschoff speaks directly to the audience — referred to as breaking the fourth wall — and plays multiple roles, including his parents, Gideon Tomaschoff and Sylvie Leone-Tomaschoff.

When he was creating the musical, he kept his folks in the dark about its contents, a move he described as “my little payback.” But when his parents first saw it performed, they really liked it, he said. With every new iteration of the script, he strives to represent them authentically, while not shying away from difficult moments.

“It’s a negotiation, but we always strive to arrive at consensus around each new version of the script, which I think it must be the first musical in history where the parents essentially have an editorial role in the writing of it,” Tomaschoff said. “But it’s another way that we kind of keep each other honest.”

Tomaschoff’s story is specific, but he said the show deals with universal themes such as identity and family crisis. He wants audiences of all ages to walk out of the show inspired to embrace honesty in their relationships.

While he’s had years to process the truth, Tomaschoff said during performances, he can still tap into the initial moment of shock.

“I think I will be able to forever because it was just such a life-changing moment.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: New poll shows deadlock between Chow and Bradford days before Toronto election
stories.summary: Several polls put candidate Bradford slightly ahead of Chow, while others still place her ahead of Bradford, indicating there is no clear favourite, according to research firms.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
New polling just days before Toronto’s mayoral election shows Brad Bradford and Olivia Chow are locked in a narrowing race prior to election day on Oct. 26.

Several polls put Bradford the challenger slightly ahead of Chow the incumbent. Others still place her ahead of Bradford, indicating there is no clear favourite, according to research firms that publish the polls.

A new Liaison Strategies survey released Wednesday puts Bradford at 49 per cent support and Chow at 47 per cent among decided and leaning voters, with three per cent choosing someone else.

In this most recent poll, Chow loses a five-point lead she had in a Liaison Strategies poll published Oct. 13 .

“It is a much less comfortable race for the mayor than it was last week,” said David Valentin, principal at Liaison in a news release.

But “this is not a result either campaign can treat as a clear lead,” he said.

Another poll published Tuesday by Mainstreet Research also revealed a very narrow race with a slight advantage for Bradford. The firm placed Bradford with 48.9 per cent support and Chow at a “nearly equal” 47.5 per cent, Mainstreet said in a statement.

Quito Maggi, president and CEO of Mainstreet, said in a news release that Bradford leads in Etobicoke and North York while Chow is ahead in Scarborough and downtown.

But research firm Pollara Strategic Insights has Chow in a much firmer lead in its new polling also published Tuesday. It found incumbent Olivia Chow ahead of Brad Bradford by seven points among decided voters, 53 per cent to 46 per cent.

That polling also found a significant gender gap in voting intentions. Chow leads among decided women (60 per cent compared to 39 per cent of women for Bradford), while slightly more men are leaning towards Bradford (52 per cent to 45 per cent).

Both candidates have been hitting the pavement daily in the final week before the Oct. 26 election to reach those precious undecided voters who May push the vote slightly more on either side. Chow and Bradford have been quick to trade barbs, with Chow accusing her opponent Tuesday of neglecting residents in his own ward, and Bradford claiming that Chow has failed to address the city’s traffic and transit woes.

While advance polls have closed, voters will have a final chance to vote on election day Monday.

Liaison Strategies surveyed a random sample of 1,000 Toronto residents from October 18 to October 19, 2026, using conventional phone and Interactive Voice Recording (IVR) technology. T he margin of error is +/- 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. The margin is higher for subsamples, including decided and leaning voters.

Mainstreet Research conducted its survey between October 16 and October 18, 2026 with a sample size of 1,000 adults, 18 years of age or older, living in Toronto. The survey was conducted using conventional phone Interactive Voice Response (IVR) technology. The margin of error for the poll is +/- 3.1% at the 95% confidence level. Margins of error are higher in each subsample.

The Pollara Strategic Insights survey was fielded October 13 to 19, 2026. It surveyed Toronto residents aged 18+ eligible to vote (695 online panel, 404 live telephone). The poll was commissioned by Cupe Local 416 (Toronto Civic Employees’ Union). It was weighted to census data by gender, age and region. It states that “because the sample includes an online panel, no margin of error applies”. A probability sample of 1,099 would carry a margin of error of +/- 3.0 percentage points, 19 times out of 20, and more for subgroups. Subgroups with an unweighted base under 100 should be read with caution, it says.

stories.title: Carney to make Turkey trip for 1st bilateral visit aimed at deepening ties
stories.summary: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson will join Prime Minister Mark Carney on the planned trip.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is travelling to Turkey on Wednesday for a three-day trip that experts say should show how his approach to international diplomacy differs from that of the previous Liberal government.

Carney’s office says this is the first official bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey. Carney met with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Turkey earlier this year as part of the Nato summit.

The prime minister will land in Ankara early Thursday for a meeting with Erdogan before heading to Istanbul to meet with Turkish business leaders on Friday.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson will join Carney on the trip.

Senior government officials providing a background briefing to reporters ahead of the trip said Canada is seeking deeper political, economic and security ties with Turkey.

Carney’s bid to diversify trade beyond the United States and find new global investors for Canadian infrastructure projects is well-suited to deeper ties with Turkey, said Kerim Uras, the former Turkish ambassador to Canada.

Both the Canadian and Turkish economies need alternatives to the increasingly protectionist U.S. market, Uras said in an interview. While neither country can replace the United States with any one partner, forging connections between middle powers should be part of the path forward, he said.

“One can summarize it like the Carney doctrine meets Turkish pragmatism,” said Uras, now a senior fellow at Carleton University’s Centre in Modern Turkish Studies.

Turkish contractors are used to doing work in periods of geopolitical turmoil, Uras said. The country sits at the crossroads between Europe and the Middle East, with the Russia-Ukraine conflict across the Black Sea to its north and southern and eastern borders with Syria, Iraq and Iran.

“I would describe Turkey as an island of stability today in a very troublesome neighbourhood,” Uras said.

After Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Turkey brokered a deal with both nations to allow for grain exports, as the war threatened crucial food supplies for numerous developing countries.

Canada and Turkey have had formal diplomatic ties since 1944. The federal government estimates there are 76,000 members of the Turkish diaspora living in Canada.

Technical talks are underway on a Canada-Turkey free-trade agreement. Two-way trade between the nations totalled $4.3 billion in 2025, with Turkish exports to Canada accounting for the bulk of that.

Uras called that trade volume “peanuts” compared to the size of the two economies.

“With a little work, we could quadruple this very fast and I’m sure there is a mutual desire to do that,” he said.

Senior government officials said Carney and Erdogan will highlight free trade and progress on other key files during the visit. They would not say whether there will be any formal announcements of any new deals from the leaders’ meetings in Ankara.

Bessma Momani is a politics professor at the University of Waterloo and senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation. She said in an interview that Canada’s relationship with Turkey has been “low stakes” to date, but there are reasons for Canada to pursue closer ties now.

While Turkey is an “industrial and consumer powerhouse,” Momani said the country’s reliance on Russia and Iran for energy is a source of weakness.

“I think their Achilles heel for them has always been energy. And that’s something that Canada has something to potentially offer,” she said.

When Anand hosted Turkish Foreign Affairs Minister Hakan Fidan in Canada in June, they toured the Darlington Nuclear Generating Station near Bowmanville, Ont.

Uras said Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRéalis — maker of the Candu reactor in operation at Darlington — is one of the leading contenders to supply two planned nuclear power plants in Turkey.

A senior government official briefing reporters said Hodgson’s presence on the trip speaks to the importance of energy projects in discussions with Turkey.

Beyond nuclear, Uras said Turkish contractors are keen on a variety of projects across Canada in industries such as critical minerals, shipping and construction. As Nato allies, Canada and Turkey also have opportunities to collaborate on defence spending, the former ambassador suggested.

Uras, who was Turkey’s ambassador to Canada from 2018 to 2023, noted his time as envoy was characterized more by what couldn’t be traded between the nations.

In 2019, Canada banned arms exports to Turkey in response to the country’s military incursion into Syria. It expanded the ban after subsequent conflicts in the region showed Canadian-made technology, specifically drone parts, had been diverted to Azerbaijan. Canada lifted that ban in 2024 in the face of criticism from Armenian diaspora groups.

Uras said he doesn’t expect any lingering issues around the arms embargo. Canada and Turkey “hit the reset button” when Carney came to power, he said.

The Erdogan government is under heavy scrutiny internationally right now over reports of official persecution of Lgbtq+ organizers in the country.

Human Rights Watch and independent experts at the United Nations have condemned co-ordinated police raids on Lgbtq+ advocacy organizations in Turkey in recent months.

Canada did not join Germany, France and others in a joint statement last month condemning the country’s Lgbtq+ raids.

Government officials would not tell reporters whether Carney plans to raise the issue in private conversations with Erdogan.

One senior official called Canada’s approach to international affairs principled and pragmatic and said Canada recognizes not all partners will share Canada’s values.

Momani said as awful as Erdogan’s Lgbtq+ raids are, Turkey is not the only country in the world sliding back from liberal values. She said she expects Carney will take an approach different from that of his predecessor Justin Trudeau.

“I just don’t think the Carney government wants to make that a priority in the way that perhaps the Trudeau government was a little more willing to see foreign policy as a tool for moralizing their preferred social values,” Momani said.

Carney has argued closed-door conversations on rights issues are more productive than “lecturing countries from afar.”

Uras agreed that “megaphone diplomacy” does not help bridge values between allies, but he said it could be a topic of conversation between the leaders.

“Instead of walking away from the table, talking about these behind closed doors at the table is a much healthier approach. I’m sure we can discuss anything together and we will listen to each other,” he said.

–with files from Dylan Robertson

Senior government officials providing a background briefing to reporters ahead of the trip said Canada is seeking deeper political, economic and security ties with Turkey.

Carney’s bid to diversify trade beyond the United States and find new global investors for Canadian infrastructure projects is well-suited to deeper ties with Turkey, said Kerim Uras, the former Turkish ambassador to Canada.

Both the Canadian and Turkish economies need alternatives to the increasingly protectionist U.S. market, Uras said in an interview. While neither country can replace the United States with any one partner, forging connections between middle powers should be part of the path forward, he said.
“One can summarize it like the Carney doctrine meets Turkish pragmatism,” said Uras, now a senior fellow at Carleton University’s Centre in Modern Turkish Studies.

Turkish contractors are used to doing work in periods of geopolitical turmoil, Uras said. The country sits at the crossroads between Europe and the Middle East, with the Russia-Ukraine conflict across the Black Sea to its north and southern and eastern borders with Syria, Iraq and Iran.
“I would describe Turkey as an island of stability today in a very troublesome neighbourhood,” Uras said.
After Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Turkey brokered a deal with both nations to allow for grain exports, as the war threatened crucial food supplies for numerous developing countries.
Canada and Turkey have had formal diplomatic ties since 1944. The federal government estimates there are 76,000 members of the Turkish diaspora living in Canada.
Technical talks are underway on a Canada-Turkey free-trade agreement. Two-way trade between the nations totalled $4.3 billion in 2025, with Turkish exports to Canada accounting for the bulk of that.
Uras called that trade volume “peanuts” compared to the size of the two economies.
“With a little work, we could quadruple this very fast and I’m sure there is a mutual desire to do that,” he said.

Senior government officials said Carney and Erdogan will highlight free trade and progress on other key files during the visit. They would not say whether there will be any formal announcements of any new deals from the leaders’ meetings in Ankara.

Bessma Momani is a politics professor at the University of Waterloo and senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation. She said in an interview that Canada’s relationship with Turkey has been “low stakes” to date, but there are reasons for Canada to pursue closer ties now.
While Turkey is an “industrial and consumer powerhouse,” Momani said the country’s reliance on Russia and Iran for energy is a source of weakness.
“I think their Achilles heel for them has always been energy. And that’s something that Canada has something to potentially offer,” she said.
When Anand hosted Turkish Foreign Affairs Minister Hakan Fidan in Canada in June, they toured the Darlington Nuclear Generating Station near Bowmanville, Ont.
Uras said Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRéalis — maker of the Candu reactor in operation at Darlington — is one of the leading contenders to supply two planned nuclear power plants in Turkey.
A senior government official briefing reporters said Hodgson’s presence on the trip speaks to the importance of energy projects in discussions with Turkey.

Beyond nuclear, Uras said Turkish contractors are keen on a variety of projects across Canada in industries such as critical minerals, shipping and construction. As Nato allies, Canada and Turkey also have opportunities to collaborate on defence spending, the former ambassador suggested.
Uras, who was Turkey’s ambassador to Canada from 2018 to 2023, noted his time as envoy was characterized more by what couldn’t be traded between the nations.

In 2019, Canada banned arms exports to Turkey in response to the country’s military incursion into Syria. It expanded the ban after subsequent conflicts in the region showed Canadian-made technology, specifically drone parts, had been diverted to Azerbaijan. Canada lifted that ban in 2024 in the face of criticism from Armenian diaspora groups.

content_blocks.text: Uras said he doesn’t expect any lingering issues around the arms embargo. Canada and Turkey “hit the reset button” when Carney came to power, he said.
The Erdogan government is under heavy scrutiny internationally right now over reports of official persecution of Lgbtq+ organizers in the country.
Human Rights Watch and independent experts at the United Nations have condemned co-ordinated police raids on Lgbtq+ advocacy organizations in Turkey in recent months.
Canada did not join Germany, France and others in a joint statement last month condemning the country’s Lgbtq+ raids.
Government officials would not tell reporters whether Carney plans to raise the issue in private conversations with Erdogan.
One senior official called Canada’s approach to international affairs principled and pragmatic and said Canada recognizes not all partners will share Canada’s values.

Momani said as awful as Erdogan’s Lgbtq+ raids are, Turkey is not the only country in the world sliding back from liberal values. She said she expects Carney will take an approach different from that of his predecessor Justin Trudeau.

“I just don’t think the Carney government wants to make that a priority in the way that perhaps the Trudeau government was a little more willing to see foreign policy as a tool for moralizing their preferred social values,” Momani said.
Carney has argued closed-door conversations on rights issues are more productive than “lecturing countries from afar.”
Uras agreed that “megaphone diplomacy” does not help bridge values between allies, but he said it could be a topic of conversation between the leaders.

“Instead of walking away from the table, talking about these behind closed doors at the table is a much healthier approach. I’m sure we can discuss anything together and we will listen to each other,” he said.

stories.title: Ottawa will ‘not budge’ from ‘sustainable’ immigration levels: Carney
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says Ottawa will "not budge" from its goal of making immigration intake numbers sustainable and the federal government is "getting them to that level now."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney is not ruling out giving Alberta more authority over immigration along the lines of a deal Ottawa signed with Quebec in the early 1990s.

Reporters on Parliament Hill asked the prime minister on Wednesday if Ottawa could reach an agreement on immigration powers with Alberta similar to the one with Quebec.

“We’ll see,” Carney replied in French.

He added that “Quebec is distinct” because of its culture and language and said Ottawa will also talk with the other provinces about immigration levels.

Following the failure of the Meech Lake accord, the federal government signed an agreement with Quebec in 1991 which granted the province the power to set its own economic immigration targets.

Carney’s comments come after just over a million Albertans voted yes on a referendum question calling for more provincial control over immigration policy to reduce the number of newcomers to “sustainable levels.”

About 53 per cent of voters said yes to that question, according to preliminary results available on Wednesday. The officially certified results are due later next week.

At a news conference in Calgary on Wednesday, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she told Carney the day before that her government is putting together a “proposal” for the federal government.

“We have been looking for some inspiration from Quebec’s 1991 Canada-Quebec accord,” she said.

In his English remarks, Carney argued his government has “retaken control” of immigration and is listening to the provinces.

“We have been having discussions with the provinces’ first ministers around getting immigration, first and foremost, to the right levels,” Carney said.

“I just want to underscore we will not budge from overall levels that are sustainable. We’re getting them to that level now.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said on Tuesday the Liberals have lost control of immigration and provinces should have more control over their intake numbers since they must deliver services for newcomers.

“Recently, the prime minister went to The New York Times, a foreign newspaper, to tell them that he wants to increase immigration. That too is a mistake,” Poilievre said in Calgary on Tuesday.

“It shows he is totally out of touch. Immigration is totally out of control.”

Carney told the U.S. newspaper last month that the next question his government faces is when to “resume some controlled increase in the population.”

The federal Conservatives sent out a fundraising email to party supporters this week saying immigration should be “dramatically reduced,” not “ramped back up.”

Immigration Minister Lena Diab did not respond to reporters’ questions when she walked into the weekly Liberal caucus meeting Wednesday. Federal immigration levels are due for an update by next month.

The federal government had set out plans to increase the national target for permanent residents to 500,000 a year. But Ottawa changed course and slashed the targets in its 2024-2025 plan.

The most recent plan sets out targets of 385,000 permanent resident admissions this year, 370,000 next year and the same figure for 2028.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

— With files from David Baxter

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: London police arrest trio sought in Fennell Crescent shooting
stories.summary: London police said two 19 year old’s and an 18 year old were taken into custody Tuesday.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Three people previously wanted in connection with a weekend shooting in south London have been arrested, according to police.

London police said two 19 year old’s and an 18 year old were taken into custody Tuesday.

All three remained in custody and were scheduled to appear in a London court Wednesday in relation to charges connected to the investigation.

Police had identified the trio as suspects in a shooting that occurred in the area of Fennell Crescent and Ernest Avenue over the weekend.

The victim remains in hospital in fair condition.

stories.title: RCMP apologizes for ‘grossly inadequate’ investigation into N.S. workplace drowning
stories.summary: The agency that reviews complaints against the RCMP says the Mounties have apologized for their “grossly inadequate” investigation into the October 2020 workplace death.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The agency that reviews complaints against the RCMP says the Mounties have apologized for their “grossly inadequate” investigation into the October 2020 workplace death of a man in Nova Scotia.

In a final report dated Oct. 14, the Civilian Review and Complaints Commission says 26-year-old engineer Andrew Gnazdowsky drowned after he jumped into a reservoir to retrieve a malfunctioning piece of equipment.

The province’s Labour Department later charged three businesses with violating of the Nova Scotia Occupational Health and Safety Act, which led to convictions and fines for failing to provide a safe workplace.

Gnazdowsky’s sister, Nicole, filed a complaint against the RCMP in 2024, saying the police force should have investigated the businesses for Criminal Code violations, such as criminal negligence causing death.

The independent commission says that aside from the RCMP’s inadequate investigation, the police force failed to understand its role in investigating a workplace death.

As well, the agency asked the Mounties to consider conducting a criminal investigation, but the RCMP responded by saying it was unlikely that any investigation would lead to a successful prosecution.

stories.title: Appeal of an N.S. RCMP officer’s sexual assault acquittal has been abandoned by Crown
stories.summary: An appeal of a Nova Scotia RCMP officer's sexual assault charge acquittal has been abandoned by the Crown.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An appeal of a Nova Scotia RCMP officer’s sexual assault charge acquittal has been abandoned by the Crown.

RCMP Const. William McNutt had been facing several charges of sexual assault and has been suspended without pay since January 2024.

On Aug. 5, he was acquitted of two counts of sexual assault in a decision by Judge Del Atwood.

Later that month, the Crown issued notice that it would appeal the acquittal on the basis that the trial judge had made errors.

Then, ON Oct. 13, the Crown abandoned the appeal.

The Public Prosecution Service says the Crown concluded there were no grounds for appeal.

McNutt is still facing one count of sexual assault relating to an alleged 2024 incident.

A provincial court is scheduled to set a trial date for this case on Nov. 2.

Four other separate sexual assault charges against him were dismissed due to court delays.

In late May, Judge Ian Hutchison entered a judicial stay for charges of committing assault by choking or strangling, uttering threats and four counts of sexual assault, due to untimely delay.

stories.title: Two taken to hospital after garage fire damages London home
stories.summary: Fire crews were called to Avenue Road just before 9:30 a.m. following reports of a fire involving an attached garage.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A garage fire in London sent two people to hospital and caused extensive damage to a home Wednesday morning.

Fire crews were called to Avenue Road just before 9:30 a.m. following reports of a fire involving an attached garage.

Upon arrival, firefighters launched an initial offensive attack and were able to quickly knock down the blaze. Crews later switched to a defensive strategy after part of the roof structure collapsed.

Officials said the fire caused extensive damage to both the attached garage and the home.

Two people were transported to Victoria Hospital. The extent of their injuries has not been released.

No information on the cause of the fire was immediately available.

The incident remains under investigation.

stories.title: Carney appoints astronaut Jeremy Hansen to advise government on new space strategy
stories.summary: Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney has appointed Jeremy Hansen as a special adviser on space.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney has appointed Jeremy Hansen as a special adviser on space — just as the United States takes note of Canada’s efforts to shift its space partnerships toward Europe.

“I’m just super excited to serve Canada in that role,” Hansen said in a video he posted Tuesday on social media.

“There’s so much opportunity to leverage this position that we’re already in, to do more to provide for our sovereignty, our security, our quality of life on the planet, and at the same time make significant contributions on the global stage.”

The role involves advising Carney and Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, Hansen said.

In April, as part of the Artemis II mission, Hansen and three other astronauts travelled around the moon and further out into space than any humans before them.

Joly said Hansen proposed helping the government “develop a new space strategy” when he left the Canadian Space Agency.

“We had a conversation of how he could continue to have an impact, to contribute, to serve,” she said at an event Tuesday.

Joly said she’s getting feedback from other Canadian astronauts and people in the aerospace sector on the strategy “in order to accelerate innovation and reinforce our international partnerships.”

The offices of Carney and Joly did not respond when asked for details of Hansen’s role, such as its end date and compensation.

On Wednesday, Defence Minister David McGuinty announced a $20 million agreement on the use of a space launch complex in southern Newfoundland, which builds on a March agreement involving a complex in Nova Scotia.

“Reliable and independent launch access will enable Canada to place critical satellites into orbit even during global uncertainty, geopolitical tensions, or disruptions in foreign launch markets,” McGuinty’s department wrote in a news release.

“With military, emergency response, and government services increasingly dependent on space-based systems, sovereign launch (capacity) protects national interests and enables continuity of operations.”

Hansen’s appointment comes as Canada looks to expand co-operation with European countries in space — and as Washington warns it could seek partners other than Canada for its space missions.

Joly spoke Tuesday at the SpaceBound 2026 Conference. U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra told that same conference that Canada has decided to “move away” from the American firm SpaceX.

“Canada has said that, ‘We’re going to take a look at the European Space Agency, we’re going do more with them,’” he said.

Hoekstra said it was helpful to know that Canada is not interested in partnering with the firm founded by billionaire Elon Musk, who has close ties to U.S. President Donald Trump.

“It’s kind of like, wow, Canada is really saying for all the investment, all the innovation, all the excellence that is being driven by Elon, we don’t want to be a part of it? OK. That’s fine,” he said.

Hoekstra said the United States will always have a “bias” toward the private sector.

“Competition breeds excellence,” he said.

“What we fight in the United States all the time is to make sure that we never come in and over-regulate it. We’ve had to fight that, in the digital world … We’ll probably have to fight this in the space realm.”

Hoekstra added that the F-35 jet is “the best fighter in the world.” He did not directly mention Ottawa’s decision to pause a planned purchase of F-35s after Trump launched his trade war and repeatedly threatened Canada’s sovereignty.

“We also recognize that Canada’s going through a re-evaluation of how they want to move forward on defence,” he said.

Hoekstra said Washington is waiting to see whether Canada wants to continue decades of airspace co-operation through Norad. He said Trump’s recent security deal with Greenland — which also followed his repeated threats to annex the island — is meant to shore up U.S. security in the North.

“We’re waiting to see exactly where Canada wants to go on this,” he said. “We’d love to do it with Canada. It would be very, very helpful. But at the same time, and I’ve said this for the past year and a half, we are not standing still.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Federal, Ontario governments to announce billions in support for key sectors, source says
stories.summary: Support to focus on tariff-stricken steel, energy and auto sectors, as well as Ontario’s Ring of Fire region
stories.author: Laura Stone, Stephanie Levitz
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced $9-billion in supports on Wednesday for the steel and auto sectors hit by U.S. tariffs and funding for roads into the province’s Ring of Fire minerals region.

The Prime Minister, alongside Mr. Ford in Ottawa, said the new “action plan” will protect jobs and make Canada more independent.

In prepared remarks, Mr. Carney said the U.S. tariffs have raised costs for Americans, while putting Ontario workers and businesses “at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty.”

“The world May have changed. But what makes Ontario and Canada great hasn’t changed. We have the minerals. We have the steel. We have the ingenuity. And we have the best workers on earth,” he said.

“Protecting what we have is not enough. We must go further. To transform our economy. To secure our future.”

It’s unclear whether all of the money announced is new funding.

The announcement includes more than $5-billion for a new Joint Steel Action Fund, which Mr. Carney says will enable mills to upgrade machinery and manufacture more products Canada needs and expand to meet demand in non-U.S. markets.

Mr. Carney said the government is also strengthening enforcement to protect against foreign steel dumping.

The new plan includes $2.5-billion for the auto sector to boost electric vehicle production and to position Canada to become what Mr. Carney says is “a global leader in EV production.”

As a result of the tariffs, the Prime Minister said Canada’s auto exports to the U.S. have declined by more than 10 per cent, while U.S. exports to Canada have fallen by more than 20 per cent, even though Canada is still the U.S.’s largest customer.

“Nobody wins from this. Tariffs make both our industries weaker and reduce choice for families. That’s why Canada remains ready to negotiate a fair deal when the U.S. is ready to sit down in good faith,” Mr. Carney said in his remarks.

“An integrated, North American auto sector will be stronger, more competitive, and provide better jobs for our workers. But we recognize these are not the objectives of the current U.S. administration. Their approach has changed, and so must ours.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled an $8.7-billion joint plan to help tariff-affected industries in the province battered by the trade war. The funds will target steel companies, the auto sector and critical mineral development in Ontario's Ring of Fire.

The Canadian Press

Ontario and the federal government also pledged to create a working group to engage with local Indigenous communities to create opportunities for economic development, as well as conservation and Indigenous protected areas.

In addition, Ottawa is also committing up to $1-billion over three years to build road infrastructure to reach the Ring of Fire critical minerals region in the far north of Ontario.

Ottawa’s funding pledge removes a key hurdle that had held back development for decades.

Located in a remote boggy region, about 550 kilometres north of Thunder Bay, the Ring of Fire has long been promoted by Ontario as holding vast quantities of critical mineral riches including nickel and chromite.

While Mr. Ford has long promised to invest $1-billion into the roads, and repeatedly pressed the federal government to follow suit, Ottawa had hesitated to pull the trigger amid questions over whether mining projects in the region were sufficiently profitable to justify building the infrastructure.

Australia’s Wyloo Pty Ltd. owns the high-grade Eagle’s Nest nickel project in the Ring of Fire, which is the most promising project in the region. The initial mine life is only about 11 years.

Since 2019, Webequie First Nation and Marten Falls First Nation have been leading federal environmental assessments into various sections of the road. Two of three assessments have been completed and early construction work has started. The assessment on the final Northern Road Link Project section hasn’t yet been completed. The roads would allow Wyloo to transport nickel to markets, and also connect the two First Nations to the provincial highway network.

Earlier this year, Mr. Ford, a perennial booster of the Ring of Fire, predicted that roads into the region should be completed by 2031, which would pave the way for mining to start.

Wednesday’s announcements in steel, critical minerals and autos are happening amid rising tensions with the Trump administration.

U.S. steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs is locked in a battle with Ottawa after its subsidiary Stelco announced last month it was laying off hundreds of workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont.

The federal government has threatened legal action, alleging Cliffs has breached legally binding job commitments from when it acquired Stelco in 2024, including maintaining at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada for five years.

Cliffs says it can no longer compete in galvanized steel in Canada, owing to both the trade war with the United States and Ottawa not doing enough to prevent a flood of cheap imports.

content_blocks.text: The Prime Minister, alongside Mr. Ford in Ottawa, said the new “action plan” will protect jobs and make Canada more independent.

stories.title: Risk to Windsor, Ont., 'very low' after Ohio chemical leak: mayor's office
stories.summary: Windsor - A spokesperson for the mayor of Windsor, Ont., says the border city is monitoring a toxic chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio that prompted evacuations on Tuesday night.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Windsor - A spokesperson for the mayor of Windsor, Ont., says the border city is monitoring a toxic chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio that prompted evacuations on Tuesday night.

The spokesperson says the risk to Windsor residents is “very low” as the city is about 90 kilometres northeast of Toledo on the shores of Lake Erie and winds are blowing in the opposite direction.

stories.title: Carney and Ford set to announce support for workers amid trade war
stories.summary: Prime Minister Carney will begin the day with a meeting of the Liberal caucus and then with Ontario Premier Doug Ford, his office said in his itinerary on Wednesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney will be with Ontario Premier Doug Ford in Ottawa on Wednesday as the two are set to announce support for tariff-hit industries and workers.

Carney will begin the day with a meeting of the Liberal caucus and then with Ford, his office said in his itinerary.

Following his meeting with Ford, the two will “make an announcement to protect workers and strengthen Ontario industries.”

Later in the day, Carney will depart for Turkey.

The announcement comes as workers at an Ontario-based steel manufacturing plant are facing imminent layoffs.

Stelco announced last month that pressure from U.S. tariffs forced it to concentrate steel production at its Lake Erie Works plant in Haldimand, and halt production at its plant in Hamilton. Some employees would be offered transfers, but many would be out of work.

A resolution of the standoff between the federal government and Stelco is a “question of days,” Industry Minister Melanie Joly said on Friday.

The federal government believes there have been “multiple breaches of the commitments” that Stelco made under the Investment Canada Act.

Stelco is facing financial penalties and “a potential forced divestiture,” which would force them to sell all their assets in Canada, Joly said.

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said on Tuesday that the federal government would release its federal budget on Nov. 5, two days after the U.S. midterm elections.

Champagne announced the date during question period on Tuesday.

The budget will be second as Carney, who changed the schedule for how federal budgets are released by moving them from spring to fall.

Carney’s second budget date comes after the Parliamentary Budget Officer trimmed the 2026 and 2027 outlook for economic growth.

The PBO now projects gross domestic product growth of 0.9 per cent for this year and 1.5 per cent for 2027, down from 1.1 per cent and 1.6 per cent respectively.

–with files from Global’s Sean Previl
