stories.title: Temporary residents outside Quebec scramble to learn French to stay in Canada
stories.summary: Many temporary residents outside of Quebec are trying to learn French in the hope of obtaining permanent residency in Canada.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
By Paula Saraza, Omni News

Posted October 21, 2026 10:36 am.

In previous federal announcements, Ottawa has stressed its commitment to prioritizing Francophone immigration outside Quebec, prompting many temporary residents to learn French in the hope of obtaining permanent residency (PR) in Canada.

“After graduating and then working for a year, you could’ve easily gotten permanent residency,” says Alyanna Chua, who came to Canada as an international student in 2019.

Chua says that, at the time, immigration policies were relatively straightforward, and the path to permanent residency was simple.

A strong PR candidate must be fluent in English, be in a younger age bracket, hold a bachelor’s degree from a Canadian institution, and have at least one year of Canadian work experience.

“It was relatively simple because the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score required to immigrate and become a permanent resident was relatively low at that time,” she says. “It was in the 400s, and my score at that time was around 474.”

However, she says the rules changed when she graduated in 2023, following the COVID-19 pandemic, as Ottawa introduced cuts to the number of permanent and temporary residents in the country.

That’s when, according to Chua, the immigration score increased to around 530 to 540, a range she says would have been impossible for her to reach without studying French.

In Canada’s Express Entry System, there’s a French-language proficiency category in which an applicant could receive up to 50 additional points toward their Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score if they pass their French exam and reach the minimum B2 level.

With her status set to expire in October 2026, Chua says she spent almost the entirety of 2024 learning French.

She says she took the test twice after failing on her first attempt in October of last year. She eventually passed the exam last November, and her CRS score increased to the 500s.

Chua received her permanent residency status in July.

Demand to learn French outside of Quebec grows as French Category-based draws for permanent residency increase.

According to immigration lawyer Lou Janssen Dangzalan, the number of PR invitations issued through French-speaking category-based draws is tremendous.

He says the trend mirrors Ottawa’s French PR admission targets: 9.5 per cent in 2026, increasing to 10 per cent next year and 12 per cent by 2028.

“This has been a program that is allowing them to hit that particular parliamentary mandate,” Dangzalan says.

However, he says it’s uncertain whether this is an effective step toward strengthening French language proficiency in the country.

The increasing demand for French lessons among non-French-speaking residents is also being felt in some sectors.

Study Live Explore Canada, an online platform initially designed to mentor international students, has changed course and transformed into a French tutoring platform.

“At first, we were just getting a few students, and now we have about 500 students, mostly Filipinos,” says founder Emmalyn de Guzman.

Aida Valdez-Cabel, a French tutor with the organization, says most of her students are from Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta.

Recently, the federal government announced changes to the Express Entry System for immigrants with high-wage jobs, but no definite details were released about Ottawa’s immigration levels plan, which is expected to be announced in November.

Experts say there’s a strong possibility that Ottawa will continue its focus on French-speaking permanent resident admissions outside Quebec.

Now a fluent French speaker, Chua says she recognizes the challenges of learning a new language, the pressure of an expiring status, and the cost of lessons and exams faced by people with temporary status.

“I still take one French class every single week,” she says. “Just to be able to maintain my French.”

Chua says that with her improved language skills, she’s confident they could lead to more opportunities as she continues building her life in Canada.

stories.title: Atlas expansion aims to boost wood products production in Clinton
stories.summary: The announcement was made Wednesday by Sarnia-Lambton MP Marilyn Gladu on behalf of Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson during a groundbreaking ceremony at the site.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Atlas Engineered Products has broken ground on a new robotics manufacturing facility in Clinton.

A $4-million investment from Natural Resources Canada, through the Investments in Forest Industry Transformation (Ifit) program, is intended to help the company expand production capacity and strengthen the wood construction supply chain through increased manufacturing of value-added building materials.

The announcement was made Wednesday by Sarnia-Lambton MP Marilyn Gladu on behalf of Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson during a groundbreaking ceremony at the site.

According to the federal government, the new facility will allow Atlas Engineered Products to modernize and expand its manufacturing operations with advanced automation and robotics technology.

The investment comes as Canada’s forest sector faces economic pressures, including trade challenges and tariffs affecting exports to the United States. Federal officials say the funding is aimed at helping Canadian forestry and wood-products companies innovate and expand production.

In a statement, Hodgson said the forestry industry remains a key economic driver for many Canadian communities and that investments in industrial-scale innovation can help companies increase capacity and develop new products.

Gladu said projects such as the Clinton facility help create jobs and support economic growth in smaller communities.

Atlas Engineered Products manufactures wood-based building components and construction products. The company says the new facility will help increase production while supporting demand for housing and other construction projects.

No timeline for the facility’s completion was immediately announced.

stories.title: Carney heads to Turkey for 1st bilateral visit to deepen ties with Nato ally
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney is travelling to Turkey on Wednesday for a three-day trip that experts say should show how his approach to international diplomacy differs from that of the previous Liberal government.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney is travelling to Turkey on Wednesday for a three-day trip that experts say should show how his approach to international diplomacy differs from that of the previous Liberal government.

Carney’s office says this is the first official bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey. Carney met with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Turkey earlier this year as part of the Nato summit.

The prime minister will land in Ankara early Thursday for a meeting with Erdogan before heading to Istanbul to meet with Turkish business leaders on Friday.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson will join Carney on the trip.

Senior government officials providing a background briefing to reporters ahead of the trip said Canada is seeking deeper political, economic and security ties with Turkey.

Carney’s bid to diversify trade beyond the United States and find new global investors for Canadian infrastructure projects is well-suited to deeper ties with Turkey, said Kerim Uras, the former Turkish ambassador to Canada.

Both the Canadian and Turkish economies need alternatives to the increasingly protectionist U.S. market, Uras said in an interview. While neither country can replace the United States with any one partner, forging connections between middle powers should be part of the path forward, he said.

“One can summarize it like the Carney doctrine meets Turkish pragmatism,” said Uras, now a senior fellow at Carleton University’s Centre in Modern Turkish Studies.

Turkish contractors are used to doing work in periods of geopolitical turmoil, Uras said. The country sits at the crossroads between Europe and the Middle East, with the Russia-Ukraine conflict across the Black Sea to its north and southern and eastern borders with Syria, Iraq and Iran.

“I would describe Turkey as an island of stability today in a very troublesome neighbourhood,” Uras said.

After Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Turkey brokered a deal with both nations to allow for grain exports, as the war threatened crucial food supplies for numerous developing countries.

Canada and Turkey have had formal diplomatic ties since 1944. The federal government estimates there are 76,000 members of the Turkish diaspora living in Canada.

Technical talks are underway on a Canada-Turkey free-trade agreement. Two-way trade between the nations totalled $4.3 billion in 2025, with Turkish exports to Canada accounting for the bulk of that.

Uras called that trade volume “peanuts” compared to the size of the two economies.

“With a little work, we could quadruple this very fast and I’m sure there is a mutual desire to do that,” he said.

Senior government officials said Carney and Erdogan will highlight free trade and progress on other key files during the visit. They would not say whether there will be any formal announcements of any new deals from the leaders’ meetings in Ankara.

Bessma Momani is a politics professor at the University of Waterloo and senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation. She said in an interview that Canada’s relationship with Turkey has been “low stakes” to date, but there are reasons for Canada to pursue closer ties now.

While Turkey is an “industrial and consumer powerhouse,” Momani said the country’s reliance on Russia and Iran for energy is a source of weakness.

“I think their Achilles heel for them has always been energy. And that’s something that Canada has something to potentially offer,” she said.

When Anand hosted Turkish Foreign Affairs Minister Hakan Fidan in Canada in June, they toured the Darlington Nuclear Generating Station near Bowmanville, Ont.

Uras said Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRéalis — maker of the Candu reactor in operation at Darlington — is one of the leading contenders to supply two planned nuclear power plants in Turkey.

A senior government official briefing reporters said Hodgson’s presence on the trip speaks to the importance of energy projects in discussions with Turkey.

Beyond nuclear, Uras said Turkish contractors are keen on a variety of projects across Canada in industries such as critical minerals, shipping and construction. As Nato allies, Canada and Turkey also have opportunities to collaborate on defence spending, the former ambassador suggested.

Uras, who was Turkey’s ambassador to Canada from 2018 to 2023, noted his time as envoy was characterized more by what couldn’t be traded between the nations.

In 2019, Canada banned arms exports to Turkey in response to the country’s military incursion into Syria. It expanded the ban after subsequent conflicts in the region showed Canadian-made technology, specifically drone parts, had been diverted to Azerbaijan. Canada lifted that ban in 2024 in the face of criticism from Armenian diaspora groups.

Uras said he doesn’t expect any lingering issues around the arms embargo. Canada and Turkey “hit the reset button” when Carney came to power, he said.

The Erdogan government is under heavy scrutiny internationally right now over reports of official persecution of Lgbtq+ organizers in the country.

Human Rights Watch and independent experts at the United Nations have condemned co-ordinated police raids on Lgbtq+ advocacy organizations in Turkey in recent months.

Canada did not join Germany, France and others in a joint statement last month condemning the country’s Lgbtq+ raids.

Government officials would not tell reporters whether Carney plans to raise the issue in private conversations with Erdogan.

One senior official called Canada’s approach to international affairs principled and pragmatic and said Canada recognizes not all partners will share Canada’s values.

Momani said as awful as Erdogan’s Lgbtq+ raids are, Turkey is not the only country in the world sliding back from liberal values. She said she expects Carney will take an approach different from that of his predecessor Justin Trudeau.

“I just don’t think the Carney government wants to make that a priority in the way that perhaps the Trudeau government was a little more willing to see foreign policy as a tool for moralizing their preferred social values,” Momani said.

Carney has argued closed-door conversations on rights issues are more productive than “lecturing countries from afar.”

Uras agreed that “megaphone diplomacy” does not help bridge values between allies, but he said it could be a topic of conversation between the leaders.

“Instead of walking away from the table, talking about these behind closed doors at the table is a much healthier approach. I’m sure we can discuss anything together and we will listen to each other,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

— with files from Dylan Robertson

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: London Knights appoint new captain
stories.summary: The London Knights have named Ryan Brown as the 55th team captain in franchise history. Brown's teammates vote...
stories.author: Ben McFadden
stories.content:
The London Knights have named Ryan Brown as the 55th team captain in franchise history.

Brown’s teammates voted him in for showing a “high level of character,” said Rob Simpson, the Knights’ associate general manager.

Already a Dallas Stars prospect, the 18-year-old was announced in the new role Monday, and is preparing to lead his team against the Sarnia Stings for his first game in the new position.

“It’s a super cool feeling and a huge privilege to be on this team, let alone the captain of it,” said Brown, who is from Newmarket, Ont.

Ryan Brown #43 Captain of London Knights Photo credit: Benjamin McFadden XFM News

“There has been some great names before me, so I’m just trying to bring my own style and be myself.”

Brown will be leading the charge against Sarnia Wednesday with alternate captains Evan Van-Gorp and Cohen Bidgood.

The Knights are 7-1 this season and sit second in the Western Conference.

As the Knights see continuous changes to their roster this new adjustment comes to the excitement of teammates who look to see No.43 lead them in the remaining season.

The Knights, won against the Erie Otters on Sunday.

Ryan Brown previously played for his hometown team the Newmarket Minor Hockey Association (MHA) and quickly rose through the ranks, he showcases amazing talent and hard-working character to inspire his team going forward.

“Growing up and seeing my brother play in his OHL games really motivated me to get to this spot now,” the new Captain said.

stories.title: One person dead after early morning blaze damages London home
stories.summary: Emergency crews were called to a residence on Lyman Street, just north of Oxford Street East, shortly after 6:30 a.m. Wednesday.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A person has died following an early morning house fire in London.

Emergency crews were called to a residence on Lyman Street, just north of Oxford Street East, shortly after 6:30 a.m. Wednesday.

London fire officials said one resident and a dog were able to safely escape the home. The individual who evacuated told firefighters there May have been another person still inside the home.

Firefighters entered the property and found a person on the main floor. Crews determined the individual was deceased.

According to deputy chief Gary Bridge, when firefighters arrived, smoke and flames were visible from the home. The fire caused significant damage to the residence.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation, and officials have not released any information about the identity of the deceased.

London fire, the London Police Service and the Ontario Fire Marshal’s Office are investigating. Authorities did not comment when asked whether the fire is considered suspicious.

With files from CTV News London’s Sean Irvine

stories.title: Expert insight: Why ‘vertical farming’ is not a fix for our food system
stories.summary: Western University experts argue that vertical farming often requires enormous amounts of energy and extensive digital infrastructure.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
The Canadian government launched its first-ever National Food Security Strategy in June 2026. The strategy aims to invest $750 million to increase year-round Canadian production of fruits and vegetables, including on so-called vertical farms.

These multi-storey towers and warehouses filled with fresh produce glowing under artificial light May seem like the future of food. Promoted as climate-resilient, land-saving and a positive form of urban development, vertical plant factories, commonly referred to as vertical farms, are drawing investment from governments and venture capital alike.

What we refer to as vertical plant factories are fully enclosed buildings or warehouses where artificial lighting, wiring, plumbing, engineered substrates and climate control systems replace sun, soil and seasons. These systems are largely oriented toward producing leafy greens and berries.

We recently took a closer look at the claims made about vertical plant factories. We examined the claims made by leading Canadian vertical farm developers and how those claims have been covered in major Canadian news outlets.

We argue that vertical plant factories are not a solution to the problems of industrial agriculture. Instead, they represent a problematic continuation of its contradictory logic.

Vertical plant factories are widely promoted as a sustainable response to mounting environmental crises and future food security challenges. They are also touted for using less water and less land.

Yet, they often require enormous amounts of energy and extensive digital infrastructure that monitors and controls production, while replacing functions otherwise provided by ecological processes and farmer knowledge.

Growing plants in a sealed building means replacing the free energy of sunlight with high-powered LEDs and temperature and ventilation systems that run around the clock. Furthermore, equipment like lighting, wiring, tubing, microchips and so on must be frequently replaced as they break down or get outdated. The result is a far more material- and energy-intensive system of production than is typically conveyed.

An important limitation of vertical plant factories is that they cannot grow staple crops. Instead, many focus on high-margin items like lettuce, microgreens and berries.

These high prices per volume are required to pay the enormous energy and infrastructure costs associated with plant factories. In fact, several high-profile bankruptcies in recent years have plagued the industry.

The types of fresh produce grown are often nutritionally limited foods that are prohibitively expensive for low-income consumers. So claims vertical plant factories can help address food insecurity into the future are misleading.

The fact that the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations does not include leafy greens in global hunger statistics is telling.

Enough food is produced globally to feed the population, but prioritizing distribution remains a problem.

Why, then, do these systems continue to attract support from investors and policymakers?

Part of the answer lies in what Sharon Stein and Evan Bowness call the “politics of continuity.” They use this to describe the struggle over what contemporary societies seek to preserve amid deepening environmental instability, what they are willing to do to achieve these ends and who bears the costs.

In the food system, the politics of continuity is visible in efforts to maintain existing expectations of abundance even as the ecological conditions and resource intensity that make them possible become more uncertain.

Canadians have grown accustomed to supermarket shelves stocked year-round with fresh produce. Vertical plant factories promise to sustain this expectation instead of adapting food systems and consumption patterns to ecological limits.

Vertical plant factories are a vivid example of the politics of continuity. Our point is that enormous technological and material investments are being mobilized to preserve the expectation that a particular version of the present can be sustained into an increasingly unstable future.

Proponents of vertical plant factories argue they promote growth and preserve consumption habits without sacrifice. This is a compelling sales pitch. For governments, they promise sleek, high-tech solutions that can serve to divert public resources toward speculative systems, while ecologically sound and community-based food alternatives remain overlooked.

Vertical plant factories command extensive energy and resource budgets – for example, 4.4 kilowatt-hours per kilogram of lettuce produced. They also command attention, policy space and imagination.

One of the great risks in this sort of capital-intensive response is that it draws attention away from better and more feasible solutions, such as the urgent need to improve access to land for new farmers. They also replace farming knowledge and labour with increasingly automated systems.

In short, attempts to preserve things as they are can foreclose other possible futures. Rather than asking how food systems might become more ecologically grounded, fair and resilient, vertical plant factories frame the question in narrow terms: how can technology allow us to meet our current expectations of abundance?

This does not mean vertical plant factory technology can never be useful. In Canada’s North, at relatively small scales (inside shipping containers, for example) and using solar power instead of diesel fuel, it could be possible to produce fresh greens in ways that make economic and environmental sense and reduce the reliance on long-distance shipping. However, broader claims about plant factories cannot credibly invoke food security or be cast as a response to the harms of industrial agriculture.

If governments are serious about building a better food system, they need to stop chasing technological fantasies and start supporting more grounded alternatives. That means investing in farmers, land access and place-based knowledge rather than capital- and material-intensive towers of leafy greens and berries.

The challenge is not to decide which technologies can keep the existing food system going, but to ask what is worth carrying forward, what needs to change, and whose futures our choices make possible.Image 1: The Conversation

Richard Bloomfield, PhD Candidate, Geography and Environment, Western University; Evan Bowness, Assistant Professor, Geography and Environment, and Tony Weis, Professor of Geography and Environment, Western University.

stories.title: Carney, Ford to announce support for steel and auto sectors hit by tariffs
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are expected to unveil a new suite of supports for the steel and auto sectors hit by U.S. tariffs.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are expected to unveil a new suite of supports for the steel and auto sectors hit by U.S. tariffs.

Carney’s itinerary says he will meet with Ford on Parliament Hill today, with a joint announcement to follow.

A source with knowledge of the announcement but not authorized to speak publicly about the details, says support for critical minerals is also on the table.

Carney and Ford’s respective finance ministers are also expected to be on hand.

On Tuesday, federal Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said the Carney government will deliver its second budget on Nov. 5.

Carney is set to depart for Ankara, Turkey later today.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

The record-setting $90 million Lotto Max jackpot was won in Alberta following Tuesday night’s draw, the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation says.

The OLG didn’t say whether there was one winner or multiple in a news release Wednesday. The jackpot climbed to $90 million after several winner-less draws.

The OLG said multiple Ontario-based players won MaxMillion and MaxPlus prizes Tuesday night. Three $1 million prizes were sold in Brant County, Toronto and online.

Twelve MaxPlus tickets each worth $100,000, and five MaxPlus tickets worth $50,000 were sold elsewhere in the province.

LottoMax draws happen every Friday and Tuesday.

stories.title: Grocery diaries: Korean-Canadian writer Ann Choi on fermented foods
stories.summary: What once had to be homemade, like kimchi, can now be found in Korean groceries in many cities
stories.author: Daniel Reale-Chin
stories.content:
When Ann Y.K. Choi was growing up in the 70s, kimchi was hard to find in Toronto, so Choi’s parents would spend a week making a season’s worth of the fermented vegetables. Her youth is marked by huge boxes of green napa cabbage, red gochugaru (Korean chili paste), white radishes and the sight of her parents – two proud Korean-Canadian variety store owners – chopping and prepping the vegetables for kimchi.

“For a week, everything smells like garlic and fish sauce,” she says.

As a child, Choi resented the pungent smell of kimchi – the sharp scent of garlic and the funk of fish sauce – and the way it lingered in her clothes and hair. As an adult, those same scents have become a source of inspiration for Choi’s writing.

The author of three books – Kay’s Lucky Coin Variety , Once Upon an Hour and her latest, All Things Under the Moon , published last year – Choi uses Korean food as a motif throughout her fiction.

Her debut novel, Kay’s Lucky Coin Variety, was published in 2016 and became the first contemporary Korean novel to be published in Canada. Much of the plot was inspired by Choi’s own upbringing: her parents, who owned a convenience store in Toronto’s Trinity-Bellwoods neighbourhood; the milk, bread and peanut butter that she saw their white customers buy; and the hours her parents spent above the shop fermenting foods and preparing banchan – side dishes of seasoned vegetables, such as spinach and soybean sprouts – for their own meals.

Seeing that contrast in how other Canadians were able to quickly purchase staples such as peanut butter and canned soups while her mother toiled away above the shop fed Choi’s rejection of Korean food.

“As a young person, I always wondered, why is Korean food so hard?”

But things have changed since the days of the Choi family variety store. Now, Choi has her choice of kimchi and fermented soy beans at the many Korean grocery and convenience stores in her neighbourhood.

Korean grocery chains such as Galleria Supermarket, H Mart and PAT Supermarket have spread rapidly across Canada to meet the demands of both Korean populations and other Canadians who enjoy the taste of Korean foods.

Kimchi, in particular, has grown in popularity, with videos touting its health benefits racking up tens of thousands of views on social media as more Canadians turn to fermented foods for their potential to improve their gut microbiome and immune function (researchers are still studying the potential benefits of these foods).

When choosing a store-bought kimchi to feed her own family – her daughter and mother (her husband, who is not Korean, does not enjoy it) – she turns to H Mart or Galleria, grocery stores that make their banchan in-house, and looks for kimchi made with napa cabbage and a strong smell of garlic and fish sauce.

“It should smell pungent. That means it has sat for a while to ferment,” she says.

How I save money on groceries: I chase weekly flyers. My mom got me into them, she gets the Korean newspaper, where they advertise. I now do it online, where it’s easy to find deals that are happening by going to the grocers’ website.

How I splurge on groceries: One thing I cannot make myself are Korean rice cakes. I absolutely love them. They’re pretty easy to find at Korean grocery stores or bakeries. Luna Bakery on Yonge St. in Toronto has amazing rice cakes, but they’re expensive: Boxes of mini rice cakes are $8.99. Because rice cakes don’t have gluten, I can still indulge despite my gluten sensitivity.

The hardest shopping habit to keep up: Trying to maintain the tradition and making stuff from scratch. I live in North York, where many Korean grocery stores such as Galleria, H Mart and PAT Supermarket exist and are within seven minutes of my house. It’s hard to resist the temptation to buy premade instead of appreciating the process of making things from scratch to teach my daughter her culture.

How I’ve changed my eating habits recently: A lot of it was when my father was diagnosed with stomach cancer. It forced my family to rethink what goes into our bodies. I now eat more intentionally, rather than eating out or eating highly processed foods often, where I can’t see what ingredients they put into their food. I also started introducing more proteins and foods into my diet that I know are high in nutrients: sardines, liver meat.

Roasted seaweed - T&T - $2.19 for a pack of three: These are low-calorie snacks that taste great.

Golden Curry Sauce Mix - S&B - $3.97 each: This brand makes Korean/Japanese curries that taste great. It’s easy to throw protein, potatoes and carrots into a pot and make a quick meal with a pack of this.

Shin Ramyun - Nongshim - $4.44 a pack: This was such a treat for us growing up, because it was something that we could make without our parents, and now it’s still a guilty pleasure for me. I try to make it healthier by topping it with eggs and green onions and serving it in a nice dish to sort of elevate it.

Mat Kimchi - Galleria - $19.99 for 1.8 kilograms: ​When I first learned to use chopsticks, I was about three or four, and kimchi was the first thing that I learned to pick up, so kimchi will always be a staple for me.

Fuji apples - 85 cents each: They’re very crisp and sweet, compared to some other apples. My mom made us eat so many apples growing up, so it also reminds me of my childhood.

stories.title: Some bright lights, but many cottage sellers see dim prospects
stories.summary: Many of the properties changing hands are in the upper tier, where buyers with deep pockets May be less swayed by fluctuations in the economic outlook and financial markets
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
In Ontario’s cottage country, buyers and sellers often aim to have a deal in place before the clocks turn back and the first dusting of snow descends.

This fall, many of the properties changing hands are in the upper tier, where buyers with deep pockets May be less swayed by fluctuations in the economic outlook and financial markets.

Some sellers also become more willing to negotiate or cut the asking price as the season winds down, agents say.

Anita Springate-Renaud, broker with Engel & Völkers Toronto Central, says sales have been more brisk in the markets she oversees in the smaller towns of Port Carling and Collingwood than in the city.

Agents in Muskoka are busy with evaluating properties for prospective sellers and touring with buyers, she says.

Ms. Springate-Renaud points to a swathe of land on a secluded bay on Lake Rosseau that sold for $8.699-million in late September.

The 11.3-acre property at 1246 Purdy Rd. with 602 feet of shoreline, a four-bedroom cottage and a two-storey boathouse was listed in early spring with an asking price of $8.999-million, then reduced to $8.699-million in August.

Meanwhile, sales in the city have stalled amid concerns about the U.S.-Canada trade war, interest rates and the economy.

“Toronto is horribly slow,” says Ms. Springate-Renaud.

Toronto and Vancouver led Canada’s housing market into reverse in September as the two most expensive cities dragged down national sales and prices, notes Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics.

Mr. Brown points to the rise in rates for fixed-term mortgages as the main factor in a 2.3 per cent drop in seasonally adjusted national sales in September compared with August.

Another reason for weak sales in the Greater Toronto Area is that homeowners who purchased during the period of ultralow interest rates and soaring prices during the COVID-19 pandemic cannot sell for the amount they paid, Ms. Springate-Renaud says.

Some are setting asking prices with the hope of breaking even or making a small profit, but buyers are not willing to pay those prices.

“They’re not going to get anywhere near what they bought it for,” she says.

The condo segment continues to struggle, she says. Agents in her office recently listed three condos, and two of the units had had no showings after several days on the market, she says.

“I have so many agents not even getting appointments.”

Ms. Springate-Renaud adds that some urban dwellers in their late 20s and early 30s figure they are priced out of buying a house, so they are renting in Toronto and buying a cottage or vacation home outside the city, she says.

Paul Crammond, broker with Chestnut Park Real Estate, sees purchasers on the large lakes of Rosseau, Joseph and Muskoka buying for the first time.

The so-called Big Three at the top end of the market command the highest prices.

He recently worked with first-time cottage buyers who paid above the $10-million mark for a large family cottage with a garage and boathouse.

The buyers had been searching for a few years, he adds.

The cottage, built approximately 10 years ago, was listed in the spring with an asking price of $13.5-million, he says, but compared with others in that price range, this property didn’t measure up.

“At that level, the buyers are usually extra-sharp and looking for fair value.”

Mr. Crammond and his business partner, broker Tracy Stewart, pointed to the sale prices of comparable listings, and the sellers were willing to negotiate.

Usually such a large gap between the amount a property is listed for and the price a buyer is willing to pay does not result in a deal, he notes.

Mr. Crammond says transactions in Muskoka fell about 4 per cent in the first half of the year compared with the first half of 2025. New listings rose 3 per cent in the same period.

Prices in the upper echelons have not declined in most cases, he says, because the supply of luxury cottages on the Big Three is scarce. A handful of sales above $20-million can skew average prices for the entire area.

“It is a tiny market,” he says. “Because it’s such a small sampling, it’s tough to get accurate stats.”

The average price on the Big Three stood at $2.1-million at the end of June compared with $1.8-million at the end of 2025, he notes.

The population is shrinking in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we put more housing there?

Sales on Muskoka’s smaller lakes have entered a more severe downturn, says Mr. Crammond, as some buyers who purchased during the pandemic have seen the value of their property fall by as much 35 or 40 per cent.

Between 2020 and 2022, bidding wars erupted, and prices skyrocketed during a stretch of low interest rates and “fear of missing out.”

“It was a frenzy,” says Mr. Crammond. “It was an absolute frenzy, and the prices made no sense.”

A cottage that sold for $1.1-million during the mania might change hands for $700,000 in the fall of 2026, he says.

That reduction in value has people who bought during COVID trapped, Mr. Crammond says. Even if they want to move up to a larger lake or better-equipped cottage, they don’t have the funds to do so.

The owner who paid $1.1-million might have a mortgage of $800,000, for example, and the cottage is worth less than that today.

“They’ve got zero equity from that place on the small lake,” he says. “That’s the same situation in the city that’s freezing the market.”

But while first-time buyers in the luxury segment do not grapple with that problem, they do have an aversion to overpaying, he adds.

Sellers need to start with a realistic asking price.

“If the properties are priced accurately, they do sell quite quickly – even over the $5-million and $10-million mark.

Sales in more modest segments have been harder hit by fears around inflation, the economy and jobs, he says, noting that a recreational property is a discretionary purchase.

“We have had buyers back off,” says Mr. Crammond. “If you’re not taking on more debt, you’re certainly taking on more expenses,” he says of the cost of ownership.

“It’s a luxury purchase even at the entry level.”

The 11.3-acre property at 1246 Purdy Rd. with 602 feet of shoreline, a four-bedroom cottage and a two-storey boathouse was listed in early spring with an asking price of $8.999-million, then reduced to $8.699-million in August.
Meanwhile, sales in the city have stalled amid concerns about the U.S.-Canada trade war, interest rates and the economy.
“Toronto is horribly slow,” says Ms. Springate-Renaud.

Toronto and Vancouver led Canada’s housing market into reverse in September as the two most expensive cities dragged down national sales and prices, notes Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics.
Mr. Brown points to the rise in rates for fixed-term mortgages as the main factor in a 2.3 per cent drop in seasonally adjusted national sales in September compared with August.

Another reason for weak sales in the Greater Toronto Area is that homeowners who purchased during the period of ultralow interest rates and soaring prices during the COVID-19 pandemic cannot sell for the amount they paid, Ms. Springate-Renaud says.
Some are setting asking prices with the hope of breaking even or making a small profit, but buyers are not willing to pay those prices.
“They’re not going to get anywhere near what they bought it for,” she says.
The condo segment continues to struggle, she says. Agents in her office recently listed three condos, and two of the units had had no showings after several days on the market, she says.
“I have so many agents not even getting appointments.”

Ms. Springate-Renaud adds that some urban dwellers in their late 20s and early 30s figure they are priced out of buying a house, so they are renting in Toronto and buying a cottage or vacation home outside the city, she says.
Paul Crammond, broker with Chestnut Park Real Estate, sees purchasers on the large lakes of Rosseau, Joseph and Muskoka buying for the first time.
The so-called Big Three at the top end of the market command the highest prices.
He recently worked with first-time cottage buyers who paid above the $10-million mark for a large family cottage with a garage and boathouse.
The buyers had been searching for a few years, he adds.
The cottage, built approximately 10 years ago, was listed in the spring with an asking price of $13.5-million, he says, but compared with others in that price range, this property didn’t measure up.
“At that level, the buyers are usually extra-sharp and looking for fair value.”
Mr. Crammond and his business partner, broker Tracy Stewart, pointed to the sale prices of comparable listings, and the sellers were willing to negotiate.
Usually such a large gap between the amount a property is listed for and the price a buyer is willing to pay does not result in a deal, he notes.
Mr. Crammond says transactions in Muskoka fell about 4 per cent in the first half of the year compared with the first half of 2025. New listings rose 3 per cent in the same period.

Prices in the upper echelons have not declined in most cases, he says, because the supply of luxury cottages on the Big Three is scarce. A handful of sales above $20-million can skew average prices for the entire area.
“It is a tiny market,” he says. “Because it’s such a small sampling, it’s tough to get accurate stats.”
The average price on the Big Three stood at $2.1-million at the end of June compared with $1.8-million at the end of 2025, he notes.
The population is shrinking in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we put more housing there?

Sales on Muskoka’s smaller lakes have entered a more severe downturn, says Mr. Crammond, as some buyers who purchased during the pandemic have seen the value of their property fall by as much 35 or 40 per cent.
Between 2020 and 2022, bidding wars erupted, and prices skyrocketed during a stretch of low interest rates and “fear of missing out.”
“It was a frenzy,” says Mr. Crammond. “It was an absolute frenzy, and the prices made no sense.”
A cottage that sold for $1.1-million during the mania might change hands for $700,000 in the fall of 2026, he says.
That reduction in value has people who bought during COVID trapped, Mr. Crammond says. Even if they want to move up to a larger lake or better-equipped cottage, they don’t have the funds to do so.
The owner who paid $1.1-million might have a mortgage of $800,000, for example, and the cottage is worth less than that today.
“They’ve got zero equity from that place on the small lake,” he says. “That’s the same situation in the city that’s freezing the market.”
But while first-time buyers in the luxury segment do not grapple with that problem, they do have an aversion to overpaying, he adds.
Sellers need to start with a realistic asking price.
“If the properties are priced accurately, they do sell quite quickly – even over the $5-million and $10-million mark.
Sales in more modest segments have been harder hit by fears around inflation, the economy and jobs, he says, noting that a recreational property is a discretionary purchase.
“We have had buyers back off,” says Mr. Crammond. “If you’re not taking on more debt, you’re certainly taking on more expenses,” he says of the cost of ownership.
“It’s a luxury purchase even at the entry level.”

stories.title: Group assisting long-planned review of firearms — including SKS — has yet to meet
stories.summary: An advisory group that's supporting a federal review of firearms classification is expected to hold its first meeting this fall, almost a year after Ottawa announced the review.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
An advisory group that’s supporting a federal review of firearms classification — including a look at the SKS rifle — is expected to hold its first meeting this fall, almost a year after Ottawa announced the review.

Public Safety Canada says members of the Firearms Classification Technical Advisory Group, appointed to provide expert advice to the department and the RCMP, “will be meeting later this fall.”

The Liberal government has faced fresh questions about the SKS after a document filed in a U.S. court said the killer in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting talked about having an SKS gun.

Eighteen-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight people in the Feb. 10 Tumbler Ridge attack before taking her own life.

The RCMP has declined to release details about firearms used in the shootings, saying its investigation is ongoing.

The SKS has been used in police killings and other high-profile shootings.

It is also commonly used in Indigenous communities to hunt for food.

Prime Minister Mark Carney recently indicated the government would look at the advice of the classification advisory group before making any decision on the status of the SKS.

Since May 2020, Ottawa has outlawed approximately 2,500 types of guns on the basis they belong only on the battlefield. It has not banned the SKS.

Gun control advocacy group PolySeSouvient has long called on the government to impose an immediate ban on new sales of the SKS, to remove from circulation modern, assault-style versions of the rifle, and to implement a voluntary buyback of older models. It calls for an exemption for Indigenous hunters who use the SKS primarily for sustenance.

In early December last year, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said the government would “shortly be launching a comprehensive review of the firearms classification regime” with an emphasis on simplicity and consistency.

“This review will be supported by an expanded advisory group, and will involve dedicated consultations with First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities, including on the SKS, to ensure Indigenous perspectives and traditions are an active part of the process,” he said in a statement.

“The review will take a broad view of the legal framework for firearms, devices, magazines and ammunition to modernize the regime and ensure Canadians’ safety.”

In response to questions this month from The Canadian Press, the Public Safety Department said more information on the Technical Advisory Group and on engagement activities related to the classification review will be made available “in the near term.”

“Members will bring diverse technical knowledge, experience, and expert views from a wide range of perspectives,” the department said.

PolySeSouvient said this week that instead of implementing a comprehensive ban on assault-style firearms and high-capacity magazines, “the government keeps announcing new consultations and panels, and each one becomes another reason to postpone actual change.”

“Lives are at stake,” the group told The Canadian Press. “The government needs to stop consulting and start acting, before more people are killed in mass shootings.”

In a recent commentary on its website, the Canadian Shooting Sports Association said many questions remain about the Tumbler Ridge shootings, including which firearms were used, how they were obtained, and which — if any — had been seized by police previously.

“Reclassifying another firearm before answering those questions May satisfy the demand for immediate action,” the commentary said. “It does not prove that banning another firearm would have prevented this mass murder.”

stories.title: ‘Hurting’: Vigil in Wainwright, Alta., for soldiers caught in deadly fire
stories.summary: Ryan Wood, pastor of the town's Church of the Nazarene, said it's important those in the Armed Forces know they're not alone after the deadly fire.
stories.author: Bill Graveland and David Baxter
stories.content:
Almost every church in Wainwright, Alta., has a parishioner who’s a soldier at the nearby military base.

Ryan Wood, pastor of the town’s Church of the Nazarene, said it’s important those in the Armed Forces know they’re not alone after a fast-moving grass fire during training on Saturday killed four and injured dozens more.

“They’re hurting. They’re struggling just like everybody else,” Wood said.

“We want to have a message that we’re together in supporting our military. We’re together in grieving. We’re together is seeking a sense of peace and even hope in all of this.”

His church is hosting a vigil Wednesday night, organized by local faith leaders, for the town of roughly 7,000 people.

It’s to be the first opportunity for the public and those on the base to formally gather and grieve.

The four killed have been identified as: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

Isaiah Mast, pastor of the Evangelical Free Church, said Albertans like to think they’re tough.

But they need to know that it’s all right not to be all right.

“These things will live with the person,” Mast said. “I think what we hope to do is to be available for those who are going to be wrestling with this for a few weeks.

“This isn’t something that just goes away.”

Flags in the town, across the country and on all federal buildings were lowered to half-mast to honour those in the fire.

A pile of flowers has also grown at the Wainwright cenotaph.

Mayor Bruce Pugh said he’s relieved church leaders are organizing the vigil.

It will go a long way toward healing, he said.

“I think this will be a big piece. We are doing things for our first responders. We’re supporting them, our health-care professionals, by just going and visiting,” Pugh said.

“I think for some, it won’t close the book, but it will help close this chapter in a sense.”

“I think for some it will be a recognition of the strength of this community and allows us to hear messages of faith.”

stories.title: A First Nation community in Ontario is using a data centre to preserve its heritage
stories.summary: Among the digital files the Wiikwemkoong Unceded Territory holds are video recordings of Anishinaabe speaking their native language
stories.author: Kelvin Chan
stories.content:
For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have passed down their traditions and culture through oral storytelling. Now, a Canadian Indigenous community is using a data centre to help preserve its heritage.

The Wiikwemkoong Unceded Territory in rural Ontario installed a small data centre as it modernized its recordkeeping systems. Among the digital files it holds are video recordings of Anishinaabe speaking their native language.

“Our language is one of the biggest things that most First Nations across the country are losing,” said Wiikwemkoong Chief Tim Ominika. “We will have our knowledge keepers, our language speakers who may be moving on to the spirit world, but their legacy is still going to be protected for many years to come by having our own data systems in place and protecting that.”

The idea of digital sovereignty has gained momentum in places like Europe, where leaders are wary of the widespread influence of American Big Tech. For the Wiikwemkoong First Nation and other Indigenous communities, it is also about asserting authority over their own information after historically being excluded from its collection and use by colonizers.

About the size of a single-car garage, the data centre installed last year also stores the community’s corporate documents, health data for residents, and security camera footage.

“The purpose of all of this is having the ownership, access, control and possession of our information,” Ominika said. It’s about preventing anyone else from “having authority or setting their guidelines on what they could do with our data.”

The First Nation has been transferring all its information from a Microsoft data centre in Toronto, about 305 kilometres south, said Michael McCormick, the community’s chief technical officer.

The facility is part of a wider effort to modernize the community’s digital infrastructure and protect its data from climate threats and external control.

The Associated Press

Wiikwemkoong is on the eastern end of Manitoulin Island in Lake Huron, an area that attracts visitors with its rugged wilderness, extensive waterways and Anishinaabe cultural offerings. The reserve prides itself on being Canada’s only “unceded territory,” because it never signed a treaty surrendering its land.

The data centre, which underpins a modernization of Wiikwemkoong’s administrative services, also has paved the way for new public safety infrastructure, including a drone fleet and a network of surveillance cameras. A backup data center on the mainland and public Wi-Fi transmitters are also planned for the community of about 4,000 people. The chief declined to disclose how much is being spent on the projects.

Improvements to data storage gained urgency after a flood in 2022 resulted in the loss of some of its digital records, which had been scattered in various offices.

“That information is very important to us. And in order to protect it, keep it safe, we said ’Why can’t we not look at developing and creating and implementing our own data sovereignty program?’” Ominika said.

Wiikwemkoong’s upgrade program is among the first for Indigenous communities in Canada that include First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Delegations from other Indigenous communities in Ontario and neighbouring Manitoba have come to check out the project, McCormick said.

The chief said he has to explain to visitors that their data centre is not like the giant ones relied on by artificial intelligence companies that require vast amounts of land and water.

Wiikwemkoong’s data centre sits in a secure bunker next to the administrative office, accessed by a facial recognition scanner. Its four racks of computer servers are cooled by a pair of fans – not water – and it has “a relatively small carbon footprint,” McCormick said.

In the U.S., a few Native American tribes like the Navajo Nation have for years been operating their own data centres for local infrastructure services.

Wiikwemkoong’s data centre is believed to be the only one on Indigenous territory in Canada, but McCormick said other Indigenous leaders are increasingly savvy about control of their data. The Chiefs of Ontario, which represents 133 First Nations in the province, held a data sovereignty conference earlier this year that included a panel on AI and data centres.

For generations, Indigenous communities worldwide have had no say in how information on them has been collected, interpreted and held by governments, researchers and institutions, said Carmen Jones, director of research and data management for the Chiefs of Ontario.

“As more information is collected and stored, it is critical that First Nations determine how that data is accessed, managed, and used,” she said.

Amid the island’s natural splendour, the community faces its share of problems that community leaders hope the technology can help address.

Since installing the data centre, McCormick’s team has added 700 surveillance cameras around the community, and a dozen drone docking stations on the administrative office’s rooftop housing a fleet of DJI drones. They are used to find people who go missing in the area’s wooded hills, look out for criminal activity, such as drug deals and break-ins, and monitor for forest fires.

Ominika said there was “a little bit of resistance” to the drone program from residents worried about privacy.

Wiikwemkoong’s drones are supplied by DJI, a Chinese company whose drones have been blocked in the United States over national security concerns. McCormick said all drone footage would be stored locally. The chief said he wanted to make sure any information the drones collect “is going to be protected” and not “used against us, moving forward, by China.”

First Nations in Canada recognized the importance of data sovereignty decades ago, drawing up their own data governance principles in 1998 because they were often the focus of research by outsiders that didn’t benefit them. That argument is reflected in current criticism of Big Tech companies building AI large language models by scraping text, video, images and other data from the internet, often without permission.

Ominika said community leaders would be cautious and thoughtful when considering the use of AI.

“Once we start to realize and understand that there is a potential of any kind of resistance or harm towards our community, then we would put a stop there,” he said.

stories.title: Food bank visits rise to 2.3M a month as grocery costs go up, report says
stories.summary: One in five food banks across Canada are reportedly running out of food before meeting the needs of all their clients, a new report by Food Banks Canada says.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
A new report from Food Banks Canada says the number of Canadians struggling with food insecurity continues to grow, as food bank visits hit a new record of more than 2.3 million in March.

The non-profit organization’s latest HungerCount report, released Wednesday, says the cost-of-living crisis and economic pressures are weighing heavily on nearly 10 million Canadians experiencing food insecurity.

Its annual survey recorded more than 2,355,000 visits to food banks across Canada in March 2026, an 8.7 per cent increase from the March 2025 record of more than two million visits.

The report says more than a third of this year’s food bank visits, or nearly 776,000, were made by children.

Food Banks Canada CEO Kirstin Beardsley says people are “running out of options” as they try to balance essential spending, such as paying rent, with rising grocery costs.

The HungerCount report says that since 2021, food prices increased by about 30 per cent, housing costs by 28 per cent and transportation by roughly 24 per cent.

One in five food banks across Canada are reportedly running out of food before meeting the needs of all their clients.

“A lot of folks who used to give to food banks are now finding themselves in need of those services,” Beardsley said.

“A job is not enough to ensure that you are not in need of a food bank anymore,” she added. “There’s no other room in their budget to do anything.”

Beardsley said the federal government’s new Canada Groceries and Essential Benefit is one “positive investment,” but it’s not nearly enough to bridge the gap she’s seeing at the community level or in northern regions, where groceries are sold at higher prices due to transport costs.

The report includes a number of policy recommendations, such as doubling the Canada Workers Benefit for low-income residents, expanding food sovereignty initiatives in the North and investing up to $500 million toward food bank infrastructure to meet the demand.

stories.title: Young anglophones are still leaving Quebec, but at much lower rates, find researchers
stories.summary: Having grown up in an English-speaking family in Montreal, Jeremy Schachter says the question of staying or leaving Quebec was a “very real” dinner-table conversation.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
Having grown up in an English-speaking family in Montreal, Jeremy Schachter says the question of staying or leaving Quebec was a “very real” dinner-table conversation.

“So many of my friends have left. It’s just, people wonder about the future of the anglophone community,” he said.

Schachter himself moved to Toronto a year ago to join his girlfriend, who works as a social worker in the city. He is part of a long-standing movement of young English-speakers leaving Quebec to move elsewhere in Canada.

Data from the federal census shows that English-speakers are more likely to leave Quebec in favour of other provinces than French-speakers, but that the trend is slowing down.

This movement was especially strong in the 1970s and 1980s, said Simon-Pierre Lacasse, who recently wrote a paper exploring the migration of young anglophones out of Quebec.

“The ‘Anglo exodus’, as it’s often referred to, is something that’s really contingent to a specific period,” Lacasse told The Canadian Press.

In their research, Simon-Pierre Lacasse and student Meghan Rulli focused on young adults, who are more likely to move between provinces.

Their research paints a picture of how the rate of this migration has slowed down in recent decades.

Their research paper, published by the Quebec English-Speaking Communities Research Network, shows close to 20 per cent of English-speakers in Quebec left the province between the late 1960s and the early 1980s, with the net loss of around 121,000 anglophones in interprovincial migration between 1976 and 1981.

Between 2016 and 2021, the interprovincial anglophone migration was almost balanced, with a net loss of around 3900 anglophones in Quebec.

At the end of the most recent period, federal statistics reveal the overall English-speaking community in the province remained strong. Over 1.6 million Quebecers spoke English at home on a regular basis in 2021, according to the census.

This represents over 19 per cent of the Quebec population.

At the same time, the census numbers show that over 35 per cent of workers in the province said they regularly spoke English while on the job.

Lacasse said the numbers appear to suggest young English-speakers are better integrated in the province’s culture today than they were in the 1970s.

“To me, that was the big surprise. … If the goal is youth retention for the vitality of English-speaking communities, then maybe there is hope,” said Lacasse.

The researchers identified many “push” factors that might drive anglophones away from Quebec, including greater career opportunities elsewhere and economic concerns. Interwoven with many of these factors is the question of language.

“Language in Quebec, perhaps more than other provinces in Canada, is directly linked to identity and is politicized,” said Lacasse.

In 2022, the provincial government passed a bill that strengthened language legislation in the province. It imposed measures like French-only services for most Quebec residents and a cap on enrolment in some English-language colleges.

The bill also caused disruptions during the recent provincial election campaign after the election authority sent out French-only guides to all voters. A Superior Court judge temporarily suspended the bill’s provisions and ordered the agency to send out bilingual reminder cards to voters.

On Ki Lin, who was born in Hong Kong but moved to Montreal when they were eight years old, said they left Quebec to study at the University of Toronto mainly because they thought this was the best place to pursue their education.

Although Lin says financial concerns are keeping them in Toronto, the former Montrealer also noted having struggled to fully integrate into Quebec culture.

“There would be some people (who) would be very abrasive and very rude because my accent wasn’t the same as theirs. Or they would assume that if I had an accent, it meant that I wasn’t fluent enough to understand what they were saying,” said Lin.

The feeling that there is no space for English-speaking identities in Quebec lingers for many, said Lacasse.

“When I was living in Montreal, the overarching sentiment was that, you live here, but are you really welcome here? I don’t know. It was not so clear to me,” said Schachter.

This affects not only feelings of identity and belonging, but also professional development, with some anglophones feeling that they are not welcome in francophone workspaces, found the paper.

But English-speaking Quebecers’ relationship with the French language is also generational, said Lacasse, pointing out that those born after the Quiet Revolution in the 1960s, a period of nationalist political and social reform marked by a strengthening of the French-speaking Quebec identity, were more likely to understand the importance of French within the province.

The paper also highlights that young English-speakers in Quebec are increasingly bilingual.

Speaking with The Canadian Press, Schachter expressed attachment to the French language. He said he was recently offended when a man sitting close to him at a hockey game became upset to hear the national anthem sung in French.

“Even though I wouldn’t consider myself francophone … I think that’s really offensive,” he said.

Lacasse added English-speakers May find it easier to move to the rest of Canada, while French-speakers May face language barriers.

Lacasse said he is curious to see what trends will appear from the 2026 census data, which is set to be released in early 2027, especially after a period of high political tensions around language in Quebec.

From their new lives in Toronto, Lin and Schachter both reminisced about Montreal and Quebec.

“I would never consider myself Québécois, really, but there’s definitely something special about Quebec,” said Schachter.

stories.title: Long lot helps in Mount Pleasant home sale
stories.summary: This three-bedroom house backing onto the cemetery sold for almost $2-million
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
699 Merton St., Toronto

Asking price: $1,995,000 (August, 2026)

Selling price: $1,955,000 (August, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $1,805,000 (September, 2021); $699,000 (May, 2006); $421,000 (July, 2002); $385,000 (December, 1989)

Taxes: $8,601 (2026)

Days on the market: 15

Listing agents: Paul Maranger and Christian Vermast, Sotheby’s International Realty Canada

This 81-year-old house has three bedrooms upstairs in a neighbourhood where four or more is the norm, and a yard backing onto Mount Pleasant Cemetery. Paul Maranger was concerned that buyers might find those factors objectionable. But the roughly 70 visitors to tour the house seemed more interested in the depth of the 25- by 156-foot lot, that it was newly landscaped, and that a fourth bedroom had been added to the home in a remodelling of the basement.

“[My clients] spent $150,000 on the lower level, wanting it extremely comfortable for family visiting,” said Mr. Maranger.

“A lot of houses backing onto cemeteries don’t have deep lots, so you’re very aware it’s there. But in this case, pine trees in that section are absolutely stunning.

“Then a year ago, [the sellers] spent money on the backyard … dividing it into three zones: one off the family room with beautiful, sliding doors to a deck, a patio area and at the back, they created a gas fire pit area.”

Within two weeks of the home’s launch, one buyer cut a deal for $1,955,000.

“It May have had a smaller buyer pool than if it had four bedrooms, but the entire home was gorgeous,” Mr. Maranger said.

“In this market, anything sold under 21 days is considered an expedited sale.”

The two-storey house has 1,423 square feet of living space, including living and dining rooms, and a family room addition with a gas fireplace, skylights and access to a deck.

The kitchen was recently upgraded with new stainless-steel appliances, and all three bathrooms were remodelled. Interior designer Sarah Richardson redesigned one with marble countertops and heated flooring.

One parking spot is at the front and the rear.

“It’s in a fabulous school district, and half a block from gorgeous cafés, bakeries, shops and restaurants on Bayview [Avenue],” Mr. Maranger said.

stories.title: Status certificate revelation cuts sale price on North York condo
stories.summary: Two-bedroom corner unit sells for $607,500
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
5444 Yonge St., No. 902, Toronto

Asking price: $659,900 (August, 2026)

Selling price: $607,500 (August, 2026)

Previous selling price: $290,000 (June, 2006)

Taxes: $3,322 (2026)

Days on the market: Eight

Listing agent: Belinda Lelli, Royal LePage Real Estate Services Ltd.

This condo unit in a 41-year-old building on Yonge Street south of Finch Avenue received a professional makeover to entice families and young professionals. One buyer, liking what they saw, placed an offer on the 1,302-square-foot space within days of its appearance on the market this summer.

“What’s good about older condos is they are a lot more spacious,” said listing agent Belinda Lelli.

“I wanted it staged and painted before we started because buyers today want something turnkey.”

The buyer’s offer of $615,000 was accepted, but a close examination of the building’s status certificate revealed that ongoing balcony repairs had depleted the reserve fund. With the expectation of an impending special assessment against owners, the buyer requested a price drop. The seller complied, knocking the selling price down to $607,500.

“We had to make a concession once the status certificate revealed that there were very large improvement undertakings that drained the reserve fund,” said Ms. Lelli.

“We were going to hit the same issue if we kept it on the market, and we’d also be incurring maintenance fees.”

The corner unit has an eat-in kitchen, separate living and dining areas, and a sunroom with access to a balcony.

stories.title: Surveillance cameras could see inside Toronto apartment, tenant says
stories.summary: Complaint about property management company’s security system has exposed vulnerabilities in Canada’s privacy rights regime
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
A complaint that a Toronto property management company’s security cameras are capturing footage from inside tenant apartments has exposed vulnerabilities in Canada’s privacy rights regime.

The advent of AI tools and facial recognition software makes the issue of what happens with footage collected by security and surveillance cameras far more complex than it was 20 years ago, when Canada’s federal government introduced the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (Pipeda). Privacy experts say this new reality puts Canadian privacy rights at risk.

“Privacy rights go well beyond recording your image,” said Alejandra Brown, a privacy expert with Kirke Management Consulting. “Video surveillance nowadays has a lot of other implications: Are you using a cloud-based vendor that is storing this information in places like the U.S.? Your vendors could use this information to train their own AI models. When you collect information for security, it doesn’t give you a blank cheque to use it for other things.”

In June, the Office of the Privacy Commissioner (OPC) issued a report that found MetCap Living Management Inc. has been inappropriately recording video from inside the apartments at 105 Isabella St., a building it manages in Toronto. Security cameras in its hallways had been angled such that when some doors opened, parts of a tenant’s private space inside could be recorded.

Moreover, the OPC report said MetCap’s failure to respond to the tenant’s request for his personal private information – and its failure to provide information about its security footage in its privacy policy – does not comply with federal law.

Javier Ruiz-Soler began pushing MetCap for answers about its security cameras in late 2024. After multiple e-mails to property management and staff, Mr. Ruiz-Soler received an e-mail from a property manager that said “We disagree that Pipeda requires us to disclose any of our internal policies to residents.”

The OPC report corrected the company on that view, noting Pipeda’s principle 4.8 states, “Organizations shall be open about their policies and practices with respect to the management of personal information. Individuals shall be able to acquire information about an organization’s policies and practices without unreasonable effort.”

Mr. Ruiz-Soler is well-versed in privacy rights; he’s a civil servant working for the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario, and believes the OPC needs to take MetCap to federal court to ensure the company changes its cameras to stop indiscriminately recording footage of the tenants, as outlined in its report.

But experts say that’s unlikely to happen.

“Pipeda doesn’t currently have teeth the way people would normally use that phrase; the powers of the commission are limited to making recommendations,” said David Elder, chief privacy officer with law firm Stikeman Elliot. Without the ability to levy fines or make orders that a federal court will uphold, the commission or involved parties need to apply to the court, an expensive process that doesn’t happen often, according to Mr. Elder.

Instead, Mr. Elder said the commission’s main tool is “public shaming” when they release summaries of their investigations and name names. In this case, the OPC hasn’t published a final summary, though Mr. Ruiz-Soler shared the June report with media.

“MetCap continues to engage with the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada regarding the matters raised in its report. As this remains an ongoing process, we are unable to comment further on specific details at this time,” wrote Michael Guyette, vice-president of operations for MetCap, which manages hundreds of buildings adding up to more than 22,000 apartments. In a different e-mail, Mr. Guyette wrote that “following a review of the camera positioning, the relevant camera angles were adjusted and supporting images were provided to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner,” but declined to answer follow-up questions as to whether the camera’s have been changed again since June, when the OPC concluded that the adjustments still left parts of tenant apartment interiors visible to security cameras.

“It would have been easy to move the cameras five inches,” Mr. Ruiz-Soler said. “If you have good intentions, why is it so hard for this landlord to comply with the law?”

In an e-mailed statement the OPC said MetCap had been co-operative and remains in communication with it about its recommendations, but declined to comment on the specifics about whether the cameras have been adjusted. “The OPC will continue to closely monitor the situation to ensure that its recommendations are complied with,” it said.

Mr. Guyette said the other issues related to privacy policy and contacts for tenants have been addressed. However, signage at the building warns tenants that a third-party contractor, SEQ Security Surveillance Services Inc., is collecting both video and audio. This May create another issue, namely that federal law makes it a criminal offence to record audio of individuals who do not consent.

MetCap’s new video surveillance policy says it does not use the cameras “for general tenant monitoring.” Mr. Guyette said Seq’s equipment at Isabella does not collect audio.

On Seq’s website, the company claims that its systems make use of sophisticated AI tools that allow for easy monitoring in buildings. “Follow anyone, anywhere in the building,” one description of its software reads. “One click follows a person’s path across every camera – lobby to elevator to floor – without touching a single camera name. Full picture, instantly.”

Ms. Brown argues that good privacy policies should disclose what kind of third-party vendors have access to video footage, and whether they are using AI tools for monitoring, since such software often comes with broad permissions to use any data fed into it for other applications.

“Consent is really the foundation,” said Mr. Elder. “So if you don’t have a privacy policy that tells people what you are doing and why, then that is really a core violation of the law.”
