stories.title: A walk through Modernist downtown Hamilton
stories.summary: The city still suffers from the effects of a plan to adopt a one-way street system for the downtown core
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
Traffic engineer Wilbur Smith, arriving from South Carolina, convinced Hamilton in 1956 to adopt a one-way street system for their downtown core. It always reminds me of the Marge vs. the Monorail episode of The Simpsons . It not only killed the downtown core’s vitality, but it also discouraged one of urban living’s greatest pleasures: walking.

Despite this, I recently had the pleasure of leading two groups, the Hamilton Burlington Association of Architects (Hbsa) and the Ontario Professional Planners Institute (Oppi), ON a downtown walking tour along streets that still suffer from the effects of the Smith plan, and those that were converted back to two-way in 2002. So, as we discuss some of the architectural highlights we ogled, I’ll also describe how we felt.

Hamilton City Hall, 71 Main St. W. (1960).

Thankfully, Stanley M. Roscoe’s magnum opus, like many city halls, is set back on a grand plaza. This allows the clean, geometric composition – one of the great Modernist buildings of Ontario – to breathe and, more importantly, to be admired. Interestingly, while Mr. Roscoe was already employed as Hamilton’s “City Architect” (Canada’s first), it took some convincing to move then-mayor Lloyd Jackson away from his wish for an ecclesiastical architect.

And while I’m not a fan of bollards, the addition of a sentrylike row along the sidewalk’s edge a few years ago does help engender an increased feeling of safety. Walking east to look at the next stops, that feeling dissipates quickly as the sidewalk narrows and city buses almost brush our elbows.

First Ontario Concert Hall, 1 Summers Lane (1973) / Hamilton Public Library, 55 Main St. W. (1913) / BDC Building, 25 Main St. W. (1971).

This cluster of buildings is wonderful. Trevor Garwood-Jones came from England in 1959 and opened his own firm a decade later. His first big commission, Hamilton Place (now First Ontario Concert Hall), showed his mastery of Brutalism, with projecting concrete fins that mimic flying buttresses. The sculpture, Canadac by Kosso Eloul, is a fitting bit of bling for its boldness and its material: it’s made of “Stelcoloy,” a weathering steel material Stelco developed in the 1970s (also used on Stelco Tower).

The Carnegie-funded library – now home to the Superior Court – is a stately, classically-proportioned reminder that Pittsburgh steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie’s money funded 125 Canadian libraries, of which 111 are in Ontario.

Across MacNab Street South is the former IBM building (now BDC), which shows the kind of moody, muscular, corporate Modernism that Mr. Roscoe (with partners) was capable of producing after leaving his post as city architect and going into private practice.

Pigott Building, 36 James St. S. (1928-29).

While it could use a power-wash, the Art Deco/Gothic skyscraper (Hamilton’s first) is still a jewel. It’s also a name-check for one of the most prolific builders in Ontario. Joseph Pigott and his brother Roy took their father’s construction firm (est. in 1885) and dialled it up several notches. In Toronto, they’re responsible for the east wing of the ROM, the original TD Centre, and the Imperial Oil Building (111 St. Clair W.); in Hamilton, there are too many to count.

Walking on James Street South, which switched back to two-way traffic in 2002, there is a considerable reduction in auto-aggression.

Hamilton GO Centre, 33 Hunter St. E. (1933).

Built as the main terminal for the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway, it’s obvious train station specialists – and Art Deco masters – Fellheimer and Wagner (NYC) were responsible for the design. It commands the view corridor from Main Street all the way down Hughson Street, and it’s bejewelled with wings, curved walls and wraparound corner windows that break the box.

Pagoda Chop Suey House neon sign, John Street North and King Street East (1942) / Capri Ristorante sign, 25 John St. N. (1962).

Once regarded as tacky and junked by the millions in the 1970s and 80s, neon, in some cities at least, is having a moment for its warmth, movement and placemaking abilities.

While Edmonton has its Neon Sign Museum, which transformed the side of an anonymous building into a tourist attraction, and Las Vegas has the must-see Neon Museum, Hamilton’s Pagoda sign, despite being restored in 2018, was dark as we walked past.

The red bands of the Capri, however, were reflecting off our smiling faces as we passed and talked about The Blue Grotto upstairs at this Italian restaurant, which looks like a cave, complete with stalactites.

This is the Gore Park neighbourhood, and there was a great deal of traffic, but the pedestrian island (with cannons) provided a good vantage point for Pagoda.

Lister Block, 28 James St. N. (1923).

Twenty years ago, the heritage architecture community watched and waited as this abandoned Classical Renaissance building (built by Pigott) swung from salvation to rumours of destruction.

Luckily, and perhaps because of public outcry and scrutiny, new owners LiUNA spent $25-million to perform a full restoration.

The best place to gaze is King William Street; despite being a one-way street, wider sidewalks, a cobblestone road surface, planters and street trees all contribute to pedestrian well-being, with drivers automatically slowing down due to visual clutter.

Hamilton City Centre, 77 James St. N. (1989-90).

Despite abandonment in 2022 and a stalled high-rise development scheme, this was once a showpiece. Adorned with Postmodern geegaws, the former Hamilton Eaton Centre cost $100-million and arrived with great fanfare. Today, it is partially covered in black paint. Here, we discuss that the next big era for heritage protection is PoMo, and wonder if perhaps new life as a place for micro-lofts with a built-in communal dining room (the food court) could be found? It’s happening all over.

While there were other stops, I’ll leave it here. And with the news that Hamilton is converting a six-kilometre stretch of Main Street back to two-way traffic, with construction to begin soon.

stories.title: Huge terrace helps sell Cobourg penthouse near asking price
stories.summary: Two-bedroom unit with extensive renovation sells for $1.12-million
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
145 Third St., No. 411, Cobourg, Ont.

Asking price: $1,149,900 (August, 2026)

Selling price: $1.12-million (September, 2026)

Previous selling price: $560,000 (February, 2015); $495,327 (May, 2005)

Taxes: $8,843 (2026)

Days on the market: 27

Listing agent: Christopher Bibby, Re/Max Hallmark Bibby Group Realty

This 1,870-square-foot penthouse is in a four-storey building across from the harbour in Cobourg, 120 kilometres east of Toronto. The unit also has a 2,500-square-foot terrace, a space so large that it is often mistaken for a common area. It has a custom pergola, fountain and barbecue station and views north, east and south.

“I haven’t encountered many units in my career with terraces this size, especially ones overlooking the water and in a smaller, boutique building,” said agent Christopher Bibby.

“The owner told me that, at one point, someone knocked on their door asking how to get to the terrace. Their joke was: ‘You have to become friends with us.’”

Fourteen buyers toured the two-bedroom unit, which also has twice the interior space than the building average. An opening offer kicked off negotiations and an agreed sale at $29,900 under the asking price.

“Because units this size also don’t come up often, we knew we could be a bit adventurous on price,” said Mr. Bibby.

“Everyone wants to negotiate; it’s part of the process.”

This corner unit has hardwood flooring, coffered ceilings, and several entrances to the terrace.

There is an updated kitchen and a living room with a gas fireplace.

The primary bedroom also has a fireplace, a walk-in closet, and a private bathroom.

There is a second full bathroom.

The unit comes with a storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $1,631 cover heating, water, cable and internet.

“A previous owner had done an extensive renovation; the unit was fairly turnkey,” Mr. Bibby said.

“There were a couple of parks to the sides of the unit, and the marina directly below. It really was a special offering.”

stories.title: Cppib, Omers to sell stakes in British port operator to IMF Investors
stories.summary: CPP Investments holds a 33.9% interest in Associated British Ports, while Omers owns 30%
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Omers have signed a deal to sell their entire stakes in Associated British Ports to IFM Investors.

Financial terms of the sale were not disclosed.

ABP is Britain’s largest port operator with 19 ports in England, Scotland and Wales.

CPP Investments holds a 33.9-per-cent interest in ABP, while Omers owns 30.0 per cent.

IFM Investors is a global asset manager, owned by Australian pension funds and British pension fund Nest.

CPP Investments and Omers first acquired their stakes in ABP in 2015 and 2006, respectively.

stories.title: More Canadians are visiting food banks than ever, with monthly visits hitting record high
stories.summary: Canadians continue to struggle with the high cost of living, with monthly food bank visits up nearly nine per cent this year compared to last. According to Food Banks Canada’s annual HungerCount report, food bank visits have soared to 2.35 million per month in 2026, a 117 per cent increase from 2019.
stories.author: Heather Wright
stories.content:
Toronto - Canadians continue to struggle with the high cost of living, with monthly food bank visits up nearly nine per cent this year compared to last.

According to Food Banks Canada’s annual HungerCount report, food bank visits have soared to 2.35 million per month in 2026, a 117 per cent increase from 2019.

“(This) is the story of what happens when millions of people are out of options,” said Food Banks Canada CEO Kirstin Beardsley.

“In the past, most people in Canada could absorb a small financial setback… those days are over. Canada’s bleak new reality is that millions of people are making impossible trade-offs every day as they choose between food or rent,” she said.

Food bank visits are up in every province and territory except Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Labrador. The most populous provinces saw the most visits, with 846,724 in Ontario (a nearly 11 per cent increase), 785,889 in Quebec (up 5 per cent) and 250,505 visits in British Columbia (a 14 per cent increase).

“This does not have to be Canada’s story,” said Beardsley, who is calling on all governments to act.

Among the recommendations in this year’s report are changes to employment insurance (EI) to include non-traditional occupations such as gig work and review eligibility thresholds; doubling the Canada Workers Benefit; enhancing the Disability Tax Credit (DTC); reviewing federal social assistance; and investing in critical infrastructure, including affordable housing.

The report also calls for more investment in Canada’s north, where food bank visits are up sharply compared to last year: 24 per cent in Yukon and 29 per cent in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut.

Food Bank Canada releases its HungerCount study every year, compiling data from more than 5,500 food banks and community organizations across the country.

The report found the cost of basic necessities has soared since 2021. Food prices have increased nearly 30 per cent, housing is up 28 per cent and transportation has risen nearly 24 per cent.

The rising cost of living has driven more employed Canadians to food banks. The report found that nearly one in five clients is employed, up from one in 10 in 2019.

stories.title: Danielle Smith’s post-referendum problem
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses what the results mean for Premier Danielle Smith and the UCP, where Alberta's separatists go from here.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Alberta has decided its fate remains within a united Canada.

More than 75 per cent of voters in Monday’s historic referendum struck down the idea of separating from the country, a result Prime Minister Mark Carney says he’s “thrilled” about.

As the results continue to roll in for the other nine questions, however, the conversation surrounding the province’s future is far from over. And so is the question of sovereignty.

Host Caryn Ceolin is speaking with political strategist Zain Velji about what question 10’s results mean for Premier Danielle Smith and the UCP, where Alberta’s separatists go from here, and how Quebec is taking note of it all.

stories.title: Young anglophones continue to leave Quebec, but study shows trend seeing a slowdown
stories.summary: Research paper also highlights that young English-speakers in Quebec are increasingly bilingual
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
Having grown up in an English-speaking family in Montreal, Jeremy Schachter says the question of staying or leaving Quebec was a “very real” dinner-table conversation.

“So many of my friends have left. It’s just, people wonder about the future of the anglophone community,” he said.

Schachter himself moved to Toronto a year ago to join his girlfriend, who works as a social worker in the city. He is part of a long-standing movement of young English-speakers leaving Quebec to move elsewhere in Canada.

Data from the federal census shows that English-speakers are more likely to leave Quebec in favour of other provinces than French-speakers, but that the trend is slowing down.

This movement was especially strong in the 1970s and 1980s, said Simon-Pierre Lacasse, who recently wrote a paper exploring the migration of young anglophones out of Quebec.

“The ‘Anglo exodus’, as it’s often referred to, is something that’s really contingent to a specific period,” Lacasse told The Canadian Press.

In their research, Simon-Pierre Lacasse and student Meghan Rulli focused on young adults, who are more likely to move between provinces.

Their research paints a picture of how the rate of this migration has slowed down in recent decades.

A recent paper by the Quebec English-speaking Communities Research Network, which operates out of Concordia University in Montreal, shows that English-speakers are more likely to leave Quebec.

The Canadian Press

Their research paper, published by the Quebec English-Speaking Communities Research Network, shows close to 20 per cent of English-speakers in Quebec left the province between the late 1960s and the early 1980s, with the net loss of around 121,000 anglophones in interprovincial migration between 1976 and 1981.

Between 2016 and 2021, the interprovincial anglophone migration was almost balanced, with a net loss of around 3900 anglophones in Quebec.

At the end of the most recent period, federal statistics reveal the overall English-speaking community in the province remained strong. Over 1.6 million Quebeckers spoke English at home on a regular basis in 2021, according to the census.

This represents over 19 per cent of the Quebec population.

At the same time, the census numbers show that over 35 per cent of workers in the province said they regularly spoke English while on the job.

Lacasse said the numbers appear to suggest young English-speakers are better integrated in the province’s culture today than they were in the 1970s.

“To me, that was the big surprise. … If the goal is youth retention for the vitality of English-speaking communities, then maybe there is hope,” said Lacasse.

The researchers identified many “push” factors that might drive anglophones away from Quebec, including greater career opportunities elsewhere and economic concerns. Interwoven with many of these factors is the question of language.

“Language in Quebec, perhaps more than other provinces in Canada, is directly linked to identity and is politicized,” said Lacasse.

In 2022, the provincial government passed a bill that strengthened language legislation in the province. It imposed measures like French-only services for most Quebec residents and a cap on enrolment in some English-language colleges.

The bill also caused disruptions during the recent provincial election campaign after the election authority sent out French-only guides to all voters. A Superior Court judge temporarily suspended the bill’s provisions and ordered the agency to send out bilingual reminder cards to voters.

On Ki Lin, who was born in Hong Kong but moved to Montreal when they were eight years old, said they left Quebec to study at the University of Toronto mainly because they thought this was the best place to pursue their education.

Although Lin says financial concerns are keeping them in Toronto, the former Montrealer also noted having struggled to fully integrate into Quebec culture.

“There would be some people [who] would be very abrasive and very rude because my accent wasn’t the same as theirs. Or they would assume that if I had an accent, it meant that I wasn’t fluent enough to understand what they were saying,” said Lin.

The feeling that there is no space for English-speaking identities in Quebec lingers for many, said Lacasse.

“When I was living in Montreal, the overarching sentiment was that, you live here, but are you really welcome here? I don’t know. It was not so clear to me,” said Schachter.

This affects not only feelings of identity and belonging, but also professional development, with some anglophones feeling that they are not welcome in francophone workspaces, found the paper.

But English-speaking Quebeckers’ relationship with the French language is also generational, said Lacasse, pointing out that those born after the Quiet Revolution in the 1960s, a period of nationalist political and social reform marked by a strengthening of the French-speaking Quebec identity, were more likely to understand the importance of French within the province.

The paper also highlights that young English-speakers in Quebec are increasingly bilingual.

Speaking with The Canadian Press, Schachter expressed attachment to the French language. He said he was recently offended when a man sitting close to him at a hockey game became upset to hear the national anthem sung in French.

“Even though I wouldn’t consider myself francophone … I think that’s really offensive,” he said.

Lacasse added English-speakers May find it easier to move to the rest of Canada, while French-speakers May face language barriers.

Lacasse said he is curious to see what trends will appear from the 2026 census data, which is set to be released in early 2027, especially after a period of high political tensions around language in Quebec.

From their new lives in Toronto, Lin and Schachter both reminisced about Montreal and Quebec.

“I would never consider myself Québécois, really, but there’s definitely something special about Quebec,” said Schachter.

stories.title: This Ontario church run by controversial 'prophet' faces 50 bylaw charges
stories.summary: Conservative MPP pledged to help the church, whose leader faces allegations of misconduct, so it could stay on protected Ontario Greenbelt
stories.author: Investigative Journalism Bureau
stories.content:
A church north of Toronto whose leader has been accused by some former congregants of sexual or financial misconduct is facing dozens of municipal bylaw charges, including charges of operating illegally on protected Greenbelt land.

Even as Miracle Arena For All Nations church has battled Vaughan, Ont., officials over its presence on protected land, it has received promises to work for a Greenbelt zoning “exception” from a provincial cabinet minister who has frequently visited the church.

In total, City of Vaughan officials have laid 50 bylaw charges against Miracle Arena — owned and run by self-proclaimed “prophet” Martin Kofi Danso — and three current or former associates, the Investigative Journalism Bureau has found. Danso himself is not charged. The bylaw issues range from alleged zoning infractions to property standards and animal welfare charges.

Danso was the subject of an IJB investigation earlier this year into allegations of sexual and financial impropriety. He has never been criminally charged and has denied all the allegations.

The dispute over zoning for the land his church is built on goes back to 2020.

Danso said in a written statement that a church was allowed on the land based on a February 2020 zoning certificate he provided to IJB reporters. The document says a church is “permitted by the relevant zoning requirements.” But it cautions that site plan approval May be required and that the property May be designated as “protected countryside” under the Greenbelt Plan, which was established in 2005 and prohibits commercial development or expansion on protected lands.

The certificate also notes that “a building permit is required” before any construction or major alterations to the property.

Through his lawyer, Danso also said that the church is operating legally on the basis of a Sept. 19, 1988, City of Vaughan bylaw that zoned its location, 10800 Weston Rd., as agricultural, which also permitted a church and a dwelling on the property.

Vaughan city officials, however, told the IJB the “provincial Greenbelt Plan supersedes the city’s zoning by-law and does not allow for a place of worship on that property.”

Miracle Arena was “not lawfully established on this property…. It did not have planning approvals or building permits,” reads the City of Vaughan statement. Danso’s zoning certificate is only valid for six months and expired before the church was constructed in late 2020, the city statement says.

After the church was founded, then expanded, ON Greenbelt land starting in 2020, Danso received support from Vaughan-Woodbridge MPP Michael Tibollo, now the province’s associate attorney general.

In June 2022, Tibollo addressed Miracle Arena congregants during his second visit in two months, pledging to assist the church in changing the Greenbelt zoning.

“One of the things we have always said is we will not touch the Greenbelt, but I think there are sometimes exceptions.… I will help and I made that commitment,” he said.

Tibollo has had public interactions with Danso at least 11 times between 2022 and 2025. He also introduced Danso on at least two occasions to Ontario Premier Doug Ford — by phone and at Tibollo’s own community summer barbecue — and encouraged other government ministers, including current Minister of Energy and Mines Stephen Lecce, to visit Miracle Arena. Scarborough Centre MPP David Smith is also among the politicians who have visited the church.

Tibollo did not respond to repeated requests for comment regarding his commitment to help change the zoning at 10800 Weston Rd. or his relationship with Danso. Ford, Lecce and Smith also did not respond to requests for comment.

The bylaw charges against Miracle Arena are to be heard in court in November and December. According to information published on the City of Vaughan’s property bylaws page, complaints and violations require “significant” investigation before a fine or penalty is issued. Charges are laid as a “last resort.”

Ontario’s Greenbelt is a protected swath of farmland, forests and wetlands spanning two-million acres across southern Ontario.

Danso and his wife, JoAnne, purchased the 12-acre plot of land where their church now sits in May 2020 for $5.6 million. The real estate listing at the time shows the property was zoned as “Greenbelt,” “agricultural” and “heritage.”

At the time, satellite images show a house and large shed on the property surrounded by dirt roads and fields littered with trucking, shipping and construction equipment. Those structures pre-date the property’s 2005 Greenbelt designation.

Once the Dansos took possession, the property began a transformation.

In videos Danso posted at the time of purchase, he described his desire to develop the land into a community with a large church and amenities such as a shopping mall, condos, a school and livestock.

In 2022, Premier Ford opened parts of the Greenbelt to housing and development, but not the parcel of land where Miracle Arena sits. Ford reversed the decision to open the Greenbelt in 2023 after investigations by Ontario’s Auditor General and Integrity Commissioner found the process favoured politically connected developers.

In May 2022, MPP Tibollo attended Miracle Arena ahead of the provincial election. Speaking to the congregation , he called Danso “an incredible leader” while detailing his own track record in the private and public sector.

A month later, Tibollo returned following his reelection and publicly thanked Danso and his congregants for their support before making his commitment to assist the church with the Greenbelt zoning issue.

Miracle Arena’s challenges reach beyond alleged breaches of Greenbelt zoning restrictions.

In an address to regional council for York Region in September 2023, Danso raised safety concerns about the sanitary conditions of the property, notably the strain on its septic tank, at a time when the church was providing shelter to African refugees.

Despite the zoning issues, Danso asked the city to help connect the building to the municipal sewage system to relieve the pressure on the septic tank.

Fitz-Roy Gordon, a current candidate for York regional council in the Oct. 26 municipal election, was working with refugees at Miracle Arena at this time through advocacy organization Anchor, founded by him and his wife, Shernett Martin.

In an interview, Gordon and Martin said “hundreds of people” shared one shower at Miracle Arena and just a few toilets. Soon the septic tank was backing up and sewage was spilling over the ground.

“It was awful. It was smelling — it was unsanitary,” Gordon recalls. “I know that the region and the city wanted them (the refugees) off that land.”

In the September 2023 address to city council, Danso said, “We were told that we need a Minister’s Zoning Order (MZO) to address some of the issues on the property.”

Vaughan City records show the church told the city it was in the process of getting an MZO. But Michael Minzak, press secretary for Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing Rob Flack, told the IJB that “no (Minister’s Zoning Order) was ever issued or contemplated.”

Speaking again before York Region councillors in January 2024, Danso characterized city orders to stop Miracle Arena’s religious services and remove structures on the church property used to house asylum seekers as “discrimination” and accused public officials of abusing their authority.

“As a clergyman, nobody has the power to stop me from exercising my spiritual duties, especially on this land,” Danso said, drawing cheers from church supporters in the council chamber.

As the IJB previously reported, several members of the church are facing criminal charges of fraud, laundering and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence related to funding of refugee housing on the property.

That matter remains before the courts. Danso has not been charged. In a press release published at the time, Miracle Arena said “the alleged conduct was undertaken independently and without the knowledge, authorization, or involvement of the Church.”

The 50 alleged regulatory bylaw infractions the church now faces date back to 2023.

Sixteen of the charges against Miracle Arena and three of its senior associates are zoning bylaw infractions; eight have to do with property standards; four are alleged site alternation bylaw infractions; while 22 charges relate to animal welfare, including that the church allegedly failed to provide food, failed to provide care and failed to keep an animal pen in sanitary conditions.

In interviews, former Miracle Arena parishioners told the IJB that the animals kept on the property — mainly alpacas, a horse and donkeys — were rehoused elsewhere after at least one animal died.

Danso did not respond to questions about allegations of animal harm or where animals were sent.

“The current land use at the property is now before the court. It would be inappropriate to comment any further on that,” reads a statement from Danso’s lawyer, Aaron Crangle.

“(Miracle Arena) has spent a considerable amount of time and money to get the property into compliance with any concerns or orders.”

The property disputes add to a controversy already surrounding Miracle Arena. A recent IJB investigation documented years of troubling allegations involving Danso and the church, ranging from allegations of sexual misconduct to alleged financial exploitation.

Several former parishioners told the IJB about alleged “grooming” behaviours by Danso. Some alleged Danso had non-consensual sexual encounters with them, including one woman who says she was a minor at the time.

Danso has never been criminally charged and previously told the IJB he denied all allegations of sexual or financial impropriety.

The church has continued to draw hundreds of parishioners to services. And as the church’s physical footprint has expanded on the Greenbelt, so too has its leader’s push for political influence.

“We need to help to do evangelism to take over the city,” said Danso in a September 2026 sermon in which he encouraged his flock to volunteer and knock on doors for certain municipal candidates. “We have to do everything we can to make sure we are taking over for the glory of God.”

“The Lord does not give a city to people by prayer,” he said in the September sermon. “Let’s do whatever we can to make it happen.… We must take it by force.”

In response to IJB questions, Danso’s written statement says “there is nothing wrong with Mafan (Miracle Arena For All Nations) supporting politicians that have demonstrated support for the work that it has done.”

Among the candidates he has recommended to his congregants is Vaughan mayoral candidate Shelly Cerrelli, the sole opponent to incumbent mayor Steven Del Duca, who has clashed with Danso over his plans for long-term refugee housing on the Greenbelt property. Cerrelli’s campaign told reporters she has no connection to the church beyond visits made as part of her campaign outreach to faith communities across the region.

Her campaign listed several faith communities she has interacted with during the campaign and said she has not promised Danso or any religious leader or organization “favourable treatment” or “municipal approvals” in exchange for prayer, encouragement or support for her candidacy.

The IJB has identified at least three candidates receiving Danso’s support who have clear ties to the church. Robert Bazil, a candidate for Toronto City Council, and Andrea Francis Bucknor, a candidate for Peel Public School Board trustee, have both publicly identified themselves as members of Miracle Arena. Neither responded to requests for comment.

Another Miracle Arena-affiliated candidate is Matthew Boateng, one of Danso’s longtime supporters and a church minister. He is also running for Toronto Council.

He is listed as a board member for the church in charity documents and named as a defendant, along with Miracle Arena and two others, in the pending bylaw charges.

On his campaign website, Boateng cites his experience as “volunteer and ministry service with Miracle Arena for All Nations” and being a church “shelter supervisor.”

During a campaign launch speech in September, Boateng credited Danso and JoAnne Danso for being the people “that gave me this push to do this.”

IJB reporters sought comment from Boateng about the bylaw charges, his relationship with Danso and his campaign.

Boateng did not directly respond to most of the Ijb’s questions, instead saying the inquiries were “harassment, voter intimidation and blatant election interference.”

The IJB also asked Boateng if Danso, Miracle Arena or other high-ranking political figures had donated money to his campaign.

Boateng denied receiving “the financial contributions in question,” but added, “according to the City of Toronto, any resident of Ontario who is a resident, can contribute to a municipal campaign.”

content_blocks.text: A church north of Toronto whose leader has been accused by some former congregants of sexual or financial misconduct is facing dozens of municipal bylaw charges, including charges of operating illegally on protected Greenbelt land.

Even as Miracle Arena For All Nations church has battled Vaughan, Ont., officials over its presence on protected land, it has received promises to work for a Greenbelt zoning “exception” from a provincial cabinet minister who has frequently visited the church.

In total, City of Vaughan officials have laid 50 bylaw charges against Miracle Arena — owned and run by self-proclaimed “prophet” Martin Kofi Danso — and three current or former associates, the Investigative Journalism Bureau has found. Danso himself is not charged. The bylaw issues range from alleged zoning infractions to property standards and animal welfare charges.
content_blocks.html: In total, City of Vaughan officials have laid 50 bylaw charges against Miracle Arena — owned and run by self-proclaimed “prophet” Martin Kofi Danso —  and three current or former associates, the Investigative Journalism Bureau has found. Danso himself is not charged. The bylaw issues range from alleged zoning infractions to property standards and animal welfare charges.

content_blocks.text: Danso was the subject of an IJB investigation earlier this year into allegations of sexual and financial impropriety. He has never been criminally charged and has denied all the allegations.
content_blocks.html: Danso was the subject of an IJB investigation earlier this year into allegations of sexual and financial impropriety. He has never been criminally charged and has denied all the allegations.

content_blocks.text: The dispute over zoning for the land his church is built on goes back to 2020.

Danso said in a written statement that a church was allowed on the land based on a February 2020 zoning certificate he provided to IJB reporters. The document says a church is “permitted by the relevant zoning requirements.” But it cautions that site plan approval May be required and that the property May be designated as “protected countryside” under the Greenbelt Plan, which was established in 2005 and prohibits commercial development or expansion on protected lands.
The certificate also notes that “a building permit is required” before any construction or major alterations to the property.

content_blocks.alt: Man in green jacket sitting at desk
content_blocks.caption: Rev. Kofi Danso at the Miracle Arena For All Nations in Vaughan, says his church has a right to be where it is. Photo by Ashlee Rezin / Chicago Sun-Times

content_blocks.alt: Man in green jacket sitting at desk
content_blocks.caption: Rev. Kofi Danso at the Miracle Arena For All Nations in Vaughan, says his church has a right to be where it is. Photo by Ashlee Rezin / Chicago Sun-Times

content_blocks.text: Through his lawyer, Danso also said that the church is operating legally on the basis of a Sept. 19, 1988, City of Vaughan bylaw that zoned its location, 10800 Weston Rd., as agricultural, which also permitted a church and a dwelling on the property.
Vaughan city officials, however, told the IJB the “provincial Greenbelt Plan supersedes the city’s zoning by-law and does not allow for a place of worship on that property.”

Miracle Arena was “not lawfully established on this property…. It did not have planning approvals or building permits,” reads the City of Vaughan statement. Danso’s zoning certificate is only valid for six months and expired before the church was constructed in late 2020, the city statement says.
After the church was founded, then expanded, ON Greenbelt land starting in 2020, Danso received support from Vaughan-Woodbridge MPP Michael Tibollo, now the province’s associate attorney general.
In June 2022, Tibollo addressed Miracle Arena congregants during his second visit in two months, pledging to assist the church in changing the Greenbelt zoning.
content_blocks.html: In June 2022, Tibollo addressed Miracle Arena congregants during his second visit in two months, pledging to assist the church in changing the Greenbelt zoning.

content_blocks.text: “One of the things we have always said is we will not touch the Greenbelt, but I think there are sometimes exceptions.… I will help and I made that commitment,” he said.

Tibollo has had public interactions with Danso at least 11 times between 2022 and 2025. He also introduced Danso on at least two occasions to Ontario Premier Doug Ford — by phone and at Tibollo’s own community summer barbecue — and encouraged other government ministers, including current Minister of Energy and Mines Stephen Lecce, to visit Miracle Arena. Scarborough Centre MPP David Smith is also among the politicians who have visited the church.

Tibollo did not respond to repeated requests for comment regarding his commitment to help change the zoning at 10800 Weston Rd. or his relationship with Danso. Ford, Lecce and Smith also did not respond to requests for comment.

The bylaw charges against Miracle Arena are to be heard in court in November and December. According to information published on the City of Vaughan’s property bylaws page, complaints and violations require “significant” investigation before a fine or penalty is issued. Charges are laid as a “last resort.”
Twelve-acre plot in question
Ontario’s Greenbelt is a protected swath of farmland, forests and wetlands spanning two-million acres across southern Ontario.

Danso and his wife, JoAnne, purchased the 12-acre plot of land where their church now sits in May 2020 for $5.6 million. The real estate listing at the time shows the property was zoned as “Greenbelt,” “agricultural” and “heritage.”
content_blocks.html: Danso and his wife, JoAnne, purchased the 12-acre plot of land where their church now sits in May 2020 for $5.6 million. The real estate listing at the time shows the property was zoned as “Greenbelt,” “agricultural” and “heritage.”

content_blocks.text: At the time, satellite images show a house and large shed on the property surrounded by dirt roads and fields littered with trucking, shipping and construction equipment. Those structures pre-date the property’s 2005 Greenbelt designation.
Once the Dansos took possession, the property began a transformation.
In videos Danso posted at the time of purchase, he described his desire to develop the land into a community with a large church and amenities such as a shopping mall, condos, a school and livestock.
content_blocks.html: In videos Danso posted at the time of purchase, he described his desire to develop the land into a community with a large church and amenities such as a shopping mall, condos, a school and livestock.

content_blocks.text: In 2022, Premier Ford opened parts of the Greenbelt to housing and development, but not the parcel of land where Miracle Arena sits. Ford reversed the decision to open the Greenbelt in 2023 after investigations by Ontario’s Auditor General and Integrity Commissioner found the process favoured politically connected developers.

In May 2022, MPP Tibollo attended Miracle Arena ahead of the provincial election. Speaking to the congregation , he called Danso “an incredible leader” while detailing his own track record in the private and public sector.

content_blocks.text: A month later, Tibollo returned following his reelection and publicly thanked Danso and his congregants for their support before making his commitment to assist the church with the Greenbelt zoning issue.

content_blocks.caption: Area MPP Michael Tibollo has visited the church on several occasions. Photo by Jennifer Hamilton-McCharles / North Bay Nugget

content_blocks.text: ‘It was awful. It was smelling’
Miracle Arena’s challenges reach beyond alleged breaches of Greenbelt zoning restrictions.

In an address to regional council for York Region in September 2023, Danso raised safety concerns about the sanitary conditions of the property, notably the strain on its septic tank, at a time when the church was providing shelter to African refugees.
content_blocks.html: In an address to regional council for York Region in September 2023, Danso raised safety concerns about the sanitary conditions of the property, notably the strain on its septic tank, at a time when the church was providing shelter to African refugees.

content_blocks.text: Despite the zoning issues, Danso asked the city to help connect the building to the municipal sewage system to relieve the pressure on the septic tank.

Fitz-Roy Gordon, a current candidate for York regional council in the Oct. 26 municipal election, was working with refugees at Miracle Arena at this time through advocacy organization Anchor, founded by him and his wife, Shernett Martin.
In an interview, Gordon and Martin said “hundreds of people” shared one shower at Miracle Arena and just a few toilets. Soon the septic tank was backing up and sewage was spilling over the ground.
“It was awful. It was smelling — it was unsanitary,” Gordon recalls. “I know that the region and the city wanted them (the refugees) off that land.”
In the September 2023 address to city council, Danso said, “We were told that we need a Minister’s Zoning Order (MZO) to address some of the issues on the property.”

Vaughan City records show the church told the city it was in the process of getting an MZO. But Michael Minzak, press secretary for Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing Rob Flack, told the IJB that “no (Minister’s Zoning Order) was ever issued or contemplated.”

Speaking again before York Region councillors in January 2024, Danso characterized city orders to stop Miracle Arena’s religious services and remove structures on the church property used to house asylum seekers as “discrimination” and accused public officials of abusing their authority.
content_blocks.html: Speaking again before York Region councillors in January 2024, Danso characterized city orders to stop Miracle Arena’s religious services and remove structures on the church property used to house asylum seekers as “discrimination” and accused public officials of abusing their authority.

content_blocks.text: “As a clergyman, nobody has the power to stop me from exercising my spiritual duties, especially on this land,” Danso said, drawing cheers from church supporters in the council chamber.

As the IJB previously reported, several members of the church are facing criminal charges of fraud, laundering and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence related to funding of refugee housing on the property.

That matter remains before the courts. Danso has not been charged. In a press release published at the time, Miracle Arena said “the alleged conduct was undertaken independently and without the knowledge, authorization, or involvement of the Church.”
The 50 alleged regulatory bylaw infractions the church now faces date back to 2023.

Sixteen of the charges against Miracle Arena and three of its senior associates are zoning bylaw infractions; eight have to do with property standards; four are alleged site alternation bylaw infractions; while 22 charges relate to animal welfare, including that the church allegedly failed to provide food, failed to provide care and failed to keep an animal pen in sanitary conditions.
In interviews, former Miracle Arena parishioners told the IJB that the animals kept on the property — mainly alpacas, a horse and donkeys — were rehoused elsewhere after at least one animal died.
Danso did not respond to questions about allegations of animal harm or where animals were sent.

content_blocks.alt: Iron gate with long driveway behind it
content_blocks.caption: One of the entrances to the Miracle Arena Church, located at 10800 Weston Rd. Photo by Peter J. Thompson / National Post

content_blocks.text: “The current land use at the property is now before the court. It would be inappropriate to comment any further on that,” reads a statement from Danso’s lawyer, Aaron Crangle.
“(Miracle Arena) has spent a considerable amount of time and money to get the property into compliance with any concerns or orders.”
Alleged sexual misconduct and financial exploitation

The property disputes add to a controversy already surrounding Miracle Arena. A recent IJB investigation documented years of troubling allegations involving Danso and the church, ranging from allegations of sexual misconduct to alleged financial exploitation.
content_blocks.html: The property disputes add to a controversy already surrounding Miracle Arena. A recent IJB investigation documented years of troubling allegations involving Danso and the church, ranging from allegations of sexual misconduct to alleged financial exploitation.

content_blocks.text: Several former parishioners told the IJB about alleged “grooming” behaviours by Danso. Some alleged Danso had non-consensual sexual encounters with them, including one woman who says she was a minor at the time.
Danso has never been criminally charged and previously told the IJB he denied all allegations of sexual or financial impropriety.
The church has continued to draw hundreds of parishioners to services. And as the church’s physical footprint has expanded on the Greenbelt, so too has its leader’s push for political influence.

“We need to help to do evangelism to take over the city,” said Danso in a September 2026 sermon in which he encouraged his flock to volunteer and knock on doors for certain municipal candidates. “We have to do everything we can to make sure we are taking over for the glory of God.”
content_blocks.html: “We need to help to do evangelism to take over the city,” said Danso in a September 2026 sermon in which he encouraged his flock to volunteer and knock on doors for certain municipal candidates. “We have to do everything we can to make sure we are taking over for the glory of God.”

content_blocks.text: “The Lord does not give a city to people by prayer,” he said in the September sermon. “Let’s do whatever we can to make it happen.… We must take it by force.”

In response to IJB questions, Danso’s written statement says “there is nothing wrong with Mafan (Miracle Arena For All Nations) supporting politicians that have demonstrated support for the work that it has done.”

Among the candidates he has recommended to his congregants is Vaughan mayoral candidate Shelly Cerrelli, the sole opponent to incumbent mayor Steven Del Duca, who has clashed with Danso over his plans for long-term refugee housing on the Greenbelt property. Cerrelli’s campaign told reporters she has no connection to the church beyond visits made as part of her campaign outreach to faith communities across the region.

Her campaign listed several faith communities she has interacted with during the campaign and said she has not promised Danso or any religious leader or organization “favourable treatment” or “municipal approvals” in exchange for prayer, encouragement or support for her candidacy.

The IJB has identified at least three candidates receiving Danso’s support who have clear ties to the church. Robert Bazil, a candidate for Toronto City Council, and Andrea Francis Bucknor, a candidate for Peel Public School Board trustee, have both publicly identified themselves as members of Miracle Arena. Neither responded to requests for comment.
Another Miracle Arena-affiliated candidate is Matthew Boateng, one of Danso’s longtime supporters and a church minister. He is also running for Toronto Council.
He is listed as a board member for the church in charity documents and named as a defendant, along with Miracle Arena and two others, in the pending bylaw charges.
On his campaign website, Boateng cites his experience as “volunteer and ministry service with Miracle Arena for All Nations” and being a church “shelter supervisor.”
During a campaign launch speech in September, Boateng credited Danso and JoAnne Danso for being the people “that gave me this push to do this.”
IJB reporters sought comment from Boateng about the bylaw charges, his relationship with Danso and his campaign.
Boateng did not directly respond to most of the Ijb’s questions, instead saying the inquiries were “harassment, voter intimidation and blatant election interference.”
The IJB also asked Boateng if Danso, Miracle Arena or other high-ranking political figures had donated money to his campaign.
Boateng denied receiving “the financial contributions in question,” but added, “according to the City of Toronto, any resident of Ontario who is a resident, can contribute to a municipal campaign.”

stories.title: Winnipeg mayoral candidates to face off in 680 Cjob debate
stories.summary: Richard Cloutier will host three of Winnipeg's mayoral candidates, incumbent Mayor Scott Gillingham, Kevin Klein and Mike Vogiatzakis, for a debate on 680 Cjob Wednesday morning.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Incumbent Mayor of Winnipeg Scott Gillingham will meet with two candidates vying for his position, Kevin Klein and Mike Vogiatzakis, ON 680 Cjob Wednesday morning.

The hour-long debate is set to begin at 9 a.m. on the radio station and will be streamed online.

Richard Cloutier , host of the News on 680 Cjob, will moderate the discussion between the three mayoral candidates. Connecting Winnipeg’s Hal Anderson will host a post-debate analysis on his show.

Wednesday morning will see the first major broadcast debate among the candidates, a week before Winnipeg voters head to the polls on Oct. 28.

As of Sunday evening, more than 25,000 early ballots were cast, according to a news release shared by the City of Winnipeg on Monday. It said that a single-day advanced voting location record was set last Friday when 1,879 votes were submitted at an advanced voting location in the St. Vital Centre.

stories.title: Cancer patients decry Ontario’s revised drug funding rules for out-of-country coverage
stories.summary: Drug treatments will now only be funded out of country if they are already funded within the province but access is temporarily unavailable or delayed
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Sabrina Apitz-Grossman was told 13 months ago that she had about 12 to 18 months to live.

A rare form of cancer in the 31-year-old’s knee had metastasized, spreading to her lungs. She has undergone radiotherapy, chemotherapy and surgeries, though the synovial sarcoma couldn’t be fully removed.

Apitz-Grossman’s doctors are recommending a treatment approved in the United States but unavailable in Ontario. She needs it urgently but the Ontario Health Insurance Plan turned her down for out-of-country coverage. An appeal failed, as did an application under a Case-by-Case Review Program to get special permission for the treatment to be administered at the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre in Toronto.

She is still fighting.

“I so desperately would love to turn 32,” she said.

Apitz-Grossman and other Ontarians with Stage 4 cancer told by their doctors that they are good candidates for treatments unavailable in the province were buoyed last month when 37-year-old Alex Shved, in a similar situation, won a court challenge against his Ohip out-of-country denial.

But their hopes were dashed when Health Minister Sylvia Jones responded to the court ruling by changing the rules.

Drug treatments will now only be funded out of country if they are already funded within the province but access is temporarily unavailable or delayed, a set of circumstances some patients see as impossibly narrow. The government said it clarified in regulation what was already long-standing policy.

“We’re protecting Ontario patients and taxpayers from price gouging and protecting their access to life-saving medications that would otherwise only be available in the United States or overseas,” Jones wrote in a statement.

“This change supports a consistent, fair and transparent approach to funding decisions, protects the integrity of Ontario’s world-class drug approval process and will help avoid up to $5.2-billion in additional costs to Ontario’s health-care system every year.”

Framing the move as a cost-saving measure is not sitting right with Apitz-Grossman.

“Are we saying that we could save like 5,000 or more people’s lives, and they’re proud of themselves for not doing that?” she said. “Is this supposed to be good news that we’re not going to save those people, so that we can instead buy a couple more private jets?”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford came under fire earlier this year for a government purchase of a $29-million private jet and quickly returned it.

The treatment Apitz-Grossman is seeking, Tecelra, is a personalized therapy made from a patient’s own T-cells, a type of white blood cell. Nearly half of patients in Apitz-Grossman’s situation respond to the treatment, and among those who respond, there is a 90 per cent chance of survival after a year and 70 per cent after two years, according to her oncologist.

But the treatment is costly, at US$727,000, Apitz-Grossman said. She feels terrible guilt for seeking such a pricey treatment, she said, but she wants to live.

“There has never been a moment where I have thought to myself, ‘Gosh, I wish that patient who was in the ICU for weeks and who it cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to save, hadn’t been saved,’” Apitz-Grossman said.

The origin of Jones’ $5.2-billion figure was unclear in her press release, and a government official later explained that it would be the additional cost if the province entirely stopped negotiating prices with drug manufacturers for public coverage in Ontario.

Ohip’s reason for denying Apitz-Grossman, Shved and others out-of-country drug treatment funding is that routinely paying for such requests while drugs are undergoing review for funding in Ontario would “undermine the incentive structure that encourages manufacturers to participate in Canada’s drug review processes.”

Kevin Nash, 59, has metastatic melanoma and is seeking the same tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy as Shved. Nash’s out-of-country application and subsequent appeal were also denied, and he does not believe the government’s reasoning.

“These companies make billions of dollars a year, not a billion, billions of dollars a year,” he said. “Do you think that they care one bit whether Kevin Nash goes to Buffalo for a treatment? That’s so preposterous.”

In Apitz-Grossman’s case, the manufacturer of Tecelra has said it has no plans to apply for approval in Canada. That means there is no review process in this case to undermine, she noted.

Holly Wardlow, 61, is in a similar boat, with the government denying coverage through its Case-by-Case Review Program for a medication to treat her rare form of liver cancer because the drug was “expected to be reviewed for public funding in Ontario.”

That’s despite the manufacturer submitting two letters telling the province it has no plans to apply for approval in Canada.

“We just thought, ‘Well, this doesn’t make any sense,’” Wardlow said.

“We provided evidence that there is not going to be a population-based review. This drug is never going to be approved in Canada, let alone Ontario, because the manufacturer is not going to make an application, and they have evidence of that. And yet they provided the same reason for denying funding.”

Wardlow and her husband have been paying $78,000 a month for her to receive infusions in Ontario every two weeks, and her tumour has been shrinking with almost no side-effects, she said.

Their savings have been depleted and they have now started a GoFundMe.

“I’m getting out there and trying to stay fit, partly because I can, and partly because the weather is beautiful, and partly because I’m thinking ahead that surgery May be possible in the future,” Wardlow said.

Kevin Nash, 59, has metastatic melanoma and is seeking the same tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy as Shved. Nash’s out-of-country application and subsequent appeal were also denied, and he does not believe the government’s reasoning.

“These companies make billions of dollars a year, not a billion, billions of dollars a year,” he said. “Do you think that they care one bit whether Kevin Nash goes to Buffalo for a treatment? That’s so preposterous.”
In Apitz-Grossman’s case, the manufacturer of Tecelra has said it has no plans to apply for approval in Canada. That means there is no review process in this case to undermine, she noted.

Holly Wardlow, 61, is in a similar boat, with the government denying coverage through its Case-by-Case Review Program for a medication to treat her rare form of liver cancer because the drug was “expected to be reviewed for public funding in Ontario.”

“We provided evidence that there is not going to be a population-based review. This drug is never going to be approved in Canada, let alone Ontario, because the manufacturer is not going to make an application, and they have evidence of that. Wardlow and her husband have been paying $78,000 a month for her to receive infusions in Ontario every two weeks, and her tumour has been shrinking with almost no side-effects, she said.
Their savings have been depleted and they have now started a GoFundMe.

“I’m getting out there and trying to stay fit, partly because I can, and partly because the weather is beautiful, and partly because I’m thinking ahead that surgery May be possible in the future,” Wardlow said.

stories.title: Monthly food bank visits hit record high as Canadians struggle with persistently high cost of living
stories.summary: Canadians continue to struggle with the high cost of living, with monthly food bank visits up nearly nine per cent this year compared to last. According to Food Banks Canada’s annual HungerCount report, food bank visits have soared to 2.35 million per month in 2026, a 117 per cent increase from 2019.
stories.author: Heather Wright
stories.content:
Toronto - Canadians continue to struggle with the high cost of living, with monthly food bank visits up nearly nine per cent this year compared to last.

According to Food Banks Canada’s annual HungerCount report, food bank visits have soared to 2.35 million per month in 2026, a 117 per cent increase from 2019.

“(This) is the story of what happens when millions of people are out of options,” said Food Banks Canada CEO Kirstin Beardsley.

“In the past, most people in Canada could absorb a small financial setback… those days are over. Canada’s bleak new reality is that millions of people are making impossible trade-offs every day as they choose between food or rent,” she said.

Food bank visits are up in every province and territory except Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Labrador. The most populous provinces saw the most visits, with 846,724 in Ontario (a nearly 11 per cent increase), 785,889 in Quebec (up 5 per cent) and 250,505 visits in British Columbia (a 14 per cent increase).

“This does not have to be Canada’s story,” said Beardsley, who is calling on all governments to act.

Among the recommendations in this year’s report are changes to employment insurance (EI) to include non-traditional occupations such as gig work and review eligibility thresholds; doubling the Canada Workers Benefit; enhancing the Disability Tax Credit (DTC); reviewing federal social assistance; and investing in critical infrastructure, including affordable housing.

The report also calls for more investment in Canada’s north, where food bank visits are up sharply compared to last year: 24 per cent in Yukon and 29 per cent in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut.

Food Bank Canada releases its HungerCount study every year, compiling data from more than 5,500 food banks and community organizations across the country.

The report found the cost of basic necessities has soared since 2021. Food prices have increased nearly 30 per cent, housing is up 28 per cent and transportation has risen nearly 24 per cent.

The rising cost of living has driven more employed Canadians to food banks. The report found that nearly one in five clients is employed, up from one in 10 in 2019.

stories.title: Canadian food bank use hits 2.3 million monthly visits due to grocery costs, report finds
stories.summary: A new report from Food Banks Canada says the number of Canadians struggling with food insecurity continues to grow, as food bank visits hit a new record of more than 2.3 million in March. The non-profit organization’s latest HungerCount report, released today, says the cost-of-living crisis and economic pressures are weighing heavily on nearly 10 […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Kerry Holt never expected she’d become a food bank client.

After losing her job nearly a year ago following major surgery, Holt said it became increasingly difficult to balance her rent, extra bills and provide for her three children.

She would have only one meal a day, suffering from fainting spells a few times, before being diagnosed with an iron deficiency because of her lack of eating.

“I was doing everything I could to find work,” she said. “My groceries and bills were so high.”

Now, Holt visits her local Indigenous food bank twice a month, always on the look out for eggs, milk, bread, granola and sometimes produce when it’s available.

“With food prices, anyone could need the food bank at any point,” she said.

A new report from Food Banks Canada says the number of Canadians struggling with food insecurity continues to grow, as food bank visits hit a new record of more than 2.3 million in March.

The non-profit organization’s latest HungerCount report, released today, says the cost-of-living crisis and economic pressures are weighing heavily on nearly 10 million Canadians experiencing food insecurity.

Its annual survey recorded more than 2,355,000 visits to food banks across Canada in March 2026, an 8.7 per cent increase from the March 2025 record of more than two million visits.

The report says more than a third of this year’s food bank visits, or nearly 776,000, were made by children.

Food Banks Canada CEO Kirstin Beardsley says people are “running out of options” as they try to balance essential spending, such as paying rent, with rising grocery costs.

“A lot of folks who used to give to food banks are now finding themselves in need of those services,” Beardsley said.

The HungerCount report says that since 2021, food prices increased by about 30 per cent, housing costs by 28 per cent and transportation by roughly 24 per cent.

One in five food banks across Canada are reportedly running out of food before meeting the needs of all their clients.

“A job is not enough to ensure that you are not in need of a food bank anymore,” she added. “There’s no other room in their budget to do anything.”

Linda Barker has been a volunteer for 15 years at the North York Harvest Food Bank, where she spends two to three days a week sorting through food donations and packing up dozens of boxes.

Barker, an avid runner in her mid-70s, said she’s been on the lookout for baby diapers to put into emergency essentials boxes for clients who need supplies last-minute. With a small team of five other volunteers, they spend their Wednesday morning moving like a well-oiled machine.

“The need is far more pressing than people realize,” she said.

Beardsley said the federal government’s new Canada Groceries and Essential Benefit is one “positive investment,” but it’s not nearly enough to bridge the gap she’s seeing at the community level or in northern regions, where groceries are sold at higher prices due to transport costs.

The report includes a number of policy recommendations, such as doubling the Canada Workers Benefit for low-income residents, expanding food sovereignty initiatives in the North and investing up to $500 million toward food bank infrastructure to meet the demand.

Ottawa Food Bank CEO Natalie Spooner said she’s seeing a “concerning” influx of food clients visiting food banks in Ottawa, mainly children and young adults.

The non-profit tries to budget for fresh produce to provide nutritious options for its clients, since that’s become unaffordable.

The organization’s clients rely heavily on local food banks, where supplies are mainly provided through community donations.

Fundraising for donations while having a limited budget comes with its own challenges when everyone is struggling economically, Spooner explained.

“Food insecurity severity is becoming more dire,” she said. “We are seeing some exhaustion in the network.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Sadeen Mohsen, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Sunshine, dry conditions expected to continue across region
stories.summary: CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison says sunny skies and dry conditions are expected to continue across southern Ontario over the next seven days.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison says sunny skies and dry conditions are expected to continue across southern Ontario over the next seven days.

The region will see plenty of sunshine Wednesday, with temperatures reaching a high of 17 C and light winds.

“It’s cool out there this morning, but by the afternoon we’ll warm up to 17 degrees,” Atchison said.

The sunny weather is expected to continue Thursday through Sunday, with daytime highs ranging between 16 C and 18 C.

Atchison said an upper ridge and surface high pressure are contributing to the stable conditions, with little change expected in the forecast over the coming week.

Despite the sunshine during the day, overnight temperatures will remain cool, with the possibility of frost.

The extended stretch of dry weather is expected to continue, with sunshine forecast throughout the next week.

stories.title: Canada can end homelessness. Even cities in the U.S. are showing it can be done
stories.summary: Treating housing as the first intervention in health care makes moral and economic sense
stories.author: Andrew Boozary
stories.content:
Dr. Andrew Boozary is a primary care physician and the founding executive director of the UHN Gattuso Centre for Social Medicine.

Whenever I raise the example of Finland – the country that nearly eradicated homelessness through treating housing as the first intervention in health care – someone online tells me it doesn’t count. The country is too socialist. Too small. Too “homogeneous,” whatever that is supposed to mean. The objection isn’t really about Finland it seems, but about preserving a failing status quo.

As a physician that works with unhoused patients in Toronto, I decided to set my clinical gaze on other jurisdictions – other cities that would be harder to wave away, especially amidst a trade war. The one I want to talk about now is not in Scandinavia. It doesn’t even have universal health care. It is in Texas.

Houston, the state’s most populous city, has housed more than 30,000 people since 2012 and cut homelessness by more than 60 per cent since 2011. As a tale of two cities, while Houston was moving people out of encampments and into housing, Toronto’s homeless population more than doubled, from about 7,300 in 2021 to more than 15,000 in the latest count . While there has been some progress in Toronto – a near 9-per-cent reduction in homelessness this past year ​– some American cities are moving toward eradicating homelessness. In my home province, I see patients pass away before their name is called on a housing wait list.

My clinical days are spent in shelters, drop-ins and social housing, and contrary to all the online vitriol, the people I treat are not sick due to a shortage of willpower. Illness is imposed on them owing to a shortage of social housing supply. Homelessness is not a social inconvenience that happens to carry health consequences. It is a pathology of poverty, and one we hold the prescription for yet keep declining to fill.

The evidence has long stopped being suggestive and become outright embarrassing. “The Public Housing Dividend” report , produced by the Canadian Centre for Economic Analysis and supported by Scotiabank, projected what investing in public housing across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton area would deliver over the next 25 years: more than 524,000 hospital bed days avoided, and roughly 156,000 fewer emergency-department visits. Every dollar in public housing returns $2.80. When major banks are joining the chorus for housing for all, it is worth asking why public policy hasn’t caught up.

Some of it lies in how we view people who are unhoused. We put the onus on them or shirk blame by assuming their circumstances are the result of something other than housing – mental health or drug use. But we have our own proof that this isn’t the case. The Mental Health Commission of Canada ran a national study, Chez Soi/Homes First, which showed the benefits of a housing-first approach through a randomized control trial in cities across the country. That we even needed a clinical trial to examine the benefits of housing speaks volumes on a moral scale.

And now, through the Social Medicine Housing Initiative at UHN Dunn House, formerly a hospital parking lot, we have seen what happens when housing is treated not as a reward for healthy behaviour but as the thing that lets people get better at all. In its first year, the 51 tenants at Dunn House saw a 52-per-cent reduction in emergency department visits and a 79-per-cent drop in time in hospital. These are not soft numbers. They are hospital beds freed up, ambulances tending to medical emergencies, and emergency department staff treating the needs they are expertly trained for. It is also human dignity restored. The hospital ward is the most expensive and least humane place to treat homelessness, and we treat a great deal of it in our health system as the last thread of the social safety net. That is why the Social Medicine Housing model is now expanding to more than 300 new homes with the support of every level of government.

Houston is not a magical place, nor is it socialist. What it built is a system: Dozens of agencies and various levels of government started co-ordinating around permanent housing as the shared goal. To be sure, its success is fragile and contested with pandemic funding drying up and Texas still allowing landlords to turn away tenants with rent vouchers. But this is why it is a useful example – it succeeded in adverse political conditions, not ideal ones.

And Houston is not alone. Denver recorded its first overall drop in homelessness in nearly a decade this year, after moving roughly 7,700 people into permanent housing since 2023; unsheltered homelessness dropped by 45 per cent in the last two years. They followed the same formula: cross-sector co-ordination and a focus on permanent housing, not shelter as the treatment.

From these cities, and yes, even Finland, there are three lessons that travel well across our border.

First, house people first. Shift investments toward social and supportive housing. The return on investment has been demonstrated at length. We cannot treat diabetes or cancer in encampments and keep blaming individuals for poor health outcomes.

Second, co-ordinate a system of compassion and sound evidence. There needs to be better integration across housing, health, justice and community sectors. The fragmentation amongst and within sectors comes at a very real human cost.

And finally, let’s acknowledge homelessness as the generational health crisis that it is. Every dollar we decline to spend in housing, we spend several times over in emergency departments, hospital wards, prison cells and shelter beds.

More than half a century ago, the Lalonde Report put forward a Canadian idea: that health is influenced far more by social conditions than the medicine patients receive. We put that insight on the world stage and many other countries took up the call. The least we can do is implement it at home.

The question was never whether housing works as good medicine. We have randomized control trial data, a major report sponsored by a major bank and now two American cities showing results in real time that it does. The question is whether we are finally willing to stop looking away from the suffering and devastation playing out in hospitals and street corners.

stories.title: Food bank use in Canada more than doubles since 2019, report shows
stories.summary: Employed Canadians make up almost a fifth of those turning to emergency assistance
stories.author: Mariya Postelnyak
stories.content:
Food bank use in Canada has more than doubled since 2019, with employed Canadians making up nearly one-fifth of those turning to emergency food assistance, new data shows.

Monthly food bank visits throughout the country reached 2.35 million in March, 2026, up nearly 9 per cent compared with the same month a year ago and up 117 per cent since 2019, according to a report from Food Banks Canada released on Wednesday.

It’s a symptom of an affordability crisis that spans food, shelter and transportation, according to Richard Matern, research director at Food Banks Canada. He said many households have little room in their budgets to absorb sudden price shocks before they are forced to turn to food banks for help.

“What’s most concerning is the sustained depth of need that’s been occurring over the last few years,” Mr. Matern said. “People are progressively losing their financial cushion.”

For around 18 per cent of food bank users, employment was their primary source of income, up from just 12 per cent in 2019 but down slightly from 19.4 per cent in 2025, the report found. Meanwhile, the share of visitors who had social assistance as their primary source of income has consistently shrunk over the same period.

“This portion of clients who were employed [was] holding at 10 or 11 per cent for like a decade,” said Mr. Matern. “And that’s when the affordability crisis started to hit.”

Food Bank Canada’s HungerCount survey is sent out to a network of nearly 3,000 food banks and affiliates across the country each February, and the data is collected for the month of March.

Grocery inflation in Canada eased at the end of the summer after two years of sustained increases, with prices up 1.7 per cent year over year in September compared with annual growth of 2.8 per cent in August.

But that simply means already-high grocery prices are rising at a slower pace. The price of a typical grocery basket is up 30 per cent since 2019, according to data from Royal Bank of Canada.

And even the modest reprieve from high food inflation looks to be short-lived , as soaring diesel prices linked to the continuing conflict in Iran are poised to make food imports in the winter months more expensive.

Those fuel costs are turning into a “double-whammy” for food banks across Canada, Mr. Matern said.

“On one hand, transportation and fuel costs affect the operational budgets of the food bank network, and on the client side, increased gas prices are another layer on the affordability challenge.”

Diesel prices are up more than 70 per cent from a year ago, and May soon have a bigger impact on grocery prices as well, warned Mike von Massow, a professor in the Department of Food, Agricultural and Resource Economics at the University of Guelph.

Currently, Canada’s harvest season is helping to keep fruit and vegetable prices in check, Prof. von Massow said. But prices typically go up in the colder months as the country begins to import more of its produce, he added.

”Those prices May be even higher with the rising price of diesel,” he said.

Then there are shelter costs, which have increased by 37 per cent since January, 2019, for renters, as measured by Statistics Canada. Roughly 72 per cent of food bank users live in market rent housing, according to Food Banks Canada.

For the most financially vulnerable Canadians, including many who earn a paycheque, incomes have not kept up with the threefold blow from years of steep food, transport and shelter cost increases, Mr. Matern said.

People in the lowest-income bracket are spending upward of 60 per cent of their disposable income on their housing alone, he said. “Resilience has been eroded at this point for a lot more people.”
