stories.title: B.C. election 2026: What to know about the parties, leaders and platforms
stories.summary: Here’s an overview of the situation as voters head to the polls on Saturday
stories.author: Moira Wyton, Globe staff
stories.content:
When B.C.’s NDP Premier David Eby called a snap provincial election last month, two years early and with the Opposition BC Conservatives in disarray, he said he needed a strong mandate to deal with U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

Some called the move opportunist, however now there’s a risk that it could backfire. Months of party chaos and infighting had the BC Conservatives looking like easy opponents, but in the weeks since the writ dropped, the Official Opposition appears to have pulled themselves together. In some surveys, interim leader Lorne Doerkson’s party is polling narrowly ahead of the NDP. The upheaval on the right didn’t reshape the province’s political landscape, and now it’s another tight two-way race, with the Greens and a couple new challengers trailing behind.

Upcoming Q&A: Ask us your questions about the B.C. election

Which parties are in the running, who are their leaders, and what do they stand for? Here’s what you need to know for Saturday’s general election.

The general election is on Saturday, Oct. 24.

The last day to vote in advance is Wednesday. Several advanced polling stations are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. PT.

On Saturday, polling stations are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. PT. To find the closest polling station, enter your address on Elections BC’s website .

There are 93 members of the Legislative Assembly of British Columbia, meaning a party must win 47 seats to form a majority government.

Seats at dissolution: 47 seats

Official party status: Yes

When David Eby called a snap election last month to try to increase his Ndp’s narrow majority, it didn’t seem like much of a gamble. The BC Conservatives – who had come within a whisker of an upset election win two years ago – were practically leaderless and had seemingly destroyed themselves from the inside. But now, the NDP are polling a few critical points behind the Conservatives, as accusations of political opportunism and the baggage of nine years in power weigh down the ruling party’s campaign.

Five takeaways from the B.C. election leaders' debate

Eby has presented himself as the only person strong enough to stand up to Donald Trump for B.C. in this “existential moment,” and leaned heavily on policies meant to invigorate the party’s centre-left base, such as raising taxes on those making more than $190,000 to pay for more health care services and capping some grocery prices. But running against Trump hasn’t worked as well for Eby as it did for Prime Minister Mark Carney during the last federal election. Criticism from the left and the right over the ballooning provincial debt, a recent billion-dollar-plus budget error , environmental policy and the state of B.C.’s stretched health care system have taken the wind out of the Ndp’s sails. If the party manages to eke out a fourth mandate, polling indicates it’s unlikely to be stronger than what they started with.

Interim leader: Lorne Doerkson

Seats at dissolution: 28

The BC Conservatives had all but imploded when the writ dropped on Sept. 22, but the party has pulled itself back together and is mounting a stiff challenge to the NDP. Two years ago, the party burst back onto the political scene, reshaped the political landscape and won 44 seats, coming within a handful of votes of forming government. But months of infighting and turmoil led to 16 MLAs leaving or being ousted, former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s resignation and several former Conservatives joining challenger parties. However, in the weeks since Lorne Doerkson took over as interim leader , he has managed to reunite much of the big-tent right-wing party, which polls now suggest could win a majority on Saturday.

Lorne Doerkson didn’t plan on leading the BC Conservatives, but he’s trying to meet the moment

Doerkson, who was little-known a month ago, has wasted no time introducing himself to British Columbians. His jobs-focused campaign includes pledges to “supercharge the economy,” freeze income taxes , reduce red-tape and “fully-fund” frontline health care services. Doerkson has also promised to repeal the province’s legislation implementing the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and to remove the sexual orientation and gender identity (Sogi) resource available for schools.

But the interim leader hasn’t clearly answered how he’ll reduce the budget deficit or where he might make cuts, and his opponents have cast doubt on his ability to govern both the province and his unruly caucus. Doerkson has already ousted two Conservative candidates – one accused of making Hitler remarks and another for racist social media posts – and the NDP and Greens have criticized others who remain on the campaign slate, including one who likened Sogi to grooming. It remains to be seen whether he can hold the party together - something his two predecessors failed to do.

Leader: Emily Lowan

Seats at dissolution: 2

The BC Greens are hoping to pull themselves back from the brink of losing official party status and become kingmakers once again. Nine years ago, they helped John Horgan’s NDP end the 16-year reign of Christy Clark’s BC Liberals. But the party has struggled since Horgan’s snap pandemic election in 2020 betrayed their confidence-and-supply agreement and boosted the NDP to a historic majority. Now, the progressive party is trying to use a fresh leader, frustration with Eby’s snap election and the Ndp’s track record on the environment and Indigenous rights to peel off left-wing votes and put itself back on the map.

Leader Emily Lowan , a 26-year-old renter, has campaigned on her youth and policies aimed at holding onto the party’s progressive base, which is largely concentrated in and around Victoria and on the Gulf Islands. The Greens are pledging a tax on the ultra-wealthy , oil and gas royalty reforms and vacancy control for renters. And while the Greens are polling a distant third, they have recruited star candidates – such as the province’s former chief coroner Lisa Lapointe – who could help give them a bit more sway in the legislature once again.

Leader: Elenore Sturko

Seats at dissolution: 8

Official party status: No

CentreBC is trying to un-unite the right and return a centrist party to the province’s legislature, two years after BC United (formerly the BC Liberals) folded its campaign and endorsed the surging BC Conservatives. Leader Elenore Sturko, a former BC United MLA, sent a shock through provincial politics when she crossed the floor to the Conservatives in 2024, where she was a star candidate and later shadow minister for John Rustad’s Official Opposition. But she was removed from caucus in 2025 and Sturko, who is gay, later claimed she was prevented from voicing her “more socially Liberal beliefs.”

CentreBC formed in the same year, and merged with the British Columbia Party last month with eight former BC Conservative MLAs on board, including Sturko. When the snap election was called, all of them took Doerkson’s invitation to rejoin caucus , except Sturko, who now finds herself unexpectedly at the helm of the party. She has described it as “socially progressive, environmentally pragmatic and fiscally responsible,” saying it would ensure a strong centrist voice in Victoria. However, a recent poll put her far behind, and it’s unclear if CentreBC could win enough votes off the Conservatives to squeak out a seat.

Leader: Dallas Brodie

Official party status: Yes

OneBC is another recent product of the Conservatives’ internal divisions. Former BC Conservative MLAs Dallas Brodie and Tara Armstrong formed the party in 2025, after Brodie was removed from caucus over comments she made about residential schools . Now, Brodie is among two incumbent MLAs running under the OneBC banner, but polls suggest the party is unlikely to win a seat or keep its official party status.

In the legislature, OneBC has proposed a bill against gender-affirming care for transgender people and another to ban land acknowledgements by public institutions and employees in the province. Brodie has also vowed to “fight against these land-back giveaways that are being done by the current government” and “stop the greed and corruption of the reconciliation industry” during the course of the campaign.

With reports from Andrea Woo, Mike Hager and The Canadian Press

But months of infighting and turmoil led to 16 MLAs leaving or being ousted, former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s resignation and several former Conservatives joining challenger parties. However, in the weeks since Lorne Doerkson took over as interim leader , he has managed to reunite much of the big-tent right-wing party, which polls now suggest could win a majority on Saturday.
Lorne Doerkson didn’t plan on leading the BC Conservatives, but he’s trying to meet the moment

Doerkson, who was little-known a month ago, has wasted no time introducing himself to British Columbians. His jobs-focused campaign includes pledges to “supercharge the economy,” freeze income taxes , reduce red-tape and “fully-fund” frontline health care services. Doerkson has also promised to repeal the province’s legislation implementing the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and to remove the sexual orientation and gender identity (Sogi) resource available for schools.

But the interim leader hasn’t clearly answered how he’ll reduce the budget deficit or where he might make cuts, and his opponents have cast doubt on his ability to govern both the province and his unruly caucus. Doerkson has already ousted two Conservative candidates – one accused of making Hitler remarks and another for racist social media posts – and the NDP and Greens have criticized others who remain on the campaign slate, including one who likened Sogi to grooming. It remains to be seen whether he can hold the party together - something his two predecessors failed to do.
Green Party of B.C.

content_blocks.caption: Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Leader: Emily Lowan
Seats at dissolution: 2

The BC Greens are hoping to pull themselves back from the brink of losing official party status and become kingmakers once again. Nine years ago, they helped John Horgan’s NDP end the 16-year reign of Christy Clark’s BC Liberals. But the party has struggled since Horgan’s snap pandemic election in 2020 betrayed their confidence-and-supply agreement and boosted the NDP to a historic majority. Now, the progressive party is trying to use a fresh leader, frustration with Eby’s snap election and the Ndp’s track record on the environment and Indigenous rights to peel off left-wing votes and put itself back on the map.

Leader Emily Lowan , a 26-year-old renter, has campaigned on her youth and policies aimed at holding onto the party’s progressive base, which is largely concentrated in and around Victoria and on the Gulf Islands. The Greens are pledging a tax on the ultra-wealthy , oil and gas royalty reforms and vacancy control for renters. And while the Greens are polling a distant third, they have recruited star candidates – such as the province’s former chief coroner Lisa Lapointe – who could help give them a bit more sway in the legislature once again.
CentreBC

content_blocks.caption: ETHAN CAIRNS/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Leader: Elenore Sturko
Seats at dissolution: 8
Official party status: No

CentreBC is trying to un-unite the right and return a centrist party to the province’s legislature, two years after BC United (formerly the BC Liberals) folded its campaign and endorsed the surging BC Conservatives. Leader Elenore Sturko, a former BC United MLA, sent a shock through provincial politics when she crossed the floor to the Conservatives in 2024, where she was a star candidate and later shadow minister for John Rustad’s Official Opposition. But she was removed from caucus in 2025 and Sturko, who is gay, later claimed she was prevented from voicing her “more socially Liberal beliefs.”

CentreBC formed in the same year, and merged with the British Columbia Party last month with eight former BC Conservative MLAs on board, including Sturko. When the snap election was called, all of them took Doerkson’s invitation to rejoin caucus , except Sturko, who now finds herself unexpectedly at the helm of the party. She has described it as “socially progressive, environmentally pragmatic and fiscally responsible,” saying it would ensure a strong centrist voice in Victoria. However, a recent poll put her far behind, and it’s unclear if CentreBC could win enough votes off the Conservatives to squeak out a seat.
OneBC

content_blocks.caption: ETHAN CAIRNS/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Leader: Dallas Brodie
Official party status: Yes

OneBC is another recent product of the Conservatives’ internal divisions. Former BC Conservative MLAs Dallas Brodie and Tara Armstrong formed the party in 2025, after Brodie was removed from caucus over comments she made about residential schools . Now, Brodie is among two incumbent MLAs running under the OneBC banner, but polls suggest the party is unlikely to win a seat or keep its official party status.

In the legislature, OneBC has proposed a bill against gender-affirming care for transgender people and another to ban land acknowledgements by public institutions and employees in the province. Brodie has also vowed to “fight against these land-back giveaways that are being done by the current government” and “stop the greed and corruption of the reconciliation industry” during the course of the campaign.

stories.title: Canada orders deportation of Toronto man who helped Iran evade sanctions
stories.summary: Amin Yousefijam was a key member of a crime group that illicitly exported materials to Iran, the Immigration and Refugee Board ruled.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
A former Tehran police lieutenant living in Toronto under a new name is being deported from Canada for his “important and critical role” in a crime group that helped Iran evade sanctions.

The Immigration and Refugee Board ruled that Amin Yousefijam was “crucial” to the sanctions-dodging scheme, according to a copy of the 36-page decision released to Global News on Tuesday.

The IRB ruled that the Iranian citizen, who has resided in Canada since 2016, was the group’s logistician and oversaw shipping arrangements for the transnational procurement operation.

The electronics, motors and other materials he exported to Iran were “dual-use,” meaning they had both civilian and military applications, and could be harnessed to manufacture weapons of mass destruction.

“Yousefijam is a member of an organization that engaged in criminal activity that directly contravened sanctions imposed by Canada and the U.S.A. against the export of certain items to Iran,” IRB Member Christopher Marcinkiewicz wrote.

“I issue a deportation order against him.”

The CBSA did not respond by deadline to questions about Yousefijam’s deportation. Reached by phone, Yousefijam said he was still in Canada.

He would not say whether he had appealed his deportation order. “This is an ongoing legal matter so I won’t be able to discuss that in the interview,” he said.

“I’m considering my options and the minister has their options, so it’s still ongoing,” he said. “Right now I’m just, you know, living my life peacefully.”

But the ruling could put an end to his life in Canada, which began a decade ago when he arrived from Tehran, where his name was Amin Riki .

Arrested in Toronto in 2021, he was extradited to Michigan to stand trial for his alleged role in the sanctions evasion gang, which was led by his brother Arash .

After pleading guilty , Yousefijam was deported to Ontario, where he changed his name again, this time to Ameen Cohen – the third identity he is known to have adopted.

In its ruling, the IRB noted that when he applied to the Ontario government for a legal name change, he was asked whether he had ever been convicted of a criminal offence.

He answered “No.”

The IRB accused him of “providing false information on a government form,” rejecting Yousefijam’s claim that a government employee told him he didn’t need to report convictions outside Canada.

“I find that his failure to declare his U.S. conviction on his name change was done intentionally,” the IRB wrote, adding Yousefijam’s conduct was “indicative of someone who will say whatever he believes serves his immediate purpose.”

The deportation order was issued in July but was only released to Global News this week. It comes amid a U.S. war on Iran and Ottawa’s continuing efforts to expel regime members from Canada.

Iranian-Canadians have long complained that members and supporters of Iran’s repressive regime, as well as their families , have been treating Canada as a safe haven .

The government banned senior Iranian officials from Canada in 2022. Since then, the CBSA has opened dozens of investigations into regime members identified across the country.

As of Oct. 1, the Canada Border Services Agency said it had found 40 top-level Iranian regime officials living in Canadian cities. Two have been deported so far while eight have left voluntarily.

Two more are awaiting removal while the rest are to be brought before the Immigration and Refugee Board, or have already had deportation hearings.

Meanwhile, Global News revealed last month that the son of Iran’s former vice president has been living in Edmonton and operating businesses under the name “Sal Ghafouri.”

Federal agencies, including the RCMP and Canadian Forces, have awarded the Iranian citizen almost $2-million in contracts, although he is under investigation over his alleged work for Iran’s military.

The CBSA’s attempt to deport Yousefijam has dragged on for more than two years. Deportation hearings began in September 2024 and ended in February 2025.

It’s unclear why it took the IRB until July 2026 to issue its decision, especially considering Yousefijam is not Canadian and was convicted in U.S. court in 2021.

The IRB said Yousefijam knew what he was doing when his brother Arash recruited him into crime group, which aimed to profit from sanctions evasion.

Yousefijam got involved “voluntarily and with knowledge and intent to defeat sanctions,” Marcinkiewicz wrote in his ruling.

“His attempt to distance himself and paint himself as an unsophisticated and ignorant individual working blindly at the behest of his brother undermines his general credibility,” he wrote.

While Yousefijam’s involvement was “more limited” than his brother’s, “it was nevertheless an important and critical role in the overall operation as it largely focused on securing shipping of sanctioned goods from the U.S.A. to Iran,” the IRB wrote.

“Without his involvement in the shipment of the items, they would not have reached their destinations in Iran,” the decision said.

“In other words, his role was not insignificant as he was tasked with contacting the seller and/or shipper in the U.S.A. and arranging or the items to be shipped and in so doing utilizing methods such as ‘cross stuffing.’”

Cross-stuffing is when goods are exported to a transit country, moved from one shipping container to another and then re-shipped to the end destination.

The Yousefijam brothers and a third member of the group used the United Arab Emirates as their hub for moving sanctioned materials to Iran, the IRB wrote.

The CBSA had argued that Yousefijam was a danger to Canada’s security because he had undermined the government’s efforts to contain Iran’s regime.

But the IRB said the CBSA had not proven that Yousefijam remained a security threat. The deportation order was issued based on his role in a criminal organization.

A U.S. court also convicted Yousefijam’s brother, but as a Canadian citizen he does not face immigration enforcement action.

The brother has now changed his name to Aurash Cohen and gone into dentistry. Ontario revoked his dental license in 2024 after Global News revealed his past.

Canada has been using sanctions to counter the threats Iran poses to international security and to its own people, according to Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand.

Since the Iran war began in February, the regime has been linked to an array of plots in Western countries, most recently at a British air base used by the U.S. military.

Iran is one of the five key states involved in foreign interference in Canada, according to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, which has called the Islamic Republic a “predator.”

“Iranian intelligence services act indirectly through agents, contacts and sympathizers, including individuals in Canada associated with organized crime groups,” CSIS wrote in its report.

Stewart.Bell@globalnews.ca

stories.title: BC NDP has fallen short of $10-a-day child care commitment, data suggests
stories.summary: Party made pledge central focus of 2017 election which first brought them to government, but has struggled with implementation
stories.author: Dave McGinn
stories.content:
The promise of $10-per-day child care in British Columbia has been a signature pledge of the NDP for almost a decade, but as voters go to the polls in a snap election call next week, the data suggests the results have fallen far short of the commitment.

Spaces at $10 a day only account for approximately 10 per cent of licensed child-care spaces in the province, according to the $10aDay Child Care Campaign.

The BC NDP made $10-a-day child care the central focus of the 2017 election which first brought them to government.

The provincial government has increased the number of licensed child-care spaces by approximately 50 per cent since 2018, adding more than 60,000 new spots. It has also ensured that fees for publicly funded, licensed child-care providers have been reduced by 50 per cent.

But in July, 2021, when British Columbia was the first province to sign on to the Canada-Wide Early Learning and Child Care agreement, B.C. promised to create 30,000 new affordable spaces within five years, 40,000 spaces within seven years, and reduce child-care fees to an average of $10 a day by March 2026.

Despite B.C.’s early enthusiasm for the plan, the province has struggled perhaps more than any other with its implementation.

It has created just over 17,000 spaces so far in the $10-a-day program, according to $10aDay.

Not only are spaces in the program scarce, but families with children in daycare centres outside of the program are paying some of the highest fees in the country . Earlier this year, the hopes of parents who had been waiting for a subsidized space were dashed when the province announced it was pausing the program to fix its flaws.

Sharon Gregson, a spokesperson for the Coalition of Childcare Advocates of B.C., said the provincial government’s many new child-care spaces, reduced fees and raised wages for many early childhood educators have been good news.

“It’s just that they have not delivered, and not only have they not delivered on their commitments, but they’ve stalled their progress in even making any incremental progress,” she said.

The $10-a-day commitment was not a talking point during the current election campaign until October 12, when, at a town hall event, NDP leader David Eby was asked about his family’s child-care arrangements.

His answer – that one of his children was in a $10-a-day space – led to critics charging that the premier was selfishly out of touch, having taken a spot that would otherwise have gone to a struggling family.

“Calling out Premier Eby for using affordable childcare is completely the wrong thing to do. The actual question is, why isn’t there more affordable, well-distributed quality childcare,” said Martha Friendly, executive director of the Childcare Resource and Research Unit, a Toronto-based think tank.

Child-care policy in the province, she added, is “a mess.”

According to a report co-authored by Ms. Friendly and released this August by the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, the median fee for infant care in Richmond is $52 per day, and $40 per day in Vancouver.

By comparison, the median fee in Toronto is $22 a day, according to the report. In Calgary it is just $15 a day.

B.C. also has also had the second highest increase, after Alberta, in for-profit full-day spaces since 2021, with 72 per cent of new spaces being for-profit, Ms. Friendly said.

Operators of these spaces tend to charge higher fees than their non-profit counterparts, Ms. Friendly said.

In February, the provincial government said it would be pausing the program until at least early 2027.

“The way the program is structured right now, it is not sustainable for $10 a day. There just simply is not enough money in the system,” Lisa Beare, B.C. Minister of Education and Child Care, told the Globe and Mail earlier this year.

On Saturday, the campaigning NDP announced that if re-elected, it would invest $80-million in new funding to create 7,200 new before- and after-school spaces on school grounds, plus an additional $250-million to expand universal child care, in partnership with the federal government.

Although the BC Conservative Party has yet to release its child-care platform, it says expansion is a priority.

“A Conservative Party of BC government is 100 per cent committed to opening more child care spaces. Child care is critically important, and we believe care should be available when and where people need it,” Alex Shiff, a spokesperson for the party, said in a statement e-mailed to The Globe and Mail.

“Nobody begrudges David Eby and his wife for their success,” Margareta Dovgal, Conservative Party of BC candidate for Vancouver-Yaletown, said in the statement.

“The Conservative Party of BC wants more British Columbians to succeed. What families will not accept is a premier who promised them $10-a-day child care, failed to deliver it, and then took one of the scarce spots for himself while a single mom working two jobs sits on a waitlist.”

The Green Party has an even more ambitious child-care plan.

paragraphs: The promise of $10-per-day child care in British Columbia has been a signature pledge of the NDP for almost a decade, but as voters go to the polls in a snap election call next week, the data suggests the results have fallen far short of the commitment.
Spaces at $10 a day only account for approximately 10 per cent of licensed child-care spaces in the province, according to the $10aDay Child Care Campaign.
The BC NDP made $10-a-day child care the central focus of the 2017 election which first brought them to government.

The provincial government has increased the number of licensed child-care spaces by approximately 50 per cent since 2018, adding more than 60,000 new spots. It has also ensured that fees for publicly funded, licensed child-care providers have been reduced by 50 per cent.

But in July, 2021, when British Columbia was the first province to sign on to the Canada-Wide Early Learning and Child Care agreement, B.C. promised to create 30,000 new affordable spaces within five years, 40,000 spaces within seven years, and reduce child-care fees to an average of $10 a day by March 2026.
Despite B.C.’s early enthusiasm for the plan, the province has struggled perhaps more than any other with its implementation.
It has created just over 17,000 spaces so far in the $10-a-day program, according to $10aDay.

Not only are spaces in the program scarce, but families with children in daycare centres outside of the program are paying some of the highest fees in the country . Earlier this year, the hopes of parents who had been waiting for a subsidized space were dashed when the province announced it was pausing the program to fix its flaws.

Sharon Gregson, a spokesperson for the Coalition of Childcare Advocates of B.C., said the provincial government’s many new child-care spaces, reduced fees and raised wages for many early childhood educators have been good news.
“It’s just that they have not delivered, and not only have they not delivered on their commitments, but they’ve stalled their progress in even making any incremental progress,” she said.

The $10-a-day commitment was not a talking point during the current election campaign until October 12, when, at a town hall event, NDP leader David Eby was asked about his family’s child-care arrangements.

His answer – that one of his children was in a $10-a-day space – led to critics charging that the premier was selfishly out of touch, having taken a spot that would otherwise have gone to a struggling family.

“Calling out Premier Eby for using affordable childcare is completely the wrong thing to do. The actual question is, why isn’t there more affordable, well-distributed quality childcare,” said Martha Friendly, executive director of the Childcare Resource and Research Unit, a Toronto-based think tank.
Child-care policy in the province, she added, is “a mess.”

According to a report co-authored by Ms. Friendly and released this August by the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, the median fee for infant care in Richmond is $52 per day, and $40 per day in Vancouver.
By comparison, the median fee in Toronto is $22 a day, according to the report. In Calgary it is just $15 a day.
B.C. also has also had the second highest increase, after Alberta, in for-profit full-day spaces since 2021, with 72 per cent of new spaces being for-profit, Ms. Friendly said.
Operators of these spaces tend to charge higher fees than their non-profit counterparts, Ms. Friendly said.
In February, the provincial government said it would be pausing the program until at least early 2027.

“The way the program is structured right now, it is not sustainable for $10 a day. There just simply is not enough money in the system,” Lisa Beare, B.C. Minister of Education and Child Care, told the Globe and Mail earlier this year.

On Saturday, the campaigning NDP announced that if re-elected, it would invest $80-million in new funding to create 7,200 new before- and after-school spaces on school grounds, plus an additional $250-million to expand universal child care, in partnership with the federal government.
Although the BC Conservative Party has yet to release its child-care platform, it says expansion is a priority.

“A Conservative Party of BC government is 100 per cent committed to opening more child care spaces. Child care is critically important, and we believe care should be available when and where people need it,” Alex Shiff, a spokesperson for the party, said in a statement e-mailed to The Globe and Mail.
“Nobody begrudges David Eby and his wife for their success,” Margareta Dovgal, Conservative Party of BC candidate for Vancouver-Yaletown, said in the statement.

“The Conservative Party of BC wants more British Columbians to succeed. What families will not accept is a premier who promised them $10-a-day child care, failed to deliver it, and then took one of the scarce spots for himself while a single mom working two jobs sits on a waitlist.”
The Green Party has an even more ambitious child-care plan.

“Child care shouldn’t be a lottery, it should be a guarantee. That’s why the BC Greens will restart the $10-a-day program and make it universal and free by 2031,” Prym Goodacre, a spokesperson for the party, said in a statement.
The party is also promising to create a wage grid for early childhood educators that will reach $35 to $45 an hour by 2028.
Since October 12, the B.C. NDP has clarified that Mr. Eby’s family has donated $3,200 to the child-care facility since mid-2024, and plans to donate another $4,800 at the end of this year.
“We felt that we did not need that discount and we wanted to make sure that the child-care centre could provide other supports for families in the community,” Mr. Eby said in a post on X.

stories.title: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith to take questions for first time since separation vote
stories.summary: Calgary - Premier Danielle Smith will take questions today for the first time since Albertans overwhelmingly rejected separation in Monday's referendum.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says her United Conservative Party is a pro-Canada party and that any members who want to stump for separation need to leave.

Smith said Wednesday it can’t risk a split in the ranks that would open the door to an Opposition NDP win in next fall’s general election.

“The United Conservative Party is not an independence party,” Smith told party members in a video posted on social media.

“We must be unified. If we aren’t, our party will split and Alberta will suffer terribly as a result.”

She said party members can have any views they wish but that she would respectfully invite those who want to actively stir up separatist sentiment “to join a different party.”

Smith also said anyone running for the party or serving it in an official capacity must toe the pro-Canada line.

One constituency president plans to defy that.

Mitch Sylvestre, president of the UCP’s Bonnyville-Cold Lake-St. Paul constituency association and a high-profile separation activist, said he’s going to keep talking up the concept of leaving Canada.

He also said he’s not going anywhere and that Smith is not his boss.

“She does not run the party; she runs the government. There’s a big difference,” Sylvestre said in an interview.

“Never will we be leaving to start a new party — not at this stage.”

Sylvestre spearheaded a petition calling for a binding separation vote. When that petition became bogged down in court earlier this year, Smith tied it to a pro-Canada petition as reason why it was time to resolve the separation question with Monday’s referendum.

In the referendum, 75 per cent of Albertans voted to keep the province in Canada, rejecting the other option of starting the process to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

The premier, in Wednesday’s video, says she knows that some who voted against Confederation are members of her UCP and she doesn’t hold “ill will” toward them.

“What matters now is that, as a party, we accept the results of the referendum and support and implement the clear mandate given to us by Albertans to pursue a strong Alberta within a united Canada,” Smith said.

Polls leading up to the vote suggested that a slight majority of UCP members were leaning in favour of a binding separation referendum. Separatist leaders have pushed it further, claiming party members who want to see Alberta go its own way represent a “supermajority” of the rank-and-file.

The referendum result and Smith’s pledge to not hold a binding vote while she’s premier has led some in the separatist movement to call for her resignation or a leadership review at the party’s annual general meeting next month.

Asked by reporters later Wednesday if she would expel or disqualify those who want to keep the separation debate alive in the party, Smith said she would wait to see if it becomes necessary.

“I’m asking people to do some self-reflection,” she said.

“If they are able to accept the results and the mandate that Albertans gave us through a free and democratic process, then we can have a reset. And those who cannot — they have opportunities through other political parties.”

Sylvestre said he didn’t think it would go over well if Smith started revoking memberships. “I don’t know how our people are gonna react to it,” he said

The next election is set for Oct. 18, 2027.

The lone member of Smith’s UCP caucus to publicly advocate for a second, binding referendum on separation was backbencher Jason Stephan. As polls closed Monday, he announced he would not run again.

University of Calgary political scientist Lisa Young said the premier’s comments suggest the 2027 election campaign has unofficially begun.

Young said drawing a line within the party suggests the premier is concerned she can’t win crucial ridings in Calgary or Edmonton unless the separation issue is stamped out.

“She clearly thinks that she’s in trouble,” she said.

”(Smith has) clearly made a calculation here that to continue to allow them to dictate party policy, she’s not going to be able to get enough support in the rest of the province from the general electorate to form a government.”

Smith also appears to be pivoting away from a slogan she has used in some fashion since 2022: A sovereign Alberta within a United Canada.

The first bill her government passed bore a similar name, and throughout the referendum campaign the language of sovereignty was prominent in government advertising.

But in a TV address Tuesday, the sovereign messaging was gone.

Instead, Smith spoke behind a lectern bearing a placard stating: Stronger Alberta within a united Canada.

She repeatedly used the phrase Wednesday, saying it’s the position of her party and government.

Her office did not immediately respond to questions about the word change.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

— with files from Lisa Johnson in Edmonton

stories.title: Ontario drug funding decision leaves cancer patients disappointed, with few options
stories.summary: Toronto - Sabrina Apitz-Grossman was told 13 months ago that she had about 12 to 18 months to live.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Sabrina Apitz-Grossman was told 13 months ago that she had about 12 to 18 months to live.

A rare form of cancer in the 31-year-old’s knee had metastasized, spreading to her lungs. She has undergone radiotherapy, chemotherapy and surgeries, though the synovial sarcoma couldn’t be fully removed.

Apitz-Grossman’s doctors are recommending a treatment approved in the United States but unavailable in Ontario. She needs it urgently but the Ontario Health Insurance Plan turned her down for out-of-country coverage. An appeal failed, as did an application under a Case-by-Case Review Program to get special permission for the treatment to be administered at the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre in Toronto.

She is still fighting.

“I so desperately would love to turn 32,” she said.

Apitz-Grossman and other Ontarians with Stage 4 cancer told by their doctors that they are good candidates for treatments unavailable in the province were buoyed last month when 37-year-old Alex Shved won a court challenge against his Ohip out-of-country denial for metastatic melanoma treatment.

Though Shved’s court decision was not necessarily directly applicable to all of their cases, they saw an opening, and their hopes were dashed when Health Minister Sylvia Jones responded to the court ruling by changing the rules.

Drug treatments will now only be funded out of country if they are already funded within the province but access is temporarily unavailable or delayed, a set of circumstances some patients see as impossibly narrow. The government said it clarified in regulation what was already long-standing policy.

“We’re protecting Ontario patients and taxpayers from price gouging and protecting their access to life-saving medications that would otherwise only be available in the United States or overseas,” Jones wrote in a statement.

“This change supports a consistent, fair and transparent approach to funding decisions, protects the integrity of Ontario’s world-class drug approval process and will help avoid up to $5.2 billion in additional costs to Ontario’s health-care system every year.”

Framing the move as a cost-saving measure is not sitting right with Apitz-Grossman.

“Are we saying that we could save like 5,000 or more people’s lives, and they’re proud of themselves for not doing that?” she said. “Is this supposed to be good news that we’re not going to save those people, so that we can instead buy a couple more private jets?”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford came under fire earlier this year for a government purchase of a $29-million private jet and quickly returned it.

The treatment Apitz-Grossman is seeking, Tecelra, is a personalized therapy made from a patient’s own T-cells, a type of white blood cell. Nearly half of patients in Apitz-Grossman’s situation respond to the treatment, and among those who respond, there is a 90 per cent chance of survival after a year and 70 per cent after two years, according to her oncologist.

But the treatment is costly, at US$727,000, Apitz-Grossman said. She feels terrible guilt for seeking such a pricey treatment, she said, but she wants to live.

“There has never been a moment where I have thought to myself, ‘Gosh, I wish that patient who was in the ICU for weeks and who it cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to save, hadn’t been saved,’” Apitz-Grossman said.

The origin of Jones’ $5.2-billion figure was unclear in her press release, and a government official later explained that it would be the additional cost if the province entirely stopped negotiating prices with drug manufacturers for public coverage in Ontario.

Ohip’s reason for denying Apitz-Grossman, Shved and others out-of-country drug treatment funding is that routinely paying for such requests while drugs are undergoing review for funding in Ontario would “undermine the incentive structure that encourages manufacturers to participate in Canada’s drug review processes.”

Kevin Nash, 59, has metastatic melanoma and is seeking the same tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy as Shved. Nash’s out-of-country application and subsequent appeal were also denied, and he does not believe the government’s reasoning.

“These companies make billions of dollars a year, not a billion, billions of dollars a year,” he said. “Do you think that they care one bit whether Kevin Nash goes to Buffalo for a treatment? That’s so preposterous.”

In Apitz-Grossman’s case, the manufacturer of Tecelra has said it has no plans to apply for approval in Canada. That means there is no review process in this case to undermine, she noted. Jones’ office said drugs that have not been approved by Health Canada are not funded in Ontario or any other province, and the recent clarification of the out-of-country rules did not change that.

Holly Wardlow, 61, is in a similar boat, with the government denying coverage through its Case-by-Case Review Program for a medication to treat her rare form of liver cancer because the drug was “expected to be reviewed for public funding in Ontario.”

That’s despite the manufacturer submitting two letters telling the province it has no plans to apply for approval in Canada.

“We just thought, ‘Well, this doesn’t make any sense,’” Wardlow said.

“We provided evidence that there is not going to be a population-based review. This drug is never going to be approved in Canada, let alone Ontario, because the manufacturer is not going to make an application, and they have evidence of that. And yet they provided the same reason for denying funding.”

Wardlow and her husband have been paying $78,000 a month for her to receive infusions in Ontario every two weeks, and her tumour has been shrinking with almost no side-effects, she said.

Their savings have been depleted and they have now started a GoFundMe.

“I’m getting out there and trying to stay fit, partly because I can, and partly because the weather is beautiful, and partly because I’m thinking ahead that surgery May be possible in the future,” Wardlow said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon to be sworn in and unveil cabinet
stories.summary: QUÉBEC - Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is set to be sworn in as Quebec's 34th premier.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
QUÉBEC - Paul St-Pierre Plamondon was sworn in as Quebec’s 34th premier on Wednesday, bringing the sovereigntist Parti Québécois back to power after more than a decade.

The premier named 22 ministers, including one who is responsible for Quebec independence, as well as a president and whip. St-Pierre Plamondon also appointed himself as homelessness minister. His cabinet includes nine women and 14 men, including the premier.

He has said his priorities are to tackle the province’s deficit and prepare for his promised referendum on Quebec independence.

“Look at the quality of my team. We were only three (legislature members) last election,” St-Pierre Plamondon said. “I am convinced that, as individuals and as a people, we must always envision the best. And we must never, ever accept being told that everything is lost or that we aren’t good enough.”

He added that his first order of business will be to make money available to municipalities to prepare to support the unhoused this winter.

The sovereigntist party won 59 seats in the Oct. 5 provincial election, falling short of the 64 needed for a majority government. Recounts are taking place in two ridings where PQ candidates finished second, potentially bringing the party closer to a majority.

For the first time in the province’s history, Quebec’s lieutenant-governor, Manon Jeannotte, was not present at the swearing-in ceremony at St-Pierre Plamondon’s request. The government’s general secretary presided over the ceremony, and Jeannotte agreed to sign appointment documents at her office immediately after.

The PQ’s elected representatives were sworn in last week, pledging allegiance to the people of Quebec rather than the King, following a 2022 change to the legislature’s rules prompted by St-Pierre Plamondon’s refusal to swear allegiance to the monarch. The Liberals and Québec solidaire representatives followed suit.

As he presented his cabinet, St-Pierre Plamondon stressed he would cut bureaucracy and spending, and balance the province’s budget. Under the Balanced Budget Act and the government’s current fiscal plan, Quebec must eliminate its multi-billion deficit by 2030. His party has also pledged to freeze provincial legislators’ salaries until Quebec balances its budget.

St-Pierre Plamondon has said his cabinet would be smaller than that of the last government, reflecting his campaign promise to reduce the size of government and rein in public spending. The previous Coalition Avenir Québec government had 28 ministers.

As a result, some ministers will have to juggle several portfolios, including Justice Minister Marie-Claude Sarrazin, who will also handle interprovincial relations, relations with anglophone Quebecers, the fight against racism, Lgbtq+ issues, access to information and secularism.

Sarrazin is a member of the Quebec bar and notably served as prosecutor during the inquiry into the cost overruns for the digital modernization of Quebec’s auto insurance board, known as the SAAQclic fiasco.

Though most of the party’s officials are new to the legislature, St-Pierre Plamondon chose to lean on experience on important files such as finance, education and the treasury board.

Joël Arseneau will serve as education minister and Pascal Bérubé as culture minister. Nicolas Marceau, who served as finance minister under Pauline Marois, is back in that same role.

Both Arseneau and Bérubé were elected alongside St-Pierre Plamondon in 2018, when the PQ only had three legislature members.

Catherine Gentilcore, first elected under the PQ banner in a byelection in 2025, was named immigration minister and minister responsible for Quebec independence. Alain Therrien, who served with both the PQ and the Bloc Québécois in Ottawa, will serve as president of the treasury board.

In order to cut bureaucracy, St-Pierre Plamondon also created a position dedicated to government efficiency, held by former Amos, Que., mayor and Survivor Quebec contestant Sébastien D’Astous.

St-Pierre Plamondon repeatedly promised to do some “much-needed housekeeping” and “reduce wasteful spending” before focusing on sovereignty. He has promised to hold a referendum on Quebec independence once U.S. President Donald Trump is out of the White House.

“Quebec’s independence is an ambitious and demanding undertaking,” the premier told his ministers. “We must restore Quebecers’ desire to dream and take initiative. We must rediscover the ambition to build and participate in things greater than ourselves.”

During the ceremony, St-Pierre Plamondon made several references to Marois, who was in the room for the ceremony. On her way into the legislature, she told journalists that she is familiar with minority governments, having led a PQ minority from 2012 to 2014.

”(St-Pierre Plamondon) said he would take inspiration from other parties’ programs, which I think will make it easier to get things done,” she said.

Marois is also tasked with giving the new PQ legislature members a workshop in the coming days.

BySamm Mohibuddin Staff Reporter

Canada’s record-breaking $90-million Lotto Max jackpot has finally been won, but the lucky ticket holder is not from Ontario.

The winning ticket for Tuesday night’s draw was sold in Alberta, according to an Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG) news release on Wednesday.

That is not to say Ontario players walked away empty handed as the province claimed most of the other major prizes in the draw, according to OLG.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Image 9Image 10

The $90-million jackpot was the largest lottery prize ever offered in Canada, surpassing the previous record of $80 million.

The jackpot reached $85 million last week before reaching the $90-million mark, which is the Lotto Max jackpot cap, according to the OLG.

The previously largest lottery prize ever won in Canada was $80 million. A British Columbia man first won a jackpot for that amount in May 2025, and then two friends from London, Ont., matched the total with their win in April.

The winning numbers for Tuesday’s jackpot were 8, 15, 19, 23, 26, 28 and 34 with 38 as the bonus number.

Samm Mohibuddin is a staff reporter with the Toronto Star. He can be reached at smohibuddin@thestar.ca

stories.title: London teenage band star in documentary premiere at Forest City Film Festival
stories.summary: Three H.B. Beal Secondary School students are taking their growing music career to stages across Canada, and now to the big screen.
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
General News

All Notices and Updates

Three H.B. Beal Secondary School students are taking their growing music career to stages across Canada, and now to the big screen.

Thunder Queens, a punk rock band featuring Grade 11 and 12 students Violet Bruneel, Clara Magnan and Lola Good, have already achieved the kind of success that many established musicians aspire to. The trio has toured Canada and shared bills with major artists including Sheryl Crow, The Beaches, Sloan and 54-40.

Earlier this year, Thunder Queens recorded their second studio album, Deep Below, in Toronto with Grammy-winning producer Dave Schiffman, whose credits include work with Smashing Pumpkins and Alanis Morissette. During a recent appearance on CBC Radio’s Q with Tom Power , Power described Deep Below as one of the best new records of the year.

Now, their journey is the subject of a new documentary, Thunder Queens , which recently celebrated its world premiere at the Forest City Film Festival. The film explores the band’s story while highlighting women in music, the importance of community and the potential of today’s youth.

Students and staff from Beal attended the premiere, where the film was met with standing ovations.

"It was an unforgettable evening filled with emotion, tears and laughter," said Andrew Parr, a teacher at Beal and staff lead for the school's Rock Band Club. "Lola, Violet and Clara are navigating this exciting journey with immense grace and maturity, and we are so fortunate to have them as Raiders! In this film they show us that their generation is to be heard and respected. I left the theatre bursting with pride and grateful to be a part of the Thunder Queens community. I encourage everyone to go see the film – you will leave inspired!"

On top of their incredible music career as Thunder Queens, Violet, Clara and Lola are also dedicated students at H.B. Beal Secondary School, where they participate in the school band as well as a number of other extracurriculars and are currently considering post-secondary education pathways in music.

Thunder Queens' accomplishments showcase the remarkable creativity and talent of Thames Valley students and demonstrate what young people can achieve when passion, opportunity and community come together.

content_blocks.text: Thunder Queens, a punk rock band featuring Grade 11 and 12 students Violet Bruneel, Clara Magnan and Lola Good, have already achieved the kind of success that many established musicians aspire to. The trio has toured Canada and shared bills with major artists including Sheryl Crow, The Beaches, Sloan and 54-40.
content_blocks.html: Thunder Queens, a punk rock band featuring Grade 11 and 12 students Violet Bruneel, Clara Magnan and Lola Good, have already achieved the kind of success that many established musicians aspire to. The trio has toured Canada and shared bills with major artists including Sheryl Crow, The Beaches, Sloan and 54-40.

content_blocks.text: Earlier this year, Thunder Queens recorded their second studio album, Deep Below, in Toronto with Grammy-winning producer Dave Schiffman, whose credits include work with Smashing Pumpkins and Alanis Morissette. During a recent appearance on CBC Radio’s Q with Tom Power , Power described Deep Below as one of the best new records of the year.

content_blocks.text: Now, their journey is the subject of a new documentary, Thunder Queens , which recently celebrated its world premiere at the Forest City Film Festival. The film explores the band’s story while highlighting women in music, the importance of community and the potential of today’s youth.

stories.title: Death investigation
stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 21, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS), along with the Ontario Fire Marshall’s Office, are investigating a residential fire that took place this morning on Lyman Street.

On Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at approximately 6:40 a.m., emergency crews responded to the area of Lyman Street and Oxford Street East in relation to a working fire at a residence.

Multiple individuals were inside the residence at the time of the fire. London Fire Department crews entered the residence and located one person deceased.

The cause of the fire is still under investigation.

Lyman Street is currently closed between Oxford Street and Krupp Streets.

The investigation has been reassigned to members of the LPS Major Crime Section, who continue to work alongside the Ontario Fire Marshall’s Office.

The investigation is in its early stages, and more information will be provided as appropriate.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Carney won't rule out granting provinces Quebec-style immigration powers after Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Quebec has held broader immigration authority since 1991. Premier Danielle Smith says Monday's vote gives her a mandate to pursue similar powers for Alberta.
stories.author: Alex Ballingall
stories.content:
Ottawa—Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says separatists are not welcome to run as candidates for her United Conservative Party and that those trying to turn it into a “vehicle for the independence movement” should leave.

In a Wednesday video address to party supporters and members, Smith drew a line against separatists within her party, two days after 75 per cent of Albertans voted to remain in Canada rather than trigger a binding vote on independence.

The premier urged her party to move on from the separation debate and focus instead on other measures backed in Monday’s referendum, including proposals for greater provincial control over immigration. Earlier Wednesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Ottawa is discussing with provinces whether they should have a larger role in selecting economic immigrants.

In her video, Smith called on party supporters to accept the results and unite behind her government’s position of a “strong Alberta within a united Canada.”

“The United Conservative Party is not an independence party,” Smith said.

“For those few who cannot reconcile this fact and remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement, I would respectfully invite them to join a different party.”

Smith said that while UCP members are free to believe what they want, candidates running for the party in next year’s election “need to be committed” to the party’s and government’s position, “from the day they take out their nomination papers” and throughout their time as an MLA in the UCP caucus.

The premier said she also expects “every member of our provincial board and members of constituency association boards across the province to uphold” the party’s position.

She delivered the directive roughly a month before the Ucp’s annual general meeting in Calgary.

It comes as some leaders within the independence movement have been urging supporters of separation to take out UCP memberships to more forcefully advocate their views within the party.

Mitch Sylvestre, one of the most prominent of Alberta’s independence leaders who presides over a UCP constituency association in Bonnyville, Alta., said demanding that positions like his be held by those who support remaining in Canada is “not the premier’s call.”

“I would have thought it would have been way better to try and unite the people that she already has that are actually going to do the work for her, instead of making everybody even angrier,” he told the Star.

“She cannot win without us, period. So if we leave and form another party, she’s not going to win.”

Smith warned a lack of unity is exactly what the Ucp’s political opponents want.

“As a party, we cannot permit the next year to be one of internal division and endless debates about separation when Albertans have spoken so clearly against it,” Smith said in her video.

“That’s what the NDP want us to do,” she added.

If Smith succeeds in steering her party away from the separation debate, one of her next political battles could centre on immigration.

Earlier in the day, Carney said his federal government is speaking with provinces about giving them more power over “economic immigration,” after slim majorities of voters in Alberta appeared to endorse taking more control over newcomers in Monday’s referendum.

Prime Minister Mark Carney tells reporters in Ottawa Wednesday the government is speaking with provinces about “sharing powers,” over “economic immigration.”

Heading into the Liberal government’s weekly caucus meeting, Carney told reporters that conversations on the subject have been held with all provinces except Quebec, which already has broader authority over immigration than the rest of Canada thanks to an accord inked in 1991.

“We’ll see,” Carney said in French, when asked if his government is open to giving Alberta the same immigration powers as Quebec.

“We’ve had conversations with all of the provinces” except Quebec, about “sharing powers concerning economic immigration,” the prime minister added.

He went on to defend Ottawa’s approach to immigration since he took office last year, citing drops in the number of new foreign students, asylum seekers and temporary foreign workers.

The prime minister said his government will for now focus on pragmatic solutions rather than constitutional reforms.

“We need to assess where we are, keep that control, be at sustainable levels, and while we’re doing that, discuss how the economic class, particularly of immigrants, can be most effectively distributed across the economy, the country,” he said.

Among the immigration proposals that Smith advanced in Monday’s referendum were several questions seeking a mandate to push for greater provincial control over immigration.

As of Wednesday evening, unofficial results showed a slim majority of voters favouring Alberta taking control for “decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government has "taken back control" of immigration and is determined to keep the system "sustainable."

The federal Conservatives have backed Smith’s push for more control over immigration, with party leader Pierre Poilievre stating in Calgary on Tuesday that Carney was wrong to urge Albertans to vote against the immigration questions in Monday’s referendum.

On Parliament Hill, Conservative MP Dane Lloyd said his party has always “sought to devolve areas of provincial responsibility back to the provinces,” and that he is watching how the Carney government responds to what Alberta is putting forward on immigration.

Corey Hogan, a Liberal MP from Calgary, said immigration has always required collaboration between Ottawa and the provinces, and that the questions in Monday’s referendum came “years late” because it is “chasing a challenge that has already been a bit resolved” by the Carney government.

He also questioned the strength of Smith’s mandate on immigration from Monday’s results, given how ballots are still being counted, and the majorities in favour are small.

“Politicians are going to be politicians. I am, however, grateful that Danielle Smith said we are going to put behind us this separation question,” Hogan said. “We’re going to move on.”

Heading into the Liberal government’s weekly caucus meeting, Carney told reporters that conversations on the subject have been held with all provinces except Quebec, which already has broader authority over immigration than the rest of Canada thanks to an accord inked in 1991.
“We’ll see,” Carney said in French, when asked if his government is open to giving Alberta the same immigration powers as Quebec.
“We’ve had conversations with all of the provinces” except Quebec, about “sharing powers concerning economic immigration,” the prime minister added.
He went on to defend Ottawa’s approach to immigration since he took office last year, citing drops in the number of new foreign students, asylum seekers and temporary foreign workers.
The prime minister said his government will for now focus on pragmatic solutions rather than constitutional reforms.

“We need to assess where we are, keep that control, be at sustainable levels, and while we’re doing that, discuss how the economic class, particularly of immigrants, can be most effectively distributed across the economy, the country,” he said.
Among the immigration proposals that Smith advanced in Monday’s referendum were several questions seeking a mandate to push for greater provincial control over immigration.

As of Wednesday evening, unofficial results showed a slim majority of voters favouring Alberta taking control for “decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government has "taken back control" of immigration and is determined to keep the system "sustainable."

The federal Conservatives have backed Smith’s push for more control over immigration, with party leader Pierre Poilievre stating in Calgary on Tuesday that Carney was wrong to urge Albertans to vote against the immigration questions in Monday’s referendum.

On Parliament Hill, Conservative MP Dane Lloyd said his party has always “sought to devolve areas of provincial responsibility back to the provinces,” and that he is watching how the Carney government responds to what Alberta is putting forward on immigration.

Corey Hogan, a Liberal MP from Calgary, said immigration has always required collaboration between Ottawa and the provinces, and that the questions in Monday’s referendum came “years late” because it is “chasing a challenge that has already been a bit resolved” by the Carney government.
He also questioned the strength of Smith’s mandate on immigration from Monday’s results, given how ballots are still being counted, and the majorities in favour are small.
“Politicians are going to be politicians. I am, however, grateful that Danielle Smith said we are going to put behind us this separation question,” Hogan said. “We’re going to move on.”

stories.title: Martin Regg Cohn: Alberta’s referendum is over, but Danielle Smith’s reckoning is just beginning
stories.summary: By courting both separatists and federalists, the premier has left each camp with a reason to turn on her
stories.author: Martin Regg Cohn
stories.content:
The country is saved.

The same cannot be said for Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

This week’s referendum rejection has come and gone, but it’s not gone forever. There will be more referendum recriminations and reckonings to come for Smith.

The pro-Canada victors gave up on her long ago, reproaching her for platforming the separatists. Federalists will never forgive her for forsaking them.

But the anti-Canada losers, too, will resent her for going only partway toward partition. The premier enabled them and weaponized their cause, but she didn’t pull the trigger — a fatal mistake in their eyes.

Hence, Smith will be targeted as a traitor to the cause. For in any referendum battle, as in any revolutionary war, the revolution eats its children.

Smith will be eaten alive by her erstwhile separatist supporters, just as her predecessor as premier, Jason Kenney, was dismembered by the base he brought to life a decade ago. Alberta’s independence politics spares no one.

To be sure, the final vote was a lopsided rejection of separation. But wait, you say, didn’t nearly 25 per cent of Albertans vote to leave the country and create their own?

This wasn’t a binding plebiscite — that would only have come later, if a majority had voted for another vote. It was merely a consultative referendum, which gave free rein to protest votes, so-called leverage votes and fantasy votes.

It’s also worth noting, and lamenting, that more than one in three eligible voters didn’t cast a ballot about the future of Alberta in or out of Canada. That’s democracy.

Even a country as spectacular as Canada can’t count on unanimous support, because people love to carp — and love conspiracies. Long after Elvis Presley (supposedly) died, public opinion surveys showed as many as one in 10 Americans believed he was still alive.

So how do you deal with the doubters in a democracy?

As premier of Alberta from 2019 to 2022, Kenney’s playbook was always about reuniting the right, replicating the path to power followed by his fellow travellers federally. But be careful what you wish for and campaign for.

Kenney’s anti-NDP coalition became a big-tent party that was stretched out of shape to accommodate the anti-Canada contingent. Under pressure from his progeny, Kenney rode the so-called sovereignty tiger until it threw him to the wolves.

In 2021, he conducted a referendum on ending Alberta’s unequal equalization transfers. That proved to be a precursor to this month’s referendum on cutting all ties to the rest of Canada.

When separatists pushed him from power, choosing the more malleable Smith in his place, Kenney was mortified by the monster he helped create. Ultimately, he campaigned passionately and patriotically against the referendum question.

He teamed up last month with his longtime NDP rival, former premier Rachel Notley, at the Democracy Forum I hosted at Toronto Metropolitan University. Kenney was scathing in his denunciations of Smith and renunciations of separatists, arguing that she had recklessly exploited divisions to consolidate her power.

But as he now knows, and as Smith will soon see, separatists never give in — and never give up a grudge. By playing both sides — separatists and federalists — Smith has overplayed her hand with both.

It is not possible to pacify separatists because their goals are non-negotiable. It is not about granting this concession or winning that argument; it is not about accommodation or elucidation.

Separatists live in a world of anti-Canadian impulses and pro-American fantasies. They demand the democratic exercise of a referendum but then make excuses for their defeat and refuse to reconcile themselves to the verdict.

The only consolation for federalists is that the separatists will turn on themselves first. Incredulity will turn to hostility as they hunt for those who let them down in the home stretch, failing to do what must be done to pry the province away from Canada.

The culprit cannot be Kenney nor Notley, nor any of their ilk — for these federalists were always deemed a lost cause by the secessionist camp. It was Smith, the putative ally who purported to be on their side, who led them on and let them down.

She cannot now lead them to the Promised Land in America. It is not enough for stalwarts in the United Conservative Party to come together to defeat New Democrats, for the NDP is yesterday’s adversary.

Now, the UCP’s separatist base has seen the enemy, and it is the enemy within. Their leader turned out to be a false prophet who failed to take them where they wanted all of us to go.

Now she must go.

Speaking of party leaders, I’ll be hosting NDP Leader Avi Lewis at the Democracy Forum at Toronto Metropolitan University on Thursday at 12 p.m. to talk about “what’s left for the left.” The event is sold out, but you can watch the livestream at thestar.com .

stories.title: Carney government eyes culture in budget as promised $600M for culture sector still frozen
stories.summary: Champagne hints Nov. 5 fiscal blueprint will back Canadian identity, but Indigenous screen and music organizations say money pledged last June has yet to arrive.
stories.author: Raisa Patel
stories.content:
Ottawa—The Carney government is signalling that Canadian culture and identity will be a focus of November’s federal budget , months after pledging urgent support for a struggling audiovisual sector that has yet to receive hundreds of millions of dollars in promised funding.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne was asked Wednesday whether next month’s fiscal blueprint would include further details about the annual $600-million commitment, which Ottawa announced back in June .

The finance minister said his top two priorities are affordability and economic growth, but also suggested the budget will reflect the importance of promoting Canada’s distinct identity.

Minister of Finance and National Revenue Francois-Philippe Champagne makes his way to a meeting of the federal cabinet on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, ON Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026.

“We have always been key allies to the cultural and arts sectors, celebrating who we are as Canadians and as Quebecers, in our official languages. The cultural community can count on us,” the minister said in French.

Cultural and audiovisual groups say they’re still in the dark about the future of the funding, which Canadian Culture and Identity Minister Marc Miller framed earlier this year as immediate support for a “suffering” sector as Ottawa reconsidered new requirements for streaming services to contribute to Canadian programming.

“We’re at risk of losing the momentum we’ve built, not just for us, but for the Indigenous companies that we support, and the storytelling that we’re seeing resonate with Canadian and global audiences,” said Kerry Swanson, the CEO of the Indigenous Screen Office.

“We have global hit shows like ‘Heated Rivalry’ and ‘North of North’ that clearly demonstrate the potential for Canada’s homegrown screen sector. The Canada brand is very strong right now, and it’s urgent that we capitalize on that to increase our economic opportunities in the global market,” Swanson told the Star.

“Am I gonna get fired?” The creator, execs, actors and more share the untold story of Crave’s unstoppable hit.

Miller said in the House of Commons on Tuesday that the money will flow “very soon,” but declined to say Wednesday whether that would be confirmed in the Nov. 5 budget.

The minister revealed in June, amid tense trade talks with the U.S., that he had asked Canada’s broadcasting regulator to review a spring decision to triple how much foreign streamers would have to pay to support the creation of Canadian film and television.

Those funding contributions — hiked in May from 5 per cent of streamers’ Canadian revenues to 15 per cent — stem from the Trudeau government’s Online Streaming Act, which subjected online giants like Netflix and Disney Plus to the same regulations that already apply to traditional television and radio broadcasters. The Canadian Radio-television and Communications Commission (Crtc) was tasked with overseeing the implementation of the law, including ensuring that streaming services, like broadcasters, would have to contribute to the funding, production and promotion of Canadian content.

Legal challenges by streaming platforms regarding several aspects of the law put those contributions on hold, prompting Miller in June to say Ottawa was “impatient” to get the money out the door.

The Carney government insisted its decision to revisit the Crtc’s rules and provide the funding itself was unrelated to trade tensions with the U.S. Instead, it cited concerns that streaming services could off-load the cost of the new requirements onto subscribers, a rationale the Star debunked earlier this year.

Swanson, whose group primarily relies on government funding to support the creation of Indigenous film and television content, said she believes the government understands the importance of boosting organizations like hers.

But she said that without additional aid, the Indigenous Screen Office cannot address a “soaring demand” for funding, noting that last year the group received $50 million in requests but only had $11 million to dole out.

The Indigenous Music Office, an organization that helps Indigenous artists compete in Canada’s music industry, also told the Star they were meant to be a recipient of the funds.

“The support from the $600 million would mean a lot to us and our community and the people we serve,” said board chair Alan Greyeyes. “We don’t have it yet, and we’re just making sure we’re ready when it does arrive.”

Reynolds Mastin, the head of the Canadian Media Producers Association, wrote in a statement Wednesday that he was “pleased” to hear about Champagne’s emphasis on Canada’s cultural sector.

“The funding was meant to immediately replace the streamer investment that was lost when the Online Streaming Act was suspended, and so it is critical that at least a portion of it be released well before the new federal fiscal year begins on April 1st,” Mastin’s statement read.

“This $600 million is essential and welcome, but it is no substitute for requiring streamers to commission independently produced Canadian content that reflects the importance of the Canadian market to their businesses.”
