stories.title: Wainwright fire shows the importance of health-care system resilience to Canadian security
stories.summary: Canada should seize this opportunity to make a clear case for health investments that strengthen defence readiness.
stories.author: Bhavini Gohel; Marcia Clark The Conversation
stories.content:
The fire that swept through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright over the weekend in Alberta killed four soldiers and injured 39 people , including 19 reported in critical condition.

The thoughts of Canadians are with the families, the military community, the people of Wainwright and the responders who answered the call.

But what happened after the fire deserves attention too. Wainwright’s hospital became a triage hub for what the town’s mayor described as the largest mass casualty event the community has ever seen. Patients were also transferred to hospitals in Edmonton, Calgary and Red Deer. The response mobilized 22 ground ambulances, six airplanes and two helicopters.

The Canadian Armed Forces relies on civilian systems for specialized services and mass casualty events. Civilian health readiness is therefore part of national defence. Thirteen months before Wainwright, Canada rehearsed the challenge of a casualty surge. Its findings deserve action.

The response to a mass-casualty event does not play out in an otherwise empty health-care system. It competes with everyday care for staff, beds, transport and supplies.

The Canadian Institute for Health Information (Cihi) reports that hospital beds increased by only four per cent between 2014–15 and 2023–24 as Canada’s population grew by 13 per cent. Beds per capita fell by seven per cent.

These national figures don’t establish Alberta’s capacity on the day of the fire, but they show why having enough infrastructure, staff and expertise is so important.

Alberta has two burn centres, in Edmonton and Calgary. That specialist capacity is an asset. But rural hospitals need staff, supplies and transportation to stabilize severely injured patients and move them safely to burn centres while continuing to serve their own communities.

Canada’s health-care system sits at the centre of what’s known as a polycrisis: several systems are under strain, each situation compounding the other.

Climate change is prolonging wildfire seasons. Inflation is squeezing budgets and supply chains. Workforce shortages are persisting after the COVID-19 pandemic. The flu season is surging. The consequences of these crises affect health system response and care.

Wainwright is experiencing its mass casualty event amid this ongoing polycrisis. The question is whether any system can absorb the next shock while still dealing with the last.

In September 2025, 79 people from health-care systems across the country, federal agencies and the Canadian Armed Forces gathered in Toronto for Exercise Canada Paratus. Paratus assessed overseas casualties, but the lessons apply to all hazards.

Four Canadian soldiers killed in a fast-moving fire during a training exercise in Alberta over

Led by key disaster management teams and leaders, the exercise simulated about 100 casualties a week arriving in provincial and territorial health-care systems in Canada from a war in Europe. The post-exercise report is blunt. Three findings are relevant to planning after Wainwright:

- Capacity: The report identified workforce challenges and the need to expand infrastructure, staffing and expertise for sustained casualty surges.

- Patient tracking: Canada has no integrated system to follow casualties as they move between military and civilian care. At Wainwright, the injured were dispersed across several hospitals within hours.

- Governance: The report called for a federal–provincial–territorial health emergency and security authority with clear leadership, roles and decision rights. At the moment, there’s no organization co-ordinating health-care system capacity across federal, provincial and territorial governments.

Nato already recognizes the link between healthcare and defence. One of its seven baseline requirements for national resilience is the ability to manage mass casualties and disruptive health crises, including functioning civilian health systems and secure medical supplies. Canada’s allies already treat health-care systems as strategic infrastructure, alongside energy grids and supply chains.

At the 2025 Hague Nato summit, allies agreed that up to 1.5 per cent of GDP within their new five per cent defence spending target could support resilience, including civil preparedness.

Finland’s comprehensive security model treats health security as a vital societal function, while Sweden’s total defence approach recognizes healthcare as essential to defence.

Canada should seize this opportunity to make a clear case for health investments that strengthen defence readiness.

Canada already has the diagnosis. As the polycrisis deepens, sudden events like Wainwright will keep exposing the cost of failing to fill gaps. Here’s how Canada should respond:

First, implement the Paratus recommendations with a public timeline.

Second, create the permanent federal–provincial–territorial health emergency body the report calls for.

Third, build patient tracking that works across civilian and military care, so every casualty can be followed from the scene to recovery.

Fourth, treat surge capacity, including rural hospitals near bases and critical infrastructure, as a defence-relevant investment.

Finally, make the next national exercise a domestic, sudden scenario that applies a sudden mass-casualty event onto a system already under strain. New tools, including AI-enabled polycrisis simulation, allow authorities to rehearse these compounding scenarios before they happen; they’re already being developed.

The clinicians and paramedics who responded at Wainwright were part of Canada’s defence capacity, regardless of whether we call them that.

Paratus asked whether our health system could survive intact if war came to us from overseas. Wainwright answered a harder question: what happens when the emergency is already here.

Third, build patient tracking that works across civilian and military care, so every casualty can be followed from the scene to recovery.
Fourth, treat surge capacity, including rural hospitals near bases and critical infrastructure, as a defence-relevant investment.

Finally, make the next national exercise a domestic, sudden scenario that applies a sudden mass-casualty event onto a system already under strain. New tools, including AI-enabled polycrisis simulation, allow authorities to rehearse these compounding scenarios before they happen; they’re already being developed.
The clinicians and paramedics who responded at Wainwright were part of Canada’s defence capacity, regardless of whether we call them that.
Paratus asked whether our health system could survive intact if war came to us from overseas. Wainwright answered a harder question: what happens when the emergency is already here.

content_blocks.text: The fire that swept through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright over the weekend in Alberta killed four soldiers and injured 39 people , including 19 reported in critical condition.

content_blocks.text: The thoughts of Canadians are with the families, the military community, the people of Wainwright and the responders who answered the call.

content_blocks.text: But what happened after the fire deserves attention too. Wainwright’s hospital became a triage hub for what the town’s mayor described as the largest mass casualty event the community has ever seen. Patients were also transferred to hospitals in Edmonton, Calgary and Red Deer. The response mobilized 22 ground ambulances, six airplanes and two helicopters.

stories.title: Complex challenges require collaborative solutions
stories.summary: As Fanshawe looks toward 2035, our leaders will share their perspectives on the issues that m
stories.content:
As Fanshawe looks toward 2035, our leaders will share their perspectives on the issues that matter. This series explores the opportunities, challenges and innovations shaping the future of education, workforce development and our community.

At Fanshawe College, one of our three areas of strategic focus is “making a difference for stronger contributions to our community and the economy”. We endeavor to do so through collaborations with strategic partners and employers in ways that embolden experiential education for our students. Such was the case when the College recently worked collaboratively with the public safety sector and the WSIB to develop and launch the new WSIB Centre of Excellence in Immersive Technologies Simulation for Workplace Safety.

Complex challenges require collaborative solutions. That’s why, at Fanshawe College, our education leaders meet regularly with industry and not-for-profit leaders to clearly understand their needs and to co-develop creative, innovative solutions together.

Such was the case when the leaders from the first responder sector (police, fire, paramedicine, and corrections) were canvassed two years ago by Fanshawe’s Corporate Training Solutions (CTS). At the time, three very important themes were identified that were consistent across the four public safety groups. Each described challenges tied to the attrition of new recruits, who, once in the field, quickly determined that the nature of the work was not as they had imagined. Each also described an inability – by virtue of cost, complexity and risk, to create physical training environments capable of mimicking real-world, high-risk environments. Each also described a much higher than average number of mental stress injuries related claims tied to cumulative exposure to human suffering, violence and death. It was through these discussions and then through the collaborative ideation and problem-solving that followed, that AI enabled extended reality (XR) simulation as a solution was born.

Co-created simulation was viewed to be an affordable, flexible and practical way for first responders to practice their response to a high-risk situation – and to allow them to fail as many times as necessary – with no real harm caused. Through repetitive engagement with simulation, mastery will eventually follow. While this solution was seen as a fit for preventative training, the same AI enabled XR simulation technology was also viewed to be an efficient and effective tool to provide clinical support to responders experiencing mental stress injury. Cognitive-behavioural simulation can reduce barriers and stigma related to seeking therapy, enhance the effectiveness of in-person treatment, and provide interim support for injured individuals who are awaiting services or have limited access to care, such as those living in rural communities.

Problems as complicated as these are rarely managed without a host of other partners also being engaged along the way. The WSIB has funded the development of a physical production and research AI/XR simulation ecosystem at Fanshawe inclusive of: simulation labs; 3D simulation rooms; motion capture and biomechanics systems; XR laboratories and an XR content creation studio. The organization also remains steadfast in its support for the operational sustainability of the initiative. Central to the ecosystem’s success were Fanshawe’s students and faculty, whose support was indispensable in bringing this vision to life.

Drawing on the expertise of students and faculty across disciplines ranging from information technology and AI to public safety, health sciences, creative media, business, and applied research, the initiative will create, test, and refine training and clinical simulation assets designed to benefit first responders across the region and the country.

Not only will the students benefit from an experiential opportunity tied to their technical area of focus, but they will leave such project work and enter the modern workforce with the invaluable soft skill of multi-disciplinary collaboration and innovation.

Now that the foundational AI/XR simulation ecosystem at Fanshawe has been firmly established, scaling to other economic priority sectors such as construction, advanced manufacturing, and transportation are inevitable, thereby multiplying social and economic impact in our communities whilst providing an even greater number of students, across an even greater number of disciplines, the opportunity to develop and master multi-disciplinary collaboration and innovation skills.

For any media inquiries, please reach out to mediainquiries@fanshawec.ca

stories.title: Galloway trial hears accuser first complained of sexual harassment to UBC campus security in 2013
stories.summary: Stephen Bohnen, a 77-year-old former UBC community relations officer, testified that he interviewed the woman when she came by the public counter at his office in July of that year
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
The University of British Columbia creative writing student who accused bestselling author Steven Galloway of sexual assault first complained to campus security about sexual harassment by him two years before she took her allegations to the university’s administration, the B.C. Supreme Court heard Tuesday.

Stephen Bohnen, a 77-year-old former community relations officer with the school’s security department, testified that he interviewed the woman when she came by the public counter at his office in July, 2013.

The woman, known as A.B. because of a publication ban, complained that Mr. Galloway was sexually harassing her by repeatedly giving her scotch in his office and propositioning her for sex, Mr. Bohnen testified during a defamation trial brought by Mr. Galloway against A.B. and three others.

“[A.B.] stated there had been a clearly sexualized atmosphere and more than one intimation of invitations to sex by Galloway,” the court heard Mr. Bohnen wrote in his report.

The author and former head of Ubc’s creative writing program was suspended in November, 2015 , amid an investigation into A.B.’s allegations.

He was dismissed the following year after a retired judge hired by UBC to investigate A.B.’s claims found he had sexually harassed her and found other instances of misconduct. The judge did not find that he sexually assaulted the woman.

In 2018, Mr. Galloway’s original defamation suit was filed against two dozen defendants, but only A.B. and three others remain: Mandi Gray, Dana Kagis and Glynnis Kirchmeier.

The case has wound its way through various courts over the years as judges have had to weigh whether those accused of sexual assault have a right to sue their accusers for defamation. In 2024, the B.C. Court of Appeal upheld a lower-court decision that said someone accused of rape must be allowed to defend their reputations in court.

Daniel Burnett, lead counsel for Mr. Galloway, asked Mr. Bohnen if he told A.B. that the professor was a “serial predator.”

The court has heard that in a letter to the UBC administration in November, 2015, A.B. complained that Mr. Galloway had sexually harassed and sexually assaulted her. She said in the letter that Mr. Bohnen made the comment when she first went to him with her complaint.

“Well, I certainly can’t remember anything like that,” Mr. Bohnen responded to Mr. Burnett.

Mr. Burnett also stated that the report mentioned the file being referred to the local detachment of the RCMP, which opened a case.

The B.C. Supreme Court has not yet heard what happened to that 2013 investigation by the Mounties or why her three allegations of sexual assault were put to school administrators two years later.

A.B.’s ex-husband told the court on Monday that while they were together, she told him the novelist had put his hands around her neck when the pair were on Mr. Galloway’s sailboat. The ex-husband testified that at that time A.B. refused to file a police report or let him talk to Mr. Galloway, instead telling her partner that she would handle the situation. He said he later learned that she had an extramarital affair with Mr. Galloway from 2011 to 2013.

Mr. Galloway was never charged with any offence and has always denied he sexually assaulted A.B.

A.B. is not testifying and, at the start of the trial, her lawyer Arden Beddoes told the court that she was withdrawing her defences of truth and fair comment – but not admitting that she spread lies about her former romantic partner. Mr. Beddoes said she had tried to kill herself twice this year because of the stress of the ordeal.

Mr. Burnett closed his submissions Tuesday morning by reading into the record sections of a 2019 cross-examination of A.B. from a related proceeding.

He read a portion from that transcript where A.B. acknowledged that her e-mail in November, 2015, to Ubc’s administrators included a false claim that the legal team for CBC’s the fifth estate TV news program had “vetted” her allegations against Mr. Galloway.

“Yes, in fact, it was false and it was made because I desperately wanted UBC to go forward with an investigation, and I was being pressured,” she said in the transcript.

“I had no legal counsel. I had to find a way to convince them to go forward with the investigation and this was my last desperate e-mail to make sure there was an investigation to protect me from the person who had strangled and raped me.”

“I don’t regret what I said because I needed to keep myself alive and safe, and there are no easy ways or safe ways for women to get their cases brought forward and investigated.”

stories.title: Smith vows to push for more Alberta autonomy
stories.summary: Premier says she will work co-operatively with Ottawa but will use ‘every legal and political tool’ to advance interests of province
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
A day after Albertans voted overwhelmingly to remain a part of Canada, Premier Danielle Smith heralded progress with Ottawa but remained defiant in her plan to extract more autonomy from the federal government, even as she pledged not to hold another separation referendum while in office.

Ms. Smith said she will work co-operatively with her federal counterparts, but also issued a warning to Prime Minister Mark Carney.

“We will use every legal and political tool at our disposal to protect and advance the interests of Albertans,” she said in a televised address on Tuesday night.

“And when Ottawa interferes with those rights, we will be unrelenting in our response.”

Ms. Smith encouraged Albertans to turn the page on separatism and said that, under her watch, the province wouldn’t hold another referendum on the issue.

“Yesterday, Albertans made their choice. Today, we begin the next chapter,” she said.

On Monday, roughly 75 per cent of voters in the province endorsed remaining in Canada without moving toward holding a future separation referendum.

The result mirrored more than a year of public-opinion polling on the issue and was met with relief from federalists and business leaders, many of whom had issued grave warnings about the dangers of a binding separation vote.

Alberta’s referendum – the first time the province has put a secession question to voters – emerged over the past year as one of the greatest stress tests of national unity in decades. It added to two active threats to Canadian sovereignty: the recent election of a minority separatist government in Quebec, and U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariff war and musings about annexation.

The separation debate has roiled Alberta’s political arena. It started to emerge as the province’s dominant issue in March, 2025, after Ms. Smith threatened an “unprecedented national unity crisis” if Mr. Carney didn’t repeal a list of environmental laws she believed were stifling Alberta’s energy sector. A month later, she lowered the threshold needed for citizens to put questions to the electorate in a referendum.

After two separatist petitions hit roadblocks in the courts, Ms. Smith announced this spring that Albertans would be asked to pick between two options: remain in Canada or start the process toward a binding separation referendum.

Tension between Alberta and Ottawa is not new. The relationship grew particularly strained during former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s decade in office.

Addressing the quarter of the electorate who voted to hold a binding separation referendum, Ms. Smith said on Tuesday that those Albertans hold “legitimate frustrations.”

“You need to know that your voices have been heard. Not just by our government, but also by your fellow Albertans and your fellow Canadians,” she said.

Relations between Alberta and Ottawa have thawed under Mr. Carney. Together, he and Ms. Smith have pursued building a bitumen pipeline to the West Coast, holding it up as proof Canada can work. The two campaigned side by side for the remain camp last week in Red Deer.

Ms. Smith’s support for remaining in Canada has not satisfied many of her critics, who’ve accused her of catering to separatists that public-opinion polls say make up a large chunk of her United Conservative Party base.

Political strategists say the referendum has weighed down her popularity, underlined in September by a shocking by-election loss to the Alberta NDP in one of the safest conservative seats in Calgary.

Mr. Carney said on Tuesday on Parliament Hill that he was “thrilled” with the referendum result: “They’ve chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward together with purpose, high ambition.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre celebrated the outcome as well, telling reporters in Calgary that it’s time to “focus on unity for everyone.”

Separatists, meanwhile, were left licking their wounds after failing to muster support for their cause. Mitch Sylvestre, chief executive of the Alberta Prosperity Project, said in an interview on Tuesday that he’s now focusing on getting more separatist allies on the UCP board and as party nominees for the next provincial election, scheduled for October, 2027, at the latest.

“We need some of our people to become MLAs,” he said.

Now, attention is likely to shift toward the nine other proposals on Albertans’ referendum ballots on issues of immigration policy and constitutional changes.

Carving out greater autonomy for Alberta has been Ms. Smith’s governing thesis since she became Premier in September, 2022, and motivated her decision to put the other nine questions to the electorate.

Elections Alberta was still counting those ballots on Tuesday and few questions appeared to receive an overwhelming mandate from Albertans.

With 90 per cent of polls reporting, 54 per cent of voters had endorsed Alberta taking increased control over immigration. Meanwhile, a slim majority – roughly 51 per cent – had rejected a proposal to let provinces opt out of federal programs without losing the associated funding.

In her TV address, Ms. Smith declared victory on the immigration proposals and said she’ll wait for the results on the constitutional questions before making a decision on how to proceed.

Some corners in Alberta’s business community have voiced concern over the immigration questions, saying the province’s proposals would increase the cost of labour and make it harder to attract talent.

While the results of those questions were unsettled on Tuesday, Mr. Carney signalled that he is willing to work with provinces on immigration, which is already a shared priority between the two levels of government.

“Where we go from here needs to be established in co-operation with the provinces, and that’s very much the spirit of at least one of the questions,” he told reporters.

Prime Minister Mark Carney thanked Albertans for taking part in the 'democratic process,' saying on Tuesday the vote to reject the referendum question on separation is a 'great result' for the country.

The Canadian Press

He was less absolute about reopening the Constitution. Ms. Smith’s constitutional proposals, besides needing federal co-operation, would require support from seven of the 10 provinces, comprising half the national population.

“Constitutional change is difficult. It’s long ... where we can find solutions that work for Canadians, we should find those solutions,” Mr. Carney said.

Ms. Smith’s government has not provided concrete details around how it would implement its immigration proposals. On Tuesday, she said her government will pursue those changes “in the coming months and years ahead.”

Leaders from across the country voiced their support for Alberta and were happy about voters’ choice to remain in Canada.

“I’m thrilled by the decisive support Albertans have shown for the country we all love,” Ontario Premier Doug Ford said.

In Quebec, newly elected premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon of the separatist Parti Québécois pointed to the early results on the nine questions as evidence that Albertans believe Canadian federation is a “straitjacket that prevents them from placing their priorities at the heart of their own public policies.”

“Prime Minister Mark Carney will therefore have to take note that Alberta residents are now questioning, just as Quebeckers did before them, the Canadian constitutional order and the abuses of power by the federal regime in areas of jurisdiction.”

stories.title: Carney to sign agreements with Turkey deepening co-operation in energy, defence, officials say
stories.summary: The two countries could also deepen co-operation in drone technology, aerospace, naval systems, Turkish envoy says
stories.author: Steven Chase
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney leaves Wednesday for Turkey where he will sign agreements to deepen co-operation on energy among other areas, a source familiar with the trip said.

Three senior government officials briefing journalists in Ottawa Tuesday said the Prime Minister’s brief visit, which spans three days, will also expand joint efforts on defence and security with Ankara, a Nato ally of Canada’s.

The Globe is not identifying these sources, who were not authorized to speak publicly.

Opinion: Turkey is the master of interest-based foreign policy. Will Canada pass this test?

With a population of 87 million people, Turkey’s economy is the 16th largest in the world. The visit comes as Mr. Carney’s government has been focused on expanding economic relationships in the midst of a trade war with the United States.

The trip will be another test of Mr. Carney’s pivot to “values-based realism” foreign policy that replaced former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s focus on progressive values. The Prime Minister has explained this new approach means no more “lecturing from afar” if Canada disagrees with another country’s conduct.

For instance, Mr. Carney’s trip to Turkey, part of his drive to reduce trade reliance on the U.S., is taking him to a country which in recent months has taken over a pro-opposition media outlet, raided Lgbtq groups and convicted a stand-up comic of insulting the country’s President.

Officials at a government briefing on Tuesday could not say if Mr. Carny planned to meet with Lgbtq community members, or journalists from Halk TV, or the comedian Deniz Goktas who was convicted and sentenced to 19 months in jail. He is free on appeal.

On Thursday, Mr. Carney will meet with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara to discuss co-operation on trade and investment, defence and people-to-people ties, officials said.

The two leaders will issue an update on negotiations for a Canada-Turkey free trade deal, officials said.

On Friday, Mr. Carney will meet with businesspeople in Istanbul. He returns to Canada on Saturday.

Turkey’s envoy in Ottawa said Ankara is hungry for what Canada has on offer.

“The sky is the limit,” Turkish ambassador Can Dizdar said of future co-operation between the two countries.

Canada hopes to sell Candu nuclear reactors to Turkey, which plans to add 20 gigawatts of nuclear power by 2050. Ottawa wants to supply Ankara with critical minerals and stoke Turkish interest in investing in related mining projects, possibly with Canadian partners, and export liquefied natural gas to Turkey.

Mr. Dizdar said Turkey and Canada could deepen co-operation in drone technology, aerospace, naval systems, shipbuilding parts, munitions production and vehicles. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute ranked Turkey as the 11th largest arms exporter in the world for the period from 2021 to 2025.

Turkey is the latest stop in Mr. Carney’s efforts to repair ties that suffered in the last decade. He will be the first Canadian prime minister in history to make a bilateral visit to Turkey, meaning a leader’s trip focused on Canada-Turkish relations instead of an international summit being held there.

He has reset diplomatic relations with China after allegations of foreign interference and hostage diplomacy, with India after accusations that New Delhi was behind the murder of a Canadian citizen on Canadian soil and now is appearing to do the same with Turkey, where ties suffered greatly after Ottawa restricted arms shipments to Ankara in recent years.

Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a new Canadian think tank on foreign policy, said Mr. Carney is in high demand from world leaders this year after his World Economic Speech in Davos where he argued that the post-Cold War rules-based order has suffered “a rupture, not a transition” and that middle powers like Canada must act together or risk being left on the menu.

“Right now , he is seen as a major player on the international stage and lots of countries would like him to visit - would like him to participate in their events,” Ms. Nadjibulla said. The fact that Mr. Carney is quickly returning to Turkey after announcing the launch of free trade talks during the July Nato leader’s summit in Ankara “shows how much importance he gives to this relationship and building a relationship with as a pivotal state in the Middle East,” she said.

“I think the timing is important because it’s not happening in 2027. It’s happening now in a fairly busy moment.”

stories.title: Poll suggests PQ referendum pledge cost party majority as Alberta vote fuels sovereignty debate
stories.summary: A post-election poll suggests the Parti Québécois could have won a majority government if it had not pledged to hold a sovereignty referendum in its first mandate.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Dan Spector
stories.content:
A new poll suggests the Parti Québécois’ pledge to hold a sovereignty referendum in its first mandate cost the party a majority government as Quebec politicians draw competing lessons from a referendum in Alberta.

The Léger survey for Le Journal de Montréal, conducted after the Oct. 5 election, found the PQ would have received 35 per cent of the vote if it had not promised to hold a referendum.

That is seven percentage points higher than the 28 per cent of the vote the party received in the election and, according to the poll, would have been enough to secure a majority government.

Instead, the PQ will enter the next legislature with a minority government.

“I think seeing this new poll just confirms what many people thought,” said Daniel Béland, political sociologist and director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada.

The same poll found just 20 per cent of respondents favour the PQ organizing a referendum during its first mandate.

“This idea of a third referendum is just not popular. It’s actually very unpopular, and even after this victory of the PQ, there is no change here,” Béland said.

The poll comes as Quebec politicians debate what lessons should be drawn from Monday night’s referendum results in Alberta, where about three-quarters of voters opted for the province to remain in Canada, rejecting a proposal for a future referendum on separation.

Albertans also voted for their province to negotiate changes to the Constitution to secure more powers from the federal government.

Premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Tuesday the results show cracks in the Canadian federation and suggested provinces could work together to gain more powers from Ottawa.

The PQ leader wrote on social media that Albertans had proven “there is nothing to fear from expressing one’s views through a referendum.”

“The message they are sending to Ottawa could not be clearer: Canada, as it stands, is not working, and the status quo is no longer acceptable,” St-Pierre Plamondon said.

“Like Quebecers, they see the Canadian federation as a straitjacket that prevents them from placing their priorities at the heart of their own public policies, in order to meet their own needs.”

St-Pierre Plamondon said Quebec, under the Coalition Avenir Québec government, had already tried and failed to get more autonomy from Ottawa. He said his predecessors’ approach “only led to rejections and setbacks for Quebec” and accused the federal government of becoming increasingly interventionist.

The PQ leader has promised Quebecers a third referendum on independence after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he sees common cause with Alberta and promised to collaborate with other provinces “that come to the same conclusion as Quebec and Albertans: change is needed.”

But Quebec’s opposition parties said the Alberta results should instead prompt St-Pierre Plamondon to abandon his referendum pledge.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said Quebecers should align themselves with Alberta to secure a balance of power in the federation, but said he does not support secession.

He urged St-Pierre Plamondon to drop his promise to hold a referendum on independence.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard made the same request, saying the Canadian federation remains the best option for Quebec.

“The results reflect a desire to unite and work to build Canada rather than divide it,” Milliard said. “Canada is the envy of the world.”

The new Quebec poll is also providing ammunition to the Liberals as they prepare to serve as the official Opposition.

Milliard received a warm welcome Tuesday as his party held its first official meeting as a sworn-in caucus.

“We’re going to have a strong official Opposition,” he said.

Liberal MNA Michel Leblanc said Quebecers will see in the coming months and years how central a referendum is to the PQ’s agenda and how it could affect Quebec’s relationship with the rest of Canada.

“Quebecers don’t want a referendum. The PQ wants one, and it will cost them,” Leblanc said.

A minority government typically lasts 18 to 24 months, and the Liberals are already looking ahead to the next election.

“We’ll make sure to be ready for the next rendez-vous électoral,” Milliard said.

Béland said the polling should also give the PQ pause over its commitment to a referendum deadline.

“This poll and other polls should give them pause about emphasizing the referendum with a hard deadline,” he said.

St-Pierre Plamondon is set to officially become premier Wednesday when he and his cabinet are formally sworn into office.

content_blocks.text: The Léger survey for Le Journal de Montréal, conducted after the Oct. 5 election, found the PQ would have received 35 per cent of the vote if it had not promised to hold a referendum.
That is seven percentage points higher than the 28 per cent of the vote the party received in the election and, according to the poll, would have been enough to secure a majority government.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Ottawa lawyer wants to force Quebec MNAs to pledge allegiance to the King'

content_blocks.text: Instead, the PQ will enter the next legislature with a minority government.
“I think seeing this new poll just confirms what many people thought,” said Daniel Béland, political sociologist and director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada.
The same poll found just 20 per cent of respondents favour the PQ organizing a referendum during its first mandate.
“This idea of a third referendum is just not popular. It’s actually very unpopular, and even after this victory of the PQ, there is no change here,” Béland said.

The poll comes as Quebec politicians debate what lessons should be drawn from Monday night’s referendum results in Alberta, where about three-quarters of voters opted for the province to remain in Canada, rejecting a proposal for a future referendum on separation.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Parti Québécois holds swearing in ceremony for MNAs'

content_blocks.text: Albertans also voted for their province to negotiate changes to the Constitution to secure more powers from the federal government.
Premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Tuesday the results show cracks in the Canadian federation and suggested provinces could work together to gain more powers from Ottawa.
The PQ leader wrote on social media that Albertans had proven “there is nothing to fear from expressing one’s views through a referendum.”
“The message they are sending to Ottawa could not be clearer: Canada, as it stands, is not working, and the status quo is no longer acceptable,” St-Pierre Plamondon said.
“Like Quebecers, they see the Canadian federation as a straitjacket that prevents them from placing their priorities at the heart of their own public policies, in order to meet their own needs.”

St-Pierre Plamondon said Quebec, under the Coalition Avenir Québec government, had already tried and failed to get more autonomy from Ottawa. He said his predecessors’ approach “only led to rejections and setbacks for Quebec” and accused the federal government of becoming increasingly interventionist.
The PQ leader has promised Quebecers a third referendum on independence after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Alberta referendum: What we can learn from past and present separatist movements'

content_blocks.text: St-Pierre Plamondon said he sees common cause with Alberta and promised to collaborate with other provinces “that come to the same conclusion as Quebec and Albertans: change is needed.”
But Quebec’s opposition parties said the Alberta results should instead prompt St-Pierre Plamondon to abandon his referendum pledge.
Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said Quebecers should align themselves with Alberta to secure a balance of power in the federation, but said he does not support secession.
He urged St-Pierre Plamondon to drop his promise to hold a referendum on independence.
Liberal Leader Charles Milliard made the same request, saying the Canadian federation remains the best option for Quebec.
“The results reflect a desire to unite and work to build Canada rather than divide it,” Milliard said. “Canada is the envy of the world.”
The new Quebec poll is also providing ammunition to the Liberals as they prepare to serve as the official Opposition.
Milliard received a warm welcome Tuesday as his party held its first official meeting as a sworn-in caucus.
“We’re going to have a strong official Opposition,” he said.
Liberal MNA Michel Leblanc said Quebecers will see in the coming months and years how central a referendum is to the PQ’s agenda and how it could affect Quebec’s relationship with the rest of Canada.
“Quebecers don’t want a referendum. The PQ wants one, and it will cost them,” Leblanc said.
A minority government typically lasts 18 to 24 months, and the Liberals are already looking ahead to the next election.
“We’ll make sure to be ready for the next rendez-vous électoral,” Milliard said.
Béland said the polling should also give the PQ pause over its commitment to a referendum deadline.
“This poll and other polls should give them pause about emphasizing the referendum with a hard deadline,” he said.
St-Pierre Plamondon is set to officially become premier Wednesday when he and his cabinet are formally sworn into office.

stories.title: Victims of Wainwright fire remembered as young people dedicated to service
stories.summary: Devastating fire at Canadian Forces Base in Alberta claimed lives of four soldiers, injured 39 others
stories.author: Lindsay Jones, Colin Freeze, Jana G. Pruden
stories.content:
Just days ago, Sergeant Morgan Wong was a volunteer medical responder with St. John Ambulance in Edmonton, excited about a recent promotion within the military, and eager to deploy on his second tour in Europe.

“He had so much potential,” his friend Rhyneice Cook said. “You know, kind of one of those people that you’re like, that guy’s going to change the world. And then, to lose him – it’s a great loss for humanity in general.”

Sgt. Wong, 26, was one of four soldiers killed in a devastating fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta on Saturday afternoon.

The others were Private Shaun Farrell and Pte. Aidan Goulding, both 23, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19.

Thirty-nine other soldiers in their battalion were injured. As of Monday, 33 remained in hospital, many with serious burns covering much of their bodies. Nineteen of them remained in critical condition.

All of the victims were members of the Canadian Armed Forces serving with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

In social-media posts, crowdfunding campaigns and media interviews, relatives and friends have described the victims as young people dedicated to serving their country and communities, and who, in some cases, were burned while trying to help other victims.

A huge pile of flowers continues to grow at the cenotaph in Wainwright after four soldiers were killed in a weekend training exercise gone fatally wrong. Strong and sudden winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire across the Prairie landscape at lightning speed, stopping soldiers in their tracks and sending 39 to hospital, 19 critically. Six have since been discharged, says the defence minister.

The Canadian Press

The military has released few details about how exactly the soldiers were injured, saying only that a grass fire burning in the area spread suddenly in gusting winds and overtook the battalion during training.

Prime Minister Mark Carney told the House of Commons on Monday that 50 investigators are on the ground in Wainwright conducting three separate probes, including a military board of inquiry , which will consider how to prevent similar events in the future.

General Jennie Carignan, Chief of the Defence Staff, told The Globe and Mail Monday that the inquiry could take a year, but promised the results would be made public.

The youngest of the victims who were killed on Saturday, Pte. Lykkemark, was remembered by his high-school rugby coach, Trevor Plater, as an athlete who stood out for his speed, fearlessness and self-confidence. But the coach said the teenager’s most exceptional attribute was how he cared.

“He took care of people,” Mr. Plater said in an interview. “There were moments where I, as a coach, was thinking about checking in on somebody or was worried about somebody, but a lot of the time he was already there, having a chat with them and supporting them.”

Nadine Dunford, who helped raise the teen in Langley, B.C., said he dreamed of being a police officer and joined the military after high school as a step toward that goal. She told CTV Vancouver she talked to Pte. Lykkemark last week and that he said he was looking forward to the exercises in Wainwright.

“It’s just not fair. It was a training exercise,” she said, breaking down. “I understand that accidents happen – but why?”

The Prime Minister spoke individually about each of the four victims in Parliament on Monday. He said Sgt. Wong’s family remembered him as “someone who was always there for those who needed him.” He described Pte. Goulding as a young man who “met every hardship with a joke,” adding, “When others struggled, he shouldered more than his share without ever being asked.”

In a statement, Pte. Goulding’s family said he was an exceptional athlete who quit his career as a mechanic to join the Army.

“Although he was making excellent money and had a good life, he decided he wanted to defend his country. His goal was to work for Special OPs and then onto Csis,” his mother, Sonia Monk, and older brother, Wylder Goulding, said.

They described him as “the guy that kept people’s spirits up,” with a contagious laugh and cheeky smile.

“Before he went to basic training, he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”

Mr. Carney said Pte. Lykkemark and Pte. Farrell were best friends who were “seldom seen apart.” Pte. Lykkemark was “known for his gift for lightening a hard day, for his quick wit,” and Pte. Farrell was “a generous and deeply loyal friend.”

He said Pte. Farrell was known in his battalion as the “grandmaster of chess” and planned to spend his career in the Armed Forces.

A statement posted online by family friend Heloise Vermeulen describes Pte. Farrell as “a young man of exceptional character” who was “absolutely devoted to serving his country.”

City officials in Prince Albert, Sask., posted a statement saying the 23-year-old will be remembered as a hometown hero.

On Tuesday, a memorial continued to grow at the front gates of CFB Wainwright, with pictures of the four men surrounded by flowers laid in the prairie grass, and another in support of the injured.

With reports from The Canadian Press

stories.title: The Alberta referendum by the numbers
stories.summary: While final results are still pending, preliminary tallies already reveal how voters have responded to the questions posed by the government
stories.author: Tom Cardoso, Chen Wang, Yang Sun
stories.content:
Five months after Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced her government would call a vote on whether the province should pursue secession from Canada, Albertans at last know the results of its historic referendum.

The separation question, as well as nine other ballot questions on issues such as immigration, social services and judicial appointments, led to intense rhetoric and fierce campaigning. In the end, roughly a quarter of ballots cast supported a new, separate vote that could begin the legal process allowing the Prairie province to secede from Canadian federation.

While final results are still pending – Elections Alberta has said a full count is expected to take several days – preliminary tallies already reveal how voters have responded to the questions posed by the government.

Here’s a look at Alberta’s referendum by the numbers.

Preliminary results show that roughly 62 per cent of the province’s 3.1 million eligible voters cast a ballot on Question 10, which asked whether the province should hold a separate vote that could commence the legal process to separate. Turnout on that question was similar to the 2023 general election, when around 60 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot.

Many voters chose to vote in advance or through a mail-in ballot. Roughly 43 per cent of eligible voters – 1.4-million people – cast a ballot this way during the referendum, according to Elections Alberta. This is far in excess of the 28 per cent of eligible voters who did so in 2023.

But an analysis also found that this turnout wasn’t uniform across the province.

While Elections Alberta has not yet published a breakdown of eligible voters in 2026 for each of the province’s 87 electoral divisions, it has done so for 2025. The Globe tallied up votes on the separation question for each district and compared that to the 2025 eligible-voter figures.

That analysis shows that turnout in divisions won by the United Conservative Party in 2023 was five percentage points higher than in areas that went to the New Democrats.

Preliminary results show that only two of Alberta’s 87 electoral divisions voted in favour of a separation referendum – and, in both cases, it was a slim majority.

Rimbey-Rocky Mountain House-Sundre, represented by United Conservative Party Finance Minister Jason Nixon, saw the strongest support for a separation question, with 51 per cent voting in favour of a referendum. The only other division to vote in favour of a separation question was Central Peace-Notley, represented by Forestry and Parks Minister Todd Loewen, also with 51-per-cent support.

In fact, the next 42 divisions with the most support for a separation referendum were all won by the United Conservative Party in 2023, the data show. On average, areas won by the UCP in 2023 voted for separation 33 per cent of the time, while divisions won by the Alberta New Democratic Party voted for separation roughly 15 per cent of the time.

The NDP district with the strongest support for separation was Banff-Kananaskis, a district located in the Rocky Mountains in southwest Alberta, at 20 per cent. The NDP division most staunchly in support of remaining in Canada was Edmonton-Strathcona, where 10 per cent of valid votes supported a separation referendum.

At a glance, a map of the votes for and against separation falls along familiar Albertan lines: The big-city NDP strongholds of Calgary and Edmonton were strongly in favour of remaining in Canada, while rural areas, which have traditionally gone to the UCP, were more likely to vote to separate.

The Globe analyzed Alberta’s 87 electoral divisions and divided them into four buckets: districts representing Edmonton, those representing Calgary, those representing other major cities and those representing the rest of the province, much of which is rural.

Edmonton and Calgary saw the strongest support for federalism, at roughly 86 and 83 per cent, respectively. Other cities hewed more closely to the provincial average, with 73 per cent of districts voting to remain.

The rest of the province, meanwhile, was more supportive of a separation referendum. Those districts, which represent lesser-populated areas like Camrose, Peace River and Lacombe, saw 60 per cent support for remaining in Canada – a 26-point difference compared to Edmonton.

Indigenous leaders in Alberta have been vocal opponents of Alberta’s separation movement, arguing that a break from Canada would infringe on their negotiated treaty rights.

While Elections Alberta’s data does not identify which votes came from Indigenous people, an analysis of polling stations located within Indigenous communities shows that voters in those areas overwhelmingly want Alberta to continue being a part of the Canadian federation.

The Globe identified 50 voting locations that sit primarily on First Nations land or Métis settlements and were reporting votes as of publication time. Of the 13,602 ballots cast at those locations, 95 per cent were in favour of Alberta remaining in Canada.

Some locations were even more vigorously opposed to separation. At a polling station located on the Tsuut’ina Nation southwest of Calgary, 98 per cent of 342 ballots cast were in favour of Alberta remaining a part of Canada. A polling location on Siksika Nation land that received 512 ballots was 99 per cent in favour of staying in Canada, and a voting location in the Tallcree First Nation, which had counted 102 votes as of publication time, did not see a single ballot cast in favour of separation.

Votes are still being counted on the nine other questions put to people in Alberta. Elections Alberta said it was giving priority to tallying votes on Question 10, which concerns separation.

paragraphs: Five months after Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced her government would call a vote on whether the province should pursue secession from Canada, Albertans at last know the results of its historic referendum.

The separation question, as well as nine other ballot questions on issues such as immigration, social services and judicial appointments, led to intense rhetoric and fierce campaigning. In the end, roughly a quarter of ballots cast supported a new, separate vote that could begin the legal process allowing the Prairie province to secede from Canadian federation.

While final results are still pending – Elections Alberta has said a full count is expected to take several days – preliminary tallies already reveal how voters have responded to the questions posed by the government.
Here’s a look at Alberta’s referendum by the numbers.

Preliminary results show that roughly 62 per cent of the province’s 3.1 million eligible voters cast a ballot on Question 10, which asked whether the province should hold a separate vote that could commence the legal process to separate. Turnout on that question was similar to the 2023 general election, when around 60 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot.

Many voters chose to vote in advance or through a mail-in ballot. Roughly 43 per cent of eligible voters – 1.4-million people – cast a ballot this way during the referendum, according to Elections Alberta. This is far in excess of the 28 per cent of eligible voters who did so in 2023.
But an analysis also found that this turnout wasn’t uniform across the province.

While Elections Alberta has not yet published a breakdown of eligible voters in 2026 for each of the province’s 87 electoral divisions, it has done so for 2025. The Globe tallied up votes on the separation question for each district and compared that to the 2025 eligible-voter figures.
That analysis shows that turnout in divisions won by the United Conservative Party in 2023 was five percentage points higher than in areas that went to the New Democrats.
Preliminary results show that only two of Alberta’s 87 electoral divisions voted in favour of a separation referendum – and, in both cases, it was a slim majority.

Rimbey-Rocky Mountain House-Sundre, represented by United Conservative Party Finance Minister Jason Nixon, saw the strongest support for a separation question, with 51 per cent voting in favour of a referendum. The only other division to vote in favour of a separation question was Central Peace-Notley, represented by Forestry and Parks Minister Todd Loewen, also with 51-per-cent support.

In fact, the next 42 divisions with the most support for a separation referendum were all won by the United Conservative Party in 2023, the data show. On average, areas won by the UCP in 2023 voted for separation 33 per cent of the time, while divisions won by the Alberta New Democratic Party voted for separation roughly 15 per cent of the time.

The NDP district with the strongest support for separation was Banff-Kananaskis, a district located in the Rocky Mountains in southwest Alberta, at 20 per cent. The NDP division most staunchly in support of remaining in Canada was Edmonton-Strathcona, where 10 per cent of valid votes supported a separation referendum.

At a glance, a map of the votes for and against separation falls along familiar Albertan lines: The big-city NDP strongholds of Calgary and Edmonton were strongly in favour of remaining in Canada, while rural areas, which have traditionally gone to the UCP, were more likely to vote to separate.

The Globe analyzed Alberta’s 87 electoral divisions and divided them into four buckets: districts representing Edmonton, those representing Calgary, those representing other major cities and those representing the rest of the province, much of which is rural.

Edmonton and Calgary saw the strongest support for federalism, at roughly 86 and 83 per cent, respectively. Other cities hewed more closely to the provincial average, with 73 per cent of districts voting to remain.

The rest of the province, meanwhile, was more supportive of a separation referendum. Those districts, which represent lesser-populated areas like Camrose, Peace River and Lacombe, saw 60 per cent support for remaining in Canada – a 26-point difference compared to Edmonton.
Indigenous leaders in Alberta have been vocal opponents of Alberta’s separation movement, arguing that a break from Canada would infringe on their negotiated treaty rights.

While Elections Alberta’s data does not identify which votes came from Indigenous people, an analysis of polling stations located within Indigenous communities shows that voters in those areas overwhelmingly want Alberta to continue being a part of the Canadian federation.

The Globe identified 50 voting locations that sit primarily on First Nations land or Métis settlements and were reporting votes as of publication time. Of the 13,602 ballots cast at those locations, 95 per cent were in favour of Alberta remaining in Canada.

Some locations were even more vigorously opposed to separation. At a polling station located on the Tsuut’ina Nation southwest of Calgary, 98 per cent of 342 ballots cast were in favour of Alberta remaining a part of Canada. A polling location on Siksika Nation land that received 512 ballots was 99 per cent in favour of staying in Canada, and a voting location in the Tallcree First Nation, which had counted 102 votes as of publication time, did not see a single ballot cast in favour of separation.
Votes are still being counted on the nine other questions put to people in Alberta. Elections Alberta said it was giving priority to tallying votes on Question 10, which concerns separation.
Preliminary results for most of the other nine other measures – including questions about Senate and judicial appointments, immigration and self-determination – are still close.

Question 5, which asks whether the government should implement stricter voter ID requirements, has the strongest support so far at 64 per cent. Seven other questions have support between 49 and 58 per cent.

As of publication time, only Question 8 – which asks whether voters support amending the Canadian Constitution to “allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education, and social services” – has a majority “no” vote, at 51 per cent. Elections Alberta has said it expects its count to take two days.

stories.title: Danielle Smith makes plea to separatists in televised speech, vows no more secession referendums
stories.summary: The Alberta premier called on disillusioned Albertans to "believe and hope in Canada again" after an emphatic vote to stay in the country.
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
In a province-wide address on Tuesday evening, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith vowed not to hold another referendum on the secession issue, while also urging separatist voters to “believe and hope in Canada again” following Monday’s referendum results.

In her first public remarks since referendum polls closed, the premier again sought to elevate the various deals and major projects her government has signed with Prime Minister Mark Carney in an effort to mend Alberta’s fractured relationship with Ottawa. Her comments came one day after Albertans voted with a decisive three-to-one margin to reject a proposal to hold a second legally-binding vote on whether to leave Confederation.

“And I want to make it clear tonight that for as long as I am premier, I will honour this mandate from Albertans and will not be holding another referendum on this issue,” she said. “It is time to move forward together as a strong and free Alberta within a united Canada.”

As of 7:00 p.m. MT on Tuesday, more than 1.95 million votes had been counted on the referendum’s 10th question, which asked whether Alberta should stay in Canada (Option 1) or hold a second vote on the matter (Option 2). Seventy-five per cent voted to stay in Canada while 25 per cent opted for the second option, with 90 per cent of voting stations reporting results.

Smith, who could now face an internal political reckoning from the very base of pro-independence supporters who helped get her elected, also made a plea to the one out of every four Albertans who supported Option 2.

“You love this province, and you want your family and neighbours to have every opportunity to succeed,” she said. “Many of you view Ottawa as having threatened your freedoms and blocked your path to prosperity. I acknowledge the legitimate frustrations you’ve felt — most especially during the Justin Trudeau Liberal-NDP coalition years.”

The premier based her optimism on a claim that the country has “changed significantly” in the last 1.5 years, evident in Ottawa’s newfound support for expanding oil and gas exports and its recent decision to desginate Alberta’s proposed West Coast oil pipeline as being in the national interest. In recent months, Smith and Carney have announced various major projects like oil project, a proposed passenger rail line between Edmonton and Calgary, and a recent $8-billion commitment toward four military bases in the provinces.

“So tonight I want to invite every Albertan who May still feel hopeless or frustrated with the past direction of our country, to believe and hope in Canada again,” Smith said.

“We are reversing course away from a lost decade and towards a bright future with Alberta’s prosperity at its centre.”

The premier called for patience among Alberta’s most disillusioned voters, who have for decades raised concerns over Ottawa’s mistreatment of the province. Many Albertans have long accused the federal government of choking off personal freedoms, overstepping its jurisdictional boundaries and enacting restrictive environmental policies that stifled oil and gas sector growth, and Smith suggested that frustrations over those matters won’t dissapear overnight.

“I am well aware that not every grievance Alberta has with Ottawa has been resolved,” she said. “There are still many political and constitutional battles ahead of us. But I am also convinced that the federal government is no longer targeting and trying to phase out and eliminate Alberta’s largest economic sectors as they attempted to do under the previous prime minister (Trudeau).”

The premier also commented on the results from the referendum’s other nine questions, for which Albertans seemed mostly poised to support. Five of the 10 referendum questions focused on immigration rates, and proposed giving Alberta more control over immigration and limiting access to some public services for non-permanent residents, among other things. Voters seemed likely to support each of those five questions as of 7:00 p.m. MT, as well as supporting other constitutional questions proposing to, for example, work with provinces to abolish the federal Senate.

“Although results are still coming in, it appears that Albertans have directed the provincial government to take greater control over immigration so we can moderate the extraordinary population growth our province has experienced and prioritize jobs and opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” Smith said. “They have given us direction to ensure temporary residents pay a portion of the cost of public services used by themselves and their families. They have spoken in favour of requiring proof of Canadian citizenship in order to vote.”

She said her UCP government would “continue to boldly assert our province’s autonomy” through provincial rights guaranteed to the provinces under the constitution.

“We will use every legal and political tool at our disposal to protect and advance the interests of Albertans,” she said. “And when Ottawa interferes with those rights, we will be unrelenting in our response.”

But I am also convinced that the federal government is no longer targeting and trying to phase out and eliminate Alberta’s largest economic sectors as they attempted to do under the previous prime minister (Trudeau).”

The premier also commented on the results from the referendum’s other nine questions, for which Albertans seemed mostly poised to support. Five of the 10 referendum questions focused on immigration rates, and proposed giving Alberta more control over immigration and limiting access to some public services for non-permanent residents, among other things. Voters seemed likely to support each of those five questions as of 7:00 p.m. MT, as well as supporting other constitutional questions proposing to, for example, work with provinces to abolish the federal Senate.

“Although results are still coming in, it appears that Albertans have directed the provincial government to take greater control over immigration so we can moderate the extraordinary population growth our province has experienced and prioritize jobs and opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” Smith said. “They have given us direction to ensure temporary residents pay a portion of the cost of public services used by themselves and their families. They have spoken in favour of requiring proof of Canadian citizenship in order to vote.”
She said her UCP government would “continue to boldly assert our province’s autonomy” through provincial rights guaranteed to the provinces under the constitution.

“We will use every legal and political tool at our disposal to protect and advance the interests of Albertans,” she said. “And when Ottawa interferes with those rights, we will be unrelenting in our response.”

stories.title: Alberta First Nations criticize lack of ballots and delays for members to vote in referendum
stories.summary: Elections Alberta says extra ballots were delivered as voter turn out was higher than expected
stories.author: Patrick White, Willow Fiddler
stories.content:
Elections Alberta ran short of ballots in several First Nations during the provincial referendum on Monday, prompting criticism of how the agency administered the vote.

Residents voted on 10 questions, including whether Alberta should remain part of Canada or trigger a subsequent secession vote and others related to immigration and constitutional issues in the referendum, which the province had been planning for months.

The question of separation was of particular interest to First Nations , who have spoken out against it for months and launched legal challenges arguing that it went against treaty rights.

In some communities the ballot shortage led to long waits at polling locations, according to a statement from Siksika Nation, a southern Alberta First Nation with nearly 8,000 members.

“It is unacceptable that First Nations communities continue to encounter barriers to participating fully in Alberta’s democratic processes,” Siksika Chief Samuel Crowfoot said in a statement. “Our people have fought too long for their democratic rights to be treated as an afterthought. The right to vote must be supported by meaningful and equitable access to the ballot box.”

Elections Alberta spokeswoman Michelle Gurney said in an e-mailed statement that the agency delivered extra ballots to five First Nations – three of which received multiple shipments.

Samson Cree Nation, Louis Bull Tribe and Ermineskin Cree Nation received three separate ballot deliveries, she said.

Whitefish First Nation and a voting location serving Siksika Nation and Blood Tribe needed at least one extra delivery.

The agency predicted the number of ballots needed at each of the province’s 1,400 polling stations based on past voter registry data. It sent 1.5 times as many ballots as it deemed necessary, Ms. Gurney said.

“This means we have seen higher turnout at these locations than we have in the past,” she said. “This is a good news story, showing higher voter engagement in these locations.”

But some First Nations leaders saw the miscalculation as a failure to appreciate Indigenous engagement in an issue that so squarely encroaches on treaty rights.

“This shouldn’t have come as a surprise because it was the First Nations people who were most vocal and most against the referendum from the beginning,” said Jay Telegdi, senior manager of intergovernmental affairs for Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation.

First Nations in Alberta have challenged the legality of provincial separation in court, arguing that it would violate treaties with the Crown and breach the government’s duty to consult Indigenous peoples on matters affecting their rights.

Two Alberta judges ruled that First Nations must be considered in the decision to call a referendum on provincial independence. In a December decision, Court of King’s Bench Justice Colin Feasby ruled that “First Nations, as founding partners in the creation of Alberta, cannot be ignored or bypassed as Alberta contemplates its future whether that is as part of Canada or not.”

Last week, a number of First Nations raised concerns that their members were not given the opportunity to vote in advanced polls , which were meant to be available from Oct. 13 through to Oct. 17, because of staff shortages.

Results from voting locations in First Nations across the province were overwhelmingly opposed to separation.

At the Tallcree First Nation band office, a total of 102 voters cast ballots with not a single one favouring independence. And at one location on the Alexis Nakota Sioux Nation, just seven of 363 voters selected separation.

Elections Alberta did not make an overall turnout figure for First Nations available.

In the lead up to the referendum, many First Nations held information sessions and rallies to encourage voting. Some issued social media posts imploring members to vote in favour of remaining in Canada.

“First Nations and Albertan voters turned out in huge numbers and stood up for our shared past, present and future in Canada and rejected a divisive proposal that would bring needless upheaval, conflict and uncertainty for everyone,” Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said in a press release. “The results of this vote speak volumes: We are stronger together.”

With a report from Matthew Scace

stories.title: Two Globe reporters shortlisted for the Lane Anderson Award for Canadian science writing
stories.summary: Greg Mercer, Eric Andrew-Gee are up for annual prize recognizing jury-selected books
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Two Globe and Mail journalists, Greg Mercer and Eric Andrew-Gee , are nominated for the Lane Anderson Award for Canadian science writing.

The annual prize recognizes jury-selected books in two categories, adult and young reader. The winners in both are awarded $10,000.

The shortlisted books in the adult category are Andrew-Gee’s The Mind Mappers: Friendship, Betrayal and the Obsessive Quest to Chart the Brain , published by Penguin Random House Canada; Mercer’s The Lobster Trap: The Global Fight for a Seafood on the Brink , published by McClelland & Stewart; and Sarah Boon’s Meltdown: The Making and Breaking of a Field Scientist , published by University of Alberta Press.

The contenders for the young reader prize are The Buzz on Wild Bees: The Little-Known Pollinators that Keep Our Planet Humming, written by Globe contributor Kira Vermond and illustrated by June Steube for Owlkids Books; The Gland Factory: A Tour of Your Body’s Goops, Juices, and Hormones , written by Rachel Poliquin and illustrated by Clayton Hanmer for Greystone Kids; and The Story and Science of Hope , written by Andrea Curtis and illustrated by Ana Suárez for Groundwood Books.

The award was created in 2010 by the Fitzhenry Family Foundation, a private charitable group founded by Robert Fitzhenry, one of the founding partners of Canadian publishing and distribution company Fitzhenry & Whiteside. The prize’s name originates from the maiden names of his mother, Margaret Lane Fitzhenry, and his wife, Hilda Anderson Fitzhenry.

Recent winners in the adult category include Jennifer Grenz’s Medicine Wheel for the Planet , John Vaillant’s Fire Weather , and Ontario’s Old-Growth Forests by Michael Henry and Peter Quinby.

Prize-takers in the young readers division include A Planet Is a Poem by Amanda West Lewis and Oliver Averill; Polar by L. E. Carmichael and Byron Eggenschwiler; and It Takes Guts by Jennifer Gardy and Belle Wuthrich.

The 2026 award winners will be announced in January at an event in Toronto.
