stories.title: Danielle Smith calls for unity after separatism rejected in Alberta referendum
stories.summary: A day after Alberta voters rejected the idea of further pursuing separating from Canada, the Premier Danielle Smith delivered a message on where the province goes from here.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
One day after Alberta voters rejected the idea of pursuing separation from Canada, Premier Danielle Smith said the turnout was a historic and a powerful testimony of the passion Albertans feel for the country and province.

“Yesterday, Albertans made their choice. Today, we begin the next chapter,” the premier said in a speech that was broadcast Tuesday night during airtime paid for by the Alberta government.

“Let us move forward not as a people divided by how we voted yesterday, but as neighbours, friends, Albertans and Canadians. Let us treat one another with respect and compassion. Let us stand proudly for this province.”

The outcome of the referendum ‘s separatism question mirrors more than half a year of polling, which since the beginning of 2026 consistently showed about 70 per cent of Albertans wanted the province to remain in Canada .

Albertans roundly rejected leaving Canada by roughly 75 per cent, with 1.9 million ballots counted for the separation question as of late Tuesday afternoon, representing about 61.9 per cent of voters so far.

“At the end of it all, the people of Alberta cast their votes in an open and democratic referendum. And the resulting vote from Albertans has given our government a clear mandate.

“Alberta will remain a province of Canada. Albertans will continue to be Canadians.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Alberta will remain a province of Canada. Albertans will continue to be Canadians."

Alberta will continue to assert its autonomy and stand up for the issues important to residents, Smith said, but disputes will be settled within the political and legal institutions rather than pursuing the option of separation.

Smith indicated the question of independence has been put to bed.

“I want to make it clear tonight that for as long as I am premier, I will honour this mandate from Albertans and will not be holding another referendum on this issue,” she said. “It is time to move forward together.”

It was a debate Smith said was many years in the making, as Albertans have struggled to address many long-standing and legitimate grievances with Ottawa .

“I acknowledge the legitimate frustrations you’ve felt.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I acknowledge the legitimate frustrations you've felt."

Nearly half a million ballots were cast in favour of continuing down the road towards leaving Canada. In some ridings such as Central Peace-Notley and Rimbey-Rocky Mountain House-Sundre, the leave votes narrowly outnumbered the ones cast to stay.

Smith addressed those voters directly on Tuesday night.

“I recognize you as loyal Albertans. You love this province, and you want your family and neighbours to have every opportunity to succeed. Many of you view Ottawa as having threatened your freedoms and blocked your path to prosperity,” she said.

“You need to know that your voices have been heard. Not just by our government, but also by your fellow Albertans and your fellow Canadians.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "You need to know that your voices have been heard. Not just by our government, but also by your fellow Albertans and your fellow Canadians."

Smith’s message was one of unity and moving forward.

“Tonight, I want to invite every Albertan who May still feel hopeless or frustrated with the past direction of our country, to believe and hope in Canada again.”

But, it doesn’t appear Smith will get her wish that all Albertans will simply accept the results of the referendum and move on.

Instead, going forward, Smith and the governing United Conservative Party will have to contend with a motivated and more organized separatist movement turning their efforts to oust the premier and take further control of the party.

Jeffrey Rath, one of the central figures in the separatist movement who had a hand in former premier Jason Kenney’s ouster, told Global News he will be pushing for a special general meeting of the party to remove Smith as well.

Smith, in her speech, made the case that Canada has changed significantly over the past 18 months and credited all Albertans for helping make happen.

“I am well aware that not every grievance Alberta has with Ottawa has been resolved. There are still many political and constitutional battles ahead of us,” she said.

“But I am also convinced that the federal government is no longer targeting and trying to phase out and eliminate Alberta’s largest economic sectors as they attempted to do under the previous prime minister.”

“In fact, both the federal Conservatives and federal Liberals are united in supporting Alberta and our key industries in a manner we haven’t seen in a generation.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "In fact, both the federal Conservatives and federal Liberals are united in supporting Alberta and our key industries in a manner we haven't seen in a generation."

Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, Smith said there is a renewed understanding that Canada cannot achieve prosperity by preventing its strongest industries from succeeding.

She said pipelines that were once declared impossible are now being built as national priorities, in reference to the Pacific Link project that received national interest designation on Oct. 1 , with the goal of construction of the line to the B.C. Lower Mainland beginning next September.

“Canada is once again producing more energy, exporting more resources, building more major projects and attracting more investment,” she said. “I believe it’s working better every day, and it can work even better in the future if we keep fighting together for it.”

Smith’s speech was pre-recorded, so she did not answer questions from journalists. Smith is slated to do that on Wednesday at an 11:30 a.m. media availability in Calgary.

While the question of leaving Canada appears to have been put to bed, the results for the other nine referendum questions have revealed Albertans are divided.

Ballots were still being counted by hand as of Tuesday afternoon, but an Elections Alberta website sharing minute-by-minute updates showed the yes option was leading on eight of the nine questions, including all five on immigration.

The leads were tight, ranging from 51 to 63 per cent provincewide .

The questions asked whether Alberta should have more say over who comes to the province to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations — and perhaps introduce fees — on temporary workers who seek access to health care and education.

The remaining four questions asked for Albertans’ blessing for Smith to lobby her provincial counterparts for support on amending the Constitution to take more power from Ottawa and abolish the Senate.

The yes side was leading on all of the immigration questions with roughly 54 to 58 per cent of the votes as of Tuesday afternoon.

One exception was Smith’s question five proposal to require proof of citizenship to vote provincially, which was leading with about two-thirds of the vote.

Broken down geographically, voters in Edmonton said no to all nine questions while in Calgary, voters said no to eight of the questions except question five.

The only question in which the no vote was leading provincewide on Tuesday afternoon — albeit by a tight 51 per cent for “no” to 49 per cent for “yes” — was question eight.

It asked if Alberans would support its government working with other provinces to opt out of federal programs like health care, education, social services without losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs.

Colin Aitchison, a former United Conservative Party press secretary turned government relations consultant, told The Canadian Press the results present a clear mandate for the premier.

“Governments get elected on less than 50 per cent in this country, and then they move forward with implementing a mandate,” said Aitchison, a managing director with Enterprise Canada.

“Regardless of the size of the mandate, it is a clear mandate, and with voter turnout, I think it’s something that (Smith) can definitely point to when she’s trying to negotiate (with Ottawa),” he said.

Smith has said immigration is beneficial to Alberta, but that it must be balanced with the high cost of social services. Her government has yet to give specifics about how the proposals would work or how they would be implemented.

Avnish Nanda, a lawyer who had campaigned against the immigration proposals, said Tuesday he was shocked by the results so far, as he was expecting the questions to pass with much larger margins.

“We thought we would be blown out,” Nanda said in an interview.

Nanda said he didn’t think the results represent the will of Albertans. He pointed to polls that suggest some voters were confused by the wording of the questions and would vote differently depending on how the question was framed.

“These are hard questions (and) a (government) propaganda campaign that has misled Albertans to vote for things that are contrary to, I think, what they actually want and what’s in their best interest.”

On Tuesday, Carney said he favours pursuing pragmatic “common solutions” with the provinces on issues under federal jurisdiction.

When speaking to reporters as he welcomed the rejection of separation , Carney said pursuing constitutional changes can be a difficult, drawn-out process.

Conservative Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre said Tuesday the Liberals allowed immigration to run “totally out of control” and he supports provinces being able to set their own levels.

The prime minister said disputes in areas like immigration can be resolved without constitutional amendments, adding his government has moved to bring immigration back under control.

Smith addressed those voters directly on Tuesday night.

stories.title: Premiers welcome separatist loss in Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Provincial leaders largely steer clear of commenting on other ballot questions about immigration, judges, Senate
stories.author: Jeff Gray
stories.content:
Provincial leaders outside Alberta welcomed the province’s rejection of separatism in Monday’s referendum, but mostly steered clear of the other questions on the ballot, including those that asked Albertans whether they endorse restricting immigration and changing the Constitution.

According to unofficial results posted by Elections Alberta on Tuesday evening, about 75 per cent of voters rejected the separation question, which asked them about holding a future, second vote on leaving Canada.

But for eight of the ballot’s other nine questions, which included proposals for Alberta to take control of immigration, appoint its own higher-court judges and abolish the federal Senate, results showed majorities voting Yes, as Premier Danielle Smith had urged.

Several of these questions raise the spectre of potentially tangled constitutional negotiations, something Canadian politicians have shied away from for decades after the wrenching national debates of the 1980s and 1990s. But some of these ballot items also echo complaints that other premiers have regularly made to Ottawa in recent years.

In a statement posted to X on Tuesday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford praised the result on separation. He also reiterated his vow to build a new pipeline to bring Alberta’s oil to refineries in Ontario, in order to avoid routes that now bring the resource through the United States.

“I’m thrilled by the decisive support Albertans have shown for the country we all love,” Mr. Ford said. “Now it’s up to the rest of Canada to deliver on our commitment to Alberta by building new pipelines, unlocking our natural resources and unleashing the prosperity that will protect the future of Canadians from coast to coast to coast.”

In Saskatchewan, which also has its own small separatist movement, Premier Scott Moe applauded Alberta’s vote to remain in Canada. But he also said the West’s grievances within Confederation need to be addressed.

“There is still work to be done on improving how Western Canada is treated by Ottawa,” Mr. Moe said on X. “But Canada is worth that effort. Saskatchewan will continue to work with Alberta to make our provinces stronger within a united Canada.”

In Quebec, where separatist Parti Québécois just returned to power, premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said the results on the other nine questions show Albertans agree with Quebeckers that Confederation, and an “increasingly interventionist” federal government, are not working.

“As in Quebec, they recognize that the Canadian federation is a straitjacket that prevents them from placing their priorities at the heart of their own public policies, in order to meet their own needs,” he said in a statement on X.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who will be sworn in as premier on Wednesday, has promised to hold a third referendum on independence in Quebec, though not before 2029.

B.C. Premier David Eby, who, as his province’s NDP Leader was campaigning for re-election in Kelowna on Tuesday, thanked Albertans who voted to stay in Canada.

“It feels like a no-brainer to me, but I am glad to see that was confirmed by the people of Alberta,” Mr. Eby said. “We’re stronger together as a country.”

Speaking to reporters in Winnipeg, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew congratulated Albertans for voting to “remain a part of the No. 1 country on Earth.”

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston also welcomed the referendum results. “Canada is stronger with Alberta as part of it, and last night’s results show the overwhelming majority of Albertans agree with this,” he said on X.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham, who leads a province that many have left to work in Alberta, said he was delighted with the vote. When asked about the quarter of Albertans who chose the separatist option, Mr. Wakeham told reporters at the techNL Summit in St. John’s that many people are frustrated with governments.

“Nothing is perfect, and so we have to find ways to keep moving forward and improve the lives of people, whether they are in our own province or in another province,” he said.

Among the other referendum questions that received majority support from Albertans was one about the province seeking more power over immigration to cut it to “more sustainable levels.” Voters also endorsed proposals that would create an “Alberta-approved immigration status,” and restrict access to health care and other services for those with non-permanent status.

Ontario and other provinces have also long advocated for more control over immigration policy, pointing to Quebec’s degree of autonomy in the area – even as Ottawa has recently slashed immigration levels.

Albertans also voted Yes to a question on changing the Constitution to appoint higher-court judges provincially, rather than federally. In a March open letter, Mr. Moe, Ms. Smith, Mr. Ford and then-Quebec-premier François Legault asked Ottawa to ensure all candidates for higher-court judicial appointments are both recommended and approved by the provincial government concerned. Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser flatly rejected the idea at the time.

With reports from Jameson Berkow, Maura Forrest and Ian Bailey

B.C. Premier David Eby, who, as his province’s NDP Leader was campaigning for re-election in Kelowna on Tuesday, thanked Albertans who voted to stay in Canada.
“It feels like a no-brainer to me, but I am glad to see that was confirmed by the people of Alberta,” Mr. Eby said. “We’re stronger together as a country.”
Speaking to reporters in Winnipeg, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew congratulated Albertans for voting to “remain a part of the No. 1 country on Earth.”

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston also welcomed the referendum results. “Canada is stronger with Alberta as part of it, and last night’s results show the overwhelming majority of Albertans agree with this,” he said on X.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham, who leads a province that many have left to work in Alberta, said he was delighted with the vote. When asked about the quarter of Albertans who chose the separatist option, Mr. Wakeham told reporters at the techNL Summit in St. John’s that many people are frustrated with governments.
“Nothing is perfect, and so we have to find ways to keep moving forward and improve the lives of people, whether they are in our own province or in another province,” he said.

Among the other referendum questions that received majority support from Albertans was one about the province seeking more power over immigration to cut it to “more sustainable levels.” Voters also endorsed proposals that would create an “Alberta-approved immigration status,” and restrict access to health care and other services for those with non-permanent status.

Ontario and other provinces have also long advocated for more control over immigration policy, pointing to Quebec’s degree of autonomy in the area – even as Ottawa has recently slashed immigration levels.

Albertans also voted Yes to a question on changing the Constitution to appoint higher-court judges provincially, rather than federally. In a March open letter, Mr. Moe, Ms. Smith, Mr. Ford and then-Quebec-premier François Legault asked Ottawa to ensure all candidates for higher-court judicial appointments are both recommended and approved by the provincial government concerned. Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser flatly rejected the idea at the time.

stories.title: Accused Toronto airport gold heist gang turned on each other in nasty fight for loot
stories.summary: As a police net tightened, suspects fled Canada, tried to dodge surveillance, hired lawyers, and viciously turned against one another.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
While suspects in the Toronto airport gold heist were under intense, around-the-clock police surveillance, one of them franticly made increasingly angry and desperate phone calls chasing down money, feeling cheated and abandoned by his friends, court heard.

“It’s already falling apart,” a caller identified in court as Parmpal Sidhu said over the phone nine months after more than $22.5 million in gold bars and cash was stolen after arriving at Pearson airport on a flight from Switzerland.

As a police net tightened around them, suspects fled Canada, tried to dodge surveillance, hired expensive lawyers and viciously turned against one another, police wiretaps show.

“Everybody’s on their own. Everybody’s worried about themselves,” he said in a call. “Everyone got money and I’m stuck here,” he said in another.

Sidhu was an Air Canada employee in the Pearson airport cargo warehouse from where the crate was stolen on April 17, 2023. He was arrested April 5, 2024, one of the first of nine men to be charged and the first to plead not guilty and face trial in the spectacular case. Only about a kilogram of the gold has been recovered.

His trial on Tuesday in Ontario Superior Court in Brampton, Ont., heard a handful of the thousands of wiretap recordings Peel Regional Police made in their probe.

“I am not paying 10 grand for this lawyer. I am going to make a f–king deal. I’m in my car. My other phone is here. It’s probably tapped. I got a tracker on my phone. I am fed up of the lies,” he said in a call.

“You guys literally threw me in the ditch. That’s what you did.

“I’ve been trying to get you guys to do the right thing. Nobody’s listening to me, and now I’m the one who’s getting all the f–king heat.”

The phone calls, by a voice identified by a Peel police officer as Sidhu’s, reveal a man facing a financial apocalypse. His credit cards were maxed; his American Express card had been declined; he took money out of his line of credit, “freaking out” his wife. He spoke of borrowing from his mother.

“I am not joking,” he said in one call, “I am telling you, I am in a hole, and I am going to have to look out for myself.”

Peel police Det. Sarah Angevine testified that people suspected of pulling off the largest gold heist in Canadian history were under police scrutiny, including physical surveillance, phone wiretaps and microphone probes planted in their homes and cars.

The wiretap recordings, most of which are partially obscured by background music and noise, show an apparent escalation of paranoia, anger, financial problems and efforts to be paid money.

Angevine said the people on the wiretaps often used code names or nicknames for people that police believed to be some of the others accused in the heist.

There are references to someone called by the Punjabi word for “Black,” believed to be code for Durante King-Mclean, the accused driver in the gold heist who is Black and the only person not of South Asian descent accused in the heist.

Someone named “Grove” is a reference to Archit Grover, Angevine said, who is accused of supplying the truck used to move the stolen gold from the airport warehouse.

There are also references to someone referred to as “Dubai.” Court heard earlier that Ansalan Chaudhary, who admitted he was one of the masterminds of the heist, had flown to Dubai after the heist.

“This is what Dubai doesn’t f–king understand: I’ll make sure if I lose my cut then f–king Grove will lose his too,” Sidhu is heard saying in one of the wiretaps, court heard. “You think Grove’s just gonna walk away unscathed? No f–king chance.”

He also complained of people leaving Canada after the heist — “who’ve just taken off and left,” he said. Grover, Chaudhary and the man who court heard was the second mastermind behind the heist, Simran Preet Panesar, a former Air Canada manager, are all known to have travelled abroad.

Sidhu complained in another call, “I didn’t know he was going to f–king vanish,” court heard. “His promises are absolutely, utterly worthless.”

He implored the person on the other end of one call to intercede on his behalf: “Make it clear. You need to explain the situation,” he said. He said the guy “didn’t believe me that I got charged.”

“You know how f–king angry it makes me, because I never cheated anybody.”

He also made apparent threats amid his anger.

“I’m going to f–king tear him apart now,” he said.

In a call on Jan. 14, 2024, he said he had been warned he “can’t go after them” or he risks being “arrested,” but that money was coming, however, it is “not going to be what you’re expecting.”’

By the sound of the calls, the payout never came.

In one call, he is heard musing with someone about sending a frightening message with what sounds like a drive-by shooting.

“Can somebody just go there and like spray them — not hurt anybody — but spray like the cars, the house, or something like that, or whatever. Something to worry?”

Court also heard that an analysis of Sidhu’s phone records showed he talked and texted with Panesar, his Air Canada manager and fellow accused in the heist, more than he did with his wife before the theft.

Court heard that three months before the Toronto airport gold heist, a bank draft for $30,000 was deposited into Sidhu’s bank account.

Const. Michael Asanin, a Peel police fraud investigator, testified that he examined 1,121 pages of bank records for Sidhu, spanning several bank accounts and pointed out a large bank draft deposit of $30,000 on Jan. 5, 2023, which was three months before the gold heist.

Sidhu’s lawyer, Shale Wagman, asked Asanin if he knew whether the gold heist plot was underway at the time of the deposit. He said he didn’t know.

Wagman asked him if the money could have an innocent source.

“I have nothing to say that this particular draft was or was not fraudulent,” Asanin said.

The trial continues.

content_blocks.text: Court also heard that an analysis of Sidhu’s phone records showed he talked and texted with Panesar, his Air Canada manager and fellow accused in the heist, more than he did with his wife before the theft.
Court heard that three months before the Toronto airport gold heist, a bank draft for $30,000 was deposited into Sidhu’s bank account.

Const. Michael Asanin, a Peel police fraud investigator, testified that he examined 1,121 pages of bank records for Sidhu, spanning several bank accounts and pointed out a large bank draft deposit of $30,000 on Jan. 5, 2023, which was three months before the gold heist.
Sidhu’s lawyer, Shale Wagman, asked Asanin if he knew whether the gold heist plot was underway at the time of the deposit. He said he didn’t know.
Wagman asked him if the money could have an innocent source.
“I have nothing to say that this particular draft was or was not fraudulent,” Asanin said.
The trial continues.

stories.title: ‘You just feel so helpless’: Family of soldier badly burned in CFB Wainwright fire holds onto hope
stories.summary: The family of a 24-year-old Canadian soldier seriously injured in a deadly fire at CFB Wainwright is holding on to hope as he faces a long and uncertain recovery.
stories.author: Kathy Le
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Edson, Alta. - The family of a 24-year-old Canadian soldier seriously injured in a deadly fire at CFB Wainwright is holding on to hope as he faces a long and uncertain recovery.

Cpl. Sean Hiatt, who grew up near Edson, Alta., suffered second-degree burns to approximately half his body in Saturday’s fire, which killed four soldiers and injured 39 others . He is being treated at the University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton, which has a specialized burn treatment unit.

“We have each other,” said Teresa Hiatt, his older sister. “And we know that Sean would want us to be strong too.”

Despite the heartbreak, Teresa and Sara Dizon, Sean’s girlfriend of four years, shared smiles as they sat together inside Teresa’s coffee shop in Edson.

The business is temporarily closed as Teresa focuses on supporting her brother. Both women are determined to remain positive, saying that’s what Sean would want.

“Sean is very easy to love,” Sara said, describing him as outgoing and bubbly.

But behind those smiles are memories of a terrifying weekend that neither woman will soon forget.

Teresa was out for dinner Saturday when she came across a social media post about an incident at CFB Wainwright. Knowing her brother was there for military training, she immediately contacted Sara to find out when she had last heard from him.

“I kept telling my husband, like, I can’t do this, I can’t do this, I can’t do this,” Teresa recalled.

Her husband began calling hospitals, eventually learning that Sean had been taken to hospital in Wainwright.

Sara, meanwhile, repeatedly tried calling her boyfriend, but received no answer.

When Sean’s mother called her in tears, Sara feared the worst.

“She was like, ‘he is alive.’ And I’m like, ‘thank God.’ That’s everything that we had to know at that time,” she recalled.

‘The nation is in mourning’: Canada’s leaders react to Wainwright tragedy

The following morning, Teresa and Sara travelled to Edmonton, where Sean had been transferred for specialized care. Nothing could have prepared them for what they saw.

Sean was sedated, with a breathing tube down his throat and bandages covering his face. His ears and nose had also been burned.

“We both broke,” Teresa said.

“You just wanted to take him into your arms and just, like, hold him and tell him it was OK,” she said. “You just feel so helpless.”

Sara said seeing the man she loves in such a condition was devastating.

“I never saw him like that. It was very hard,” she said. “And I can’t stop imagining what he’d been through.”

The tragedy unfolded Saturday afternoon as soldiers conducted live-fire training at the military base in Alberta. Military officials say a nearby grass fire, initially considered under control, was driven by a sudden shift in powerful winds, rapidly overtaking soldiers in the training area.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

For Sean’s family, the immediate concern is getting him through the critical early stages of recovery.

What happened at Wainwright? Canada’s top general tells CTV News the inquiry findings will be made public.

Teresa said doctors are focused on stabilizing his condition while assessing the extent of his injuries, including possible damage from smoke inhalation. He May require surgeries and skin grafts.

Doctors have warned the family that recovery will be a marathon, not a sprint.

For now, even the smallest movements offer hope.

“When we said goodbye to him last night, he actually wiggled his thumb,” Teresa recalled. “We were just so happy to see that.”

For the family, it was a small but meaningful moment as they wait for signs of recovery.

Sean comes from a family of 11 siblings, with relatives living in different communities and provinces. His parents are staying in Edmonton, while other family members are trying to balance work, children and travel to be at his bedside.

Teresa said the support from the military community has been overwhelming, with veterans, restaurants and others providing food and assistance to families at the hospital.

“The military family is very close. We’re getting a glimpse of that, and now I know why he loved it,” she said.

The tragedy has also left the family grieving for the soldiers who died. Teresa said one of those killed was someone Sean knew from his military unit, adding another emotional challenge he May face during his recovery.

For Sara, the message to her boyfriend is simple: his loved ones will be waiting and fighting alongside him for as long as it takes.

“We’re just here for him,” she said. “We’re not giving up this easy. And we know that he’s not giving up too.”

“He’s very tough. He doesn’t go down that easy.”

stories.title: Local developer commits to affordable apartments under $1,000 a month
stories.summary: Royal Premier Homes is constructing an eight-storey, 170 unit, apartment building at 801 Sarnia Rd. that will include 17 highly-affordable units renting at just $990 per month for the next 10 years.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Royal Premier Homes is constructing an eight-storey, 170 unit, apartment building at 801 Sarnia Rd. that will include 17 highly-affordable units renting at just $990 per month for the next 10 years.

“We’re from London. We’re building London,” explained V.P. Dimen Noory. “We really like to make positive commitments, (and) positive attributes to anything that we do in our builds.”

On Tuesday, Royal Premier Homes held an event at the construction site to announce its commitment that 10 per cent of the units in the building will be highly-affordable housing.

Jared Zaifman, CEO of the London Home Builders Association (Lhba) says its members are aware of the growing demand for very affordable units.

“The challenge for our members is simply the cost to build these days has escalated so much that, unfortunately, trying to create units that are below $1,000 to rent per month is very challenging,” Zaifman told CTV News.

Mayor Josh Morgan said a decision by city council earlier this term that allowed developers to stack financial incentives for affordable units together was crucial.

“We said to (city) staff, we’ve got to align the Dollars for Doors program with the Cmhc (Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation) incentives,” Morgan explained. “When you put those two things together, you can actually drive a deeper level of affordability than what we’ve been seeing across the city.”

Zaifman agreed that it takes coordination by all three levels of government, “Seeing close to 20 units here in this building is really amazing, but it wouldn’t happen without the partnership with the city, with the province, and with the federal government.

Royal Premier Homes began constructing single family homes over 20 years ago, and more recently started constructing townhomes.

The building on Sarnia Road is their first venture into apartment buildings.

“It’s going to be oriented to all renting groups, so we’re happy to welcome everyone when the doors open,” Noory said.

Construction is on schedule to have tenants begin moving in by next September.

stories.title: ‘Old school’ singer Sass Jordan was known for her raw vocal power
stories.summary: The Juno winner shared stages with some of the world’s biggest rock acts, including Van Halen, AC/DC and Aerosmith, and later found a new audience as a judge on Canadian Idol
stories.author: Alexander Hackett
stories.content:
It is rare now for professional musicians to perform without in-ear monitors, especially in front of large audiences. Going without them involves the risk of poor sound, deafening volumes and not being able to hear yourself sing.

But Sass Jordan, undaunted, did just that at Toronto’s SARSstock benefit concert in 2003, in front of 500,000 people.

“Sass was old school,” said Derek Sharp, her husband and musical partner of 30 years. “From the first song, she unplugged her in-ears and sang the whole show without them. It’s just a skill from another time.”

Ms. Jordan, who died on Oct. 2 at the age of 65 of an undisclosed illness, was a Canadian rock icon and a raw-throated, powerhouse vocalist. She was also known to television audiences as a judge on Canadian Idol , appearing in all six seasons of the reality show from 2003 to 2008.

She spent a freewheeling youth in the rock ‘n’ roll trenches, leaving home at age 14, establishing herself in the local music scene and later touring for years throughout Quebec, Ontario and the Maritimes. She never looked back – an embodiment of the rock and roll road warrior.

Following the release of her debut Tell Somebody in 1988, she won a Juno Award for most promising female vocalist and relocated to Los Angeles. Her 1992 album Racine sold 450,000 copies in the United States and Canada, propelled by the hard-rocking, gospel-tinged single Make You A Believer . Billboard Magazine named her 1992’s Top Female Rock Artist of the year.

Trust In Me , a duet with Joe Cocker, appeared on the soundtrack to Whitney Houston movie The Bodyguard , which sold 45 million copies – the highest-selling film soundtrack of all time. Her success led her to tour and share stages with acts such as Van Halen, AC/DC, Aerosmith and the Steve Miller Band.

“Sass was tough, but also kind and generous,” her former manager and fellow Canadian Idol judge Jake Gold said. “That comes from years and years of being on the road. She was a trailblazer. There weren’t a lot of women fronting rock bands in the 80s and 90s, y’know?”

“There was a wisdom to her,” said singer-songwriter Emm Gryner. “Of all the bands I’ve been in, from David Bowie to Gowan, I learned the most about singing from Sass. She sang how she lived, which is just full out.”

Ms. Jordan’s professional life was interwoven with some of the biggest rock acts of her day – a situation her husband called “very Forrest Gump-like.”

At a Foo Fighters show in Toronto in 2015, the band invited her onstage for a cover of the Faces song Stay With Me . Drummer Taylor Hawkins introduced her as the person who had “taught a 22-year-old greenhorn like me how to be in a rock band, and gave me my first rock and roll cheque.”

Singer Dave Grohl went further: “If it weren’t for Sass Jordan, Taylor Hawkins wouldn’t be in the Foo Fighters!”

“We used to joke that if you played with her, you’d go on to be the biggest thing ever,” Mr. Sharp said. Mr. Hawkins went on to tour with Alanis Morissette, while another former bandmate, Peter Barbeau, joined Céline Dion’s band.

Born in Birmingham, England, ON Dec. 23, 1960, Sarah (Sass) Jordan moved to Montreal with her family when she was three and grew up in Westmount. Her father, Albert Jordan, was a professor of French literature at Sir George Williams University (now Concordia) and her mother, Jean Lanceman, was a classically trained dancer who performed for the Rambert Dance Company in London in the 1950s.

Sass’s first turns in front of the camera came as a girl in the NFB documentary The India Trip, which came out in 1971. Her family had moved to Pondicherry for a year, and those events were documented by filmmaker Bill Davies.

“We crossed the Atlantic on a Russian freighter and got off in Karachi, I think it was,” said her brother, Daniel Jordan. “We had a grand old time. In the film, you can see glimpses of Sass when she was nine, singing at the school she attended, and sitting with Indian girls picking nits out of each other’s hair.”

In India the Jordans rode the last of the country’s old steam trains, and spent time with the spiritual guru Mirra Alfassa, also known as The Mother. These experiences were formative for Sass and sowed a seed of deep spirituality within her.

The family home in Montreal was filled with classical music, but rock ’n’ roll came as a revelation. She started singing and playing guitar with friends in Westmount Park in the early 1970s, and by 16 was fronting bands in Montreal clubs. She sang and played bass for the local outfit the Pinups, and got used to the touring grind early on.

“They did the Quebec and northern Ontario circuit, all the little towns,” Mr. Sharp explained. “You had to play, like, six sets a night, until 3 a.m. You’d play for six nights, and you’d travel on Sunday, and then play the next week somewhere else. It was this constant playing of covers and then you’d slip in an original here and there. That’s how it was back then.”

Championed by local impresario Donald K. Donald in the early 1980s, she signed with Montreal’s Aquarius Records, home to acts such as April Wine and Corey Hart. The label paid her rent while she trekked across town every day to hone her songwriting chops with friend and musical partner Bill Beaudoin.

Around this time, she joined Montreal new wave band the Box as a backup singer. “I met her in 1982,” said Jean-Marc Pisapia, the Box’s lead singer and songwriter. “She came to an audition with [Québec singer] Marie Carmen, who also went on to do her own thing. They stayed with us for four and five years, respectively.”

“She was an incredible trooper, not bothered by the darker sides of the industry,” Mr. Pisapia added. “She navigated it all like she’d be doing it her whole life. I remember her at breakfast in the hotels checking out the hockey scores in the Journal de Montréal. . . She was an extremely versatile person, and very, very intelligent. She just adapted. And I think it showed in her career. That was Sass Jordan.”

In such a well-lived life, there are inevitably too many stories to tell. But standout tales include being courted to sing for Van Halen and charming LSD guru Timothy Leary so completely that he invited her to his death party.

On a blog post on her website, Ms. Jordan recalled being invited for secretive jams with Eddie and Alex Van Halen in Los Angeles, without realizing they were auditioning her to be their new singer. “When she found out, she said ‘That’s the worst idea in the world – a female singer in Van Halen!’” Mr. Sharp said. The gig went to Gary Cherone instead.

Of Mr. Leary, Mr. Sharp said, “They met in L.A. and she didn’t know who he was, but he took to her right away. He invited her to his death party, and wrote her this letter about how much he loved her.” Mr. Leary eventually died in his sleep, but Ms. Jordan was present in the days before, along with people like Oliver Stone and Yoko Ono.

There’s no justice in the music industry, and after Racine there was a sense that she never reached the level of success that others had predicted for her. Angsty grunge music took over the airwaves, musical tastes shifted, and her style of blues-tinged rock fell out of favour somewhat.

But she kept working. In the early 2000s she starred in theatrical productions of the Vagina Monologues in Toronto and Winnipeg, and Love, Janis, an off-Broadway musical stage show about Janis Joplin, which led to the Canadian Idol gig.

Her last moments, surrounded by family, “couldn’t have been more beautiful,” Mr. Sharp said. She didn’t want a funeral or anything. She didn’t want people to make a fuss.”

“She did not believe in death,” added her brother. “She believed that when you die, you return to your natural state. You come into this life to do three or four things – those things are going to happen, no matter what. Everything in between is free will. She marched straight into this life, and she exited stage right. Then she was gone. She wouldn’t have had it any other way.”

Sarah (Sass) Jordan leaves her husband, Mr. Sharp; daughter, Stella Jordan-Sharp; stepdaughter, Brianne Sharp; brother, Daniel Jordan; and father, Albert Jordan.

paragraphs: It is rare now for professional musicians to perform without in-ear monitors, especially in front of large audiences. Going without them involves the risk of poor sound, deafening volumes and not being able to hear yourself sing.
But Sass Jordan, undaunted, did just that at Toronto’s SARSstock benefit concert in 2003, in front of 500,000 people.

“Sass was old school,” said Derek Sharp, her husband and musical partner of 30 years. “From the first song, she unplugged her in-ears and sang the whole show without them. It’s just a skill from another time.”

Ms. Jordan, who died on Oct. 2 at the age of 65 of an undisclosed illness, was a Canadian rock icon and a raw-throated, powerhouse vocalist. She was also known to television audiences as a judge on Canadian Idol , appearing in all six seasons of the reality show from 2003 to 2008.

She spent a freewheeling youth in the rock ‘n’ roll trenches, leaving home at age 14, establishing herself in the local music scene and later touring for years throughout Quebec, Ontario and the Maritimes. She never looked back – an embodiment of the rock and roll road warrior.

Following the release of her debut Tell Somebody in 1988, she won a Juno Award for most promising female vocalist and relocated to Los Angeles. Her 1992 album Racine sold 450,000 copies in the United States and Canada, propelled by the hard-rocking, gospel-tinged single Make You A Believer . Billboard Magazine named her 1992’s Top Female Rock Artist of the year.

Trust In Me , a duet with Joe Cocker, appeared on the soundtrack to Whitney Houston movie The Bodyguard , which sold 45 million copies – the highest-selling film soundtrack of all time. Her success led her to tour and share stages with acts such as Van Halen, AC/DC, Aerosmith and the Steve Miller Band.

“Sass was tough, but also kind and generous,” her former manager and fellow Canadian Idol judge Jake Gold said. “That comes from years and years of being on the road. She was a trailblazer. There weren’t a lot of women fronting rock bands in the 80s and 90s, y’know?”

“There was a wisdom to her,” said singer-songwriter Emm Gryner. “Of all the bands I’ve been in, from David Bowie to Gowan, I learned the most about singing from Sass. She sang how she lived, which is just full out.”
Ms. Jordan’s professional life was interwoven with some of the biggest rock acts of her day – a situation her husband called “very Forrest Gump-like.”

At a Foo Fighters show in Toronto in 2015, the band invited her onstage for a cover of the Faces song Stay With Me . Drummer Taylor Hawkins introduced her as the person who had “taught a 22-year-old greenhorn like me how to be in a rock band, and gave me my first rock and roll cheque.”
Singer Dave Grohl went further: “If it weren’t for Sass Jordan, Taylor Hawkins wouldn’t be in the Foo Fighters!”

“We used to joke that if you played with her, you’d go on to be the biggest thing ever,” Mr. Sharp said. Mr. Hawkins went on to tour with Alanis Morissette, while another former bandmate, Peter Barbeau, joined Céline Dion’s band.

Born in Birmingham, England, ON Dec. 23, 1960, Sarah (Sass) Jordan moved to Montreal with her family when she was three and grew up in Westmount. Her father, Albert Jordan, was a professor of French literature at Sir George Williams University (now Concordia) and her mother, Jean Lanceman, was a classically trained dancer who performed for the Rambert Dance Company in London in the 1950s.

Sass’s first turns in front of the camera came as a girl in the NFB documentary The India Trip, which came out in 1971. Her family had moved to Pondicherry for a year, and those events were documented by filmmaker Bill Davies.

“We crossed the Atlantic on a Russian freighter and got off in Karachi, I think it was,” said her brother, Daniel Jordan. “We had a grand old time. In the film, you can see glimpses of Sass when she was nine, singing at the school she attended, and sitting with Indian girls picking nits out of each other’s hair.”

In India the Jordans rode the last of the country’s old steam trains, and spent time with the spiritual guru Mirra Alfassa, also known as The Mother. These experiences were formative for Sass and sowed a seed of deep spirituality within her.

The family home in Montreal was filled with classical music, but rock ’n’ roll came as a revelation. She started singing and playing guitar with friends in Westmount Park in the early 1970s, and by 16 was fronting bands in Montreal clubs. She sang and played bass for the local outfit the Pinups, and got used to the touring grind early on.

“They did the Quebec and northern Ontario circuit, all the little towns,” Mr. Sharp explained. “You had to play, like, six sets a night, until 3 a.m. You’d play for six nights, and you’d travel on Sunday, and then play the next week somewhere else. It was this constant playing of covers and then you’d slip in an original here and there. That’s how it was back then.”

Championed by local impresario Donald K. Donald in the early 1980s, she signed with Montreal’s Aquarius Records, home to acts such as April Wine and Corey Hart. The label paid her rent while she trekked across town every day to hone her songwriting chops with friend and musical partner Bill Beaudoin.

Around this time, she joined Montreal new wave band the Box as a backup singer. “I met her in 1982,” said Jean-Marc Pisapia, the Box’s lead singer and songwriter. “She came to an audition with [Québec singer] Marie Carmen, who also went on to do her own thing. They stayed with us for four and five years, respectively.”

“She was an incredible trooper, not bothered by the darker sides of the industry,” Mr. Pisapia added. “She navigated it all like she’d be doing it her whole life. I remember her at breakfast in the hotels checking out the hockey scores in the Journal de Montréal. . . She was an extremely versatile person, and very, very intelligent. She just adapted. And I think it showed in her career. That was Sass Jordan.”

In such a well-lived life, there are inevitably too many stories to tell. But standout tales include being courted to sing for Van Halen and charming LSD guru Timothy Leary so completely that he invited her to his death party.

On a blog post on her website, Ms. Jordan recalled being invited for secretive jams with Eddie and Alex Van Halen in Los Angeles, without realizing they were auditioning her to be their new singer. “When she found out, she said ‘That’s the worst idea in the world – a female singer in Van Halen!’” Mr. Sharp said. The gig went to Gary Cherone instead.

Of Mr. Leary, Mr. Sharp said, “They met in L.A. and she didn’t know who he was, but he took to her right away. He invited her to his death party, and wrote her this letter about how much he loved her.” Mr. Leary eventually died in his sleep, but Ms. Jordan was present in the days before, along with people like Oliver Stone and Yoko Ono.

There’s no justice in the music industry, and after Racine there was a sense that she never reached the level of success that others had predicted for her. Angsty grunge music took over the airwaves, musical tastes shifted, and her style of blues-tinged rock fell out of favour somewhat.

But she kept working. In the early 2000s she starred in theatrical productions of the Vagina Monologues in Toronto and Winnipeg, and Love, Janis, an off-Broadway musical stage show about Janis Joplin, which led to the Canadian Idol gig.
Her last moments, surrounded by family, “couldn’t have been more beautiful,” Mr. Sharp said. She didn’t want a funeral or anything. She didn’t want people to make a fuss.”

“She did not believe in death,” added her brother. “She believed that when you die, you return to your natural state. You come into this life to do three or four things – those things are going to happen, no matter what. Everything in between is free will. She marched straight into this life, and she exited stage right. Then she was gone. She wouldn’t have had it any other way.”
Sarah (Sass) Jordan leaves her husband, Mr. Sharp; daughter, Stella Jordan-Sharp; stepdaughter, Brianne Sharp; brother, Daniel Jordan; and father, Albert Jordan.

stories.title: Under cross-examination woman maintains she was sexually assaulted
stories.summary: The woman at the centre of a sexual assault case involving a retired London high school teacher spent the entire day on the stand under heavy cross-examination from the defence.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
The woman at the centre of a sexual assault case involving a retired London high school teacher spent the entire day on the stand under heavy cross-examination from the defence.

Lawyer Lakin Afolabi who represents the accused questioned the woman’s memory.

She has testified that Murray MacDonald, now 68, sexually assaulted her in the mid-1980’s when he was her biology teacher and swim coach at Central Secondary School in downtown London.

The woman who cannot be identified has told the court that the alleged incident took place when she was in grade 11 and they ran into each other at The Bavarian, a one-time bar located in Cherryhill Village Mall on Oxford Street West.

She has testified that it happened when he drove her home, claiming that she was groped and forced to perform a sexual act in a dark parking lot.

The court has heard about a troubled home life and that’s why she said, “I had no one to tell, no one at home to tell, no one at school.”

She said that’s why she kept it to herself.

She also testified about how MacDonald acted as a swim coach on the pool deck with comments to students about muscles and massaging, “I recall there was a feeling of inappropriate behaviour by him.”

Afolabi questioned her about her memory, “If I suggest to you that those things didn’t happen?” She replied, “Those things did happen...I’m not fabricating anything.”

When asked about the four decades that have passed before going to police she said, “I’ve had the same memories for 40 years.”

MacDonald who has since retired as a teacher and principal, has plead not guilty to one count of sexual assault.

The woman who is now in her mid-50s has since moved out of London.

When she completed her testimony, the Crown wrapped up its case.

The trial is now in the hands of the defence when the case resumes on Wednesday.

stories.title: Expert weighs in on MS misdiagnoses after celebrity’s revelation
stories.summary: Misdiagnosis of the disease is uncommon, says director of the Multiple Sclerosis Research Unit at the Ottawa Hospital
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
American actress Christina Applegate, who is often remembered for her role as Kelly Bundy on the hit TV show Married With Children that aired from the late 80s to late 90s, said this week that she was wrongly diagnosed with multiple sclerosis.

Ms. Applegate first announced in 2021 that she had been diagnosed with the disorder that causes the immune system to attack the cells in the central nervous system.

On Tuesday, The Globe and Mail spoke with Dr. Mark Freedman, an internationally recognized neurologist who serves as director of the Multiple Sclerosis Research Unit at the Ottawa Hospital, to learn more about the disease and how common it is to be misdiagnosed.

MS is considered an autoimmune disease. There are many autoimmune diseases. Every organ of the body has an autoimmune disease associated with it.

In MS, the autoimmune target is the insulation of the wires of the central nervous system, called myelin.

Anywhere you have the central nervous system, myelin is open to attack from the immune system. It includes what some people don’t realize: the optic nerve.

The optic nerve is an extension of the brain and it’s coated with myelin, similar to the way the rest of the brain and spinal cord are.

Your brain controls everything, right? So depending on where the attack occurs, you could have a multitude of different symptoms, or you could have no symptoms at all.

We actually just published a brand-new series of criteria about a year ago. This was an international effort at trying to really line up the clues for MS.

Every rendition of our diagnostic criteria had two things in mind. Number one: make sure that if you put the label of MS, it really is MS. The second is to try to diagnose the disease earlier, so there’s an opportunity for treatments. The earlier you introduce an effective treatment, the better the long-term outcome.

In Canada, I would say it’s very uncommon. Most of the neurologists in our country are highly trained in usually large academic centres. We always train fellows. That’s not the case in other countries, such as the U.S.

The disease has become so complex, not only in terms of the diagnosis but also in the therapies that we apply.

Quite frankly, there’s not enough trained MS specialists in the U.S. to handle all their patients.

Psychologically, would you really want to be labelled with a disease you don’t have? I would err on the side of “This could be MS, but I’m not convinced of it, and I need to do more tests or I need more time.”

The drugs that we’re using today are actually quite complex and very expensive. Do I want to commit a patient to a therapy they don’t need and could be potentially harmful to them? I don’t want to do that. Our Hippocratic Oath when we became doctors is to first do no harm.

Yes. The data varies a little bit, but most of the time we say that if you have a first-degree relative – mother, father, sister, brother – with MS, your chances are 30 to 50 times the population risk. So about three-to-five-per-cent lifetime risk, because the incident rate in Canada overall is about one in 1,000.

There’s so much that we need to know.

Years ago, we pioneered the use of autologous stem cell treatment for MS in Ottawa. We are still the leading centre in Canada that does these treatments for people who have very aggressive forms of the disease. In those individuals, we’ve been able to stop it cold and they’ve done very well.

It’s quite an extreme procedure to completely remove an immune system and replace it with patients’ own stem cells. We still do one or two a month from all over Canada.

Even if we stop all inflammation in patients, some patients still continue to progressively get worse. That is a different type of inflammation that is not currently targeted by the therapies we have, but there are some new ones on the horizon.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

stories.title: U.S. food importer sues Trump administration over 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
stories.summary: Gellert Global Group argues Trump lacked authority to invoke a never-before-used section of U.S. law to order the levies against Canada.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
The Trump administration is being sued over the imposition of 50 per cent tariffs on an array of Canadian goods, the latest in a string of cases that broadly accuse the president of trying to achieve his trade agenda by asserting a taxing power that belongs to Congress.

The lawsuit, filed on Tuesday, comes amid an ongoing trade war between the U.S. and one of its largest trading partners. The food import business that sued argues President Donald Trump lacked authority to invoke a never-before-used section of U.S. law to order the levies against Canada and that this is part of a trend of unlawful tariff actions by the administration.

The suit centers on tariffs imposed under Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which took effect at the end of August after weeks of negotiations aimed at lowering trade tensions between the U.S. and Canada. Negotiators had appeared to agree on the broad terms of a preliminary deal before it fell apart.

The initial 50 per cent tariffs applied to roughly US$20 billion of Canadian goods, and were followed by later presidential actions to alter and expand the list of covered products. Prime Minister Mark Carney responded with retaliatory tariffs, which took effect on Sept. 8, and the Trump administration eventually excluded certain Canadian goods, including motorcycles, alcoholic beverages and whey products, from being imported to the U.S. at all.

Section 338 was meant to address discrimination against U.S. commerce, but the challengers contend that Congress “abandoned” the statute several years later in favour of a more “comprehensive scheme” and that no president ever issued tariffs under it. Even if the statute is still operative, the suit alleges that Trump’s rationale for the Canadian tariffs failed to meet the necessary criteria and that the 50 per cent rate isn’t tethered to the law’s requirement that it “offset” the actual “burden or disadvantage.”

The challenger, Gellert Global Group Corp., specializes in food imports, including Canadian cheese that is subject to the Section 338 tariffs. The case was brought by Liberty Justice Center, a nonprofit involved in earlier rounds of litigation against Trump’s tariffs.

“No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” Liberty Justice Center Chairman Sara Albrecht said in a statement.

Following the lawsuit filing on Tuesday, an administration official who wasn’t named said in an email that Canada continues to discriminate against U.S. industry, including dairy, alcoholic beverages and auto exports, and that the Trump administration would defend the president’s actions in court.

The president has faced a slew of legal challenges to his tariff policies. The U.S. Supreme Court struck down his first attempt at global tariffs last year under an economic emergency powers law, a loss that has forced customs authorities to refund the US$166 billion collected from importers before the justices ruled, plus interest. A court fight over the president’s second attempt at multicountry tariffs was pending when those levies expired in July.

The trade court is poised to rule in the coming weeks on the fate of Trump’s third round of global tariffs on dozens of economies under a provision of U.S. trade law known as Section 301 that deals with forced labor concerns. A three-judge panel heard arguments in late September.

The case is Gellert Global Group Corp v. Trump, 26-cv-4636, U.S. Court of International Trade (New York).

stories.title: Championship trophy forgotten by Saskatoon Hilltops to be handed to Regina Thunder
stories.summary: The Regina Thunder's president is in possession of the Prairie Football Conference championship trophy after the Saskatoon Hilltops forgot to bring it to Sunday's game.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The Regina Thunder will soon get their hands on the Prairie Football Conference (PFC) championship trophy after it was forgotten by the Saskatoon Hilltops at Sunday’s title game.

The championship trophy is currently in the hands of the president of the Regina Thunder Football Club, Murad Al-Katib, as of Tuesday afternoon. He said he plans to take the prize to Regina from his Saskatoon office Wednesday.

His plan comes after the trophy was forgotten by the Canadian Junior Football League (Cjfl) team’s rival, the Saskatoon Hilltops, which prompted an apology from the defending champs on social media. The Hilltops forgot to bring the prairie conference prize to Sunday’s championship game where Regina defeated Saskatoon. The final score was 44-19.

At the end of the game, the Thunder could not hoist the trophy in front of their home crowd.

“Obviously, when you have the high of winning a championship, there’s a lot of work that goes into it. So, there was just a little bit of confusion at first, but then a little bit of disappointment,” Al-Katib told Global News in an interview Tuesday.

“We were recognized as the winners, and we found out after that the trophy had been missed.”

Following the mishap, the Hilltops issued an apology on social media Monday.

“As the defending champions, it was our responsibility to ensure the trophy was there to be presented to this year’s winner,” the Saskatoon Hilltops wrote.

“We know firsthand how much hard work, dedication, and sacrifice goes into winning a championship. The Regina Thunder earned the right to celebrate that special moment with the trophy in their hands.”

The apology was addressed to the Regina Thunder organization and its players, coaches and fans. According to the president of the Thunder, the Hilltops are forgiven.

“The Saskatoon Hilltops recognize their mistake, and they’ve issued a public apology, not at our request,” he said, adding that “it’s nice when someone apologizes when you don’t ask for an apology. There was an acknowledgement that there was an oversight and we arranged to have it delivered.”

“When I got the apology, I was grateful. And we’ve already moved on because we got a national semifinal championship to win.”

The Thunder are set to play the Sault Ste. Marie Cougars Saturday evening. If they win, the Regina squad will travel to B.C. for the national championship game next month.

stories.title: Bruce Power halfway through 13-year, $13B refurbishment project
stories.summary: The 13-year, $13-billion construction project to refurbish six of the eight reactors at the Bruce Power Nuclear site has reached it’s halfway point.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The 13-year, $13-billion construction project to refurbish six of the eight reactors at the Bruce Power Nuclear site has reached it’s halfway point.

“What we have going on here at the Bruce site is one of the largest infrastructure projects in Canada. The Major Component Replacement (M.C.R) isn’t just about refurbishing the unit and bringing it back, it’s about positioning that unit for another 30 to 40 years. So, we’re really talking about mega projects in Canada, that are nation building,” said Bruce Power’s Chief Operating Officer and Executive Vice-President, James Scongack.

Work to refurbish two of the six reactors under the Major Component Replacement program, has been completed. A third reactor just passed a major milestone, replacing 480 calandria tubes, 25 days faster than the previous reactor.

“We’re able to, with the same units, do the work repetitively, find efficiencies, find innovation, so everyone improves in safety, quality, cost and schedule,” said Scongack.

The work that will extend the life of Bruce Power’s eight reactor fleet to 2064 has been on time, and on budget. In some cases, ahead of budget, and ahead of time said Bruce Power officials.

Remote robotics are amongst the many innovations being used by the 5,000 people working on the Major Component Replacement at Bruce Power, at any given time including Rory Ingham, in Fuel Handling Operations.

“It’s right at the brink of technological development within nuclear. Bruce Power seems to have a leg up compared to other nuclear utilities in the country, and I think even the world. We’re constantly developing our technological processes. Our engineering groups are really engaged, everyone really cares about what they’re doing here, and being a little part of that within fuel handling is a lifetime achievement for myself. I really am proud to be a part of it,” said Ingham, who has worked at Bruce Power since 2005.

The refurbishment project isn’t just replacing the parts in each reactor, and putting it back as it was.

Improvements are being made to squeeze even more power production from each reactor as it’s refurbished.

“Our goal is to be a 7000 megawatt (MW) site for the 2030’s. And, if you look at that from where we started at 6300 MW, that’s the equivalent of two Small Modular Reactors at peak generation. So, it provides the incremental power to the province that it needs, but most importantly, it’s one of the most cost effective, lowest cost, incremental power, we can get,” said Scongack.

It’s a project, Ingham plans to see from start to finish, as refurbishment work is set to be completed by 2033.

“These are mega projects that cost millions of dollars to complete, but it will allow us to continue operation well into the future, and make power for Ontario’s grid for many years into the future,” he said.

Refurbishment work on Unit 5 at Bruce Power begins in November, with Units 7 and 8 to follow in the years to come.

stories.title: CFB Wainwright fire victim ‘always there’ for anyone who needed him: family
stories.summary: Tributes have poured in from across Canada from politicians, community leaders and the everyday Canadians, who Wong's family recognized in their statement.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
The family of the sergeant killed in a deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is describing him as someone who was there for anyone who needed him and are thanking the public for its support.

Sgt. Morgan Wong was one of four Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) members who died Saturday when a grass fire overtook soldiers during a live-fire exercise at the base.

“We are shocked and deeply saddened by Morgan’s death,” the family said in a statement. “We loved Morgan very much and we are extremely proud of him.”

Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, B.C. and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C. also died.

Another 39 members were taken to hospital with 19 in critical condition. As of Tuesday morning, federal Defence Minister David McGuinty said 33 remain in hospital.

Wong’s family said he was “extremely proud to serve” with the CAF.

“He was an incredible person who was always there whenever anyone needed him,” they said. “He loved being active and spending time with his friends and family.”

The 26-year-old was born in Edmonton and graduated from the University of Alberta in 2022 with a Bachelor of Commerce degree. He also held certificates in real estate and civil-military leadership.

In November 2022, Wong’s family said he began to serve as a medical first responder with St. John Ambulance.

He joined the CAF in December 2017 and served on Operation Reassurance in Latvia from October 2024 to June 2025.

The live-fire exercises he participated in on Saturday was part of training in preparation for potential deployment overseas, including in Latvia and other regions, Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland told reporters Sunday. Rutland was commander of the 1st Canadian Division.

According to Wong’s family, he was training in Wainwright to prepare to deploy on his second tour in Europe.

Tributes have poured in from across Canada from politicians, community leaders and the everyday Canadians, who Wong’s family recognized in their statement.

“We are grateful for the support that the public has shown for the military community after what happened at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Oct. 17,” they said. “Our thoughts are with the families of the other soldiers who were killed, and with those who were injured.”

An investigation continues into the fire and how it started and how the fatal incident unfolded.

stories.title: Ontario begins probe of eight private career colleges over alleged Osap ‘fraud’
stories.summary: The government said investigators "gathered information and interviewed individuals" at the unnamed career colleges and suggested it plans to widen the inspections.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Provincial investigators have begun in-person inspections at eight private career colleges looking for potential evidence of “irregularities or fraud,” as the Ford government continues to deal with the fallout of the alleged criminal use of the student assistance program.

The government said investigators “gathered information and interviewed individuals” at the unnamed career colleges and suggested it plans to widen the inspections to additional schools, and to the “sector as a whole.”

In early October, the province said students all 242 private career colleges in the province would be barred from accessing the Ontario Student Assistance Program (Osap) as the province investigated “serious concerns” raised by the federal government, advocacy groups and internal audits and inspections.

The government alleged that some private career colleges were co-owned by immigration services and recruitment firms, could not validate students or provide verification that they were enrolled in courses and that there was a “high concentration of Osap applications” from the same geographic locations.

Those findings, uncovered by external audit firm Kmpg, have been referred to the OPP for an official investigation.

The system-wide Osap suspension, however, has been met with an outcry from college administrators who insist the government is blindly targeting schools without evidence of any wrongdoing.

Trinity College, which offers health, business, technology and trades programs, suspended in class instruction last week “to establish viable financial arrangements following the province-wide pause in Osap funding,” according to an internal memo obtained by Global News.

Meanwhile, other colleges have warned the government they might have to shut their doors if Osap funding dries up.

While the Ford government said the pleas from colleges and students are “not lost on us,” the province will only revive Osap access once “integrity to the system” has been restored.

“We are working to develop a strengthened validation process for private postsecondary institutions associated with Osap approvals for the 2026-27 academic year,” Ontario’s Minister of Colleges and Universities said in a statement.

“This process is expected to be implemented in the new year. Osap will not resume for private postsecondary institutions until the strengthened validation process is in place.”

Quinn said the government plans to introduce caps on Osap-funded enrollment at the colleges, exclude online-only programs, and will enhance student identification and verification controls.

Meanwhile, the government said it’s still working on connecting thousands of students with banks and financial institutions for bridge loans to cover the cost of their education, but that the province is still working on the “program criteria.”

These include common ownership, the involvement of immigration services firms and co-location between private career colleges and immigration recruitment or immigration services firms, inadequate student validation and verification of course enrolment and outcomes, and unusually high concentrations of Osap applications submitted from the same geographic locations.

The government alleged that some private career colleges were co-owned by immigration services and recruitment firms, could not validate students or provide verification that they were enrolled in courses and that there was a “high concentration of Osap applications” from the same geographic locations.
Those findings, uncovered by external audit firm Kmpg, have been referred to the OPP for an official investigation.
The system-wide Osap suspension, however, has been met with an outcry from college administrators who insist the government is blindly targeting schools without evidence of any wrongdoing.

Trinity College, which offers health, business, technology and trades programs, suspended in class instruction last week “to establish viable financial arrangements following the province-wide pause in Osap funding,” according to an internal memo obtained by Global News.
Meanwhile, other colleges have warned the government they might have to shut their doors if Osap funding dries up.
While the Ford government said the pleas from colleges and students are “not lost on us,” the province will only revive Osap access once “integrity to the system” has been restored.

“We are working to develop a strengthened validation process for private postsecondary institutions associated with Osap approvals for the 2026-27 academic year,” Ontario’s Minister of Colleges and Universities said in a statement.
“This process is expected to be implemented in the new year. Osap will not resume for private postsecondary institutions until the strengthened validation process is in place.”
Quinn said the government plans to introduce caps on Osap-funded enrollment at the colleges, exclude online-only programs, and will enhance student identification and verification controls.

Meanwhile, the government said it’s still working on connecting thousands of students with banks and financial institutions for bridge loans to cover the cost of their education, but that the province is still working on the “program criteria.”

These include common ownership, the involvement of immigration services firms and co-location between private career colleges and immigration recruitment or immigration services firms, inadequate student validation and verification of course enrolment and outcomes, and unusually high concentrations of Osap applications submitted from the same geographic locations.

stories.title: A high school in Saint-Jérôme, Que., suspends 78 students following disruptions
stories.summary: Montreal - A high school about 40 kilometres north of Montreal has suspended 78 students after disruptions on school grounds on Friday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The school board told The Canadian Press that the school in Saint-Jérôme, Que., was closed Monday as the administration worked to shed light on the event.

The school administration told parents in a letter Friday that these incidents happened after a call to action by students.

Article continues below

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Classes resumed on Tuesday, but several parents said on social media that their children felt unsafe at the thought of returning to school.

The administration told parents in a subsequent letter about new security measures for Monday, including hiring security guards and increased police presence.

The school has more than 3,400 students and approximately 330 staff members.

Videos of the disruptions Friday show students crowding the halls, with some pushing through the group and others throwing a garbage can in the air.

On Monday, school staff reviewed video recordings to identify the students “who instigated or participated in Friday’s events,” Nadyne Brochu, spokesperson for the Rivière-du-Nord school board, said in an email.

“The consequences for each student will be determined based on the severity of their actions,” Brochu wrote.

“Parents will need to be involved in the process and work with the school staff,” she added.

The school also said that it has adjusted the its staff’s schedules “to ensure maximum adult supervision.”

In a letter sent to parents on Monday, school director Nathalie Flamand said further disruption could lead to serious consequences.

“No gathering or behaviour that could compromise the safety or the proper functioning of the school will be tolerated,” she wrote.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

— With files from Mathieu Paquette and Frédéric Lacroix-Couture

The Canadian Press
