stories.title: Chow and Bradford neck-and-neck with days left in Toronto mayoral election campaign
stories.summary: As the race is in its final stretch, Bradford and Chow are shoring up their main talking points with the goal of moving the needle to their benefit.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Matthew Bingley
stories.content:
With less than a week until election day, the race to become Toronto’s next mayor has narrowed into a tight match-up between Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford.

As the race is in its final stretch, Bradford and Chow are shoring up their main talking points with the goal of moving the needle to their benefit, while taking shots at each other’s records.

For Chow, that meant returning to 500 Dawes Road on Tuesday, an apartment building in Bradford’s Beaches-East York ward that had been notorious for derelict conditions and severe pest issues.

In May, Chow sent city by-law officers to the site to complete emergency repairs. Residents in the building had long advocated that their landlord refused to maintain basic living conditions and that the city needed to step in to help. Chow told reporters in May that $200,000 in fines were issued at the building.

Speaking outside the building Tuesday, flanked by renters, Chow criticized Bradford for not doing enough to help the tenants as their city councilor.

“For years, they asked for help,” she said.

“I came here, I listened and I took action. People of Toronto, renters of Toronto, need someone to back them up,” she said. She said her phone is “buzzing” with requests from tenants daily, looking for help in fighting negligent landlords.

“My office has really intervened and brings together all the city staff to make sure their needs are dealt with,” she said.

Chow also took the opportunity to level criticism against Bradford.

“If you cannot represent your own people in your own ward, and do your job properly as councilor, you don’t deserve to be mayor of the city of Toronto,” she said. Helping tenants in his ward is Bradford’s job and “he’s not doing it,” she said.

Chow has promised that if re-elected, she will create a task force within the RentSafeTO bylaw enforcement program to go after bad landlords who perpetually violate basic maintenance standards.

Bradford’s team was quick to fire back against Chow’s claims at 500 Dawes Road, stating that she waited until an election year to take real action. He’s said he’s used municipal tools at his disposal for years to tackle building violations prior to Chow stepping in as mayor.

Several tenants and advocacy groups have disputed Bradford’s telling of the 500 Dawes saga, as some have told media that he failed to meet with them or connect with tenants’ rights groups like Acorn.

Transit and congestion were Bradford’s focus on Tuesday, with the candidate promising to get rid of reduced speed zones on the TTC if elected.

Known as TTC slow zones, the measure has trains travel at slower speeds, sometimes at 15 km an hour, while track maintenance is complete. The TTC currently caps its slow zones to 12.

“As mayor, I’m going to set the target at zero. I am going to raise our standards and I am going to hold the city and the TTC to account,” he said.

Any slow zones would have to be justified with a published reason and a published repair date, he said. Bradford also announced that he would implement an independent track condition audit and a track renewal program for the subway.

“If you want a city that respects your time, respects your commute, then you have to vote for it,” he said. He said Chow has “made her peace” with less and “business as usual.”

Chow’s team published a news release responding to Bradford’s announcement Tuesday. Her campaign said that as a TTC Commissioner, Bradford supported budgets that allowed the TTC to age and preventative maintenance to stop, leading to the track work being done now.

“As I’ve said, even one slow zone is too many and I will eliminate them,” said Chow in the release. “Bradford helped create the maintenance challenges the TTC is fixing now. Of course we must do more; I will keep working to make critical repairs,” she said.

A new Mainstreet Research poll published Tuesday indicated a very narrow race. The firm placed Bradford with 48.9 per cent support and Chow at a “nearly equal” 47.5 per cent, Mainstreet said in a statement.

Quito Maggi, president and CEO of Mainstreet, said in a news release that Bradford leads in Etobicoke and North York while Chow is ahead in Scarborough and downtown.

Research firm Pollara Strategic Insights has Chow in a much firmer lead in its new polling also published Tuesday. It found incumbent Olivia Chow ahead of Brad Bradford by seven points among decided voters, 53 per cent to 46 per cent.

That polling also found a strong gender gap in voting intentions. Chow leads among decided women (60 per cent compared to 39 per cent of women for Bradford), while slightly more men are leaning towards Bradford (52 per cent to 45 per cent).

Toronto’s mayoral election is being held on Oct. 26.

stories.title: ‘More than a headline’: Manitoba family wants public inquiry, following inquest into daughter’s fatal 2020 shooting
stories.summary: The family of a 16-year-old First Nations girl, who was fatally shot by Winnipeg police in 2020, is calling for accountability and change following an inquest into her death.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Winnipeg — The family of a 16-year-old First Nations girl, who was fatally shot by Winnipeg police in 2020, is calling for accountability and change following an inquest into her death.

The conclusion of the inquest comes more than six years after Eishia Hudson was shot and killed by police.

“It’s been a tough six and a half years,” said William Hudson, Eishia’s father, at a press conference on Tuesday.

“The wounds don’t close; they remain open.”

Eishia was shot on April 8, 2020, after police responded to reports of a robbery at a liquor store and chased a stolen Jeep. Police have said the stolen vehicle, “rammed” into a police cruiser and hit other cars during a pursuit before shots were fired.

The inquest heard that Eishia was driving the Jeep when three of the four people in the vehicle with her committed the robbery.

Hudson’s parents and other family members attended two days of closing submissions in court last week, where numerous recommendations were presented to help prevent similar deaths in the future.

‘I just want changes’

The lawyer for the Winnipeg Police Service (WPS) opposed many of the recommendations relating to police training. CTV News reached out to the WPS but did not hear back.

A spokesperson from WPS told CTV News they cannot comment on any recommendations at this time since they have not yet been made by the court.

“When the court releases its report, the WPS will review any recommendations made and comment at that time,” a spokesperson said in a statement.

Eishia’s family testified during the inquest along with several police officers, including the one who shot the teen. The inquest also heard from some of those who were in the vehicle with Eishia.

“Our daughter is more than a headline,” Hudson said.

“I just want changes so our people don’t have to go through this again.”

Protests followed Eishia’s death and there are continued calls for a public inquiry into police-related deaths of Indigenous Peoples.

She was one of three First Nations people killed in a 10-day period in Winnipeg that year.

“This inquest has raised serious concerns about policing, systemic racism, child and family services, youth justice and accountability,” said Kyra Wilson, Grand Chief of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs.

The inquest is examining whether the officer’s use of force was appropriate and whether systemic racism played a role in the shooting. Police had initially identified the robbery suspects as Indigenous.

“As important as this process is, no recommendation, no report or outcome will ever bring Eishia back to her family,” said Melissa Robinson, a community advocate.

The inquest into Eishia’s death began in February.

Judge Margaret Wiebe of the Manitoba Court of King’s Bench, who presided over the case, now has six months to write a report outlining final recommendations.

-With files from The Canadian Press

The inquest heard that Eishia was driving the Jeep when three of the four people in the vehicle with her committed the robbery.
Hudson’s parents and other family members attended two days of closing submissions in court last week, where numerous recommendations were presented to help prevent similar deaths in the future.
‘I just want changes’
The lawyer for the Winnipeg Police Service (WPS) opposed many of the recommendations relating to police training. CTV News reached out to the WPS but did not hear back.
A spokesperson from WPS told CTV News they cannot comment on any recommendations at this time since they have not yet been made by the court.
“When the court releases its report, the WPS will review any recommendations made and comment at that time,” a spokesperson said in a statement.
Eishia’s family testified during the inquest along with several police officers, including the one who shot the teen. The inquest also heard from some of those who were in the vehicle with Eishia.
“Our daughter is more than a headline,” Hudson said.
“I just want changes so our people don’t have to go through this again.”
Protests followed Eishia’s death and there are continued calls for a public inquiry into police-related deaths of Indigenous Peoples.
She was one of three First Nations people killed in a 10-day period in Winnipeg that year.

“This inquest has raised serious concerns about policing, systemic racism, child and family services, youth justice and accountability,” said Kyra Wilson, Grand Chief of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs.

The inquest is examining whether the officer’s use of force was appropriate and whether systemic racism played a role in the shooting. Police had initially identified the robbery suspects as Indigenous.
“As important as this process is, no recommendation, no report or outcome will ever bring Eishia back to her family,” said Melissa Robinson, a community advocate.
The inquest into Eishia’s death began in February.
Judge Margaret Wiebe of the Manitoba Court of King’s Bench, who presided over the case, now has six months to write a report outlining final recommendations.

stories.title: Pause on Osap at private post-secondary institutions to stay in effect until new year
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's colleges and universities minister says a pause on student financial assistance payments across all private post-secondary institutions will stay in effect until at least the new year.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A pause on student financial assistance payments across all private post-secondary institutions in Ontario will stay in effect until at least the new year, the province’s colleges and universities minister announced Tuesday.

Nolan Quinn said in a late afternoon statement that the government intends to strengthen the approval process for career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions under the Ontario Student Assistance Program, but that work is not yet done.

“Proposed measures will include caps on Osap-funded enrolment, the exclusion of predominantly online-only programs, and strengthened student identification and verification controls,” he wrote.

“While necessary to protect the integrity of Osap and to protect Ontario taxpayers from abuse, we understand the impact that this work is having on students and families across the province. This impact is not lost on us as we work to restore integrity to the system and provide students with greater certainty and stability as quickly as possible.”

The new validation system is expected to be implemented in the new year, he wrote, and Osap payments will not resume until that time.

The government is also still working on securing third-party loans for students through banks, he said.

Quinn tasked Kpmg with an audit of the sector in August and said earlier this month that preliminary findings raised serious enough concerns that he has referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police.

Ministry investigators launched in-person inspections last week at eight career colleges, he said. That is on top of six institutions the government cut off from Osap eligibility earlier this year.

Career Colleges Ontario, students and institutions including a divinity school and Canada’s National Ballet School have decried the government’s broad approach of pausing Osap at all private post-secondary schools, but Quinn’s office has said there is evidence of systemic issues.

Angele Proulx, a student at Trillium College in St. Catharines, called Quinn’s statement outrageous.

“That does not seem to me that they are looking out for the students’ best interest,” said Proulx, in the college’s community development support worker program.

“We are due to graduate Feb. 4, 2027, just after the new year. If they don’t do something about it from now until then, we will not graduate, but they will expect full payment. So that is not taking into consideration the students that are innocent in all of this.”

Trillium College announced late last week that it was suspending its academic operations as a result of the pause. It is offering interest-free payment arrangements, but many students have said they cannot make those payments without Osap funding, the school said in a notice to students.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request showed large increases in Osap usage at a relatively small number of career colleges from 2020-21 to 2024-25.

The seven career colleges that had the highest Osap usage in 2024-25 received $385 million in provincial grants – the same amount that went to students at all of Ontario’s publicly funded colleges that year.

Court records show that ministry officials who inspected three career colleges found evidence they allege suggests third parties were completing the coursework — sometimes entire courses in one day — and a few students who couldn’t name their school or program.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Justice minister orders review of decades-old unsolved murder investigation in P.E.I.
stories.summary: The provincial justice minister in P.E.I. has ordered a review of the investigation into a decades-old unsolved murder case after charges were withdrawn last week.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The provincial justice minister in P.E.I. has ordered a review of the investigation into a decades-old unsolved murder case after charges were withdrawn last week.

Crown prosecutors in the province withdrew charges against Todd Joseph Gallant after Charlottetown police lost crucial evidence, including a knife that would have been used as an exhibit in court.

Police charged Gallant with first-degree murder and interfering with human remains in 2024 following an investigation into the 1988 killing of teacher Byron Carr.

The allegations against Gallant were not tested in court.

Darren MacDougall, Charlottetown’s interim chief of police, blamed a lack of consistent “property management systems” for the missing evidence.

Carr was 36 when he was strangled and stabbed in his Charlottetown home by someone who left a handwritten note on a wall that read, “I will kill again.”

Bloyce Thompson, the justice minister, has directed the Office of the Police Commissioner to appoint a third party to conduct the review.

“This is a troubling situation for all those involved, particularly the friends and family of the late Mr. Carr,” the minister said in a statement. “The community deserves answers, and we need to ensure public confidence in our justice system.”

stories.title: St. Thomas city council considers $1M funding request to help save railway museum
stories.summary: St. Thomas city council is considering a grant request of $1 million to help save the Elgin County Railway Museum (Ecrm).
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
St. Thomas city council is considering a grant request of $1 million to help save the Elgin County Railway Museum (Ecrm).

It follows the building’s abrupt closure earlier this year due to structural issues.

“There’s so much railway heritage that has left our town. That’s the reason to save it. You need these places,” exclaimed Ecrm CEO Wil Zufelt.

On Monday, council formally received the grant request, which will be dealt with by the incoming council. Spread out over five to 10 years, the money would help to preserve and revitalize the popular attraction.

“Now I think it is a worthy project, and it certainly identifies our past and has an opportunity to be a pillar of our future. But I think that we should do due diligence and not only see how it fits with in our budget but that it is a sustainable plan,” said Coun. Jeff Kohler during Monday’s council discussion.

“We’ve always bragged about our railway heritage being St. Thomas. And I really believe we need to keep the museum,” added Coun. Jim Herbert.

The ask is part of an $8.5 million capital campaign. The federal and provincial governments will be asked to match municipal funding.

Zufelt says three quarters of the overall project funding has already been identified.

“What you’re going to see is about an 18,000 sq. ft. new museum here. Taking the existing museum right now, making the footprint smaller. Making it accessible, and making it sustainable,” said Zufelt.

Zufelt says they’re hoping to reopen the museum in 2029.

stories.title: The PQ bypassed the monarchy. It was met with a shrug in Quebec and Ottawa
stories.summary: 'We will let Quebec make its own decisions, and for our part, we will promote cooperative federalism,' said Industry Minister Mélanie Joly.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Parti Québécois’ decision to have the swearing-in ceremony of its cabinet ministers on Wednesday without the Quebec Lieutenant-Governor physically present in the room did not cause as much as a ripple from political friends and foes.

Quebec Premier-elect Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who has promised to cut ties with the monarchy, wrote to Manon Jeannotte earlier this week to ask her to not attend the ceremony and to instead sign the necessary documents from her office.

In a statement to National Post, Jeannotte’s office confirmed that she will abide by the incoming government’s wishes and will follow the ceremony with a television feed.

“There is no requirement for the Lieutenant-Governor to attend, and she does not wish to become the focus of attention. Her priority is the continuity of government in accordance with the Constitution,” said Ian Préfontaine, her media relations manager.

St-Pierre Plamondon’s request does not come as a total surprise, as he has vowed to defund her office, but he still must contend with the current constitutional realities.

That means the lieutenant-governor’s signature is still needed to appoint the premier and his cabinet ministers, to ratify orders-in-council issued by the cabinet and, most importantly, to grant royal assent to bills passed in the Quebec provincial legislature.

Still, many politicians in Quebec and Ottawa did not have a strong reaction when questioned about the PQ’s decision to push Jeannotte to the sidelines.

Reacting to the news, Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said he has “no problem” with the PQ government going ahead with this symbolic gesture.

“Well, it’s certainly true that I’m not a monarchist — I don’t think that comes as any surprise to you,” he told reporters in Quebec City on Tuesday.

That said, Duhaime said he has questions should the PQ be tempted to permanently remove the role of lieutenant-governor which would require constitutional changes.

“I don’t think there’s much appetite in Quebec for heading down that path,” he added.

In Ottawa, the reactions to the news from Quebec MPs were a mix of disinterest and apathy — a sign of just how much the monarchy means to people in the province.

“We will let Quebec make its own decisions, and for our part, we will promote cooperative federalism, because we believe we can work effectively with the government,” said Industry Minister Mélanie Joly on her way to a cabinet meeting.

Liberal MP Jean-Yves Duclos, who briefly served as Quebec lieutenant under Justin Trudeau, echoed Joly’s comments that it is the Quebec government’s decision.

Duclos said the federal government will focus “on what we believe is important.”

“Personally, it doesn’t bother me. I’m a Quebecer,” said Conservative MP Jacques Gourde of the PQ’s decision to exclude Jeannotte from their swearing-in ceremony. “I understand those who like the monarchy, and it doesn’t bother me if others don’t.”

Even Bloc Québécois MPs — who support the idea of abolishing the monarchy — had a relatively muted reaction, with some refusing to comment or politely endorsing it.

The exclusion of the Quebec Lieutenant-Governor from the swearing-in ceremony for ministers is just the latest in a series of affronts to the monarchy.

Jeannotte was also excluded from swearing-in ceremonies for members of the National Assembly to date as all of them chose to swear an oath to “the people of Quebec” instead of King Charles III — as it is possible to do since a law was passed in 2022.

The law, known as Bill 4, added a clause to the Constitution Act of 1867 stating that the oath to the monarch is optional as it no longer applies to Quebec legislators.

On Monday, even the very federalist Quebec Liberals opted to swear an oath to “the people of Quebec” at the behest of its leader Charles Milliard. He said he thought it was a “good idea” and that there was consensus inside his caucus to follow his example.

There is, however, a legal challenge of Bill 4 underway that could ultimately force the incoming MNAs to swear an oath to the King — whether they like it or not.

On Tuesday, the Quebec Superior Court heard from Lawrence David, a professor at the University of Ottawa’s faculty of law and founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute, who filed an emergency injunction claiming Bill 4 is unconstitutional.

David said in an email he expects a “possible urgent appeal” by either side once a decision will be rendered by Justice Ian Demers in the following days.

The Quebec legislature is expected to reconvene on Nov. 24.

In a statement to National Post, Jeannotte’s office confirmed that she will abide by the incoming government’s wishes and will follow the ceremony with a television feed.

“There is no requirement for the Lieutenant-Governor to attend, and she does not wish to become the focus of attention. Her priority is the continuity of government in accordance with the Constitution,” said Ian Préfontaine, her media relations manager.
St-Pierre Plamondon’s request does not come as a total surprise, as he has vowed to defund her office, but he still must contend with the current constitutional realities.

That means the lieutenant-governor’s signature is still needed to appoint the premier and his cabinet ministers, to ratify orders-in-council issued by the cabinet and, most importantly, to grant royal assent to bills passed in the Quebec provincial legislature.
Still, many politicians in Quebec and Ottawa did not have a strong reaction when questioned about the PQ’s decision to push Jeannotte to the sidelines.
Reacting to the news, Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime said he has “no problem” with the PQ government going ahead with this symbolic gesture.
“Well, it’s certainly true that I’m not a monarchist — I don’t think that comes as any surprise to you,” he told reporters in Quebec City on Tuesday.
That said, Duhaime said he has questions should the PQ be tempted to permanently remove the role of lieutenant-governor which would require constitutional changes.
“I don’t think there’s much appetite in Quebec for heading down that path,” he added.
In Ottawa, the reactions to the news from Quebec MPs were a mix of disinterest and apathy — a sign of just how much the monarchy means to people in the province.

“We will let Quebec make its own decisions, and for our part, we will promote cooperative federalism, because we believe we can work effectively with the government,” said Industry Minister Mélanie Joly on her way to a cabinet meeting.
Liberal MP Jean-Yves Duclos, who briefly served as Quebec lieutenant under Justin Trudeau, echoed Joly’s comments that it is the Quebec government’s decision.
Duclos said the federal government will focus “on what we believe is important.”

“Personally, it doesn’t bother me. I’m a Quebecer,” said Conservative MP Jacques Gourde of the PQ’s decision to exclude Jeannotte from their swearing-in ceremony. “I understand those who like the monarchy, and it doesn’t bother me if others don’t.”
Even Bloc Québécois MPs — who support the idea of abolishing the monarchy — had a relatively muted reaction, with some refusing to comment or politely endorsing it.
The exclusion of the Quebec Lieutenant-Governor from the swearing-in ceremony for ministers is just the latest in a series of affronts to the monarchy.

Jeannotte was also excluded from swearing-in ceremonies for members of the National Assembly to date as all of them chose to swear an oath to “the people of Quebec” instead of King Charles III — as it is possible to do since a law was passed in 2022.
The law, known as Bill 4, added a clause to the Constitution Act of 1867 stating that the oath to the monarch is optional as it no longer applies to Quebec legislators.

On Monday, even the very federalist Quebec Liberals opted to swear an oath to “the people of Quebec” at the behest of its leader Charles Milliard. He said he thought it was a “good idea” and that there was consensus inside his caucus to follow his example.
There is, however, a legal challenge of Bill 4 underway that could ultimately force the incoming MNAs to swear an oath to the King — whether they like it or not.

On Tuesday, the Quebec Superior Court heard from Lawrence David, a professor at the University of Ottawa’s faculty of law and founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute, who filed an emergency injunction claiming Bill 4 is unconstitutional.
David said in an email he expects a “possible urgent appeal” by either side once a decision will be rendered by Justice Ian Demers in the following days.
The Quebec legislature is expected to reconvene on Nov. 24.
National Post calevesque@postmedia.com

stories.title: Galloway defamation trial hears of ‘inflated and outrageous’ email rhetoric
stories.summary: A former creative writing student testifying in author and former UBC professor Steven Galloway's defamation trial says she was "shocked" and "horrified" at language used in a mass email by a fellow student investigating misconduct allegations against Galloway.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Vancouver — A former creative writing student told a B.C. Supreme Court defamation trial that she was “shocked” and “horrified” at language used in a mass email by a fellow student who was investigating misconduct allegations against author and former UBC professor Steven Galloway.

Cara Woodruff, a UBC creative writing graduate, told the civil trial where Galloway alleges defamation that she received an email in November 2015 from Chelsea Rooney, who was collecting complaints against Galloway.

Woodruff said the email from Rooney contained “inflated and outrageous” rhetoric and urged recipients to anonymously contact a reporter from The Canadian Press about allegations against Galloway.

She told the court that Rooney had been speaking on behalf of a woman identified only as A.B. because she was vulnerable and in need of support, but A.B. “had mentioned before that she didn’t like Chelsea. She didn’t trust her, so I didn’t understand why Chelsea was coming in like a detective.”

Woodruff said she didn’t believe that Galloway sexually assaulted A.B. and she kept asking the woman to go to the police to have it investigated “properly.”

Rooney issued a public apology to Galloway this month, just days before the trial began.

Her statement said she understood her conduct toward him was “serious and harmful,” and that she deeply regretted “contributing to the harm Mr. Galloway has suffered.”

Woodruff told the court on Tuesday that she felt “blindsided” when she learned of the allegations because she had been friends with A.B., and it “was very unclear” to Woodruff if there was a criminal investigation.

“It was so vague,” she said. “But it was a very complex situation. It just didn’t make sense to me.”

A.B. is not testifying in the trial, and the court has heard she is not asserting in her defence that the allegations she made against Galloway are true.

Galloway, the author of novels including “The Cellist of Sarajevo” and “The Confabulist” was a tenured professor and the chair of the creative writing program at the University of B.C.

He was never charged over the allegations by A.B., whose name is under a publication ban, though he was fired from his job.

Rooney said in her apology that she had been asked by the university, A.B. and faculty members to gather complaints against Galloway, but she had “no information” that the “very serious and unproven allegations” against Galloway were true.

The court also heard on Tuesday from Stephen Bohnen, a former UBC community relations officer, who first documented A.B.’s sexual harassment complaint against Galloway in 2013.

Galloway’s lawyer asked Bohnen about an email sent by A.B. that referred to the head of campus security named “Steve,” alleging he’d called Galloway a “serial predator.”

Bohnen said he was not the head of security, and when asked if it was him who referred to Galloway that way, he said “I certainly can’t remember anything like that. I have no reason to think of him as anything but a professor at the university.”

He said A.B. had not reported sexual assault, but rather sexual harassment.

Glynnis Kirchmeier, a defendant representing herself in the case alleged to have defamed Galloway in a Twitter post, questioned Bohnen about how the university handled complaints against professors.

Justice Neena Sharma paused Kirchmeier’s questioning, asking her about the relevance to the defamation case.

“I intend to argue that part of the downstream liability that I share with A.B. comes from UBC not handling her report correctly,” Kirchmeier said.

She said it would demonstrate that it was “ reasonable for me to believe A.B., first of all, and why it would (not be) malicious for me to be distrustful of the findings” of a report by a former judge hired by UBC who’d deemed the allegations unsubstantiated.

“I’ll let you continue, although I’m not sure I completely understand that,” Sharma said.

The court also heard that A.B. had admitted in 2019 during cross-examination on an affidavit she swore that she had falsely claimed that the CBC’s legal team had vetted her story.

Galloway’s lawyer Daniel Burnett read from a transcript where A.B. said she made the claim because she “desperately wanted UBC to go forward with an investigation.”

“I don’t regret what I said because I needed to keep myself alive and safe, and there are no easy ways for safe, or safe ways for women to get their cases brought forward and investigated,” A.B. said in transcript read into court.

Later Tuesday, A.B.’s lawyers argued against admitting into evidence a report by a publishing industry expert, as Galloway alleges his writing career was destroyed after the allegations surfaced.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

stories.title: 'Stay the hell out of bargaining': Unions blast Bill C-39's labour provisions during committee testimony
stories.summary: Unions called on the federal government to repeal Section 107 from the Canada Labour Code during committee testimony on Tuesday.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa — Unions called on the federal government to repeal Section 107 from the Canada Labour Code during committee testimony on Tuesday, as members of Parliament study a bill that seeks to clarify its uses for ending strikes.

“We’ve maintained … since (Section) 107 was starting to be used by this government, that governments should stay the hell out of bargaining,” said Mark Hancock, national president at the Canadian Union of Public Employees (Cupe).

“The only place a collective agreement should be found, can be found, is at a bargaining table with both sides,” he added.

Committee hearings began in the House of Commons and the Senate this week, with testimony from expert witnesses, ON the Liberal government’s latest major projects bill.

Bill C-39, which builds on the government’s Bill C-5, is intended to fast-track the regulatory approval process of all major projects, not just those deemed within the national interest.

The bill also makes changes to the Canada Labour Code, including changes to collective bargaining and giving the labour minister “guardrails” on when they can intervene to end a lockout or strike.

Over the last few years, the Liberal government has relied on Section 107 of the labour code to end lockouts and strikes at airlines, ports and railways. There are currently four different court challenges brought forward by unions on what they view as the federal government’s misuse of Section 107.

In August of last year, the use of Section 107 was invoked by Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu to force 10,000 Air Canada flight attendants back to work, which backfired when flight attendants defied the order by the Canada Industrial Relations Board and stayed on the picket line. A deal was secured a few days later following hours of negotiations between Cupe and Air Canada.

Unions have maintained that the expectation of ministerial intervention in a strike or lockout leads to bad faith bargaining, because employers expect binding arbitration.

“When you have arbitration, not only do we believe that the court will find it to be unconstitutional, but it will also create an environment where problems stack up, labour relations deteriorate, and that will follow our business and our business reputation far more than any problem that this bill purports to resolve,” said Tim Perry, president of the Air Line Pilots Association.

Hajdu has said Bill C-39’s labour provisions give “guardrails” to her use of Section 107, including a special mediator report and a national interest test.

During her testimony on Monday, Hajdu said that a report issued publicly by the special mediator will have a shaming effect on employers, should the report show they are acting in bad faith. She also argued Bill C-39 protects the right to strike even “more vigorously” with those guardrails in place.

“So not only will the minister have that special mediators report, but all of Canada will know exactly what’s happening at that table,” she said. “That will be very illuminating for union members, for employee groups, employer groups, for customers, for shareholders.”

David Chartrand, Canadian general vice-president of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, said Hajdu can consider the report, but she is not bound by it.

“It’s economic harm that is one of the factors to be weighed, even though economic pressure is the very purpose of a strike, that is far too much power to place in the hands of one individual,” he added.

Perry said the national interest provision is far too broad and does not think the guardrails are sufficient.

Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, agreed with Perry that this will lead to bad outcomes in collective bargaining.

“I don’t believe for a minute that this legislation will improve the collective bargaining process,” she said. “I think this will improve employers to hold out and not to get to a deal.”

Hancock said the purpose of Bill C-39 is not to provide guardrails for the minister, but to protect the federal government from legal challenges.

“I think one of the things this government’s attempting to do is to to shelter themselves from court challenges, and I think they’ve done a decent job of that, but at no point will we, as the union, give up our right to strike, and no guardrails are going to take away our right to strike,” said Hancock.

The bill passed the House of Commons, with the help from the Conservative Party. However, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has said his party plans to bring amendments to “protect the rights of workers.”

Notably, the Liberal government has not yet released a Charter statement on Bill C-39’s potential effects.

The legislative committee has given itself until Nov. 16 to hear from expert witnesses, before they begin clause-by-clause consideration of the bill.

Some experts during testimony in front of the Senate committee warned a bill of this magnitude warrants further study.

“The time frame for this review is really completely unrealistic and unfeasible,” said Arlene Kwasniak, University of Calgary professor, to senators on Monday. “I recommend that either you somehow make longer time frames or just reject the bill in its entirety and start over.”

stories.title: Albertans want more control over immigration and limits on newcomers' access to social services
stories.summary: Albertans seem to want a say in how many newcomers they accept and appear willing to crack open the Constitution to abolish the Senate.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
More than half the Albertans who voted in Monday’s referendum want more control over immigration to the province and to limit new immigrants’ access to social services.

While the star of the historic vote was the question on whether Albertans wanted a referendum to leave Canada — more than three-quarters of those who voted nixed that option — nine other questions on the ballots delved into whether Alberta should wrest power away from Ottawa.

Albertans seem to want a say in how many newcomers they accept and appear willing to crack open the Constitution to abolish the Senate and choose their own judges.

Official results, with 86 per cent of the votes counted, show more than 840,000 Albertans voted yes when asked if they support the government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration “for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities.” Just over 700,000 voted no on this question.

When asked if they support the government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that “only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” will be eligible for health care, education and other social services, more than 736,000 voted yes, and over 592,000 voted no.

Ottawa will consider the vote results in the nine questions, “and look where we can find solutions together,” Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters Tuesday morning in Ottawa.

“What I favour is working now pragmatically to common solutions,” he said.

“Constitutional change is difficult. It’s long. We have an amending formula generated originally out of Alberta, and where we can find solutions that work for Canadians, we should find those solutions that work for Canadians.”

Carney pointed out that the federal government “has recognized from the start the need to take back control on immigration, and we’ve done so. You know the numbers, but I think it’s important to underscore them for all Canadians: reduction in asylum seekers of 17 per cent, reduction in temporary foreign worker flows of 60 per cent, reduction in foreign students of 80 per cent over the course of the last 18 months.”

Canada is moving to a “more sustainable pace of immigration now,” Carney said.

“I’m not saying that that stabilization is complete, but where we go from here needs to be established in cooperation with the provinces, and that’s very much the spirit of at least one of the questions.”

More than 705,000 answered yes when asked if they “support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially funded social support programs.” More than 514,000 voted no.

More than 660,000 indicated they “support the Government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family’s use of the health care and education systems.”

More than 489,000 said no to that question.

“In large measure, immigration falls mostly within federal jurisdiction,” said Wayne MacKay, a professor emeritus at Dalhousie University’s Schulich School of Law.

Immigration laws can be tweaked, he said.

“But as with most things there are trade-offs,” he said. “In some areas, we certainly still need immigrants to keep the population up. Like many countries, we don’t have enough immigration. We don’t have enough workers to operate the economy.”

More than 736,000 indicated they support “the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election.” More than 418,000 voted no.

MacKay questioned whether the effect would be “more focused on vulnerable groups” who May have more difficulty producing evidence of citizenship. “That one’s a little tricky. You do have to be a citizen to vote, so if they’re upping the requirement to do that, and they do it consistently, then I suppose that’s legitimate.”

More than 570,000 Albertans said yes to whether they support “the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King’s Bench and Appeal courts.” More than 527,000 voted no.

Provinces already have “quite a bit of input” into who is appointed to the bench, MacKay said. “Increasingly there are independent selection committees that try to take some of the politics out of this.”

More than 569,000 said yes when asked if they support “the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?” More than 490,000 voted no.

That would require a constitutional amendment, MacKay said, noting it would take unanimous consent from Ottawa and the provinces. “It’s a pretty high hurdle to meet and therefore might be not a very wise exercise in time and energy trying to do it.”

More than 526,000 voted no when asked if they “support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs.” More than 512,000 voted yes on that question.

The vote skewed slightly to the yes side (more than 520,000) when Albertans were asked if they “support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province’s laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province’s laws and federal laws conflict.” More than 500,000 voted no to this question.

That would be “a big reversal of existing constitutional structure, where if there’s valid federal and provincial laws in the same area, the federal one kind of prevails,” MacKay said.

“What they’re really arguing for is a significant round of constitutional amendment giving more power to the provinces and less power to the federal government. And as we know from way back with Meech Lake and all the other various attempts to amend the Constitution, amending our Constitution is a very difficult, lengthy and not very successful process.”

You know the numbers, but I think it’s important to underscore them for all Canadians: reduction in asylum seekers of 17 per cent, reduction in temporary foreign worker flows of 60 per cent, reduction in foreign students of 80 per cent over the course of the last 18 months.”
Canada is moving to a “more sustainable pace of immigration now,” Carney said.

“I’m not saying that that stabilization is complete, but where we go from here needs to be established in cooperation with the provinces, and that’s very much the spirit of at least one of the questions.”

More than 705,000 answered yes when asked if they “support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially funded social support programs.” More than 514,000 voted no.

More than 660,000 indicated they “support the Government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family’s use of the health care and education systems.”
More than 489,000 said no to that question.
“In large measure, immigration falls mostly within federal jurisdiction,” said Wayne MacKay, a professor emeritus at Dalhousie University’s Schulich School of Law.
Immigration laws can be tweaked, he said.

“But as with most things there are trade-offs,” he said. “In some areas, we certainly still need immigrants to keep the population up. Like many countries, we don’t have enough immigration. We don’t have enough workers to operate the economy.”

More than 736,000 indicated they support “the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election.” More than 418,000 voted no.

MacKay questioned whether the effect would be “more focused on vulnerable groups” who May have more difficulty producing evidence of citizenship. “That one’s a little tricky. You do have to be a citizen to vote, so if they’re upping the requirement to do that, and they do it consistently, then I suppose that’s legitimate.”

More than 570,000 Albertans said yes to whether they support “the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King’s Bench and Appeal courts.” More than 527,000 voted no.

Provinces already have “quite a bit of input” into who is appointed to the bench, MacKay said. “Increasingly there are independent selection committees that try to take some of the politics out of this.”

More than 569,000 said yes when asked if they support “the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?” More than 490,000 voted no.

content_blocks.text: That would require a constitutional amendment, MacKay said, noting it would take unanimous consent from Ottawa and the provinces. “It’s a pretty high hurdle to meet and therefore might be not a very wise exercise in time and energy trying to do it.”

More than 526,000 voted no when asked if they “support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs.” More than 512,000 voted yes on that question.

The vote skewed slightly to the yes side (more than 520,000) when Albertans were asked if they “support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province’s laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province’s laws and federal laws conflict.” More than 500,000 voted no to this question.
That would be “a big reversal of existing constitutional structure, where if there’s valid federal and provincial laws in the same area, the federal one kind of prevails,” MacKay said.

“What they’re really arguing for is a significant round of constitutional amendment giving more power to the provinces and less power to the federal government. And as we know from way back with Meech Lake and all the other various attempts to amend the Constitution, amending our Constitution is a very difficult, lengthy and not very successful process.”

stories.title: Federal government says it will take Fsin to court to repay $12.4M in spending
stories.summary: Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) says it will be filing a statement of claim against the Fsin for repayment of $12.4 million in unsupported spending in a year-long audit dispute.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) says it will file a statement of claim against the Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations (Fsin) to recover millions of dollars in spending, after issuing the group a final repayment notice last week.

ISC says it issued the organization, which represents 74 First Nations in Saskatchewan, a recovery letter seeking repayment of close to $12.4 million in funding, according to a statement shared with Global News.

The decision follows a similar legal threat issued last week by the Fsin , which said it does not accept the federal government’s conclusion or its claim that the expenditures are ineligible and is taking the department to court.

While the Fsin has not shared additional information about its legal action, Global News has obtained federal court documents filed by the organization in August, where the group is asking for a judicial review of what it alleges is unfair treatment by ISC, including the withholding of funds since being asked to repay what the department says is ineligible spending.

Isc’s final repayment notice to Fsin marks the latest development in a year-long dispute that earlier this year saw Indigenous Services Canada identify $28.7 million in ineligible and unsupported expenses between April 2019 and March 2024.

That figure was taken from the findings of a forensic audit ordered by ISC and conducted by Kpmg, which last fall flagged $34 million in questionable, ineligible and unsupported spending related to COVID-19 expenditures, travel and payments made to a former employee.

The Fsin has consistently disputed the findings of this audit and has defended its spending.

ISC says it continues to meet with Fsin but will not provide details of those encounters or what transpired over the past seven months, during which the repayment amount dropped by over $16 million.

“Due to privacy requirements and contractual obligations between Canada and the recipient, we are not in a position to share the letter, discuss its contents nor disclose any details of any subsequent meetings between ISC officials and the Fsin Executive,” said ISC spokesperson Carolane Gratton in a statement.

ISC says department officials, not Minister Mandy Gull-Masty, are involved in its audit processes, and that ISC auditors met regularly with Fsin officials to share updates and request more documents.

The statement comes after Fsin disputed the audit decision and said the minister had only communicated with the organization through the media, despite repeated attempts to reach her by phone and email.

In its statement last week, the Fsin said the organization participated fully in the federal review and held extensive line-by-line discussions with a negotiation team appointed by ISC, adding the two sides had substantially narrowed the disputed amount by June 12.

According to the Fsin, federal representatives had confirmed that all purchases of personal protective equipment, accounting for almost $8 million of the current $12.4-million claim, were substantiated as purchased and delivered and had been removed from the list of ineligible or questionable expenditures.

The organization said it was surprised those expenses were subsequently added back to the amount being claimed.

In its statement, ISC says the Fsin has until Nov. 13, 2026 to “communicate with ISC for the repayment of the total amount to the Receiver General of Canada.” However, in the letter sent to Fsin, the department said this was the deadline for payment in full.

ISC has not provided additional information surrounding its statement of claim or clarification surrounding the deadline.

Global News has reached out to Fsin Chief Bobby Cameron for comment but has not heard back.

Policy expert Ken Coates says it is unusual for federal departments to seek legal action for repayment from organizations they support, as they typically have longstanding relationships with them.

“In fact, critics of federal government spending have actually said for many years that they’ve been far too lax about doing that,” he said.

The case going to court will likely spur a larger conversation about federal funding approvals and decisions made during the COVID-19 pandemic, Coates said.

“We’re gonna see what’s underneath the mushroom cap and we’re not gonna like it,” he said.

“We’re going to look and see how the Government of Canada authorized money. How did they make their decisions during the pandemic? What was the immediate oversight that was provided?”

With files from Alessia Simona Maratta

stories.title: 'Perfect storm': Extreme weather fuelled Wainwright military base fire, expert says
stories.summary: A wildfire expert says powerful winds with shifting directions and dry weather contributed to rapid expansion of the fire at a military base in Wainwright, Alta., that left four soldiers dead and 39 others wounded.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Powerful winds with shifting directions and dry weather contributed to rapid expansion of the grass fire at a military base in Wainwright, Alta., that left four soldiers dead and 39 others wounded, a wildfire expert said.

Environment and Climate Change Canada had issued a severe weather alert for swaths of Alberta on Saturday, warning of powerful wind gusts of up to 90 kilometres per hour in the region where the base is located, 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

stories.title: N.B. RCMP officer did not commit crime while breaking man’s nose in arrest: watchdog
stories.summary: New Brunswick's police watchdog says an RCMP officer who broke a man's nose during an arrest did not commit a crime.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
New Brunswick’s police watchdog says an RCMP officer who broke a man’s nose during an arrest did not commit a crime.

The Serious Incident Response Team (SiRT) investigated after an officer injured a man while police executed a search warrant at a residence in Moncton on June 2.

The watchdog’s report says one of the four people at the residence did not co-operate with police and the officer pinned him against a forklift and took him to the ground, breaking his nose.

It also says the man who was injured told SiRT he has a hearing impairment and did not know what the officer was saying to him.

The watchdog found the officer acted reasonably while using force to secure the man in handcuffs because the man did not follow his commands.

New Brunswick RCMP said a 55-year-old Moncton man was injured during the intervention and later charged with 38 offences, including 25 counts of possession of property obtained by crime over $5,000.

stories.title: Happy hour is back
stories.summary: As workers go into the office more regularly, a chance to socialize with colleagues – and some good deals – May be drawing them out to bars and restaurants again
stories.author: Daniel Reale-Chin
stories.content:
It is 3:30 p.m. on a Thursday, and despite the overcast, chilly autumn weather, the rooftop deck at Cactus Club Cafe in Toronto’s Financial District feels warm and inviting. It is exactly the feeling that Katherine Baldock was looking for when choosing where to bring her client.

“You need this energy: the music, the atmosphere. It makes me seem more fun as a salesperson because I’m in a fun environment,” she says.

Perched at a two-top table with her laptop open, Baldock spends a few moments making notes, reflecting on the meeting she has just finished and sending updates to her team at Tundra Technical Solutions, a Toronto-based staffing firm. Like many at the tables around her – insurance agents in suits, university students catching up after class and salespeople with their clients – she is taking part in happy hour, the few hours between lunch and dinner when discounts at restaurants and bars draw people out of their workplaces.

In the past year, happy hour has made a resurgence as office towers in the city fill back up following return-to-office mandates from Canada’s largest financial institutions. According to OpenTable’s 2026 Restaurant Dining Trends Report , reservations between 4 and 4:59 p.m. increased by 30 per cent between January and the end of August, 2025, compared to the same time span in the year before. And the trend is expected to grow – 42 per cent of Canadians surveyed for the report say they would like to see more happy hour and value promotions in 2026.

Andrej Holly, General Manager of Cactus Club Cafe in First Canadian Place, says the restaurant has had a 30- to 35-per-cent growth in reservations from last year.

“A lot of that growth is just from happy hour,” says Holly. “People looking for a deal on drinks, food, and a good vibe and service.”

That hunger led Sebastian Rosado Mustafa, a 29-year-old senior software engineer, to create cheaperdrinks.now , an interactive map of 421 Toronto restaurants and their current happy hour offerings with detailed, up-to-date information. Since launching the site in March this year, the website has grown in visits, with 1,400 clicks in September and 450 unique visitors during the first week of October.

Creating the site came naturally for Rosado Mustafa, who was already keeping tabs on happy hour deals as a way to continue going out with friends and colleagues after work or enjoy a meal with his girlfriend for less.

“I think people resonate with the idea of finding a good deal and putting down their phone to connect,” says Rosado Mustafa, whose favourite happy hour in Toronto is at Mexican restaurant Anejo, featuring $4 tacos and $7.50 margaritas (which typically cost $12.50 during regular hours).

At the downtown Toronto Cactus Club, reservations have been on the rise. Customers are looking for good deals and ‘a good vibe,’ says general manager Andrej Holly.

While the downsides of consuming alcohol remain a big deterrent for many Canadians – last year, The Globe and Mail reported on the uptick in sales of non-alcoholic drinks as health groups pushed for warning labels on alcoholic products – drinking is starting to make a comeback.

In Canada, alcohol consumption among Gen Z , rose to 73 per cent this year, up from 56 per cent three years ago, according to the latest Bevtrac survey conducted by Iwsr, the leading organization on global beverage data, which spoke with thousands of drinking age adults in 15 countries, including Canada. It also found that Gen Z drinkers were the most likely to consume alcoholic beverages with five or more people on their last occasion, suggesting that Gen Z considers drinking a way to connect.

Gen Z had a reputation for moderation, but these latest numbers bring it in line with the overall consumption rate across generations. The survey reports that Millennials remain the generation with the highest participation numbers for drinking, at 81 per cent, Generation X at 77 per cent, and Boomers at 71 per cent.

Edward Slingerland, a University of British Columbia professor and author of the book Drunk: How we Sipped, Danced and Stumbled Our Way to Civilization has been studying the evolutionary roots of humanity’s appetite for intoxication. The primary advantages of sharing a drink, he says, are creativity and social co-operation: Alcohol helps people relax and feel more comfortable sharing ideas with others.

The pandemic interrupted human sociality and after the lockdowns opened back up a lot of the negative consequences of the pandemic persisted, says Singerland. Gen Z workers, in particular reported feeling that their social skills were stunted by the pandemic and found more difficulty maintaining workplace relationships in the following years versus other generations. After years on Zoom calls and of working in hybrid environments, getting together socially in person can provide opportunities for career networking and building relationships.

Of course, happy hour meeting go-ers should be mindful about consumption. Booze can cloud judgement: alcohol downregulates your prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain that weighs choices, predicts the consequences of actions and inhibits inappropriate urges, warns Slingerland. “There are ways to capture the benefits while mitigating the risks,” he says, pointing to tools such as mocktails and non-alcoholic beers as ways for people to feel that they are still bonding at happy hour without being intoxicated.

Colleagues Ravish Kamath and Nathan VanWyk work in insurance and now operate on a hybrid in-office schedule, which requires them to work downtown most days per week. They attend happy hour about twice a month as a way to connect with other people from work over cheap drinks and a bite to eat.

On Thursday, the 30- and 25-year-old attended happy hour at Cactus Club with three friends from work. Most were sipping a pint of beer, but one had a mocktail.

“I think the biggest reason we come out for happy hour is happiness. We’re not all from the same team, so it’s nice to go out for an hour with people from our office around our age and grab a cheap drink and just talk for a bit,” says VanWyk.
paragraphs: It is 3:30 p.m. on a Thursday, and despite the overcast, chilly autumn weather, the rooftop deck at Cactus Club Cafe in Toronto’s Financial District feels warm and inviting. It is exactly the feeling that Katherine Baldock was looking for when choosing where to bring her client.
“You need this energy: the music, the atmosphere. It makes me seem more fun as a salesperson because I’m in a fun environment,” she says.

Perched at a two-top table with her laptop open, Baldock spends a few moments making notes, reflecting on the meeting she has just finished and sending updates to her team at Tundra Technical Solutions, a Toronto-based staffing firm. Like many at the tables around her – insurance agents in suits, university students catching up after class and salespeople with their clients – she is taking part in happy hour, the few hours between lunch and dinner when discounts at restaurants and bars draw people out of their workplaces.

In the past year, happy hour has made a resurgence as office towers in the city fill back up following return-to-office mandates from Canada’s largest financial institutions. According to OpenTable’s 2026 Restaurant Dining Trends Report , reservations between 4 and 4:59 p.m. increased by 30 per cent between January and the end of August, 2025, compared to the same time span in the year before. And the trend is expected to grow – 42 per cent of Canadians surveyed for the report say they would like to see more happy hour and value promotions in 2026.
Andrej Holly, General Manager of Cactus Club Cafe in First Canadian Place, says the restaurant has had a 30- to 35-per-cent growth in reservations from last year.
“A lot of that growth is just from happy hour,” says Holly. “People looking for a deal on drinks, food, and a good vibe and service.”

That hunger led Sebastian Rosado Mustafa, a 29-year-old senior software engineer, to create cheaperdrinks.now , an interactive map of 421 Toronto restaurants and their current happy hour offerings with detailed, up-to-date information. Since launching the site in March this year, the website has grown in visits, with 1,400 clicks in September and 450 unique visitors during the first week of October.

Creating the site came naturally for Rosado Mustafa, who was already keeping tabs on happy hour deals as a way to continue going out with friends and colleagues after work or enjoy a meal with his girlfriend for less.

“I think people resonate with the idea of finding a good deal and putting down their phone to connect,” says Rosado Mustafa, whose favourite happy hour in Toronto is at Mexican restaurant Anejo, featuring $4 tacos and $7.50 margaritas (which typically cost $12.50 during regular hours).
At the downtown Toronto Cactus Club, reservations have been on the rise. Customers are looking for good deals and ‘a good vibe,’ says general manager Andrej Holly.

While the downsides of consuming alcohol remain a big deterrent for many Canadians – last year, The Globe and Mail reported on the uptick in sales of non-alcoholic drinks as health groups pushed for warning labels on alcoholic products – drinking is starting to make a comeback.

In Canada, alcohol consumption among Gen Z , rose to 73 per cent this year, up from 56 per cent three years ago, according to the latest Bevtrac survey conducted by Iwsr, the leading organization on global beverage data, which spoke with thousands of drinking age adults in 15 countries, including Canada. It also found that Gen Z drinkers were the most likely to consume alcoholic beverages with five or more people on their last occasion, suggesting that Gen Z considers drinking a way to connect.

Gen Z had a reputation for moderation, but these latest numbers bring it in line with the overall consumption rate across generations. The survey reports that Millennials remain the generation with the highest participation numbers for drinking, at 81 per cent, Generation X at 77 per cent, and Boomers at 71 per cent.

Edward Slingerland, a University of British Columbia professor and author of the book Drunk: How we Sipped, Danced and Stumbled Our Way to Civilization has been studying the evolutionary roots of humanity’s appetite for intoxication. The primary advantages of sharing a drink, he says, are creativity and social co-operation: Alcohol helps people relax and feel more comfortable sharing ideas with others.

The pandemic interrupted human sociality and after the lockdowns opened back up a lot of the negative consequences of the pandemic persisted, says Singerland. Gen Z workers, in particular reported feeling that their social skills were stunted by the pandemic and found more difficulty maintaining workplace relationships in the following years versus other generations. After years on Zoom calls and of working in hybrid environments, getting together socially in person can provide opportunities for career networking and building relationships.

Of course, happy hour meeting go-ers should be mindful about consumption. Booze can cloud judgement: alcohol downregulates your prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain that weighs choices, predicts the consequences of actions and inhibits inappropriate urges, warns Slingerland. “There are ways to capture the benefits while mitigating the risks,” he says, pointing to tools such as mocktails and non-alcoholic beers as ways for people to feel that they are still bonding at happy hour without being intoxicated.

Colleagues Ravish Kamath and Nathan VanWyk work in insurance and now operate on a hybrid in-office schedule, which requires them to work downtown most days per week. They attend happy hour about twice a month as a way to connect with other people from work over cheap drinks and a bite to eat.
On Thursday, the 30- and 25-year-old attended happy hour at Cactus Club with three friends from work. Most were sipping a pint of beer, but one had a mocktail.

“I think the biggest reason we come out for happy hour is happiness. We’re not all from the same team, so it’s nice to go out for an hour with people from our office around our age and grab a cheap drink and just talk for a bit,” says VanWyk.

stories.title: Halifax Forum meeting to be rescheduled, councillors raise concerns over project pause
stories.summary: The 98-yera-old Halifax Forum is a municipal heritage property, and any redevelopment would require a legal process that includes public engagement.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
Discussions around the future of the aging Halifax Forum are back on track, after Halifax Regional Council voted in favour Tuesday of setting a new date for a community meeting on the proposed demolition of the heritage building.

The nearly century-old recreation centre is a municipal heritage property, and any redevelopment would require a legal process that includes public engagement.

The meeting was originally planned for Oct. 1, but was cancelled last month.

HRM staff announced the cancellation on Sept. 25, and said they would need to pause the redevelopment project to re-evaluate financial options.

According to staff, the updated project costs exceeded the $126 million approved by council by 10 to 12 per cent.

The decision blindsided the Halifax Forum Community Association.

“Nobody reached out prior to this and said something’s going on. This was an 11th-hour decision late on the Friday,” said Paul Card, chair of the association board, ON Sept. 29.

At Tuesday’s council meeting, councillors said they too felt they weren’t properly briefed before the process was paused.

“That (community) meeting does need to happen at some point and it’s better to have it now than later because the cost could have increased from just waiting for that meeting to come up four or five months later,” said District 8 Coun. Virginia Hinch.

Some councillors said they didn’t understand why the meeting on the building’s heritage status was cancelled.

“Whether or not we vote to continue with this project or whether or not we’re going down where the mayor wants to go and sell off the land and demolish the place, it doesn’t matter,” said District 5 Coun. Sam Austin.

“Either way, you got to do the heritage piece.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Either way, you got to do the heritage piece."

Municipal staff say a report they intend to release in December will have a more fulsome look at the status of the Forum project, as well as third-party insight into the cost increases.

Other councillors raised concerns about why staff had enough information to cancel the meeting, but couldn’t share all the details with council.

“So if there was enough information to cancel the public information meeting, why does council have to wait until December to get the report?” said District 10 Coun. Kathryn Morse.

Mayor Andy Fillmore said he sees value in moving things forward while staff continue working on the next steps.

“There’s no reason why we can’t have the staff going ahead and getting that third-party verification of cost while we proceed with a public consultation on demolition that we know has to happen anyway,” he said.

“So I think this is a good way to keep the ball rolling.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "So I think this is a good way to keep the ball rolling."

The motion to reschedule the public meeting was passed unanimously. While a specific date hasn’t been set yet, the meeting is expected to take place sometime in November.

Coun. Hinch stressed that the decision isn’t just about preventing delays but also about rebuilding community trust.

“If we’re going to do something, just do it, especially when it comes to public meetings,” she said. “I believe that we just need to keep to our word.”

stories.title: Trump’s 50% tariffs on Canada hit by new lawsuit from U.S. food importer
stories.summary: The 50 per cent tariffs were imposed when trade talks broke down in August after the prime minister said the deal would have given U.S. power to control who it could trade with.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:
A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs targeting Canada has been filed in the United States Court of International Trade.

The lawsuit, filed today by the non-profit Liberty Justice Center on behalf of U.S. food importer Gellert Global Group, argues Trump’s use of a Depression-era trade statute exceeds his power as president.

Trump used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap an array of Canadian goods with a 50 per cent levy after trade talks broke down in August.

The same statute was used the following month to ban the import of other Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products.

Liberty Justice Center CEO Sara Albrecht says in a news release that no president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans.

The lawsuit asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful and order a refund.
