stories.title: As Stelco reports soaring earnings, how solid is their layoff legal case?
stories.summary: U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs said on Monday that it saw its strongest quarterly financial results since the year before acquiring Stelco in 2024.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs said on Monday that it saw its strongest quarterly financial results since the year before acquiring Stelco in 2024.

This comes as Stelco continues to lay off hundreds of workers at its steel plant in Hamilton, Ont., while citing pressure from U.S. tariffs , a decision the federal government says breaches its binding agreement to maintain jobs.

Cleveland-Cliffs said it saw net earnings of US$612 million in the third quarter, up from $286 million in the previous quarter.

Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves in the report said, “Third quarter was our strongest quarter in three years,” and added that the figure was higher than the $575 million guidance they provided three months earlier.

On Tuesday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly spoke outside the House of Commons.

“We took good note of the earnings call that happened yesterday where the CEO of Stelco again mentioned that he was in favour of American tariffs against steelworkers in Canada and therefore we’ve hired the best lawyers to advise us on what to do next,” said Joly.

“I’ll have more to say in the coming days, but we’re following this very closely. We’ve been working also with the union as they’re providing important proof for a legal case.”

Several legal experts say that, based on publicly available information, the federal government could have a strong case.

“The federal government’s case, from everything we’ve heard, is rock solid and they should be seeking injunctive relief against the layoffs entirely and recalling the workers.”

Stelco announced last month that pressure from U.S. tariffs forced it to concentrate steel production at its Lake Erie Works plant in Haldimand, Ont., and halt production at its plant in Hamilton. Although the company said some of those workers would be offered positions at the Haldimand facility, hundreds are still expected to be out of work.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs include a 50 per cent duty on various Canadian steel products, and Stelco claims that has severely impacted its sales.

Here’s how the two arguments stack up, according to legal experts.

When Cleveland-Cliffs acquired Stelco in 2024, the federal government approved the deal under the Investment Canada Act. The full legally binding agreement has not been made public, although a summary of its terms was released in 2024 .

According to the summary, the agreement with Cleveland-Cliffs includes a commitment “To continue to employ at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees as were employed when the transaction was announced.”

The federal government’s stance is that by using tariffs to justify laying off workers, Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs breached the agreement.

“But again, it’s based on what we’ve heard and I’m surprised the federal government has not released the actual documents. But I’m also surprised, if the owner of Stelco has a real good defence, that they haven’t released the actual documents.”

Joly sent Stelco’s president a letter on Oct. 5 demanding the company outline how it plans to abide by its commitments, including preserving jobs.

In addition, Joly said last week that Goncalves has been a vocal supporter of U.S. tariffs on steel, and therefore the company cannot use tariffs as an excuse for layoffs.

“He’s in favor of these U.S. tariffs against steel,” she said to reporters on Oct. 7.

“They cannot say that this is now an act of God or force majeure.”

Employment lawyer Christopher Achkar, managing partner at Achkar Law, says that in this context, Stelco using tariffs as an excuse for layoffs amounts to trying to “have your cake and eat it too.”

“You can’t say that you are in favor of something, and then when it actually happens, say, ‘oh, it is out of my hands,’ — you are the one who was in favor of that,” he says.

“I think Stelco’s positions from a practical standpoint are quite weak.”

Further, Achkar says that Stelco would likely have a tough time arguing that tariffs forced it to lay off workers, when it also refused financial assistance from the federal government to mitigate those risks.

Stelco’s president, Paul Simon, responded to Joly’s letter on Oct. 9.

The seven-page response detailed the company’s stance, and said the federal government’s accusations are “false.”

“Stelco submitted its annual report confirming its compliance with the employment undertakings in November 2025. That report highlighted that Stelco was facing significant challenges due to the unforeseen consequences stemming from unprecedented U.S. tariffs and Canada’s failure to advance an effective ‘Fortress North America’ trade regime,” the letter said.

“Your representation that Stelco’s planned layoffs cause it to breach its undertakings is false as the undertakings do not stipulate a commitment to avoid layoffs.”

The company is describing the cuts as indefinite layoffs, while the union is treating them as temporary under its collective agreement, which Levitt says is a key detail.

“You can lay off some without paying them anything, as long as you maintain benefits for 35 weeks, if it’s a temporary layoff. But Stelco announced this is an ‘indefinite’ layoff — in my mind, that’s a termination, not a layoff.”

The letter also says its exports of cold-rolled and coated steel to the United States have plunged 58 per cent from pre-trade-war levels as foreign imports continue to undercut Canadian-made steel.

Achkar says the wording in the letter suggests Stelco May seek to argue its case based on a technicality.

“Their argument is going to be that they are still technically employees and the headcount is still technically the same,” he says.

Achkar also explains that the Investment Canada Act stipulates to avoid terminating workers, while these tariff-related layoffs are considered by the company to be temporary measures until market conditions improve.

“Stelco is saying that a layoff doesn’t mean that they’re no longer an employee, and if our undertaking says that we are going to maintain the same headcount, the question is, is it staying the same with a temporary layoff?”

Ultimately, Achkar expects the case will not go to the Supreme Court because Stelco’s case May not be strong enough to justify it. Instead, he believes the case will likely wind up being a negotiated settlement.

“They are in breach, whether they can justify the breach May fall on a technicality. My estimation of it is it would probably be a weak one and will not succeed,” he says.

After she confirmed receipt of the letter from Stelco over the Thanksgiving long weekend, Joly was asked by reporters on Oct. 14 if she still believes the case will go to court.

“We expect Stelco to follow the undertakings that they’ve committed to, to the Government of Canada, and right now, a business decision or even a change in market conditions cannot be used to not follow the commitment. So we’re reviewing the Stelco letter,” Joly said.

“A few possible outcomes of a court process can lead to financial penalties towards a company, forcing them to abide by the commitment, and also a forced divestiture, so forcing them to sell their Canadian assets. Everything is on the table.”

She added: “I’m always open to sit down with the company and find a solution, but we’re looking at everything that is possible to keep jobs in Canada.”

stories.title: Protesters return to defence trade show as attendees position for increased defence spending
stories.summary: A defence industry trade show that sparked protests and arrests last year remained peaceful on Tuesday morning.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A defence industry trade show that sparked protests and arrests last year remained peaceful on Tuesday morning.

The return of the Best Defence Conference coincides with increased federal government military spending.

The conference is billed as an opportunity for industry and public safety contractors to connect with military officials and government procurement agencies. It attracts southwestern Ontario’s growing defence industry.

On Tuesday, a smaller group of protesters threw jeers at attendees arriving at RBC Place.

They also called on passersby to challenge the show’s presence.

“This is your city that they are manufacturing death in!” said one person with a megaphone.

In 2025 , things were much more heated.

London Police made an arrest after portions of RBC Place were damaged.

Weeks later, police executed search warrants across the province, leading to more counts.

This year, barricades blocked ground-level entrances except for the main doors.

Uniform police officers were positioned to check IDs throughout the day.

“We can say that we have police resources on hand in the event that they are needed. And if there are any instances of violence or property damage, they will be investigated,” said London Police Sergeant Sandasha Bough.

Protester Kellin Johnson told CTV News they did not want a repeat of 2025.

“We had some issues last year. This year, keeping it completely peaceful is our plan. We don’t want any conflict. We want to show up that we are on the side of peace and not war.”

The protesters called on conference attendees to walk away from the trade show, which according to its website was sponsored by General Dynamic Land Systems-Canada, Western University, and other groups.

Although not directly involved in the show, the London Chamber of Commerce later commented on how vital the defence sector is to the region.

Kristen Duever, Chief Operating Officer said, “Defence is an economic issue as much as anything. It creates very high-paying jobs, skilled jobs in advanced manufacturing, innovation, and technology. So, it’s very important to our economy as well as to the country’s defence.”

stories.title: The end of the beginning: Alberta’s real referendum message for Carney
stories.summary: Albertans May have rejected separation for now, but they also endorsed an agenda for changing Canada that has considerable support elsewhere in the country.
stories.author: Darrell Bricker
stories.content:
On Monday, Albertans voted in a provincewide referendum that could have important consequences for Canada’s future. But the question attracting the most attention May not be the one that matters most.

The tenth question asked Albertans whether they want to remain in Canada or take the next step toward separation. As of the time of writing, only a quarter of Alberta voters opted for another referendum. Three-quarters opted against another referendum and said they wanted to remain in Canada.

But results from the other nine questions May tell a more interesting story. All but Question 10 garnered majority support. Ipsos polling for Global News also found that Canadians outside Alberta supported eight of the nine proposals by majority. Albertans May have rejected separation for now, but they also endorsed an agenda for changing Canada that has considerable support elsewhere in the country.

Prime Minister Mark Carney seems to understand the message he received. At a rally in Calgary on October 15, he urged Albertans to reject the other nine questions with the slogan “No to the Nine.” Carney wasn’t simply campaigning against separation. He was taking a position against proposals that could reshape our country.

The remaining nine questions cover two broad areas. The first five concern immigration and access to public services. They propose greater provincial control over immigration, lower immigration levels, employment preferences and restrictions on access to publicly funded services for temporary residents. They also address proof of citizenship for provincial voting.

The other four concern the federal system itself. They propose provincial control over appointments to superior courts, abolition of the Senate, the right to opt out of federal programs without losing funding and provincial laws taking precedence over federal laws in areas of provincial or shared jurisdiction.

Some proposals would require constitutional changes. Others could be addressed through existing legislation. None automatically becomes law even though Albertans voted for them. But majority support has given Premier Danielle Smith justification to pursue them.

Quebec’s recent election adds another layer. Voters there have just elected a sovereigntist Parti Québécois government. Alberta and Quebec have different objectives, but both could find common cause in demanding greater provincial autonomy. Ottawa could soon face demands from two provinces with very different motivations seeking fundamental changes to Confederation.

For the past year, Donald Trump’s trade war against Canada has dominated Canadian politics. The threat from Washington has encouraged Canadians to rally around the flag. But national unity in the face of an external threat hasn’t eliminated the disagreements within Canada.

One of the most persistent has been the conflict between Alberta and Ottawa. It intensified during the Trudeau years, particularly over energy and environmental policy. For many Albertans, the dispute became a question of whether Ottawa was treating their province fairly.

Carney has tried to change that relationship. His support for a new pipeline to tidewater represents a significant departure from the direction many Albertans associated with the previous Liberal government. But a pipeline remains a promise until it is built. Alberta’s demands for greater provincial autonomy extend well beyond energy.

A poll can show support for a proposal, but it doesn’t reflect support for the negotiations required to make it happen. Canadians May like abolishing the Senate without agreeing on what should replace it. They May favour greater provincial autonomy without wanting to reopen the Constitution.

But dismissing these results would miss the point. The public opinion exists, and it isn’t confined to Alberta. What’s missing is a political agenda capable of bringing these attitudes together. stories.title: Albertans largely support measures aimed at reducing immigration, split on constitutional questions
stories.summary: Close results mean there isn’t any obvious immediate impact, law professor says
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
The preliminary count in Alberta ’s referendum shows that a small majority of voters support reducing immigration. On questions of whether Premier Danielle Smith ’s government should pursue constitutional reform on issues such as appointing judges or abolishing the federal Senate, voters are split.

Beyond the main question on separation, voters in Alberta marked ballots on nine other referendum questions.

Ms. Smith and her government campaigned in favour of voting no to separation but yes to the other nine questions. In a social media post Monday morning, the Premier made one last push for “Yes to the Nine” and said it would mean Alberta “gets a real say” over immigration and “constitutional reforms that protect this province’s authority no matter who sits in Ottawa.”

As of midafternoon Tuesday, the yes votes were leading in all but one of those additional questions, with 88 per cent of polls reporting. Ms. Smith has said she will use the results to push for negotiations with Ottawa and other provinces while also proposing her own policies, likely after next year’s scheduled provincial election.

On some questions, however, the results remained too close to call.

Preliminary results showed 54 per cent of voters answered yes to a proposal that Alberta take greater control of immigration, in part to limit the number of newcomers.

Three related questions about limiting services such as health care to some newcomers, or charging fees, garnered 55-, 57- and 58-per-cent support.

On constitutional questions, support for reform ranges from 49 per cent to 54 per cent.

Those figures held steady as votes were tallied Tuesday.

As the final ballots are counted, it is unclear what impact the questions will have on government policy or any response from other provinces and Ottawa.

Five years ago, 62 per cent of Albertans voted in favour of a referendum question about removing equalization from the Constitution. But turnout was low, and nothing tangible happened.

Constitutional reform in Canada is difficult, requiring the support of at least seven provinces representing more than half the country’s population, alongside Ottawa’s backing.

In Ottawa on Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the federal government will work with the provinces on immigration, arguing that jibes with the spirit of one of Alberta’s referendum questions.

The slim majority on some questions and split result on the rest means there won’t be any obvious, immediate impact, said Shaun Fluker, a law professor at the University of Calgary.

“There really aren’t any legal consequences flowing directly from the outcome of these nine questions,” he said in an interview Tuesday.

Prof. Fluker called the results of the immigration questions disappointing and described them as divisive, adding that Ms. Smith’s government did “such a poor job informing Albertans about the context of the questions.”

He pointed to Question 6, which asked Albertans to back the provincial government in seeking the support of other provinces to amend the Constitution so the provinces, rather than the federal government, name judges to the top two courts in each province, the superior and appeal courts. Fifty-one per cent of voters said yes.

In the Constitution, the federal government has the power to name judges to these courts, but an appointment system in place for the past four decades solicits a range of input on potential candidates, who apply to judicial advisory committees. Each province gets some input on appointments to their own courts, including from the provincial justice minister and chief justice.

Richard Mailey, director of the Centre for Constitutional Studies at the University of Alberta’s law school, said the referendum results in general don’t make a strong case for an Alberta mandate to negotiate, but judicial appointments May be an exception.

“This is one area where I see some room to manoeuvre, despite the small size of the majority that supported it in the referendum,” Prof. Mailey said.

He cited potential support from Ontario and Quebec and the fact that constitutional reform isn’t necessary for Ottawa to offer provinces more input on appointments by increasing their power on the judicial advisory committees.

Two weeks ago, the federal government named two new judges in Alberta: Justice Thomas Rothwell, a judge on the Court of King’s Bench, was elevated to the Court of Appeal; and Malcolm Lavoie, deputy minister of justice in Ms. Smith’s government, was appointed to the Court of King’s Bench to replace Justice Rothwell.

The day after the appointments, the Alberta government put out a news release praising the appointments, an unusual move.

“Alberta’s government welcomes the federal government’s willingness to meaningfully collaborate on these judicial appointments,” Alberta Justice Minister Mickey Amery said in a statement, adding that the province’s top courts “should reflect Albertans and the province they serve.”

“Our government looks forward to continuing our collaboration with the federal government while hearing from Albertans about the future of judicial appointments in our province,” Mr. Amery said on Oct. 9.

Mr. Lavoie was a law professor at the University of Alberta before he joined Ms. Smith’s government at the start of 2024. During his time in government, he worked on the province’s various uses of the notwithstanding clause in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and last March argued at the Supreme Court of Canada in favour of no new restrictions on the clause in the landmark Bill 21 case from Quebec.

Justice Rothwell had been an assistant deputy minister in Alberta’s Justice Department before he became a judge in 2020. Early in his career, he served as a clerk to John Major, a former Supreme Court justice from Calgary.

stories.title: Bradford slightly ahead of Chow in Toronto mayoral race, two new polls show
stories.summary: But the number of undecided voters are large enough to put either candidate in the mayor's office.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Two new polls from Mainstreet Research and Build Canada have put Toronto mayoral candidate Brad Bradford ahead of the incumbent mayor, Olivia Chow, with less than a week to go before Oct. 26, voting day in Canada’s largest city.

Among decided voters (including those who have already marked their ballots in advance polls), Bradford has a slight edge over Chow, with 48.9 per cent support for the Beaches-East York councillor, against 47.5 per cent who favour the current mayor. (The remaining 3.6 per cent were split among 46 other candidates, with no one candidate receiving even a single percentage point.)

Taking undecided voters into account reveals a similar split, with 42.4 per cent favouring Bradford and 41.1 per cent on the side of Chow. However, a further 13.4 per cent said they remain undecided, meaning that group has the power to swing the election one way or the other.

“This race is truly too close to call, but Bradford now has the upper hand” Quito Maggi, President & CEO of Mainstreet Research, said in a statement.

“This represents a seismic shift in the Mayoral election in Toronto,” he added. “While we have seen this race tighten significantly throughout October, Chow had previously led wire to wire and led in three of four regions of Toronto.”

He concluded: “This race will come down to turnout and get-out-the-vote efforts from these campaigns. Bradford continues to lead among older voters who are more likely to vote, so he maintains that advantage.”

The Build Canada poll asked participants to say who they would vote for or, if they were undecided, who they were leaning towards. It found 48 per cent support for Bradford against 44 per cent for Chow, and eight per cent split among the remaining candidates.

Build Canada also asked respondents a variety of questions about life in Toronto, and priorities for the next municipal government. Asked to choose between “Toronto’s next mayor and council should try new ideas, even if some of them fail,” and “they should be careful, even if that means slower progress,” two thirds (67 per cent) opted for new ideas, while 23 per cent said play it safe.

Most of those polled (55 per cent) also said City Hall moved too slowly when making decisions, versus eight per cent who said it was too fast, and 16 per cent who thought it moved at the right pace.

The poll also found dissatisfaction with property taxes. Only five per cent of respondents said they got very good value for the tax they paid, while a quarter chose “fairly good value” and another quarter said “fairly poor value.” The largest group, at 37 per cent, said they got very poor value for their property taxes.

The Mainstreet poll also asked potential voters how likely they were to go to the ballot box, with a strong majority saying they planned to. Of those who had not voted already, 82.4 per cent said they definitely would, while another 8.1 per cent said they would probably vote. Only 3.5 per cent said they definitely would not be voting.

This is a marked departure from most municipal elections. In the 2023 election that brought Chow to the office of mayor, the turnout was 38.5 per cent, a nine per cent increase over the previous election in 2022.

However, the city has noted that advance voting is already far higher than in other recent elections. Over the six days of advance voting this month, 222,5550 eligible votes were cast. That’s almost double the number from the 2023 election, which saw almost 130,000 advance votes.

In an interview with National Post, Maggi also noted that past polls have always shown more people who claim to vote than actual do. He also pointed out that “the type of people who take time to complete a poll are also the type who are likely to vote.”

Mainstreet also asked Toronto voters to rate the importance of several issues in the election. Affordability and the cost of living was the highest ranked issue at 38.3 per cent, followed by traffic and transit (22.4 per cent) and crime and safety (16.4 per cent).

Perhaps looking to tap into that feeling, Bradford released a campaign ad yesterday in which his wife and daughter drop by a public appearance and find him promising people “a city that’s safer, a city that’s more affordable; I have a plan to get Toronto unstuck,” before adding: “But if we want to change the city, we have to change the mayor.”

The slick-looking ad drew some online comments that it might have been produced by AI, but the post on X now carries reader-generated content that it wasn’t. This includes behind-the-scenes photos and statements from the production team.

The Mainstreet poll was conducted Oct. 16 through Oct. 18 and involved 1,000 adult Toronto residents. It has a margin of error of 3.1 per cent, 19 times out of 20. Build Canada’s survey involved 991 randomly selected Toronto adults between Oct. 11 and Oct. 16, with the same margin of error.

stories.title: Slowing economy will mean more red ink and debt costs for Carney's budget, PBO says
stories.summary: The Canadian economy will slow to a crawl over the coming months, Ottawa's fiscal watchdog said Tuesday in a new report.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Canadian economy will slow to a crawl over the coming months, which will lead the Carney government to increase both its borrowing and interest payments more than what was expected just four months ago, Ottawa’s fiscal watchdog said Tuesday in a new report.

With the federal budget scheduled for Nov. 5, the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) added to the government’s fiscal squeeze by projecting that the Canadian economy will grow this calendar year by just 0.9 per cent and 1.5 per cent in 2027, down from the 1.1 per cent and 1.6 per cent that were forecast just four months ago. The slower growth is primarily a function of the Canada-United States trade war escalation that started in June.

The Pbo’s Economic and Fiscal Outlook also said that the federal deficit for this year is projected to be $59.3-billion, climbing to $83-billion by 2030-31, in part because of increased borrowing and higher rates on accumulated debt. Projected deficits are now expected to be an average of $3-billion higher per year than what was expected just four months ago.

That will mean that federal debt charges, the budget’s fastest-growing expense, are projected to more than double from $24.5 billion in 2021‑22 to $59.3 billion during this fiscal year, and are projected to reach $83.0 billion by 2030‑31.

The PBO report said that Ottawa has been raking in more revenue than what was expected last spring, due largely to inflation and higher prices for oil and other commodities. But that additional spending of $10.5-billion a year will more than use up that windfall over the coming years.

Ottawa continues to swim in an increasingly large pool of red ink. The federal government has now accumulated $1.27-trillion in total debt, almost half of which has been added over the last five years. Using the Pbo’s new figures, Ottawa is expected to add $333.3-billlion in additional debt over the next five years, a 26.2 per cent increase in the government’s total debt.

Meanwhile on Tuesday, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told the House of Commons that the federal budget will be held Nov. 5.

The PBO report will only add pressure on the Carney government to reduce its annual deficit, while still investing in infrastructure and other projects designed to improve the productivity of the economy.

The government has already said that it’s identified $60-billion in savings over the next five years, which will help pay for some of the additional spending on infrastructure, defence, tax cuts and other priorities.

The PBO said that the success of those productivity efforts will go a long way in determining Canada’s economic future. “Over the longer term, Canada’s economic and fiscal outlook will depend heavily on whether recent capital budget investments can translate into stronger productivity, economic capacity and prosperity.”

But many economists continue to warn about the dangers of escalating debt charges.

Franco Terrazzano, federal director of the Canadian Taxpayers Federation, said the federal government has no plan to stop borrowing money. “Debt interest payments continue to spiral out of control because government spending continues to spiral out of control,” he said in a release.

The PBO says federal debt charges are now projected to climb next year to $1,419 per Canadian, up from $640 in 2021-22, and on track to reach $1,952 per person in 2030-31. And according to PBO figures, Ottawa’s debt per capita will rise from $29,811 in 2021-22 to $33,436 in 2026-27 and reach $39,191 in 2030-31.

stories.title: Lawsuit filed challenging Trump's tariffs on Canada
stories.summary: A lawsuit challenging U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs targeting Canada has been filed in the United States Court of International Trade.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A U.S. food importer has filed a lawsuit in the United States Court of International Trade challenging U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs targeting Canada.

The lawsuit, filed Tuesday by the non-profit Liberty Justice Center on behalf of Gellert Global Group in the New York-based court, argued Trump’s use of a Depression-era trade statute exceeds his power as president.

“No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” Liberty Justice Center CEO Sara Albrecht said in a news release.

Trump used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap an array of Canadian goods with a 50 per cent levy after trade talks broke down in August.

The same statute was used the following month to ban imports of other Canadian goods, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products.

The White House has said Section 338 empowers the president to impose tariffs when a country puts U.S. exporters at a disadvantage relative to exporters in other countries — even though the law had never been used for that purpose.

U.S. officials have said the latest duties are a response to provincial bans on U.S. liquor, Canada’s supply managed dairy system and quotas on certain U.S. vehicles.

Tuesday’s lawsuit said the Canadian policies don’t justify the sweeping tariffs imposed by the Trump administration.

It notes two of the measures — auto quotas and liquor bans — were actually a response to Trump’s own tariff measures. The lawsuit also said Canada’s dairy supply management involves policies agreed to under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as Cusma, which was negotiated during the first Trump administration.

A Trump administration official, commenting on background, said the president’s actions will be vigorously defended in court. The official added that Tuesday’s lawsuit won’t deter the president’s commitment to levelling the playing field for American workers, farmers and firms.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said Tuesday that in the Trump administration’s view, Canada and the United States are not in a trade war.

“We are negotiating some tariffs,” Hoekstra said at a conference in Gatineau, Que.

“From our perspective, we don’t view the relationship as ruptured. I know that the Canadians look at it differently.”

But the Trump administration’s actions are leading to consequences for American businesses.

Thomas Gellert, co-chief executive officer of New Jersey-based Gellert Global Group, said the company has “spent generations building trusted relationships with suppliers, customers and partners across the food industry.”

“These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain,” Gellert said in the news release.

The company is being hit by the trade war on all sides, the news release said. It pays a 50 per cent tariff on imports of Canadian cheese but is also slammed by Ottawa’s retaliatory tariffs on American-made cheeses its Canadian division sells in Canada.

The company cites the experience of one of its Canadian cheese suppliers to show how the integrated North American market is being disrupted by the tariff dispute. It gets milk from dairy farmers in Upstate New York, which is processed into brie in Canada, which is then sent back to the United States.

“The tariffs hit American farmers and businesses on both sides of that transaction,” the news release said.

The case raises concerns beyond Canada, the news release added. If the duties remain unchecked, any president could use Section 338 to impose tariffs and trade restrictions without meaningful congressional control.

The Liberty Justice Center was previously involved in the legal challenge against Trump’s use of the International Economic Emergency Powers Act of 1977 for the so-called “Liberation Day” and fentanyl-related tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China.

In February, America’s top court concluded it was not legal for Trump to use the statute, known as Ieepa, because the U.S. Constitution very clearly gives Congress power over taxes and tariffs.

The president replaced those duties with a stopgap tariff statute — which also faced a legal challenge — before putting in place levies of 10 to 12.5 per cent on most nations around the world, citing forced labour in supply chains.

A coalition of U.S. states is challenging the use of Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to hit the world with the forced-labour duties.

Tuesday’s lawsuit argues that Section 338 is defunct and has been superseded by other laws, including Section 301. It also says Trump’s tariffs don’t meet various requirements for invoking the law, such as a 30-day waiting period.

“Congress already gave the executive branch a tool for responding to unfair foreign trade practices: Section 301, which requires an investigation, public comment and other safeguards,” Liberty Justice Center Senior Counsel Jeffrey M. Schwab said in the news release.

“The administration cannot skip those protections by reaching for a 1930 statute that no president had ever used to impose a tariff.”

The lawsuit asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful and order a refund.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Three ‘armed and dangerous’ suspects sought after weekend shooting
stories.summary: London police are looking for three suspects as one person remains in hospital after a shooting over the weekend.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
London police are looking for three suspects as one person remains in hospital after a shooting over the weekend .

Investigators say they have identified the three suspects in relation to the incident. All three are currently wanted by the London Police Service and have not been located.

Owen Barclay, 19, of London is charged by way of warrant of arrest with the following offences:

Attempt to commit murder using a firearm;

Discharge firearm with intent to wound/endanger life;

Occupy motor vehicle with firearm; and

Possess restricted or prohibited firearm knowingly not holding a licence.

Tyler Lewis McLaughlin, 19, and Julianna Marie Smith, 18, both of London, are charged jointly by way of warrant of arrest with the following offences:

Aggravated assault;

Police say the suspects should be considered armed and dangerous. Members of the public are advised not to approach them. Anyone who has information about their whereabouts is asked to call 911 immediately.

The victim remains in hospital in fair condition.

The investigation is ongoing, and additional information will be provided as appropriate.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Mother of First Nation woman who couldn’t get medical transport and died seeks reform
stories.summary: The 31-year-old mother of three from Fort Severn First Nation died on Sept. 8, weeks after asking people on social media to seek action in case of her death.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
If only. It’s a phrase that plays over and over again in Eva Mamakwa’s mind.

If only her daughter, Miranda Mamakwa, had made it to at least one followup appointment after open-heart surgery, she May be alive.

If only Indigenous Services Canada’s non-insured health benefits program had arranged travel for just one of her four missed appointments, Miranda May be alive.

The 31-year-old mother of three from Fort Severn First Nation died on Sept. 8, weeks after asking people on social media to seek action in case of her death.

“I don’t want this to happen to anyone else,” Eva Mamakwa said in an interview with The Canadian Press from her home before falling quiet, overcome with emotion. She is speaking out about her daughter’s death for the first time.

Since Miranda Mamakwa’s death, more than a dozen First Nations and tribal councils have filed a human rights complaint that alleges widespread neglect of their communities’ health needs, while chiefs have demanded reform from the federal agency in charge of arranging medical travel for remote First Nation people.

Indigenous Services Canada said it’s working to improve delivery of the service, while the minister in charge has said she requested a fact-finding mission on the circumstances that led to Miranda Mamakwa’s death.

Months ago, Mamakwa’s family was filled with hope as she underwent surgery at the University of Ottawa Heart Institute in April to replace a valve in her heart. She recovered over two weeks at the hospital in Ottawa, then two more weeks at the Thunder Bay Regional Health Sciences Centre.

On May 24, she arrived home in Fort Severn First Nation, the most northerly community in Ontario that sits near the mouth of the Severn River on Hudson Bay.

Her doctors wanted to see her for several followups. She had blood clots and had been put on blood thinners, which required testing on an ongoing basis, Eva Mamakwa said. Doctors booked her daughter for an echocardiogram and an appointment with a vascular surgeon in Thunder Bay.

Miranda Mamakwa was thrilled to be back home; her children were excited and her mother was caring for her.

That excitement would soon abate.

Eva Mamakwa said she went to the First Nation’s nursing station to begin the administrative process to arrange travel back to Thunder Bay for her daughter’s first followup appointment. Nurses soon faxed Miranda’s documentation to the non-insured health benefits program — faxes are protocol — and the family waited to hear back on travel plans.

She said the agency never responded and her daughter missed her first appointment on May 28. Eva Mamakwa then called Nihb’s office in Sioux Lookout, Ont., and got someone on the line.

“I told her that it was extremely important that Miranda go to her followup appointments,” she said. “I talked to her and she listened to me and she said they would send her travel, but travel never came.”

She said the Nihb told her the request never arrived despite more than one tranche of faxes being sent.

The same thing occurred for followup appointments on June 11, July 2 and Aug. 6, Eva Mamakwa said, despite multiple faxes and phone calls.

“They didn’t care at all,” she said.

As the summer progressed, Miranda Mamakwa became more tired, slept more and started losing feeling in her fingers.

On Aug. 19, she wrote a Facebook post about the problems with Nihb and the missed appointments.

“If I die, pls go after (them),” she wrote.

On Sept. 6, she started to feel sick. Her stomach hurt and she began vomiting. “We just thought she might have caught the flu from her kids,” her mother said.

But Eva Mamakwa soon realized that “something was terribly wrong.”

Her daughter needed immediate help. Later that day, Skycare, which operates on behalf of provincial air and land ambulance Ornge, arrived, and airlifted her to the intensive care unit of the Thunder Bay Regional Health Sciences Centre, some 850 kilometres away.

The next day, Eva Mamakwa and Mike Bluecoat, Miranda’s father, got a call from the ICU doctor.

“He told me that Miranda had a lot of bleeding in her brain, she was hemorrhaging,” she said. “Even if they send her down south (to Toronto), to try and help her, that she wouldn’t have survived it.”

The doctor told them to fly to Thunder Bay so they did, with Miranda’s children in tow. Eva Mamakwa’s oldest daughter was already at the hospital to support her sister.

They arrived to crushing news.

“There was no brain activity at all and we had to make a very difficult decision to take her off life support or not,” Eva Mamakwa said through tears.

“As much as I wanted to keep her, it wouldn’t have been a good idea because it was the machine that was helping her breathe,” she said.

“It was very, very heartbreaking seeing my daughter being disconnected. But up until the end, when her heart stopped, and everything shut down, her children were beside her. All of us were beside her. And then we watched her go.”

Eva Mamakwa’s words failed, briefly, as tears rolled down her cheeks while she relived the nightmare.

“Today my daughter would be here if her travel was made to attend her appointments, but sadly it didn’t happen,” she said. “I am holding Nihb accountable for my daughter’s passing.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Today my daughter would be here if her travel was made to attend her appointments, but sadly it didn't happen," she said. "I am holding Nihb accountable for my daughter's passing."

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty has said her department would review the circumstances of the case, and that Mamakwa’s community and family deserved answers.

The woman’s death became a clarion call to First Nation leadership across Canada. It came after hundreds of people staged a sit-in at the Nihb office in Sioux Lookout over missed medical appointments, calling for urgent reform.

Chief Archie Wabasse of Wunnumin Lake First Nation, a remote fly-in community some 500 kilometres north of Thunder Bay and 330 kilometres south of Fort Severn, broke into tears as he discussed the issue in a recent interview.

He said that in his community of 800 people, about 80 residents had a total of 147 missed medical appointments between March 2025 and March 2026 due to lack of transport.

There is no full-time doctor in the First Nation, but one rotates in for a week or two every month, for 12 to 14 visits a year. Demand for the doctor’s time far exceeds availability, and those visits lead to referrals to specialists in southern parts of the province.

“The problem is getting worse for my people,” an emotional Wabasse said.

He lists a number of community members who need help. One, with a pacemaker, who has already missed a few appointments. Another who needs dialysis in a few days, but has not heard back from Nihb about his travel. In one case, the band paid about $3,000 to send an elder to a specialist in Winnipeg after Nihb did not return calls, he said.

Wabasse said he met with the Indigenous Services minister to talk about the issue, months before Miranda Mamakwa’s death.

He said Gull-Masty told the chiefs in attendance about improvements being made to Nihb, but she declined their request to sit down with them and resolve on the spot what he sees as a relatively straightforward administrative issue.

“It is a solvable problem, but what we’re trying to do here is advocating, telling the minister, the decision makers, the prime minister, this could be solved in one day,” Wabasse said.

When asked about Wabasse’s description of that meeting with the minister, Indigenous Services Canada said regular dialogue with First Nations leaders about Nihb “has been an important part of our work to improve service levels.”

More than 12 First Nations and tribal councils filed a complaint on Oct. 1 with the Canadian Human Rights Commission against Indigenous Services Canada over what they say is effectively a denial of health care in their communities.

The joint complaint from Wunnumin Lake First Nation, Matawa Chiefs Council and Windigo First Nations Council alleges the federal department’s non-insured health benefits program is failing to meet the needs of community members for medical transportation.

The Nihb program for First Nations and Inuit people covers medical, dental and mental health care not available through private insurance or provincial health plans. First Nations leaders and physicians have long said the program is not working for communities, and that its employees are notorious for being slow in responding to queries, requests and filing reimbursements.

The complainants say Nihb fails to consistently arrange medical transportation, or it informs patients so late about the transport that they are forced to miss their appointments.

They say Eabametoong First Nation community members miss about 50 appointments per month, while North Caribou First Nation members missed almost 100 appointments in the past year.

The complaint said First Nations have attempted to raise the issue with Indigenous Services Canada from as early as 2014, to no avail.

“Due to Isc’s actions, First Nations are suffering and dying. This is known to ISC, and yet nothing has been done to change it,” the complaint said. “Years of Nihb failing to approve requests on a timely basis, considered in the context of costs associated with First Nation service-provision and remoteness, represents a choice to deny First Nations health care.”

The complainants are requesting a formal review and reform of the benefits program, along with $20,000 in compensation for each individual who missed an appointment due to Nihb’s failures, and an additional $20,000 for pain and suffering.

“The continued failure regarding medical transportation is the newest chapter in a long history of Canada’s colonial practices devaluing the health and safety of Indigenous people,” the complaint said.

Indigenous Services Canada spokesperson Carolane Gratton said the department recognizes the serious impacts any gaps in service can have on people who rely on Nihb for medical transportation, and that it’s working to strengthen the delivery of the service.

The department implemented a simplified travel submission process in early October, meant to provide clients with more direct support from local medical transportation co-ordinators and create a “more consistent and streamlined experience,” Gratton wrote in an emailed statement. She said the department is looking into other actions that could improve call centre performance.

Indigenous Services Canada did not provide details when asked if there is a service standard for arranging medical transportation, nor how often that standard is met.

Gratton said the department takes seriously any complaints to the Canadian Human Rights Commission, and that it would respond “through the appropriate process.”

Julian Falconer, a longtime human rights lawyer who is representing the First Nations and tribal councils in the case, said their complaint is not about “simple negligence.”

“We are talking recklessness when it comes to the sanctity of life,” he said. “It’s an outrage.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We are talking recklessness when it comes to the sanctity of life," he said. "It's an outrage."

The government’s response is a “perfect parallel” to what happened to Miranda Mamakwa after her surgery, he said.

“The ignoring continues to this day,” Falconer said. “The minister promised an urgent review. We’re six weeks out and it’s crickets.”

Pediatrician and infectious disease specialist Anna Banerji, who travels to see patients in northern communities, said administration of the Nihb is discriminatory.

She said First Nations children, some of whom have serious health issues, are often no-shows for their appointments.

“Their flights were not booked,” she said.

Lack of transport has also led to missed mammogram appointments, allowing cancers to spread, and high-risk pregnancy symptoms that aren’t caught early and lead to complications for mothers and babies, she said.

Banerji said when concerns have been raised to Nihb, it’s like a “black hole.”

“(Patients) don’t know if the flight is booked, or when it’s booked, and if you try to communicate with (Nihb) again, no one ever picks up the phone. They can send faxes, and no one responds to the faxes,” she said.

“At the last minute they’ll say, ‘You have a flight in an hour.’ Well, (patients) have other responsibilities. They have other children, they have elderly people at home, they have jobs and suddenly they have to drop everything they’re doing last minute to go on a flight. It’s just disrespectful.”

Banerji said if the Nihb was any other system in Canada, it would be dismantled.

“My conclusion is, after 30 years of observing it, this is all racism. It’s a double standard. It’s discriminatory,” she said.

“I would go so far as to say when you give one group of people certain rights and you deny that to another group based on race … it’s called apartheid.”

Banerji said Miranda Mamakwa’s death was preventable, but not unpredictable, and called for a national inquiry into the system.

For Mamakwa’s family, the past month has been difficult.

Her children, aged 7, 9 and 11, are struggling. Eva Mamakwa said her youngest grandson often says, “I want my mom back.”

They trek to her grave to visit. They’re just trying to get through the days.

“My grandson, he wakes up early in the morning and he cries and in the evenings, that’s when it gets really hard for all of us,” Eva Mamakwa said, choking up.

“I cry every day. There are times I get extremely angry. What happened with our daughter? I miss her. I miss talking to her.”

The complainants are requesting a formal review and reform of the benefits program, along with $20,000 in compensation for each individual who missed an appointment due to Nihb’s failures, and an additional $20,000 for pain and suffering.

content_blocks.text: “The continued failure regarding medical transportation is the newest chapter in a long history of Canada’s colonial practices devaluing the health and safety of Indigenous people,” the complaint said.

Indigenous Services Canada spokesperson Carolane Gratton said the department recognizes the serious impacts any gaps in service can have on people who rely on Nihb for medical transportation, and that it’s working to strengthen the delivery of the service.

The department implemented a simplified travel submission process in early October, meant to provide clients with more direct support from local medical transportation co-ordinators and create a “more consistent and streamlined experience,” Gratton wrote in an emailed statement. She said the department is looking into other actions that could improve call centre performance.
Indigenous Services Canada did not provide details when asked if there is a service standard for arranging medical transportation, nor how often that standard is met.
Gratton said the department takes seriously any complaints to the Canadian Human Rights Commission, and that it would respond “through the appropriate process.”
Julian Falconer, a longtime human rights lawyer who is representing the First Nations and tribal councils in the case, said their complaint is not about “simple negligence.”

“We are talking recklessness when it comes to the sanctity of life,” he said. “It’s an outrage.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "We are talking recklessness when it comes to the sanctity of life," he said. "It's an outrage."

content_blocks.text: The government’s response is a “perfect parallel” to what happened to Miranda Mamakwa after her surgery, he said.
“The ignoring continues to this day,” Falconer said. “The minister promised an urgent review. We’re six weeks out and it’s crickets.”
Doctor says system is a ‘black hole’
Pediatrician and infectious disease specialist Anna Banerji, who travels to see patients in northern communities, said administration of the Nihb is discriminatory.
She said First Nations children, some of whom have serious health issues, are often no-shows for their appointments.
“Their flights were not booked,” she said.

Lack of transport has also led to missed mammogram appointments, allowing cancers to spread, and high-risk pregnancy symptoms that aren’t caught early and lead to complications for mothers and babies, she said.
Banerji said when concerns have been raised to Nihb, it’s like a “black hole.”

“(Patients) don’t know if the flight is booked, or when it’s booked, and if you try to communicate with (Nihb) again, no one ever picks up the phone. They can send faxes, and no one responds to the faxes,” she said.

“At the last minute they’ll say, ‘You have a flight in an hour.’ Well, (patients) have other responsibilities. They have other children, they have elderly people at home, they have jobs and suddenly they have to drop everything they’re doing last minute to go on a flight. It’s just disrespectful.”
Banerji said if the Nihb was any other system in Canada, it would be dismantled.
“My conclusion is, after 30 years of observing it, this is all racism. It’s a double standard. It’s discriminatory,” she said.
“I would go so far as to say when you give one group of people certain rights and you deny that to another group based on race … it’s called apartheid.”
Banerji said Miranda Mamakwa’s death was preventable, but not unpredictable, and called for a national inquiry into the system.
For Mamakwa’s family, the past month has been difficult.
Her children, aged 7, 9 and 11, are struggling. Eva Mamakwa said her youngest grandson often says, “I want my mom back.”
They trek to her grave to visit. They’re just trying to get through the days.
“My grandson, he wakes up early in the morning and he cries and in the evenings, that’s when it gets really hard for all of us,” Eva Mamakwa said, choking up.
“I cry every day. There are times I get extremely angry. What happened with our daughter? I miss her. I miss talking to her.”

stories.title: Sarnia Police seek public’s help identifying break-and-enter suspect captured on surveillance
stories.summary: Sarnia Police are appealing to the public for assistance in identifying a suspect involved in a pair of early morning break-and-enters that happened around 4 am Tuesday morning.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
Sarnia Police are appealing to the public for assistance in identifying a suspect involved in a pair of early morning break-and-enters that happened around 4 am Tuesday morning.

Surveillance footage captured an individual smashing a business door, stealing a cash register tray, and fleeing the scene on a scooter.

The Sarnia Police Service reported responding to calls regarding broken windows at two businesses located in the Northgate Plaza, situated in the 500 block of Exmouth Avenue. The incidents took place shortly after 4 am.

Officers arriving at the scene found that glass doors had been broken. While no suspect was present at the time of the initial police response, surveillance video obtained from one of the businesses provided crucial details of the crime.

The footage shows the suspect throwing an object to shatter the glass door, entering the premises, and then vaulting over a counter. The individual proceeded to rip the cash register tray from its housing before making a swift exit on a scooter.

The suspect is described as a male, believed to be between 20 and 30 years of age.

At the time of the incident, the individual was wearing a grey “CAT” brand hooded sweater, dark jeans, white and black high-top shoes, and a black hat.

A key identifying feature is an orange bandana worn to cover the face. The suspect also wore mismatched gloves, one black and one yellow. Multiple layers of clothing were apparent, with a white shirt visible underneath the hooded sweater.

Individuals with any relevant information are asked to contact the Sarnia Police Service directly at 519-344-8861. Alternatively, anonymous tips can be submitted through Crime Stoppers by calling 1-800-222-8477 or by visiting their website at www.p3tips.com .

stories.title: Liberals to table 2026 federal budget on Nov. 5
stories.summary: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says the Liberal government will table its 2026 federal budget on Nov. 5.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says the Liberal government will table its 2026 federal budget on Nov. 5.

The upcoming fiscal plan will be the second delivered under Prime Minister Mark Carney and comes as Canada’s economy faces sharp headwinds from U.S. tariffs and other geopolitical forces.

Since taking office, Carney has tried to reorient federal spending away from the day-to-day operations of government and instead focus borrowing on an aggressive infrastructure agenda.

Canada’s economy showed some resilience in the second quarter but growth is under fresh pressure after the collapse of trade talks with the United States in August.

The parliamentary budget officer expects federal deficits will be an average of $3 billion higher annually over the next five years than the office projected in June.

But a stretch of higher gas prices tied to war in the Middle East has also lifted federal revenues in the near term, which the PBO expects will lower the deficit for this fiscal year.

stories.title: Hiking the West Coast Trail reminded me to take a good look around
stories.summary: In a world that often celebrates excess, it was a welcome relief on this adventure to embrace a simpler mindset
stories.author: Kelly Carlson
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

Hiking Canada’s West Coast Trail – the 75-kilometre, remote trek that hugs the rugged coastline of Vancouver Island – has been on my bucket list since my 20s.

So when long-time friends asked my husband and me if we wanted to join them in Pacific Rim National Park Reserve, we jumped at the opportunity. Now that we’re in our early 50s, we knew the hike would be a challenge. What I didn’t anticipate was how much the trail would remind me of basic life lessons.

Our adventure started at Pachena Bay. Heavy rain, a daytime high of 11 C and a black bear skirting the edges of our first camp made for a harrowing start. Here, however, is where the hike reminded me that perspective is everything. Over the eight days that we spent on the trail, all challenges were put in reference to that first day – “At least it’s not raining,” one of us would say. And suddenly, no matter how tough things were, they instantly felt easier.

Our time unfolded in a predictable pattern – long days of hiking followed by evenings cozied up by the fires we would build on the beach. We would refresh ourselves in cold, rainforest streams and then stretch our aching bodies across the warm sand before eating dinner as a group. We shared what treats we had brought – chocolate, penny candy, popcorn. Our days reminded me that less truly is more. In a world that often celebrates excess, it was a welcome relief to embrace a simpler mindset.

The trail saw us navigating deep pockets of mud and water, climbing over boulders and fallen trees, scaling endless ladders and shuffling along slippery, rocky platforms. Regardless of the terrain, the job was the same every day – to put one foot in front of the other. Given the challenging topography, I often stumbled and lost my footing. Forced to pause, I would take in my surroundings – the enormous trees that towered above me or the watery tide pools at my feet with their colourful sea anemones. In these moments I was reminded that it’s important to stop every now and then and take a good look around. If all you’re doing is working, you’ll miss out on so much beauty.

When my girlfriend, who has successfully completed multiple Ironman-distance races, told me that hiking the West Coast Trail was the hardest thing she had ever done, I panicked. But, as the kilometres unfurled beneath my feet, I slowly came to the realization that although the hike was hard, it didn’t mean that I couldn’t do it. After all, here I was, a 30-pound knapsack on my back, steadfastly powering myself through every single kilometre thrown at me. The trail helped to remind me that even if something is difficult, it doesn’t mean it’s impossible.

Our travel companions were well versed in the West Coast Trail as they had completed the hike two years earlier. From the moment we started planning they were generous with their time and knowledge, sending us detailed packing lists as well as helping us to understand potential challenges we might encounter. In addition to their valuable insight, our friends also brought a relentlessly positive attitude – an attitude that helped to set the tone for our trip and, in my opinion, helped our group complete the trail with grace. Their mindset and wisdom reminded me that life is easier when you have good people alongside you.

The photos from our final morning on the trail show the wear on our faces of having travelled almost 75 km by foot. They also highlight the easy companionship amongst our group as we sip coffee around the fire together. Surrounded by a heavy ocean mist, it is clear that we are in no hurry to leave. Hours later, at the terminus of the trail, another photo shows our group sporting huge smiles. We are done!

Truthfully, I was excited to be finished. I was tired, sore and unable to push my body much more. But, I also felt a strong sense of melancholy. No longer would I be able to step outside of my tent in the morning and see a long spout of water emerging from a whale’s blowhole or watch a bald eagle soar overhead. I would also have to say farewell to our friends and the day-to-day rhythm we had built over the week. Once we left the trail, normal life, with all of its expectations and obligations, would return. In these final moments, the West Coast Trail reminded me that life is about the journey and not the destination.

Upon our return to civilization, friends would comment on how we “conquered the trail!” It was not a philosophy that we had subscribed to in our planning or execution of the trip. Although I was humbled by the hike in many ways, once I was back in the city, I quickly came to realize that the goal was never to conquer the trail. It was about spending time with our friends. It was about exploring a part of the world unknown to us and enjoying all it had to offer. It was about challenging ourselves both mentally and physically. And, as it turns out, it was also a chance to remind myself of some valuable life lessons.

Kelly Carlson lives in Ottawa.

Although I was humbled by the hike in many ways, once I was back in the city, I quickly came to realize that the goal was never to conquer the trail. It was about spending time with our friends. It was about exploring a part of the world unknown to us and enjoying all it had to offer. It was about challenging ourselves both mentally and physically. And, as it turns out, it was also a chance to remind myself of some valuable life lessons.

stories.title: Fact File: Misinformation spreads after deadly fire at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: False and misleading claims spread online this week about the fire that killed four soldiers and injured 39 others.
stories.author: Marissa Birnie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A fire that tore through a Canadian Armed Forces training ground in Wainwright, Alta., ON Saturday killed four soldiers and injured 39 others. False and misleading claims about the fire and its cause spread online this week. Here is a look at some of them.

The post claimed someone shot a high explosive round that went off course and struck a gas well, which then exploded and started the fatal fire. The post also claimed the explosion destroyed three structures with about 300 soldiers inside.

Similar posts on X and Facebook suggested the fire was caused by a live fire drill triggering the explosion of a gas well.

Defence officials have not released the official cause of the fire.

Early news reports in the immediate aftermath of the fire did suggest a gas well could have been involved.

Global News, citing multiple military sources, initially reported that a live-fire training exercise hit a gas line or gas well on the base, causing an explosion.

Global later updated its story, writing, “A preliminary investigation suggests a munition from the live training exercise sparked a fast-moving grass fire, which caused an explosion.”

The latest information from military officials as of Monday says strong and sudden winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire toward 84 members of Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry who were in a training area.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said most of the soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a range while 10 others were doing a simulated attack on an enemy.

He said leaders were aware of the grass fire that had ignited roughly a kilometre away, but the fire was “right on top” of the group within 30 seconds to a minute.

Rutland said army officials do not believe the fire was the result of an explosion from natural gas infrastructure. A full investigation is underway.

The Alberta Energy Regulator said that while it maintains oil and natural gas infrastructure at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, it has not received reports of incidents regarding that infrastructure.

“The AER continues to monitor the situation and has not been engaged by the lead agency or other provincial agencies in any response at this time,” the regulator said in a statement Sunday.

A TikTok video from Oct. 18 shows someone speaking about the incident in front of a green screen, which shows multiple separate videos. One clip shows an explosion in what appears to be a residential area; another shows a burnt landscape; other clips show large plumes of smoke.

The video received more than 200,000 views.

The video of the burnt landscape was posted to an Alberta Facebook group by a user who lists the location as south of Wainwright.

But the video of the explosion is unrelated. A reverse image search shows the clip is of an explosion at an ammunitions factory in Italy in August, as reported by multiple local and international media outlets.

One of the videos depicts the aftermath of a U.S. air force bomber crash in California in June, and The Canadian Press was unable to link it or any of the other smoke plume videos to CFB Wainwright.

An Oct. 19 X post claimed the federal government’s Earthquakes Canada website recorded a 3.7 magnitude earthquake in Wainwright at the time of the fire.

The Prime Minister and other officials “only talk of a fast moving fire — not an explosion,” the post reads.

Earthquakes Canada, which records earthquakes using data from seismic stations across Canada, did not record any seismic events the day of the fire.

It recorded a 3.7 magnitude earthquake in Canmore, Alta., the day before. Canmore is more than 500 kilometres northeast of CFB Wainwright.

In an X post Sunday, a user claimed a Canadian Army major with the last name Singh had confirmed that a PFC, or private first class, fired an artillery shell at a natural gas well during windy conditions.

The post received around 4,500 likes, with many users seeming to take the post at face value.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland is the military official who has shared details publicly about the fire. There is no record of the military personnel named in the post or the supposed comments made by a major with the last name Singh.

The X user has a history of making racist, false and inflammatory posts.

stories.title: Canada’s federal budget date revealed as trade war continues to bite
stories.summary: Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne says the federal budget will be released on Nov. 5 — two days after the U.S. midterm elections.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne says the federal budget will be released on Nov. 5 — two days after the U.S. midterm elections.

Champagne announced the date during question period on Tuesday.

The budget will be Prime Minister Mark Carney’s second, who changed the schedule for how federal budgets are released by moving them from spring to fall.

Carney’s second budget date comes after the Parliamentary Budget Officer trimmed the 2026 and 2027 outlook for economic growth.

The PBO now projects gross domestic product growth of 0.9 per cent for this year and 1.5 per cent for 2027, down from 1.1 per cent and 1.6 per cent respectively.

That forecast comes as U.S. tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs remain in effect and as the Republicans are just two weeks out from the midterm elections scheduled for Nov. 3.

In addition to a lower GDP, the PBO also projected a budgetary deficit of $63.3 billion for the 2026-27 fiscal year, which will peak at $70.2 billion in the following year.

All eyes will be on the government for its upcoming budget, after the U.S. trade war with Canada ramped up after Carney had his negotiators walk away in August from a trade deal that he said would’ve granted the U.S. power to control who Canada could trade with.

U.S. President Donald Trump enacted his previously threatened 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods in August, leading to new counter-tariffs issued in retaliation.

— with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadian man guilty of animal cruelty after stealing a flamingo in Las Vegas as a drunken joke
stories.summary: Police said photographs and video recovered from Fairburn’s phone showed him aggressively choking the bird and throwing it to the floor.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
The Canadian man accused of stealing and injuring a flamingo in a Las Vegas hotel in March has been found guilty of animal cruelty.

Mitchell Fairbarn, 34, from Ontario was charged with two counts of animal cruelty, one stemming from his treatment of the animal, known as Peachy, while it was still in its habitat, the second for his treatment of the bird in the hotel back in March, reports Kvvu , the Fox News affiliate in Las Vegas.

Peachy is a Chilean flamingo that had been kept in an enclosure at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino.

The prosecutors opened Fairbarn’s trial by showing surveillance video, photos and Snapchat clips showing him smiling, laughing and grabbing the flamingo by the neck, while he was with two friends. Video then showed him walking to the hotel elevator alone in the hallway, holding Peachy.

During his testimony, Fairbarn spoke about having experience with animals. He said he grew up on a farm, owns dogs and a parrot, and said he previously rescued an abandoned llama and six ducks. He attempted to use that experience to explain why he entered the Flamingo hotel’s wildlife habitat during the early morning hours of March 3. He claimed he noticed that the flamingo had uneven wings. And then he claimed he went inside the enclosure thinking something might be wrong with Peachy.

Investigators presented a different picture, reports Newsweek, with surveillance footage showing a shirtless Fairburn handling the flamingo by its neck and legs. Police said photographs and video recovered from Fairbarn’s phone showed him aggressively choking the bird and throwing it to the floor.

'It’s kind of serious stuff,' Vegas hotel tells 911 after Canadian man's alleged flamingo theft

Canadian accused of Las Vegas flamingo theft, torture pleads not guilty

Investigators said Fairbarn laughed in one clip, while saying he was “taking the bird home.” A “large bloody feather” was later found in his hotel room. Animal control officials said Peachy suffered a wing injury that required stitches and testified that the wing had been pulled from the bird’s body.

Fairbarn denied having any malicious intent to hurt or kill the bird. Instead, he testified that he took Peachy as a drunken “silly pranky joke” after drinking between 30 and 40 beers.

Fairbarn also spoke about how his family has been affected by news of the incident, including break-ins, death threats and his children having to change schools.

Peachy has been doing well physically since the incident. Fairburn remains under house arrest and is scheduled to be sentenced on December 1.

stories.title: Trump drops threats against Bombardier – here’s why
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump has dropped threats against Canadian jet maker Bombardier to ban it from the U.S. market and instead vowed to take "good care" of the company's workers.
stories.author: David Shepardson and Allison Lampert
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has dropped threats against Canadian jet maker Bombardier to ban it from the U.S. market and instead vowed to take “good care” of the company’s workers in Kansas.

Trump’s threats in September against Bombardier became a political issue in Kansas, where it employs 1,500 workers in Wichita. The threatened ban prompted calls to the White House from Kansas lawmakers including Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who is facing a tough re-election bid.

“We’re going to take care of Bombardier,” Trump told 12 News in Kansas, citing Marshall’s involvement.

At a speech Monday, Trump said he would help Bombardier.

“I’m going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away… I’ll be helping them because I always viewed them as a Canadian company,” Trump said.

“But now I find out they have a presence here, and we’re not hurting them if they’re in Kansas. So we’ll take care of those people and the jobs.”

Bombardier’s shares rose four per cent Tuesday after Trump’s comments. The White House declined to comment and referred questions to Trump’s TV interview.

Bombardier, which in 1990 acquired Learjet and established its US headquarters in Kansas, has ​3,500 jobs in the US, more than 40 per cent of which are in Wichita.

Bombardier recently announced a North American Learning Center in Kansas and has said it workforce in the state is growing. Last week, it announced a $50 million investment in Wichita, where it has its defence headquarters, and also plans to open a facility in Fort Wayne, Indiana.

Last month, the Trump administration banned a broad swath of Canadian alcoholic beverages, motorcycles and dairy products from import, effective September 29, but took no action against Bombardier.

The action came after Canada’s own retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect in early September. Those were prompted after Washington imposed tariffs on some $20 ‌billion of Canadian goods in August, after several rounds of negotiations collapsed.

Reuters reported last month it was not immediately clear how Trump could bar Bombardier private jets from being delivered to American customers since they have been approved by ​the US Federal Aviation Administration.

Threats by Trump in February to decertify Bombardier aircraft over a certification spat involving US rival Gulfstream Aerospace never materialized, with regulator Transport ‌Canada eventually ⁠approving the American-made jets.

stories.title: London police seek three ‘armed and dangerous’ suspects after weekend shooting
stories.summary: London police are looking for three suspects as one person remains in hospital after a shooting over the weekend.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
London police are looking for three suspects as one person remains in hospital after a shooting over the weekend .

Investigators say they have identified the three suspects in relation to the incident. All three are currently wanted by the London Police Service and have not been located.

Owen Barclay, 19, of London is charged by way of warrant of arrest with the following offences:

Attempt to commit murder using a firearm;

Discharge firearm with intent to wound/endanger life;

Occupy motor vehicle with firearm; and

Possess restricted or prohibited firearm knowingly not holding a licence.

Tyler Lewis McLaughlin, 19, and Julianna Marie Smith, 18, both of London, are charged jointly by way of warrant of arrest with the following offences:

Aggravated assault;

Police say the suspects should be considered armed and dangerous. Members of the public are advised not to approach them. Anyone who has information about their whereabouts is asked to call 911 immediately.

The victim remains in hospital in fair condition.

The investigation is ongoing, and additional information will be provided as appropriate.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Canada's Culture Minister touts commercial deals with creative sector in China
stories.summary: Ottawa - Culture Minister Mark Miller has returned from a five-day trip to China that aimed to deepen cultural ties between the two countries.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Miller travelled to Shanghai, Shenzhen and Suzhou this month with dozens of representatives from Canadian creative industries.

His office says seven new commercial agreements worth more than $4.2 million were signed during the trip.

Article continues below

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Almost 50 representatives from 36 Canadian companies and organizations took part, most of them from the interactive digital media industry.

A government news release says Miller met with his Chinese counterpart Sun Yeli and the pair discussed ways to build commercial partnerships and create jobs in the cultural sector.

In Beijing earlier this year, Prime Minister Mark Carney outlined steps to build a new strategic partnership with China, including more cultural exchanges and “people-to-people” ties.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Quebec opposition parties want Parti Québécois to take note of Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Two opposition leaders in Quebec are urging the incoming Parti Québécois government to take note of Monday night's referendum results in Alberta.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Quebec’s premier-designate says the results of the Alberta 10-question referendum reveal cracks in the Canadian federation and suggested the provinces could work together to gain more powers from Ottawa.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon wrote Tuesday on social media that the people of Alberta have proven that “there is nothing to fear from expressing one’s views through a referendum.”
