stories.title: Saskatchewan honours fallen soldiers after Wainwright tragedy
stories.summary: The death of four soldiers in Wainwright is being felt deeply in Saskatchewan. Private Shaun Farrell was killed when a fire ripped through the area during a training exercise.
stories.author: Chris Carr
stories.content:
The death of four soldiers in Wainwright is being felt deeply in Saskatchewan. Pte. Shaun Farrell, from Prince Albert, was killed when a fast-moving fire ripped through the area during a training exercise. Dozens more were critically injured.

Flags are flying at half-mast in Saskatchewan in honour of the victims of the tragedy.

Nutana Legion Branch 362 president Bill Flahr says he wants people to remember the fallen soldiers, the injured and the families who are impacted.

“The sacrifices that our military members make, and our military families make really come to the forefront with this type of tragedy,” Flahr said. “Military families sacrifice as much as the serving members do and I think we need to acknowledge that and recognize that.”

Flahr said legion members are looking for ways to support the families impacted. He said they are waiting for guidance on how they can step in financially to assist.

The financial aid would come through the Poppy Trust Fund, which is a controlled financial trust run through the Royal Canadian Legion.

Meanwhile, condolences are pouring in from across the province, including from the mayor of Prince Albert, the city Pte. Shaun Farrell called home.

Mayor Bill Powalinksy said in a statement that his city is grieving alongside those who knew and loved Shaun and that he recognizes the profound sorrow this tragedy has brought to his family.

Premier Scott Moe has offered condolences to the families impacted in a statement paying tribute to Pte. Farrell, saying in part, “Shaun was a young man full of promise who chose to serve his country. His loss will be felt deeply…”

For many, the tragedy is a harsh reminder that even though Canada is not actively engaged in a war, there are always dangers in serving in the military.

“We won’t forget the sacrifices they made while serving the country. And I will be thinking of them on Remembrance Day,” said Flahr.

On Oct. 18, 84 members of 3rd Battalion of Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were training with live munitions in the area.

Most of the soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a range, while 10 soldiers were doing simulations of an attack on enemies. The exercise was in preparation for potential deployment overseas to Latvia and other regions.

Training leaders were aware of a nearby grass fire about a kilometre from the soldiers, but it was not immediately determined to be a threat.

Saskatchewan had played a role in the response, with Stars dispatching air ambulances from Saskatoon, transferring three patients.

A coordinated emergency response involving health care teams across Alberta and Saskatchewan, coming together.

Investigators say it could be weeks before details of how the fire started would be known.

stories.title: B.C. heads to the polls on Saturday. Ask us your questions about the provincial election
stories.summary: The Oct. 24 snap vote comes just after municipal elections and disarray within the B.C. Conservatives
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
British Columbia is heading to the polls once again, barely two years since the last provincial election.

On Sept. 22, Premier David Eby called a snap provincial election, citing the “existential” threat of U.S. President Donald Trump . The NDP leader’s decision followed months of disarray within the B.C. Conservatives, who’s leader resigned just days before the election was called.

Now, the Conservatives have a new interim leader, and voters must return to the ballot box after having just gone through their local municipal elections.

On Thursday, Oct. 22 at 10 a.m. PT, reporters Mike Hager and Ian Bailey and columnist Gary Mason will be answering your questions about the coming provincial election, what the big issues are and how calling the snap vote might affect Eby’s chances.

Share your questions in the box below, or send us an e-mail at audience@globeandmail.com .

stories.title: Major projects bill would put decades of labour stability at risk: union leader
stories.summary: Ottawa - The president of the Canadian Labour Congress says proposed amendments to Canada's labour code outlined in Bill C-39 could put decades of labour stability at risk.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Proposed amendments to Canada’s labour code outlined in Bill C-39 could put decades of labour stability at risk, Canadian Labour Congress President Bea Bruske told a parliamentary committee on Tuesday.

The 243-page bill seeks to fast-track approvals for major projects, cut their review times and create zones of “national interest” to pre-approve certain types of projects.

The bill also proposes changes to Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to state that a minister can order a business under federal jurisdiction to resume operations, or put parties into binding arbitration.

Bruske told MPs on the special House of Commons committee struck to review the bill that those proposed new powers effectively eliminate the right to strike.

“What looks like greater stability on paper is going to create more instability,” she told members of Parliament at the committee meeting.

Canadian Union of Public Employees national president Mark Hancock told the committee that when companies know the government will bail them out during a strike, they won’t put their best offers forward in contract negotiations.

“Bill C-39 doesn’t encourage employers to bargain,” he said. “It encourages them to lowball workers and wait for the minister to do their dirty work.”

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu defended the legislation at a meeting of the C-39 committee on Monday.

Hajdu said the bill strengthens the right to strike by removing the ability to use Section 107 before a labour disruption. She argued the government has a responsibility to act during an “exceptionally consequential” dispute.

“Protecting workers and protecting the national interest go hand in hand,” she said.

The Canadian Labour Congress has proposed amendments that would ensure Section 107 does not give the minister the power to end legal strikes. Bruske said the group also has proposed striking an independent panel of experts to assess whether ongoing strikes have created a genuine national economic emergency.

“The panel would advise government, and if intervention were necessary, government would have to introduce legislation and make its case in Parliament,” she said.

Through C-39, the Liberals are proposing to introduce a new special mediator position. The special mediator would document both sides’ arguments in a labour dispute and publish a report to identify sticking points before talks break down.

It’s a tool the government sees being used in cases where unions and employers have a history of acrimony.

If passed, C-39 would require the jobs minister to consider the special mediator’s report before triggering Section 107. The minister must also conclude that the labour disruption is adversely affecting the “national interest” before taking the extraordinary step of ending a strike.

Bruske said her organization has proposed that special mediators be independent of government.

“Our experience under the Public Service Labor Relations Act raises some concerns that the proposed special mediator process could delay settlements rather than help achieve them,” she said.

The Liberals have used Section 107 numerous times in recent years leaned to end strikes in federally regulated sectors such as rail, ports and air transportation.

Labour experts have said the new language in C-39 likely does confer additional powers on the minister — and those powers will be subject to Charter challenges questioning their constitutionality.

A Charter statement for the bill says the changes around Section 107 May potentially engage section 2(d) of the Charter — the freedom of association.

It says a ministerial direction to the Canada Industrial Relations Board to order employees to resume their duties, extend a collective agreement, or impose a binding method of resolving outstanding issues, May engage the right to strike.

“The amendments would not generally prohibit strikes or lockouts. Rather, the proposed authority could be exercised when a strike or lockout is already underway and would be subject to specified conditions,” says the statement. “These considerations constrain the circumstances in which the authority May be exercised.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Kelowna bucks Okanagan trend as mayor wins re-election in tight race
stories.summary: Tom Dyas narrowly defeated challenger Ron Cannan by 969 votes, securing another term with a margin of about 2.5 percentage points after a nail-biting election night.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
As voters across the Okanagan ushered in new leadership, Kelowna bucked the trend, re-electing Mayor Tom Dyas in one of the province’s tightest mayoral races.

Dyas narrowly defeated challenger Ron Cannan by 969 votes, securing another term with a margin of about 2.5 percentage points after a nail-biting election night.

“It was very, very nerve-wracking, very, very close as everybody knows, but at the end of the day, we took it,” Dyas said as he celebrated with supporters.

For some Kelowna residents, the result was a vote of confidence in the mayor’s first term.

“I think it’s fantastic. I think he’s done a good job,” said Ken Hart, a Kelowna resident.

Others, who call Kelowna home, found the choice less clear-cut.

“You know, it was a tough choice between the two,” voter Lyn Mainwaring said.

For some, the outcome came as a surprise.

“I didn’t think that Tom would get re-elected…just because it’s time for a change and a lot of people talked about time for a change,” said Kelowna resident Michele Nojonen.

That desire for change was a recurring theme throughout the campaign, particularly around public safety issues related to homelessness, drug addiction and mental health.

With Cannan securing nearly half the vote, Dyas acknowledged that concerns remain and said the campaign had made clear the issue would need greater attention.

“I think we all kind of heard it substantially throughout this campaign, so it will become that much more of a bigger issue with regards to our priorities,” Dyas said.

The election result in Kelowna stood in contrast to several other Okanagan communities where incumbent mayors lost their seats, including Penticton, Peachland, Lake Country, Vernon, Armstrong and Enderby.

But while Kelowna voters opted to keep their mayor, the city’s council is set for a significant shake-up, with five of its eight seats going to new councillors, including three people in their 20s and 30s.

For voter Rob Peters, the election results reflected his support for a younger generation of leaders.

“I think three or four of the people that I voted for got in. I voted for younger people,” Peters said.

Nicole Richards also welcomed the incoming councillors, saying it can benefit the city.

“I think fresh faces and different perspectives are always healthy and the change is healthy,” Richards said.

Attention now turns to the upcoming provincial election and whether voters will deliver a similar change at the provincial level.

stories.title: La Bola Negra movie review: Netflix’s epic Oscar hopeful takes a big swing, and misses
stories.summary: Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s wannabe epic mistakes enormity for majesty and a dogpile of narratives for depth
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
Directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi

Written by Javier Calvo, Javier Ambrossi and Alberto Conejero

Starring Guitarricadelafuente, Carlos González and Penélope Cruz

Classification N/A; 159 minutes

Opens in Toronto Oct. 23, Vancouver and Montreal Oct. 30, and other Canadian cities Nov. 6; streaming on Netflix starting Dec. 2

If there is an unfortunate fad in film writing this year, it is critics (or more often that amorphous collective known as “influencers”) throwing around the meaningless term “big swing” to cushion the blows left by movies that don’t live up to their grand self-stated ambitions.

We’re told, even though it is in fact a preening work of nothingness, that Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger is a big swing of a movie, admirable in its alleged extremes. The same goes for Boots Riley’s provocative-in-concept but aggravating-in-execution comedy I Love Boosters . And now, to make this trend complete with a perfect comes-in-three example, we can add the Spanish-language drama La Bola Negra to the list of big-swing movies that mistakes enormity for majesty and a dogpile of narratives for depth.

The film, which took home the coveted People’s Choice Award at Tiff last month, is far from Digger -level in its abrasiveness. But as the movie inevitably staggers its way through the upcoming awards conversation – the title is Netflix’s big and perhaps only Oscar hopeful for 2027, the streaming giant having acquired the film after its Cannes premiere – it is helpful to remember that not every cinematic fault line can be masked by even the best, biggest-swing intentions.

The latest collaboration from the creative duo Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo (the pair known in Spain as simply “Los Javis”), La Bola Negra follows three stories separated by decades whose threads begin to tie themselves together toward the end of a sometimes inspired, sometimes soggy journey through Spanish history and the queer men who survived it.

The first narrative follows a boyish industry scion named Carlos (Milo Quifes) who, in 1932 Granada, struggles to balance his closeted sexuality with acceptance into a social club governed by the local elite. The second story, and easily the most emotionally and thematically rich, is set a few years later, during the Spanish Civil War, when a young trumpeter named Sebastien (played by the musician known as Guitarricadelafuente) is conscripted to join the Nationalist forces as they fight against the country’s Republican faction, both sides never clear as to where their allegiances should reside. Finally, a third section set in 2017 traces the journey of the jaded historian Alberto (Carlos González) who, restless with his boyfriend and family, begins to research the origins of an unfinished play, also called La Bola Negra (or The Black Ball ), written by the real-life Spanish poet Federico García Lorca.

On their own, each one of the film’s stories offer substantial intrigue, the uniting theme of suppressed desire inflating some of the thinner characterizations found in the first and third chapters. And the performances are strong across the film’s century of broken men, with González especially compelling in a role that could have reduced a lesser performer to adopt whiny affectations.

Yet in Ambrossi and Calvo’s desire to imbue their film with magnificent importance, the directors embrace a kind of superficial audaciousness at every possible moment. Not every film needs a sense of restraint, but there is a weightlessness to this wannabe epic’s maximalism that drains its ultimate impact.

For every sequence that truly pops, such as Penélope Cruz’s extended cameo, in which she plays a 1930s showgirl who bewitches Sebastien and his fellow troops for 10 beguiling minutes, there are far more scenes that struggle to convey just how important they’re meant to be. (Although many English-language audiences will be pleasantly surprised with just how well Glenn Close, who briefly appears in the 2017 section, speaks Spanish.)

When the film premiered at the tail end of the Cannes Film Festival this past spring, it was greeted as something like the second coming of cinema. But it’s hard to shake the feeling that was only because the first half of the festival felt so unusually muted. The to-the-rafters-and-beyond volume of La Bola Negra makes it impossible to ignore, sure. But there is a yawning gap between grudging admiration and sincere devotion, and Los Javis never leap across that chasm. No matter how big their collective swing.

And now, to make this trend complete with a perfect comes-in-three example, we can add the Spanish-language drama La Bola Negra to the list of big-swing movies that mistakes enormity for majesty and a dogpile of narratives for depth.

The film, which took home the coveted People’s Choice Award at Tiff last month, is far from Digger -level in its abrasiveness. But as the movie inevitably staggers its way through the upcoming awards conversation – the title is Netflix’s big and perhaps only Oscar hopeful for 2027, the streaming giant having acquired the film after its Cannes premiere – it is helpful to remember that not every cinematic fault line can be masked by even the best, biggest-swing intentions.

The latest collaboration from the creative duo Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo (the pair known in Spain as simply “Los Javis”), La Bola Negra follows three stories separated by decades whose threads begin to tie themselves together toward the end of a sometimes inspired, sometimes soggy journey through Spanish history and the queer men who survived it.

The first narrative follows a boyish industry scion named Carlos (Milo Quifes) who, in 1932 Granada, struggles to balance his closeted sexuality with acceptance into a social club governed by the local elite. The second story, and easily the most emotionally and thematically rich, is set a few years later, during the Spanish Civil War, when a young trumpeter named Sebastien (played by the musician known as Guitarricadelafuente) is conscripted to join the Nationalist forces as they fight against the country’s Republican faction, both sides never clear as to where their allegiances should reside. Finally, a third section set in 2017 traces the journey of the jaded historian Alberto (Carlos González) who, restless with his boyfriend and family, begins to research the origins of an unfinished play, also called La Bola Negra (or The Black Ball ), written by the real-life Spanish poet Federico García Lorca.

On their own, each one of the film’s stories offer substantial intrigue, the uniting theme of suppressed desire inflating some of the thinner characterizations found in the first and third chapters. And the performances are strong across the film’s century of broken men, with González especially compelling in a role that could have reduced a lesser performer to adopt whiny affectations.

Yet in Ambrossi and Calvo’s desire to imbue their film with magnificent importance, the directors embrace a kind of superficial audaciousness at every possible moment. Not every film needs a sense of restraint, but there is a weightlessness to this wannabe epic’s maximalism that drains its ultimate impact.

For every sequence that truly pops, such as Penélope Cruz’s extended cameo, in which she plays a 1930s showgirl who bewitches Sebastien and his fellow troops for 10 beguiling minutes, there are far more scenes that struggle to convey just how important they’re meant to be. (Although many English-language audiences will be pleasantly surprised with just how well Glenn Close, who briefly appears in the 2017 section, speaks Spanish.)

When the film premiered at the tail end of the Cannes Film Festival this past spring, it was greeted as something like the second coming of cinema. But it’s hard to shake the feeling that was only because the first half of the festival felt so unusually muted. The to-the-rafters-and-beyond volume of La Bola Negra makes it impossible to ignore, sure. But there is a yawning gap between grudging admiration and sincere devotion, and Los Javis never leap across that chasm. No matter how big their collective swing.

stories.title: Alberta referendum result removes a ‘major’ uncertainty, businesses say
stories.summary: After the majority of Albertans voted to remain in Canada, the Canadian dollar increased in value and some business leaders say the result should bring confidence to businesses.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
After the majority of Albertans voted to remain in Canada , the Canadian dollar increased in value and some business leaders say the result should bring confidence to consumers and business owners alike.

“Businesses, workers and communities can feel more confident with this result. As we digest the results of this process, we are reminded that we can never take national unity for granted. It is cultivated day by day,” said Candace Laing, president and CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, in a statement.

“Alberta is central to economic security and opportunity in Canada and we must now turn our attention squarely to the needed work to collaboratively build a stronger, resilient, united economy from coast to coast to coast.”

The Business Council of Alberta’s president, Adam Legge said in a statement it’s “delighted” with the results as it “provides an important foundation” for the province’s economy, as well as families and workers to move forward with more certainty.

“While today’s result settles the question of separation, the concerns that brought it to the forefront remain. We urge the governments of Canada and Alberta to continue working together to pursue fairness for Alberta,” said Legge.

Alberta’s small business leaders also said the referendum results should provide small and medium-sized business owners with some relief.

Keyli Loeppky, senior director of Alberta and interprovincial affairs at the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, said in a statement that the referendum vote result should provide “greater certainty for small businesses at a time when they are already facing significant economic challenges.”

“Small business owners value stability, predictability, and access to customers, suppliers, and workers across Canada,” said Loeppky.

“This result removes a major source of uncertainty and allows businesses to focus on growing their operations rather than navigating questions about Alberta’s future constitutional status.”

Elections Alberta began releasing the results of the province’s referendum decision late Monday night, with around 76 per cent of Albertans voting to remain part of Canada.

The separatism question asked voters if Alberta should remain in Canada or if the provincial government should begin the legal process of holding a future binding referendum on whether to separate.

Monday’s results mirror more than half a year of polling, which since the beginning of 2026, has consistently shown about 70 per cent of Albertans want the province to remain in Canada .

In January, an Ipsos poll found about three in 10 residents supported independence , but a deeper dive revealed that when faced with the costs and consequences, only half of those interested in separatism were truly committed to following through.

The referendum vote also comes as Canada faces an ongoing trade war, with U.S. tariffs especially hammering the economy and job market, and as the Iran war and Russia’s war with Ukraine lead to rising oil and gas prices and threaten to continue accelerating inflation .

Amid these economic challenges, the federal government has been seeking to unify Canada by easing interprovincial trade restrictions and working with individual provinces and territories, including Alberta, to find ways to maximize Canada’s economic potential.

Earlier this month, the newly announced Pacific Coast Pipeline was officially designated as a project of national interest , and falls under Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Major Projects Office, a government branch meant to speed federal approvals for significant economic initiatives. The pipeline, which will run mostly parallel to the current Trans Mountain pipeline, is expected to increase the output of Alberta oil to Asian markets via B.C. by one million barrels per day.

The future of the pipeline was hanging in the balance prior to Monday’s vote as some separatist leaders suggested leaving Alberta would mean taking the pipeline and its revenue with it.

The loonie also popped once the referendum results came in.

Shortly after polls in Alberta closed on the evening of Oct. 19, the Canadian dollar’s value began to rise by about a third of a U.S. cent to 71.2 cents as of publication.

Derek Holt, vice president and head of Capital Markets Economics at Scotiabank said in a statement that the loonie’s reaction was more likely reflective of higher oil prices worldwide, as well as rising expectations that the Bank of Canada will be increasing interest rates sooner than later.

After the referendum vote Holt also said, “Canada emerges from the vote in stronger fashion.”

“There should be some accountability for having called this waste of taxpayer money in the first place and the risk that a surprise Brexit-like vote could have been a risk.”

Holt continued: “How separatists exact their vengeance on the provincial administration remains uncertain.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and the governing United Conservative Party (UCP) will have to contend with a motivated and more organized separatist movement turning their efforts to oust the premier and take control of the party.

Jeffrey Rath, one of the central figures in the separatist movement who had a hand in former premier Jason Kenney’s ouster, told Global News he will be pushing for a special general meeting of the party to remove Smith.

Rath said Alberta independence will never be realized as long as Smith, who he called an “avowed federalist,” remains leader.

“Moving forward from here, our hundreds of thousands of members and volunteers are going to be committed to taking back ownership of the (UCP),” Rath said.

– with files from Global News’ Karen Bartko and Alex Boutilier

stories.summary: Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy will run consecutively with 40-year sentence he is serving for plotting mass-casualty terrorist attack in NYC.

stories.content:
Ontario man Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, has been sentenced to 50 years in prison after stabbing two prison guards at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood in Pennsylvania, an attack that led to one of them losing his eye.

The sentence for El Bahnasawy will run consecutively with the 40-year sentence he is already serving for his part in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of Isis.

The attack at Allenwood occurred on Dec. 7, 2020, when El Bahnasawy went at the two guards using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell. He stabbed one officer in the head and face. Then, when a second officer responded, El Bahnasawy stabbed her in the hand . The first officer eventually lost his right eye because of Bahnasawy’s attack.

El Bahnasawy’s attack on the guards was “once again on behalf of Isis,” said John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, in a press release from the U.S. Department of Justice on Monday. “Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time.”

Pennsylvania U.S. attorney Brian Miller said the justice department “will prosecute those who aid, attempt to aid, or commit violence on behalf of the pernicious Isis ideology wherever they May be found,” adding that the sentence reflects an “unwavering commitment to fight those who perpetrate violence in the name of Isis even behind prison walls.”

When El Bahnasawy was finally restrained, corrections officers found a note in his sock that read, “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq was also found taped inside the locker door in El Bahnasawy’s prison cell.

He pleaded guilty in November 2025 to assault, assault with intent to commit murder, possession of contraband inside a prison, as well as providing material support to Isis, a designated foreign terrorist organization.

As previously reported by National Post , El Bahnasawy led a sheltered existence in Mississauga, Ont. before getting involved with Isis. He suffered from “serious” mental-health problems. As a teenager, his world revolved around his parents, his older sister and the people he met while being treated for an opioid addiction. He never got past Grade 11. He went on with two men to plot bombings and shootings in the name of Isis amid heavily populated areas of New York City during Ramadan in 2016.

El Bahnasawy pleaded guilty Oct. 13, 2016 to conspiring to bomb Times Square, attack passengers on the subway and shoot up crowds at unnamed concerts.

Initially was represented by federal public defenders after his arrest, but as reported by National Post , he later hired a new legal team linked to Dennis Edney, the celebrated Alberta lawyer who acted for Omar Khadr, citing entreaties from his parents.

The terrorist plot was infiltrated by an undercover FBI agent, posing as an Isis supporter. Subsequently, the FBI arrested El Bahnasawy in May 2016 after he had travelled from Canada to the New York City area intending to carry out the planned attacks.

He has been in custody ever since.

stories.title: McDonald's drone drop at Quebec maximum-security prison highlights contraband risks
stories.summary: Ottawa - It was after dark last Wednesday when a drone dropped silently from the sky over the special handling unit of a maximum-security prison in Quebec.
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - It was after dark last Wednesday when a drone dropped silently from the sky over the special handling unit of a maximum-security prison in Quebec.

Slipping into the gap between the chain-link fencing and the window — which was broken from the inside — it delivered its contraband contents to the man waiting within: a McDonald’s meal and a bottle of alcohol.

Prison guards making the rounds in the morning found the intoxicated inmate along with the remains of his late-night snack.

Frédérick Lebeau, national president of the Union of Canadian Correctional Officers, said the fact that this happened in this particular high-security unit should serve as a warning.

“It’s kind of a funny thing, the McNugget trio … but it could be worse. It could be firearm, it can be a ceramic knife,” he said.

“We are seeing an increase of violence in every institution in this country.”

Lebeau said security cameras on the outside of the Regional Reception Centre at Ste-Anne-des-Plaines, Que., failed to capture the drone drop. Counter-drone technology also did not pick up the intrusion.

Drone deliveries of contraband are an ongoing problem at prisons across the country.

The Office of the Correctional Investigator’s annual report in 2024 said there are different counter-drone systems in use, including detector dogs.

There were 90 drone incidents at corrections facilities reported in the first six months of that year, and the report found 98 per cent of them were detected. It also noted that the perceived risk of a drone drop at facilities with large outdoor yards led the correctional service to limit inmates’ outdoor time or to provide access only to fenced-in “mini-yards” that were much smaller than the caged spaces provided for the dogs at those facilities.

Correctional Service Canada uses measures like radio frequency detection to alert staff when a drone is in the area. Lebeau said that technology is not sophisticated enough to catch the newer drones.

A pilot project announced in March 2025 uses technology capable of blocking cellphone and drone signals at prisons. Lebeau said the Regional Reception Centre is part of that pilot program — and still, this drone made it through.

“There’s a huge gap in our correctional facilities in Canada and we need to address it sooner than later because one day we will have a major incident,” he said.

A spokesperson for Correctional Service Canada said incidents like this “underscore the need for ongoing investment in technologies and infrastructure.”

Kevin Antonucci said in an email that the correctional service is implementing “physical mitigation measures” such as nets at the Regional Reception Centre.

“These measures are designed to disrupt and prevent the delivery of contraband, such as drugs, weapons, and other prohibited items that can threaten the safety of staff, inmates, and the public,” he wrote.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree called the incident unacceptable.

“Minister Anandasangaree has spoken with the CSC commissioner about this incident,” Simon Lafortune wrote in an email.

“CSC is responsible for security at federal correctional institutions, and the minister expects CSC to identify what went wrong and take the necessary corrective action.”

Lebeau said stepped-up measures were put in place after the incident was reported by Quebec media last week, but extra outdoor patrols at the facility were ended on Monday.

He said the federal government needs to spend a lot more money to prevent this kind of thing from happening. He pointed out that Correctional Service Canada is facing the same budget cuts as every other department.

“We need to take it seriously,” he said.

Conservative public safety critic Frank Caputo agreed, noting the budget cuts at Correctional Service Canada have hit things like perimeter security and dog handlers.

Caputo said he’s outraged that the government isn’t taking the “huge issue” of drone incursions more seriously, despite the known involvement of organized crime groups.

“It is a matter of time before a firearm gets into a federal penitentiary,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

stories.title: No immediate changes to military training after CFB Wainwright fire kills four soldiers: defence minister
stories.summary: Defence Minister David McGuinty said no changes have been made to military training procedures following a deadly fire at CFB Wainwright that killed four soldiers and sent 39 others to hospital during a training exercise on Saturday.
stories.author: Graham Richardson
stories.content:
Ottawa - Defence Minister David McGuinty said no changes have been made to military training procedures as of now, following a deadly fire at CFB Wainwright that killed four soldiers and sent 39 others to hospital during a training exercise on Saturday.

Ahead of a cabinet meeting on Parliament Hill on Tuesday, McGuinty was asked whether he had directed any changes to existing protocols. He told reporters that it was too soon to make adjustments before the facts are known.

“It’s very difficult to provide advice on the merits of how the protocols, which are in place, ought to be amended until we get the facts,” McGuinty said.

Pressed on why no interim measures have been introduced before formal inquiries are completed, McGuinty said decisions about training adjustments rest with Canadian Armed Forces officials.

“Listen, I’m going to leave it right now to the chief of defence, the commander of the army and the professionals who conduct these processes, to take the time they need to evaluate,” McGuinty said. “This happened 48 hours ago.”

Sgt. Morgan Wong and Privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark were killed during the training exercise. The soldiers, who served with Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were preparing to deploy to Latvia next year.

Military lawyer and former soldier Col. Michel Drapeau told CTV News Monday, the military should not investigate itself given the scale of the tragedy.

Drapeau called for a public coroner’s inquest instead.

stories.title: Trump jokingly says Canada can keep hockey and O Canada in his latest '51st state' offer
stories.summary: President Donald Trump said that while he liked Canada's national anthem, the country has been "screwing" the United States.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
The comments were made about half way through his speech in Park City, where he was supporting U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in the midterm election. Trump mentioned how car plants were thriving in the United States, but were leaving Mexico and Canada.

“They’re leaving O Canada,” he said, in reference to the beginning of the country’s national anthem. “Canada’s been ripping us off for so many years. People got used to it. I didn’t get used to it. We got it under control.”

He questioned why Americans would even need Canadian-made cars, but added: “I do like their national anthem.”

He followed up his offer by adding that he was “only kidding” and “having a good time.”

“But they have been screwing us,” he said, adding that now Canada wants to make a deal. The U.S. does very little business with Canada, while the northern country does 95 per cent of business with Americans, he said. The U.S. loses $90 billion a year because of this, according to Trump.

“I would say that’s a little too much for the privilege of having people live through very cold weather,” he said.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has not specifically addressed Trump’s claim that Canada is the cause of a $90 billion deficit in the U.S. However, Canadian-founded research institute Centre for Future Work published an article earlier this month, debunking some of Trump’s “big lies about Canada.”

“The true deficit for 2025, based on official U.S. government data , was $27 billion. That consisted of a $55 billion deficit on merchandise, partly offset by a $28 billion U.S. surplus on services,” the post said.

Raymond J. de Souza: Is Trump's desertion of Ukraine betrayal, stupidity or avarice?

“That’s just 3 per cent of the massive two-way $900 billion bilateral flow. America’s trade with Canada is far more balanced than with the rest of the world – adding to the mystery of why Canada is suddenly Public Enemy Number One.”

Trump made reference to the border between the two countries, saying it was a straight line drawn by “some guy with a ruler” who said, “Let those people have that cold air.”

“I’m going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away,” he said.

“We’ll take care of those people,” said Trump.

Along with broaching the prospect of separation, the Alberta referendum posed nine other questions related to immigration and constitutional issues. Voters marked “yes” to indicate support for the proposals of Premier Danielle Smith and her government, and “no” to reject them.

Elections Alberta continues to tally the ballots. See below for voting results from Tuesday evening. As of 9:47 p.m. MT, over eight per cent of polls (462 of 5,583) had not yet reported.

stories.title: Trump walks back threat to ban Bombardier sales in U.S.
stories.summary: Montreal - U.S. President Donald Trump is backing down on a threat to ban Bombardier Inc. plane sales in the United States.
stories.author: Christopher Reynolds The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - U.S. President Donald Trump has backed down on a threat to ban Bombardier Inc. plane sales in the United States, allowing the aerospace sector to breathe a sigh of relief after tempers flared and tariffs rose in an escalation of the trade war last month.

Speaking at a campaign rally Monday night, Trump said he’s changed his perception of the Montreal-based business jet maker as a purely Canadian manufacturer.

“I’m going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away,” he told a crowd in a suburb of Wichita, Kan., where Bombardier employs 1,500 workers.

“I always viewed them as a Canadian company ... but now I find out they have a presence here, and we’re not hurting them if they’re in Kansas. So we’ll take care of those people, all right, and the jobs.”

Wichita serves as the home base of Bombardier’s defence division. The company employs about 3,500 American workers across plants in Kansas, Texas, California and other states.

Kansans are already feeling first-hand the effects of the president’s policies. Midwestern farmers have seen the diesel that powers their tractors and combines rise to near-record prices due to the Iran war. Kansas has now turned into a political battleground as Republicans and Democrats fight for control of the typically red state ahead of next month’s midterm elections.

Trump said Monday that a phone call from Kansas Republican Sen. Roger Marshall helped convince him to walk back his threat against Bombardier. Polls show Marshall is running neck and neck with Adam Hamilton, a Democrat in a state that has not elected one to the Senate since 1932.

Last month, Trump suggested he would bar Bombardier aircraft sales in the United States unless it moved its operations there, despite the harm experts said such a move would inflict on American workers.

“NO More Selling Bombardier IN THE United States!” he posted on social media on Sept. 7. “If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank.’”

Bombardier responded that it pays more than US$2.5 billion to some 2,800 American suppliers across 47 states each year, indirectly supporting tens of thousands of jobs.

“The American aerospace industry is a clear winner on trade and exports,” Bombardier stated in September, adopting the language of the president and his fixation on triumph and trade surpluses.

Last week, the company inaugurated a skills development centre for new aircraft technicians and mechanics in Wichita, part of a US$50-million investment in the site.

America enjoys a US$109-billion aerospace and defence trade surplus with the world, according to the U.S. Aerospace Industries Association.

Bombardier does the final assembly of its Challenger and Global business jets in Canada, while more than half of its revenue stems from American customers.

“We view the removal of this regulatory uncertainty as positive for sentiment as it alleviates an important headline overhang for investors,” said James McGarragle, an analyst at RBC Dominion Securities.

Trump’s threat did not have a “tangible impact” on demand for the luxury jets among American customers over the past six weeks, he added.

Bombardier shares rose $13.85 or about 4.5 per cent to close at $325.32 on Tuesday.

Despite U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and other goods, aerospace manufacturing remains deeply integrated across the continent and beyond.

Most Bombardier planes feature at least 40 per cent U.S. content, analysts say. Over half of the value of the ultra-long-range Global 7500 luxury jet derives from American parts.

Blocking a major manufacturer from the market would “undoubtedly” cause revenue and job losses at American parts producers, said National Bank analyst Cameron Doerksen last month.

A ban would have also been “massively disruptive” to the many American jet fleet operators awaiting Bombardier deliveries, he said.

Trump’s fist-shaking went down a day before Ottawa’s retaliatory tariffs on American goods took effect on Sept. 8, a response to the 50 per cent duties Washington imposed on Canadian goods in August.

Trump then proceeded to ban most Canadian alcoholic drinks, some dairy products and motorcycles, among other products, and slapped a 50 per cent levy on more items.

Since then, however, the cross-border feud has seemingly entered a holding pattern, with fewer outbursts against Canada from America’s head of state.

Trump’s Truth Social post marked the second time this year Bombardier has come into the president’s crosshairs.

In January, he singled out Bombardier in a threat to ground all Canadian-made aircraft and slap them with a 50 per cent tariff unless Ottawa approved Gulfstream business jets — assembled in Savannah, Ga. — marking an earlier escalation of trade tensions between the two countries.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Canadian dollar hits four-week high as market cheers Alberta remain vote
stories.summary: Strategist: ‘The Alberta vote could not have ⁠gone better from a market perspective’
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
The Canadian dollar strengthened to a four-week ​high against its U.S. counterpart ‌on Tuesday, boosted by a narrower gap between Canadian and U.S. interest rates and after Alberta voted by a large majority to remain part ⁠of ​Canada

The loonie was trading 0.5 per cent higher at 1.4045 per U.S. dollar, or 71.20 U.S. cents, after touching its strongest intraday level since September 22 at 1.4033. Among Group of ​10 currencies, only sterling posted a bigger ‌gain.

“The Canadian discount to the US has fallen sharply in the last few days which has helped fuel this correction in the Canadian dollar,” said Marc Chandler, chief market strategist at Bannockburn Capital Markets.

The ‌gap between ​Canada’s 2-year yield ‌and the U.S. equivalent has narrowed to 146 basis points ​from about 160 basis points earlier this ⁠month as investors raised bets on a Bank ⁠of Canada interest rate hike next week.

Swap market data indicates an ​80-per-cent chance the BoC raises its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.50 per cent on October 28. It follows hawkish comments by Governor Tiff Macklem on Saturday and evidence on Monday of rising long-term inflation expectations.

The ⁠remain side won 76 per cent of tallied votes in Alberta’s first-ever referendum on separation, handing Prime Minister Mark Carney a much-needed win as he attempts to unify the country amid a trade war with the U.S..

“The Alberta vote could not have ⁠gone better from a market perspective,” Chandler ​said. “This is the least disruptive alternative because it preserves the status ⁠quo.”

The price of oil, one of Canada’s major exports, pulled back from its ‌highest level since April as traders priced in Houthi attacks on Saudi ​infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf. U.S. crude oil futures were trading 0.9 per cent lower at US$102.75 a barrel.

Canadian government bond yields moved lower across ​the curve, with the 10-year down 6.8 basis points at 3.894 per cent.

stories.title: Health care, affordability and the economy are the priorities in N.B. throne speech
stories.summary: Fredericton - Health care and new export markets outside the U.S. are among the priorities in the New Brunswick government’s throne speech.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Fredericton - New Brunswick’s Liberal government named health care and new export markets outside the United States among its priorities as the provincial legislature kicked off a new session Tuesday.

In a throne speech delivered by Lt.-Gov. Louise Imbeault, the government said it will open its 30 planned collaborative care clinics by the end of next year — ahead of its self-imposed deadline of 2028.

The province first started opening the clinics in the spring of 2025, saying it was one of the ways to address doctor shortages by connecting patients with a variety of health care professionals.

Premier Susan Holt’s government announced new health care plans, as well.

The ruling Liberals said they will name a mental health advocate and launch a health and long-term care workforce strategy.

And the province plans to work with non-profit organizations to develop individual case management programs to help people suffering from poor mental health and addictions.

“Your government is determined to ensure New Brunswickers can access the health care they need, when and where they need it,” Imbeault said.

“They will continue making investments to deliver your health care close to home.”

As U.S. tariffs on Canadian forestry products, seafood and beer continue to drag on New Brunswick’s economy, the Liberals want to diversify where the province’s exports go.

Via the throne speech, the government said it will create a diversification plan for markets beyond the U.S. that align well with the province’s exports.

“Their objective is to build a more resilient export economy, one that balances international market development with domestic supports,” Imbeault told the legislature.

“This will allow our industries to compete globally while deepening connections with new trade partners in Europe, Asia and beyond.”

As well, Holt’s administration teased new affordability measures to tackle the rising cost of living and an overhaul to the landlord and tenants law.

The throne speech confirmed the government’s draft data centre framework will be used to guide changes to New Brunswick’s Electricity Act.

Imbeault said the framework will have “high environmental, social, economic and energy standards that data centre projects will be required to meet” to receive approval for building.

Some New Brunswick residents who live near sites of proposed data centres have criticized the government for considering approvals before finalizing a policy for the energy-hungry projects.

The Liberal provincial government sees the plants as a potential opportunity to generate economic growth through tax revenue, private sector buy-in and job creation.

Overall, the throne speech delivered by the lieutenant-governor largely recapped the Holt government’s record so far and included few details about their new proposals.

Daniel Allain, the newly-elected leader of Progressive Conservatives, said the Liberals gave a “recycled throne speech” that lacked long-term vision.

He said the government did not include plans to reverse the multibillion-dollar provincial debt, which is expected to increase in the next two Liberal budgets.

“For a government whose mid-mandate (speech) was titled delivering change, I thought it was more like delivering chaos or fiscal disorder,” Allain said in an interview Tuesday.

Allain, who said he watched the throne speech from the public gallery, is a former one-term provincial legislator who does not currently have a seat in the house.

He appointed two-term legislator and former fisheries minister Margaret Johnson to serve as Official Opposition leader inside the legislature on his behalf.

Allain said he plans to run for a seat next year.

Meanwhile, Holt in a statement Tuesday said her government is “focused on delivering results” in health care and affordability.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

— With files from Devin Stevens.

stories.title: Fire burned for hours before CFB Wainwright tragedy: satellite data
stories.summary: Training continued at CFB Wainwright on Saturday even though a fire had been burning on the base since noon and forecasts warned of high winds and an approaching cold front.
stories.author: Ashleigh Stewart
stories.content:
The military let training continue at CFB Wainwright on Saturday even though a fire had been burning on the base since noon and forecasts had already warned of high winds, dry conditions and an approaching cold front.

Hours later, a grass fire overtook soldiers during a live-fire exercise at the base, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, killing four members of the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) and injuring 39, 19 of them critically.

The military says a sudden shift in wind turned a fire it believed was contained into a deadly one.

“The fire was a kilometre away when the wind shifted. It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds,” said Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division.

But satellite imagery reviewed by Global News and weather records reveal warning signs around four hours before the blaze expanded.

Forecasters had also flagged unusually powerful winds days earlier.

Satellite data from Nasa’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (Firms) detected 59 possible fire hotspots across an area roughly 1.6 kilometres wide at CFB Wainwright at approximately 12:20 p.m. Saturday. Global News could not independently confirm whether it was the same fire that turned fatal.

Mike Flannigan, a wildfire researcher at Thompson Rivers University, said the data definitively showed at least one fire burning on the base roughly four hours before the tragedy, although he could not rule out multiple fires.

To be detectable by satellite, he said, it likely started “at least half an hour before that, maybe even hours before that.”

The detections do not show the fire’s size, when it began, or whether the blaze that later turned deadly was the one detected.

The Office of the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal declined to answer questions from Global News about the event, as the investigation is ongoing and requires co-operation from multiple agencies.

As the afternoon wore on, strong-wind forecasts escalated into Environment Canada warnings, while warm, dry conditions and an approaching cold front created what wildfire experts call a potentially lethal combination.

“This was just a confluence of really extreme conditions that all played out at the exact moment when they had an active fire in the area,” says Jen Beverly, an associate professor of wildland fire at the University of Alberta.

Rutland said at a press conference Sunday that a fire burned on the base “for several hours,” but training continued “for a certain amount of time” because commanders believed the fire was contained.

“The weather for the majority of the day was well within standard procedures, well below 50 kilometres,” he added. “This was uncommon, rapid, and I certainly hadn’t seen anything like it. Certainly we train in all types of conditions because you don’t know where you’re going to operate.”

Three former senior military officers interviewed by Global News said training exercises often continue while a fire burns nearby, provided the base’s Range Control deems it safe. They also said strong winds alone wouldn’t necessarily be grounds to suspend training.

The Wainwright area is consistently windy, partly because of its exposed prairie landscape. Environment Canada records from nearby Lloydminster – the closest available long-term climate data – show prevailing westerly winds for most of the year, with stronger average winds outside the summer months.

But more than a dozen residents interviewed by Global News described the gusts as stronger than anything they’d ever experienced. The same winds tore across the province before they reached Wainwright, kicking up dust storms, damaging property and even pushing semi-trailer trucks off the highway.

“I was outside, and it almost blew me away. I had to seek shelter in the building as the wind went through,” says Roger Holmes, editor of the town’s Star Edge newspaper.

“I’ve lived in this town for over 30 years, and I’ve never seen a wind storm like that come through.”

Dry, blustery conditions had already gripped the Wainwright area in the days leading up to the deadly blaze.

Environment Canada issued separate wind warnings for the region Wednesday, which remained in effect into early Thursday. The Weather Network and news outlets, including Global News, forecast a cold front crossing Alberta on Saturday with powerful winds.

“It was well advertised days in advance. Computer models knew there would be winds gusting 80 to 100 kilometres an hour,” said Global News meteorologist Anthony Farnell.

The area was also in an extended dry spell.

Weather records show Wainwright had received just 3.5 millimetres of rain this October, with no significant rainfall. The last substantial rainfall was on Sept. 7, when approximately 23.5 millimetres fell, roughly six weeks earlier.

By Saturday, wildfire danger across much of southern Alberta, including Wainwright, was rated “extreme,” according to provincial data and the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System.

That appears to contradict an internal memo issued Sunday by the military’s Strategic Joint Staff (SJS), which rated the fire risk as low.

It is unclear whether the memo referred to broader fire-weather conditions or the risk posed by the exercise.

Nasa satellite data show possible fire activity at CFB Wainwright at two different times Saturday.

The first detections came at 12:17 p.m., when Nasa’s Landsat 8 satellite identified 59 possible fire hotspots across an area roughly 1.6 kilometres wide.

More than two and a half hours later, at 2:49 p.m., a second satellite system, Viirs, detected additional hotspots in the area.

Landsat can detect smaller fires with greater precision, while Viirs provides more frequent observations. The timestamps reflect when the satellites passed over the area, rather than when the fires began.

The detections do not establish the size of the fire, exactly when it began or whether it was the same blaze that later turned deadly.

Wildfire researcher Mike Flannigan said the fire likely started “at least half an hour before that, maybe even hours before that,” for satellites to detect it.

Within an hour, powerful winds were sweeping through the Edmonton region, where the international airport reportedly recorded a gust of 117 kilometres an hour around 1 p.m. Residents described massive dust clouds, property damage and power outages.

Around the same time in Wainwright, conditions were comparatively calm, with temperatures hovering around a balmy 20 C and winds moving at approximately 15 kilometres an hour.

But at 2:15 p.m., Environment Canada issued a wind warning for the Lloydminster region, which includes Wainwright, forecasting gusts of up to 100 kilometres an hour.

By 3 p.m., weather records show, temperatures at the base had climbed above 23 C — before plunging more than 10 degrees in an hour.

Relative humidity was also falling, creating what fire scientists call “crossover fire conditions”, when the temperature in degrees Celsius exceeds the relative humidity percentage.

A cold front can also swing the wind abruptly, dramatically changing how a fire spreads, she explained.

“It means that the flank or side of your fire can suddenly become the head of the fire.”

Around 3 p.m., Environment Canada extended its wind warning in a separate alert, with forecasters expecting gusts up to 90 kilometres an hour. But strong winds alone would not necessarily halt military training, said retired Col. Ryan Jurkowski, director of the Conference of Defence Associations.

“In my 30 years of training with the Canadian Armed Forces for infantry training, wind has never been a factor.”

He said he’d trained with higher gusts, and that inclement weather “adds to the value of the training.”

By 4 p.m., Environment Canada data showed gusts at CFB Wainwright reaching 48 kilometres an hour. The agency also recorded an 82-kilometre-an-hour gust that day, though its public data does not say when. Environment Canada did not respond to a request for clarification.

“That wind was so strong, and it was blowing me over trying to carry my baby and the cats,” says Madison Keller, who lives on the edge of the military base.

Her father called to warn her about an approaching fire, she said, but within moments, it was upon her. She scrambled to gather her one-year-old baby, pets and a bag of essentials and fled.

“It just came out of nowhere. No noise, besides the wind. That’s all we heard was wind.”

As the winds shifted, Rutland said, the once-contained fire became a fast-moving inferno.

“I spoke to my commander on the ground last night and this morning, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute, they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them.”

Wildfire experts say that kind of speed would be extraordinary.

Flannigan said grass fires typically spread at about one-tenth the speed of the wind, while Beverly says that even under extreme conditions, Canada’s fire-behaviour prediction system might forecast a grass fire spreading at around 20 kilometres an hour.

But Rutland’s account suggests the Wainwright fire was moving between 60 and 120 kilometres an hour — several times faster than those estimates.

“If the fire was spreading at the rate that they described, it’s not impossible, but it would be on record as the fastest moving fire ever recorded in Canada,” says Beverly, adding that such speeds have been recorded in rural Australia grass fires and during the 2023 Hawaii wildfires.

Brian MacDonald, who advised then-defence minister Peter MacKay in 2008, said it was “fairly routine” for military exercises to continue even when a fire was burning nearby, provided it was considered safe.

“There’s usually a detailed meteorological report that’s provided, but of course those are often imperfect, and the imperative is to continue on with the mission,” he said.

Locals confirmed the base was known for fires.

Wainwright resident Annette Nesbitt said plumes of smoke rising above the base rarely caused alarm.

“We say that the base was on fire again, but it is always on fire… you don’t think anything of it.”

She did not hear an explosion, as has been widely reported. Neither did several other residents Global News interviewed. Some heard loud “booms,” but said that’s common near the base. “We’re used to hearing the guns, you don’t think anything of it,” Nesbitt said.

“You go to sleep hearing that sound, and the joke is – if something serious happened, how long would it take us to realize?”

This isn’t the first time a fire on an Alberta military base has spread out of control.

In September 2017, a grass fire broke out as soldiers at CFB Suffield were destroying an unexploded artillery shell. Fuelled by dry conditions and strong winds, it scorched across roughly 36,000 hectares, destroyed a ranch, killed more than 160 cattle and forced dozens of residents to evacuate.

The military subsequently pledged to improve its firefighting and fire-prevention procedures.

What sparked the deadly Wainwright fire remains unanswered, with politicians, community leaders and military officials largely unwilling to speculate while the investigation continues.

Rutland offered few details about the possible cause, other than ruling out any involvement of oil and gas infrastructure or “outside interference.”

“There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area yesterday: grenade launcher, grenades, small arms, ammunition. Quite frankly, it could have been any of that or none of it,” he said.

But beyond what ignited the flames, the 50 investigators deployed to Wainwright face another question: whether the deaths and injuries could have been avoided.

Retired Canadian Armed Forces Maj.-Gen. Denis Thompson cautioned against drawing conclusions before the investigation is complete, but said one question remains central.

“The real question here is, was this a preventable accident or incident? Or was it non-preventable?”

“I spoke to my commander on the ground last night and this morning, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute, they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them.”
Wildfire experts say that kind of speed would be extraordinary.

Flannigan said grass fires typically spread at about one-tenth the speed of the wind, while Beverly says that even under extreme conditions, Canada’s fire-behaviour prediction system might forecast a grass fire spreading at around 20 kilometres an hour.
But Rutland’s account suggests the Wainwright fire was moving between 60 and 120 kilometres an hour — several times faster than those estimates.

“If the fire was spreading at the rate that they described, it’s not impossible, but it would be on record as the fastest moving fire ever recorded in Canada,” says Beverly, adding that such speeds have been recorded in rural Australia grass fires and during the 2023 Hawaii wildfires.

Brian MacDonald, who advised then-defence minister Peter MacKay in 2008, said it was “fairly routine” for military exercises to continue even when a fire was burning nearby, provided it was considered safe.
“There’s usually a detailed meteorological report that’s provided, but of course those are often imperfect, and the imperative is to continue on with the mission,” he said.
Locals confirmed the base was known for fires.
Wainwright resident Annette Nesbitt said plumes of smoke rising above the base rarely caused alarm.
“We say that the base was on fire again, but it is always on fire… you don’t think anything of it.”

She did not hear an explosion, as has been widely reported. Neither did several other residents Global News interviewed. Some heard loud “booms,” but said that’s common near the base. “We’re used to hearing the guns, you don’t think anything of it,” Nesbitt said.
“You go to sleep hearing that sound, and the joke is – if something serious happened, how long would it take us to realize?”
Questions remain
This isn’t the first time a fire on an Alberta military base has spread out of control.

In September 2017, a grass fire broke out as soldiers at CFB Suffield were destroying an unexploded artillery shell. Fuelled by dry conditions and strong winds, it scorched across roughly 36,000 hectares, destroyed a ranch, killed more than 160 cattle and forced dozens of residents to evacuate.
The military subsequently pledged to improve its firefighting and fire-prevention procedures.
What sparked the deadly Wainwright fire remains unanswered, with politicians, community leaders and military officials largely unwilling to speculate while the investigation continues.
Rutland offered few details about the possible cause, other than ruling out any involvement of oil and gas infrastructure or “outside interference.”

“There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area yesterday: grenade launcher, grenades, small arms, ammunition. Quite frankly, it could have been any of that or none of it,” he said.
But beyond what ignited the flames, the 50 investigators deployed to Wainwright face another question: whether the deaths and injuries could have been avoided.
Retired Canadian Armed Forces Maj.-Gen. Denis Thompson cautioned against drawing conclusions before the investigation is complete, but said one question remains central.
“The real question here is, was this a preventable accident or incident? Or was it non-preventable?”

stories.title: 'Is this a joke?': Cruise ship heading for the Bahamas rerouted to Nova Scotia instead
stories.summary: About 5,000 passengers aboard a Royal Caribbean cruise ship expecting to visit the Bahamas Tuesday will instead make port in Halifax, N.S.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A cruise ship carrying 5,000 passengers that embarked from New Jersey is heading to Nova Scotia, not Nassau as they thought, because of heavy weather at sea.

Royal Caribbean’s Oasis of the Seas left Cape Liberty, N.J., ON Sunday, diverting course from its original itinerary of Florida, then the Bahamas, to sail instead for Halifax, where passengers will spend 24 hours of their seven-day cruise. It’s not clear where the ship will go next, but it’s about a three-day sail to the Bahamas from Nova Scotia and the cruise is due back on Sunday.

“The funny thing is I was on board Vision of the Seas in September, and it was supposed to go to Canada, but it was rerouted to the Caribbean because of a storm and now I have the opposite happening,” passenger Debra DelCamp wrote in a message to the National Post.

“I don’t think it’s a big deal; It’s cruise life. For first-time cruisers, I can understand it being confusing or upsetting, but for regulars it’s just cruising.”

The saddest story she has heard about the itinerary swap was from a family aboard the Oasis of the Seas who had planned to scatter their late father’s ashes while the 362-metre-long cruise ship was in the Bahamas.

“It was to celebrate their father’s last trip on Oasis that actually went to Nassau,” DelCamp said. “So, they were very sad to be releasing ashes in Canada.”

Another passenger, David Hess of Ephrata, Penn., heard about the itinerary swap after boarding Oasis of the Seas.

“We mostly packed summer clothes, tank tops, booty shorts,” Hess wrote on social media. “My question is: is it as warm in Canada as the Bahamas?”

Daisy Mungin from Greenville, S.C., responded: “I’m on the boat with you,” she said. “It’s freezing.”

Passenger Nicole Borowicz-Byler seemed taken aback by the destination swap.

“Instead of the Bahamas it now says we’re going to Canada,” she wrote on social media. “Is this a joke?”

Passenger Mikayla Iverson wrote that she’d driven eight hours to board the ship. “Now I’ve gotta go buy something warm to wear.”

Cruise ships are regular visitors to the Port of Halifax, which saw 184 of them stop in the N.S. capital last year, carrying a total of about 357,000 passengers.

The accidental N.S. tourists, who are slated to land in the province Tuesday evening just before sunset, will have lots on offer once they get to Halifax, according to Giacomo Bruno, director of sales and marketing with Ambassatours Gray Line, which organizes outings for visiting cruise ships.

“We’re offering the Harbour Hopper Tour (#1 boat tour in Halifax); tours to Georges Island National Historic Site, bus tour to Peggy’s Cove, a Waterfront Walking Tour and trips to McNabs Island,” Bruno said in an email.

“If folks didn’t pack for the cold, we have a charming shop on the waterfront where we sell East Coast Lifestyle … Tall Ship Silva hoodies and full zip sweatshirts, and Harbour Hopper Tours sweaters.”

Halifax Mayor Andy Fillmore was practically effusive about this week’s unplanned stop for the sun-seeking cruisers aboard Oasis of the Seas.

“To the 5,000 visitors who packed their swimsuits for the Bahamas but woke up headed for Nova Scotia — welcome to Halifax!” Fillmore said in an email to the National Post.

“You May be come-from-aways, but we’re delighted you’re here.”

The ship is slated to arrive Tuesday evening and stay in Halifax for most of Wednesday. The weather forecast calls for cloudy skies both days and highs between 13 C and 15 C while the Oasis of the Seas is in port. Meanwhile, the temperature in sunny Nassau Tuesday was 28 C.

“We can’t promise you tropical temperatures, but we can promise you a warm welcome — with zero chance of sunburn,” Fillmore said.

“So, trade the flip-flops for Blundstones, and the palm trees for pine trees. Grab a toque, find a good bowl of seafood chowder, and explore our wonderful local restaurants, pubs, and shops. And tell them the Mayor sent you! Who knows — you might just discover that the best part of your Caribbean cruise was Canada.”

stories.title: Alberta separatists vow to fight on after referendum loss: 'Tonight isn't the finish line'
stories.summary: Alberta separatists advocates Mitch Sylvestre , Jeffrey Rath, Keith Wilson and others aren't giving up their fight following a referendum loss.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
The results of Monday’s Alberta referendum question on separation from Canada won’t be official for more than a week, but all indications are that the separatist movement was handed a sound defeat.

As the earliest numbers showed about 76 per cent in favour of remaining in Confederation, a figure that hasn’t changed much as of 10 a.m. MT , separatist leader Jeffrey Rath expressed optimism about the political movement and re-emphasized the need to take control of the United Conservative Party of Alberta from Premier Danielle Smith, whom he said conspired with “fake news” and the “entire Canadian political establishment” to campaign against independence.

“It’s time to have a serious discussion as to whether or not a supermajority of the (UCP) want to continue to be led by a federalist who’s in bed with Naheed Nenshi, Mark Carney, Rachel Notley, and the rest of the socialists and globalists that have literally been ruining this province and ruining this country,” Rath told Global News late Monday night at a downtown Edmonton pizza parlour.

During his interview, the self-described “ constitutional lawyer ” and co-founder of the Alberta Prosperity Project (APP) estimated that, by night’s end, anywhere from 600,000 to 700,000 people will have voted in favour of starting the formal process of Alberta seceding from Canada. Elections Alberta, with 78 per cent of polls reported, counted 458,923 as of 10 a.m. Official results are due on Thursday, Oct. 29.

Rath said supporters of independence won’t be swayed from their cause.

“We roll up our sleeves and we work harder because that’s who we are as people,” he said.

As for Smith, she said on X that she was “very pleased” with the initial results on the separation question and promised to address the province at 6:45 p.m. local time on Tuesday, “to discuss the results of all referendum questions for which results are available, and where our province goes from here.”

“They can underestimate us. They can throw every obstacle imaginable in our way, and believe me, they have, but they cannot stop what has already started. Tonight isn’t the finish line,” he said.

“It’s another chapter in something much bigger than any one of us. We have awakened something in this province, and that spirit isn’t going anywhere.”

Sylvestre also addressed UCP co-founder and former Alberta premier Jason Kenny, a staunch opponent of the separatist movement, who last week said supporters of separatism were facing a post-referendum reckoning.

“We certainly don’t need lectures from those who have already underestimated us once before,” Sylvestre said.

The true reckoning, he said, is a group of Albertans that are “organized, integrated, and not putting up with the corruption and the failure.”

After Kenny posted on X Monday that secession talk only pushed election-deciding “mainstream centre-right voters” away from conservative parties towards the NDP, Republican Party of Alberta leader Cameron Davies, another fierce separatism advocate, countered that they’re gravitating because conservatives are “acting and governing like liberal lite.”

“Fake conservatives are kryptonite for any real conservative movement,” he wrote.

In Calgary, Let Alberta Decide founder Keith Wilson, formerly of the 2022 Freedom Convoy, noted that at least a quarter “feel that Alberta needs to be treated better, that Alberta can do better.”

David Parker, founder of conservative group Take Back Alberta, called Monday’s result “bleak.”

Cory Morgan, founder of Pathway to Independence, said it’s not the Ucp’s role to become a separatist party. He said a single advocacy group should lead the effort and that the recent campaign was hurt by not collectively addressing voters.

“We had six or seven different groups speaking throughout the campaign. You don’t run a general election that way; it would just be a dog’s breakfast,” he said.

Meanwhile, as the results were taking shape, pro-separation MLA Jason Stephan (Red Deer-South), announced on X that he would not seek re-election in next year’s provincial general election.

“The status quo is not the right way for Albertans. Empty words and platitudes do not make it otherwise,” he wrote in an open letter. “Some say they want Unity, but their actions say otherwise. Does fearmongering, name calling labelling, and gaslighting produce unity?”

stories.title: Seven taken to hospital after Oxford collision
stories.summary: The lone occupant of an SUV and the six occupants of the minivan were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A collision in South-West Oxford sent seven occupants out of two vehicles to hospital Monday afternoon, according to police.

Oxford OPP along with Oxford County Fire and Oxford County Paramedic Services, responded to a two-vehicle collision at the intersection of Foldens Line and Clarke Road at about 2 p.m. on Monday.

Police said a sport utility vehicle and a minivan collided at the intersection.

The lone occupant of the SUV and the six occupants of the minivan were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

A 32-year-old driver from the minivan has been charged with careless driving under the Highway Traffic Act.

Police did not release the identities of those involved.
