paragraphs: Albertans have voted against separating from Canada in a historic referendum, according to preliminary results released in the early hours of Tuesday morning.

The results, however, will likely do little to silence separatist sentiment across the province and could further escalate questions about whether Alberta Premier Danielle Smith can maintain control of her party – and the province.

The political fallout will now take centre stage as Alberta’s United Conservative Party, Opposition New Democratic Party, federalists and separatists decide how to leverage this pivotal moment in the province’s history.
Here are five key takeaways following Monday’s vote.

Elections Alberta tallied the results of the separation question first. At 3:01 p.m. MT (5:01 p.m. ET) on Tuesday, with 88 per cent of voting locations reporting, the agency said almost 1.45 million Albertans supported staying in Canada, or 75 per cent, while more than 477,000 elected to launch the legal process to hold a second referendum on secession, or 25 per cent.

Early results indicate voters in Calgary and Edmonton threw their weight behind Confederation at a rate outpacing their rural counterparts. The more the spread widens, the more difficult it will be for the Premier to keep the peace within the United Conservative Party.

There were roughly 3.15 million eligible voters in Alberta, and residents came out in droves. Nearly 1.36 million Albertans cast an advance vote or special ballot before referendum day, exceeding the turnout for the 2023 provincial election. Just over 43 per cent of eligible electors voted in advance, compared with 27.5 per cent in 2023.
The ballots are being hand counted because the province no longer allows electronic tabulators. Polls closed later than planned Monday after delays in opening at multiple voting locations.
The outcome of Monday’s vote didn’t matter: Separatists have been clear that their work is far from over.

Mitch Sylvestre, leader of the Alberta Prosperity Project, one of the province’s most prominent separatist organizations, said his first option in trying to advance his agenda was the referendum. Now, he’s looking at other options.
“You have to get involved in government. That’s the different way,” he said, though he added he believes an independence party would have slim chances of winning a general election.
Mr. Sylvestre said he would meet with “independence leaders” for breakfast on Tuesday to decide next steps.
His partner at the Alberta Prosperity Project, Jeff Rath, was more defiant in defeat, taking aim at the Premier.
“The next phase for us moving forward is an institutional phase where we move forward to take control back of our party, which is the United Conservative Party of Alberta,” Mr. Rath said.

Lawyer Keith Wilson, who co-founded the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, said Monday night that the results show many people want change. “At least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better, that Alberta can do better.”
Federalists will be pleased that Albertans have voted to stay in Canada but the outcome is unlikely to position Ms. Smith as an ally to the movement.

The Premier has a contentious relationship with the pro-Canada crowd, who have accused her of pandering to separatists and voiced dissatisfaction with her muddled messaging on Alberta’s place within Canada.

While Ms. Smith has said repeatedly that she wants Alberta to be part of a “united Canada,” she has been relentless in her push to squeeze Ottawa for additional powers for the province. It has also not gone unnoticed by many federalists that there is significant overlap between the people who pushed her into power and the separatists.

Former Alberta deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk, the head organizer of Forever Canadian, the largest federalist group, said he isn’t confident that Ms. Smith won’t hold another referendum in the future.

Ms. Smith is now left with the difficult task of maintaining control of her party while broadly appealing to Albertans. Already, some separatists are rallying UCP members to oust her at next month’s annual party gathering.

The Alberta NDP, which has positioned itself as staunchly pro-Canada, has capitalized on widespread opposition to the referendum, gaining political momentum in recent months after a long period of stagnation.
A sign that the separatism debate was weighing down the Ucp’s popularity came in September when NDP candidate Kyle Campbell won a by-election in the reliable conservative riding of Calgary-Shaw.

Ms. Smith blamed the stunning upset on a vote split between two conservative parties and low voter turnout. But political strategists argued the referendum turned the by-election into a protest vote against separation.
Recent polling also suggests that the divide between the UCP and NDP has narrowed, with the two parties locked in a virtual tie.
NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said the referendum has hit a nerve with voters. His job now, he said, is to make sure Albertans hold on to that feeling until the next provincial election.
“My challenge is really to help Albertans remember what happened, remember how frustrated they were today but also remember that they deserve better,” Mr. Nenshi said on Monday night.
Still, it’s a full year before a scheduled provincial election, giving the UCP significant runway to calm any lingering tensions from the referendum.

Ms. Smith’s relationship with Prime Minister Mark Carney has warmed over the past year, particularly over his approach to energy and pipelines. On Friday, the pair stood side by side in Red Deer to rally support for Alberta to remain in Canada.
But the complicated – and often tense – relationship between the province and Ottawa is a tale as old as Alberta.

The two leaders still have areas of disagreement, including on the other nine questions included in the referendum. While Ms. Smith urged voters to say yes to proposals on topics including immigration, health care and constitutional reform that would wrest power away from Ottawa, Mr. Carney wanted voters to reject them.
Votes on the other nine questions were still being tallied early Tuesday. The full count is expected to take two days to complete.

Ms. Smith has said that the new mandate from the other ballot questions would be used as leverage to increase provincial autonomy, shaping the federal-provincial relationship in the days and months to come.

stories.title: How the son of the original ‘Iceman’ furthered his father’s legacy
stories.summary: Growth required a fresh perspective and a willingness to cede some control of The Iceman. Unexpected exposure from Drake hasn’t hurt either
stories.author: Nickie Shobeiry
stories.content:
Right after university graduation in 2011, Jake Silva put on his “investor glasses” for a Toronto ice-distribution business even though he didn’t have a financial stake in the company.

He had the fresh eyes of a younger generation that could bring new ideas and perspective to The Iceman, which his father John Silva had started 24 years earlier.

Jake saw a reputable company with steady demand, but also an operation that lacked structure and that had unrealized potential. Payroll would take days, clients still used paper invoices and filing cabinets were filled with physical records.

Jake decided to apply his degree in commerce and finance from Concordia University to the family business – involvement that would eventually fulfill expansion aspirations that John had always held but had never acted on.

However, transforming the regional ice distributor into a manufacturer with a production facility in Ontario and one in Alberta was a years-long process that required the founder to give up some power.

“I’m very hands-on,” John, 64, acknowledges. “I try to control stuff, and you can’t be like that” to grow.

The business moved away from having most decisions revolve around John, which had created bottlenecks. He is now much better at allowing departments to run their own teams, says Jake, who joined The Iceman full-time in 2012 and has been president since 2020. “I don’t think we would have grown as much as we have without him [ceding] some control.”

The founder of a business entering a new chapter must allow incoming leaders to “exercise real authority,” says Jill Renton, executive director of Kpmg Canada’s family office. Succession is ideally a gradual transfer where the next generation proves their capability over time, she adds.

Transitioning The Iceman’s leadership is an example of such progression. Jake, now 37, grew up delivering bags of ice by golf cart each summer to bars, restaurants and events such as pride parades as well as running and car races. Once he joined permanently, he held a wide variety of roles throughout the enterprise.

When John’s business partner at the time wanted out in 2017, Jake, who was handling all accounting and finance matters, bought a stake. Until then, The Iceman was primarily a distributor, relying on an ice manufacturer that was also its competitor for product. “The dynamic was problematic,” Jake says, “because they could really control which kind of customers we could go after and which ones we couldn’t.”

He devised a business plan for The Iceman to build its own ice plant. His father was excited, Jake recalls, saying it’s something that John had always wanted to do, “but maybe he wasn’t able to put together all the pieces” when it came to financing and bank loans.

Jake secured the necessary funding and the company opened its first ice plant in 2018 in Vaughan, north of Toronto. The facility makes about 50 metric tonnes of ice daily but they’ve had to turn away clients in the last two years because of a lack of capacity. A second Toronto-area plant set to open early next year is expected to triple output.

Today, The Iceman supplies restaurants, events and businesses including Costco with cocktail cubes, packaged ice and dry ice, as well as heat-relief water bottles and freezers for construction sites. It also sells, rents and services ice machines. In 2024, it acquired an Edmonton company that produces and distributes ice across Alberta. The Iceman has grown to 80 employees in the summertime from around 30 when Jake first joined.

He also helped move the company toward software-based payroll, accounting, invoicing and dispatch systems. “If we had the old way of doing things, growing would have just been so painful,” Jake says.

John, who now manages The Iceman’s sales and customer relationships, appreciates his son’s leadership: “I see Jake’s done what he’s done and I’m very happy and lucky that he’s taken over.”

While Jake says he sometimes still seeks his father’s advice, “I’m already driving the bus, and he’s happy to have the role he’s in now.”

Ms. Renton notes that it’s important for a successor to understand the founder’s “unique qualities” that allowed the business to flourish in the first place. New leaders must treat their predecessors as “an important point of continuity,” she says.

John entered the industry in the mid-1970s when an ice plant in downtown Toronto closed and his parents’ nearby variety store became a local ice collection point. When restaurants asked if they could send taxis to the shop to retrieve bags of ice, John began delivering them himself in a pickup truck. He later bought a truck that doubled as both a delivery vehicle and storage for six pallets of ice and then expanded into dry ice and ice-machine rentals and repairs.

“I always learned how to hustle,” John says. However, in the early days, “I didn’t have the whole business plan together.”

The company’s profile got an unexpected boost this spring through a collaboration with the musical artist Drake, tied to the rollout of his 2026 album Iceman . After connecting through a mutual friend, the Canadian rapper and singer filmed video footage at The Iceman’s plant.

The attention sent millions of people to The Iceman’s website every day. “People pay a lot of money for a viral moment like that, so the fact that we were able to get it very coincidentally – it was great,” Jake says.

The Drake partnership sparked demand for The Iceman merchandise – previously only available to employees – such as jackets, hoodies and hats. Within two weeks of Drake’s single release, the company added an online store, selling more than 1,200 orders since, Jake says.

“It’s kind of cool to think that there’s people all over the world wearing Iceman T-shirts.”

stories.title: Police asking for public’s help finding missing George Nash, 80
stories.summary: London police have asked residents of a southeast London neighbourhood to search their yards, sheds, garages a...
stories.author: Georgia Chambers
stories.content:
London police have asked residents of a southeast London neighbourhood to search their yards, sheds, garages and cars for an 80-year-old man, who was last reported seen a week ago.

Police say them and George Nash has been missing since Oct. 14, when he was seen near Wellington Road and Weston Street. He is vulnerable and his family is concerned for his well being, police said.

There have been no updates since Saturday, when police announced they would be searching the Chelsea Green neighbourhood.

“The investigation is ongoing and the most recent media release that was shared asking members of the public to search their properties and outbuildings,” is still the message police are sending, said Sergeant Sandasha Bough in a comment today

There will be a bigger police presence in the Chelsea Green neighbourhood as they officers continue to search for him, police said in an October 17 update.

George Nash, 80 Photo Credits: London Police Service

Nash is desribed as white, around 5’2 and 120lbs, with balding white hair and blue eyes.

He was last seen in a light blue shirt, a dark blue striped jacket, casual pants and a beige baseball hat.

Police are asking that if anyone has any information to call them at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477.

stories.title: Woman dies after single-vehicle crash in London
stories.summary: Emergency crews were called to the 600-block of Upper Queen Street at about 1:20 a.m. for reports of a serious crash.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A woman has died following a single-vehicle collision in London early Tuesday morning, according to police.

Emergency crews were called to the 600-block of Upper Queen Street at about 1:20 a.m. for reports of a serious crash.

Police said a female passenger was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries. She later died from those injuries.

The male driver was arrested at the scene and remains in police custody.

Police continue to investigate the collision and have not released the identities of those involved or details about what led to the crash.

Upper Queen Street remains closed between Chiddington Avenue and Ferndale Avenue while investigators examine the scene. Motorists are being advised to avoid the area and use alternate routes.

A section of Upper Queen Street has been closed in London following a motor vehicle collision that required a rescue by fire crews.

London police said Upper Queen Street is closed between Chiddington Avenue and Ferndale Avenue as officers investigate the crash. Motorists are being asked to avoid the area and use alternate routes.

Fire crews responded to the scene and extricated one person from a vehicle involved in the collision.

Police have not released information about the extent of any injuries or how the crash happened.

The road is expected to remain closed for an undetermined amount of time.

stories.title: Albertans mixed on other referendum questions after rejecting separation
stories.summary: Albertans decisively rejected moving toward separation in Monday’s referendum, while several of the remaining questions produced narrower margins.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Albertans decisively rejected moving toward separation in Monday’s referendum , while several of the remaining questions produced narrower margins.

Elections Alberta reported results from 75 per cent of voting locations as of 5 a.m. MT Tuesday. The figures remain unofficial and May change as counting continues. Official results are expected on Oct. 29.

The referendum posed 10 questions, including one asking if the province should hold a formal referendum on separation. Around 76 per cent of respondents said no .

The margins on several of the nine other questions were considerably narrower. Five involved immigration and services for non-permanent residents, while four concerned potential constitutional changes.

The immigration questions asked if Alberta should have more say on who comes to the province to work, and whether it’s time to put more limitations — or even fees — on some who seek access to health care and education.

The constitutional questions asked whether the province should pursue constitutional negotiations with other governments on gaining control from Ottawa and abolishing the Senate.

Unofficial results showed nearly 59 per cent in favour for the first question, which sought support for increased provincial control for the purpose of decreasing immigration.

A similar result was reported for the second question on access limits for programs like health care, education and social services. About 57 per cent supported limiting those programs to citizens, permanent residents and those with approved immigration status.

Roughly 63 per cent supported requiring proof of citizenship to vote, which was asked in question five.

Question six, which asked if Albertans want the government to try and amend the constitution to allow provinces to select justices for provincial courts, had 50.7 per cent support.

About 52 per cent opposed the proposal in question eight, which asked if Alberta should opt out of federal programs like health care, education, social services without losing federal funding.

Nearly 51 per cent supported question nine, which asked if the government should try to amend the constitution to give provincial laws priority over federal laws when they conflict.

Global News continues to track the live results to each question, which can be viewed here .

stories.title: Home seller rejects weak spring offer, waits for a better one
stories.summary: Four-bedroom house has 2,510 square feet of living space and finished basement with direct access to heated garage and driveway
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
64 Thompson Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $3,548,000 (August, 2026)

Previous asking price: $3,698,000 (April, 2026)

Selling price: $3.5-million (September, 2026)

Previous selling price: Not available

Taxes: $12,867 (2026)

Days on the market: 13

Property days on market: 128

Listing agent: Luisa Piccirilli, Re/Max West Realty Inc.

This four-bedroom house has 2,510 square feet of living space and a finished basement with direct access to a heated garage and driveway. There’s also a rear exit to a hot tub and cabana on the 35- by 120-foot lot. Though buyers this spring were intrigued by the home’s design and convenient location a block from Bloor Street West, there was only one offer, and that was far below the asking price.

“There are excellent schools in the area that certainly attract a lot of young families,” said agent Luisa Piccirilli.

“It was a very spacious house, but a lot of feedback was [that buyers] wanted it a little bigger. Otherwise, the upgrades more than made up for that.”

In August, the home was relisted with the asking price cut by $150,000. Within two weeks, one buyer negotiated a deal at $3.5-million, with another potential buyer waiting in the wings.

“All of a sudden, we had so many more eyes on the listing,” Ms. Piccirilli said.

“I like to work with one offer at a time, but we could have had a choice of other offers. We had someone potentially waiting if something went south with this offer.”

This two-storey house has an office and open-concept living and dining areas with 10-foot ceilings.

The kitchen has an island, a pantry and sliding doors to the patio. There is a barbecue station, a cabana with a wet bar and a powder room.

There are five bathrooms, and a sauna in the basement. Also downstairs is a recreation area with a wet bar and heated flooring.

“The cabana was great because it was multifunctional,” said Ms. Piccirilli.

“It could have been a yoga studio, definitely an office or even a cigar lounge.”

There’s also a rear exit to a hot tub and cabana on the 35- by 120-foot lot. Though buyers this spring were intrigued by the home’s design and convenient location a block from Bloor Street West, there was only one offer, and that was far below the asking price.
“There are excellent schools in the area that certainly attract a lot of young families,” said agent Luisa Piccirilli.
“It was a very spacious house, but a lot of feedback was [that buyers] wanted it a little bigger. Otherwise, the upgrades more than made up for that.”
In August, the home was relisted with the asking price cut by $150,000. Within two weeks, one buyer negotiated a deal at $3.5-million, with another potential buyer waiting in the wings.
“All of a sudden, we had so many more eyes on the listing,” Ms. Piccirilli said.
“I like to work with one offer at a time, but we could have had a choice of other offers. We had someone potentially waiting if something went south with this offer.”
This two-storey house has an office and open-concept living and dining areas with 10-foot ceilings.
The kitchen has an island, a pantry and sliding doors to the patio. There is a barbecue station, a cabana with a wet bar and a powder room.
There are five bathrooms, and a sauna in the basement. Also downstairs is a recreation area with a wet bar and heated flooring.
“The cabana was great because it was multifunctional,” said Ms. Piccirilli.
“It could have been a yoga studio, definitely an office or even a cigar lounge.”

stories.title: A family looks for just enough space in Niagara Falls
stories.summary: What can this downsizing family get for $550,000?
stories.author: Andrea Yu
stories.content:
Dhana Dias immigrated from her native Brazil to Toronto in 2016. Three years later, in 2019, she met fellow Brazilian Ronald Augusto, a 41-year-old data analyst, through Toronto’s Brazilian community. In 2021, the two became roommates, sharing an apartment near Wellesley Station before their friendship evolved into romance. Ms. Dias, 39, became pregnant, and just before their son, Max, was born, the couple moved to a larger two-bedroom condo in Humber Bay Shores, which they rented for $2,600 a month.

As Max got older, the family felt cramped in their condo (they also had two cats). After visiting friends who lived in Welland, Ont., just west of Niagara Falls, they fell in love with the area. “It was so quiet and seemed so safe,” Ms. Dias explains. They moved into a new three-bedroom townhouse rental in Welland at the end of 2022, paying $2,200 a month. But the couple struggled with loud neighbours. Their second son, Alex, was born in 2023, and they moved to a four-bedroom detached home in the Brown area of Niagara Falls in 2024, paying $2,700 per month.

At the same time, Ms. Dias was undergoing a career change and became a real estate agent. Her work brought her in and out of homes for sale and opened the couple’s eyes to what might be possible for their family. “Seeing people with a similar background and making the same money as we were … affording a house. We thought, maybe we can do it,” Mr. Augusto explains. They figured they could buy a smaller house and spend roughly the same amount on a mortgage as they did on rent. “We realized we didn’t need all this space,” Ms. Dias explains.

Home Run: With a $1.5-million budget for a new home, what did this expecting Toronto couple buy?

Because Ms. Dias was now self-employed, they had to wait until she had two years of tax returns as proof of income to qualify for a mortgage. By early April, 2026, they filed their 2025 taxes, were pre-approved for a mortgage and hit the ground running.

The couple wanted at least three bedrooms, plus an additional bedroom or a finished basement for guests and a kids’ playroom. A garage was a must to park their car in the winter, as was a good backyard for the kids to play in. But the most important element was location: they wanted to be close to Forestview, where their kids’ daycare was located. “It’s a very family-friendly neighbourhood,” Ms. Dias says. “People tend to take care of their homes and yards with a bit more care.”

With their preapproval in place and additional help from savings back in Brazil, they set themselves a budget of $550,000. Here were their top three options:

Small three-bedroom townhouse in Forestview

Mr. Augusto and Ms. Dias were eager to see this home because it was within walking distance to their sons’ daycare, a public school, and a great playground. It was a newer home, around ten years old and move-in ready. It had three bedrooms and three bathrooms, but the basement wasn’t finished, leaving no space for guests or a kids’ playroom. And while the family was up for downsizing, at 1,125 square feet, they worried the house would be too small for them. The layout had less natural light, so the home felt darker. But it did have a single-car garage and a nice fenced-in backyard for their kids to play in. The listing price of $520,000 was also under their budget.

Older four-bedroom detached home in Dorchester

Despite the fact that it was 15 minutes east of their target neighbourhood, Ms. Dias had viewed this home with a client and thought it might work for her family, so she returned with Mr. Augusto. The home felt spacious at 1,512 square feet, and it had four bedrooms and two bathrooms. It was an older house that had been recently renovated, but the basement was unfinished. In addition, one of the bathrooms in the basement needed some renovation work that the couple wasn’t keen to take on. There wasn’t any carpet in the home, which they saw as a bonus, since it’s easier to keep clean with kids and pets. It had a detached garage and a sizable backyard with a shed. But the neighbourhood was noisier and closer to the tourist district, which meant more traffic. It was listed just under their top budget, at $549,999.

Spacious three-bedroom townhouse in Fernwood Estates

The couple wasn’t initially going to see this home in Fernwood Estates, just west of Forestview, because it was over their budget, priced at $579,900. But Ms. Dias figured the sellers might be willing to negotiate. They loved that the neighbourhood was in an enclave with one entrance and exit, which felt safe and private. The neighbours’ homes were very well-kept with tidy front yards, which they liked. The 1,501-square-foot house had a one-and-a-half-car garage, three bedrooms and a finished basement. The backyard was spacious and fenced in, which would be great for the kids to play in. However, there was only one full bathroom – the second bath was just a powder room – and there was carpet on the top level, which they felt wasn’t ideal with two cats and two kids under five.

Their home: The spacious three-bedroom townhouse in Fernwood Estates

Mr. Augusto and Ms. Dias worried that the detached home in Dorchester wasn’t the best neighbourhood for their kids, and an older home would require too much maintenance. They actually submitted an offer on the small three-bedroom townhouse in Forestview for $500,000, but an administrative oversight resulted in another buyer with the same bid getting the property. The couple was glad it turned out that way since, in retrospect, they believe that home would have been too small for their family. They liked that the Fernwood Estates townhouse was bigger and brighter. “It was love at first sight, for sure,” Mr. Augusto explains.

The couple offered $545,000 for the spacious three-bedroom townhouse. Since Ms. Dias was a realtor, she was able to waive her 2 per cent commission, which she thinks helped sweeten the deal. The purchase was finalized at the end of April, 2026, only a few weeks after they first started looking for a home, and the family moved in by June.

Right now, their two sons are sharing a bedroom (“They love it,” says Mr. Augusto. “They wanted to sleep together.”) while the couple is in the primary bedroom and the third bedroom is their shared office. The kids have enjoyed turning the basement into their playroom, running around in the backyard and biking to a nearby playground.

Downsizing from 2,500 square feet to 1,500 square feet as a family of four might seem like a less-favourable transition. But Mr. Augusto and Ms. Dias believe it was the right move for them. “We didn’t even have enough furniture for the whole house,” Ms. Dias says about their former rental home. “It was a lot to clean and a lot of work for us.”

While they initially thought the fourth bedroom in their old home would be great for overnight guests, they realized that having a larger house just for occasional visitors wasn’t worth the space or expense. The couple plans to add a sofa bed to the finished basement to host guests in the future.

As their sons grow older and need separate bedrooms, Ms. Dias and Mr. Augusto will think about upgrading in about five years. Meanwhile, they’re enjoying life in their new home. “Every day, I wake up and say, ‘I love this house,’” Ms. Augusto says.

stories.title: Porter flights prompt London Transit Commission to explore better bus service to YXU
stories.summary: Recent announcements by Porter Airlines about new flights coming to London International Airport (YXU) has prompted the London Transit Commission (LTC) to investigate improving bus service for travellers.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Recent announcements by Porter Airlines about new flights coming to London International Airport (YXU) has prompted the London Transit Commission (LTC) to investigate improving bus service for travellers.

On Monday, a motion by London Transit Commissioner Coun. Sam Trosow called for a review before the next LTC meeting, “The airport is currently served by Route 36 which runs from Fanshawe College, and the purpose of this motion is request a staff report about the potential for direct service from downtown London to the airport.”

“It’s generally felt in this city that the connections to the airport are very poor,” Trosow told CTV News after the meeting. “People are forced to take very expensive connections, or use a motor vehicle, so this would be a great opportunity for us to up our service.”

Trosow’s motion received no support from colleagues on the commission, but it was followed by a related motion from Mayor Josh Morgan.

Morgan’s motion directed the LTC to engage with the airport and city hall about potential passenger volumes and possible destinations within the city for those arriving or departing from the airport.

It also didn’t exclude a direct link to the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) stop at Fanshawe College.

Trosow broadened the scope of the motion with an amendment that added consultation with Tourism London and the RBC Place Convention Centre.

“I want Tourism London and the Convention Centre to be part of this discussion because they’re going to have a lot of information about how many people might be affected,” Trosow explained. “We might want to use the front of the Convention Centre or some other downtown depot as a starting place for this. Let’s make it easy for people when they get off the plane in London to see that there are alternative routes to get into downtown.”

In August, Porter announced it would begin offering winter flights from London to sun destinations in Florida, Mexico and Jamaica.

Earlier this month the airline announced it will begin domestic flights to Edmonton, Halifax, Montreal, Ottawa and Vancouver in Spring 2027.

stories.title: Sunshine and autumn colours on display across southwestern Ontario
stories.summary: A stretch of sunny and mild fall weather is expected across southwestern Ontario this week, with temperatures remaining above seasonal norms and plenty of opportunities to enjoy the region’s autumn colours.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A stretch of sunny and mild fall weather is expected across southwestern Ontario this week, with temperatures remaining above seasonal norms and plenty of opportunities to enjoy the region’s autumn colours.

CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison said the region can expect mainly sunny skies Tuesday with a high of 17 C and light winds.

“It’s going to be beautiful, gorgeous, mainly sunny,” Atchison said.

The pleasant conditions are expected to continue through the remainder of the work week. Atchison said full sunshine is forecast Wednesday through Friday, with daytime highs ranging from 17 C to 18 C.

While overnight temperatures will be cool, Atchison said a gradual warming trend is expected heading into the weekend.

A mix of sun and cloud is forecast for Saturday and Sunday, with daytime highs expected to range between 16 C and 19 C.

Atchison said the weather will provide an ideal backdrop for residents hoping to take in the area’s fall colours.

“We have some gorgeous fall colours. Make sure you get outside and enjoy,” she said.

stories.title: Keith Morrison and Diana Swain on the case of Elizabeth Bain
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses the disappearance of Elizabeth Bain, and the resurfacing of a previous theory as to what happened to her.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Elizabeth Bain was 22 years old when she went missing from Toronto on June 19, 1990. The details of her disappearance have kept Canadians wondering for years what happened to her.

More than 35 years later, new, unreported evidence could bring her case back into focus for investigators and law enforcement alike.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Diana Swain, host of Dateline Canada, and Keith Morrison, award-winning correspondent for Dateline NBC, to discuss the mystery millions of Canadians have been trying to solve, and the resurfacing of a previous, struck-down theory as to what happened on that day in June.

Dateline Canada premieres Thursday, November 26 at 8 p.m. ET/PT on Citytv and Citytv+.

stories.title: Lorne Doerkson didn’t plan on leading the BC Conservatives, but he’s trying to meet the moment
stories.summary: Affable MLA is sharpening his attacks on the NDP as his party holds on to a narrow lead in the polls
stories.author: Jesse Winter, Mike Hager
stories.content:
Of the last five premiers of British Columbia , two were lawyers and three were political staffers before running for office.

If BC Conservative Party interim leader Lorne Doerkson pushes his party to power, his CV before entering politics will look vastly different. The 58-year-old would also become the first premier from outside the South Coast since Dan Miller spent six months shepherding the New Democrats into the current century.

Mr. Doerkson was elected six years ago with the now-defunct BC Liberals as an MLA in the rural Interior. Before that, he said he tried his hand at bareback rodeo riding, and at selling advertisements for community newspapers across the region before becoming a publisher. He then ran a Chevrolet dealership and a “glass shop that didn’t go as perfect as I had hoped,” he told The Globe and Mail during a recent editorial board meeting. He then briefly ended up in the financial-services industry.

Now, the affable Williams Lake resident, who prioritized good relations with all colleagues as deputy speaker in the last legislature, is sharpening his attacks on the NDP.

Most polls are showing the Conservatives with a narrow lead over the NDP. Leading a party in chaos into an early election and finding himself in the position of potentially becoming premier wasn’t something he had planned.

Mr. Doerkson said he, like everyone else, had heard concerning allegations about his predecessor Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s leadership. But he had been staying out of the fray – amid a push by business leaders and conservative operatives to install a new leader – and had no designs on taking over the party that was clearly heading into a snap election two years ahead of schedule.

“I didn’t know that she was about to quit and it was a surprise to me too,” he said.

Angelo Isidorou, the BC Conservatives’ former executive director and current adviser, said Mr. Doerkson was unanimously voted to become leader last month, likely because he offered a clean break from the recrimination and defections that characterized Ms. Findlay’s mere four months as leader.

“The calculation they had made was who is the guy in this room who everybody can always point to and say ... ‘That’s a good guy and I trust him because I think he’s a good person,’ ” he said.

Mr. Doerkson himself is so uncontroversial he was not mentioned in a 200-page dossier of internal “oppo research” into the views and conduct of BC Conservatives that was compiled by BC United staffers before the two parties merged in a bid to unseat the NDP last election.

The night Mr. Doerkson learned he’d been tapped to lead, he called a handful of people for advice.

High on that list was Donna Barnett, his long-time mentor who plucked him from relative political obscurity and set him on the path to replace her as Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA.

Speaking from 100 Mile House, where Ms. Barnett has served in municipal politics for years, she said she was not surprised that Conservative party insiders chose Mr. Doerkson to step into the breach.

“He’s a real public person. He likes people. He likes helping. So it was not difficult, believe you me. He’s the right guy for the job,” she said.

At the outset of the campaign, Global TV re-aired footage it captured five summers ago, showing Mr. Doerkson, face smudged with soot, holding a hose and helping fight a wildfire on a neighbour’s property.

Ms. Barnett said that’s as apt an encapsulation of him as one could find.

“He’s just a real down-to-earth person who believes in helping,” she said.

Mr. Doerkson’s diplomacy skills have been tested this campaign by the NDP, which has trained its sights on portraying the BC Conservatives as intolerant or worse. He’s also had to spend time taming his own teammates, tempering them from promoting views on the fringes of modern conservative thought.

Mr. Doerkson has said his number-one priority if his party forms government is to repeal the province’s reconciliation act with First Nations. That goal and his comments about it on the campaign trail has him running afoul of an important neighbour: the Xeni Gwet’in First Nation.

Xeni Gwet’in Chief Roger William said Mr. Doerkson has often attended ceremonial gatherings and events, and that “wherever he sees you, he says hello, so in that way he’s good.”

But, Mr. Doerkson’s commitment to repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People Act, or Dripa, is deeply worrying to Mr. William.

In 2014, Xeni Gwet’in, as part of the larger Tsilhqot’in Nation, won a landmark Supreme Court case against the B.C. government that – for the first time in Canadian history – declared the existence of aboriginal rights and title over 1,750 square kilometres of Crown land in the Nemaiah Valley.

One of the outcomes of that ruling is to negotiate and manage relationships with tenure and private land holders within the Xeni Gwet’in title lands, something Mr. William said he’s spent years doing alongside the B.C. government.

“There is private land within the title lands. There are tenure holders within title land. There are even B.C. Parks within title land,” Mr. William said. “We’re still working together with B.C. We’re working with tenure holders.”

But since becoming MLA in 2020, Mr. William said Mr. Doerkson has not shown up to help in that work.

“If anything, he seemed to be the cheerleader on the other side,” he said.

Mr. William said Mr. Doerkson has participated in and continues to spread fear among British Columbians that their private property needs to be protected from Indigenous claims.

“He says he wants to work with First Nations … but in the time that he’s been in, he hasn’t done that,” Mr. William said.

Mr. Doerkson definitely has the attention of his main opponent, even if Mr. Eby didn’t see him coming before this snap election of his choosing.

“I would have gone down a list of a lot of Conservative MLAs before I ended on Mr. Doerkson,” Mr. Eby said during his recent editorial board meeting with The Globe. “No shade, he just wasn’t a person that was very prominent in the legislature. He obviously was respected by his colleagues sufficiently to be chosen leader, but he wasn’t someone that I noticed.”

stories.title: Eby set out to tackle B.C.’s biggest problems. Now, he must convince voters his efforts are working
stories.summary: The NDP Leader’s past four years in office have been marked by both progress and challenges
stories.author: Andrea Woo, Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Before David Eby was sworn in as British Columbia’s 37th premier, he set his sights on the province’s toughest challenges: housing, health care and public safety.

“My goal,” he told reporters as premier-designate in October, 2022, “will be to work through with our team what the world of the possible is.”

Four years later, as the NDP Leader seeks another mandate, he must convince British Columbians that his government’s efforts are beginning to bear fruit. On the campaign trail since last month’s snap election call, Mr. Eby has pointed to falling rents after a housing policy overhaul, thousands of additional doctors and nurses, and a program targeting repeat violent offenders that has significantly reduced police interactions.

At the same time, Mr. Eby has contended, B.C. is facing unprecedented threats from both U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and a Conservative Party that risks taking the province backward.

Saturday’s election will test whether voters trust Mr. Eby to see the job through.

Mr. Eby was born and raised in Kitchener, Ont., and moved to Vancouver after law school to article with the federal Justice Department. He began his career in 2005 with the Pivot Legal Society in the Downtown Eastside, advocating for the city’s most marginalized. In 2008, he was named executive director of the BC Civil Liberties Association.

In 2013, Mr. Eby unseated then-premier Christy Clark in Vancouver-Point Grey to become an NDP MLA. After the NDP took power in 2017, he served as attorney-general and housing minister under premier John Horgan. Mr. Eby was acclaimed party leader in 2022 after a messy race in which his only challenger was disqualified, and he was sworn in as premier that November.

His record in office has been marked by both progress and persistent challenges. In the 2024 campaign, he pledged that every B.C. resident who wanted a family doctor or nurse practitioner would be connected to one by the end of 2025. His government introduced a new family doctor payment model , streamlined the process for international medical graduates and recruited hundreds of health care workers from the United States. However, more than a million people still don’t have family doctors and specialist wait times remain long.

The Ndp’s response to the toxic drug crisis has satisfied few: Opponents blame its experiments with drug decriminalization and prescribed alternatives to illicit drugs for making things worse, while proponents of the interventions say the government undermined its own efforts by failing to fully implement them and retreating under pressure.

Mr. Eby has also taken positions that seem at odds with the progressive advocacy that defined his early career. His push to expand involuntary treatment for people with concurrent mental-health and substance-use disorders, for instance, has drawn criticism from the civil liberties association he once led.

In an interview, Mr. Eby countered that a drastically altered illicit drug supply and the brain injuries that it has caused require a more intensive response, including in Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside.

“I think it’s safe to say that the responses that the neighbourhood needs now are different from the ones I believe they needed in 2008,” he said. “And that includes things like involuntary care for people who are struggling and unable to ask for help.”

The unravelling of NDP climate commitments has disappointed some. In his first speech as premier-designate, Mr. Eby said expanding fossil-fuel infrastructure is incompatible with reaching climate goals; his government has since helped to advance a wave of liquefied natural gas projects.

On this, Mr. Eby said Mr. Trump’s effort to “destroy the Canadian economy” had forced a reassessment of the province’s priorities.

“That means we have to move really quickly to diversify our markets around the world, find new sources of income, and that has shifted the calculus quite dramatically on things like LNG,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Conservatives point to B.C.’s projected $13.8-billion deficit as evidence of the Ndp’s fiscal mismanagement. In response, Mr. Eby said the preceding Liberal government ran “massive infrastructure debts” that his government has worked to remedy, including multibillion-dollar upgrades to the Highway 1 corridor, the Surrey Langley SkyTrain extension, and upgrades to schools and hospitals.

His party has proposed a tax increase on income over $190,000 , which it says would reduce the projected deficit to $12-billion by 2028-29. Critics counter that similar forecasts in previous budgets failed to materialize.

The opposition has also taken aim at the Ndp’s approach to reconciliation. After a B.C. Court of Appeal ruling raised questions about the practical and legal effects of the province’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act , Mr. Eby had considered amending or suspending the legislation before committing instead to working with First Nations to address concerns.

He has said that the legislation has nonetheless enabled partnerships with Indigenous communities that have paved the way for major projects.

Those who have worked closely with Mr. Eby describe a self-assured leader who can be difficult to read. Former NDP cabinet minister Katrina Chen likened him to a scientist and said he has a cerebral leadership style.

“As a leader, it’s kind of hard to know what he’s thinking,” said Ms. Chen, who co-chaired Mr. Eby’s leadership campaign.

Mr. Eby is a “firm, articulate guy” intent on convincing people of his point of view, she added.

Former finance minister Selina Robinson, a vocal critic of Mr. Eby’s since he removed her from cabinet in February, 2024, said she had left a surplus when she vacated the finance portfolio and advised the Premier to be mindful of a slipping economy.

“He didn’t take my advice, and that’s been my experience of David,” Ms. Robinson said in an interview. “I don’t think he takes the advice of his people who know, and so he does his own thing. And I think he has made some bad decisions.”

For all the unfinished business, Mr. Eby has argued that voters should judge his government against the alternative, warning that a Conservative victory would reverse hard-won progress on housing, health care and Indigenous reconciliation.

“I know that I haven’t been perfect. Our government hasn’t been perfect,” Mr. Eby said in his closing remarks at a leaders’ debate last week. “But we have always been, and we always will be, committed to fight for you.”

stories.title: After decisive defeat, Alberta separatists turn their attention to Smith and the UCP
stories.summary: Separatist leader Jeffrey Rath says they’ve built a movement of thousands of committed volunteers and will try to “take ownership” of Alberta’s governing party.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Bruised but not yet broken, Alberta’s separatist movement is turning its attention toe Premier Danielle Smith and the governing United Conservative Party.

As results continued to trickle in early Tuesday morning, the separatists’ defeat proved even more decisive than months of public polling predicted — with 75.7 per cent of Albertans voting to remain in Canada, and just 24.3 per cent voting to trigger an independence referendum.

It was a staggering blow to the separatist movement, and a massive win for the volunteers and politicians who campaigned for months against independence. The impact of the vote was less clear for Smith — who despite officially supporting the remain side, was seen as being sympathetic to the separatist cause and triggered the vote in the first place.

It doesn’t appear that Smith will get her wish that Albertans will simply accept the results of the referendum and move on.

Instead, Smith and the governing United Conservative Party (UCP) will have to contend with a motivated and more organized separatist movement turning their efforts to oust the premier and take control of the party.

Jeffrey Rath, one of the central figures in the separatist movement who had a hand in former premier Jason Kenney’s ouster, told Global News he will be pushing for a special general meeting of the party to remove Smith.

Rath said Alberta independence will never be realized as long as Smith, who he called an “avowed federalist,” remains leader.

“Moving forward from here, our hundreds of thousands of members and volunteers are going to be committed to taking back ownership of the (UCP),” Rath said.

“It’s time to have a serious discussion as to whether or not a supermajority of the United Conservative Party of Alberta want to continue to be led by a Federalist (in Smith) who’s in bed with Naheed Nensi, Mark Carney, Rachel Notley and the rest of the socialists and globalists that have literally been ruining this province and ruining this country.”

Polling released on the eve of the referendum suggested that the separatists’ biggest pool of support was found within the UCP ranks. Abacus Data’s findings suggest 52 per cent of UCP supporters would vote for a referendum, with just 44 per cent voting to remain

“By comparison, 93 per cent of NDP supporters would vote remain,” David Coletto, Abacus’ CEO, wrote in an analysis of the numbers.

“Indeed, 77 per cent of everyone who would vote (for a referendum) currently supports the UCP. The referendum continues to divide the governing party’s own coalition.”

The polling revealed UCP supporters are less likely than other partisans to feel a connection to Canada. Just 39 per cent of the party’s supporters expressed a strong attachment to the country, while 68 per cent of UCP voters feel a strong attachment to Alberta. More NDP voters (84 per cent) said they felt a strong attachment to Canada, while 42 per cent said the same about attachment to their province.

Another risk for Smith and the UCP is the political blowback for forcing Albertans to vote on independence in the first place.

While a strong current within their own party, Tuesday’s results clearly show that most Albertans do not have separatist sympathies. In forcing the issue, Smith risked wearing the separatist cause in voters eyes — while failing to satisfy the die-hard independence movement within her own party.

Polling aggregator 338Canada’s numbers suggest a tightening of the provincial horse race polls , with Naheed Nenshi’s NDP pulling within the margin of error with Smith’s governing party. That tightening of the provincial political race roughly coincided with Smith’s decision to put separation on the ballot.

stories.title: After Wainwright tragedy, one lawyer is calling for a coroner’s inquest
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says there are 50 investigators on the ground probing how one of the worst peacetime tragedies unfolded at an Alberta military base.
stories.author: Judy Trinh
stories.content:
Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney says there are 50 investigators on the ground probing how one of the worst peacetime tragedies unfolded at an Alberta military base.

On Saturday, four soldiers were killed during a scheduled training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, Alta.

Thirty-nine military members were hospitalized, with 19 people in critical condition.

A battalion of soldiers conducting live-combat training with grenades and artillery was overtaken by a fast-spreading fire whipped by strong winds.

When asked by reporters, if he trusts the military to investigate itself, Carney said, “Absolutely.”

“We will give them all the resources that they need … We will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy as expeditiously and transparently as necessary,” Carney said after paying tribute in the House of Commons to the four soldiers who died.

Sgt. Morgan Wong, and privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark were killed during a training exercise.

The young men, who were serving with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were preparing to deploy to Latvia next year.

Military lawyer and former soldier, Col. Michel Drapeau says the scope of the tragedy demands more than an internal investigation, it deserves an inquiry “under the glare of the public.”

Drapeau says the military cannot investigate itself because the Department of National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces “lacks the impartiality, neutrality, objectivity and disinterest” to analyze the evidence and report on the outcome.

Drapeau said a coroner’s inquest is an ideal mechanism to get answers.

“Let there be an open audience. People can attend. People can listen and people can testify.”

He said that soldiers May not tell Armed Forces investigators the full story of what they saw or experienced because they’re nervous or afraid of being blamed. Only when testimony is given under oath, and there’s cross examination can the “bare truth come out,” Drapeau said in an interview with CTV News.

“The purpose of this is to prevent recurrence, to prevent (future) fatalities. We need to get to the bottom of it - not assign blame.”

Drapeau, whose firm has represented soldiers and veterans in legal battles with the Department of National Defence, is also concerned a large swath of the public could be “suspicious” of the findings if an investigation is not done by an independent actor.

What defence officials have said at this point is that the battalion was doing “live-fire training.”

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, the commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said the group was practising a simulated attack, while a fire was burning about a kilometre away was being monitored by range control.

Rutland said the cause of that fire was under investigation – and that there was a variety of ordnance moving through the area. He said the source could have been “grenade launchers, grenades, small arms, ammunition.”

“Quite frankly it could have been any of that or none of it,” Rutland told reporters one day after the tragedy.

The military official said that the battalion didn’t see a fire, but then around 4 p.m., within “30 seconds to a minute … there was a fire right on top of them.”

“This was a very uncommon occurrence. That being said, the reason why there was an investigation is to decide if it was a preventable, non-preventable, or to what extent something was preventable.” Rutland said.

On Oct. 17, the forecast from Environment Canada warned of strong winds that could gust up to 90 kilometres an hour.

But according to the hourly data report for the airfield at CFB Wainwright , wind gusts at 4 p.m. on that day registered at 42 km/h.

stories.title: Canadians quickly falling behind on their mortgages: Benchmark Canada
stories.summary: The share of homeowners who fell seriously behind on payments has doubled from its 2022 low, the steepest rise in the G7, figures show.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
Countries don’t typically get report cards, but there are hard facts that can be collated, assessed and compared. Enter Benchmark Canada, a new project from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute that brings together more than 40 different metrics that measure this nation’s performance. This fall, the National Post is examining many of those findings.

Canadians have a reputation for paying their mortgages on time, but more homeowners are falling behind, a potential warning sign for the country’s housing market.

Canada has the second-lowest mortgage arrears rate in the G7, but the share of homeowners who fell seriously behind on payments has doubled from its 2022 low, according to Benchmark Canada.

That’s the steepest rise in the G7.

The Macdonald-Laurier Institute project finds that 0.29 per cent of Canadian mortgages were in arrears in September, up from 0.14 per cent in August 2022. Apart from Japan, which enjoys a healthy mortgage arrears rate of 0.20 per cent, the rest of the G7 fared worse — with the United States standing at 1.43 per cent and the United Kingdom at 0.89 per cent. Italy had the highest rate at 2.10 per cent.

Ron Butler, a mortgage broker at Butler Mortgage, says condo investors are among the Canadian borrowers in greatest difficulty, facing higher financing costs, lower asking rents and more vacancies. Some owners find themselves underwater on their investment and unable to sell their units to repay the mortgage, ultimately forced to keep putting money into a losing investment.

“You find you can’t sell it, or if you sell it, it doesn’t cover the mortgage,” he said. “You’re losing money every month. You’re going backwards.”

Benjamin Tal, deputy chief economist at Cibc, said Canada’s increase in arrears came as borrowers renewed mortgages taken out at exceptionally low rates in 2021 when the Bank of Canada made extraordinary moves to shield the economy during the COVID-19 pandemic. Meanwhile, mortgage lenders are managing potential damage by approaching homeowners facing sharp payment increases and extending the time they have to repay their loans.

How Canada's short-term thinking sparked a national housing crisis

Tal said housing data show delinquencies of 30 to 60 days had risen while those of 60 to 90 days were flat, which he attributes in part to lenders intervening with borrowers before they fall further behind.

“What happened is that banks became much more proactive,” he said.

Tal thinks the number of borrowers facing steep payment increases when renewing their mortgage has likely already peaked. While arrears will continue to rise, lenders have so far managed the renewal pressure better than feared, he said.

“The fact that we are still standing is actually very reassuring,” Tal said.

Butler said red flags would be raised if national delinquencies climbed beyond the 0.40 to 0.50 per cent mark. However, he cautions against treating a low arrears rate as evidence that homeowners are financially comfortable.

“People will go into their personal lines of credit and use their credit cards to pay for everyday stuff just to make sure their mortgages are paid,” Butler said.

Butler said some borrowers who cannot meet stringent bank requirements have turned to more expensive alternative financing, although the Benchmark Canada data exclude private lenders and credit unions.

“The eternal belief is that if I just keep this house, eventually it’ll go back up in value and life will be great,” he said. “The fear of never being able to get a mortgage again is very, very big.”

Tal said Canada’s smaller market for high-risk mortgages also helps explain the low arrears datapoint. He regards the country’s mortgage borrowers as a better credit risk than those in many other markets, including those in the G7.

Canadian households never went through the drastic reduction in debt that followed the U.S. housing crash in 2008, Tal noted. Canadian household debt-to-income ratio kept growing – now roughly $1.76 in debt for every dollar of household disposable income – leaving them more sensitive than Americans to interest-rate increases if inflation forces borrowing costs to rise higher again.

Ontario, by virtue of being the most populous province, also leads the country in mortgage delinquencies, data from the Canadian Bankers Association show. Enter Benchmark Canada, a new project from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute that brings together more than 40 different metrics that measure this nation’s performance. This fall, the National Post is examining many of those findings.

Canada has the second-lowest mortgage arrears rate in the G7, but the share of homeowners who fell seriously behind on payments has doubled from its 2022 low, according to Benchmark Canada.
That’s the steepest rise in the G7.

The Macdonald-Laurier Institute project finds that 0.29 per cent of Canadian mortgages were in arrears in September, up from 0.14 per cent in August 2022. Italy had the highest rate at 2.10 per cent.

Some owners find themselves underwater on their investment and unable to sell their units to repay the mortgage, ultimately forced to keep putting money into a losing investment.
“You find you can’t sell it, or if you sell it, it doesn’t cover the mortgage,” he said. “You’re losing money every month. You’re going backwards.”

Benjamin Tal, deputy chief economist at Cibc, said Canada’s increase in arrears came as borrowers renewed mortgages taken out at exceptionally low rates in 2021 when the Bank of Canada made extraordinary moves to shield the economy during the COVID-19 pandemic. Meanwhile, mortgage lenders are managing potential damage by approaching homeowners facing sharp payment increases and extending the time they have to repay their loans.

stories.title: Ontario public-sector unions push province for workplace AI safeguards
stories.summary: Local bargaining units are being told to investigate how AI is showing up in workplaces and to identify potential risks.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Unions representing tens of thousands of public sector workers in Ontario are racing to inject artificial intelligence safeguards into multiple contract negotiations, Global News has learned, as workers express concerns about how Crown agencies plan to use the technology.

The Ontario Public Service Employees Union (Opseu), which represents more than 200,000 public sector workers, said language around the current or potential use of AI is being introduced at nearly every bargaining table across the province.

“The implication of AI becomes more and more clear in almost every sector we represent,” said Opseu President JP Hornick.

“We have teams working on bargaining guides around AI in almost every area I can think of.”

Hornick said among the top concerns are job losses, the replacement of job functions and employers potentially using AI to monitor work.

“We don’t want to see AI rolled out without workers’ voices being present,” said Hornick.

The Canadian Union of Public Employees (Cupe), which represents nearly 310,000 workers in Ontario, has also created bargaining guidelines on AI to ensure protective language can be negotiated in collective agreements.

Local bargaining units are being told to investigate how AI is showing up in workplaces, to identify potential risks and review collective agreements for language clauses related to AI.

“Left unchecked, AI and other digital innovations can have harmful consequences for work quality and workers’ rights,” Cupe states on its website.

Among the demands: that employers should be prevented from collecting or using biometric data, emotional or facial recognition tools or any “human behaviour manipulation tool.”

Cupe also wants language to ensure that AI systems are controlled by humans and that employees will not be subject to any decisions made entirely by AI.

Unions like Opseu have been met with some roadblocks around AI negotiations.

In August, contract talks between the union and the Ontario Hospital Association on behalf of 14,000 hospital employees went to arbitration, where the use of artificial intelligence in hospitals was a key point of negotiation.

Opseu sought advance notice of hospitals’ “anticipated” use of AI, but the arbitration board rejected the union’s proposal. It claimed current contract language was enough to capture any technological changes related to AI.

It would be too “onerous,” the board also said, for hospitals to provide notice to the union about anticipated AI use.

“The use of A.I. in high-tech equipment is ubiquitous and is often guarded as intellectual property by third parties. It would be nearly impossible for hospitals to comply with notice requirements for the ‘anticipated use’ of A.I.,” the arbitration board said.

In late 2024, the Ford government introduced new directives on how ministries and agencies are expected to use artificial intelligence tools.

Those directives, which also apply to all public service workers, mandate that the use of AI must be “human rights affirming” and always transparent and accountable.

The Treasury Board Secretariat, which oversees labour relations between the government and the public service, said AI provides the Ontario Public Service (OPS) with tools to “modernize” and “improve how we work.”

The OPS, a spokesperson said, is “leveraging AI to drive innovation,” while also ensuring it’s used “safely and responsibly to safeguard the interest of the people and businesses of Ontario.”

The NDP, however, claims more than one million public sector jobs could be at risk if AI is fully implemented in the OPS.

“Despite these concerns, the Ford government hasn’t moved with any urgency to protect workers,” NDP Labour Critic Jamie West told Global News.

Instead, West said Premier Ford is focused on “making an all-in push on data centres” and “inviting American tech giants” to invest in Ontario.

“Throwing unions and workers into chaos as they try to get a handle on this rapidly evolving technology is unacceptable,” said West.

When asked if unions are correct to be concerned about AI in the public service, a spokesperson for Treasury Board President Kinga Surma said “issues that May be raised in collective bargaining are matters to be addressed by the parties through the negotiation process.”

stories.title: An election debate over public disorder frays nerves in Toronto’s Gay Village
stories.summary: The rising anger over what goes on in Barbara Hall Park shows how urban disorder has become a potent issue
stories.author: Marcus Gee, photography by Laura Proctor
stories.content:
About this series

The Globe is reporting from cities and towns in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia to hear from residents about the issues affecting their communities and their votes in the municipal elections. Explore the entire series here .

Barbara Hall Park in Toronto’s Gay Village is an unusual kind of park. It has a splash pad and a dog run, but more paving stones than grass. The benches are painted in rainbow colours. It surrounds a community centre called the 519, renowned for advocating for gay rights and social justice.

At the heart of the park is a memorial for the victims of AIDS. Opened in 1993, it features a row of concrete pillars with the names of those who died of the disease engraved on stainless steel plaques.

Barbara Hall, named after a former mayor, was meant to be an inclusive, urban space that honoured gay history and life, but welcomed everyone.

Yet, in recent years, many local residents say it has become something else: A round-the-clock hangout for people dealing with addiction, mental illness and homelessness.

As of Oct. 14, Toronto police had made 227 arrests in the park this year, up from 177 for the same period last year. The charges included assault, theft and possession of drugs for the purpose of trafficking. A hardware store just down the street has had its window smashed.

Unhoused people and security guards keep an eye out for each other in Barbara Hall Park. Shouting matches are common here, and police arrests have been higher in 2026 compared with last year.

Go by the park on any given day, and you are almost sure to see someone drawing on a drug pipe or slumped over in a state of deep intoxication. On one recent afternoon, a skinny young woman wearing only one shoe did a jerky dance, singing an incoherent song. On another, a shirtless man walked out of the park and into the street, stopping traffic.

That upsets neighbours such as Vera Tarman, whose home backs onto the park. As an addiction doctor, she sympathizes with people who find themselves in the thrall of today’s potent street drugs.

But as a proud lesbian who saw AIDS tear through the LGBTQ community in the 1980s and 1990s, she is appalled to see people dealing drugs, strewing garbage and even relieving themselves in a place that is home to a memorial where many people come to remember those they have lost.

Fires, fights and shouting matches break out all the time, she says. Ambulances and police cars pull up, sirens blaring. Ms. Tarman, who is 69, no longer feels comfortable walking through the park with her little dog, Maddie.

She is so exasperated that she finds herself wishing the city would send in more police to clean the place up, a position she is a bit surprised to find herself taking. “That’s not who Vera was 20 years ago.”

Her feelings are far from unusual these days. Confronted with scenes of conflict and despair on sidewalks, parks and public transit, even liberal-minded city dwellers are getting fed up, making urban disorder a potent issue in this fall’s cycle of municipal elections.

Some candidates say the answer is to crack down on street disorder, with more policing and even mandatory treatment for those with addictions or severe mental illnesses. Others say the emphasis should be on providing better housing and health care for vulnerable people.

The debate is playing out across the country. In Winnipeg, which will hold its vote on Oct. 28, all the main candidates for mayor are pledging to improve public safety. A recent survey from Abacus Data found that, despite a drop in the crime-severity index, more than two-thirds of Winnipegers felt less safe now than they did four years ago.

In Oshawa, which votes on Monday, drug use and disorder in the heart of the historic automaking community east of Toronto have become a major campaign issue. A months-long police crackdown that just wrapped up led to almost 500 arrests, many for drug-related crimes, according to the Durham Regional Police Service.

In Toronto, city councillor Brad Bradford has made public safety one of the main thrusts of his campaign to unseat Olivia Chow, a former NDP stalwart who is seeking a second term as mayor.

Under the slogan “a city that is not safe is not free,” he is pledging to hire 1,000 police officers, though police stats show a drop in several types of offences.

The question is what to do about it. The debate is especially sharp in Toronto Centre, a dense downtown ward that, along with the Village, includes soaring condo towers and big public housing estates.

On one side is Daniel Tate, a candidate for area councillor who complains on his website that the city’s “parks and public spaces have been overtaken by crime, disorder and open drug use.” He is the founder of a provocative watchdog group, IntegrityTO, that routinely posts stark videos of urban disorder. He was scheduled to hold a press conference at Barbara Hall on Tuesday, with Ms. Tarman at his side to speak about her concerns.

On the other is Curran Stikuts, a former head of advocacy for the 519 who is also running for council. He says the park has suffered from the province’s decision to cut funding for supervised drug-use sites and the city’s decision to wind up homeless encampments – moves that he says pushed many people to Barbara Hall. “I don’t think that anybody across the political spectrum thinks that it’s acceptable for a parent to have to step over a needle to go use a park,” Mr. Stikuts says. But he thinks the stress should be on help, not enforcement.

Those who aren’t running for office are divided, too.

Ginette Hahn was passing through Barbara Hall on her daily walk on a recent morning, pushing a shopping cart. She said that, years ago, she was part of a group of mothers who came to the park with their children. Back then, “it was a joy to come here, but now it’s an embarrassment. It’s a drug park, that’s all it is.”

But Rowan Jetté Knox, who has a popular new cafe just down the block, says it would be a mistake just to lower the boom, because “what we are seeing in the park is folks who are not having their needs met at a systemic level.”

Ms. Tarman has suggested putting a fence around the park and closing it at night, like a cemetery. After all, she said, with the AIDS memorial and a trans memorial just next to it, “We have two sacred grounds there.”

But Joel Moffatt, 43, a long-time crystal methamphetamine user who was visiting the park one day last week, said fencing the park would only force people onto the street, where they would be more visible and disruptive. He said most users don’t take their drugs when families or children are around anyway, so “there’s enough respect here for people and the property” as it is.

At a city hall committee meeting in June, many residents and advocates spoke against the fence idea, but the sitting councillor, Chris Moise, says he is open to putting it forward again if he is re-elected on Monday.

In the meantime, says Mr. Moise, a former police officer and health care worker, the city has put in “layers and layers of supports” to make the park more livable: posting security guards there day and night, sending in squads of health and housing workers, and dispatching cleaners three times a day to sweep up debris. The city, he says, is “using every tool that’s legally available to it.”

That does not wash with Ms. Tarman, who says anyone who passes by the park can see that something is terribly wrong. She is frustrated not just with the condition of Barbara Hall, but with being scolded on Facebook for speaking up about it. “Whenever we complain about something like this, the response is: ‘You’re a bad person,’” she says. “It’s very demoralizing.”

The Globe is reporting from cities and towns in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia to hear from residents about the issues affecting their communities and their votes in the municipal elections. Explore the entire series here .

Barbara Hall Park in Toronto’s Gay Village is an unusual kind of park. It has a splash pad and a dog run, but more paving stones than grass. The benches are painted in rainbow colours. It surrounds a community centre called the 519, renowned for advocating for gay rights and social justice.

At the heart of the park is a memorial for the victims of AIDS. Opened in 1993, it features a row of concrete pillars with the names of those who died of the disease engraved on stainless steel plaques.
Barbara Hall, named after a former mayor, was meant to be an inclusive, urban space that honoured gay history and life, but welcomed everyone.
Yet, in recent years, many local residents say it has become something else: A round-the-clock hangout for people dealing with addiction, mental illness and homelessness.

As of Oct. 14, Toronto police had made 227 arrests in the park this year, up from 177 for the same period last year. The charges included assault, theft and possession of drugs for the purpose of trafficking. A hardware store just down the street has had its window smashed.
Unhoused people and security guards keep an eye out for each other in Barbara Hall Park. Shouting matches are common here, and police arrests have been higher in 2026 compared with last year.

Go by the park on any given day, and you are almost sure to see someone drawing on a drug pipe or slumped over in a state of deep intoxication. On one recent afternoon, a skinny young woman wearing only one shoe did a jerky dance, singing an incoherent song. On another, a shirtless man walked out of the park and into the street, stopping traffic.
That upsets neighbours such as Vera Tarman, whose home backs onto the park. As an addiction doctor, she sympathizes with people who find themselves in the thrall of today’s potent street drugs.

But as a proud lesbian who saw AIDS tear through the LGBTQ community in the 1980s and 1990s, she is appalled to see people dealing drugs, strewing garbage and even relieving themselves in a place that is home to a memorial where many people come to remember those they have lost.

Fires, fights and shouting matches break out all the time, she says. Ambulances and police cars pull up, sirens blaring. Ms. Tarman, who is 69, no longer feels comfortable walking through the park with her little dog, Maddie.

She is so exasperated that she finds herself wishing the city would send in more police to clean the place up, a position she is a bit surprised to find herself taking. “That’s not who Vera was 20 years ago.”

Her feelings are far from unusual these days. Confronted with scenes of conflict and despair on sidewalks, parks and public transit, even liberal-minded city dwellers are getting fed up, making urban disorder a potent issue in this fall’s cycle of municipal elections.

Some candidates say the answer is to crack down on street disorder, with more policing and even mandatory treatment for those with addictions or severe mental illnesses. Others say the emphasis should be on providing better housing and health care for vulnerable people.

The debate is playing out across the country. In Winnipeg, which will hold its vote on Oct. 28, all the main candidates for mayor are pledging to improve public safety. A recent survey from Abacus Data found that, despite a drop in the crime-severity index, more than two-thirds of Winnipegers felt less safe now than they did four years ago.

In Oshawa, which votes on Monday, drug use and disorder in the heart of the historic automaking community east of Toronto have become a major campaign issue. A months-long police crackdown that just wrapped up led to almost 500 arrests, many for drug-related crimes, according to the Durham Regional Police Service.
In Toronto, city councillor Brad Bradford has made public safety one of the main thrusts of his campaign to unseat Olivia Chow, a former NDP stalwart who is seeking a second term as mayor.
Under the slogan “a city that is not safe is not free,” he is pledging to hire 1,000 police officers, though police stats show a drop in several types of offences.

The question is what to do about it. The debate is especially sharp in Toronto Centre, a dense downtown ward that, along with the Village, includes soaring condo towers and big public housing estates.

On one side is Daniel Tate, a candidate for area councillor who complains on his website that the city’s “parks and public spaces have been overtaken by crime, disorder and open drug use.” He is the founder of a provocative watchdog group, IntegrityTO, that routinely posts stark videos of urban disorder. He was scheduled to hold a press conference at Barbara Hall on Tuesday, with Ms. Tarman at his side to speak about her concerns.

On the other is Curran Stikuts, a former head of advocacy for the 519 who is also running for council. He says the park has suffered from the province’s decision to cut funding for supervised drug-use sites and the city’s decision to wind up homeless encampments – moves that he says pushed many people to Barbara Hall. “I don’t think that anybody across the political spectrum thinks that it’s acceptable for a parent to have to step over a needle to go use a park,” Mr. Stikuts says. But he thinks the stress should be on help, not enforcement.
