She said that, years ago, she was part of a group of mothers who came to the park with their children. Back then, “it was a joy to come here, but now it’s an embarrassment. But Joel Moffatt, 43, a long-time crystal methamphetamine user who was visiting the park one day last week, said fencing the park would only force people onto the street, where they would be more visible and disruptive. He said most users don’t take their drugs when families or children are around anyway, so “there’s enough respect here for people and the property” as it is.

At a city hall committee meeting in June, many residents and advocates spoke against the fence idea, but the sitting councillor, Chris Moise, says he is open to putting it forward again if he is re-elected on Monday.

In the meantime, says Mr. Moise, a former police officer and health care worker, the city has put in “layers and layers of supports” to make the park more livable: posting security guards there day and night, sending in squads of health and housing workers, and dispatching cleaners three times a day to sweep up debris. stories.title: Nova Scotia claims its winds are ‘world class.’ It needs data to back that up
stories.summary: Understanding wind conditions is a must when selecting a site for an expensive offshore wind farm
stories.author: Matthew McClearn
stories.content:
“World class” is among the superlatives used by Nova Scotia’s government to describe the strength of the province’s offshore breezes. The phrase is echoed by federal officials, industry associations, engineering consultants and virtually everyone else who promotes Wind West, the broad plan to build expansive offshore wind farms off the province’s coasts.

Yet federal officials tacitly acknowledge that hard evidence for that claim is sparse. Tim Hodgson, the federal Energy and Natural Resources Minister, announced last week that Ottawa had committed $100-million to Wind West , $5-million of which was immediately allocated “to the deployment of floating light detection and ranging (FLiDAR)–mounted buoys” to begin measuring offshore wind and ocean conditions.

Four years after its unveiling as one of Atlantic Canada’s prime economic development schemes, much of the basic data collection needed to prove Wind West’s viability has only just begun, and willingness from the province and private investors to commit funds remains unclear. But it’s already a recipient of a wide range of federal support, including significant open-end financing, and is a candidate for accelerated permitting with the Major Projects Office.

Tim Hodgson, Canada’s minister of energy, announced $100-million in support for Nova Scotia’s Wind West offshore energy project on Oct. 15, 2026, in Dartmouth, N.S.

The Canadian Press

In 2022, the government of Premier Tim Houston announced plans to open offshore wind development seabed leases to competitive bids in 2025, with the goal of developing five gigawatts of generating capacity by 2030. Nothing about the proposal was modest; it was nearly double the province’s entire installed capacity at the time. Yet Mr. Houston went further, asserting that his province’s offshore wind resource could represent as much as 66 gigawatts of capacity – enough, he said, to meet more than one quarter of Canada’s electricity requirements.

In its 2023 budget, the federal government earmarked $3-billion over 13 years for a variety of electricity projects, including “science-based activities to help capitalize on Canada’s offshore wind potential” off Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador.

Mr. Houston wants Ottawa to refer Wind West to its new Major Projects Office. Although that hasn’t happened, the MPO has identified Wind West as a component of an even larger project it seeks to advance, dubbed the Atlantic Energy Strategy.

Wind conditions are obviously relevant when selecting a site for an offshore wind farm. Seemingly minor differences can matter because the relationship between wind speed and power generated is exponential: A turbine spinning in a wind that’s blowing 20 kilometres an hour will generate double the electricity of one in a 15-kilometre-per-hour breeze.

A high-level plan published in 2023 said the province had carried out “preliminary geospatial analysis” to assess offshore wind resources, including wind speed, and found “relatively consistent economic potential for offshore wind.”

But there was a problem: The underlying data was scant at best.

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s map of marine observation buoys and coastal stations, which capture atmospheric, oceanographic and meteorological data, shows only seven monitoring buoys moored off Nova Scotia, six operated by Environment and Climate Change Canada. Not one is located in areas designated for future offshore wind development, says Larry Hughes, a research fellow at the MacEachen Institute for Public Policy at Dalhousie University.

In a recent commentary published in allNovaScotia, an online news publication, he contrasted that paltry number with Noaa’s proliferation of buoys along the length of the U.S. Eastern Seaboard; even Lake Ontario and Lake Erie have more. He explained that Nova Scotia’s buoy data is largely supplemented by ship logs and meteorological data on storms.

“What it boils down to is, other than people saying we have a great wind resource, we really don’t know much about it,” he said in an interview.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration shows only seven buoys off Nova Scotia, none of which are located in areas proposed for offshore wind farms – leaving a data gap concerning wind conditions that Ottawa is eager to bridge.

Buoy locations are approximate john sopinski/the globe and mail, Source: novascotia.cl; noaa

Wind West’s backers, including Natural Resources Canada, understood from the outset that the project faces numerous data gaps. A study by consultancy Power Advisory LLC suggested that high-resolution wind speed data was required, with minimum cell sizes of one square kilometre, and that wind speed measurements were needed at two elevations, perhaps 80 metres and 120 metres above the sea’s surface.

Engineering consulting firm Stantec and wind energy software company WindSim later simulated Atlantic Canada’s wind resources and assembled what it described as a “high-resolution wind atlas.” But the government clearly believes that kind of modelling is not sufficient to satisfy developers. Only $5-million of the federal government’s $100-million commitment was explicitly allocated in last week’s announcement. Ms. Power said the money is “being drawn from existing Government of Canada resources,” including the natural resources department’s Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program.

But it’s already a recipient of a wide range of federal support, including significant open-end financing, and is a candidate for accelerated permitting with the Major Projects Office.

In 2022, the government of Premier Tim Houston announced plans to open offshore wind development seabed leases to competitive bids in 2025, with the goal of developing five gigawatts of generating capacity by 2030. Nothing about the proposal was modest; it was nearly double the province’s entire installed capacity at the time. Yet Mr. Houston went further, asserting that his province’s offshore wind resource could represent as much as 66 gigawatts of capacity – enough, he said, to meet more than one quarter of Canada’s electricity requirements.

In its 2023 budget, the federal government earmarked $3-billion over 13 years for a variety of electricity projects, including “science-based activities to help capitalize on Canada’s offshore wind potential” off Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador.

Mr. Houston wants Ottawa to refer Wind West to its new Major Projects Office. Although that hasn’t happened, the MPO has identified Wind West as a component of an even larger project it seeks to advance, dubbed the Atlantic Energy Strategy.

Wind conditions are obviously relevant when selecting a site for an offshore wind farm. Seemingly minor differences can matter because the relationship between wind speed and power generated is exponential: A turbine spinning in a wind that’s blowing 20 kilometres an hour will generate double the electricity of one in a 15-kilometre-per-hour breeze.

A high-level plan published in 2023 said the province had carried out “preliminary geospatial analysis” to assess offshore wind resources, including wind speed, and found “relatively consistent economic potential for offshore wind.”

He explained that Nova Scotia’s buoy data is largely supplemented by ship logs and meteorological data on storms.
“What it boils down to is, other than people saying we have a great wind resource, we really don’t know much about it,” he said in an interview.

stories.title: Why we should be skeptical of digital traffic control
stories.summary: Yes, other countries have done it, but we should invest in qualified air-traffic controllers, not digital solutions
stories.author: Lucas Aykroyd
stories.content:
Lucas Aykroyd is a Vancouver-based travel and sports journalist.

In 2026, I have flown on assignment as a journalist to Addis Ababa, Tokyo, and Zurich. Before year’s end, I will fly to Ottawa, Winnipeg, and Edmonton. I thus have a continuing interest in monitoring global and Canadian flight safety standards, including air-traffic control policies.

The launch of Canada’s first digital aerodrome air-traffic tower in Kingston, Ont., is concerning and premature at best. Over time, it looks likely to increase the risk of accidents, undermining a worldwide trend of declining aviation fatalities since the 1990s.

The AI-assisted Kingston Digital Facility (KDF) lets air-traffic controllers view inbound and outbound aircraft, not with eyes on airport runways, but via multiple cameras, from a centralized control room with video screens. According to Nav Canada , the non-profit private company that marks its 30th anniversary of overseeing Canadian civil air navigation this year, Kingston will become a digital hub that could provide remote air-traffic control services to up to 20 airports.

However, this approach is foolhardy. Transportation Safety Board of Canada statistics from 2015 to 2025 show that “the largest number of airplane accidents involve events that happen during the landing ... and takeoff ... phases of flight.”

Of course, those are also the two phases of flight best observed with direct visual contact from a traditional control tower. Why should travellers trust that video screens and AI-powered sensors will do a better job?

Nav Canada touts its rigorous testing procedures, along with the implementation of infrared technology and on-screen highlighting to improve detection of objects that could interfere with aircraft. That sounds nice. But what happens when the screens go black during a peak period? A full system crash would hamstring off-site controllers.

Remote systems can also be hacked. And AI often spits out wrong answers, based on misinterpreted or fabricated data. So much for enhanced “situational awareness.”

The primary motive, I believe, for transitioning to remote air-traffic control is not to offer better tools for controllers, let alone safer conditions for passengers. It is – like most things associated with AI and remote work – to save money for organizations like airports and make money for tech firms like Kongsberg Geospatial, Nav Canada’s Ottawa-based partner on the KDF.

The big-picture vision isn’t hard to grasp. Less bricks-and-mortar infrastructure. Easier hiring of Gen Z and millennial trainees who might, say, refuse to relocate to Thunder Bay but agree to work remotely from Kingston. Blithe acceptance of the magical thinking that AI will soon run everything anyway and that since countries like Norway and Britain have already implemented digital air-traffic control facilities, Canada should simply follow suit.

Unfortunately, quick, cost-effective, and acceptable-ish AI-driven solutions are not ideal for life-and-death situations like air-traffic control.

There are about 2,000 controllers Canada-wide. Nav Canada acknowledges it could use about 200 more. Overwork and understaffing – exacerbated by a tide of retirements – is a nagging problem.

The answer should be to invest in more quality people, not machines.

The danger of cognitive offloading is a well-documented phenomenon linked to AI and automation. It May not matter much when a middle manager at a cosmetics company writes increasingly mindless thank-you emails with Claude. It matters a lot when air-traffic controllers become mentally lazy and incapable of averting a runway collision without AI-led hand-holding.

Licensed tower controllers earn upward of $104,000 under the current collective agreement with the Canadian Air Traffic Control Association (Catca).

This is a stressful occupation that requires great concentration and communication skills. So why not pump up the pay to attract more prospective high-calibre controllers? It could save lives.

A pertinent cautionary tale here is the 2019 crash of Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, which claimed 157 lives minutes after departing from Addis Ababa. A faulty sensor automatically made the Boeing 737 MAX 8 nose-dive, overriding manual commands by the pilots.

Point being, nobody wants to die in a plane crash caused by AI confidently or maliciously hallucinating an empty runway. Right now, air travel remains safe overall. So let’s keep it that way.

Kingston will host the annual Travel Media Association of Canada (Tmac) conference in June, 2027. I served on the Tmac B.C. board for more than 10 years, and respect my colleagues who are organizing the upcoming event. Still, due to the KDF, I will not go to Kingston, despite benefiting from the 2026 conference in Richmond, B.C.

Until we get meaningful AI regulation at the federal and international levels, consumer pressure is the only message that hits home in any sector.

stories.title: Alberta referendum results: Province rejects separation; Albertans appear split on immigration in early vote counts
stories.summary: Albertans voted on whether to remain in Canada or begin the formal process of separation.
stories.author: Star staff and wire services
stories.content:
Alberta rejects separation in referendum vote ; early results show province appears split on immigration. This file is no longer updating.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is seen in an image taken from a video as she speaks in a televised address Wednesday night after Alberta residents voted to remain part of Canada in the province’s referendum on separation.

Edmonton — Alberta Premier Danielle Smith slammed the door on holding any further referendums on independence, declaring in a speech Tuesday night that Albertans have spoken and want to remain in Canada.

“I want to make it clear tonight that for as long as I am premier, I will honour this mandate from Albertans and will not be holding another referendum on this issue,” she said.

Premier Danielle Smith says that Albertans have spoken in Monday's referendum and, as long as she’s in power, separation is a dead issue. Smith, in a TV address to the province, also says challenges with Ottawa will be handled in the courts or through political channels. (Oct. 20, 2026)

Speaking in a live televised address, Smith called for unity and delivered a staunchly pro-Canada message. It was “time to move forward,” she said, from the debate that has raged across the province for months, saying she knows the province-wide exercise was at times “passionate.”

About 75 per cent of Albertans voted Tuesday to stay and roughly 25 per cent backed a second binding referendum on leaving the country.

The premier vowed to stand up for provincial jurisdiction and fight back against Ottawa when it is seen as interfering in areas that are not its own.

“But those disputes will be settled within the political and legal institutions of our nation, rather than pursuing the option of separation.”

Earlier in the day, as Smith prepared her address, the man behind the independence push that led to Monday’s vote delivered to her a message of his own.

“You made a choice. You made a choice. You’re going to possibly have to suffer the consequences,” Mitch Sylvestre told the Star on Tuesday as he drove from Edmonton to his home in Bonnyville, Alta.

Such a warning is just one example of the furor directed at Smith, particularly from independence supporters who see her decision to back remaining in Canada as a betrayal of the party’s base, many of whom support independence.

Smith spoke to a province divided by the referendum but united in its anger: some resent that the vote happened at all, while others are angry that she chose Canada’s side.

Even when the premier joined Prime Minister Mark Carney at a brewery outside Red Deer, Alta., last week to meet federalist supporters and organizers, her efforts to campaign for Alberta remaining in Canada did little to persuade those in the crowd.

“I was told, if you can’t say something nice, don’t say anything,” said Sue Peters, a 45-year resident of Red Deer.

Smith began her speech by outlining her rationale for bringing the independence question forward in the first place, describing her actions as being done “out of respect for” democracy after two petitions under a provincial set of rules had been submitted on the issue, one of which came from Sylvestre, which was quashed by a judge.

Speaking to the Star on Tuesday, Sylvestre candidly admitted he’s had better days.

He travelled a long road to Monday’s vote, first criss-crossing the province to collect more than 300,000 signatures from Albertans who felt there was nothing left for Canada to offer after decades of perceived grievance.

So seeing his side garner only about 24 per cent of the vote, despite hundreds of town halls and thousands of volunteer hours devoted to the cause, isn’t sitting well. The federalist side won roughly 75 per cent.

“I was expecting way better,” he said. How much better? At least 40 per cent, Sylvestre said.

Smith in her speech addressed those who voted to hold a second referendum and encouraged them to give Canada a second chance.

“You need to know that your voices have been heard, not just by our government, but also by your fellow Albertans and your fellow Canadians.”

For his part, looking at the scale of his side’s loss Sylvestre points the finger at mail-in ballots, hundreds of thousands of which poured into Elections Alberta.

The provincial elections agency has worked to dispel the concerns being voiced online about mail-in voting, telling one X user on Tuesday that such ballots have been around in the province since the 1980s and that obtaining one requires the same identification as receiving a paper ballot for in-person voting does.

The explosion in requests for them happened in part because Smith’s United Conservative Party government previously eased access to mail-in ballots to make that form of voting more convenient. Federalist organizers also urged supporters to vote early, warning that if they stayed home, separatists could secure a binding referendum vote.

The strategy paid off.

“I don’t accept them as they’re reported now,” Sylvestre said of the results, “but I have no proof otherwise. So, you know what? I’m just going to wait and see what happens.”

Federalist campaigns were also waiting Tuesday afternoon to see what would happen next.

While celebrating an overwhelming victory against holding a binding referendum on separation, they were also watching the results of nine other questions proposing greater provincial control over immigration and constitutional reform.

As unofficial results showed Smith’s proposed immigration reforms winning , including a question requiring proof of citizenship to vote in provincial elections, a spokesperson for a federalist group opposed to the measures took comfort in the narrower margins on some other questions.

“I don’t think it’s as clear a mandate as she May suggest it is,” said Avnish Nanda, who leads Our Alberta Advantage, a referendum initiative launched by the Alberta Advantage Immigrant Support Society.

“I want her to call an election,” he said.

Smith told Albertans on Tuesday that she would “be pursuing the reforms approved by Albertans through this referendum in the coming months and years ahead.”

While she noted having a mandate to move on the immigration questions, she said the results of the constitutional questions will be better known “in a couple of days.”

With the referendum over, United Conservatives will turn their attention to two matters: the next provincial election, set for 2027, and preparations for next month’s annual gathering of UCP members in Calgary.

Sylvestre presides over the Ucp’s riding association in Bonnyville. While he has yet to call a meeting on whether the board will vote to trigger a special leadership review of Smith, he predicts it will.

At least 22 of the party’s riding associations would have to vote to hold a review of Smith’s leadership for a vote to actually happen. Such was the process Sylvestre and others used to oust party founder and former Alberta premier Jason Kenney over his handling of COVID-19.

Asked whether he was prepared to organize against Smith, Sylvestre said “it’s a little soon.”

He said whatever happens next is in the hands of the party’s boards.

But, he said, independence supporters across the party base are “livid.”

“Danielle’s crossed the floor already once, so you know as far as we’re concerned, she’s done it again, and you know I don’t think there’s a strike three here.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks during a news conference in Calgary earlier this year.

Edmonton—As Alberta Premier Danielle Smith prepares to address the province, the man behind the independence push that led to Monday’s vote has his own message for her.

When Smith speaks at 8:45 p.m. EDT, she will do so to a province divided by the referendum but united in its anger: some resent that the vote happened at all, while others are angry that she chose Canada’s side.

The time is ticking down before Alberta Premier Danielle Smith delivers a live address after Monday’s referendum results.

The stakes are high for the premier. The referendum has unleashed a lot of anger. Some resent the fact she added an independence question to the ballot in the first place. Anger is also brewing among independence supporters who once saw her as an advocate but feel betrayed that she came out in support of Canada.

Mitch Sylvestre, who presides over a United Conservative Party board in Bonnyville, Alta., told the Star he has his own message for the premier.

“You made a choice. You made a choice. You’re going to possibly have to suffer the consequences.”

Those on the federalist side also question how much of a mandate she will have once all the results are counted for nine remaining reforms she was asking Albertans to vote “yes” to. Those included pursuing immigration and constitutional reforms.

Prime Minister Mark Carney applauds as Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe speaks at Canada’s national investment summit, in Toronto, ON Monday, Sept. 14, 2026.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe, speaking in Saskatoon, says things have changed under Prime Minister Mark Carney compared with under his predecessor, Justin Trudeau.

He says the approach is much more collaborative, and that the impact of that “did shine through” in the Alberta referendum results.

Let’s remember that, like Alberta, Saskatchewan railed against federal climate policies that Carney has since walked back or cancelled. That includes the consumer carbon price and a planned cap on emissions from the oil and gas sector. Moe also pushed back against previous federal rules to restrict coal-fired power generation that he plans to continue in Saskatchewan.

Moe seemed to also endorse the idea that provinces should have more control over immigration , which is something that was also on the ballot in Monday’s Alberta referendum.

“I welcome the co-operative federalism that the prime minister is bringing,” Moe said, encouraging him to bring the same spirit to immigration as well.

Watch Premier Danielle Smith’s address to the Alberta delivered Oct. 20 at 6:45 p.m. MT.

In a post on X, she says will be addressing the province in a speech that will be carried live by numerous broadcasters beginning at 8:45 p.m. Eastern time.

She says the focus will be on “what comes next.”

“Albertans picked up a pencil yesterday and answered ten hard questions about our future,” she wrote.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks at the Canada Strong and Free conference in Calgary, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.

As results began to roll in less than 24-hours ago, Smith announced that she would be addressing the province, celebrating the fact that the remain side came out on top by an overwhelming margin.

Results are still coming in for the other nine questions Smith put to Albertans, asking for a mandate to pursue constitutional reforms and take more control over immigration.

While the numbers are not final yet, the “yes” side to these questions is leading but by some narrow margins.

Assembly of First Nations national chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak responded to the referendum result, saying “people of Alberta and First Nations stood together and chose a future in Canada built on Treaty and sharing, over division and chaos.”

First Nations and Albertan voters “turned out in huge numbers and stood up for our shared past, present and future in Canada and rejected a divisive proposal that would bring needless upheaval, conflict and uncertainty for everyone,” she said in a written statement.

Eleanor Olszewski, the lone Liberal cabinet minister representing a seat in Alberta, said she is “beyond pleased,” with the referendum results.

“I know that the way that the prime minister and our government views the referendum is that, you know, today or October 19th, that was not the finish line at all.”

Olszewski, who represents a seat in Edmonton, suggested the government’s focus on Alberta, with the prime minister having made more than a dozen stops since his election last year, would not cease in light of the separatist push being defeated.

“We need to continue doing the hard work with Alberta, and we have every intention of doing that,” she told the Star from a government office in Edmonton on Tuesday.

Having spent the past few months travelling the province, the minister says she’s noted “a palpable difference in people’s views towards the government,” something she says she spoke to Carney about when he visited Red Deer, Alta., last week.

“Albertans feel heard,” she said.

With 85 per cent of the vote counted, the unofficial results from Elections Alberta showed that all but one of the nine questions proposing reforms like taking more control of immigration and pursuing constitutional changes like abolishing the Senate were passing.

Olszewski voted “no the nine,” which was a phrase federalist organizers use to urge supporters to reject these questions, warning they advanced a separation-minded agenda.

She dismissed the idea that a referendum was needed to address Alberta’s concerns around immigration.

“You know, from my perspective, we didn’t really need a referendum to tell the Prime Minister to tell our government that there were issues that we needed to work on with Alberta.”

As for the around 24 per cent of Albertans who voted to hold a binding referendum on separating from Canada, Olszewski acknowledged that for some, there’s nothing that can be done to persuade them otherwise.

“They’re probably very firmly entrenched in their views.”

She still believes there is a chance to reach those who cast a ballot for that option looking more to send Ottawa a message.

“There are people that, over time, we’ll be able to work with, and hopefully convince that cooperative federalism is working.”

Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre talks to reporters during a press conference the day after Albertans voted not to pursue a referendum to leave Canada, in Calgary, Alberta, Canada October 20, 2026.

At a news conference in Calgary Tuesday, as votes were still being counted, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre said after two days in Wainwright, he has “never been so proud to be Canadian” in the face of the courage of soldiers, first responders and rescuers who dealt with the weekend tragedy.

Poilievre said he’ll fight for a strong federal response to the tragedy when he returns to Parliament Wednesday, and then went on to blast the Liberal government of Mark Carney , saying his Conservative caucus would fight to restore the “promise of Canada” in Ottawa.

“Conservatives are thrilled to see Albertans vote for a stronger province within a United Canada,” he said.

But he said it was “inappropriate” for Carney last week to tell Albertans to vote “no to the nine” questions.

“It does appear that Albertans have rejected Mark Carney’s direction on this. They have said they want to take back control of immigration after a decade of reckless, unvetted mass migration and open borders. That means cutting off the deluxe benefits that the federal government is imposing on provinces, that go to people who have never paid into the system and are not even Canadian permanent residents. Things that Canadians don’t even get. We’ve got to cut back on that.”

On the immigration questions asked by the referendum — levels, limiting access to services or charging premiums to non-permanent residents — Poilievre said in French, “I should say I am entirely in favour of the proposals that were put to Albertans, and at this moment it seems that Albertans are as well.”

Poilievre called Carney “completely disconnected from reality” on immigration, saying “Liberal immigration levels are totally out of control,” and Ottawa needs to “deport criminals” and cut back on numbers of immigrants.

He offered a scathing view of the prime minister’s economic record, saying Carney has brought “stagflation” to Canada, and failed to address the affordability crisis facing Canadians.

Conservatives will fight for Canadians “facing despair no matter what province they are in,” said Poilievre.

“We need real results in the real lives of real people. Mr. Carney will be judged on that, and we deliver those results. I believe we will have a country that is more united than ever.”

But he dodged a question about whether he would open the constitution to address some of the changes Alberta is seeking, saying he’d await until all the vote results are finalized.

Federal Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne welcomed the result for the Liberal government’s efforts to draw investment to Canada. “The world has been watching” the Alberta referendum, he said, adding, “Now the message is clear.”

“It will reassure investors, it will reassure certainly the markets. And it gives momentum.”

“So now we continue to build. We have a lot to do together,” he said.

Champagne, who is widely expected to announce a federal budget date for early November, said there is major “structural change in the world economy” with renewed focus on critical minerals and energy which are “going to be fundamental in the economy of the 21st century.”

“That’s why I see Alberta front and centre in building the economy, that will provide benefits across the nation. You know, so I think this is a very powerful message to, obviously, all Canadians, but also you know people who are watching and saying you know Canada is united. Canada is building, and Canada is going to be leading.”

Former Alberta premiers Rachel Notley, right, and Jason Kenney discuss their assessment of the possible economic cost of Alberta’s referendum at an Edmonton Chamber luncheon, in Edmonton, ON Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.

In a joint statement, two former Alberta premiers, Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley, who co-chaired the Canadian Chamber of Commerce’s initiative called Stronger Together, hailed the results.

“Businesses, workers and communities in Alberta understand that connections to the rest of Canada are a source of strength,” said Kenney.

“At a historic time of unstable market access for them, they know there’s no advantage in cutting reliable customers and neighbours off. These results amplify the fact that Albertans remain overwhelmingly united that we’re better off with Canada, especially when we partner and help set a win-win economic agenda with the rest of the federation. That’s who Alberta is and will always be.”

Notley said, “small businesses in particular have been battered by years of economic barriers. This period of added uncertainty has not been welcome for them or those thinking of starting a business. Business knows that communities depend on them, and they conversely depend on others across Canada to help stock their shelves, build new things or innovate their service.”

“Going it alone isn’t a recipe for a better, stronger economy. I know many Alberta businesses and possible investors are counting on this question being settled once-and-for-all. As we move forward, let’s commit to delivering that finality for them.”

Supporters of the Forever Canadian group, who want Alberta to remain in Canada, react after Alberta residents voted to remain part of Canada in a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty.

Alberta's rejection of separation is making headlines south of the border, where American news outlets are casting the referendum results as another test of Canadian unity in the shadow of U.S President Donald Trump's increasingly strained relationship with Canada.

In a brief news story published Tuesday morning, the Washington Post framed the result as a testament of Canadian unity amid Trump’s trade war and annexation threats to make Canada the “51st state.” The newspaper even highlighted Prime Minister Mark Carney’s warnings of “outside forces” meddling with Canada’s identity, where he said they are “working to break us so they can own us.”

American news outlets weighed in after the province voted to reject a second binding referendum

But the vote also exposed the extent to which Alberta’s separatist movement has attracted attention in Washington. In a Tuesday morning story, Axios gave a spotlight to the reported meetings between Alberta’s separatist leaders and U.S officials, as well as comments from U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent describing Alberta as a natural partner for the United States.

The New York Times, under the headline “Voters in Oil-Rich Alberta Reject Leaving Canada,” touched on Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s role in the vote, noting she had “managed to provoke the ire of people on both sides” of the debate.

Fox News had no mention of the referendum results on its website as of Tuesday morning, but a Monday report noted the economic ties between Alberta and the U.S, though the outlet acknowledged that some separatists rejected becoming America’s “51st state.”

The Associated Press framed the result as a victory for Carney, whose appeals to national unity came amidst tension with Washington. The wire service noted a rise in Canadian nationalism, even in a provinces where Liberal prime ministers have historically struggled to win support.

“Well over a million Albertans came together to give us something all too rare these days, a moment of hope,” NDP Leader Avi Lewis said about Alberta’s referendum results.

NDP leader Avi Lewis said the result from the referendum is a relief and a sign of Canadians coming together during a difficult time.

“At a time when our country is under threat and when we need to come together as Canadians. This result represents a clear rejection of the politics of division,” Lewis said outside of the House of Commons Tuesday morning.

He thanked Albertans for getting out to the polls and showing support for Canada.

“Well over a million Albertans came together to give us something all too rare these days, a moment of hope,” he said.

He said there are obviously concerns in Alberta about the cost of living, healthcare and education, as there are in the rest of the country, but said those problems don’t get addressed by splitting up the country.

“As so many Albertans have shown us, we don’t fix our problems by turning on each other. We fix them by coming together,” he said.

Lewis blamed Alberta Premier Danielle Smith for the vote even taking place and said she had stoked division.

“The entire process was unnecessary, nobody asked for it. Danielle Smith’s career has been defined by a slow walk towards separation. All of the questions are designed to stoke division in Alberta and she is the one who is responsible for that.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney , building on his written statement earlier, told reporters he was “thrilled” at the referendum result on Canada’s unity.

He spoke to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith this morning about the results and about the devastating accident at CFB Wainwright.

And he pledged to work with all provinces on changes, for example to immigration reform.

Carney did not close the door to constitutional change if necessary, but downplayed the necessity of opening up the country’s foundational governing document as a first resort.

“Look,” he told reporters. “There’s one approach which is to say ‘oh let’s wait until — we’re just going to park the important issues, whether it’s immigration, whether it’s the judiciary, other aspects, let’s just park that unless we have constitutional change’ or ‘let’s work together..”

“Let’s find common solutions now, and then if it were to become necessary — it’s this question of priorities and starting. And this is a government that very much is focused on results for Canadians.

“It’s very focused on working with the provinces. It’s very focused on working with Indigenous peoples and finding solutions now to the issues that our country faces, and really, above all, seizing the many opportunities for Canadians.”

At another point he said, “what I favor is working now pragmatically to common solutions. Constitutional change is difficult. It’s long.”

Take a closer look at the unofficial results for the nine additional referendum questions compared to the main vote in Alberta.

Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre said the Alberta referendum result sent a strong message from the people of the province that “the promise of Canada is worth fighting for.”

He said the result showed that Albertans had “decisively voted for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada.”

But his social media post Tuesday made no mention of the other nine questions on the referendum slate, which had to do with the province taking greater control over immigration and pushing for amendments to the Canadian Constitution—most notably to abolish the Senate.

Speaking ahead of a 2013 Supreme Court of Canada hearing, Poilievre—then minister of state for democratic reform—told reporters that the upper chamber needed to be reformed or abolished in line with Conservative Party policy under prime minister Stephen Harper.

“The Senate must change or vanish,” he said. “The status quo is not acceptable.”

Alberta NDP leader Naheed Nenshi leaves after casting his referendum vote at an advance polling station in Calgary, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.

Alberta’s opposition NDP leader Naheed Nenshi reacted overnight to the referendum results about holding a vote on separating from Canada.

Nenshi posted a photo of himself against a Canadian flag, with a message of thanks.

“We saved Canada,” he wrote early Tuesday morning. “Now, we save Alberta.”

Recent opinion polls have put Nenshi’s NDP neck-and-neck with Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party.

The next provincial election is scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027, but there is speculation that Smith could take Albertans to the polls soon after the referendum results are counted.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford woke up on the right side of the bed Tuesday morning, saying he was “thrilled by the decisive support Albertans have shown for the country we all love.”

“Alberta voters have overwhelmingly chosen a stronger, more prosperous future for their province by remaining in Canada,” he wrote on X.

But Ford said there is now an obligation on the rest of the country to love-bomb Alberta by building new pipelines, exploiting natural resources and “unleashing the prosperity that will protect the future of Canadians from coast to coast to coast.”

Last summer while at the Calgary Stampede, the Ontario and Alberta premiers stood together to propose construction of a new oil pipeline—the Northern Shield Energy Corridor —running from Hardisty, Alta., to refineries in Sarnia.

Last month, Ford said Ontario taxpayers would back the 3,300-kilometre construction project, which could cost tens of billions of dollars.

Ford referred to this as “the cost of defending Canada’s sovereignty.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney meets Alberta Premier Danielle Smith at his office in Ottawa on May 8.

Plenty will be claiming victory now that Alberta has voted against separatism , but the days and weeks ahead will show what’s been lost, too, with this democracy gambit.

The decisive majority — over 75 per cent with most polls reporting — is a clear win for Mark Carney , whose stock in Alberta has only climbed throughout the referendum campaign. The prime minister does not have to relive the Brexit drama, as he constantly cited as an example Alberta should not follow.

“Albertans chose Canada,” Carney said in a brief statement as the majority became clear.

Albertans have voted in droves to stay in Canada. The result was satisfying for the pro-Canada movement, but separatists say it's just the beginning. (Oct. 20, 2026)

Premier Danielle Smith will be wanting to call this a win for her, too, but what she’s unleashed with this referendum May be hard to put back in the box, including threats to her own leadership of the United Conservative Party.

Even before a single vote was counted, Alberta separatists were saying that their cause has been strengthened by the referendum. In fact, that was the uniting battle cry at the big, final rally for Alberta independence on the weekend.

“Regardless of what happens on Monday, we’ve already won,” Keith Wilson, head of Let Alberta Decide, told the crowd.

Jeffrey Rath, also one of the leading separatist voices, hammered home that same, already-won theme in a lengthy post on X the next day.

“We have forced federal politicians to come to Alberta to help prove how Canadian federalism is failing Albertans,” Rath wrote.

Now they’re coming for Smith, too, he said. “We have forced a federalist provincial government to hold a vote on independence that will force a leadership change of the governing party of Alberta.”

If those voices remain loud, Smith could be in for a rough-and-tumble gathering when the UCP meets next month.

Wilson, in a subdued speech as results were still coming in, told his supporters: “Tonight concludes a campaign, but the conversation about Alberta’s future in Canada and our place in Canada and our role in Canada will continue.” He told one supporter as well: “We’re not giving up.”

So much for Smith’s assertions that this referendum will put to rest the issue.

As for the other nine questions on the ballot, there’s a lot of unfinished business lurking here too, for Alberta and the country.

Albertans were leaning toward Yes on the five immigration questions as polls were reporting, giving Smith some political cover to press Ottawa for more provincial control over who comes to the province. She warned Carney at their joint appearance in Red Deer late last week that other premiers were on her side on this issue.

But the immigration questions in the referendum stirred the waters on an issue that has become volatile, sometimes even dangerous, in many parts of the world right now. Smith’s New Democratic opponents flatly accused her of courting racism. Throughout the campaign, there were periodic reports that immigrants and diverse communities felt less safe because they’d been put on the ballot.

Questions No. 1 through No. 4 sought a mandate to reduce the number of immigrants settled in Alberta and restrict their access to pricey social

Saima Jamal, co-founder of the Calgary Immigrant Support Society, told Global News in late August: “Right now racism and hate is on steroids and I’ve never seen this level of hatred toward immigrant communities.”

Is that the kind of thing that Smith can put back in the box?

Also unresolved on the day after is Alberta’s relationship with Indigenous people, who in large numbers have rejected the whole idea of a referendum being used to haggle over constitutional arrangements that could affect treaty rights.

Whatever Smith believes is settled by Monday’s vote, Alberta-Indigenous relations aren’t among them.

In the larger sense, one is left wondering what this referendum achieved, beyond a vent of Alberta grievances. The 10 questions, in sum, were a grocery list of all the things that’s alleged to be wrong with the province’s place in the federation — the chips on the shoulder. They all but declare that Alberta is getting screwed on the Senate, ON judicial appointments, or on financing for health care and social services.

Every Albertan who voted had to consider that list. Many May have walked away from the ballot box, or the referendum debate overall, feeling more aggrieved, seeing that list in black and white. It’s hard to argue that this venting exercise did anything for Canadian unity.

The problem is that unity is exactly the thing that Canada needs now, in the face of the challenges coming from Donald Trump’s America.

Carney didn’t sugar-coat that reality when he was out making his final pitches in Alberta before the referendum. “This referendum comes at the worst possible time,” he said.

Given all that’s been whipped up during it — from separatism to anti-immigrant sentiments and the relentless hammering away at grievance — the time after the referendum isn’t looking exactly ideal for the times either.

The main question of whether to hold a referendum on Alberta’s independence has resulted in a decisive victory for federalists in the province.

Canada can celebrate that it has been spared an Alberta separation vote with the results of Monday’s referendum — at least one in the near future.

But the other nine questions on the ballot risk causing a federal hangover that could be felt for years to come.

Overshadowed through much of the campaign by the headline threat of the independence movement in Canada’s energy rich province, the other questions put to Albertans deal with immigration and constitutional reform.

Backed by Alberta Premier Danielle Smith , questions No. 1 through No. 4 sought a mandate to reduce the number of immigrants settled in Alberta and restrict their access to pricey social programs like health care and education.

Questions No. 6 through 9 asked whether Alberta should try to amend the Constitution to abolish the Senate, to appoint its own judges, to be able to opt out of federal funding programs and give priority to its own laws in case of conflict with Ottawa.

The other results provide a more troubling glimpse into voters’ satisfaction levels within the Canadian federation.

As of Tuesday morning, eight of the nine questions are backed by majorities that favour a change to the status quo.

Question No. 8, which asks about amending the Constitution to be able to opt out of federal funding programs, continued to be a close-fought battle between voters opposed and in favour.

This shouldn’t come as a complete surprise.

Alberta is, after all, the birthplace of Western alienation: the complaint that Western Canadians drive the national economy but are often overlooked when federal politicians gather in Ottawa to debate issues and pass laws.

Part of that sentiment has been fuelled by the special attention and treatment afforded by the federal government to Quebec with the aim of keeping the momentum and threat of the province’s sovereigntists at bay following independence referendum votes in 1980 and 1995.

Turmoil around immigration and Alberta-Indigenous relations that were unleashed with this referendum May be hard to put back in the box.

The Alberta referendum questions seeking more powers over immigration—particularly Question No. 1, which asks about cutting numbers “to more sustainable levels”— are undoubtedly inspired by the control over immigration that Quebec has negotiated for itself over decades.

Alberta’s push for constitutional amendments will also have taken its inspiration from federal efforts to address Quebec discontent after the 1980 Quebec referendum, in which 60 per cent of Quebecers voted against sovereignty association.

After the votes were counted, then-prime minister Pierre Trudeau pledged in a victory speech to “renew the Canadian federation.” He repatriated the Constitution in 1982, but he did so over the Quebec government’s objections and without the province’s signature.

Prime minister Brian Mulroney’s attempts to make amends with Quebec resulted in two unsuccessful attempts to renegotiate some of the terms of the Canadian Constitution.

The drama and division of those attempts have scared successive federal governments away from trying for their own amendments, whether it was then-Conservative leader Stephen Harper on Senate reform or Justin Trudeau’s pledge to change the Canadian electoral system.

In a podcast interview last week , he said that he “(got) the point about an unelected Senate,” and admitted that “the Constitution is not unamendable.”

“But it requires building a real consensus around what’s necessary to change and why it (should) change and which elements you are going to change,” he told host Ryan Jespersen .

At the same time, Carney has also cast the idea of bickering over the Constitution as a political distraction from the real job at hand, which is bolstering the Canadian economy and diversifying away from the United States.

Carney’s time in power has been focused on clearing away distractions and roadblocks that stand in the way of his government’s agenda.

But Danielle Smith, whose UCP party is being challenged by the Alberta NDP in opinion polls, May welcome the distraction of a battle to amend the Canadian Constitution — particularly now that she is armed with ammunition from the referendum.

An Alberta referendum hot take from one of America’s most prominent Canadian-born political commentators, David Frum.

A writer for The Atlantic and a podcast host, Frum weighed in Tuesday morning and declared that the Alberta referendum vote was U.S. President Donald Trump’s “first midterm defeat.”

The cheeky comment is a likely reference to the segment of Alberta separatists who were attracted—not repelled—by Trump’s calls to make Canada the 51st state as well as reports that organizers of the province’s independence movement held meetings with Republican Party operatives and U.S. State Department officials.

A man walks near an advance voting station during the Alberta Referendum as Albertans head to the polls in Tofield, Alberta, ON October 16, 2026.

Good morning, and welcome back to the Star’s coverage of the Alberta referendum. The results on the main question of whether to hold a referendum on Alberta’s separation from Canada are holding steady this morning, with about 70 per cent of Albertans opting for Canadian unity.

The other nine referendum questions are sending a more nuanced message of frustration within the federation.

With the ballots still being counted, there are clear but narrow majorities who voted yes to questions one through four, which ask whether the Alberta government should take a harder line on immigration.

The ballot questions, which are supported by Premier Danielle Smith’s government, ask about decreasing the number of immigrants who can settle in the province and limiting their access to social programs such as health care and education.

And the early results also indicate that Albertans are evenly divided over questions about whether the government should push for amendments to the Canadian Constitution —a traumatic matter in Canada, which has seen numerous failed efforts to enact constitutional change.

Referendum questions six through nine ask whether Alberta should seek amendments that would allow it to: appoint its own judges; abolish the Senate; opt out of federal funding programs for provincial matters like education and healthcare; and giving priority to provincial laws when there is a conflict with the federal government.

A man registers to vote in a voting station during the Alberta Referendum as Albertans head to the polls in Calgary, Oct. 19, 2026.

Edmonton — A turbulent campaign that pitted federalists against separatists over Alberta’s future in Canada ended with the remain side securing an overwhelming victory.

With votes still being counted on Tuesday morning, about 76 per cent of Albertans voted to remain in Canada and roughly 24 per cent backed a second binding referendum on leaving the country.

At a watch party in Edmonton hosted by the federalist group “Forever Canadian,” a crowd of fewer than 100 jumped to its feet, hugging, cheering and waving Canadian flags as the call was made.

“Canada, Canada, Canada,” the crowd chanted.

The projections came before Elections Alberta had released complete official results. More than 100 polling stations that opened late stayed open past the scheduled closing time, delaying the count until after midnight.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on X that she would address Albertans Tuesday at 8:45 p.m. Eastern time regarding the results “and where our province goes from here.”

“I’m very pleased to see the initial results from Elections Alberta show widespread support for remaining in Canada. Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith wrote.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Mark Carney issued a statement celebrating the results, saying the province had “made a clear choice” in Monday’s vote.

“Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

He said that while all of the results have not yet been counted, “the defining question of separation” has been decided and victory for the federalist camp means that the country can now return to the job of advancing Canada “with renewed purpose and high ambition,” referring to his government’s agenda of increasing international trade and developing infrastructure, mining and energy projects across the country.

He said that Canada was “unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta at its core.”

While federalists celebrated Monday’s victory, many were quick to note that 23 per cent of Albertans choosing the option to hold a vote on separation was not something to cheer about.

“I was hoping it would be like 85 per cent,” Dee Winn, a volunteer with the “Forever Canadian” campaign, told the Star as the early results came in.

Amid the cheers and applause, Thomas Lukaszuk, who spearheaded the federalist group, told the crowd those voters could not be ignored.

“These are Albertans. These are Canadians,” he said from the stage, adding that something had to be done to address what was driving their anger and frustration.

“We cannot go on like this.”

Before the polls even closed, Mitch Sylvestre, a key separatist leader, told a crowd of volunteers and other independence supporters gathered at a nearby Edmonton bar that their movement had become something that was not going to disappear.

“Alberta has changed,” he said.

Monday’s vote took place under the shadow of tragedy after four people were killed and 39 others injured when extreme winds pushed an already burning fire onto troops conducting exercises at CFB Wainwright on Saturday.

Polls opened as scheduled, with some voters in Wainwright worried about what would happen to the base, an integral part of the community’s identity and economy, should Alberta one day separate from Canada.

“This is a federal town,” said Greg Granger, who works in IT at CFB Wainwright.

Elsewhere, the polarization that has taken hold across the province during the referendum campaign was on full display.

Olivia Hughes, an Edmonton resident living with disabilities, walked to a polling station at an Anglican church in the city on Monday, wondering, “Why the f—- do I have to be out here?”

Besides contemplating the impact secession would have on her quality of life, she said: “I’m a Canadian, I’m not just an Albertan.”

“I would like to remain a Canadian, so that’s why I’m here.”

Others arrived feeling fed up.

“I think we’ve been screwed over by the other provinces,” said fellow Edmonton voter Bill Lewis, who cast his ballot at a polling station in one of the city’s strip malls for the option to begin the process of holding a future vote to leave Canada.

“I think our money should stay here instead of us getting nothing and the other provinces getting it all.”

A record-breaking 1.3 million Albertans had already cast their ballots through advance polls or by mail, comprising 43 per cent of the province’s eligible voters.

How Alberta came to this moment is a mix of historic grievance, COVID-fuelled populism and a premier who was unwilling to close the door on separatists.

While Western alienation is nothing new in the country’s largest oil-producing province, successive public opinion polls suggested an uptick in the sentiment after the election of Prime Minister Mark Carney, whose victory was viewed by some as another blow to the deep-blue Conservative province.

Anger had been brewing for years during the tenure of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, whose environmental policies were viewed by many in the province as stymying resource development. Even before that, the Trudeau name triggered distrust among some Albertans, who remembered the legacy of the long-dismantled National Energy Program introduced by his father, former prime minister Pierre Trudeau.

But while Carney has sought to reset relations with Alberta, working with Premier Danielle Smith to advance a new million-barrel-a-day oil pipeline to the West Coast and overhauling federal regulatory processes with the goal of getting more major energy and infrastructure projects off the ground, another movement was brewing in the province.

Independence organizers who entered Alberta’s political arena through opposition to COVID-19 pandemic measures got to work pushing for a referendum.

Sylvestre, the owner of a sporting goods store in Bonnyville, Alta., spent the dead of winter travelling the province collecting 300,000 signatures for a petition under provincial citizen-initiative rules to trigger a referendum on leaving Canada.

Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier in a Progressive Conservative government, was busy collecting tens of thousands of signatures for his own “Forever Canadian” initiative under the same provincial rules in response to the separatist push.

Things came to a head this May when an Alberta judge quashed the separatist petition over concerns about the failure to properly consult First Nations.

One evening in late May, Smith addressed Albertans to announce that her United Conservative Party government would add an independence question to a previously decided set of nine referendum questions focused on taking greater control over immigration and pursuing constitutional reforms such as abolishing the Senate.

That sparked criticism from all corners. Carney called the referendum a “dangerous bluff.” Other premiers panned the move, while federalists in Alberta mobilized supporters who wanted to remain in Canada to turn out and vote, warning that separatism remained a minority view but a vocal and highly motivated one.

Independence leaders also expressed ire at Smith, particularly over her public support for remaining in Canada, viewing it as a betrayal of her party base, where support for independence is popular.

Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney visits supporters of a Vote to Stay event ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty, in Red Deer, Alta., October 16, 2026.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has issued a statement celebrating the Alberta referendum results, saying the province “made a clear choice” in the Monday vote.

He said that while all of the results have not yet been counted, “the defining question of separation” has been decided and victory for the federalist camp means that the country can now return to the job of advancing Canada “with renewed purpose and high ambition,” Carney said, referring to his government’s agenda of increasing international trade and developing infrastructure, mining and energy projects across the country.

Supporters cheer as results begin to display at the pro Canada watch party in Edmonton, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026.

Both CBC News and CTV News are projecting the remain side has won.

CBC made the call, showing the remain side leading with 76.6 per cent of the vote, as compared to 23 per cent for the independence option.
paragraphs: Alberta rejects separation in referendum vote ; early results show province appears split on immigration. This file is no longer updating.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is seen in an image taken from a video as she speaks in a televised address Wednesday night after Alberta residents voted to remain part of Canada in the province’s referendum on separation.

Edmonton — Alberta Premier Danielle Smith slammed the door on holding any further referendums on independence, declaring in a speech Tuesday night that Albertans have spoken and want to remain in Canada.
“I want to make it clear tonight that for as long as I am premier, I will honour this mandate from Albertans and will not be holding another referendum on this issue,” she said.

Premier Danielle Smith says that Albertans have spoken in Monday's referendum and, as long as she’s in power, separation is a dead issue. Smith, in a TV address to the province, also says challenges with Ottawa will be handled in the courts or through political channels. (Oct. 20, 2026)

Speaking in a live televised address, Smith called for unity and delivered a staunchly pro-Canada message. It was “time to move forward,” she said, from the debate that has raged across the province for months, saying she knows the province-wide exercise was at times “passionate.”
About 75 per cent of Albertans voted Tuesday to stay and roughly 25 per cent backed a second binding referendum on leaving the country.
The premier vowed to stand up for provincial jurisdiction and fight back against Ottawa when it is seen as interfering in areas that are not its own.
“But those disputes will be settled within the political and legal institutions of our nation, rather than pursuing the option of separation.”
Earlier in the day, as Smith prepared her address, the man behind the independence push that led to Monday’s vote delivered to her a message of his own.
“You made a choice. You made a choice. You’re going to possibly have to suffer the consequences,” Mitch Sylvestre told the Star on Tuesday as he drove from Edmonton to his home in Bonnyville, Alta.

Such a warning is just one example of the furor directed at Smith, particularly from independence supporters who see her decision to back remaining in Canada as a betrayal of the party’s base, many of whom support independence.
Smith spoke to a province divided by the referendum but united in its anger: some resent that the vote happened at all, while others are angry that she chose Canada’s side.

Even when the premier joined Prime Minister Mark Carney at a brewery outside Red Deer, Alta., last week to meet federalist supporters and organizers, her efforts to campaign for Alberta remaining in Canada did little to persuade those in the crowd.
“I was told, if you can’t say something nice, don’t say anything,” said Sue Peters, a 45-year resident of Red Deer.

Smith began her speech by outlining her rationale for bringing the independence question forward in the first place, describing her actions as being done “out of respect for” democracy after two petitions under a provincial set of rules had been submitted on the issue, one of which came from Sylvestre, which was quashed by a judge.
Speaking to the Star on Tuesday, Sylvestre candidly admitted he’s had better days.

He travelled a long road to Monday’s vote, first criss-crossing the province to collect more than 300,000 signatures from Albertans who felt there was nothing left for Canada to offer after decades of perceived grievance.

So seeing his side garner only about 24 per cent of the vote, despite hundreds of town halls and thousands of volunteer hours devoted to the cause, isn’t sitting well. The federalist side won roughly 75 per cent.
“I was expecting way better,” he said. How much better? At least 40 per cent, Sylvestre said.
Smith in her speech addressed those who voted to hold a second referendum and encouraged them to give Canada a second chance.
“You need to know that your voices have been heard, not just by our government, but also by your fellow Albertans and your fellow Canadians.”
For his part, looking at the scale of his side’s loss Sylvestre points the finger at mail-in ballots, hundreds of thousands of which poured into Elections Alberta.

The provincial elections agency has worked to dispel the concerns being voiced online about mail-in voting, telling one X user on Tuesday that such ballots have been around in the province since the 1980s and that obtaining one requires the same identification as receiving a paper ballot for in-person voting does.

The explosion in requests for them happened in part because Smith’s United Conservative Party government previously eased access to mail-in ballots to make that form of voting more convenient. Federalist organizers also urged supporters to vote early, warning that if they stayed home, separatists could secure a binding referendum vote.
The strategy paid off.
“I don’t accept them as they’re reported now,” Sylvestre said of the results, “but I have no proof otherwise. So, you know what? I’m just going to wait and see what happens.”
Federalist campaigns were also waiting Tuesday afternoon to see what would happen next.

While celebrating an overwhelming victory against holding a binding referendum on separation, they were also watching the results of nine other questions proposing greater provincial control over immigration and constitutional reform.

As unofficial results showed Smith’s proposed immigration reforms winning , including a question requiring proof of citizenship to vote in provincial elections, a spokesperson for a federalist group opposed to the measures took comfort in the narrower margins on some other questions.

“I don’t think it’s as clear a mandate as she May suggest it is,” said Avnish Nanda, who leads Our Alberta Advantage, a referendum initiative launched by the Alberta Advantage Immigrant Support Society.
“I want her to call an election,” he said.
Smith told Albertans on Tuesday that she would “be pursuing the reforms approved by Albertans through this referendum in the coming months and years ahead.”
While she noted having a mandate to move on the immigration questions, she said the results of the constitutional questions will be better known “in a couple of days.”

With the referendum over, United Conservatives will turn their attention to two matters: the next provincial election, set for 2027, and preparations for next month’s annual gathering of UCP members in Calgary.

Sylvestre presides over the Ucp’s riding association in Bonnyville. While he has yet to call a meeting on whether the board will vote to trigger a special leadership review of Smith, he predicts it will.

At least 22 of the party’s riding associations would have to vote to hold a review of Smith’s leadership for a vote to actually happen. Such was the process Sylvestre and others used to oust party founder and former Alberta premier Jason Kenney over his handling of COVID-19.
Asked whether he was prepared to organize against Smith, Sylvestre said “it’s a little soon.”
He said whatever happens next is in the hands of the party’s boards.
But, he said, independence supporters across the party base are “livid.”
“Danielle’s crossed the floor already once, so you know as far as we’re concerned, she’s done it again, and you know I don’t think there’s a strike three here.”
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks during a news conference in Calgary earlier this year.
Edmonton—As Alberta Premier Danielle Smith prepares to address the province, the man behind the independence push that led to Monday’s vote has his own message for her.

When Smith speaks at 8:45 p.m. EDT, she will do so to a province divided by the referendum but united in its anger: some resent that the vote happened at all, while others are angry that she chose Canada’s side.
The time is ticking down before Alberta Premier Danielle Smith delivers a live address after Monday’s referendum results.

The stakes are high for the premier. The referendum has unleashed a lot of anger. Some resent the fact she added an independence question to the ballot in the first place. Anger is also brewing among independence supporters who once saw her as an advocate but feel betrayed that she came out in support of Canada.
Mitch Sylvestre, who presides over a United Conservative Party board in Bonnyville, Alta., told the Star he has his own message for the premier.
“You made a choice. You made a choice. You’re going to possibly have to suffer the consequences.”

Those on the federalist side also question how much of a mandate she will have once all the results are counted for nine remaining reforms she was asking Albertans to vote “yes” to. Those included pursuing immigration and constitutional reforms.
Prime Minister Mark Carney applauds as Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe speaks at Canada’s national investment summit, in Toronto, ON Monday, Sept. 14, 2026.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe, speaking in Saskatoon, says things have changed under Prime Minister Mark Carney compared with under his predecessor, Justin Trudeau.
He says the approach is much more collaborative, and that the impact of that “did shine through” in the Alberta referendum results.

Let’s remember that, like Alberta, Saskatchewan railed against federal climate policies that Carney has since walked back or cancelled. That includes the consumer carbon price and a planned cap on emissions from the oil and gas sector. Moe also pushed back against previous federal rules to restrict coal-fired power generation that he plans to continue in Saskatchewan.
Moe seemed to also endorse the idea that provinces should have more control over immigration , which is something that was also on the ballot in Monday’s Alberta referendum.
“I welcome the co-operative federalism that the prime minister is bringing,” Moe said, encouraging him to bring the same spirit to immigration as well.
Watch Premier Danielle Smith’s address to the Alberta delivered Oct. 20 at 6:45 p.m. MT.
In a post on X, she says will be addressing the province in a speech that will be carried live by numerous broadcasters beginning at 8:45 p.m. Eastern time.
She says the focus will be on “what comes next.”
“Albertans picked up a pencil yesterday and answered ten hard questions about our future,” she wrote.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks at the Canada Strong and Free conference in Calgary, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.
As results began to roll in less than 24-hours ago, Smith announced that she would be addressing the province, celebrating the fact that the remain side came out on top by an overwhelming margin.
Results are still coming in for the other nine questions Smith put to Albertans, asking for a mandate to pursue constitutional reforms and take more control over immigration.
While the numbers are not final yet, the “yes” side to these questions is leading but by some narrow margins.

Assembly of First Nations national chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak responded to the referendum result, saying “people of Alberta and First Nations stood together and chose a future in Canada built on Treaty and sharing, over division and chaos.”

First Nations and Albertan voters “turned out in huge numbers and stood up for our shared past, present and future in Canada and rejected a divisive proposal that would bring needless upheaval, conflict and uncertainty for everyone,” she said in a written statement.
Eleanor Olszewski, the lone Liberal cabinet minister representing a seat in Alberta, said she is “beyond pleased,” with the referendum results.
“I know that the way that the prime minister and our government views the referendum is that, you know, today or October 19th, that was not the finish line at all.”

Olszewski, who represents a seat in Edmonton, suggested the government’s focus on Alberta, with the prime minister having made more than a dozen stops since his election last year, would not cease in light of the separatist push being defeated.
“We need to continue doing the hard work with Alberta, and we have every intention of doing that,” she told the Star from a government office in Edmonton on Tuesday.

Having spent the past few months travelling the province, the minister says she’s noted “a palpable difference in people’s views towards the government,” something she says she spoke to Carney about when he visited Red Deer, Alta., last week.
“Albertans feel heard,” she said.

With 85 per cent of the vote counted, the unofficial results from Elections Alberta showed that all but one of the nine questions proposing reforms like taking more control of immigration and pursuing constitutional changes like abolishing the Senate were passing.
Olszewski voted “no the nine,” which was a phrase federalist organizers use to urge supporters to reject these questions, warning they advanced a separation-minded agenda.
She dismissed the idea that a referendum was needed to address Alberta’s concerns around immigration.
“You know, from my perspective, we didn’t really need a referendum to tell the Prime Minister to tell our government that there were issues that we needed to work on with Alberta.”

As for the around 24 per cent of Albertans who voted to hold a binding referendum on separating from Canada, Olszewski acknowledged that for some, there’s nothing that can be done to persuade them otherwise.
“They’re probably very firmly entrenched in their views.”
She still believes there is a chance to reach those who cast a ballot for that option looking more to send Ottawa a message.
“There are people that, over time, we’ll be able to work with, and hopefully convince that cooperative federalism is working.”

Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre talks to reporters during a press conference the day after Albertans voted not to pursue a referendum to leave Canada, in Calgary, Alberta, Canada October 20, 2026.

At a news conference in Calgary Tuesday, as votes were still being counted, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre said after two days in Wainwright, he has “never been so proud to be Canadian” in the face of the courage of soldiers, first responders and rescuers who dealt with the weekend tragedy.

Poilievre said he’ll fight for a strong federal response to the tragedy when he returns to Parliament Wednesday, and then went on to blast the Liberal government of Mark Carney , saying his Conservative caucus would fight to restore the “promise of Canada” in Ottawa.
“Conservatives are thrilled to see Albertans vote for a stronger province within a United Canada,” he said.
But he said it was “inappropriate” for Carney last week to tell Albertans to vote “no to the nine” questions.

“It does appear that Albertans have rejected Mark Carney’s direction on this. They have said they want to take back control of immigration after a decade of reckless, unvetted mass migration and open borders. That means cutting off the deluxe benefits that the federal government is imposing on provinces, that go to people who have never paid into the system and are not even Canadian permanent residents. Things that Canadians don’t even get. We’ve got to cut back on that.”

On the immigration questions asked by the referendum — levels, limiting access to services or charging premiums to non-permanent residents — Poilievre said in French, “I should say I am entirely in favour of the proposals that were put to Albertans, and at this moment it seems that Albertans are as well.”

Poilievre called Carney “completely disconnected from reality” on immigration, saying “Liberal immigration levels are totally out of control,” and Ottawa needs to “deport criminals” and cut back on numbers of immigrants.
He offered a scathing view of the prime minister’s economic record, saying Carney has brought “stagflation” to Canada, and failed to address the affordability crisis facing Canadians.
Conservatives will fight for Canadians “facing despair no matter what province they are in,” said Poilievre.
“We need real results in the real lives of real people. Mr. Carney will be judged on that, and we deliver those results. I believe we will have a country that is more united than ever.”
But he dodged a question about whether he would open the constitution to address some of the changes Alberta is seeking, saying he’d await until all the vote results are finalized.

Federal Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne welcomed the result for the Liberal government’s efforts to draw investment to Canada. “The world has been watching” the Alberta referendum, he said, adding, “Now the message is clear.”
“It will reassure investors, it will reassure certainly the markets. And it gives momentum.”
“So now we continue to build. We have a lot to do together,” he said.

Champagne, who is widely expected to announce a federal budget date for early November, said there is major “structural change in the world economy” with renewed focus on critical minerals and energy which are “going to be fundamental in the economy of the 21st century.”

“That’s why I see Alberta front and centre in building the economy, that will provide benefits across the nation. You know, so I think this is a very powerful message to, obviously, all Canadians, but also you know people who are watching and saying you know Canada is united. Canada is building, and Canada is going to be leading.”

Former Alberta premiers Rachel Notley, right, and Jason Kenney discuss their assessment of the possible economic cost of Alberta’s referendum at an Edmonton Chamber luncheon, in Edmonton, ON Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.
In a joint statement, two former Alberta premiers, Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley, who co-chaired the Canadian Chamber of Commerce’s initiative called Stronger Together, hailed the results.
“Businesses, workers and communities in Alberta understand that connections to the rest of Canada are a source of strength,” said Kenney.

“At a historic time of unstable market access for them, they know there’s no advantage in cutting reliable customers and neighbours off. These results amplify the fact that Albertans remain overwhelmingly united that we’re better off with Canada, especially when we partner and help set a win-win economic agenda with the rest of the federation. That’s who Alberta is and will always be.”

Notley said, “small businesses in particular have been battered by years of economic barriers. This period of added uncertainty has not been welcome for them or those thinking of starting a business. Business knows that communities depend on them, and they conversely depend on others across Canada to help stock their shelves, build new things or innovate their service.”
