“Going it alone isn’t a recipe for a better, stronger economy. I know many Alberta businesses and possible investors are counting on this question being settled once-and-for-all. As we move forward, let’s commit to delivering that finality for them.”
Supporters of the Forever Canadian group, who want Alberta to remain in Canada, react after Alberta residents voted to remain part of Canada in a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty.

Alberta's rejection of separation is making headlines south of the border, where American news outlets are casting the referendum results as another test of Canadian unity in the shadow of U.S President Donald Trump's increasingly strained relationship with Canada.

In a brief news story published Tuesday morning, the Washington Post framed the result as a testament of Canadian unity amid Trump’s trade war and annexation threats to make Canada the “51st state.” The newspaper even highlighted Prime Minister Mark Carney’s warnings of “outside forces” meddling with Canada’s identity, where he said they are “working to break us so they can own us.”
American news outlets weighed in after the province voted to reject a second binding referendum

But the vote also exposed the extent to which Alberta’s separatist movement has attracted attention in Washington. In a Tuesday morning story, Axios gave a spotlight to the reported meetings between Alberta’s separatist leaders and U.S officials, as well as comments from U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent describing Alberta as a natural partner for the United States.

The New York Times, under the headline “Voters in Oil-Rich Alberta Reject Leaving Canada,” touched on Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s role in the vote, noting she had “managed to provoke the ire of people on both sides” of the debate.

Fox News had no mention of the referendum results on its website as of Tuesday morning, but a Monday report noted the economic ties between Alberta and the U.S, though the outlet acknowledged that some separatists rejected becoming America’s “51st state.”

The Associated Press framed the result as a victory for Carney, whose appeals to national unity came amidst tension with Washington. The wire service noted a rise in Canadian nationalism, even in a provinces where Liberal prime ministers have historically struggled to win support.
“Well over a million Albertans came together to give us something all too rare these days, a moment of hope,” NDP Leader Avi Lewis said about Alberta’s referendum results.
NDP leader Avi Lewis said the result from the referendum is a relief and a sign of Canadians coming together during a difficult time.

“At a time when our country is under threat and when we need to come together as Canadians. This result represents a clear rejection of the politics of division,” Lewis said outside of the House of Commons Tuesday morning.
He thanked Albertans for getting out to the polls and showing support for Canada.
“Well over a million Albertans came together to give us something all too rare these days, a moment of hope,” he said.

He said there are obviously concerns in Alberta about the cost of living, healthcare and education, as there are in the rest of the country, but said those problems don’t get addressed by splitting up the country.
“As so many Albertans have shown us, we don’t fix our problems by turning on each other. We fix them by coming together,” he said.
Lewis blamed Alberta Premier Danielle Smith for the vote even taking place and said she had stoked division.

“The entire process was unnecessary, nobody asked for it. Danielle Smith’s career has been defined by a slow walk towards separation. All of the questions are designed to stoke division in Alberta and she is the one who is responsible for that.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney , building on his written statement earlier, told reporters he was “thrilled” at the referendum result on Canada’s unity.
He spoke to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith this morning about the results and about the devastating accident at CFB Wainwright.
And he pledged to work with all provinces on changes, for example to immigration reform.
Carney did not close the door to constitutional change if necessary, but downplayed the necessity of opening up the country’s foundational governing document as a first resort.

“Look,” he told reporters. “There’s one approach which is to say ‘oh let’s wait until — we’re just going to park the important issues, whether it’s immigration, whether it’s the judiciary, other aspects, let’s just park that unless we have constitutional change’ or ‘let’s work together..”
“Let’s find common solutions now, and then if it were to become necessary — it’s this question of priorities and starting. And this is a government that very much is focused on results for Canadians.

“It’s very focused on working with the provinces. It’s very focused on working with Indigenous peoples and finding solutions now to the issues that our country faces, and really, above all, seizing the many opportunities for Canadians.”
At another point he said, “what I favor is working now pragmatically to common solutions. Constitutional change is difficult. It’s long.”
Take a closer look at the unofficial results for the nine additional referendum questions compared to the main vote in Alberta.
Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre said the Alberta referendum result sent a strong message from the people of the province that “the promise of Canada is worth fighting for.”
He said the result showed that Albertans had “decisively voted for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada.”

But his social media post Tuesday made no mention of the other nine questions on the referendum slate, which had to do with the province taking greater control over immigration and pushing for amendments to the Canadian Constitution—most notably to abolish the Senate.

Speaking ahead of a 2013 Supreme Court of Canada hearing, Poilievre—then minister of state for democratic reform—told reporters that the upper chamber needed to be reformed or abolished in line with Conservative Party policy under prime minister Stephen Harper.
“The Senate must change or vanish,” he said. “The status quo is not acceptable.”
Alberta NDP leader Naheed Nenshi leaves after casting his referendum vote at an advance polling station in Calgary, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026.
Alberta’s opposition NDP leader Naheed Nenshi reacted overnight to the referendum results about holding a vote on separating from Canada.
Nenshi posted a photo of himself against a Canadian flag, with a message of thanks.
“We saved Canada,” he wrote early Tuesday morning. “Now, we save Alberta.”
Recent opinion polls have put Nenshi’s NDP neck-and-neck with Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party.
The next provincial election is scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027, but there is speculation that Smith could take Albertans to the polls soon after the referendum results are counted.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford woke up on the right side of the bed Tuesday morning, saying he was “thrilled by the decisive support Albertans have shown for the country we all love.”
“Alberta voters have overwhelmingly chosen a stronger, more prosperous future for their province by remaining in Canada,” he wrote on X.

But Ford said there is now an obligation on the rest of the country to love-bomb Alberta by building new pipelines, exploiting natural resources and “unleashing the prosperity that will protect the future of Canadians from coast to coast to coast.”

Last summer while at the Calgary Stampede, the Ontario and Alberta premiers stood together to propose construction of a new oil pipeline—the Northern Shield Energy Corridor —running from Hardisty, Alta., to refineries in Sarnia.
Last month, Ford said Ontario taxpayers would back the 3,300-kilometre construction project, which could cost tens of billions of dollars.
Ford referred to this as “the cost of defending Canada’s sovereignty.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney meets Alberta Premier Danielle Smith at his office in Ottawa on May 8.
Plenty will be claiming victory now that Alberta has voted against separatism , but the days and weeks ahead will show what’s been lost, too, with this democracy gambit.

The decisive majority — over 75 per cent with most polls reporting — is a clear win for Mark Carney , whose stock in Alberta has only climbed throughout the referendum campaign. The prime minister does not have to relive the Brexit drama, as he constantly cited as an example Alberta should not follow.
“Albertans chose Canada,” Carney said in a brief statement as the majority became clear.
Albertans have voted in droves to stay in Canada. The result was satisfying for the pro-Canada movement, but separatists say it's just the beginning. (Oct. 20, 2026)

Premier Danielle Smith will be wanting to call this a win for her, too, but what she’s unleashed with this referendum May be hard to put back in the box, including threats to her own leadership of the United Conservative Party.

Even before a single vote was counted, Alberta separatists were saying that their cause has been strengthened by the referendum. In fact, that was the uniting battle cry at the big, final rally for Alberta independence on the weekend.
“Regardless of what happens on Monday, we’ve already won,” Keith Wilson, head of Let Alberta Decide, told the crowd.
Jeffrey Rath, also one of the leading separatist voices, hammered home that same, already-won theme in a lengthy post on X the next day.
“We have forced federal politicians to come to Alberta to help prove how Canadian federalism is failing Albertans,” Rath wrote.
Now they’re coming for Smith, too, he said. “We have forced a federalist provincial government to hold a vote on independence that will force a leadership change of the governing party of Alberta.”
If those voices remain loud, Smith could be in for a rough-and-tumble gathering when the UCP meets next month.

Wilson, in a subdued speech as results were still coming in, told his supporters: “Tonight concludes a campaign, but the conversation about Alberta’s future in Canada and our place in Canada and our role in Canada will continue.” He told one supporter as well: “We’re not giving up.”
So much for Smith’s assertions that this referendum will put to rest the issue.
As for the other nine questions on the ballot, there’s a lot of unfinished business lurking here too, for Alberta and the country.

Albertans were leaning toward Yes on the five immigration questions as polls were reporting, giving Smith some political cover to press Ottawa for more provincial control over who comes to the province. She warned Carney at their joint appearance in Red Deer late last week that other premiers were on her side on this issue.

But the immigration questions in the referendum stirred the waters on an issue that has become volatile, sometimes even dangerous, in many parts of the world right now. Smith’s New Democratic opponents flatly accused her of courting racism. Throughout the campaign, there were periodic reports that immigrants and diverse communities felt less safe because they’d been put on the ballot.
Questions No. 1 through No. 4 sought a mandate to reduce the number of immigrants settled in Alberta and restrict their access to pricey social

Saima Jamal, co-founder of the Calgary Immigrant Support Society, told Global News in late August: “Right now racism and hate is on steroids and I’ve never seen this level of hatred toward immigrant communities.”
Is that the kind of thing that Smith can put back in the box?

Also unresolved on the day after is Alberta’s relationship with Indigenous people, who in large numbers have rejected the whole idea of a referendum being used to haggle over constitutional arrangements that could affect treaty rights.
Whatever Smith believes is settled by Monday’s vote, Alberta-Indigenous relations aren’t among them.

In the larger sense, one is left wondering what this referendum achieved, beyond a vent of Alberta grievances. The 10 questions, in sum, were a grocery list of all the things that’s alleged to be wrong with the province’s place in the federation — the chips on the shoulder. They all but declare that Alberta is getting screwed on the Senate, ON judicial appointments, or on financing for health care and social services.

Every Albertan who voted had to consider that list. Many May have walked away from the ballot box, or the referendum debate overall, feeling more aggrieved, seeing that list in black and white. It’s hard to argue that this venting exercise did anything for Canadian unity.
The problem is that unity is exactly the thing that Canada needs now, in the face of the challenges coming from Donald Trump’s America.
Carney didn’t sugar-coat that reality when he was out making his final pitches in Alberta before the referendum. “This referendum comes at the worst possible time,” he said.

Given all that’s been whipped up during it — from separatism to anti-immigrant sentiments and the relentless hammering away at grievance — the time after the referendum isn’t looking exactly ideal for the times either.
The main question of whether to hold a referendum on Alberta’s independence has resulted in a decisive victory for federalists in the province.
Canada can celebrate that it has been spared an Alberta separation vote with the results of Monday’s referendum — at least one in the near future.
But the other nine questions on the ballot risk causing a federal hangover that could be felt for years to come.

Overshadowed through much of the campaign by the headline threat of the independence movement in Canada’s energy rich province, the other questions put to Albertans deal with immigration and constitutional reform.

Backed by Alberta Premier Danielle Smith , questions No. 1 through No. 4 sought a mandate to reduce the number of immigrants settled in Alberta and restrict their access to pricey social programs like health care and education.

Questions No. 6 through 9 asked whether Alberta should try to amend the Constitution to abolish the Senate, to appoint its own judges, to be able to opt out of federal funding programs and give priority to its own laws in case of conflict with Ottawa.
The other results provide a more troubling glimpse into voters’ satisfaction levels within the Canadian federation.
As of Tuesday morning, eight of the nine questions are backed by majorities that favour a change to the status quo.
Question No. 8, which asks about amending the Constitution to be able to opt out of federal funding programs, continued to be a close-fought battle between voters opposed and in favour.
This shouldn’t come as a complete surprise.

Alberta is, after all, the birthplace of Western alienation: the complaint that Western Canadians drive the national economy but are often overlooked when federal politicians gather in Ottawa to debate issues and pass laws.

Part of that sentiment has been fuelled by the special attention and treatment afforded by the federal government to Quebec with the aim of keeping the momentum and threat of the province’s sovereigntists at bay following independence referendum votes in 1980 and 1995.
Turmoil around immigration and Alberta-Indigenous relations that were unleashed with this referendum May be hard to put back in the box.

The Alberta referendum questions seeking more powers over immigration—particularly Question No. 1, which asks about cutting numbers “to more sustainable levels”— are undoubtedly inspired by the control over immigration that Quebec has negotiated for itself over decades.

Alberta’s push for constitutional amendments will also have taken its inspiration from federal efforts to address Quebec discontent after the 1980 Quebec referendum, in which 60 per cent of Quebecers voted against sovereignty association.

After the votes were counted, then-prime minister Pierre Trudeau pledged in a victory speech to “renew the Canadian federation.” He repatriated the Constitution in 1982, but he did so over the Quebec government’s objections and without the province’s signature.
Prime minister Brian Mulroney’s attempts to make amends with Quebec resulted in two unsuccessful attempts to renegotiate some of the terms of the Canadian Constitution.

The drama and division of those attempts have scared successive federal governments away from trying for their own amendments, whether it was then-Conservative leader Stephen Harper on Senate reform or Justin Trudeau’s pledge to change the Canadian electoral system.
In a podcast interview last week , he said that he “(got) the point about an unelected Senate,” and admitted that “the Constitution is not unamendable.”
“But it requires building a real consensus around what’s necessary to change and why it (should) change and which elements you are going to change,” he told host Ryan Jespersen .

At the same time, Carney has also cast the idea of bickering over the Constitution as a political distraction from the real job at hand, which is bolstering the Canadian economy and diversifying away from the United States.
Carney’s time in power has been focused on clearing away distractions and roadblocks that stand in the way of his government’s agenda.

But Danielle Smith, whose UCP party is being challenged by the Alberta NDP in opinion polls, May welcome the distraction of a battle to amend the Canadian Constitution — particularly now that she is armed with ammunition from the referendum.
An Alberta referendum hot take from one of America’s most prominent Canadian-born political commentators, David Frum.
A writer for The Atlantic and a podcast host, Frum weighed in Tuesday morning and declared that the Alberta referendum vote was U.S. President Donald Trump’s “first midterm defeat.”

The cheeky comment is a likely reference to the segment of Alberta separatists who were attracted—not repelled—by Trump’s calls to make Canada the 51st state as well as reports that organizers of the province’s independence movement held meetings with Republican Party operatives and U.S. State Department officials.
A man walks near an advance voting station during the Alberta Referendum as Albertans head to the polls in Tofield, Alberta, ON October 16, 2026.

Good morning, and welcome back to the Star’s coverage of the Alberta referendum. The results on the main question of whether to hold a referendum on Alberta’s separation from Canada are holding steady this morning, with about 70 per cent of Albertans opting for Canadian unity.
The other nine referendum questions are sending a more nuanced message of frustration within the federation.

With the ballots still being counted, there are clear but narrow majorities who voted yes to questions one through four, which ask whether the Alberta government should take a harder line on immigration.

The ballot questions, which are supported by Premier Danielle Smith’s government, ask about decreasing the number of immigrants who can settle in the province and limiting their access to social programs such as health care and education.

And the early results also indicate that Albertans are evenly divided over questions about whether the government should push for amendments to the Canadian Constitution —a traumatic matter in Canada, which has seen numerous failed efforts to enact constitutional change.

Referendum questions six through nine ask whether Alberta should seek amendments that would allow it to: appoint its own judges; abolish the Senate; opt out of federal funding programs for provincial matters like education and healthcare; and giving priority to provincial laws when there is a conflict with the federal government.
A man registers to vote in a voting station during the Alberta Referendum as Albertans head to the polls in Calgary, Oct. 19, 2026.
Edmonton — A turbulent campaign that pitted federalists against separatists over Alberta’s future in Canada ended with the remain side securing an overwhelming victory.
With votes still being counted on Tuesday morning, about 76 per cent of Albertans voted to remain in Canada and roughly 24 per cent backed a second binding referendum on leaving the country.
At a watch party in Edmonton hosted by the federalist group “Forever Canadian,” a crowd of fewer than 100 jumped to its feet, hugging, cheering and waving Canadian flags as the call was made.
“Canada, Canada, Canada,” the crowd chanted.

The projections came before Elections Alberta had released complete official results. More than 100 polling stations that opened late stayed open past the scheduled closing time, delaying the count until after midnight.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on X that she would address Albertans Tuesday at 8:45 p.m. Eastern time regarding the results “and where our province goes from here.”
“I’m very pleased to see the initial results from Elections Alberta show widespread support for remaining in Canada. Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith wrote.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Mark Carney issued a statement celebrating the results, saying the province had “made a clear choice” in Monday’s vote.
“Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

He said that while all of the results have not yet been counted, “the defining question of separation” has been decided and victory for the federalist camp means that the country can now return to the job of advancing Canada “with renewed purpose and high ambition,” referring to his government’s agenda of increasing international trade and developing infrastructure, mining and energy projects across the country.
He said that Canada was “unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta at its core.”
While federalists celebrated Monday’s victory, many were quick to note that 23 per cent of Albertans choosing the option to hold a vote on separation was not something to cheer about.
“I was hoping it would be like 85 per cent,” Dee Winn, a volunteer with the “Forever Canadian” campaign, told the Star as the early results came in.
Amid the cheers and applause, Thomas Lukaszuk, who spearheaded the federalist group, told the crowd those voters could not be ignored.
“These are Albertans. These are Canadians,” he said from the stage, adding that something had to be done to address what was driving their anger and frustration.
“We cannot go on like this.”

Before the polls even closed, Mitch Sylvestre, a key separatist leader, told a crowd of volunteers and other independence supporters gathered at a nearby Edmonton bar that their movement had become something that was not going to disappear.
“Alberta has changed,” he said.

Monday’s vote took place under the shadow of tragedy after four people were killed and 39 others injured when extreme winds pushed an already burning fire onto troops conducting exercises at CFB Wainwright on Saturday.

Polls opened as scheduled, with some voters in Wainwright worried about what would happen to the base, an integral part of the community’s identity and economy, should Alberta one day separate from Canada.
“This is a federal town,” said Greg Granger, who works in IT at CFB Wainwright.
Elsewhere, the polarization that has taken hold across the province during the referendum campaign was on full display.
Olivia Hughes, an Edmonton resident living with disabilities, walked to a polling station at an Anglican church in the city on Monday, wondering, “Why the f—- do I have to be out here?”
Besides contemplating the impact secession would have on her quality of life, she said: “I’m a Canadian, I’m not just an Albertan.”
“I would like to remain a Canadian, so that’s why I’m here.”
Others arrived feeling fed up.

“I think we’ve been screwed over by the other provinces,” said fellow Edmonton voter Bill Lewis, who cast his ballot at a polling station in one of the city’s strip malls for the option to begin the process of holding a future vote to leave Canada.
“I think our money should stay here instead of us getting nothing and the other provinces getting it all.”
A record-breaking 1.3 million Albertans had already cast their ballots through advance polls or by mail, comprising 43 per cent of the province’s eligible voters.
How Alberta came to this moment is a mix of historic grievance, COVID-fuelled populism and a premier who was unwilling to close the door on separatists.

While Western alienation is nothing new in the country’s largest oil-producing province, successive public opinion polls suggested an uptick in the sentiment after the election of Prime Minister Mark Carney, whose victory was viewed by some as another blow to the deep-blue Conservative province.

Anger had been brewing for years during the tenure of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, whose environmental policies were viewed by many in the province as stymying resource development. Even before that, the Trudeau name triggered distrust among some Albertans, who remembered the legacy of the long-dismantled National Energy Program introduced by his father, former prime minister Pierre Trudeau.

But while Carney has sought to reset relations with Alberta, working with Premier Danielle Smith to advance a new million-barrel-a-day oil pipeline to the West Coast and overhauling federal regulatory processes with the goal of getting more major energy and infrastructure projects off the ground, another movement was brewing in the province.
Independence organizers who entered Alberta’s political arena through opposition to COVID-19 pandemic measures got to work pushing for a referendum.

Sylvestre, the owner of a sporting goods store in Bonnyville, Alta., spent the dead of winter travelling the province collecting 300,000 signatures for a petition under provincial citizen-initiative rules to trigger a referendum on leaving Canada.

Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier in a Progressive Conservative government, was busy collecting tens of thousands of signatures for his own “Forever Canadian” initiative under the same provincial rules in response to the separatist push.
Things came to a head this May when an Alberta judge quashed the separatist petition over concerns about the failure to properly consult First Nations.

One evening in late May, Smith addressed Albertans to announce that her United Conservative Party government would add an independence question to a previously decided set of nine referendum questions focused on taking greater control over immigration and pursuing constitutional reforms such as abolishing the Senate.

That sparked criticism from all corners. Carney called the referendum a “dangerous bluff.” Other premiers panned the move, while federalists in Alberta mobilized supporters who wanted to remain in Canada to turn out and vote, warning that separatism remained a minority view but a vocal and highly motivated one.
Independence leaders also expressed ire at Smith, particularly over her public support for remaining in Canada, viewing it as a betrayal of her party base, where support for independence is popular.
Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney visits supporters of a Vote to Stay event ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty, in Red Deer, Alta., October 16, 2026.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has issued a statement celebrating the Alberta referendum results, saying the province “made a clear choice” in the Monday vote.

He said that while all of the results have not yet been counted, “the defining question of separation” has been decided and victory for the federalist camp means that the country can now return to the job of advancing Canada “with renewed purpose and high ambition,” Carney said, referring to his government’s agenda of increasing international trade and developing infrastructure, mining and energy projects across the country.
Supporters cheer as results begin to display at the pro Canada watch party in Edmonton, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026.
Both CBC News and CTV News are projecting the remain side has won.
CBC made the call, showing the remain side leading with 76.6 per cent of the vote, as compared to 23 per cent for the independence option.

stories.title: Alberta referendum a notable chapter in long history of grievance with Ottawa
stories.summary: While the majority of Albertans opted to stay in Canada, the referendum highlighted grievances towards the federal government that go back nearly a century.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Alberta will remain in Canada following Monday’s historic referendum result , despite hundreds of thousands of votes cast in favour of asking the provincial government to begin the process of separating.

The referendum asked residents 10 government-initiated questions, with the lion’s share of public and political attention focused on the 10th question asking Albertans whether they wanted to remain in Canada or proceed to another, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

While about 76 per cent of voters opted to stay as of early Tuesday morning, the referendum brought to a head grievances in the province towards the federal government that go back nearly a century.

Starting in the 1930s, many Alberta farmers opposed the monopoly the Canadian Wheat Board (CWB) had over wheat and barley prices and their sales.

Established in 1935, for much of its history the CWB was the sole buyer and seller of Prairie wheat and barley destined for export from Canada.

It became illegal for farmers to sell their grains elsewhere in order to facilitate Canadian sales to Britain during the Second World War , at a time when many were struggling to survive following the Great Depression.

Many Alberta grain farmers — viewing their operations as independent commercial businesses rather than state-managed entities — strongly opposed the single-desk system.

They argued the CWB restricted their freedom to sell grain to private buyers , negotiate independent contracts and capture better market prices.

Changes to loosen restrictions were made in later decades until the board was dissolved in 2012.

Anger boiled over in the 1980s when Pierre Trudeau’s National Energy Program (NEP) devastated jobs and investment in the province’s oil and gas sector.

The program kept domestic oil prices below world levels to promote Canadian energy security and increase the federal share of oil revenues.

Opposition led by Peter Lougheed, who served as Alberta premier from 1971 to 1986, viewed the program as an unconstitutional federal intrusion into provincial resource ownership.

The province retaliated by ordering a cut to oil production and suspension of oil sands projects.

Lougheed’s battles with Trudeau over Alberta’s oil revenues and the NEP were legendary, sparking the famous bumper sticker reading: “Let the Eastern bastards freeze in the dark.”

Anger amongst Albertans lingered long after Lougheed and Trudeau developed a grudging friendship and worked together on constitutional reform.

For many Albertans, the NEP became a lasting symbol of federal interference.

The Reform Party of Canada rose to prominence in the late 1980s largely from Western Canadian, and particularly Albertan, frustration with the federal government.

Founded in 1987 by Preston Manning, the party tapped into a belief that Ottawa routinely prioritized the interests of central Canada, especially Ontario and Quebec, over the west.

The Progressive Conservative government of Brian Mulroney alienated many westerners through constitutional debates, particularly the Meech Lake Accord, and decisions such as awarding a major CF-18 maintenance contract to Quebec rather than Manitoba.

Under the slogan “The West Wants In,” Reform advocated greater Western influence in federal politics, Senate reform, fiscal conservatism and decentralization.

In the 1993 federal election, the Reform Party won 52 seats — overwhelmingly in Western Canada — while the governing Progressive Conservatives collapsed.

As feelings of Western alienation began to resurface in 2019, Manning once again issued a warning to politicians about rising separatist sentiment, saying, “There’s real reasons for why people are angry and disillusioned.”

Manning said problems with the energy sector and the inability to get resources to tidewater and world markets were fueling the fire.

More recent grievances included the Justin Trudeau government’s policies on energy investment and public health restrictions during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The anti-Ottawa mood ramped up in 2019, when the United Conservative Party under former premier Jason Kenney came to power in Alberta, capitalizing on discontent over federal rules and policies deemed to impair Alberta’s ability to create wealth, particularly in oil and gas.

Kenney fought for more independence from Ottawa but remained a staunch advocate for the province staying in Confederation.

stories.title: McGill law students petition for convicted murderer to return to studies
stories.summary: Some McGill law students are calling on the university to allow a convicted murderer on day parole to return to his studies amid a growing campus controversy.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Amanda Jelowicki
stories.content:
Some McGill University law students are calling on the school to allow a convicted murderer on day parole to return to his studies, as controversy over his admission continues to divide students.

Jeffrey George Ewert, now in his 60s, began studying in McGill’s law faculty in September. He was convicted in the 1980s of second-degree murder and attempted murder involving violent attacks on two women, one of whom was 15 years old.

Ewert spent 40 years in federal prison and was granted day parole in 2025. News of his studies spread in early October and he has since been barred from campus.

The revelation has prompted sharply divided reactions among students.

McGill student Leah Kropf told Global News “it’s scary and it’s kind of unbelievable,” that many students apply and aren’t accepted, but Ewert was.

Other students have defended Ewert’s opportunity to pursue an education.

“I believe in second chances. I believe in rehabilitation,” McGill student Ines Keita said. “People make mistakes and I also feel like if he got liberated, he has the right to rehab, do something with his life and get an education.”

But student Isabelle Munoz said she isn’t comfortable with the idea. “I would not feel safe being in class with him. I would not feel safe being on campus around him,” she said.

But some students within the law faculty are now pushing for Ewert to be allowed to return. Law student Raymond Johnson-Brown, who met Ewert a year ago, has started a petition urging McGill to allow him to resume his studies. The petition has collected 128 signatures from law students.

“We know that education supports reintegration,” Johnson-Brown said. “I do have faith in the criminal justice system that there are checks and balances to ensure the safety, that if there is any gross misconduct, that he would immediately return to jail,” he said.

McGill told Global News that privacy laws prevented it from discussing individual student cases, but said the safety and security of its students is paramount.

The university also said it would actively review its admissions processes to ensure a similar situation does not happen again.

In a letter sent to students over the weekend, the McGill administration said it remained committed to second chances and the power of education to transform lives. It also said student safety comes first and the matter was being reviewed by the university.

Constitutional lawyer Julius Grey said proper rehabilitation reduces recidivism and argued Ewert should be allowed to continue his studies.

“This man has to be somewhere. He has to be able to earn a living, and I believe that we have to unfortunately be less sensitive about these risks,” Grey said.

stories.title: Montreal man faces massive medical bills after emergency spinal surgery
stories.summary: A Montreal man from the Philippines says he could face more than $1 million in medical bills after undergoing emergency spinal surgery without provincial health coverage.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Dan Spector
stories.content:
A Montreal man from the Philippines says he could face more than $1 million in medical bills after undergoing major spinal surgery without provincial health insurance.

Alvin John Reyes, who came to Canada in 2023 and is living in Montreal on a work permit, underwent back surgery in mid-September after being diagnosed with spinal stenosis.

Alvin is now bedridden and says he will need months of rehabilitation before he is able to walk again. His brother, Allan Reyes, said the family already owes close to $200,000 to the McGill University Health Centre (Muhc).

Alvin’s wife and three children are in Canada on study permits, while his work permit is tied to his wife’s student permit. His family is eligible for government health insurance, but he is not.

Alvin, who says he works in marketing and pays taxes, said he applied three times for coverage through Quebec’s health insurance board, the Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (Ramq). “I got rejected every time,” he told Global News.

Earlier this year, he began experiencing weakness in his legs and eventually had difficulty walking. He went to the emergency room, where he said he had to pay $1,600 because he did not have Ramq coverage.

He was diagnosed with spinal stenosis and was told he needed a major operation. The family says a doctor waived most of the fees associated with the surgery, but Alvin still needed to be hospitalized for a month at a cost of $7,000 a day.

“Money is money. I can always earn it in the future and pay for it,” he said. “But the problem is, if I don’t get to walk, that’s a bigger issue. Because who will pay for my family’s bills?”

He now needs medication, round-the-clock care and as much as six months of rehabilitation, which the family says could cost another $7,000 a day.

His brother said the resulting bill could reach between $1.2 million and $1.4 million.

“It’ll take us like two lifetimes to pay that,” Allan said.

Allan, a Canadian citizen who has been in the country for 16 years, said to help pay for his brother’s care, he sold a house he purchased for his mother.

The brothers said they hope health authorities will agree to cover at least some of the rehabilitation costs. “Sometimes there’s special reasons or special cases that they can give exemptions for,” Alvin said.

The Ramq said in an email to Global News that it does not have discretionary power to make exceptions to the law. The agency outlined its eligibility requirements and said people whose work permits are tied to a spouse’s student permit are not among those eligible.

Immigrant advocate Frantz Andre said cases such as Alvin’s are “definitely more common than we think.” Andre said he believes taxpaying workers such as Alvin should be given more flexibility, but said current anti-immigrant sentiment is pushing policy in the opposite direction.

“It’s only going to get worse,” he said.

Alvin is now advising others in similar situations to purchase adequate private health insurance. His own policy only covers $25,000.

He has also launched a GoFundMe to help cover his expenses.

Alvin said he had dreamed of buying a house in Canada, but his financial future now looks very different. “It looks more like paying a medical bill my entire life.”

Alvin John Reyes, who came to Canada in 2023 and is living in Montreal on a work permit, underwent back surgery in mid-September after being diagnosed with spinal stenosis.

Alvin is now bedridden and says he will need months of rehabilitation before he is able to walk again. His brother, Allan Reyes, said the family already owes close to $200,000 to the McGill University Health Centre (Muhc).

content_blocks.alt: A Montreal man from the Philippines says he could face more than $1 million in medical bills after undergoing emergency spinal surgery without provincial health coverage.
content_blocks.caption: A Montreal man from the Philippines says he could face more than $1 million in medical bills after undergoing emergency spinal surgery without provincial health coverage. Courtesy Alvin John Reyes

content_blocks.text: Alvin’s wife and three children are in Canada on study permits, while his work permit is tied to his wife’s student permit. His family is eligible for government health insurance, but he is not.

Alvin, who says he works in marketing and pays taxes, said he applied three times for coverage through Quebec’s health insurance board, the Régie de l’assurance maladie du Québec (Ramq). “I got rejected every time,” he told Global News.

Earlier this year, he began experiencing weakness in his legs and eventually had difficulty walking. He went to the emergency room, where he said he had to pay $1,600 because he did not have Ramq coverage.

He was diagnosed with spinal stenosis and was told he needed a major operation. The family says a doctor waived most of the fees associated with the surgery, but Alvin still needed to be hospitalized for a month at a cost of $7,000 a day.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'BC on the hook for more than $200M in unpaid medical bills'

content_blocks.text: “Money is money. I can always earn it in the future and pay for it,” he said. “But the problem is, if I don’t get to walk, that’s a bigger issue. Because who will pay for my family’s bills?”
He now needs medication, round-the-clock care and as much as six months of rehabilitation, which the family says could cost another $7,000 a day.
His brother said the resulting bill could reach between $1.2 million and $1.4 million.
“It’ll take us like two lifetimes to pay that,” Allan said.
Allan, a Canadian citizen who has been in the country for 16 years, said to help pay for his brother’s care, he sold a house he purchased for his mother.

The brothers said they hope health authorities will agree to cover at least some of the rehabilitation costs. “Sometimes there’s special reasons or special cases that they can give exemptions for,” Alvin said.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Health Matters: Alberta takes new steps to restrict MAID access'

content_blocks.text: The Ramq said in an email to Global News that it does not have discretionary power to make exceptions to the law. The agency outlined its eligibility requirements and said people whose work permits are tied to a spouse’s student permit are not among those eligible.

Immigrant advocate Frantz Andre said cases such as Alvin’s are “definitely more common than we think.” Andre said he believes taxpaying workers such as Alvin should be given more flexibility, but said current anti-immigrant sentiment is pushing policy in the opposite direction.
“It’s only going to get worse,” he said.
Alvin is now advising others in similar situations to purchase adequate private health insurance. His own policy only covers $25,000.
He has also launched a GoFundMe to help cover his expenses.
Alvin said he had dreamed of buying a house in Canada, but his financial future now looks very different. “It looks more like paying a medical bill my entire life.”

stories.title: We asked Canadians 55 years and older what it’s like to look for employment. Here’s what they said
stories.summary: When Jennifer Kolppanen received an email to visit her school principal’s office at the end of the day in June, she imagined one of two things would happen: Either she gets laid off, or she is asked to split her time between two schools.
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
When Jennifer Kolppanen received an email to visit her school principal’s office at the end of the day in June, she imagined one of two things would happen: Either she gets laid off, or she is asked to split her time between two schools.

She recalled going into shock after being told it was the former.

“They handed me this letter and told me to read it, which I couldn’t. I tried (but) I was so in shock,” the 55-year-old said.

By then, she had been working for 29 years as a library technician and was 16 months away from receiving her pension. Instead, she received a six-month severance and six weeks’ worth of pay in lieu of notice.

While she wasn’t surprised her position was eliminated, she hoped that she would receive an early retirement offer or enough severance to be able to receive her pension.

“I was wrong,” she said.

Before, she had envisioned retiring in the short term and spending her time volunteering. Instead, four months later, Kolppanen was living with her parents and visiting employment advisers for help with job applications.

“I’ve just learned what ‘Linked In’ is but I’m not sure how to use it or if I want to learn,” she wrote in an email.

CTV News asked readers aged 55 and older what it has been like to look for employment as an older person.

Those who responded described grappling with a job market vastly different from the one they had experienced at the beginning of their careers. Others spoke of applying for jobs they felt overqualified for and feeling passed over for younger candidates with less experience. Some spoke to re-entering the job market after being let go, only a few years or less before the age of retirement and having to contend with finding new employment rather than making plans for the golden years.

“I’ve taken 29 years to turn this into a job that I really love doing,” Kolppanen said. “It’s so daunting to think I’m going to have to do that all over again.”

Older Canadians working longer

More older Canadians are staying longer in the workforce, data shared last week by Statistics Canada showed. Those aged 65 and older accounted for 23.2 per cent of the working age population, up from 20.5 per cent in September 2019.

A StatCan report published in April found that the percentage of Canadian seniors, aged 65 and older, rose for the fifth consecutive year to 15.2 per cent in 2025.

“For years, the trend had been the other way,” Rafael Gomez, a professor of employment relations and human resources at University of Toronto, told CTVNews.CA on Thursday.

But in the last decade, the “nature of work” has changed, he said.

“Old jobs were physically taxing” with a lot of “wear-and-tear – literally – on the body,” Gomez said. However, he added today’s jobs have “a longer lifespan” and that “you can work productively for longer in these jobs.”

The elimination of a working-age cap has also meant that people can work beyond the age of 65 and choose when they want to retire.

“So now we had workers who no longer were being pushed out,” he said.

Last week, StatCan also reported that the unemployment rate in September inched up to 6.5 per cent, which means a net 68,300 jobs across the country were lost.

The drop followed a decline of 41,700 jobs in August .

According to the October report, the unemployment rate among people aged 55 and older rose 0.2 percentage points to 5.3 per cent in September.

“If we have rising unemployment, then it stands to reason that even in that group, since they’re more engaged in the labour market, they too will see more unemployment,” he said.

Job-hunting instead of retiring

Louis Labelle, who lives in Ottawa, said she had been laid off in August 2025, two months after turning 65.

Since then, she has interviewed for five other similar roles but hasn’t received an offer.

“If I don’t find a job in the next six months, I will have to give up my apartment and live out of my car,” she wrote in an email. “I’m not in any position to retire.”

Mike Miller, 64, who lives in B.C., said he was “one year from retirement.”

“I have very slim retirement savings,” he said. “I’ve been doing this for over a year.”

Kolppanen had planned to work for two more years before deciding whether to continue or retire.

“I (was) just going to see how I feel,” she said. Her bank adviser had recommended she work for five more years.

She said she had been looking forward to days where she could volunteer if she felt like it, rather than being tied to a working schedule.

“I don’t have those luxuries (anymore),” she said of her current situation.

Passed over for younger candidates

After losing her job in 2017, Celina Mantler, now 58, decided to get her master of business administration degree after being told it would help her advance in her career.

After graduating in 2022, she described repeatedly losing opportunities to “younger people with far less experience and ... less education.”

Labelle stated she was told by an employer that he “typically” hires people with young families.

Gomez said employers are likely to question whether they can hire someone who is at the end of their career with higher salary expectations, while seniors May have to contend with a boss who is much younger than they are.

“The problem for older workers is finding the next job,” he said.

New job screening, requirements

After finding a job listing for the city’s public library, Kolppanen fished out her resume and compared it to common job requirements recently posted .

She realized her resume was outdated, she said, and had to take a few days to work on it. When seeking help with an employment adviser, she found herself “floored” when she was told employers run application documents through an AI screening program.

“They’re going to throw out my resume because AI doesn’t like it?” she recalled asking.

Lisa Bennett, 60, who lives in Ottawa, said she wanted to return to part-time work in early childhood education with 30 years of experience in the field.

When she attempted to reinstate her registration with the College of Early Childhood Education, she said she was denied as the criteria had since changed.

“My registration would still be valid today had fees been maintained,” she wrote in an email. “As a 60-year‑old professional, this feels like unintended age discrimination. Older members are being held to new requirements that did not exist when our credentials were granted."

stories.title: Military lawyer calls for coroner’s inquest into Wainwright tragedy
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says there are 50 investigators on the ground probing how one of the worst peacetime tragedies unfolded at an Alberta military base.
stories.author: Judy Trinh
stories.content:
Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney says there are 50 investigators on the ground probing how one of the worst peacetime tragedies unfolded at an Alberta military base.

On Saturday, four soldiers were killed during a scheduled training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, Alta.

Thirty-nine military members were hospitalized, with 19 people in critical condition.

A battalion of soldiers conducting live-combat training with grenades and artillery was overtaken by a fast-spreading fire whipped by strong winds.

When asked by reporters, if he trusts the military to investigate itself, Carney said, “Absolutely.”

“We will give them all the resources that they need … We will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy as expeditiously and transparently as necessary,” Carney said after paying tribute in the House of Commons to the four soldiers who died.

Sgt. Morgan Wong, and privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark were killed during a training exercise.

The young men, who were serving with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were preparing to deploy to Latvia next year.

Military lawyer and former soldier, Col. Michel Drapeau says the scope of the tragedy demands more than an internal investigation, it deserves an inquiry “under the glare of the public.”

Drapeau says the military cannot investigate itself because the Department of National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces “lacks the impartiality, neutrality, objectivity and disinterest” to analyze the evidence and report on the outcome.

Drapeau said a coroner’s inquest is an ideal mechanism to get answers.

“Let there be an open audience. People can attend. People can listen and people can testify.”

He said that soldiers May not tell Armed Forces investigators the full story of what they saw or experienced because they’re nervous or afraid of being blamed. Only when testimony is given under oath, and there’s cross examination can the “bare truth come out,” Drapeau said in an interview with CTV News.

“The purpose of this is to prevent recurrence, to prevent (future) fatalities. We need to get to the bottom of it - not assign blame.”

Drapeau, whose firm has represented soldiers and veterans in legal battles with the Department of National Defence, is also concerned a large swath of the public could be “suspicious” of the findings if an investigation is not done by an independent actor.

What defence officials have said at this point is that the battalion was doing “live-fire training.”

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, the commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said the group was practising a simulated attack, while a fire was burning about a kilometre away was being monitored by range control.

Rutland said the cause of that fire was under investigation – and that there was a variety of ordnance moving through the area. He said the source could have been “grenade launchers, grenades, small arms, ammunition.”

“Quite frankly it could have been any of that or none of it,” Rutland told reporters one day after the tragedy.

The military official said that the battalion didn’t see a fire, but then around 4 p.m., within “30 seconds to a minute … there was a fire right on top of them.”

“This was a very uncommon occurrence. That being said, the reason why there was an investigation is to decide if it was a preventable, non-preventable, or to what extent something was preventable.” Rutland said.

On Oct. 17, the forecast from Environment Canada warned of strong winds that could gust up to 90 kilometres an hour.

But according to the hourly data report for the airfield at CFB Wainwright , wind gusts at 4 p.m. on that day registered at 42 km/h.

Drapeau, whose firm has represented soldiers and veterans in legal battles with the Department of National Defence, is also concerned a large swath of the public could be “suspicious” of the findings if an investigation is not done by an independent actor.
What defence officials have said at this point is that the battalion was doing “live-fire training.”

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, the commander of the 1st Canadian Division, said the group was practising a simulated attack, while a fire was burning about a kilometre away was being monitored by range control.

Rutland said the cause of that fire was under investigation – and that there was a variety of ordnance moving through the area. He said the source could have been “grenade launchers, grenades, small arms, ammunition.”
“Quite frankly it could have been any of that or none of it,” Rutland told reporters one day after the tragedy.
The military official said that the battalion didn’t see a fire, but then around 4 p.m., within “30 seconds to a minute … there was a fire right on top of them.”

“This was a very uncommon occurrence. That being said, the reason why there was an investigation is to decide if it was a preventable, non-preventable, or to what extent something was preventable.” Rutland said.
On Oct. 17, the forecast from Environment Canada warned of strong winds that could gust up to 90 kilometres an hour.
But according to the hourly data report for the airfield at CFB Wainwright , wind gusts at 4 p.m. on that day registered at 42 km/h.

stories.title: A look at past referendums in Canada as Albertans reject future separation vote
stories.summary: Albertans voted in a referendum Monday against separation. In early results, about 76 per cent of said they wanted the province to stay in Canada, while 24 per cent said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Albertans voted in a referendum Monday against separation. In early results, about 76 per cent said they wanted the province to stay in Canada, while 24 per cent said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Here’s a look at some of the other referendums held across Canada:

2021 — Alberta on daylight time

The province asked residents whether it should adopt year-round daylight time — the time often used across Canada in the summer — to put an end to twice-yearly clock changes.

Out of more than 1 million votes, 50.2 per cent were against the idea, while 48.8 per cent were in favour of ditching clock changes.

Premier Danielle Smith announced this year that starting Nov. 1, the province is adopting year-round daylight time.

She said it’s to gauge opinion and that most people will agree. She said if she’s wrong, the government could put the matter to a vote in 2027.

2019 — Prince Edward Island electoral reform

Voters weighed in on electoral reform alongside the provincial election.

It followed similar votes in 2016 and 2005, which both failed to eliminate the voting practice known as “first past the post.”

The referendum asked: “Should Prince Edward Island change its voting system to a mixed member proportional voting system?”

The threshold for a win in either direction would have been 17, but neither side was able to secure that number — 13 districts voted against, while 14 voted in favour.

2018 — British Columbia electoral reform

After failed votes in 2009 and 2005, the province held a third referendum on electoral reform.

Out of all ballots received, 61.3 per cent voted to keep first past the post, while proportional representation got 38.7 per cent.

2007 — Ontario electoral reform

The referendum asked voters to chose between the existing first-past-the-post or the mixed-member proportional systems.

Voters overwhelmingly rejected mixed-member proportional representation, with Elections Ontario figures showing roughly 1.5 million people voted for change, while nearly 2.7 million voted against it.

2001 — New Brunswick video lottery terminals

Voters were asked whether the province should ban VLTs, following a 1999 campaign promise by former premier Bernard Lord.

“Should the province of New Brunswick continue to permit the legal and regulated operation of video gaming devices, commonly known as video lottery terminals?”

About 53 per cent were in favour of keeping VLTs, while 47 per cent were opposed.

New Brunswick was the first to allow VLTs after Ottawa, in 1985, allowed provinces and territories to operate the machines.

1997 — Newfoundland education

Newfoundlanders voted in on the churches’ role in the province’s education system.

The referendum asked: “Do you support a single school system where all children, regardless of their religious affiliation, attend the same schools where opportunities for religious education and observances are provided?”

More than 70 per cent of voters wanted to create a non-denominational public education system still allowing religious instruction and observance, ending the church-run school system.

In a similar vote two years earlier, voters narrowly approved the government’s plan to reform the church-run education system.

1995 — Quebec sovereignty

A razor-thin majority rejected the idea of the province leaving Confederation and becoming its own country.

In a dramatic campaign, the sovereigntist side came from behind to take a lead in the polls in the final weeks before the vote. In the end, 50.58 per cent voted no.

A previous vote in 1980 also rejected sovereignty.

1992 — Charlottetown accord

Ottawa asked Canadians to vote on constitutional changes that would have given Quebec greater powers to protect its culture. It would have also created a “Triple-E” senate — equal, elected and effective.

Canadians voted against the accord, with 54 per cent opposed and 45 per cent in favour.

The majority of voters in Ontario, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Newfoundland supported the accord. Those in Quebec, Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia opposed it.

1980 — Quebec sovereignty-association

Quebec’s government asked voters to give it a mandate to negotiate “sovereignty-association” with the rest of Canada. It would have given the province more powers but maintain an economic partnership with Canada.

Quebecers rejected the question, with 60 per cent of voters opposed and 40 per cent in favour.

1942 — Conscription

The federal government asked Canadians to vote on conscription during the Second World War.

Canadians voted to support the measure, with 64 per cent in favour.

Quebecers, however, were overwhelmingly opposed to conscription, with 73 per cent voting against it.

1898 — Alcohol Prohibition

In Canada’s first federal referendum, Ottawa had asked Canadians to vote on prohibiting alcohol.

The yes side narrowly won with 51 per cent in favour of the measure, and 49 per cent opposed it.

With such a close result, Prime Minister Wilfrid Laurier decided there wasn’t enough support for legislating Prohibition.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

Aaron Sousa, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Albertans split in early returns on remaining 9 referendum questions
stories.summary: Edmonton - While Albertans roundly rejected separation in Monday’s referendum, results were decidedly closer in early returns on nine other questions.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says her government will be moving ahead with sweeping changes to immigration after Monday’s referendum.

But, in a TV address to Albertans Tuesday, she hinted it could be some time before her government takes action.

The remaining ballots were still being tallied late Tuesday, but it appears Albertans will approve eight of the nine immigration and constitutional questions Smith put to voters, while also overwhelmingly rejecting separation.

The constitutional questions appear to be coming down to the wire, but Smith said Albertans have given her a mandate to take action on immigration.

Those questions ask whether Alberta should have more say on who comes to the province to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations — and perhaps introduce fees — on temporary residents who seek access to health care and education.

She acknowledged there were more ballots to count but said it appeared the yes vote would win out. As of Tuesday evening, four of the immigration proposals were leaning towards the yes side with single-digit majorities. The fifth proposal to require proof of citizenship at provincial election polls had nearly two-thirds approval.

Smith said the mandate voters have given her will see the province take greater control over immigration to stabilize population growth and make sure Albertans are prioritized for jobs.

“We will be pursuing the reforms approved by Albertans through this referendum in the coming months and years ahead,” Smith said.

The premier didn’t promise action on the constitutional questions, saying she was waiting for Elections Alberta’s final count. The agency has said all ballots will be counted by Wednesday.

The Constitution questions sought Albertans’ blessing for Smith to lobby provincial counterparts to assist in amending the Constitution to reduce Ottawa’s power over provinces and to abolish the Senate.

As of Tuesday evening, the yes option was leading on three of those four questions by razor-thin margins with almost all polls reporting.

“We will know the answer to those questions in a couple of days,” Smith said.

The lone question with the no side in the lead was whether provinces should be allowed to opt out of federal programs without losing federal funding.

Smith has said she needs a yes to the nine questions so she can better bargain with Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Carney told reporters in Ottawa that the federal government will “take into account” the votes on the nine questions but cautioned that constitutional change can be a “difficult” and drawn-out process.

Critics have called the immigration questions anti-immigrant dog-whistling, and some, including Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi, say the results seem to be an underwhelming mandate for the premier and called on her to move on.

“If she wanted a mandate, she should have been able to get 85 per cent on questions like this, and she was unable to carry the day,” Nenshi told reporters earlier Tuesday. He called on Smith to stop scapegoating immigrants and “be a premier for all Albertans.”

Colin Aitchison, a former United Conservative Party press secretary turned government relations consultant, said the result was a mandate for the premier.

“Governments get elected on less than 50 per cent in this country, and then they move forward with implementing a mandate,” said Aitchison, with Enterprise Canada.

Smith’s government has yet to give specifics on how the proposals would work or how they would be implemented.

Avnish Nanda, a lawyer who had campaigned against the immigration proposals, said he was shocked by the results as he was expecting the questions to pass with much larger margins.

“We thought we would be blown out,” Nanda said.

Nanda said he didn’t think the results represent the will of Albertans. He pointed to polls that suggest some voters were confused by the wording of the questions. He said they May have also been misled by the government advertising campaign.

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said he was proud to see a majority of voters in his city reject the immigration proposals, saying it affirms Calgary as a welcoming place for newcomers.

Farkas also said Ottawa was already acting to address immigration concerns. “That, to me, kind of leads me to ask, ‘What was the point of this whole exercise to begin with?’” Farkas said.

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack also called for Smith to ditch the immigration questions.

“I don’t want our neighbours to feel like they’re not welcome in our city,” Knack said late Monday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

— With files from Lisa Johnson in Edmonton and Dayne Patterson in Calgary

content_blocks.html: EDMONTON - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says her government will be moving ahead with sweeping changes to immigration after Monday’s referendum.

content_blocks.text: But, in a TV address to Albertans Tuesday, she hinted it could be some time before her government takes action.
content_blocks.html: But, in a TV address to Albertans Tuesday, she hinted it could be some time before her government takes action.

content_blocks.text: The remaining ballots were still being tallied late Tuesday, but it appears Albertans will approve eight of the nine immigration and constitutional questions Smith put to voters, while also overwhelmingly rejecting separation.
content_blocks.html: The remaining ballots were still being tallied late Tuesday, but it appears Albertans will approve eight of the nine immigration and constitutional questions Smith put to voters, while also overwhelmingly rejecting separation.

content_blocks.text: The constitutional questions appear to be coming down to the wire, but Smith said Albertans have given her a mandate to take action on immigration.
content_blocks.html: The constitutional questions appear to be coming down to the wire, but Smith said Albertans have given her a mandate to take action on immigration.

content_blocks.text: Those questions ask whether Alberta should have more say on who comes to the province to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations — and perhaps introduce fees — on temporary residents who seek access to health care and education.
content_blocks.html: Those questions ask whether Alberta should have more say on who comes to the province to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations — and perhaps introduce fees — on temporary residents who seek access to health care and education.

content_blocks.text: She acknowledged there were more ballots to count but said it appeared the yes vote would win out. As of Tuesday evening, four of the immigration proposals were leaning towards the yes side with single-digit majorities. The fifth proposal to require proof of citizenship at provincial election polls had nearly two-thirds approval.

content_blocks.text: Smith said the mandate voters have given her will see the province take greater control over immigration to stabilize population growth and make sure Albertans are prioritized for jobs.

content_blocks.text: “We will be pursuing the reforms approved by Albertans through this referendum in the coming months and years ahead,” Smith said.

stories.title: 'Very much an open question': Carney's West Coast pipeline project could run into legal pitfalls
stories.summary: The pipeline, called Pacific Link, is the first project to be designated within the national interest under the government's Bill C-5.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government has promised to have shovels in the ground in the less than a year on the construction of a new pipeline to the West Coast, but lawyers and legal academics are warning the project could face legal challenges in court.

The pipeline, called Pacific Link, is the first project to be designated within the national interest under the federal government’s Bill C-5, also known at the Building Canada Act.

The legislation allows Cabinet to give projects in the national interest a fast-tracked regulatory process.

Robin Junger, counsel on Indigenous law and the environment at McMillan LP, said he is anticipating court challenges on two fronts: the Crown’s duty to consult under Section 35 of the Constitution Act and the federally legislated United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (Undrip).

“They passed a law that talks about consulting First Nations before they designate a project in the national interest, and then the statute talks about consulting First Nations and development of conditions,” said Junger.

“But that’s a different way of approving projects than previously; I’ll say it’s at best untested, and whether that’s going to complicate potential legal challenges is very much an open question,” he added.

Junger said the federal government could end up reviewing the major projects legislation if there is uncertainty there.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the national interest designation of Pacific Link earlier this month, promising the country will remain one of high standards, but not necessarily slow decisions.

The newly formed Major Projects Office undertook consultations with over 130 Indigenous communities between July 3 to Sept. 18, before the designation was announced. The MPO will begin its review of the project in early 2027, with public hearings held by the commission of the Canada Energy Regulator. The MPO is expected to finalize a conditions document by Sept. 1, 2027.

First Nations have been clear that they view Bill C-5 as a violation of the Undrip. In July, Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse-Nepinak said that fast-tracking projects will not come at the expense of First Nations’ rights.

“A one-year timeline, principally designed to attract investment, subordinates the honour of the Crown to commercial imperatives,” she said, during her opening remarks at the Afn’s annual meeting.

A note published by Osler, Hoskin & Harcourt LLP last December warned that the consultation process under Bill C-5 could be challenged in court.

“An accelerated BCA (Building Canada Act) process May result in legal challenges where Indigenous consultation is perceived to be truncated or otherwise inadequate to fulfill the federal government’s obligations,” the report said, adding that proponents can mitigate these risks by consulting early, proactively and responsively to Indigenous communities.

“However, if a project is designated as an (National Interest) Project and faces Indigenous opposition, there is a risk a court will find that Crown consultation prior to designation of the (National Interest) Project was inadequate,” the report added.

Dwight Newman, professor of law at the University of Saskatchewan, said there is ample case law about the duty to consult, which the courts have made clear does not give Indigenous communities final say on whether a project moves forward.

However, the federally legislated Undrip has added an extra layer of uncertainty, which was first passed by the federal government in 2021. This is because Undrip includes Free, Prior and Informed Consent (Fpic), which allows Indigenous communities to say no to a project development.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser told reporters last year that Undrip does not allow “a blanket veto power” to Indigenous communities, but later apologized for his comments after criticism, noting that speaking about Undrip in that way makes an assumption that Indigenous people and the federal government are working against each other.

Newman said the federally legislated Undrip does not go as far as the one in British Columbia, where it has become an provincial election issue, but is still having an impact on case law across the country.

Newman said a recent Federal Court of Appeal decision last Friday, in the case of Canadian Nuclear Laboratories and the Kebaowek First Nation in Quebec, has determined that Undrip does not change the duty to consult.

“The lower court in that case had said that the duty to consult turned into free, prior, and informed consent because Canada adopted the UN Declaration Act, and the Federal Court of Appeal has overturned that reasoning, and they’ve said the duty to consult doctrine hasn’t changed,” said Newman.

However, the case could go to the Supreme Court of Canada, which means the issues surrounding Undrip are not finalized.

Junger said it’s hard to say how Undrip will court challenges going forward.

“Is the federal government going to rescind the Undrip Act, or is it going 60 miles an hour into a brick wall?”

“Or am I wrong? Those are all possibilities, but they are the possibilities, and that’s separate from the duty to consult,” he added.

Newman, like Junger, noted that the court challenges could also come in the initial phase of consultations that took place prior to the national interest designation.

Heather Exner-Pirot, senior fellow at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, said the federal government would have already run a risk assessment on the likelihood of court challenges facing the project and are preparing accordingly.

“I think everyone knew that there would be court challenges,” she said. “I think it was anticipated, and they prepared for it, especially on the designation process.”

That's a different way of approving projects than previously ... and whether that's going to complicate potential legal challenges is very much an open question

Last week, Major Projects Office CEO Dawn Farrell had a candid moment with the BC Assembly of First Nations, noting that the frustrations over lack of consultations on the Pacific Link project made her feel “like Canada is never going to work” according to a report by the Canadian Press.

Farrell said members of her team had “very, very big scars” while working on the Trans Mountain Expansion Project.

“The projects that we have to deliver out of our office have to achieve your rights. We have to make sure that we go through your processes,” Farrell said.

“We can’t just make stuff up. The courts will just come and overturn the projects and we’ll be like Canada’s always been, 10, 15 years, dragging stuff around in the ditch and not getting it done and wasting time and money and resources, and your time and your people’s resources. We can’t keep doing that.”

Exner-Pirot said the federal government has learned its lesson from the court challenges against TMX, with the final case dismissed in 2020.

The decision from the Federal Court of Appeal concluded that “consultation means that Canada consider and address the rights claimed by Indigenous peoples in a meaningful way” but cannot be used to create a “de facto veto right.”

Exner-Pirot said the federal government has also learned from its court losses, including in the case of Enbridge’s Northern Gateway Project, which ultimately led to the federal government’s decision not to move forward.

“There’s a lot more knowns this time,” she said. “And regulators are conservative, and they are slow, but part of it is because they’re hyper aware that the durability of the approval once they do give it must be airtight, and it’s a disaster for a regulator’s decision to be overturned because the regulator did not meet the Crown’s obligations.”

However, Exner-Pirot admitted that Undrip certainly could complicate matters in the courts, noting that Undrip was not federal law during the TMX court decision in 2020.

Newman said ultimately no project development is without legal risk, and the federal government has decided this pipeline is worth facing those pitfalls.

“It would be difficult to say there are no legal risks because there are some legal risks there, but sometimes governments have to take legal risks, and they’re saying this is in the national interest, and they need to make some decisions in the national interest,” said Newman.

“And sometimes there are legal risks attached to doing that, but they’re making the decision that they’re going to do that,” he added.

“The projects that we have to deliver out of our office have to achieve your rights. We have to make sure that we go through your processes,” Farrell said.

“We can’t just make stuff up. The courts will just come and overturn the projects and we’ll be like Canada’s always been, 10, 15 years, dragging stuff around in the ditch and not getting it done and wasting time and money and resources, and your time and your people’s resources. We can’t keep doing that.”
Exner-Pirot said the federal government has learned its lesson from the court challenges against TMX, with the final case dismissed in 2020.

The decision from the Federal Court of Appeal concluded that “consultation means that Canada consider and address the rights claimed by Indigenous peoples in a meaningful way” but cannot be used to create a “de facto veto right.”

Exner-Pirot said the federal government has also learned from its court losses, including in the case of Enbridge’s Northern Gateway Project, which ultimately led to the federal government’s decision not to move forward.

“There’s a lot more knowns this time,” she said. “And regulators are conservative, and they are slow, but part of it is because they’re hyper aware that the durability of the approval once they do give it must be airtight, and it’s a disaster for a regulator’s decision to be overturned because the regulator did not meet the Crown’s obligations.”
However, Exner-Pirot admitted that Undrip certainly could complicate matters in the courts, noting that Undrip was not federal law during the TMX court decision in 2020.
Newman said ultimately no project development is without legal risk, and the federal government has decided this pipeline is worth facing those pitfalls.

“It would be difficult to say there are no legal risks because there are some legal risks there, but sometimes governments have to take legal risks, and they’re saying this is in the national interest, and they need to make some decisions in the national interest,” said Newman.
“And sometimes there are legal risks attached to doing that, but they’re making the decision that they’re going to do that,” he added.
