stories.title: What U.S. media are saying about Alberta’s referendum: Trump’s ‘first midterm defeat’ — and a win for Carney
stories.summary: American news outlets are examining Alberta’s rejection of separation against the backdrop of Donald Trump’s annexation threats and the province’s political ties to the U.S.
stories.author: Samm Mohibuddin
stories.content:
Alberta’s rejection of separation is making headlines south of the border, where American news outlets are casting the referendum results as another test of Canadian unity in the shadow of U.S. President Donald Trump’s increasingly strained relationship with Canada .

Preliminary results from Monday’s referendum showed roughly 76 per cent of Albertans voting to remain part of Canada, while about 24 per cent supported a second binding referendum on independence.

For some American news outlets, the referendum has become a story that’s more than just Alberta’s complex relationship with Ottawa and the rest of the country, with coverage examining the influence of Trump’s politics on the separatist movement, Premier Danielle Smith’s position the issue and whether the independence campaign can survive such a decisive defeat.

Albertans have voted in droves to stay in Canada. The result was satisfying for the pro-Canada movement, but separatists say it's just the beginning. (Oct. 20, 2026)

Here’s what they’re saying:

Canadian-born American political commentator David Frum saw Alberta’s rejection of separation as a political loss for Trump.

The Atlantic writer and podcast host called the result Trump’s “first midterm defeat” in a post on X Tuesday morning.

Frum’s comment is likely a reference to reports that organizers of the province’s independence movement held meetings with Republican Party operatives and U.S. State Department officials.

Alberta’s separatists had sought U.S. support, but on Monday voters delivered a “definitive blow” against it, CNN reported Tuesday .

Journalists Max Saltman and Lex Harvey traced the movement’s American connections, including reported meetings between separatist organizers and members of Trump’s administration.

At a 2025 rally, some supporters wore red hats modelled on Trump’s Make America Great Again merchandise.

CNN also revisited an earlier interview with separatist Jeffrey Rath, who said Trump’s administration represented the movement’s best opportunity to secure American recognition of an independent Alberta.

But the U.S. president’s tariffs and repeated suggestions that Canada become the “51st state” also fuelled a wave of Canadian patriotism.

Prime Minister Mark Carney attends a national unity rally in Red Deer, Alta., alongside, from left, Monte Solberg, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, and former premier Ed Stelmach on Friday.

For the Washington Post, the referendum result was a victory for Canadian unity at a time when relations with Washington remain strained.

The newspaper’s story placed the vote against the backdrop of Trump’s trade war and annexation threats, highlighting Prime Minister Mark Carney’s warnings about threats to Canada’s sovereignty.

At a campaign rally last week, Carney warned of outside forces “working to break us so they can own us.”

Residents react after Alberta rejects move toward independence from Canada in victory for Mark Carney. (Oct. 20, 2026)

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith found herself in an awkward political position long before the ballots were counted.

She opposed separation but called the referendum, a position that drew criticism from both independence supporters and Albertans who did not want the question put to a vote.

That dilemma was central to the New York Times’ report, headlined “Voters in Oil-Rich Alberta Reject Leaving Canada.”

Smith now faces the challenge of keeping her United Conservative Party together while addressing the frustrations that helped drive the separatist campaign.

While Albertans rejected the proposed separation process, the movement’s reported dealings with Washington remained part of the story.

Axios referenced reported meetings between Alberta separatist leaders and U.S. officials , along with comments from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent describing Alberta as a natural partner for the United States.

Those connections have raised concerns in Ottawa, where officials have faced questions about possible foreign influence in the province’s independence campaign.

Axios also highlighted polling suggesting the separatist movement could remain a force in Alberta politics even after its defeat in the referendum.

Edmonton supporters of the Forever Canadian group, who want Alberta to remain in Canada, react after Alberta residents voted to remain part of Canada in a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty on Monday.

Some Alberta separatists see more common ground with their neighbours south of the border than with politicians in Ottawa.

That was one of the themes explored in a Fox News report published Monday, before the referendum results were known.

Journalist Christopher Guly spoke with separatist organizer Cory Morgan, who argued that Albertans shared American attitudes toward individual freedoms and property rights.

Morgan suggested many residents would rather have a beer with someone from Great Falls, Mont., than someone from Ottawa.

But a closer cultural relationship with the United States did not necessarily mean separatists wanted to join it. Morgan told Fox News that only a vocal minority supported Alberta becoming America’s 51st state, and that many were unhappy with Trump.

With files from Allan Woods

stories.title: Answering your questions about the Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Richard Warnica will take your questions on Alberta’s referendum, from the vote to remain in Canada to what comes next.
stories.author: Richard Warnica
stories.content:
The result has already set off a wave of reaction across the country. Wondering what the result says about the other nine questions? Curious how the separatist movement will continue? Want to know what it means for the provincial government’s relationship with the rest of the country?

That’s where senior opinion writer Richard Warnica comes in. Join him on Wednesday, Oct. 21 at 11 a.m. for a live Q&A on all things Alberta referendum, including the results, the political fallout and what to watch for next.

Here’s how to submit questions and join the chat:

The live Q&A will take place in the comment section below. There is no live stream video. Richard will instead respond to questions by replying to individual comments.

To ask a question, log into our site or app and submit you query via the comment section. When your question is answered, there will be a button below your comment that says “Show reply.” Click to see the reporter’s response.

Any reader can ask a question as long as they are registered and logged in to the Star. Nonregistered readers can still view the live chat.

Like all conversations on the Star, questions and comments are subject to moderation and the Star’s Code of Conduct.

Richard Warnica is a Toronto-based senior opinion writer for the Star. Reach him via email: rwarnica@thestar.CA.

stories.title: Respiratory Therapy graduate helps explore AI’s potential to improve lung ultrasound diagnosis
stories.summary: Welcome to Spotl
stories.content:
Welcome to Spotlight, a new digital content series showcasing high-impact, good news stories from the Fanshawe community.

For Keya Patel, the impact of a research project she began as a student has taken on new meaning now that she is working as a registered respiratory therapist at William Osler Health System.

“It truly is a feeling like no other to be able to stand on both sides of innovation—both as a clinician who sees the challenges at the bedside and as a researcher contributing to potential solutions,” says Patel, a 2026 graduate of Fanshawe's Respiratory Therapy program.

Patel was one of 55 Respiratory Therapy students who participated in a multi-phase applied research project exploring whether artificial intelligence could help clinicians interpret lung ultrasound images more accurately and confidently.

The project, “Evaluating the Effectiveness of AI Assisted Technology for Detecting Lung Sliding on Lung Ultrasound,” examined the use of AI-assisted interpretation to identify lung sliding, an important indicator of a healthy lung.

Point-of-care lung ultrasound is increasingly used in emergency medicine because it can allow clinicians to rapidly assess serious and potentially life-threatening conditions at the bedside, often without waiting for traditional imaging such as X-rays or CT scans.

For Patel, the research had particular meaning because of what she has experienced in clinical practice.

“In my clinical practice, I have seen first-hand the consequences of suboptimal diagnostics, particularly in time-sensitive situations, which has given me a strong appreciation for the need to advance technology at the bedside,” she says.

Those experiences stayed with her throughout more than a year of working on the study and helped connect the research to the realities of patient care.

The first phase of the project, conducted in partnership with biotechnology engineering researchers at the University of Waterloo, evaluated a virtual reality training tool designed to teach students how to obtain accurate diagnostic images of the lungs.

The second phase, conducted in collaboration with physicians at London Health Sciences Centre, focused on clinical image interpretation. Students completed 100 lung ultrasound interpretations without AI assistance and another 100 with AI support.

The results showed significant improvements in diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity and overall confidence when AI-assisted technology was used.

“After more than a year of working on the study, seeing such promising results has been incredibly fulfilling,” says Patel. “What is especially exciting is recognizing the possibilities that extend beyond the study itself—the potential for this technology to improve diagnostic accuracy, support clinical decision-making, enhance patient safety, and ultimately contribute to better patient outcomes.”

The project also gave students an opportunity to experience research from beginning to end, including ethics approval, data collection, analysis and knowledge dissemination.

That hands-on experience is a key part of Fanshawe's Student–Faculty Research Committee, says Julie Brown, faculty and coordinator of the Respiratory Therapy program.

“This project is a great example of how applied research can directly enhance both student learning and patient care,” says Brown. “By evaluating AI-assisted interpretation of lung ultrasound, our students were exposed to emerging clinical technologies while contributing to research that has real relevance for rapid, high-stakes respiratory assessment.”

The experience continued beyond the research itself.

In May, Patel and fellow Respiratory Therapy student Brady Hurley presented the study's findings at the Canadian Society of Respiratory Therapists’ National Forum. Hurley delivered an oral presentation, while Patel presented the research poster, representing Fanshawe alongside respiratory therapy professionals, researchers and educators from across Canada.

“It was a proud moment for us to showcase our findings and contribute to a community so dedicated to advancing respiratory therapy through research and innovation,” says Patel.

The experience represented an opportunity to contribute to the future of her profession while gaining a deeper understanding of how research can influence patient care.

The experience also encouraged her to pursue additional research opportunities and explore how respiratory therapists can play a greater role in advancing innovation and improving patient care.

“Being able to contribute to that kind of progress is incredibly meaningful,” she says.

For any media inquiries, please reach out to mediainquiries@fanshawec.CA

content_blocks.text: In May, Patel and fellow Respiratory Therapy student Brady Hurley presented the study's findings at the Canadian Society of Respiratory Therapists’ National Forum. Hurley delivered an oral presentation, while Patel presented the research poster, representing Fanshawe alongside respiratory therapy professionals, researchers and educators from across Canada.

content_blocks.text: “It was a proud moment for us to showcase our findings and contribute to a community so dedicated to advancing respiratory therapy through research and innovation,” says Patel.

content_blocks.text: The experience also encouraged her to pursue additional research opportunities and explore how respiratory therapists can play a greater role in advancing innovation and improving patient care.

stories.title: 5 ways Canada can take on the social media giants to make the internet safer for kids
stories.summary: “You've got to start looking at business disruption; you’ve got to start looking at access to market."
stories.author: Omar Mosleh
stories.content:
In the brave new world of ubiquitous smartphones, artificial intelligence chatbots and social media tech giants operating with impunity, many parents are grappling with the question of how we protect our kids online.

On Tuesday at the MaRS Centre, the Star’s Raisa Patel hosted advocates, researchers and policy experts Diana Fox Carney, Beeban Kidron and Ava Smithing to discuss regulating a digital world that one panellist described as having “less rules than an air fryer.”

Here are five key takeaways.

Protecting children from online harms is often framed as the responsibility of politicians and parents to build a wall around negligent social media platforms.

We need a law that prioritizes the protection of children over profit. We need clear rules that hold companies accountable when they fail to

Kidron made the case that, with some guidance, kids can recognize online harms, sharing an anecdote of a child who grabbed a mic at an event and yelled, “I passed my exam because they turned off TikTok notifications at night!”

Kidron said the Age Appropriate Design Code, which she helped shape and became part of the U.K.’s Data Protection Bill , includes standards for how social media companies should operate, such as restricting geolocation for youth and turning off targeted ads by default.

Of the 15 standards, 12 were directly inspired by comments she heard from youth — “It was their experience of life that made me understand what was necessary to design it differently.”

One of the overarching themes of the panel discussion is that no single country can take on the tech giants, with Smithing remarking that “companies are acting as a nation that has a seat at the table” — and May be more wealthy than a nation-state.

Social media companies rarely introduce protective features unless compelled to and have not used their profits to proactively make their platforms safer, several panellists said.

Fox Carney said she was “shocked” when she learned reports of how the Tumbler Ridge shooter consulted with an OpenAI chatbot on how to perpetrate a mass shooting. Although internal employees flagged alarming content on the perpetrator’s account, that information didn’t make it to law enforcement until after the mass shooting.

Here’s hoping a new lawsuit against OpenAI inspires Ottawa to find the courage to challenge Big

If anything good can come out of this, it’s progress in the way these companies flag and address these issues, Fox Carney said.

Fox Carney said during a recent conversation that the first lady of Romania said protecting children online “is a shared responsibility and it must be met with shared standards.”

“Surely we should be moving in a direction where we can negotiate internationally on some baseline standards,” Fox Carney said.

The U.K. Online Safety Act sets out legal and financial consequences for companies that fail to protect users, especially children, from harmful and illegal content.

Kidron said Canada can learn from the U.K.’s approach to enforcement, which she nonetheless believes could be stronger. She said governments need to recognize that for companies with billions at their disposal, fines can be a price of doing business.

“You’ve got to start looking at business disruption; you’ve got to start looking at access to market,” Kidron said.

Toronto Star Editor-in-Chief Nicole MacIntyre speaks following the panel discussion.

While the panellists acknowledged the importance of social media companies being legally required to remove harmful and illegal content, they emphasized that it’s equally important to target the inherent design features that make social media platforms addictive.

Smithing cited the approach of California’s recently passed Bill 1709, which prohibits certain functions for minors such as infinite scrolling, autoplay and algorithm-driven recommendation feeds that can suggest inappropriate content.

“Instead of banning children from being able to access platforms, it bans platforms from being able to access children,” Smithing said.

Kidron added that protective features need to be built into the platforms, and the onus shouldn’t be on parents to find them and toggle them on.

“There is phenomenal evidence that optional tools are not used, but by default settings absolutely were,” Kidron said.

It’s a common refrain that parents need to know what their kids are up to online. But parents playing the role of enforcer can result in an “enormously difficult relationship” between parent and child, Fox Carney said.

“We set rules, but we don’t want to be constant police in our house,” Fox Carney said.

Parents can’t do it alone, Kidron added. Governments need to act, but sometimes simply setting a positive example can affect children’s relationships to their devices. Kidron said in her time speaking to youth, one of the most frequent answers when asked what is most important to them is, “Can you ask our parents to put their phones down?”

stories.title: CFB Wainwright’s live-fire drills went against guidance for high-risk fire months
stories.summary: The base’s safety rules raise questions about the blaze that killed four soldiers during late-afternoon exercises.
stories.author: Alex Ballingall
stories.content:
Ottawa—The military should hold shooting drills in the early morning to prevent dangerous fires during the “high-risk” month of October, according to CFB Wainwright’s own safety rules — a revelation that raises more questions about the blaze that killed four soldiers and injured dozens during late-afternoon training exercises at the army base Saturday.

CFB Wainwright’s “Range Standing Orders,” which the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) provided to the Star on Tuesday, say units at the base should plan to practise shooting before about 10 a.m. between August and October, when the “fire hazard is normally low enough to permit the firing of most ammunition.”

A high-ranking officer describing the deadly incident to reporters this weekend, however, said the army responded to a “serious” grass fire that started inside the base’s training area — where soldiers were practising with grenades and other weapons — at around 4 p.m. MT on Saturday.

The Department of National Defence declined to answer questions from the Star on Tuesday, including why the exercises were held in the afternoon, citing ongoing investigations conducted by the military’s investigation service, along with health officials in Alberta, the RCMP and military police. Prime Minister Mark Carney said a day earlier that the “original cause” of the fire is still not known.

Four Canadian soldiers killed in a fast-moving fire during a training exercise in Alberta over the weekend are being remembered by their families

“As with any investigation of this nature, time is needed to establish a complete understanding of the facts,” said defence spokesperson Laura McIntyre-Grills in an emailed statement.

“The investigation remains active, and commenting on specific details at this stage would be inappropriate.”

Mike Flannigan, a professor of emergency management and fire science at Thompson Rivers University, said the fact that exercises were held in the afternoon during a high-risk month for fires, when the base’s own safety rules advise against that, is a red flag that “raises all sorts of questions.” Mornings are generally safer, he said, because of lower temperatures and gentler winds.

Flannigan said he also wonders why training exercises proceeded during what he deems to have been textbook conditions for rapidly spreading grassfires on the Alberta prairie.

As Flannigan explained, the autumn months are riskier for fires in the region. This year in particular saw a wet spring that caused more grass to grow — meaning there was more fuel to burn when conditions are drier in the fall, he added.

Weather conditions Saturday were also hazardous for fires, he said. A cold front in the afternoon caused the wind to pick up and change direction, Flannigan said, creating ideal conditions for a fire to spread rapidly.

He noted that Environment Canada released a wind warning , and that the federal government’s Canadian Wildland Fire Information System determined the “fire weather index” that measures risk around Wainwright was “extreme” shortly after 1 p.m. MT on Saturday.

Data from Nasa satellites captured at 2:17 p.m. MT also show heat signatures that indicate a fire in the area, Flannigan said.

“It was a classic situation of a very active day — or at least afternoon — burning period, with the strong, gusty winds shifting direction with the cold front (and) the grass being so dry,” Flannigan said.

“This is prime time for grass fires. And, yeah, we had a deadly one.”

On Parliament Hill, Defence Minister David McGuinty said 33 injured soldiers remain in hospitals, down from 39 on Sunday, stating that burn victims, their families and health-care workers have been “traumatized.”

“This is not the moment for, I think, me or for us as a government to be speaking about the merits of the circumstances of what did or did not happen through this tragic incident,” McGuinty said, declining to answer questions about the circumstances of the fire.

Speaking to the Star in Edmonton on Tuesday, Emergency Preparedness Minister Eleanor Olszewski said some of the injured soldiers have burns on more than 40 per cent of their bodies, which will require “significant rehabilitation” and support.

Bruce Moncur, a retired army corporal and advocate for veterans, said the magnitude of the tragedy at CFB Wainwright should spur the Canadian Armed Forces to develop stronger safety protocols, especially because of climate change. Currently, different bases have different “standing orders” for training safety, which Moncur said could mean some units have more stringent protocols than others.

“There’s a lapse in the system that needs to be fixed,” Moncur said.

The safety orders for CFB Wainwright discuss how vegetation can “ignite readily and spread rapidly, endangering troops and destroying equipment.” The base updates “fire hazard condition” signs every day based on the perceived risk. At an “extreme” level, the base does not allow the use of pyrotechnic tracers that make visible trails behind ammunition or white phosphorus “at any time,” the orders say. Units are also supposed to have brooms and shovels “on site” to help with ground cover firefighting.

Meanwhile, the orders for CFB Petawawa in Ontario include a longer list of restrictions when fire risk is deemed “extreme.” This includes restrictions for training with grenades, explosives and different types of ammunition. That base also has an extra risk level called “extreme plus” that prohibits the firing of “any ammunition of any type.”

Documents obtained through an Access to Information request show the military was in the process of changing its overall safety programs late last year after identifying “systemic gaps.” The documents say there were 27 different safety programs “without a unified framework or co-ordinated governance,” which led to “duplication, inefficiencies and unclear Authorities, Responsibilities, and Accountabilities.”

This situation “increases the likelihood of preventable incidents” like “accidental death, injury, illness,” the documents say.

The Department of National Defence did not respond to questions Tuesday about why fire safety protocols differ on CAF bases, or whether its changes to overall safety programs will create uniform fire prevention rules.

Meanwhile, the orders for CFB Petawawa in Ontario include a longer list of restrictions when fire risk is deemed “extreme.” This includes restrictions for training with grenades, explosives and different types of ammunition. That base also has an extra risk level called “extreme plus” that prohibits the firing of “any ammunition of any type.”

Documents obtained through an Access to Information request show the military was in the process of changing its overall safety programs late last year after identifying “systemic gaps.” The documents say there were 27 different safety programs “without a unified framework or co-ordinated governance,” which led to “duplication, inefficiencies and unclear Authorities, Responsibilities, and Accountabilities.”
This situation “increases the likelihood of preventable incidents” like “accidental death, injury, illness,” the documents say.

The Department of National Defence did not respond to questions Tuesday about why fire safety protocols differ on CAF bases, or whether its changes to overall safety programs will create uniform fire prevention rules.

stories.title: Air Canada adds $30 fee for phone bookings
stories.summary: Travellers who book an Air Canada flight via its call centre should brace for an extra charge of $30 per passenger, as the airline encourages customers to opt for its “digital tools” instead.
stories.author: Ethan Morneau
stories.content:
A Canadian airline is putting a price on phone calls.

Travellers who book an Air Canada flight via its call centre should brace for an extra charge of $30 per passenger, as the airline encourages customers to opt for its “digital tools” instead.

The new fee — which came into effect on Oct. 15 — does not apply to customers who purchase tickets via the Air Canada website or app.

But for those who do call to reserve, the fee is non-refundable, even after cancelling a ticket or booking, according to Air Canada. For a booking with two passengers, the fee would equal $60.

“The booking fee will appear as its own charge … not included in the airfare or carrier-imposed charges associated with your ticket,” the airline says on its webpage announcing the fee .

Air Canada is highlighting its “easy self-serve options,” encouraging customers to use its website or app to book flights.

“Using these digital tools for everyday travel needs helps reduce wait times and allows our Contact Centre agents to focus their expertise on situations that require personalized support,” it says.

Some customers exempt from fee

Call agents remain available over the phone for bookings — and some customers can forego the additional fee, which already applied to Aeroplan flight reward bookings made by phone.

“Customers who require specialized care and support, including those with accessibility needs, are exempt…” Air Canada says.

“There is also no change to the support available to you, and no booking fee will apply if your trip is affected by a delay, cancellation or other travel disruption,” the airline adds on its website.

“The booking fee will continue to apply for Aeroplan flight reward bookings made through our Contact Centre.”

Customers can still call Air Canada for help with existing reservations, travel disruptions and other questions without paying the new fee.

Other Canadian airlines, including WestJet and Flair , already charge a service fee for bookings made over the phone.

stories.title: B.C. soldier who died at CFB Wainwright ‘loved his army family’, mom says
stories.summary: His mother told Global News that her son wouldn't want anyone to dwell on his death, but to pray for his fellow wounded soldiers.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Grace Ke
stories.content:
The deadly fire at a Canadian military base in Alberta on Saturday claimed the lives of four Canadian Armed Forces members, including two from B.C.

Private Aidan Goulding was only 23 years old.

His mother told Global News that her son wouldn’t want anyone to dwell on his death, but to pray for his fellow wounded soldiers.

That’s the kind of man Aidan was, she said.h

Losing Aidan has left a huge hole in our family,” Sonia Monk said.

“He was the one who made us laugh and made us proud and made us incredibly resourceful.

We can rest in the thought that he died with his brothers. He loved his army family just as much as he loved us. I’m thankful that every conversation we had there was an ‘I love you’ at the end.”

Aidan was from North Vancouver and served with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

His brother, Wylder, said Aidan inspired him and that they weren’t just brothers, they were best friends.

“My beautiful brother, no one will ever truly understand the bond Aidan and I shared,” Wylder said.

“You could walk into a room and light it up with his big bright eyes and his contagious laugh. He had a way of making everything brighter just by being there.”

Nineteen-year-old Private Hayden Lykkemark was from Langley and also served with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

Officials say a grass fire quickly overwhelmed soldiers at the base on Saturday as a sudden change in wind direction and strength expanded the fire over a large area. Investigators say it could be weeks before details of how the fire started can be determined.

Dozens were injured in the incident.

Goulding’s family says their thoughts are with those still recovering.

-with files from Ariel Rabinovitch

stories.title: Ex-husband of Steven Galloway’s accuser testifies in defamation trial
stories.summary: Woman refused to go to police after she told him that Galloway put his hands around her neck, ex-husband said in testimony
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
The ex-husband of a woman who accused author Steven Galloway of sexual assault and harassment testified that she told him that Mr. Galloway had put his hands around her neck while the two were on his sailboat, but that she refused to file a police report or let her partner “go have a little talk with him.”

The woman, who is known as A.B. because of a publication ban on her name, had said she wasn’t going to the authorities and instead would take care of the alleged incident herself, her ex-husband testified on Monday in B.C. Supreme Court.

“She said she was going to ‘destroy him,’ were her direct words,” said the ex-husband, who was called as a witness by Mr. Galloway’s legal team.

The Globe and Mail is not naming the ex-husband because of the publication ban on A.B.’s identity.

His testimony was part of a defamation trial Mr. Galloway brought against the woman and three others who later repeated her allegations that he sexually assaulted and sexually harassed her. Mr. Galloway, a bestselling author who was head of the University of British Columbia’s creative writing program, was suspended from that role in November, 2015, amid an investigation into the allegations.

He was dismissed the following year after a retired judge hired by UBC to investigate A.B.’s claims found he had sexually harassed her and other instances of misconduct leading to his firing, but did not find that he sexually assaulted the woman.

A.B.’s ex-husband testified that he had wanted to confront Mr. Galloway about “a pass at my wife,” but she was worried he would get into a fight and convinced him otherwise.

He testified that the pair married in 2011, separated in 2014 and divorced some years later. A.B.’s ex-husband did not put a date on the alleged sailboat incident, but the court heard earlier this month that A.B. and Mr. Galloway had a two-year affair and that she later alleged three instances of sexual assault.

Court heard that she alleged in a complaint to UBC that he grabbed her by the throat, kissed her and threw her up against the bed in the bow when she tried to escape during a visit to his sailboat in False Creek in the spring of 2011. Mr. Galloway testified this was false and that the boat was too small to throw anyone into its covered bow without seriously injuring them.

A.B.’s ex-husband began his testimony explaining how he met Mr. Galloway when his then-wife was attending the creative writing program and they would all go drinking at a legion on Vancouver’s hip Main Street. In the early days, the married couple also received tickets to Vancouver Canucks games from the author and professor, who she viewed as nerdy, her ex-husband testified.

He said in the spring of 2013, he drove A.B. to Banff so she could attend a two-week writing workshop, and that Mr. Galloway was her planned ride back to Vancouver. Then, he said, he got a frantic call from A.B. asking him to come pick her up because she was very angry with Mr. Galloway, but she wouldn’t explain further beyond saying he was being “an asshole” and “wasn’t paying any attention to her.” He recalled driving all day and arriving in Banff to meet A.B. socializing with her writing cohort and Mr. Galloway, whom he said he bought a scotch to have a word with.

“I gave him a scowl and walked away,” A.B.’s ex-husband testified.

He told the court he didn’t find out about A.B.’s affair until her allegations of sexual assault went public when the university suspended Mr. Galloway, kicking off an online firestorm and sparking CanLit controversy.

Earlier Monday, bestselling Canadian novelist and UBC creative writing professor Timothy Taylor testified about an “unprecedented” meeting in November, 2015, before Mr. Galloway’s suspension, where faculty at the program were told of allegations made against him by a student. Mr. Taylor recalled being one of nine people at the Sunday afternoon meeting held at the home of a fellow professor, Linda Svendsen.

Mr. Galloway, who was then chair of the program, but in Ohio for a speaking engagement, was not present and was unaware the meeting was taking place. Mr. Taylor testified that at that meeting, attendees were told about sexual-assault allegations made by A.B., and played two voicemails Mr. Galloway had left her.

The messages, Mr. Taylor testified, were presented in way that suggested they were “statements of culpability in the rape allegations they had just heard.”

The faculty were told that another former student, Chelsea Rooney, had been dispatched to find other students or former students who also had allegations against Mr. Galloway. Mr. Taylor said those at the meeting were told seven other women had come forward with similar allegations.

By the time another meeting was called the next day at UBC, that number had ballooned to 19 others with allegations.

“It struck me that Ms. Rooney was carrying out her duties with some enthusiasm,” Mr. Taylor told the court.

After the close of proceedings on Monday, A.B.’s ex-husband was seen outside the courtroom with one arm wrapped tightly around Mr. Galloway’s shoulders, the pair locked together in what appeared to be an intense conversation.

His testimony was part of a defamation trial Mr. Galloway brought against the woman and three others who later repeated her allegations that he sexually assaulted and sexually harassed her. Mr. Galloway, a bestselling author who was head of the University of British Columbia’s creative writing program, was suspended from that role in November, 2015, amid an investigation into the allegations.

He was dismissed the following year after a retired judge hired by UBC to investigate A.B.’s claims found he had sexually harassed her and other instances of misconduct leading to his firing, but did not find that he sexually assaulted the woman.
A.B.’s ex-husband testified that he had wanted to confront Mr. Galloway about “a pass at my wife,” but she was worried he would get into a fight and convinced him otherwise.

He testified that the pair married in 2011, separated in 2014 and divorced some years later. A.B.’s ex-husband did not put a date on the alleged sailboat incident, but the court heard earlier this month that A.B. and Mr. Galloway had a two-year affair and that she later alleged three instances of sexual assault.

Court heard that she alleged in a complaint to UBC that he grabbed her by the throat, kissed her and threw her up against the bed in the bow when she tried to escape during a visit to his sailboat in False Creek in the spring of 2011. Mr. Galloway testified this was false and that the boat was too small to throw anyone into its covered bow without seriously injuring them.

A.B.’s ex-husband began his testimony explaining how he met Mr. Galloway when his then-wife was attending the creative writing program and they would all go drinking at a legion on Vancouver’s hip Main Street. In the early days, the married couple also received tickets to Vancouver Canucks games from the author and professor, who she viewed as nerdy, her ex-husband testified.

He said in the spring of 2013, he drove A.B. to Banff so she could attend a two-week writing workshop, and that Mr. Galloway was her planned ride back to Vancouver. Then, he said, he got a frantic call from A.B. asking him to come pick her up because she was very angry with Mr. Galloway, but she wouldn’t explain further beyond saying he was being “an asshole” and “wasn’t paying any attention to her.” He recalled driving all day and arriving in Banff to meet A.B. socializing with her writing cohort and Mr. Galloway, whom he said he bought a scotch to have a word with.
“I gave him a scowl and walked away,” A.B.’s ex-husband testified.

He told the court he didn’t find out about A.B.’s affair until her allegations of sexual assault went public when the university suspended Mr. Galloway, kicking off an online firestorm and sparking CanLit controversy.

Earlier Monday, bestselling Canadian novelist and UBC creative writing professor Timothy Taylor testified about an “unprecedented” meeting in November, 2015, before Mr. Galloway’s suspension, where faculty at the program were told of allegations made against him by a student. Mr. Taylor recalled being one of nine people at the Sunday afternoon meeting held at the home of a fellow professor, Linda Svendsen.

Mr. Galloway, who was then chair of the program, but in Ohio for a speaking engagement, was not present and was unaware the meeting was taking place. Mr. Taylor testified that at that meeting, attendees were told about sexual-assault allegations made by A.B., and played two voicemails Mr. Galloway had left her.
The messages, Mr. Taylor testified, were presented in way that suggested they were “statements of culpability in the rape allegations they had just heard.”

The faculty were told that another former student, Chelsea Rooney, had been dispatched to find other students or former students who also had allegations against Mr. Galloway. Mr. Taylor said those at the meeting were told seven other women had come forward with similar allegations.
By the time another meeting was called the next day at UBC, that number had ballooned to 19 others with allegations.
“It struck me that Ms. Rooney was carrying out her duties with some enthusiasm,” Mr. Taylor told the court.

After the close of proceedings on Monday, A.B.’s ex-husband was seen outside the courtroom with one arm wrapped tightly around Mr. Galloway’s shoulders, the pair locked together in what appeared to be an intense conversation.

stories.title: Stevenson resurrects BRT debate about north and west routes, Morgan refutes claim
stories.summary: Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson would tap the brakes on work underway at city hall that lays the groundwork to potentially expand London’s Bus Rapid Transit system with routes in the north and west parts of the city.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson would tap the brakes on work underway at city hall that lays the groundwork to potentially expand London’s Bus Rapid Transit system with routes in the north and west parts of the city.

“BRT 2.0 is already moving through the planning process,” Stevenson warned at the beginning of her campaign announcement.

She held up documents from a Request for Pre-Qualification procurement process seeking a consultant to do preliminary design, determine property requirements, update cost estimates, and implementation planning.

The anticipated study schedule runs from Fall 2026 to Fall 2027.

“I’m calling for a pause on further commitments to the north and west BRT expansion until Londoners have the costs, the traffic impacts and a real opportunity to weigh the alternatives,” Stevenson announced while standing in the middle of a transit stop along the yet-to-be-completed East London Link route.

Specifically she called for the following steps before Council decides on a path forward:

Full cost disclosure covering existing commitments, proposed expansion, confirmed funding, and exposure to overruns.

A coordinated construction plan addressing traffic, business access, emergency routes, and overlapping roadwork.

Costed alternatives and public input including frequency, express service, and better connections to jobs and growing neighbourhoods

“Josh Morgan is all about bike lanes and BRT, with the goal of getting people out of their cars, and yet the BRT business case only predicted a 5% increase in ridership,” Stevenson emphasized.

However, incumbent mayoral candidate Josh Morgan emphasized that a public decision to extend the BRT system would come after the consultants’ reports are finished.

Morgan pointed to the 25-year Mobility Master Plan (MMP) approved by council this term.

“At best this is a misunderstand of the process, and at worst it’s just an irresponsible way to try to plan transit in the city,” Morgan said about Stevenson’s announcement. “This is part of the Master Mobility Plan, an integrated plan that is not just for rapid transit, or conventional transit, but how we move cars and how we build active transportation across the city.”

“I know it was approved in the Master Mobility Plan, but I don’t know that Londoners are really on board with this,” explained Stevenson. “When I got elected, people were shocked that we were moving forward with the BRT. They thought that they’d voted no to it at election time.”

The 2018 municipal election was dominated by debate about BRT, and whether London should accept provincial and federal funding for the mega-project.

stories.title: NDP Leader Eby vows not to use Wainwright tragedy for political gain
stories.summary: Eby’s promise follows criticism from the BC Conservatives
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Tensions rose on the campaign trail in British Columbia on Monday as B.C. NDP Leader David Eby scrambled to explain comments he made earlier in the day about the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, which followed suggestions that some BC Conservatives harbour separatist sentiments.

BC Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson called the remarks unacceptable.

Later in the day speaking in Hope, B.C., Mr. Eby said he didn’t use the tragedy for political gain and will steer clear of the topic through to voting day.

“Let me say unreservedly I would never, ever use the sacrifice of these young men, the grief of their families for political advantage to attack another party,” Mr. Eby said.

Earlier, he referenced the loss of the four soldiers lives in the fire as being “our true heroes” who had put their lives on the line to defend Canada.

“What we can do for them is stand up for a united Canada, to stand up for our country,” he said.

During the same appearance, he drew a contrast with three Conservative candidates – Bryan Tepper, Heather Maahs and David Williams – who the NDP said are present in openly separatist Facebooks groups, including the BC Prosperity Project advocacy group, which is associated with an Alberta group advancing sovereignty.

“They are enabling and legitimizing a fringe political project in British Columba to try and separate us from Canada, and that is how you end up with a referendum on separation,” Mr. Eby said.

But hours later, Mr. Eby acknowledged that Mr. Doerkson had criticized Mr. Eby for using the horrific events in Alberta for political purposes.

And that’s when Mr. Eby sought to clarify his commentary.

Mr. Doerkson said that his party “unequivocally” stands for a strong and united Canada.

“That is who I am, that is who our team is, and no desperate attack from David Eby will change it,” Mr. Doerkson said in a statement,

“Invoking soldiers we lost this weekend in an attempt to save his own job is beyond the pale. Their sacrifice belongs to their families and to our country, never to a premier’s re-election campaign. This is a pathetic, desperate distraction from his record.”

The BC Conservatives did not respond to an e-mailed request for comment regarding Mr. Eby’s allegations. E-mailed requests for comment from the three candidates were not returned.

The back and forth played out as Albertans went to the polls to decide whether the province should pursue separation through a future binding referendum.

Also, in the House of Commons, MPs held a moment of silence and adjourned the House of Commons for the day in honour of the victims of the fire.

Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke of the four soldiers killed. “These were sons, brothers, partners, and friends. Young men with bright futures who chose to serve our country and who died in that cause. We will honour them always.”

B.C.’s advanced polls are open through Wednesday and the general provincial election is Saturday.

stories.title: In just minutes, tiny Wainwright hospital became scene of horrors and heroism
stories.summary: The small town’s 20-bed hospital transformed into something resembling a war-zone trauma centre
stories.author: Jana G. Pruden, Pippa Norman
stories.content:
Brandon Simmons heard the Code Orange announced in the hallways on Saturday afternoon.

“Code orange, attention everyone. Code orange, all units.”

Mr. Simmons, who became quadriplegic after a truck accident and lives in the long-term care area of the Wainwright Health Centre, then watched as the hospital roared into action. Nurses began preparing medical supplies and lining up stretchers and gurneys and machines around the entrance, then down the hallways of the small community hospital.

When a friend told Mr. Simmons there had been an explosion at the military base, he wheeled outside and tucked himself into a corner near the emergency doors, out of the way of people coming and going, and sheltered from a wind so strong it was bending trees near the hospital almost in half.

Mr. Simmons was recording video as the first vehicles arrived with injured soldiers from the base. It didn’t take long for him to see the scope of the tragedy that had occurred, and get a sense of what was coming.

“I knew that hell was about to break loose,” he says.

Mayor Bruce Pugh calls the Health Centre “our little Wainwright hospital,” a small facility in a small town, where the people working May personally know the patients they’re working on. Even if the hospital had been completely empty, and it wasn’t, there are only 20 acute care and surgical beds. The disaster for which doctors and nurses were bracing on Sunday afternoon would bring double – or even triple – that number of injured.

The Department of National Defence has said that around 4 p.m. a grass fire that had been burning for hours on the base rapidly changed direction toward personnel that were taking part in live-fire exercises.

The first vehicle to pull up to the hospital was a white SUV, which parked in the emergency bay at 4:11 p.m. Mr. Simmons’s video shows four men in army greens emerging, and moving quickly but carefully into the hospital. Two had their pants hanging in tatters below the knee.

A large military truck pulled up next.

Military personnel unloaded one person and carried them into the hospital on a stretcher. Someone was screaming. Another victim, limping into the hospital himself on burned legs. Another, wrapped in a foil blanket. Another, unmoving on a gurney. Someone was moaning. The wind blew pillows and sheets onto the gravel.

And then ambulances, one after the other, after the other.

At some point, Mr. Simmons turned the camera away.

“I didn’t want to even have it on film,” Mr. Simmons said. “I didn’t even want to see it with my own eyes.”

Dr. John Damian Paton-Gay was on-call for the Stars air ambulance service on Saturday night, when he got a call that help was needed in Wainwright.

The wind was so strong it wasn’t clear whether they’d even be able to fly, but a shift in the weather allowed them to get off the ground in Edmonton with a helicopter full of supplies.

They landed at the Wainwright hospital 45 minutes later to an almost unbelievable scene.

By the time Dr. Paton-Gay arrived, the injured from CFB Wainwright had already filled up the tiny emergency department and were overflowing into the rest of the small facility.

He saw injured people in every corner and upstairs. About 30 patients crammed into a small space, with staff moving quickly around them. A scene, he says, “that would make a medical TV show look fairly tame.”

Burns are measured both in severity and surface area. The injuries Dr. Paton-Gay saw on Saturday evening had no specific patterns, but a consistently high total body surface area burned. This type of injury meant the conditions of the patients were deteriorating rapidly.

“All of the personnel there knew that that was the case,” he said. “They knew they had to move through the first wave of injured very quickly and prepare for the next ones who were going to get sicker. That was very palpable. The sense of urgency was very clear.”

Even as a specialist working in critical care and trauma for almost a decade, the scene was unlike anything he’d ever seen. It was more like a “mass casualty that would happen in a war or a natural disaster,” he said.

Nurses and doctors sped to the hospital. Throughout the evening, help kept coming. Medical supplies were brought from other communities by truck, medical equipment flown in by helicopter, and additional hands arrived from the sky, as paratroopers landed in the next - door football field.

The injured were stabilized and then sent by ambulance or air to other hospitals around Alberta and Saskatchewan.

As of Monday, there were four soldiers dead and 39 others injured, 19 of those in critical condition.

Mr. Pugh acknowledges the health centre itself was “built for a different time and place,” and that the medical needs of the area have long outgrown the building. Local officials in the town of 7,000 have been working to get a new hospital built for nearly 20 years. It’s the place where Mr. Pugh was born, where all his children were born, and where his parents died. A place where friends and family work.

“But how could you prepare for an event like the one that happened on Saturday?” he added.

Mr. Pugh says he was told that none of the injured died at the hospital in Wainwright and that all of the victims were transported alive to bigger hospital facilities to continue the care. He toured the facility privately, away from the cameras and media, ON Monday to thank those who came to the soldiers’ aid, with federal dignitaries who made the visit.

He said he is praying none of them have to go through something like that again and is hoping that they can look back at what they did with pride.

“I hope, in a sense, some of them will be able to look back and say, “You know what? We did it.”

Long before the paratroopers landed and the last ambulance sped away, Mr. Simmons stopped recording and went back to his room, inside the long-term care area of the hospital. He has posted some of his videos online, but not that one.

“You can hear the guy in the back crying and screaming. Those are our strongest people,” he said. “Those are the sounds that will never get out of my head. No matter if I delete that stuff.”

With a file by Stephanie Chambers and Matthew Scace

stories.title: Two charged, 127 kg of cocaine seized at Ambassador Bridge: Cbsa
stories.summary: Canada Border Services Agency says two men were charged after the seizure of 127 kilograms of suspected cocaine at Ambassador Bridge border crossing in Windsor, Ont., last month.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
Canada Border Services Agency says two men were charged after the seizure of 127 kilograms of suspected cocaine at Ambassador Bridge border crossing in Windsor, Ont., last month.

The Cbsa alleges the drug was seized from a commercial truck arriving from the United States after it was referred for a secondary examination on Sept. 11.

The federal agency says officers discovered the cocaine in the truck’s trailer with the help of a detector dog.

Officials say Cbsa officers arrested a 61-year-old and a 41-year-old, both from Mississauga, and transferred them to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

They say both suspects were charged with the importation and possession cocaine for the purpose of trafficking by the Mounties.

The Cbsa says its southern Ontario region has seized 1.67 metric tonnes of cocaine so far this year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Retired teacher faces historical sexual assault trial
stories.summary: A London courtroom heard on Monday that Murray MacDonald, 68, was a biology teacher and swimming coach at Central Second School in London between 1985 and June 1986.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
A London courtroom heard on Monday that Murray MacDonald, 68, was a biology teacher and swimming coach at Central Second School in London between 1985 and June 1986.

When testifying she told the court that when she was in grade 11 she went to The Bavarian, a one-time bar in Cherryhill Mall on Oxford Street West.

She said she got in using fake ID and that once there she ran into MacDonald. “I remember him buying drinks...more than one drink,” she said. “I had no interest in this person, we had no relationship.”

She said near the end of the night, MacDonald offered to drive her home and when they got to her apartment building she said, “He drove me to the far left end of the parking lot and it was pretty dark.”

While fighting back tears on the stand she said, “All of a sudden he was all over me, hands up my shirt and hands down my pants...I remember feeling frozen.”

She then said she was forced to perform a sexual act. “It just seemed it was over very quickly...I got out of the car as fast as possible... I went to the bathroom and made myself throw up.”

The woman who was on a fast track to complete high school said the alleged incident changed her life. “I just remember being terrified...I knew I couldn’t tell my parents, I couldn’t tell the school...I’m going to be blamed and marked,” she added. “My life just fell apart. I never swam again, I never did anything again.”

The woman said she transferred to other high schools before attending university but that the night would always haunt her. “It didn’t go away so I had to address it finally...I didn’t want to be a victim.”

Then years later while living in another city she looked MacDonald up on the College of Teachers registry and in 2024 she contacted police.

“I just wanted him to turn in his licence and I want him to apologize to me because I lost about a decade of my life.”

Seated next to his defence lawyer Lakin Afolabi, MacDonald has plead not guilty to sexual assault.

The court has heard that the female complainant is expected to be the only witness to be called by the Crown.

The trial resumes on Tuesday.

stories.title: Amira Elghawaby launches portal to turn Muslim research into policy briefs
stories.summary: Online hub from ex-envoy offers community groups, journalists and politicians short, usable summaries of studies on Canadian Muslims
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
When the Carney government pulled the plug on her role as the Special Representative on Combating Islamophobia in February, Amira Elghawaby walked away, feeling the weight of unfinished business.

In Ottawa, the former cabinet adviser had raised awareness within government and through public campaigns about the scourge of Muslim hate. She commissioned research and wrote a seminal guide on Islamophobia.

But despite the research from her and others, in the form of numerous reports and policy recommendations made to the federal government, little seemed to change.

Meanwhile, she has seen and spoken publicly about disturbing reports of hate. In recent months, shots were fired at a Winnipeg mosque, a fake severed, bloodied hand was thrown into a Montreal mosque and an imam was attacked in Victoria, B.C., and left with a fractured jaw.

Elghawaby has launched a global research and policy portal — said to be the first of its kind dedicated to research on Muslim communities — that will publish available studies on Muslims and make them accessible for community members and elected officials by using the recommendations in the studies to create policy briefs.

Elghawaby spoke to the Star just before her office released a new guide on understanding and addressing Islamophobia in Canada.

The resource will help community members and policymakers find information in digestible bits they can use to help keep the issues in the spotlight.

“We keep saying the same things, and official studies come out to say them, but nobody remembers,” Elghawaby said. “And nobody is keeping anybody accountable for that.”

The Muslim Communities Research Observatory (Mcro) portal, called macro for short, goes live Friday. It will be a global hub, a one-stop shop for advocacy groups who May “not even be aware of what research is out there” and for academics who “struggle with knowledge mobilization.”

“This is about raising the ability to ask for policy changes that are fully rooted in the evidence,” she said.

The site will be an important platform to disseminate a new five-year survey of Muslims in Canada by the University of Toronto’s Institute of Islamic Studies on social issues, faith and belonging that will also be announced Tuesday.

The last research on Muslim identities was the landmark Environics Survey in 2016, in which a question was, “Do Muslims want to embrace Canadian values or Muslim values?” said lead author Anver Emon. In this survey, researchers did away with that binary and found a majority of Muslims and non-Muslims saying Muslims in Canada want to adopt both Canadian and Muslim values.

It also found that while first-generation Muslim immigrants would overwhelmingly choose to immigrate to Canada again, nearly half (47.5 per cent) of second- and later-generation Canadian Muslims would choose to live in another country over concerns of affordability and inequality. The study reflects the perceptions of 903 Muslim households and 1,072 non-Muslim households across Canada, making it the largest sample of Canadian Muslims surveyed to date, Emon said.

Mcro is an ideal partner for the dissemination of research, said Emon, because, “as academics, we’re not the best at putting our ideas in 30-second sound bites, let’s be honest, right?”

Elghawaby’s experience with government, knowledge of policy and background as a journalist makes her “ideally suited” to translate that knowledge, he said.

While sites such as Georgetown University’s Bridge Initiative exist, Elghawaby said Mcro, which has a team of three people, will function as more than a library — it will break down the data into accessible policy fact sheets.

She hopes this will help members of the public meeting politicians, journalists looking for context in a hurry, and politicians seeking information to inform policy on Muslim lives.”

For example, a constituent at a mosque wants to ask a visiting mayoral candidate a question but doesn’t know what to ask. Mcro’s tool kit could offer a brief on the issue of parking near mosques on Friday. Having access to policy priorities would allow people to feel confident when they’re engaging with politicians “so that it becomes less a photo-op and more of a conversation,” Elghawaby said.

Mcro is a project of the Muslim Fund, a grassroots charity organization.

Elghawaby said the initiative comes based on some of her learnings in government.

“The relationship between our communities and the federal government has weakened,” she said.

Former prime minister Justin Trudeau and the revenue minister had promised the Muslim community that they were going to address the issue of disproportionate scrutiny of Muslim charities, she said. She commissioned research for which academics, including Emon, spent nine months finding a policy solution before producing a report.

When she met Prime Minister Mark Carney in the summer of 2025, she reminded him of the promise made and said he told her it would be addressed by summer of 2026.

“But nothing has been done,” she said. The Prime Minister’s Office referred the Star’s query to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA).

A CRA spokesperson said charities are selected for audit based on potential non-compliance with tax rules and not on faith, denomination, or religious affiliation. The agency has implemented recommendations made by other reviews of its auditing processes and is committed to ensuring “its compliance activities are conducted in a fair, evidence-based, and unbiased manner,” Sylvie Branch said.

“Sometimes,” Elghawaby said, explaining the rationale that pushed her toward founding Mcro, “if you’re waiting for the government, even if you’ve got the promise from the highest person in government, the prime minister, himself or herself, it will not trickle down into the bureaucracy. You have to come with the solution essentially written up, with a bow on top.”

stories.title: Six charts that show how B.C.’s fiscal outlook has gotten worse
stories.summary: Provincial election on Oct. 24 pits the NDP and Conservatives’ economic visions against a complex and grim reality
stories.author: Jason Kirby
stories.content:
Regardless of which party comes out on top in British Columbia ’s impending election, the next government faces the grinding task of putting the province’s troubled fiscal house back in order.

Over the last four years, under Premier David Eby’s New Democratic Party, the B.C. government has swung from a small surplus to a deep and prolonged deficit outlook. As of the latest quarterly fiscal update, released in September, the province’s deficit was expected to hit $13.8-billion this fiscal year, or 2.9 per cent of GDP – the largest budget shortfall since at least 1991.

Yet, despite a backdrop of rising deficits, a mounting debt load and tumbling credit ratings, neither of the main parties in the Oct. 24th race – the NDP and Lorne Doerkson’s Conservative Party of B.C. – has provided a clear path back to fiscal stability in the near or even medium term.

At the same time, the headwinds facing the B.C. economy, from slower immigration numbers to the effect of U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs, is adding to anxiety about the province’s finances within the private sector.

That nervousness among businesses in B.C. “likely points to continued slow growth in the province and, regardless of the election outcome, a weaker fiscal impulse – or reduced government contribution to growth,” Ali Jaffery, chief economist at Kpmg Canada, wrote in a recent note. “Bond markets will have little tolerance for high deficit spending in a province with weak private demand growth.”

Here are six charts showing how B.C.’s fiscal situation has deteriorated and why the province is at a critical juncture with its finances.

No path back to balance from either party. Both the NDP and Conservative parties have now released costed platforms and neither goes very far in bringing B.C.’s budget back to balance.

The Ndp’s plan shows the deficit falling from roughly $13.8-billion this fiscal year (after adjusting for the government’s pause to its planned expansion of provincial sales taxes on professional services) to $11.97-billion in fiscal 2028-29.

To achieve even that modest reduction, the party’s plan relies on a tax increase on high-income earners and up to $730-million a year of new revenue from “targeted economic growth” tied to major projects. However, planned new spending would absorb most of the new revenue.

Meanwhile, the Conservatives said their plan will bring B.C.’s annual deficit down to $10.8-billion by 2029-30, though that would still be more than twice the province’s 2023-24 shortfall. To reach its target, the party said it would reduce the province’s contingency reserve fund, enact a hiring freeze, review spending at most ministries and cut outside consultants. The plan bakes in $2.6-billion of extra revenue from faster growth over three years, but tax cuts of about $3.4-billion a year would offset most of those measures.

B.C.’s debt picture has eroded faster than other large provinces. Four years of growing deficits have piled up and caused the province’s debt load to balloon. Taxpayer-supported debt is set to more than triple to $187-billion in 2028-29, as compared to when Mr. Eby took office in the 2022-23 fiscal year. That pace of debt growth far outstrips other large provinces. B.C.’s net debt relative to gross domestic product, which measures total liabilities less financial assets as a share of the economy, has soared to a projected 27.4 per cent for this fiscal year from 17.2 per cent three years ago.

Nearly 10 cents of every dollar that B.C. collects will soon go to debt payments. As recently as fiscal 2022-23, the province had the lowest debt charges relative to its revenues, but an explosion of debt has rapidly redrawn that picture. Interest costs are now rising far faster than in Ontario, Quebec and Alberta.

That means an ever-larger share of B.C.’s revenues is being eaten up by making payments on its debt, with 9.5 per cent of what the province takes in annually projected to go to interest charges by 2028-29, according to RBC Economics. As an increasing share of revenue goes to interest, that will leave less to cover for services, and threatens to push B.C.’s deficit even higher unless taxes rise or spending is cut.

The province has faced a barrage of credit-rating downgrades. None of this has gone unnoticed by bond markets and credit rating agencies. “Under Premier Eby’s administration, B.C. has been downgraded eight times in total by the main credit rating agencies,” Derek Holt, head of capital markets economics at Scotiabank, wrote in a recent note.

Fitch, one of the most recent rating agencies to downgrade B.C. debt in April, said the rating cut “reflects our expectation that meaningful erosion of debt metrics is likely given projected operating deficits and capital spending. With only modest offsetting actions so far and no plan to return to balance in the near term, further erosion is possible.”

Against that backdrop, he also noted that investors now demand a premium to hold B.C.’s 10-year bonds that is nearly as large as Quebec’s, the widest among Canada’s four largest provinces. And increasingly, those higher interest payments are heading south. Between April 1 to June 30, B.C. borrowed $14.9-billion in long-term debt from domestic and foreign markets with the latter, largely U.S. investors, accounting for 82 per cent of that lending.

The province’s public-sector hiring spree never slowed down. B.C. has added public-sector workers far faster than it has created private-sector jobs. Since the start of 2023, the province added four times as many workers in public administration, health care and education than in private jobs, according to numbers reported by Statistics Canada. But while all provinces and the federal government ramped up public-sector hiring during the pandemic, B.C. never reversed that trend in the way some other governments have recently.

While the NDP costed plan makes no mention of what public hiring would look like under a new Eby government, the Conservative plan set out a hiring freeze; a review of ministries outside of health, education and a few others; and a target of returning administrative and management staffing to where it would have been relative to population growth since 2016-17, though it did not provide a proposed headcount.

Top earners in B.C. face a steep tax hike under Mr. Eby’s plan. A key part of the Ndp’s re-election platform proposes new measures to tax the province’s top earners, including a new top bracket for incomes above $1-million, taxed at a rate of 24.5 per cent. Income in the $265,545 to $1-million range would increase by two percentage points to 22.5 per cent, starting next year.

Once added to the federal government’s top marginal rate of 33 per cent, the province’s combined top rate would be one of the highest among countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development.

The NDP said the higher taxes on top earners would generate roughly $1-billion a year in additional revenue by fiscal 2028-29. However, the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, a left-leaning think tank, estimated the additional revenue from the tax moves would be closer to $750-million.
paragraphs: Regardless of which party comes out on top in British Columbia ’s impending election, the next government faces the grinding task of putting the province’s troubled fiscal house back in order.

As of the latest quarterly fiscal update, released in September, the province’s deficit was expected to hit $13.8-billion this fiscal year, or 2.9 per cent of GDP – the largest budget shortfall since at least 1991.

Yet, despite a backdrop of rising deficits, a mounting debt load and tumbling credit ratings, neither of the main parties in the Oct. 24th race – the NDP and Lorne Doerkson’s Conservative Party of B.C. – has provided a clear path back to fiscal stability in the near or even medium term.

At the same time, the headwinds facing the B.C. economy, from slower immigration numbers to the effect of U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs, is adding to anxiety about the province’s finances within the private sector.

That nervousness among businesses in B.C. “likely points to continued slow growth in the province and, regardless of the election outcome, a weaker fiscal impulse – or reduced government contribution to growth,” Ali Jaffery, chief economist at Kpmg Canada, wrote in a recent note. “Bond markets will have little tolerance for high deficit spending in a province with weak private demand growth.”
Here are six charts showing how B.C.’s fiscal situation has deteriorated and why the province is at a critical juncture with its finances.
No path back to balance from either party. Both the NDP and Conservative parties have now released costed platforms and neither goes very far in bringing B.C.’s budget back to balance.

The Ndp’s plan shows the deficit falling from roughly $13.8-billion this fiscal year (after adjusting for the government’s pause to its planned expansion of provincial sales taxes on professional services) to $11.97-billion in fiscal 2028-29.

To achieve even that modest reduction, the party’s plan relies on a tax increase on high-income earners and up to $730-million a year of new revenue from “targeted economic growth” tied to major projects. However, planned new spending would absorb most of the new revenue.

Meanwhile, the Conservatives said their plan will bring B.C.’s annual deficit down to $10.8-billion by 2029-30, though that would still be more than twice the province’s 2023-24 shortfall. To reach its target, the party said it would reduce the province’s contingency reserve fund, enact a hiring freeze, review spending at most ministries and cut outside consultants. The plan bakes in $2.6-billion of extra revenue from faster growth over three years, but tax cuts of about $3.4-billion a year would offset most of those measures.

stories.title: Coven Fest 2026
stories.summary: London's first Coven Fest took place on Oct. 17 on Dundas block. The fest was a pop-up market with over 30 ven...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
London’s first Coven Fest took place on Oct. 17 on Dundas block. The fest was a pop-up market with over 30 vendors, featuring tattoos and piercings, tarot card readings, and photo opportunities.

This event was made to connect people, share experience, and grow the alternative and occult community in London. Attendees came from London and surrounding to show their support.

“I came to see the good energy that’s around, see the nice Halloween spirit, the costumes, the vendors, and to show my support.” said Darnell Gomez an attendee who just moved to London.

Vendors and business owners came from all over Ontario to join Coven Fest.

Photo by: Samantha Luis (Coven Fest pumpkin photo stand)

“It’s a nice opportunity just to welcome everybody. Everyone’s in good spirits and it’s nice to see everyone out supporting the community.” said Steve Ianni, the owner of Raven and Rune in Dutton.

“When we travel, we travel with a very small portion so we’ll always bring our incense and smudging. We do mystery bags, blind date with a bag or blind date with a book.” said Jennifer Haralampopoulos, owner of Sacred Spells in Tillsonburg.

Lots of items were on display across vendors including broomsticks, hats, candles, tarot cards, and books with a large majority being handmade.

“Next year I want it bigger and better. I want double the vendors, to expand, to bring Hex House to a household name, and I want the community in London to know there’s always a place.” said Katey Sawyers, host of Coven Fest and owner of Hex House.

Sawyers also said that she was quite happy with the turnout this year.

stories.title: Mounties investigate after man flashes knife at youth in Tumbler Ridge, B.C.
stories.summary: Mounties in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., say a man is in custody after flashing a knife at youth over the weekend.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Tumbler Ridge — Mounties in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., say a man is in custody after flashing a knife at youth over the weekend.

They say the incident happened late Saturday evening in the small town, which gained international attention earlier this year after a mass shooter killed eight victims, including six children, before turning the weapon on herself.

Police say officers responded to the knife report at the 100-block of Kinuseo Avenue and apprehended the man under the Mental Health Act.

They say he was brought to a hospital by officers but was released Monday and brought back to Tumbler Ridge, where he will remain in custody until he attends court.

Cpl. Jennifer Cooper says the Mounties want to assure the public that they are taking the situation very seriously and there is no further risk to the public, though the investigation is ongoing.

stories.title: Election results are tied between mayoral candidates in Lytton, B.C.
stories.summary: Lytton - The municipal election in Lytton, B.C., has resulted in a tie between two mayoral candidates with differing views on the community's recovery from a devastating wildfire that destroyed much of the village five years ago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Lytton - The municipal election in Lytton, B.C., has resulted in a tie between two mayoral candidates with differing views on the community’s recovery from a devastating wildfire that destroyed much of the village five years ago.

The results posted to the village’s website on Monday show Denise O’Connor, the incumbent, and challenger Jennifer Thoss each received 45 votes.

stories.title: Alberta voting locations extend hours after late openings, delaying referendum results
stories.summary: Elections Alberta says that for various reasons some locations opened late, so it cannot release unofficial results until 10 p.m. when the last polling station closes.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
Several voting locations in Alberta will remain open later Monday after delays prevented them from opening on time, affecting when unofficial referendum results will be released.

Elections Alberta officials said unofficial results will only begin to be released once all voting locations across the province are confirmed closed. Because of delays earlier in the day, the last voting location is not expected to close before 10 p.m.

Chief Electoral Officer Gordon McClure authorized extended hours at affected locations to ensure voters receive the full advertised hours of service.

Officials said the late openings were caused by various issues that have since been resolved. The release did not provide further details about those issues in the material provided.

Regular voting hours at all other locations are from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Officials are also asking Albertans to be patient and respectful toward election workers.

The following locations will have extended voting hours.
