stories.title: Witness at Toronto gold heist trial says snitching is never 'a positive thing' but his sudden memory loss isn't out of fear
stories.summary: The Crown asked Arsalan Chaudhary if his reticence to answer questions was more about fear of snitching consequences than mental health.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The star witness at the Toronto airport gold heist trial — who admitted to being a mastermind of one of the biggest gold heists in history — said several times that he didn’t have an opinion on snitching, but it turned out he really did.

After days of court testimony marked by low-energy, little memory, and complaints of “feeling triggered” by questions, Arsalan Chaudhary was asked if his reticence was more about prison culture than mental health.

“It’s hard giving evidence against someone when you yourself are in custody,” Crown prosecutor Jelena Vlacic asked him.

“I have no opinion,” Chaudhary replied.

“It’s challenging to snitch against someone, particularly when you’re in custody,” she asked again.

“I have no comment, ma’am.”

Vlacic reminded him that when he was previously testifying as a prelude to his own guilty plea — during which he gave detailed testimony — he asked in court if there were “any newspapers here,” and was told there weren’t. “You were concerned about the media attention,” Vlacic said, before noting that reporters were in court in Brampton, Ont., this time.

He agreed he was snitching but on Simran Preet Panesar, one of the co-accused in the heist who is considered a fugitive and living in India, but not against the accused currently on trial, Parmpal Sidhu. Vlacic suggested it was easier to snitch against someone who isn’t in the country.

Chaudhary became more animated, his voice clearer and louder, his replies much longer.

“When you’re in jail and when you snitch on somebody, it doesn’t matter where they are. If snitching is a snitch, it doesn’t make a difference,” he said. “People in jail, they don’t look at one snitch compared to another snitch any differently. So it doesn’t matter if I’m snitching on somebody who’s out of the country or someone who’s in the country. It doesn’t make a big difference in jail.”

“I guess you do have some opinion on it, then, right?” Vlacic said. She asked him if snitching was a positive thing in prison.

“I don’t think so, ma’am. It’s never been a positive thing anywhere.”

“I’m feeling triggered,” Chaudhary said when asked for details about the gold heist. “It just takes me to a place where it makes me very uncomfortable,” he said. “I’m just getting triggered by everything, and kind of nerve shaking, bringing me back memories.”

Chaudhary, 43, of Mississauga, Ont., has pleaded guilty to theft for the 2023 heist, when a crate containing more than $22.5 million worth of almost pure gold and cash was stolen from the Air Canada cargo warehouse at Pearson airport soon after arriving on an Air Canada flight from Zurich, Switzerland. He is serving a four-year sentence.

He was a reluctant witness, ordered by a judge to be brought from his cell and into court to take the stand at Sidhu’s trial.

He admitted that he was one of two masterminds who planned and orchestrated the astonishing gold heist. The other, he said, was the inside man at Air Canada, Panesar, who was a manager in the cargo facility and came up with the plan.

Chaudhary started testifying last week and easily recalled details of his harrowing attempt to flee to his native Pakistan, where he said he was kidnapped by Pakistani police who tortured him into giving up all his loot. When he was asked by Vlacic about the others who helped him pull off the heist, his memory evaporated.

After two days of him telling court he couldn’t remember, and that post-traumatic stress from his kidnapping and poor treatment in prison diminished his memory and state of mind, Judge Gordon Cudjoe of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Brampton ordered last Wednesday that Chaudhary be returned to his federal prison where he could take his medication and catch up on sleep before returning to the stand.

His testimony Monday reconvened with little apparent change of heart or state of mind.

“I don’t remember, ma’am,” was a frequent response.

After being shown his previous sworn testimony, the transcript of his guilty plea hearing, an agreed statement of fact he and his lawyer agreed to in court, and copies of text messages extracted from a phone police seized from his apartment, he still couldn’t recall much of it.

He asked the judge to let him speak to his lawyer. He said reading the transcript “will hurt me mentally.”

She asked him about text messages about melting gold after the heist that were extracted from a phone police seized in his condo. He repeatedly said he didn’t recognize the messages, didn’t know what they meant, and couldn’t say who sent them. He didn’t recognize the phone or remember his phone number.

He said he didn’t recognize who was in photos he was shown, including himself, and didn’t recognize what the Crown suggested was his Range Rover.

He testified with a scowl on his face and occasionally rubbing his head with both hands.

Eventually, Vlacic asked Cudjoe for permission to treat Chaudhary as an adversarial witness so she could more directly challenge his answers, which was granted.

Chaudhary said he communicated with Sidhu but had only vague recollection of what was said. Mainly it was about him passing messages to Panesar, Chaudhary said. He previously said he spoke with Sidhu three times on the day of the heist, but on Monday he wasn’t so sure.

Chaudhary said he and Panesar agreed to split the gold, with Panesar getting 70 per cent and Chaudhary getting 30 per cent. He previously said he needed to take care of others he had used in the plot and Panesar was going to do the same, but in court he didn’t know whether Panesar did that or who he might have shared it with.

In previous testimony he agreed he exchanged text messages with Sidhu including receiving a message asking: “you manage to melt down all that gold yet lol.”

“Theres too much heat right now,” was the reply. “We’re gonna have to wait now. Melt gold is a process lol,”

“I heard they call you 2 chains of tdot,” Sidhu allegedly texted, using a slang term for Toronto.

“I wish I had it. Love to be called 2 chains lol.”

He said in court Monday he doesn’t remember the exchange, but he recalls hearing about the “2 chains” joke.

“I’ve read this in the newspaper many times,” he testified. “That 2 chain line, everybody talked about it in jail.”

He also said the prosecutors overestimated his intelligence.

“I haven’t finished my high school. I’m trying to do that thing right now, actually, so I don’t know how smart you think I am,” he said when he claimed he didn’t know what the word “delegated” meant.

He said he was born in Pakistan and moved to the United States when he was very young and then came to Canada when he was around 12 and became a citizen. He grew up speaking English, he said, but still didn’t know the word the prosecutor used.

Vlacic eventually got him to agree that the things he agreed to at his own court hearing for his guilty plea were “probably, mostly” said because he believed them to be true at the time. “I’m not saying it’s not true.”

Under cross-examination by Sidhu’s lawyer, Shale Wagman, Chaudhary said he doesn’t know how much Sidhu would have known about the heist plans, and that for Chaudhary he was primarily a conduit to reach Panesar.

Chaudhary agreed that he never saw Sidhu at his condo or at his second condo he used as a stash house, and he had no financial dealings with Sidhu.

The trial continues.

He said in court Monday he doesn’t remember the exchange, but he recalls hearing about the “2 chains” joke.
“I’ve read this in the newspaper many times,” he testified. “That 2 chain line, everybody talked about it in jail.”
He also said the prosecutors overestimated his intelligence.
“I haven’t finished my high school. I’m trying to do that thing right now, actually, so I don’t know how smart you think I am,” he said when he claimed he didn’t know what the word “delegated” meant.

He said he was born in Pakistan and moved to the United States when he was very young and then came to Canada when he was around 12 and became a citizen. He grew up speaking English, he said, but still didn’t know the word the prosecutor used.

Vlacic eventually got him to agree that the things he agreed to at his own court hearing for his guilty plea were “probably, mostly” said because he believed them to be true at the time. “I’m not saying it’s not true.”

Under cross-examination by Sidhu’s lawyer, Shale Wagman, Chaudhary said he doesn’t know how much Sidhu would have known about the heist plans, and that for Chaudhary he was primarily a conduit to reach Panesar.
Chaudhary agreed that he never saw Sidhu at his condo or at his second condo he used as a stash house, and he had no financial dealings with Sidhu.
The trial continues.

content_blocks.text: The star witness at the Toronto airport gold heist trial — who admitted to being a mastermind of one of the biggest gold heists in history — said several times that he didn’t have an opinion on snitching, but it turned out he really did.

After days of court testimony marked by low-energy, little memory, and complaints of “feeling triggered” by questions, Arsalan Chaudhary was asked if his reticence was more about prison culture than mental health.
“It’s hard giving evidence against someone when you yourself are in custody,” Crown prosecutor Jelena Vlacic asked him.
“I have no opinion,” Chaudhary replied.
“It’s challenging to snitch against someone, particularly when you’re in custody,” she asked again.
“I have no comment, ma’am.”

Vlacic reminded him that when he was previously testifying as a prelude to his own guilty plea — during which he gave detailed testimony — he asked in court if there were “any newspapers here,” and was told there weren’t. “You were concerned about the media attention,” Vlacic said, before noting that reporters were in court in Brampton, Ont., this time.

He agreed he was snitching but on Simran Preet Panesar, one of the co-accused in the heist who is considered a fugitive and living in India, but not against the accused currently on trial, Parmpal Sidhu. Vlacic suggested it was easier to snitch against someone who isn’t in the country.
Chaudhary became more animated, his voice clearer and louder, his replies much longer.

“When you’re in jail and when you snitch on somebody, it doesn’t matter where they are. If snitching is a snitch, it doesn’t make a difference,” he said. “People in jail, they don’t look at one snitch compared to another snitch any differently. So it doesn’t matter if I’m snitching on somebody who’s out of the country or someone who’s in the country. It doesn’t make a big difference in jail.”
“I guess you do have some opinion on it, then, right?” Vlacic said. She asked him if snitching was a positive thing in prison.
“I don’t think so, ma’am. It’s never been a positive thing anywhere.”

“I’m feeling triggered,” Chaudhary said when asked for details about the gold heist. “It just takes me to a place where it makes me very uncomfortable,” he said. “I’m just getting triggered by everything, and kind of nerve shaking, bringing me back memories.”

content_blocks.text: Chaudhary, 43, of Mississauga, Ont., has pleaded guilty to theft for the 2023 heist, when a crate containing more than $22.5 million worth of almost pure gold and cash was stolen from the Air Canada cargo warehouse at Pearson airport soon after arriving on an Air Canada flight from Zurich, Switzerland. He is serving a four-year sentence.
He was a reluctant witness, ordered by a judge to be brought from his cell and into court to take the stand at Sidhu’s trial.

He admitted that he was one of two masterminds who planned and orchestrated the astonishing gold heist. The other, he said, was the inside man at Air Canada, Panesar, who was a manager in the cargo facility and came up with the plan.

Chaudhary started testifying last week and easily recalled details of his harrowing attempt to flee to his native Pakistan, where he said he was kidnapped by Pakistani police who tortured him into giving up all his loot. When he was asked by Vlacic about the others who helped him pull off the heist, his memory evaporated.

After two days of him telling court he couldn’t remember, and that post-traumatic stress from his kidnapping and poor treatment in prison diminished his memory and state of mind, Judge Gordon Cudjoe of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Brampton ordered last Wednesday that Chaudhary be returned to his federal prison where he could take his medication and catch up on sleep before returning to the stand.
His testimony Monday reconvened with little apparent change of heart or state of mind.
“I don’t remember, ma’am,” was a frequent response.

After being shown his previous sworn testimony, the transcript of his guilty plea hearing, an agreed statement of fact he and his lawyer agreed to in court, and copies of text messages extracted from a phone police seized from his apartment, he still couldn’t recall much of it.

content_blocks.text: He asked the judge to let him speak to his lawyer. He said reading the transcript “will hurt me mentally.”

She asked him about text messages about melting gold after the heist that were extracted from a phone police seized in his condo. He repeatedly said he didn’t recognize the messages, didn’t know what they meant, and couldn’t say who sent them. He didn’t recognize the phone or remember his phone number.
He said he didn’t recognize who was in photos he was shown, including himself, and didn’t recognize what the Crown suggested was his Range Rover.
He testified with a scowl on his face and occasionally rubbing his head with both hands.

stories.title: Politics Insider: The final push for unity – or separation
stories.summary: Albertans vote today on whether to remain in Canada or begin the process of pursuing separation
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. I’m Laura Stone, filling in for Ian Bailey this week. Let’s look at what happened today.

Albertans vote today on whether to remain in Canada or begin the process of pursuing separation, the culmination of a campaign that has divided the province and transfixed the country.

Premier Danielle Smith announced in May that she would use a previously planned referendum on a range of other issues to also ask Albertans to weigh their future in this country.

As Matthew Scace reports, the separatist and federalist camps made their final pitches in duelling rallies at the Alberta legislature in Edmonton over the weekend, part of a last-minute push that also saw Prime Minister Mark Carney make several stops in the province late last week urging Albertans to vote to remain in Canada.

The referendum has inflamed debate about national unity at a time when the country’s sovereignty is also being challenged by the trade policy and rhetoric of the Trump administration in the United States. And today’s vote takes place just two weeks after Quebec’s provincial election brought a separatist government to power there.

This is the daily Politics Insider newsletter, curated by

. It is available exclusively to our digital subscribers. You can sign up for more than 20 other newsletters on

Canada’s top soldier has pledged to make public the official board of inquiry probe into a grass fire that left four soldiers dead and 39 wounded during a live-fire training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Saturday.

Committee hearings have started on the Liberal government’s latest bill aimed at fast-tracking major projects, with MPs working on a tight timeline that critics say is inappropriate given the legislation’s complexity.

Cleveland-Cliffs chief executive Lourenco Goncalves criticized Prime Minister Mark Carney for “snatching defeat from the jaws of victory” in trade, as the U.S. steelmaker remains locked in conflict with Ottawa over hundreds of job losses in Canada.

With 10 days remaining in a campaign where Toronto’s notoriously clogged roads have been a central issue, the City has released figures that could shift the tone of the mayoral debate.

On our radar

“To their friends, to their families, to their colleagues, to the people of Wainwright, please know that you have the entire nation at your side, because in Canada, we take care of one another.” - Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking during a tribute to the soldiers who died this weekend after a fire ripped through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright’s training grounds in Alberta on Saturday.

In 2024, the Royal Canadian Geographical Society discovered the wreck of famed explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton’s last ship, Quest, at a depth of 390 metres, off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador. In what year did the famed polar explorer die suddenly during an Antarctic voyage?

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

Perspectives

Alberta’s separation referendum is coming: What happens in the days and weeks and months after?

What does the post-referendum Alberta agenda look like? What cards does Premier Danielle Smith play next? What does the federal government do? Where do Albertans and Canadians go from there? — Shannon Proudfoot

But timid tax reform is not just bad policy. It’s bad politics. — Andrew Coyne

The future of this country is being diminished because of how much it costs to build big things, and how often they go terribly off the rails. — Matti Siemiatycki

stories.title: Poilievre defends Alberta referendum, says ‘the goal should not be to beat one side or the other’
stories.summary: Federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre defended holding a referendum that puts a path to Alberta separation on the ballot.
stories.author: Bill Kaufmann
stories.content:
Wainwright — As some of the last voters cast their ballots on a referendum offering a path to Alberta independence, federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre asked people to vote for Canada.

Some critics, including the opposition Alberta NDP, say the referendum is a waste of money — possibly costing more than $130 million — and places a dangerous strain on the country’s unity in the face of threats from the U.S.

But Poilievre said he hopes the vote’s aftermath will see a greater sense of unity and that he understands grievances separatists have with Ottawa.

“I hope there’s a strong result for Canada tonight, and then tomorrow we can begin the work of healing the divisions,” he said.

“I think the goal should not be to beat one side or the other.”

Poilievre defended the UCP government’s decision to include referendum questions on giving the province more power over immigration. Other questions centre around charging some newcomers fees for health care and constraining education eligibility.

He said the immigration questions are based on important issues of sustainability.

“There’s no question we have to get immigration under control, we need to cut back on the deluxe benefits that are given to people here illegally,” said the opposition leader, who’s MP for Battle River—Crowfoot, which includes Wainwright.

He rejected accusations by critics that the UCP government is scapegoating immigrants for their own failure to keep pace with population growth.

“I don’t think that’s an accurate characterization either of what the critics are saying or what the situation is,” said Poilievre.

“Nobody’s blaming individual people, they’re blaming Liberal immigration policies.”

The federal government has made moves to reduce immigration and Alberta’s intake of them has recently dramatically plummeted, but Poilievre said those levels are still too high.

When asked if separatist forces should give up their fight to break Alberta away from Canada if they lose Monday’s vote, he urged the pro-independence side to give Canada a chance.

“I don’t like the term ‘give up,’ I’d rather them join and be part of making the Canadian family everything they hoped for,” said Poilievre, who was in Wainwright to lend the community support after last weekend’s grass fire that killed four soldiers at the nearby training base.

“We don’t need to look at beating people in this referendum.”

Some separatist leaders say they’ll continue to fight for an independent Alberta regardless of the referendum’s outcome.

Successive public opinion polls have shown the pro-Canada side to be the significant majority in Alberta.

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to correct an inaccurate paraphrasing of Poilievre’s comments and the headline on this story was edited to reflect the change.

“I think the goal should not be to beat one side or the other.”

Poilievre defended the UCP government’s decision to include referendum questions on giving the province more power over immigration. Other questions centre around charging some newcomers fees for health care and constraining education eligibility.
He said the immigration questions are based on important issues of sustainability.

“There’s no question we have to get immigration under control, we need to cut back on the deluxe benefits that are given to people here illegally,” said the opposition leader, who’s MP for Battle River—Crowfoot, which includes Wainwright.
He rejected accusations by critics that the UCP government is scapegoating immigrants for their own failure to keep pace with population growth.
“I don’t think that’s an accurate characterization either of what the critics are saying or what the situation is,” said Poilievre.
“Nobody’s blaming individual people, they’re blaming Liberal immigration policies.”
The federal government has made moves to reduce immigration and Alberta’s intake of them has recently dramatically plummeted, but Poilievre said those levels are still too high.
When asked if separatist forces should give up their fight to break Alberta away from Canada if they lose Monday’s vote, he urged the pro-independence side to give Canada a chance.

“I don’t like the term ‘give up,’ I’d rather them join and be part of making the Canadian family everything they hoped for,” said Poilievre, who was in Wainwright to lend the community support after last weekend’s grass fire that killed four soldiers at the nearby training base.
“We don’t need to look at beating people in this referendum.”
Some separatist leaders say they’ll continue to fight for an independent Alberta regardless of the referendum’s outcome.
Successive public opinion polls have shown the pro-Canada side to be the significant majority in Alberta.

stories.title: Repair bills piling up for aging Sarnia Police Headquarters
stories.summary: After a failed bid to fund a new facility, the Sarnia Police Service Board (Spsb) now says it needs $3.5 million for urgent repairs to the existing station.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
The repair bills continue to pile high for the aging Sarnia Police Headquarters.

After a failed bid to fund a new facility, the Sarnia Police Service Board (Spsb) now says it needs $3.5 million for urgent repairs to the existing station.

“There hasn’t been any money spent inside the police services building. Not just the last three years, it’s been a lot of years. But there’s been no major investment into that building,” said Spsb chairperson, Kelly Ash.

Broken concrete, rusted rebar, orange cones, yellow tape, and a long metal barricade greet visitors to the Christina Street headquarters.

In August, the Ontario Ministry of Labour ordered the stairs to be closed.

People are now directed to enter the building via the ramp next to the stairs.

Ash says that out of the $3.5 million dollar projected costs, the stairs alone will cost $1 million. That’s because they form part of the actual structure of the building. The problem was explained at a recent Spsb meeting by Deputy Chief Mike Van Sickle.

“In the best possible terms, if you were to scrape away our stairs, you’re going to look into the basement of the police service. So, it’s not something that can simply just be removed. What leads to that is water intrusion,” he told the board.

Other immediate needs include replacing a fuel tank, Hvac upgrades, parking lot security improvements, expanding the sally port for police transport vehicles, improving emergency alert system, electrical upgrades for an emergency generator.

“They put no money away for repairing the building on the belief they were going to get a $120 million police station,” exclaimed Sarnia Mayor Mike Bradley.

The must-do repair list follow’s Bradley’s veto last year of the board’s bid to build a new police headquarters.

“They think we’re the bank of Sarnia. And there’s been a 44 per cent increase in the last four years in the police budget. Forty-four per cent. They’ve also drained our reserves that are there for the rainy days. We don’t have the money there right now. We will have to find a way to deal with this. It is a labour, occupational health issue. That part I get. But it’s really sad how they’ve approached this,” he said.

Bradley says the next city council will be tasked with dealing with the $3.5 million dollar repair bill. Senior governments will also be approached for funding.

stories.title: Canada’s 2-year measles outbreak officially over: Phac
stories.summary: The measles outbreak started in October 2024 and has continued for about two years, with more than 6,400 cases reported during that time.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Canada’s measles outbreak that lost the country its global elimination status is officially over after two years.

The Public Health Agency of Canada (Phac) said Monday the multi-jurisdictional outbreak is over because more than two months have passed since the last case linked to the outbreak was reported.

It began in October 2024 in New Brunswick and saw more than 6,400 cases reported across 10 provinces and territories.

In total, 6,417 cases were linked to the outbreak, including 1,032 reported this year. Ontario saw the highest number of total cases with 2,390 reported, followed by 2,299 in Alberta and 1,033 in Manitoba. Other cases were seen in all provinces and territories except Yukon, Nunavut and Newfoundland and Labrador.

Most of the people who became ill had not been vaccinated against measles, Phac said.

The agency said in November 2025 that the Pan American Health Organization (Paho) had notified Phac about losing its elimination status.

At the time, Phac said a Paho commission had reviewed recent epidemiological and laboratory data, “confirming sustained transmission of the same measles virus strain in Canada for a period of more than one year.”

Global elimination status can be regained. Canada will need to keep the strain stamped out for at least 12 months, but also show it’s beefed up its surveillance systems and ability to quickly stop outbreaks if measles cases arise, according to Paho.

Canada’s Chief Public Health Officer Dr. Joss Reimer commended the work of public health authorities, health-care providers, community organizations and families across the country for their work to end the outbreak.

But her comments came with a cautionary note while urging Canadians to ensure routine vaccinations, like measles, are up to date to prevent future outbreaks.

“While this milestone is encouraging, measles continues to circulate globally, and we can expect to see further travel-related cases here at home,” she said in a news release.

Phac’s announcement the national outbreak had ended comes only a few days after Manitoba declared on Oct. 16 its 20-month outbreak was over , following weeks without a confirmed case. The last confirmed instance of measles was reported in August, the provincial government said in a news release.

Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel said in a news release Monday that cases are still being seen around the world.

“So while the outbreak is over, our work to increase vaccination rates and protect the health of Canadians continue,” she said.

Measles is still being seen in Canada, but recent cases have not been linked to the two-year outbreak. According to the federal government, three new confirmed cases were reported between Oct. 4 and Oct. 10.

stories.title: B.C. victim of Wainwright fire was everybody's best friend, says rugby coach
stories.summary: The former rugby coach for Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, one of four soldiers who died in a fire at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, says all of the teenager's team and his schoolmates thought of him as their best friend.
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The former rugby coach for Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, one of four soldiers who died in a fire at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, says all of the teenager’s team and his schoolmates thought of him as their best friend.

Trevor Plater, who coached Lykkemark in his senior year at Langley Secondary School in Langley, B.C., says Lykkemark was “always looking out for everybody.”

stories.title: BC Ferries vessel collides with humpback whale in Howe Sound near Metro Vancouver
stories.summary: Vancouver - A humpback whale has been struck by a BC Ferries vessel in waters near Metro Vancouver.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Fisheries and Oceans Canada says in an email that they were alerted to the collision on Sunday, when the Queen of Surrey reportedly struck the whale near Keats and Grace islands in Howe Sound.

The 139-metre-long Queen of Surrey provides regular service between Vancouver-Horseshoe Bay terminal and the Sunshine Coast.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Image 9Image 10

The DFO says witnesses reported two humpback whales near the ferry at the time of the collision, and one was struck after it surfaced in front of the vessel.

The federal agency says the whale was seen behind the vessel after the collision, and investigators are working to identify it and assess its condition.

BC Ferries has also confirmed the collision and is co-operating with the DFO, adding that initial reports showed crew had “very little time to react.”

“We recognize how upsetting this is, particularly for those who witnessed the collision, including our crews,” BC Ferries spokeswoman Lilian Kim says in a statement. “They work on these waters every day and care deeply about protecting the marine life around them.”

Kim says BC Ferries crew receive special training on whale awareness, and vessels operate under specific protocols to reduce collision risks.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada would not comment on whether the whale has been found, only stating that the agency is “currently reviewing the situation.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada would not comment on whether the whale has been found, only stating that the agency is “currently reviewing the situation.”

stories.title: Alberta referendum sparks Chinese community push to vote
stories.summary: With Albertans voting on the province's referendum, Chinese community leaders are mobilizing to help voters understand its 10 complex questions.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
With Albertans voting on the province’s referendum on Monday, Chinese community leaders are mobilizing to help voters understand its 10 complex questions.

Many voters are struggling to understand the ballot, but community leaders say the desire to vote has never been stronger.

“Even English-speaking Canadians, people born and raised here, many don’t fully understand these 10 questions, because altogether they’re over 400 words, and they’re not asked in a direct way,” said Teresa Woo-Paw, chair of the Acct Foundation.

The 10 questions cover a wide range of issues. Beyond the question on Alberta’s separation, the other nine address a range of topics from immigration to the constitutional division of powers.

“This referendum, I believe, is the largest and most complex vote in Canadian history,” Steven Tsang, a member of Asian Canadian for United Canada, said.

Former Alberta MLA Woo-Paw says that since July, community leaders have built a cross-ethnic coalition to address the information gap.

Woo-Paw and Tsang say they believe most Chinese voters support Alberta remaining in Canada.

“We believe that among ethnic communities, over 90 per cent support Alberta remaining in Canada,” Woo-Paw said.

Geopolitical commentator Sam Choi says the referendum carries particular significance for first-generation immigrants.

“The government doesn’t know who you voted for, but it knows whether you voted. Technology is so advanced now, they type in your surname and they know how many Chinese voted or didn’t vote,” Woo-Paw said. “If we don’t vote, we’re not important; when they make decisions on how to allocate resources.”

Choi says participation offers an opportunity for Chinese Canadians to better understand Canada’s political system.

“For Chinese to come out and vote is a very good opportunity,” Choi said. “A channel for the community to understand our federal system, the division of powers with the provinces, and how to further improve going forward.”

Results for the 10 questions on the referendum will be released in batches. Meanwhile, the results of the stay-or-leave question is expected early Tuesday morning.

stories.title: Marginalized patients have increased risk of early death from newly diagnosed metastatic breast cancer, study finds
stories.summary: A Western University-led study found higher risks of early death for marginalized people with de novo metastatic breast cancer
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
People who are marginalized or lack access to a primary care provider are at greater risk of early death from newly diagnosed metastatic breast cancer, according to research in Cmaj (Canadian Medical Association Journal) .

The Ontario study found nearly one-quarter of people with stage four metastasized breast cancer that has already spread to other sites in the body when it is found – also known as de novo breast cancer – died within six months of diagnosis.

The study was led by researchers at Western University’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry, including Dr. Priya Thomas, a plastic surgery resident and Dr. Phillip Blanchette, professor of oncology and medical oncologist at London Health Sciences Centre, along with their collaborators.

“The relationship between early death from breast cancer and a person’s sociodemographic factors hasn’t been previously examined in Canada,” Thomas said. “It’s important to investigate the role of factors like income and housing because patients with existing barriers can be especially vulnerable to disparities in health equity, including access to care.”

One in nine women will receive a diagnosis of breast cancer within their lifetime and 3,000 patients are diagnosed annually in Ontario. The type of breast cancer the team studied, de novo metastatic breast cancer, makes up three to six per cent of all breast cancer diagnoses.

Survival rates are steadily increasing for metastatic breast cancer, with numerous new treatments available, but there are long wait times for specialty care and disparities in accessing it.

The research team looked at Ices data from 4,004 patients with de novo metastatic breast cancer who were treated in Ontario between 2010 and 2019. They used the Ontario Marginalization Index tool to understand if other factors influence the risk of death, including housing stability, income, age and employment status.

An increased risk of early death (within six of their metastatic breast cancer diagnosis) was associated with age, concurrent health illnesses and marginalization and observed in 23 per cent of the study population.

For people who were treated for breast cancer, rural residence was also associated with early death, possibly because of challenges travelling for tests or treatment, which is commonly coordinated in larger urban centres.

People linked to a family physician had 26 per cent lower odds of early death. Of those, 60 per cent had received a mammogram within two years of diagnosis, compared to 42 per cent of people without a primary care provider.

The study underscores the critical role of primary care in Canada.

“Access to a primary care provider is a growing challenge in Canada, with one in four Canadians lacking regular access to primary care,” said Thomas. “Without the ability to be seen by a family doctor, people with advanced breast cancer May face delays in getting diagnosed and starting treatment.”

That’s essential to help Canadians – and a strained health-care system, the researchers said.

“Our study highlights the need for better primary care access. It is pivotal in preventing and diagnosing cancer, as well as managing symptoms and treatment side effects, mental health concerns and palliative care,” Blanchette said.

“The demand for cancer care is rising exponentially, and specialist oncologists are unlikely to be able to meet these care needs alone.”

stories.title: U.S. won’t drop digital issues in trade talks: former negotiator
stories.summary: While digital issues will continue to be a source of trade tensions with the United States, Canada can gain strength if it teams up with other allies that have similar interests, Canada’s former chief trade negotiator said Monday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Steve Verheul said the United States won’t simply drop issues like the Online News Act and digital sovereignty that it has identified as trade irritants.

“They’ve listed them as fairly fundamental concerns that they have and tend to pursue,” he said at the Canadian Chapter of the International Institute of Communications conference in Ottawa.

“The Online Streaming Act, the Online News Act, the sovereign cloud issue, control over data in Canada more broadly, that’s where the real battleground going forward with the U.S. is going to be on these kinds of issues.”

Verheul said the United States views policies targeting big tech companies as discriminatory. He said it’s difficult to design non-discriminatory policies because of how many of the largest digital companies are American.

Canada needs to work more closely with allies like the European Union to develop a more unified position on digital issues, he said.

Verheul said while Canada “needs to to maintain some level of independence on these issues,” it also must work with other countries that have similar interests.

“And we need to find some ways to move forward,” he added.

Eric Miller, president of the consulting group Rideau Potomac Strategy Group, spoke on a separate panel at the conference and gave the example of Netflix, which gets more than half of its revenue outside the U.S.

“If you begin to have policies which are unfavourable to large U.S. tech companies, it doesn’t take too many markets like Canada and the European Union co-ordinating to see how this would have very detrimental effects to them,” he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has been working on establishing closer links with Europe, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed Canada could become the first associate member of the European Union.

Canada will host an Canada-EU Summit in Montreal at the end of October, where the two sides are expected to announce the next steps in the deepening partnership.

Canada cut off the latest round of trade negotiations with the United States in August citing several reasons, including American demands related to rules about Canadian content on streaming platforms, also known as discoverability. The Crtc is in the process of implementing those rules under the Online Streaming Act.

It’s not clear exactly which element of the Online Streaming Act is the source of the conflict. Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said in late August the United States had withdrawn its position on discoverability.

But U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said the issue for the United States is streaming companies having to make financial contributions toward Canadian content — a proposal the Liberal government has backed away from.

Meredith Lilly, a professor at Carleton University’s Norman Paterson School of International Affairs, took part in the panel with Miller. She said Canada and the United States are likely to come to an agreement.

“I think that there is a landing zone that both sides will be able to agree on, and I anticipate that that will be keeping mandatory payments off … and Canada is going to be able to keep the discoverability piece of that,” she said.

The conference also heard that the cultural exemption Canada has under the current trade agreement allows the Americans to automatically retaliate if it is used.

Lilly said that means the United States could retaliate on things like cars or canola. “And so there is some potential that is going to pit parts of Canada against the cultural sector,” she said.

She said while the United States might have tolerated the cultural exemption when Canada was using it to subsidize arts and culture, that might not be the case if it extends to demanding financial contributions from American companies for Canadian content.

“If we start trying to use it to extract capital from large American firms to subsidize the creation of Canadian content and they can’t even use those subsidized funds, they are going to play hardball with us and it could be the end of the cultural exemption,” Lilly said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.
Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Steve Verheul said the United States won’t simply drop issues like the Online News Act and digital sovereignty that it has identified as trade irritants.
“They’ve listed them as fairly fundamental concerns that they have and tend to pursue,” he said at the Canadian Chapter of the International Institute of Communications conference in Ottawa.

“The Online Streaming Act, the Online News Act, the sovereign cloud issue, control over data in Canada more broadly, that’s where the real battleground going forward with the U.S. is going to be on these kinds of issues.”

Verheul said the United States views policies targeting big tech companies as discriminatory. He said it’s difficult to design non-discriminatory policies because of how many of the largest digital companies are American.
Canada needs to work more closely with allies like the European Union to develop a more unified position on digital issues, he said.
Verheul said while Canada “needs to to maintain some level of independence on these issues,” it also must work with other countries that have similar interests.
“And we need to find some ways to move forward,” he added.

Eric Miller, president of the consulting group Rideau Potomac Strategy Group, spoke on a separate panel at the conference and gave the example of Netflix, which gets more than half of its revenue outside the U.S.

“If you begin to have policies which are unfavourable to large U.S. tech companies, it doesn’t take too many markets like Canada and the European Union co-ordinating to see how this would have very detrimental effects to them,” he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has been working on establishing closer links with Europe, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed Canada could become the first associate member of the European Union.
Canada will host an Canada-EU Summit in Montreal at the end of October, where the two sides are expected to announce the next steps in the deepening partnership.

Canada cut off the latest round of trade negotiations with the United States in August citing several reasons, including American demands related to rules about Canadian content on streaming platforms, also known as discoverability. The Crtc is in the process of implementing those rules under the Online Streaming Act.

It’s not clear exactly which element of the Online Streaming Act is the source of the conflict. Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said in late August the United States had withdrawn its position on discoverability.

But U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said the issue for the United States is streaming companies having to make financial contributions toward Canadian content — a proposal the Liberal government has backed away from.

Meredith Lilly, a professor at Carleton University’s Norman Paterson School of International Affairs, took part in the panel with Miller. She said Canada and the United States are likely to come to an agreement.

“I think that there is a landing zone that both sides will be able to agree on, and I anticipate that that will be keeping mandatory payments off … and Canada is going to be able to keep the discoverability piece of that,” she said.
The conference also heard that the cultural exemption Canada has under the current trade agreement allows the Americans to automatically retaliate if it is used.
Lilly said that means the United States could retaliate on things like cars or canola. “And so there is some potential that is going to pit parts of Canada against the cultural sector,” she said.

She said while the United States might have tolerated the cultural exemption when Canada was using it to subsidize arts and culture, that might not be the case if it extends to demanding financial contributions from American companies for Canadian content.

“If we start trying to use it to extract capital from large American firms to subsidize the creation of Canadian content and they can’t even use those subsidized funds, they are going to play hardball with us and it could be the end of the cultural exemption,” Lilly said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.
Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Bombers can secure CFL playoff spot with victory
stories.summary: The Winnipeg Blue Bombers enter the final week of the CFL regular season controlling their playoff fate.
stories.author: n The Canadian Pressn
stories.content:
Toronto – The Winnipeg Blue Bombers enter the final week of the CFL regular season controlling their playoff fate.

Winnipeg (8-9) faces the B.C. Lions (10-7) on Friday night needing a win to make the playoffs. Watching intently, though, will be the Calgary Stampeders (9-9), who end the season on a bye week.

The Saskatchewan Roughriders (9-8) have already cemented a playoff spot but can finish either third or fourth in the West. The Riders meet the Edmonton Elks (13-4) on Saturday.

If the Bombers and Riders both win, Saskatchewan finishes third and faces B.C. in the West semifinal Oct. 31. Winnipeg would take fourth and visit the Toronto Argonauts (9-8) in the East semifinal.

A Winnipeg win and Saskatchewan loss would leave the Bombers third and visiting B.C. in the West semifinal. The Riders would end up fourth and cross over to take on Toronto.

Should Winnipeg lose and Saskatchewan win, the Riders will finish third. Calgary would get fourth and head to Toronto.

And finally, if Winnipeg and Saskatchewan both lose, Calgary would finish third ahead of the fourth-place Roughriders.

Edmonton and B.C. have cemented the top two spots in the West. Likewise, the Montreal Alouettes (13-4) and Toronto had clinched first and second, respectively, in the East.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

Argos mum on QB Kelly’s injury, playing status

Graves willing to do anything the Raptors ask him

stories.title: Alberta referendum live: When to expect results on 10 questions as historic separation vote underway
stories.summary: Alberta is holding a nonbinding referendum to ask residents if they want to remain part of Canada. Follow the Star's live coverage and analysis.
stories.author: Star staff and wire services
stories.content:
Results continue to trickle in after Albertans went to the polls on Monday, deciding to remain in Canada.

A man registers to vote in a voting station during the Alberta Referendum as Albertans head to the polls in Calgary, Oct. 19, 2026.

Edmonton — A turbulent campaign that pitted federalists against separatists over Alberta’s future in Canada ended with the remain side securing an overwhelming victory.

With votes still being counted on Tuesday morning, about 76 per cent of Albertans voted to remain in Canada and roughly 24 per cent backed a second binding referendum on leaving the country.

At a watch party in Edmonton hosted by the federalist group “Forever Canadian,” a crowd of fewer than 100 jumped to its feet, hugging, cheering and waving Canadian flags as the call was made.

“Canada, Canada, Canada,” the crowd chanted.

The projections came before Elections Alberta had released complete official results. More than 100 polling stations that opened late stayed open past the scheduled closing time, delaying the count until after midnight.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on X that she would address Albertans Tuesday at 8:45 p.m. Eastern time regarding the results “and where our province goes from here.”

“I’m very pleased to see the initial results from Elections Alberta show widespread support for remaining in Canada. Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith wrote.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Mark Carney issued a statement celebrating the results, saying the province had “made a clear choice” in Monday’s vote.

“Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

He said that while all of the results have not yet been counted, “the defining question of separation” has been decided and victory for the federalist camp means that the country can now return to the job of advancing Canada “with renewed purpose and high ambition,” referring to his government’s agenda of increasing international trade and developing infrastructure, mining and energy projects across the country.

He said that Canada was “unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta at its core.”

While federalists celebrated Monday’s victory, many were quick to note that 23 per cent of Albertans choosing the option to hold a vote on separation was not something to cheer about.

“I was hoping it would be like 85 per cent,” Dee Winn, a volunteer with the “Forever Canadian” campaign, told the Star as the early results came in.

Amid the cheers and applause, Thomas Lukaszuk, who spearheaded the federalist group, told the crowd those voters could not be ignored.

“These are Albertans. These are Canadians,” he said from the stage, adding that something had to be done to address what was driving their anger and frustration.

“We cannot go on like this.”

Before the polls even closed, Mitch Sylvestre, a key separatist leader, told a crowd of volunteers and other independence supporters gathered at a nearby Edmonton bar that their movement had become something that was not going to disappear.

“Alberta has changed,” he said.

Monday’s vote took place under the shadow of tragedy after four people were killed and 39 others injured when extreme winds pushed an already burning fire onto troops conducting exercises at CFB Wainwright on Saturday.

Polls opened as scheduled, with some voters in Wainwright worried about what would happen to the base, an integral part of the community’s identity and economy, should Alberta one day separate from Canada.

“This is a federal town,” said Greg Granger, who works in IT at CFB Wainwright.

Elsewhere, the polarization that has taken hold across the province during the referendum campaign was on full display.

Olivia Hughes, an Edmonton resident living with disabilities, walked to a polling station at an Anglican church in the city on Monday, wondering, “Why the f—- do I have to be out here?”

Besides contemplating the impact secession would have on her quality of life, she said: “I’m a Canadian, I’m not just an Albertan.”

“I would like to remain a Canadian, so that’s why I’m here.”

Others arrived feeling fed up.

“I think we’ve been screwed over by the other provinces,” said fellow Edmonton voter Bill Lewis, who cast his ballot at a polling station in one of the city’s strip malls for the option to begin the process of holding a future vote to leave Canada.

“I think our money should stay here instead of us getting nothing and the other provinces getting it all.”

A record-breaking 1.3 million Albertans had already cast their ballots through advance polls or by mail, comprising 43 per cent of the province’s eligible voters.

How Alberta came to this moment is a mix of historic grievance, COVID-fuelled populism and a premier who was unwilling to close the door on separatists.

While Western alienation is nothing new in the country’s largest oil-producing province, successive public opinion polls suggested an uptick in the sentiment after the election of Prime Minister Mark Carney, whose victory was viewed by some as another blow to the deep-blue Conservative province.

Anger had been brewing for years during the tenure of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, whose environmental policies were viewed by many in the province as stymying resource development. Even before that, the Trudeau name triggered distrust among some Albertans, who remembered the legacy of the long-dismantled National Energy Program introduced by his father, former prime minister Pierre Trudeau.

But while Carney has sought to reset relations with Alberta, working with Premier Danielle Smith to advance a new million-barrel-a-day oil pipeline to the West Coast and overhauling federal regulatory processes with the goal of getting more major energy and infrastructure projects off the ground, another movement was brewing in the province.

Independence organizers who entered Alberta’s political arena through opposition to COVID-19 pandemic measures got to work pushing for a referendum.

Sylvestre, the owner of a sporting goods store in Bonnyville, Alta., spent the dead of winter travelling the province collecting 300,000 signatures for a petition under provincial citizen-initiative rules to trigger a referendum on leaving Canada.

Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier in a Progressive Conservative government, was busy collecting tens of thousands of signatures for his own “Forever Canadian” initiative under the same provincial rules in response to the separatist push.

Things came to a head this May when an Alberta judge quashed the separatist petition over concerns about the failure to properly consult First Nations.

One evening in late May, Smith addressed Albertans to announce that her United Conservative Party government would add an independence question to a previously decided set of nine referendum questions focused on taking greater control over immigration and pursuing constitutional reforms such as abolishing the Senate.

That sparked criticism from all corners. Carney called the referendum a “dangerous bluff.” Other premiers panned the move, while federalists in Alberta mobilized supporters who wanted to remain in Canada to turn out and vote, warning that separatism remained a minority view but a vocal and highly motivated one.

Independence leaders also expressed ire at Smith, particularly over her public support for remaining in Canada, viewing it as a betrayal of her party base, where support for independence is popular.

Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney visits supporters of a Vote to Stay event ahead of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty, in Red Deer, Alta., October 16, 2026.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has issued a statement celebrating the Alberta referendum results, saying the province “made a clear choice” in the Monday vote.

He said that while all of the results have not yet been counted, “the defining question of separation” has been decided and victory for the federalist camp means that the country can now return to the job of advancing Canada “with renewed purpose and high ambition,” Carney said, referring to his government’s agenda of increasing international trade and developing infrastructure, mining and energy projects across the country.

Lawyer Keith Wilson speaks to independence supporters at Saturday’s rally outside the provincial legislature in Edmonton.

By the time Keith Wilson, one of the key organizers of the Alberta independence movement, took the stage Monday night, even his own party was looking pretty sparse.

Only about a dozen supporters remained in the room to hear the top separatist fundraiser speak on a night when the Alberta separatist movement appeared headed for a resounding defeat.

Wilson approached the podium at just after midnight local time. He did his best to spin a result that made Alberta independence seem less like a danger to confederation than a fringe obsession

“I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it’s fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better, that Alberta can do better,” Wilson told the crowd. “Tonight concludes a campaign, but the conversation about Alberta’s future in Canada and our place in Canada and our role in Canada will continue.”

After his brief speech, Wilson, a lawyer who gained national prominence defending members of the anti-COVID lockdown Freedom Convoy, stepped into the remaining crowd. “We’re not giving up,” he said as he shook hands with a moustached man in a tan cowboy hat. “We’re still going, man.”

Forever Canadian founder Thomas Lukaszuk speaks at the pro-Canada watch party in Edmonton, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026.

Thomas Lukaszuk took the stage in Edmonton to celebrate projections showing the remain side winning with 76 per cent.

Lukaszuk said that such a figure sends a message that Albertans want to remain in Canada. He was cautious in his celebrations, saying while it was a good sign, he wasn’t going to start popping champagne just yet.

He also spoke to the fact that 23 per cent of voters picked the option to hold a vote on separation.

Lukaszuk told the crowd these people are Albertans and Canadians and need to be listened to. He described the need to find a way to talk to them.

He also made a message for Alberta Premier Danielle Smith: “We are not packing our bags yet.”

The mood at the “Let Alberta Decide” headquarters in Calgary is somewhere between distracted and resigned. Some supporters have already started leaving. But Keith Wilson, the group’s leader, told me that he isn’t giving up hope just yet.

“It’s too early to tell” what’s going to happen, Wilson said outside the small hotel meeting room where his supporters were gathered. “Our predictions were that we would (struggle) early on.”

As the results trickled in, the sound remained off on the projection screen TV at the Wilson party. One supporter took to livestreaming a new broadcast on his phone in the lobby. He sat in a canopied chair, swinging gently, frowning at the screen.

Inside the room, a handful of supporters sat watching Global News in silence. Small groups were gathered chatting around cocktail tables.

Supporters cheer as results begin to display at the pro Canada watch party in Edmonton, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026.

Both CBC News and CTV News are projecting the remain side has won.

CBC made the call, showing the remain side leading with 76.6 per cent of the vote, as compared to 23 per cent for the independence option.

The crowd at the “Forever Canadian” event in Edmonton reacts as the first results, as reported by CBC News, show the remain side has a commanding lead.

A “Forever Canadian” beer from the Red Hart Brewing Company on display at a pro-Canadian unity party in Edmonton, Oct. 19, 2026.

This beer is but one of the many pieces of cultural swag that the Alberta referendum has created.

It was brewed in Red Deer County at a brewery that Prime Minister Mark Carney visited during his two day whirlwind stop in Alberta last week.

The separatists have their own swag, too.

Supporters mingle at a small Alberta independence party in downtown Calgary on Oct. 19, 2026.

I’m struck, looking at Stephanie’s photos from Edmonton and my own view from Calgary, how small this all feels for a referendum on the future of our country.

Supporters at the “Forever Canadian” referendum party in Edmonton, Oct. 19, 2026.

Keith Wilson’s Let Alberta Decide raised almost $600,000, more money than any other third party group in this campaign. And yet, with the polls officially closed there still can’t be more than 30 people at his official election event.

It doesn’t sound, from what Stephanie’s reporting, that the crowd at Thomas Lukaszuk’s event in Edmonton is any more robust.

The last poll was projected to close at 10 p.m. MT, 12 p.m. ET.

That means Elections Alberta can start posting results.

It had already begun counting the 1.3 million votes that were cast through advance voting and mail-in ballots — a historic figure.

Keith Wilson speaks at the launch of Alberta independence organization “Let Alberta Decide” in Calgary, Friday, June 19, 2026.

I just spoke to Let Alberta Decide leader Keith Wilson outside his party at the Alt Hotel in downtown Calgary. He told me he’s feeling both excited and anxious as the clock ticks down.

“I’ve got this funny little glimmer of hope,” he said. Wilson is expecting the pro-sovereignty side to get somewhere north of 35 percent of the vote. “But then there’s this little sliver of me that goes, well, wait a minute,” he said. “When you look at Brexit, and you look at the first election of Donald Trump … the polls got them all wrong.”

Wilson still believes there are quiet sovereigntists who aren’t comfortable talking to pollsters who May still turn out and swing the referendum his way. “I’ve spoken with many people from all walks of life — school teachers, firefighters, and importantly, leaders of industry, presidents of companies — who have shared with me in confidence that public facing, they’re either going to be neutral or leaning more toward the stay side in their public statements,” he said. “But no matter what, they’re voting option two, because they want this change.”

Regardless of the outcome Monday night, Wilson said the independence fight will continue. Will there be another referendum? I asked. “Oh I think certainly there will be,” he replied.

Supporters at the “Forever Canadian” referendum party in Edmonton stood and sang O Canada for a band that has just wrapped up.

Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski who represents an Edmonton riding is here. Earlier today she was in Wainwright, Alta., meeting with first responders and staff at the local hospital who cared for those injured in Saturday’s fire at the base.

There’s lots of red and white in tonight’s crowd, which is relatively small compared to the size of the room booked.

Supporters mingle at a small Alberta independence party in downtown Calgary Monday night.

I have relocated to Keith Wilson’s Let Alberta Decide party across the river downtown in Calgary.

There are maybe two dozen Alberta independence supporters in the room and an equal number of reporters and influencers, including one wearing sunglasses over a blue mask and a custom hockey jersey in Buffalo Sabres colours.

Volunteers for pro-Canada group Alberta’s Voice mingle at the Ruberto Ostberg Gallery in NW Calgary, Oct. 19, 2026.

I’m in Calgary at an event for the pro-Canada group Alberta’s Voice. The mood here two hours before results start coming is cautiously jubilant.

Alberta’s Voice founder Stephen Carter told me he thinks the remain side should easily win on question 10. “I’ve got 77 (per cent) to 23 (per cent),” he said while drinking what he told me was a non-alcoholic beer.

“I don’t see them going over 25 (per cent),” Carter added. “A bad loss for us might be 28 (per cent.) But Keith Wilson thinks he’s got magic votes. So what do I know?”

Carter, for now, is more concerned with the outcome of the other referendum questions. It was his group that coined the slogan “No to the Nine,” urging Albertans to reject all of Danielle Smith’s proposals on immigration and the constitution.

“It looks like the four constitutional questions are going down for sure,” he said. “Which was the whole f—-ing point.”

The Alberta’s Voice party was being hosted at an art gallery/bar in NW Calgary. Attendees include Calgary Liberal MP Corey Hogan. Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas was scheduled to arrive around 9 p.m. local time, Carter said.

I asked Carter what he thinks should happen next if the separation referendum does fail tonight. His answer: He believes Alberta Premier Danielle Smith should resign.

Mitch Slyvestre addresses supporters, saying "Alberta has changed." (Oct. 19, 2026)

In a speech to supporters shortly before 8:30 p.m. MT, Mitch Slyvestre declared that regardless of what happens with the vote, “Alberta has changed.”

He told the crowd “there’s no going back.”

After he spoke, the crowd erupted into chanting “Freedom, freedom.”

Supporters of the Forever Canada group, who want Alberta to remain in Canada, sit as they wait for the results of a non-binding referendum on Alberta sovereignty in Edmonton, Oct. 19, 2026.

Polls have officially closed in Alberta, save for the more than 100 which will be open later because of delays in opening or interruptions during the day

Elections Alberta confirms that counting will begin for ballots cast at the polling stations whose hours were not extended past 8 p.m. MT.

Independence party headquarters in Edmonton, Oct. 19, 2026.

The crowd is filling out and the TVs are now on at independence party headquarters in Edmonton.

Man of the hour Mitch Slyvestre is preparing to appear on CBC News, one of the channels on in the bar, as voting in the referendum enters the home stretch.

Remember: No results will be removed until the last poll closes at 10 p.m. MT, which is midnight for those in Ontario and later the further east you live.

Tyrone Polanski and partner Dianne watch referendum results with the independence party in Edmonton, Oct. 19, 2026.

Tyrone Polanski says he and his love, Dianne, are celebrating their 26th anniversary and to mark it are watching Alberta’s referendum results roll in with the independence crowd.

Polanski, who says he moved to Edmonton about a year-and-a-half ago, marked Option 2 on his ballot because he says he wants to see “changes.”

As for whether he thinks change will happen in terms of Alberta separating from Canada? Not so much.

“Realistically, I don’t think we’re going to separate,” he told the Star. “It affects people’s pensions.”

“It affects a lot of things that, when people look at the big picture, the infrastructure, you just can’t separate like that. Not in our lifetime, anyway. I think it’s more … sending a message.”

As for what he believes the showing for Option 2 needs to be in order to successfully send Ottawa that message, Polanski figures “at least” close to 50 per cent.

Chrystia Freeland, former finance minister and deputy prime minister of Canada.

Canadians can “breathe a sigh of relief” if 20 per cent or fewer Albertans vote in favour of separation, says former finance minister and former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland.

“If it is more than 30 (per cent) I would be really, really, very worried and upset,” she said.

Freeland, originally from Peace River, Alta., spoke this evening with the Star’s business columnist Adam Radwanski in front of a sold-out crowd at Toronto’s Soulpepper Theatre Company. The two discussed Freeland’s new book: “Unreliable Boyfriend: An Insider’s View of Dealing with a Chaotic Superpower, Plutocrats, and Other Complicated People.”

Freeland had started the evening by offering her compassion to the families affected by the military disaster at a base near Wainwright, Alta.

When asked about the referendum, Freeland said she considers herself a daughter of Alberta and noted she is glad the campaign to keep Alberta in Canada was made a non-partisan issue.

Freeland said she is awaiting the referendum results with her “fingers crossed.”

“I am cautiously optimistic that it’s going to be a good result tonight,” she said.

Leader of the Alberta Prosperity Project, Mitch Sylvestre, at his group’s referendum reception, Oct. 19 2026.

Mitch Slyvestre is getting the rock star treatment tonight at his group’s referendum reception.

He knows most of the people in the room. They worked to make this vote happen, fanning out across the province to urge supporters to vote “Option 2.”

Slyvestre said he voted this morning in his town of Bonnyville.

“It’s kind of given me a little bit of peace,” he said, citing how his campaigning for independence has been ramped up since last December.

It’s hard for Slyvestre to get very far in this reception room. People want to shake his hand. Some want photos.

“I didn’t realize how tall you were,” says one man, who asks Slyvestre for a photo with him as well as his wife.

Prime Minister Mark Carney meets with Premier of Alberta Danielle Smith at his office in Ottawa on Friday, May 8, 2026.

The doors have opened for the referendum party being hosted by the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent separatist group heavily involved in making this vote even happen.

Mitch Slyvestre, the group’s leader, was behind the signature petition drive that pushed this issue.

As of around 5 p.m. MT, he was chatting with members of the media gathered at the group’s event for the evening hosted at a bar in Edmonton.

Both Slyvestre and Jeffrey Rath, another prominent voice in the push for independence, are expected to deliver speeches later.

Elections Alberta is confirming that reporting of referendum results will be delayed until after the last polling station closes at 10 p.m. MT.

That means those following along living in the eastern time zone won’t start hearing results until midnight.

Elections Alberta issued a news release late Monday confirming that nearly 90 polling stations across the province would be kept open past the expected closing time of 8 p.m. MT.

That came as a result of many polling stations opening later than the slated time of 9 a.m. MT.

The latest a polling station will stay open is 10 p.m. MT.

Elections Alberta previously said that was the result of a polling station in one Edmonton neighborhood having to shut down for several hours after workers saw the need to reconfigure the room.

Edmonton—Referendum day in Alberta is today.

The provincial referendum has 10 questions about immigration policy, constitutional reform, and whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a binding, second referendum on quitting the country.

Over 1,400 polling stations will be open Monday from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Here’s what to expect when you go to vote:

How long will it take?

Get familiar with the ballot questions ahead of time, which are on the Elections Alberta website. Officials say it will help avoid confusion and delays.

They say they’re expecting a record turnout of between 80 and 85 per cent of Alberta’s nearly three million electors.

You have as much time as you want to fill in the 10 ballots, but officials estimate it will take most people about two minutes.

What identification is needed?

You should get a “where to vote” card in the mail ahead of time if you’re registered. Otherwise, visit Elections Alberta’s website to find out where to vote.

You must vote in your electoral division during advance voting or at your assigned location on Monday.

You’ll need one government-issued ID with your correct name, current address and photo, such as a driver’s licence. You can use two pieces of ID that both have your full name, with one showing your current address.

There are 50 forms of acceptable ID listed on Elections Alberta’s website that can be one of those two pieces, from a library card or a hunting licence to a bank statement or vehicle registration.

Elections Alberta says it will accept expired forms of ID, including a certificate of Indian Status Card, provided it still has the correct name.

Another option, in special circumstances, is to bring an attestation form signed by an authorized person such as a First Nation band manager or a student housing staffer.

What if I’m not registered to vote?

A voting officer will ask you to sign a declaration that confirms your eligibility — including that you are a Canadian citizen, at least 18 years old and that you normally reside in Alberta.

How many ballots are there?

There are 10 ballots, in different colours for easy identification. You can mark some of them, all of them or none. Your choice.

The ballots go into separate boxes to make it easier to count them and to lessen the chances of a mistake spoiling one long ballot.

What if I’m still in line when the polls close at 8 p.m.?

Stay in line. Don’t leave. You will be allowed to vote.

How long before I know the results?

By law, the votes need to be counted by hand within 48 hours.

Question 10 — about separation — is to be counted first. Officials say early results are to be released after 8 p.m. Monday, with the final count announced in the early hours Tuesday.

The results of the other nine questions should be completed and announced by Wednesday.
