stories.title: Investors buying unsold Toronto condos at 40% discount to original selling price, report finds
stories.summary: Six bulk buyers in the Toronto region bought 339 units in the most recent quarter, or 45% of new condo purchases, Urbanation report says
stories.author: Rachelle Younglai
stories.content:
Large investors bought unsold newly built condos in the Toronto region at a 40-per-cent discount to the original selling price and accounted for nearly half the preconstruction sales in recent months.

These investors paid an average of $763 per square foot for a completed and unsold unit in the third quarter, according to a report from condo research firm Urbanation Inc.

They often buy a minimum of a few dozen units from a developer as a bulk purchase. In the most recent quarter ended in September, there were six bulk buyers in the Toronto region that bought 339 units. The bulk buys accounted for 45 per cent of the 760 new condo purchases in the quarter.

Real estate companies or investment funds have gotten a cheaper price than individual buyers trying to find a deal among the glut of unsold units in the Toronto and Hamilton area.

Individuals paid an average of $1,033 per square foot for a newly built condo in the third quarter, according to Urbanation.

“Two straight quarters of higher sales show that buyers will step in at the right price,” Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand said in a news release. “Bulk investors are acquiring completed units at heavily discounted prices.”

The bulk purchases included a transaction by High Art Capital, an Ontario government-backed fund that is turning a portion of its units into affordable rentals. High Art paid $22.3-million for 43 units in a condo complex called Line 5 in midtown Toronto, The Globe and Mail first reported in September.

That works out to about $518,000 per unit and is close to the typical selling price of a condo on the resale market in the Toronto region. That is unusual because newly built condos normally sell at a significant premium to those on the resale market

This is the second quarter since the federal and Ontario governments’ HST rebate on new homes has been in place. It is also the second period where new condo sales have been markedly higher than last year.

Buyers can get a maximum of $130,000 rebate on the HST for new homes priced up to $1.5-million until the end of March, 2027. The temporary tax break went into effect in April and is designed to help developers get rid of unsold inventory, which it has managed to do to some extent.

At the end of September, there were 5,127 newly built units that were unsold. That was down 7 per cent from the end of June. (The unsold inventory does not include the units that developers have had to take back because buyers have defaulted on their purchases.)

Those who bought preconstruction units at the height of the market have seen the value of their units plunge over the past four years, according to realtors and property appraisers.

Many preconstruction buyers have not been able to close if their lender does not provide them with a mortgage at the original purchase price.

For the many individual investors who have been able to close, they are losing money on their investment because they either cannot find renters or the rent is not enough to cover the cost of their mortgage payments, condo fees and other property expenses.

That has led to a drop in preconstruction condo sales, which is a precursor to a condo tower being built. In the third quarter, there were only 60 condo units in the preconstruction phase that were sold in the Toronto and Hamilton region.

Mr. Hildebrand called the preconstruction market dormant and said this will lead to a major decline in new condos being built.

stories.title: Alberta votes on leaving Canada: 1.4 million ballots cast in advance; record turnout expected today
stories.summary: More than 800,000 advanced ballots were already cast before voting day, with results expected to roll in late Monday night.
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
Polls opened for Alberta’s historic referendum on Monday, with voters lining up to cast a ballot over whether the province should consider separating from Canada.

Voting day follows months of debate over the separation question, which has divided many in the province and prompted both sides to ramp up efforts to sway public opinion in recent weeks.

The referendum, which includes one question on proposed separation and another nine on various other constitutional matters, is expected to draw record numbers to the ballot box. Elections Alberta estimates record turnout as high as 85 per cent, compared with an average of just over 50 per cent in recent general elections. According to the agency, 1.4 million voters, or 43.1 per cent of eligible voters, have already cast advanced ballots or special ballots before Monday. That compares with 809,988 advanced and special ballots cast in the 2023 election, or 27.5 per cent of eligible voters.

Monday’s referendum vote is not explicitly a vote to leave Canada, but gives voters the option of either remaining in Canada or holding a second vote on whether to secede.

Polls opened at 9 a.m. MT and will remain open until 8 p.m. local time. However, some polling stations reportedly opened late on Monday and will remain open past 8 p.m. Elections Alberta will start counting advanced and special ballots starting at 5 p.m. MT. Early results will start rolling in after the final vote has been cast.

The separation question will be counted first and results are expected late Monday night. Check back here for the latest results after polls close. Results for the other nine questions will be announced within 48 hours.

The other nine questions ask Albertans whether Alberta should be given more control over immigration rates, work with other provinces to abolish the federal Senate, or give the province the right to opt out of certain federal programs, among others. Five of the 10 questions relate to immigration policy, including asking whether the province should halt some public services like health care to non-permanent residents.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has repeatedly said she prefers that the province remain in Canada, despite the fact that it was her government that changed the law to enable the referendum on separation to be held. The premier has called for an “independent Alberta within a united Canada” and has been working closely with Prime Minister Mark Carney to repair the province’s fractured relationship with Ottawa.

Together, the pair have announced a flurry of joint projects in an effort to shore up support for the federalist side, including Carney’s promise to back the province’s proposed West Coast oil pipeline and pump $8 billion in new military spending in the province.

Carney was in Alberta last week for a final campaign aimed at pushing Albertans to vote to remain, saying the country is stronger united, particularly in the face of what he calls a dangerous and divided world.

Meanwhile, Alberta’s pro-separatist advocates have also been calling on voters to get out the vote, with some arguing a vote for separation can give the province useful leverage in its negotiations with Ottawa.

While results of the referendum are unlikely to be known until late Monday night, polling has consistently shown that roughly three quarters of voters support remaining in Canada, while the other 25 per cent are sympathetic to the separatist cause.

1. Do you support the Government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?

2. Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially-funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?

3. Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially-funded social support programs?

4. Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family’s use of the health care and education systems?

5. Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?

6. Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King’s Bench and Appeal courts?

7. Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

8. paragraphs: Polls opened for Alberta’s historic referendum on Monday, with voters lining up to cast a ballot over whether the province should consider separating from Canada.
Voting day follows months of debate over the separation question, which has divided many in the province and prompted both sides to ramp up efforts to sway public opinion in recent weeks.

The referendum, which includes one question on proposed separation and another nine on various other constitutional matters, is expected to draw record numbers to the ballot box. Elections Alberta estimates record turnout as high as 85 per cent, compared with an average of just over 50 per cent in recent general elections. According to the agency, 1.4 million voters, or 43.1 per cent of eligible voters, have already cast advanced ballots or special ballots before Monday. That compares with 809,988 advanced and special ballots cast in the 2023 election, or 27.5 per cent of eligible voters.
Monday’s referendum vote is not explicitly a vote to leave Canada, but gives voters the option of either remaining in Canada or holding a second vote on whether to secede.

Polls opened at 9 a.m. MT and will remain open until 8 p.m. local time. However, some polling stations reportedly opened late on Monday and will remain open past 8 p.m. Elections Alberta will start counting advanced and special ballots starting at 5 p.m. MT. Early results will start rolling in after the final vote has been cast.

The separation question will be counted first and results are expected late Monday night. Check back here for the latest results after polls close. Results for the other nine questions will be announced within 48 hours.

The other nine questions ask Albertans whether Alberta should be given more control over immigration rates, work with other provinces to abolish the federal Senate, or give the province the right to opt out of certain federal programs, among others. Five of the 10 questions relate to immigration policy, including asking whether the province should halt some public services like health care to non-permanent residents.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has repeatedly said she prefers that the province remain in Canada, despite the fact that it was her government that changed the law to enable the referendum on separation to be held. The premier has called for an “independent Alberta within a united Canada” and has been working closely with Prime Minister Mark Carney to repair the province’s fractured relationship with Ottawa.

Together, the pair have announced a flurry of joint projects in an effort to shore up support for the federalist side, including Carney’s promise to back the province’s proposed West Coast oil pipeline and pump $8 billion in new military spending in the province.

Carney was in Alberta last week for a final campaign aimed at pushing Albertans to vote to remain, saying the country is stronger united, particularly in the face of what he calls a dangerous and divided world.

Meanwhile, Alberta’s pro-separatist advocates have also been calling on voters to get out the vote, with some arguing a vote for separation can give the province useful leverage in its negotiations with Ottawa.

While results of the referendum are unlikely to be known until late Monday night, polling has consistently shown that roughly three quarters of voters support remaining in Canada, while the other 25 per cent are sympathetic to the separatist cause.

1. Do you support the Government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?

2. Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially-funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?

3. Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially-funded social support programs?

4. Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family’s use of the health care and education systems?

5. Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?

6. Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King’s Bench and Appeal courts?
7. Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

8. Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?

9. Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province’s laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province’s laws and federal laws conflict?

10. Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

stories.title: Members of Quebec's official Opposition Liberals sworn in at the legislature
stories.summary: QUÉBEC - Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Millard urged his caucus to serve with clarity and humility today as they were sworn in at the provincial legislature.
stories.author: Caroline Plante The Canadian Press
stories.content:
QUÉBEC - Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Millard urged his caucus to serve with clarity and humility today as they were sworn in at the provincial legislature.

Millard said his party’s work isn’t done after a strong Oct. 5 election result.

The party more than doubled its seat count, going from 18 to 40 and will serve as the official Opposition to the minority Parti Québécois government.

Former premier Jean Charest was on hand to watch as his son Antoine was sworn in as the new representative for the Verdun riding.

All of the Liberals opted to swear the oath to the Quebec people and not to the King, after the oath to the monarch was made optional in 2022.

One member, Affine Lwalalika, was not sworn in since a judicial recount is underway in her riding.

Milliard told his elected members to be proud, but also urged them to approach the role with “a healthy dose of clarity and humility.”

“If our work of rebuilding were complete, we would be the ones forming the government today,” he said, adding, “There are still many regions to win back.”

“The result on Oct. 5 is certainly an important milestone, but it is by no means the culmination of all our efforts.”

He said it’s unclear how long the minority PQ government led by Paul St-Pierre Plamondon will last, and called for both discipline and teamwork.

“When it comes to resolving crises, the government will find in us a reliable and open partner, but when it comes to creating crises … it will find in us a tough and unyielding opponent,” he said.

Milliard also stated that the Quebec Fleur-de-lis is “just as striking alongside the Maple Leaf,” in a plea for federalism that drew thunderous applause.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: B.C. designer Bob Masse created groovy poster art for leading rock bands
stories.summary: With an art style featuring ornate Art Nouveau lines and distorted, hand-drawn lettering, he did work for Sixties groups including the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane; and he had a career revival later in life that saw him designing posters for U2, Neil Young and the Tragically Hip
stories.author: Tom Hawthorn
stories.content:
Bob Masse tuned in to the 1960s California scene, turned on to copious mind-altering substances, and dropped some of the grooviest psychedelic posters of the era.

The British Columbia graphic artist befriended band members of the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane, partied with Janis Joplin and hung out with musicians living in Laurel Canyon in the Hollywood Hills, including a fellow Canadian by the name of Joni Mitchell, whom he described as a “skinny little girl with buckteeth.”

Mr. Masse, who has died at 81, created far-out concert posters for such bands as the Dead, the Doors, Jefferson Airplane, the Steve Miller Band, and Country Joe and the Fish.

Mr. Masse was a rare poster artist from the 1960s to continue working well into the next century.

Years after his initial success, he was rediscovered and his career revived, a flashback of sorts, as he enjoyed a long, fruitful span crafting glorious posters for such performers as Tori Amos, Pearl Jam, Alanis Morissette, Smashing Pumpkins and the Red Hot Chili Peppers.

Youthful looking throughout his life, he was often asked to reminisce about the events and characters of the Sixties, though it must be said the chaotic nature of those times and his own indulgences left his memories somewhat foggy.

As he once said, “I got my mind blown in San Francisco.”

It was while he was in California hanging out with hippie bands that he came across a 50-year-old graphic design manual that changed his life.

Robert Joseph Masse was born in Vancouver on April 5, 1945, the first of four children for the former Lillian Mae Sharp and Joseph Frank Masse. Joe was serving with an artillery unit of the Canadian Army during the Second World War when he went on a blind date with Lill, a packer for a wholesale grocery firm. They married in 1944. After leaving the armed services, the elder Mr. Masse worked as a furniture polisher and refinisher with Woodward’s department store.

Young Bob liked to draw in the basement of the family’s home in Burnaby, a community adjacent to Vancouver. He got a formal education in design at the Vancouver School of Art (now the Emily Carr University of Art + Design).

A practicum sent him across the street to the Queen Elizabeth Theatre, where he offered to create for free a concert poster for a folk singer from Minnesota via Greenwich Village who was about to make his debut in the city. The poster featured six candid black-and-white photographs of the tousled, unkempt, smoking, guitar-strumming poet-singer in two vertical rows, with the date and place in all lower case, sans-serif letters. Dozens of the posters were placed around town before anyone realized Mr. Masse had rendered Bob Dylan’s surname as “Dylon.”

Mr. Masse created posters for coffeehouses featuring folk music such as the Inquisition and the Bunkhouse before doing the same for teenaged promotor Jerry Kruz, whose Afterthought promotions included light shows and the new sounds coming from California bands, as well as local talent. He was paid $10 per poster.

A trip to San Francisco introduced Mr. Masse to concert posters – by the likes of Wes Wilson, Stanley Mouse and others – featuring ornate Art Nouveau lines and distorted, hand-drawn, barely legible lettering.

“I went through a structured system [at art school], and all of a sudden people were coming out with totally bizarre designs,” he said. “It was a total breakdown in the rules.”

At the same time, he came across a copy of Strong’s Book of Designs , a 1917 manual by Charles Jay Strong featuring a phantasmagoria of ribbons, borders, show cards, airbrush designs and illustrations of such objects as butterflies, as well as fanciful typography, much of it reproduced in glorious colour.

He crashed for free in an old Victorian house at 710 Ashbury St., the communal home and headquarters of the Grateful Dead. When the band came to British Columbia, Mr. Masse agreed to meet them at the border.

“They were driving this psychedelic-painted bus, like a Ken Kesey bus, and the border officials almost fainted when they saw these guys,” he told Neal Hall of the Vancouver Sun in 2007.

Mr. Masse produced several memorable posters for the band’s shows in Vancouver, as well as for the Trips Festival, an 11-hour concert held at a hockey rink in suburban Richmond in 1967 featuring such acts as the Jefferson Airplane, Magic Fern, the Collectors and Painted Ship (the latter two both from Vancouver), as well as the Cougar and Darks Pandemonium Light Show Company (the latter being a whimsical name for the lighting crew). He also made posters for shows at Dante’s Inferno and the Retinal Circus, nightclubs at the same address on Davie Street in downtown Vancouver.

Mr. Masse returned to California where he designed posters and newspaper advertisements for the Whiskey A Go Go while living in an apartment above the Los Angeles nightclub. He later lived in a garage in Laurel Canyon, an area that was home to many of the city’s rock musicians.

He hung out backstage with the Doors and Ms. Joplin, who once complained to him about a lack of male groupies. “Nobody chases me,” she told him. “I’m not getting any action here.” Mr. Masse later confessed regret at not having taken the hint.

On his return to British Columbia in the 1970s, Mr. Masse adopted a softer, more pastoral style with more pastel colours, influenced by the imagery of Alphonse Mucha, the Mitteleuropean artist who became known for his theatrical posters for Sarah Bernhardt in the 1890s.

Mr. Masse abandoned poster making for years, as clients demanded edgier designs than he cared to create, supporting himself through commercial and advertising work.

One day, he called friend Rob Frith, a poster collector and record store owner, about a cache of old posters his parents had kept in their basement. When Mr. Frith visited the artist’s apartment, he discovered to his horror that Mr. Masse was using his old work to light fires in his fireplace. He bought the entire stack.

In 1992, Mr. Frith offered to pay for the printing if Mr. Masse made a poster for a forthcoming show by the Scottish musician Donovan on his Mellow Yellow Tour. With the deadline looming, the artist recycled an old image he had used years earlier for Honey’s Creative Sandwiches, a lunch spot next to his studio in Vancouver’s Gastown. In the original, a bare-chested nymph in a flowing, diaphanous robe with flowers in her hair is depicted holding a sandwich. For the concert poster, the food was replaced by a crystal ball.

He once again became an in-demand poster designer with his signature style called on by such artists as U2, Neil Young and the Tragically Hip. He also designed covers for the front page of the Georgia Straight newspaper on its 30 th and 50 th anniversaries, homages to the publication’s underground roots.

As well, his earlier work was rediscovered. One of his posters was included in The Art of Rock , a 1987 coffee-table book considered a vital reference for collectors of such rock ’n’ roll ephemera as posters, tickets, handbills and backstage passes.

When Mr. Frith sought to get approval for a reissue of a Grateful Dead poster, he called the band for permission. They well knew the poster; an original was hanging in their office. For Mr. Masse, this was the beginning of a profitable period of selling reproductions.

Among his many other notable works were album covers, including for the Collectors, which became the band Chilliwack. He also did the cover art for two albums issued by Mr. Frith featuring the sounds of Vancouver, including one released in August.

For all his psychedelic and pastoral works, his most ubiquitous design was likely an orange cartoon fox with heavy-lidded eyes drawn for Cfox, a Vancouver rock radio station.

“He’s everywhere, that little bugger,” he once lamented.

Mr. Masse, a resident of Salt Spring Island, where he maintained a studio, died in hospital there on Sept. 21 from Parkinson-plus syndrome, a group of neurodegenerative diseases. He had earlier suffered a minor stroke and was recuperating from the lingering effects of a motorcycle accident. He leaves Claire Norris, his partner of 33 years. He also leaves a sister, Bonnie, and brothers Ray and Len, the latter who drew a DoodleArt poster titled Ecology that sold more than a million copies. An earlier marriage for Mr. Masse ended in divorce. He had no children.

The artist’s career spanned a time when the government went from prosecuting possession of weed to selling it. As well, the posters for which he was once paid a pittance have become valuable collectibles. paragraphs: Bob Masse tuned in to the 1960s California scene, turned on to copious mind-altering substances, and dropped some of the grooviest psychedelic posters of the era.

The British Columbia graphic artist befriended band members of the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane, partied with Janis Joplin and hung out with musicians living in Laurel Canyon in the Hollywood Hills, including a fellow Canadian by the name of Joni Mitchell, whom he described as a “skinny little girl with buckteeth.”
Mr. Masse, who has died at 81, created far-out concert posters for such bands as the Dead, the Doors, Jefferson Airplane, the Steve Miller Band, and Country Joe and the Fish.
Mr. Masse was a rare poster artist from the 1960s to continue working well into the next century.

Years after his initial success, he was rediscovered and his career revived, a flashback of sorts, as he enjoyed a long, fruitful span crafting glorious posters for such performers as Tori Amos, Pearl Jam, Alanis Morissette, Smashing Pumpkins and the Red Hot Chili Peppers.

Youthful looking throughout his life, he was often asked to reminisce about the events and characters of the Sixties, though it must be said the chaotic nature of those times and his own indulgences left his memories somewhat foggy.
As he once said, “I got my mind blown in San Francisco.”
It was while he was in California hanging out with hippie bands that he came across a 50-year-old graphic design manual that changed his life.

Robert Joseph Masse was born in Vancouver on April 5, 1945, the first of four children for the former Lillian Mae Sharp and Joseph Frank Masse. Joe was serving with an artillery unit of the Canadian Army during the Second World War when he went on a blind date with Lill, a packer for a wholesale grocery firm. They married in 1944. After leaving the armed services, the elder Mr. Masse worked as a furniture polisher and refinisher with Woodward’s department store.

Young Bob liked to draw in the basement of the family’s home in Burnaby, a community adjacent to Vancouver. He got a formal education in design at the Vancouver School of Art (now the Emily Carr University of Art + Design).

A practicum sent him across the street to the Queen Elizabeth Theatre, where he offered to create for free a concert poster for a folk singer from Minnesota via Greenwich Village who was about to make his debut in the city. The poster featured six candid black-and-white photographs of the tousled, unkempt, smoking, guitar-strumming poet-singer in two vertical rows, with the date and place in all lower case, sans-serif letters. Dozens of the posters were placed around town before anyone realized Mr. Masse had rendered Bob Dylan’s surname as “Dylon.”

Mr. Masse created posters for coffeehouses featuring folk music such as the Inquisition and the Bunkhouse before doing the same for teenaged promotor Jerry Kruz, whose Afterthought promotions included light shows and the new sounds coming from California bands, as well as local talent. He was paid $10 per poster.

A trip to San Francisco introduced Mr. Masse to concert posters – by the likes of Wes Wilson, Stanley Mouse and others – featuring ornate Art Nouveau lines and distorted, hand-drawn, barely legible lettering.
“I went through a structured system [at art school], and all of a sudden people were coming out with totally bizarre designs,” he said. “It was a total breakdown in the rules.”

At the same time, he came across a copy of Strong’s Book of Designs , a 1917 manual by Charles Jay Strong featuring a phantasmagoria of ribbons, borders, show cards, airbrush designs and illustrations of such objects as butterflies, as well as fanciful typography, much of it reproduced in glorious colour.

He crashed for free in an old Victorian house at 710 Ashbury St., the communal home and headquarters of the Grateful Dead. When the band came to British Columbia, Mr. Masse agreed to meet them at the border.
“They were driving this psychedelic-painted bus, like a Ken Kesey bus, and the border officials almost fainted when they saw these guys,” he told Neal Hall of the Vancouver Sun in 2007.

Mr. Masse produced several memorable posters for the band’s shows in Vancouver, as well as for the Trips Festival, an 11-hour concert held at a hockey rink in suburban Richmond in 1967 featuring such acts as the Jefferson Airplane, Magic Fern, the Collectors and Painted Ship (the latter two both from Vancouver), as well as the Cougar and Darks Pandemonium Light Show Company (the latter being a whimsical name for the lighting crew). He also made posters for shows at Dante’s Inferno and the Retinal Circus, nightclubs at the same address on Davie Street in downtown Vancouver.

Mr. Masse returned to California where he designed posters and newspaper advertisements for the Whiskey A Go Go while living in an apartment above the Los Angeles nightclub. He later lived in a garage in Laurel Canyon, an area that was home to many of the city’s rock musicians.

He hung out backstage with the Doors and Ms. Joplin, who once complained to him about a lack of male groupies. “Nobody chases me,” she told him. “I’m not getting any action here.” Mr. Masse later confessed regret at not having taken the hint.

On his return to British Columbia in the 1970s, Mr. Masse adopted a softer, more pastoral style with more pastel colours, influenced by the imagery of Alphonse Mucha, the Mitteleuropean artist who became known for his theatrical posters for Sarah Bernhardt in the 1890s.
Mr. Masse abandoned poster making for years, as clients demanded edgier designs than he cared to create, supporting himself through commercial and advertising work.

One day, he called friend Rob Frith, a poster collector and record store owner, about a cache of old posters his parents had kept in their basement. When Mr. Frith visited the artist’s apartment, he discovered to his horror that Mr. Masse was using his old work to light fires in his fireplace. He bought the entire stack.

In 1992, Mr. Frith offered to pay for the printing if Mr. Masse made a poster for a forthcoming show by the Scottish musician Donovan on his Mellow Yellow Tour. With the deadline looming, the artist recycled an old image he had used years earlier for Honey’s Creative Sandwiches, a lunch spot next to his studio in Vancouver’s Gastown. In the original, a bare-chested nymph in a flowing, diaphanous robe with flowers in her hair is depicted holding a sandwich. For the concert poster, the food was replaced by a crystal ball.

He once again became an in-demand poster designer with his signature style called on by such artists as U2, Neil Young and the Tragically Hip. He also designed covers for the front page of the Georgia Straight newspaper on its 30 th and 50 th anniversaries, homages to the publication’s underground roots.

As well, his earlier work was rediscovered. One of his posters was included in The Art of Rock , a 1987 coffee-table book considered a vital reference for collectors of such rock ’n’ roll ephemera as posters, tickets, handbills and backstage passes.

When Mr. Frith sought to get approval for a reissue of a Grateful Dead poster, he called the band for permission. They well knew the poster; an original was hanging in their office. For Mr. Masse, this was the beginning of a profitable period of selling reproductions.

Among his many other notable works were album covers, including for the Collectors, which became the band Chilliwack. He also did the cover art for two albums issued by Mr. Frith featuring the sounds of Vancouver, including one released in August.
For all his psychedelic and pastoral works, his most ubiquitous design was likely an orange cartoon fox with heavy-lidded eyes drawn for Cfox, a Vancouver rock radio station.
“He’s everywhere, that little bugger,” he once lamented.

Mr. Masse, a resident of Salt Spring Island, where he maintained a studio, died in hospital there on Sept. 21 from Parkinson-plus syndrome, a group of neurodegenerative diseases. He had earlier suffered a minor stroke and was recuperating from the lingering effects of a motorcycle accident. He leaves Claire Norris, his partner of 33 years. He also leaves a sister, Bonnie, and brothers Ray and Len, the latter who drew a DoodleArt poster titled Ecology that sold more than a million copies. An earlier marriage for Mr. Masse ended in divorce. He had no children.

The artist’s career spanned a time when the government went from prosecuting possession of weed to selling it. As well, the posters for which he was once paid a pittance have become valuable collectibles. One of Mr. Masse’s original Grateful Dead posters, for which he believed he had been paid $100 in 1967, sold at auction in the United States five years ago for more than $15,000. As the Grateful Dead sing on Truckin’ , “What a long, strange trip it’s been.”

stories.title: Measles outbreak over after two years, Phac says
stories.summary: More than 6,400 people were infected across 10 provinces, Public Health Agency of Canada says
stories.author: Hannah Alberga
stories.content:
A measles outbreak that spanned two years and infected thousands of people in Canada is over.

The Public Health Agency of Canada made the declaration in a press release Monday, stating that more than 6,400 people were infected across 10 provinces.

Two infants in Ontario and Alberta who were infected with measles while in the womb died after they were born.

The outbreak began in New Brunswick in October 2024 and about a year later led to the loss of Canada’s measles elimination status due to ongoing transmission of the highly contagious disease for more than 12 months.

Canada’s Chief Public Health Officer Dr. Joss Reimer says that although it’s encouraging to see the outbreak declared over, it doesn’t mean that measles is gone.

Infectious disease experts have attributed the return of measles to declining vaccination rates, misinformation-fuelled vaccine hesitancy and distrust of authority, as well as disruptions to routine immunizations during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“Measles continues to circulate globally, and we can expect to see further travel-related cases here at home,” Reimer said in a statement.

Ontario, which was one of the most affected provinces, declared its outbreak over last fall, while Alberta’s ended in July. Public health officials in Manitoba said the province’s last laboratory-confirmed case was in August.

content_blocks.text: Infectious disease experts have attributed the return of measles to declining vaccination rates, misinformation-fuelled vaccine hesitancy and distrust of authority, as well as disruptions to routine immunizations during the COVID-19 pandemic.

By The Canadian Press

The province says the funding from its Community Economic Development Fund is going to the Nova Scotia Boatbuilders Association.

It says the association will use the money to promote local companies at industry trade shows and missions, in trade publications and through online communications and strategic partnerships.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Donna Skelly home

Image 9Image 10Image 11

The Nova Scotia Boatbuilders Association was established in 1998 to diversify the industry beyond the domestic fishing boat market.

The province says the investment will help local boatbuilders deliver on national defence priorities and compete internationally for naval contracts.

The executive director of the Nova Scotia Boatbuilders Association says the boatbuilding industry maintains small vessels for several of the province’s key industries, including fisheries and defence.

“This investment helps to ensure the ongoing health of our industry, and the rural communities where much of the work takes place, as we navigate an unusually complex trade environment,” said a statement from executive director Jan Fullerton.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 26, 2026.

stories.title: Pjhl Recap - Oct 23rd to Oct 25th
stories.summary: The Merchants celebrated two wins, the Braves suffered two losses, and the Trojans had a mixed weekend.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Monday, 26 October 2026 at 08:36

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

The Merchants celebrated two wins, the Braves suffered two losses, and the Trojans had a mixed weekend.

PJHL - It was a great weekend for the Norwich Merchants, but a not so great weekend for the Tavistock Braves.

The Merchants beat the Dorchester Dolphins 4-3 in a shootout on Friday and celebrated a 4-3 overtime victory over the Braves yesterday. Ethan Osborne scored the game winning goal on Friday and Tyler McDole secured the victory for Norwich yesterday.

The Braves were also shutout by the Paris Mounties 5-0 on Friday.

The Thamesford Trojans celebrated a 7-3 victory over the Petrolia Flyers on Friday with Brady Snedden, Owen Eldridge, Ryan Rodney, Andrew Kalantzakos, Nathan Enwright, and Ben Siroen scoring for the home team. However, the Trojans did suffer a 4-3 overtime loss to the North Middlesex Stars on Saturday, with Noah Vandenburg scoring the game winning goal about 30 seconds into overtime.

The Braves still top the Doherty Division standings with 22 points. They're followed by the Wellesley Applejacks with 20 points, the New Hamburg Firebirds with 19 points, and the Merchants with 14 points. The Dolphins are in fifth place with 11 points, the Mounties sit in sixth place with 10 points, and the Hespeler Shamrocks are at the bottom of the standings with six points.

The Trojans are in fifth place in the Yeck Division standings with 12 points, ahead of the sixth place Lucan Irish with nine points and the last place Port Stanley Sailors with seven points.

The Stars top the Yeck Division standings with 18 points and they're followed by the Mount Brydges Bulldogs with 17 points, and the Exeter Hawks and Aylmer Spitfires are tied for third place with 16 points each. The Flyers are in fourth place with 13 points.

Navy Vets Recap - Oct 23rd Oct 25th The Woodstock Navy Vets are in eighth place in the GOHL Western Conference standings.

UPDATE: More Assault Charges Laid in Tillsonburg The suspect is facing 13 counts of sexual assault and one count of sexual interference, stemming from five victims.

Municipal Election Day in Oxford County You have until 8:00 p.m. to cast your ballot in the 2026 municipal election.

WITAAR Supports Local Classrooms WITAAR's annual classroom supply drive has helped many classrooms across the County this year.

Ingersoll Pumpkin Fest Returns this Saturday Each family will go home with a free pumpkin, while supplies last.

PJHL Preview - Oct 23rd to Oct 25th The Braves, Trojans and Merchants all have home games tonight.

Norfolk OPP Briefs - October 23rd, 2026 Briefs include two incidents in Waterford; a break and enter on Green Street and a stolen vehicle on Concession 8 Townsend.

Wolverines to Face WPS in Friday Night Lights Charity Classic The Woodstock Wolverines will face off against members of the Woodstock Police Service in the first annual Friday Night Lights Charity Classic on October 30th.

Blandford-Blenheim Candidate Profile - Nancy Demarest When the ballots are cast, a current councillor in Blandford-Blenheim is seeking re-election. Nancy Demarest is seeking a third term on council.

stories.title: Americans in Canada urge fellow expats to vote in high-stakes midterm elections
stories.summary: Ottawa - American Democrats living in Canada are prepared to shout their political choices from the rooftops ahead of next month's midterm elections — while some of those who back Republican candidates seem leery of speaking out fearing a backlash from their neighbours.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - American Democrats living in Canada are prepared to shout their political choices from the rooftops ahead of next month’s midterm elections — while some of those who back Republican candidates seem leery of speaking out fearing a backlash from their neighbours.

Tammy Wilsker Mermelstein, a Texas voter who moved to the Greater Toronto Area last year, will be voting in a U.S. election from Canada for the first time.

While she used to be a Republican and voted that way until 2016, Wilsker Mermelstein said she has never voted for U.S. President Donald Trump. She said it’s crucial for people to vote this year as “Texas is in play.”

“Texas has not elected a Democrat in high office for at least two decades, probably longer, and this is the first solid chance,” she said. “They say every vote counts. This is really going to be an election where every vote matters, even in states where people aren’t used to having their vote matter if they’re in the minority.”

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections which could see the Democrats seize control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives from the Republicans. Democratic control of one or both chambers could significantly alter the path of Trump’s presidency, including the possibility of new impeachment proceedings against him, and investigations of some of his key allies and agency heads.

Expat participation in U.S. elections is typically low, though the Federal Voting Assistance Program estimates there were more than 430,000 eligible U.S. voters in Canada as of 2024.

The organization estimates turnout among Americans in Canada was about 10 per cent in the 2024 general election, while the domestic voting rate that year was about 76 per cent. The organization estimates the overall turnout among all eligible overseas U.S. citizens at 11 per cent.

Kathryn Sikkink, a professor at the Harvard Kennedy School who has volunteered with the U.S. Vote Foundation, said participation in voting abroad may be low because some citizens find it difficult. Some, she said, don’t even realize they’re eligible to vote.

The U.S. Department of State website says U.S. citizens can get an absentee ballot by mail, email or fax, or by downloading it from the internet, though options vary by state.

Most U.S. citizens can vote absentee for federal office candidates in U.S. primary and general elections. Some states also allow U.S. citizens living abroad to vote for local and state office candidates, and on referendums.

Georganne Burke, the chapter lead for Republicans Overseas in Canada, said it has been a “contentious year” as Americans living in Canada have watched “the back and forth” between the two governments over trade.

“They want to make sure that whatever’s going on in the States stays kind of healthy in case they have to go back home. So people, they are more engaged, I think, than they have in the past,” she said.

A dual citizen, Burke moved back to the U.S. a few months ago after spending 38 years in Toronto and Ottawa.

A Republican and Trump supporter, Burke said she estimates there is a roughly three-to-one Democrat to Republican ratio among American expats living in Canada.

“I know that most Republicans are very motivated to vote,” she said. “They’re very quiet about it. They don’t talk because they’re not received in a very friendly way in Canada, which is kind of unfortunate.

“Democrats are also motivated to vote, especially if they’re in one of those toss-up states, like Michigan.”

When The Canadian Press sought to speak with various American voters via social media pages and message boards, lots of Democrats stepped forward. Not one Republican did.

Burke said it’s a civic duty to vote in elections. She also said while some of the things Trump says and does make her “cringe,” she focuses on his accomplishments.

“A lot of the thing that he has done in the United States have made a huge difference for Americans, including dealing with the border problem in Mexico,” she said. “And I know it drives people crazy, but he is reshoring, as he puts it, American industry to the United States to employ Americans. That’s his job.”

Trump’s trade war with Canada has become a leading ballot box issue in some key states ahead of the U.S. midterms.

Trump rapidly escalated his trade war and rhetoric against Canada after trade negotiations fell apart in August. The president signed an order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America and the United States hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs. A few weeks later, Ottawa responded with its own retaliatory duties.

Jessica Matwick, a dual citizen who lives in Ottawa and is involved with Democrats Abroad and Indivisible Ottawa, said every eligible voter should get out and vote “to put a stop to an unhinged administration and a legislative body that has abdicated their responsibility to keep the executive in check.”

“The attacks on Canadian sovereignty and destructive tariff war are actions I cannot remain silent about,” said Matwick, who moved back to Canada in late 2016 and votes in Virginia. “I still have family living in the U.S. and many friends who I am concerned about.

“My heart hurts knowing that the damage that has been done in a relatively short period of time will take years and years to repair.”

Cody Littlefield, who moved to Canada from the U.S. in 2019 and now lives in Calgary, said he tries to vote in every election. A California voter, he said this election presents an opportunity for voters to send a message that what’s happening in the U.S. “is not acceptable.”

“The future of the country really matters to me,” said Littlefield, adding that he and his family may eventually move back to the U.S.

“There are some people who will never go back and maybe they just really don’t care about the domestic stuff, but I would say the foreign policy still does affect them.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Cuban ambassadors ask Canada to renew its rejection of U.S. embargo and fuel blockade
stories.summary: Ottawa - Havana is urging Ottawa not to drop its public opposition to the decades-long U.S. embargo as Washington ramps up pressure on countries supporting Cuba.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Havana is urging Ottawa not to drop its public opposition to the decades-long U.S. embargo as Washington ramps up pressure on countries supporting Cuba.

“We are confident that Canada will stay with us, as they have done in the past,” Cuban Ambassador to Canada Rodrigo Malmierca Diaz told The Canadian Press.

“The blockade and this intensification is, in practice, killing people.”

The United Nations is set to vote next week on a motion Cuba has put forward nearly every year since 1992. It calls for the termination of “the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba.”

Cuban Ambassador Rodrigo Malmierca Diaz is urging Canada to not change its public opposition to the decades-long U.S. embargo in a United Nations vote next week. The Trump administration has been ramping up pressure on countries supporting Cuba, where Canada has sent aid to respond to a humanitarian crisis stemming from the U.S. fuel blockade. (Oct. 24, 2026)

Canada has voted in favour of this motion multiple times.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has been trying to overthrow Cuba’s Communist government through a de facto oil blockade. Washington cut off Venezuelan shipments in January and has threatened to impose tariffs on countries that sell oil to the island nation.

President Donald Trump on Friday told a rally for candidates in South Florida that U.S. warships returning from the Middle East could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war, his latest suggestion of taking an interventionist approach to the nearby country. (Oct. 23, 2026)

Washington claims Cuba poses a national security threat to the United States. Malmierca said the Caribbean nation is being collectively punished by an American pressure campaign that is harming the health and education of Cubans.

An economic crisis has gripped Cuba since 2020, triggering critical shortages and severe blackouts that peaked after January’s fuel blockade.

Havana insists its economic struggles stem from six decades of American sanctions, but critics point to the inefficiency of its Communist regime. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International say Cuba’s government engages in arbitrary arrests, tortures political prisoners and limits media and political parties.

Cuba produces only 40 per cent of the fuel it needs. Shortages have led to frequent blackouts that have threatened health care systems and crippled the island’s economy. Air Canada and other airlines cancelled flights to Cuba in February because of shortages of aviation fuel.

Ottawa has pledged to distribute $13 million in humanitarian aid for Cubans through international organizations — not the Cuban government. Past Canadian development funding has gone to things like solar panels aimed at making the island less reliant on foreign fuel.

“The people are resisting because we are convinced that the most valuable thing we have is the independence, the sovereignty of Cuba. And we are not going to surrender that,” Malmierca said.

“We would like to have a normal relationship with the U.S. We are ready for dialogue.”

Malmierca said countries that have supported Cuba have told Havana they’re being warned by Washington their access to American trade or aid could be curbed if they continue supporting UN motions to end the blockade.

He said Cuba is “not naive” and knows Canada is facing its own economic pressure from the Trump administration.

“This year is a particular moment because of all this aggressivity of the U.S. government against Cuba,” he said. “They are in a kind of offensive with other countries, trying to exercise influence for them to change their votes. We know they are using threats.”

The Canadian Press asked the U.S. State Department for comment but didn’t receive a response.

U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz this week urged countries to vote against the motion, dismissing it as a product of “70 years of propaganda” meant to distract from corruption in Havana. He said Washington has been lobbying European countries to vote against the motion.

“Do not let them abuse your vote for their oppression,” he said at a Monday event he hosted. “Do not give in to this lie.”

In a statement, Global Affairs Canada said it is still pondering how it will vote on the UN motion next week.

“As with all UN resolutions, Canada’s voting position is being considered in advance of the vote,” wrote spokesperson Thida Ith.

“Canada continues to call for the Cuban government to implement needed reforms to respect the political and economic rights of the Cuban people, and to release all political prisoners.”

In July, Havana called for a UN debate on the American embargo in the context of the island’s fuel crisis. Washington suggested it was a waste of resources to debate a motion that had already been debated nine months prior, and insisted that the decision to hold a debate be put to a recorded vote.

The vote passed and a debate was held. Canada was among 30 countries that abstained from the motion on holding a debate.

Civil society groups such as the Canadian Network on Cuba said they fear Ottawa may be pulling back from Cuba.

A document The Canadian Press obtained through a freedom-of-information request shows Ottawa had frank exchanges with Cuba about its liquidity crisis before Trump ramped up pressure on the Communist government.

The document — a briefing book prepared by Global Affairs for its deputy minister — shows the deputy minister met with three Canadian firms during a visit to Havana in February 2023 to discuss their Cuban clients’ unpaid bills.

The document says the aim of the meeting was to reassure the three firms that Ottawa “has their back … without unduly encouraging new investors and traders who risk not being paid for their goods/services.”

The companies mentioned in the document are the National Bank, mining firm Sherritt and hotel chain Blue Diamond, now called Royalton. None of the companies responded to The Canadian Press when asked whether they still have accounts in arrears in Cuba.

Sherritt and Royalton have both ceased operations in Cuba. Havana has blamed their withdrawal on American pressure tactics.

The briefing book for the deputy minister reveals some of the nature of Canada’s discussions with Cuba, with Ottawa pushing for details on small and medium-sized enterprises and Havana requesting more aid.

“Canadian firms are facing mounting payment arrears with Cuban buyers. Many Canadian firms in Cuba are SMEs and the situation is threatening their sustainability,” reads the February 2023 document for the deputy minister.

“We sought bilateral meetings for you, that would allow you, for example, to engage on human rights and new economic actors (private sector SMEs and entrepreneurs). The Cuban side wanted rather to talk to you about new tourism initiatives and more Canadian international development projects.”

The briefing book proposed that Canada “leverage Cuba’s desire for increased assistance in our dialogue on other priorities (e.g. human rights)” — but added that the cheapest and most effective things Canada could offer would be technical help with reforming the agriculture sector and rules for smaller businesses.

Malmierca said Cuba is implementing 176 reform measures which came out of parliamentary and public consultations. He said these measures will allow a larger role for the private sector, foreign investment incentives and municipal autonomy.

“In Cuba, we work according to the rule of law,” he said. “Cuba is a society that is continuously trying to improve.”

He said a trade fair in Havana next month is going largely virtual due to the current electricity shortages, and Cuba will hold an event in Toronto ahead of time to drum up interest from Canadian entrepreneurs.

“We can maintain not only the economic relationship, but we can increase it in better conditions in the near future.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has been trying to overthrow Cuba’s Communist government through a de facto oil blockade. Washington cut off Venezuelan shipments in January and has threatened to impose tariffs on countries that sell oil to the island nation.

President Donald Trump on Friday told a rally for candidates in South Florida that U.S. warships returning from the Middle East could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war, his latest suggestion of taking an interventionist approach to the nearby country. (Oct. 23, 2026)

Washington claims Cuba poses a national security threat to the United States. Malmierca said the Caribbean nation is being collectively punished by an American pressure campaign that is harming the health and education of Cubans.
An economic crisis has gripped Cuba since 2020, triggering critical shortages and severe blackouts that peaked after January’s fuel blockade.

Havana insists its economic struggles stem from six decades of American sanctions, but critics point to the inefficiency of its Communist regime. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International say Cuba’s government engages in arbitrary arrests, tortures political prisoners and limits media and political parties.

Cuba produces only 40 per cent of the fuel it needs. Shortages have led to frequent blackouts that have threatened health care systems and crippled the island’s economy. Air Canada and other airlines cancelled flights to Cuba in February because of shortages of aviation fuel.

Ottawa has pledged to distribute $13 million in humanitarian aid for Cubans through international organizations — not the Cuban government. Past Canadian development funding has gone to things like solar panels aimed at making the island less reliant on foreign fuel.
“The people are resisting because we are convinced that the most valuable thing we have is the independence, the sovereignty of Cuba. And we are not going to surrender that,” Malmierca said.
“We would like to have a normal relationship with the U.S. We are ready for dialogue.”

Malmierca said countries that have supported Cuba have told Havana they’re being warned by Washington their access to American trade or aid could be curbed if they continue supporting UN motions to end the blockade.
He said Cuba is “not naive” and knows Canada is facing its own economic pressure from the Trump administration.

“This year is a particular moment because of all this aggressivity of the U.S. government against Cuba,” he said. “They are in a kind of offensive with other countries, trying to exercise influence for them to change their votes. We know they are using threats.”
The Canadian Press asked the U.S. State Department for comment but didn’t receive a response.

U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz this week urged countries to vote against the motion, dismissing it as a product of “70 years of propaganda” meant to distract from corruption in Havana. He said Washington has been lobbying European countries to vote against the motion.
“Do not let them abuse your vote for their oppression,” he said at a Monday event he hosted. “Do not give in to this lie.”
In a statement, Global Affairs Canada said it is still pondering how it will vote on the UN motion next week.
“As with all UN resolutions, Canada’s voting position is being considered in advance of the vote,” wrote spokesperson Thida Ith.
“Canada continues to call for the Cuban government to implement needed reforms to respect the political and economic rights of the Cuban people, and to release all political prisoners.”

In July, Havana called for a UN debate on the American embargo in the context of the island’s fuel crisis. Washington suggested it was a waste of resources to debate a motion that had already been debated nine months prior, and insisted that the decision to hold a debate be put to a recorded vote.
The vote passed and a debate was held. Canada was among 30 countries that abstained from the motion on holding a debate.
Civil society groups such as the Canadian Network on Cuba said they fear Ottawa may be pulling back from Cuba.

A document The Canadian Press obtained through a freedom-of-information request shows Ottawa had frank exchanges with Cuba about its liquidity crisis before Trump ramped up pressure on the Communist government.

The document — a briefing book prepared by Global Affairs for its deputy minister — shows the deputy minister met with three Canadian firms during a visit to Havana in February 2023 to discuss their Cuban clients’ unpaid bills.

The document says the aim of the meeting was to reassure the three firms that Ottawa “has their back … without unduly encouraging new investors and traders who risk not being paid for their goods/services.”

The companies mentioned in the document are the National Bank, mining firm Sherritt and hotel chain Blue Diamond, now called Royalton. None of the companies responded to The Canadian Press when asked whether they still have accounts in arrears in Cuba.
Sherritt and Royalton have both ceased operations in Cuba. Havana has blamed their withdrawal on American pressure tactics.

The briefing book for the deputy minister reveals some of the nature of Canada’s discussions with Cuba, with Ottawa pushing for details on small and medium-sized enterprises and Havana requesting more aid.

“Canadian firms are facing mounting payment arrears with Cuban buyers. Many Canadian firms in Cuba are SMEs and the situation is threatening their sustainability,” reads the February 2023 document for the deputy minister.

“We sought bilateral meetings for you, that would allow you, for example, to engage on human rights and new economic actors (private sector SMEs and entrepreneurs). The Cuban side wanted rather to talk to you about new tourism initiatives and more Canadian international development projects.”

The briefing book proposed that Canada “leverage Cuba’s desire for increased assistance in our dialogue on other priorities (e.g. human rights)” — but added that the cheapest and most effective things Canada could offer would be technical help with reforming the agriculture sector and rules for smaller businesses.

Malmierca said Cuba is implementing 176 reform measures which came out of parliamentary and public consultations. He said these measures will allow a larger role for the private sector, foreign investment incentives and municipal autonomy.
“In Cuba, we work according to the rule of law,” he said. “Cuba is a society that is continuously trying to improve.”

He said a trade fair in Havana next month is going largely virtual due to the current electricity shortages, and Cuba will hold an event in Toronto ahead of time to drum up interest from Canadian entrepreneurs.
“We can maintain not only the economic relationship, but we can increase it in better conditions in the near future.”

stories.title: British Columbians vote in early election, with David Eby's job on the line
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbians go to the polls today in an early election called by NDP Leader David Eby in the biggest gamble of his political life.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - Just over five weeks ago, Lorne Doerkson was an obscure British Columbia legislator whose party was falling apart at the seams.

He is now set to become premier at the head of a majority government, soundly defeating the New Democrats in Saturday’s snap election that backfired spectacularly on outgoing Premier David Eby, who announced his resignation as NDP leader.

It took a little over an hour after polls closed at 8 p.m. for The Canadian Press decision desk to call the race, underscoring the stunning nature of Doerkson’s win.

Outgoing NDP Leader David Eby told supporters he takes responsibility for losing Saturday's snap election to the Conservatives. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says he'll follow through on campaign promises to supercharge the province's economy. (Oct. 25, 2026)

The Conservatives had won or were leading in about two-thirds of the province’s 93 ridings about three hours after the polls closed.

He said in a victory speech set to fireworks and Fleetwood Mac’s “Don’t Stop” that “B.C. is definitely blue.”

Doerkson emerged from obscurity to unify a fractured Opposition that was a political basket case just six weeks ago.

Doerkson said he would do everything in his power to get the province “back on track.”

“Together our best days are still ahead of us my friends,” he told supporters at a party in Vancouver, adding that he would follow through on a promise to “supercharge” the province, his voice cracking as he said serving as premier would be the honour of his lifetime.

Doerkson, 58, returned from a trip to Africa and assumed the interim leadership of the Conservatives on Sept. 20, Kerry-Lynne Findlay having resigned after a tumultuous four-month reign.

He took over a party that had been losing legislators at a frantic pace, amid concerns about Findlay’s strategies and what one defector, Bruce Banman, called ideological “purity tests.”

After the 2024 election, the party had 44 legislators and was within three ridings of government, but their ranks had dwindled into the 20s by the time Doerkson took charge.

He swiftly wooed disgruntled Conservatives back to the fold, including seven out of the eight legislators who had announced days earlier they were joining the CentreBC party.

Just two days after Doerkson’s elevation, Eby called the snap election that he initially said was needed to tackle the challenge posed by U.S. President Donald Trump; he would later pivot to say the election was needed to overcome the frustrations of governing with a one-seat majority.

Whatever the reason, the election call was the biggest gamble of Eby’s political career, and it would ultimately cut short his premiership of less than four years.

Former federal Conservative cabinet minister Stockwell Day said at the B.C. Conservatives’ election night party in Vancouver that people “just want back to normal” and British Columbians were going to get “a well-deserved break from radical politics.”

“I think the other part of the strategy was just stand back and let Mr. Eby keep talking, and it seems to have worked,” he said.

Eby told his disconsolate supporters in Vancouver that he had called Doerkson to concede and offer his congratulations.

“The people of B.C. have asked us to be the official Opposition, which is obviously not the result that any of us wanted,” Eby said. “It breaks my heart and I accept full responsibly for that outcome.”

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson is wasting no time after his Conservatives swept into power last night in British Columbia.

Doerkson was gracious in victory.

He told his supporters that Eby had “given to the province for years,” a remark that was greeted with warm applause.

Doerkson also congratulated BC Green Leader Emily Lowan, who won her bid for a place in the legislature, and said British Columbians could be “grateful for her passion.”

At a party in Brentwood Bay on Vancouver Island, BC Green Party Leader Emily Lowan celebrated her party’s two-seat win, though she told supporters that she was scared of what a Conservative government would mean.

“The Conservative agenda is one of cuts to the programs that we rely on the most. It’s one of culture wars and needless attacks on human rights and the basic tenets of a dignified life. It stands against everything that brought this movement together,” she said.

Doerkson campaigned on his vow to supercharge the economy, pledging to bring down the record deficit with the help of growth his platform forecast to reach 3.2 per cent, a prediction Eby and other critics suggested was optimistic at best.

He promised no tax increases and to raise B.C.’s basic personal income tax exemption from $13,216 to $32,000, resulting in a $1,000 tax cut for most individual workers.

But he said his top priority would be repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, and he also promised to end sexual orientation and gender identity guidelines for schools.

The NDP promised a new tax bracket for those making more than $1 million to help fund health care, price caps on some basic groceries and a training program for international medical graduates already living in B.C.

Eby promised more before- and after-school spaces, but was criticized for having two children in coveted $10-a-day daycare spots. He said he and his wife paid to make up the difference with the previous cost.

Both parties singled out Surrey, B.C.‘s second-largest city, for special attention, pledging new hospitals and a SkyTrain extension for the region.

The Conservatives were the only party to initially field a full slate of 93 candidates this election but tossed two candidates for online remarks, one commenting about Hitler and the other saying the driver of a car that rammed a pro-Palestinian protest should have “reversed too.”

Doerkson acted quickly to disavow them.

VANCOUVER - Voters gave Lorne Doerkson’s B.C. Conservatives a two-thirds majority government on Saturday, now members of his party need to do …

But he stood by Conservative campaign director Katy Merrifield, who Eby said should have been removed over social media posts that included describing Islam as an “abhorrent ideology.” Doerkson defended her as a survivor of sexual assault who commented out of anger.

The legislature at dissolution consisted of 47 New Democrats, 29 Conservatives, two Greens, and 13 Independents, with two vacant seats.

But that did not take into account that most of the nominal Independents were Conservatives who returned to the party after Doerkson became interim leader. They may not all have been reflected in the official numbers, but the Conservatives went into the election holding about 37 seats.

The election win caps a remarkable rise not just for Doerkson but for the B.C. Conservatives, whose last premier, Simon Fraser Tolmie, was elected in 1928.

As recently as the 2020 election, the party received less than two per cent of the vote, but the collapse of BC United, formerly known as the B.C. Liberals, paved the way for its rise to official opposition status and now government.

Questions remain about Doerkson’s status as an interim leader, since the Conservative constitution prohibits interim leaders seeking the position permanently, with constitutional changes requiring the support of a two-thirds majority of members.

The party has said it would “pursue the appropriate means under the party’s constitution and bylaws and the Societies Act” to keep Doerkson on as leader.

The Conservative win ends nine years of NDP government that began under the late John Horgan, before he stepped aside and Eby won the NDP leadership in 2022.

His tenure was not smooth.

He inherited a budget surplus from Horgan but the province is now facing a $14 billion projected deficit this year.

Eby eked out a slim win over the Conservatives in the 2024 election, but faced pressure over health care, law and order, a failed drug decriminalization project, and legal challenges related to Indigenous rights.

In the final week of the campaign, his party trailing in opinion polls, Eby appealed to Green supporters, asking them to consider voting NDP to avoid splitting the vote and helping the Conservatives.

He faced criticism over the early election call, with a campaign period that overlapped with the Oct. 17 municipal elections.

“It’s very clear that they just want to do it before the Conservatives get it all together,” said Queena Li, a student voting on Saturday in Eby’s riding of Vancouver-Point Grey.

Eby said on Friday his biggest regret of the campaign was failing to explain to B.C. that he called the election due to the difficulties of working with a bare majority in a “stalled out” legislature.

He must now be regretting that he called it at all.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 24, 2026

— With files by Nono Shen in Brentwood Bay and Ashley Joannou in Vancouver
