After the 2024 election, the party had 44 legislators and was within three ridings of government, but their ranks had dwindled into the 20s by the time Doerkson took charge.
He swiftly wooed disgruntled Conservatives back to the fold, including seven out of the eight legislators who had announced days earlier they were joining the CentreBC party.

Just two days after Doerkson’s elevation, Eby called the snap election that he initially said was needed to tackle the challenge posed by U.S. President Donald Trump; he would later pivot to say the election was needed to overcome the frustrations of governing with a one-seat majority.
Whatever the reason, the election call was the biggest gamble of Eby’s political career, and it would ultimately cut short his premiership of less than four years.

Former federal Conservative cabinet minister Stockwell Day said at the B.C. Conservatives’ election night party in Vancouver that people “just want back to normal” and British Columbians were going to get “a well-deserved break from radical politics.”
“I think the other part of the strategy was just stand back and let Mr. Eby keep talking, and it seems to have worked,” he said.
Eby told his disconsolate supporters in Vancouver that he had called Doerkson to concede and offer his congratulations.

“The people of B.C. have asked us to be the official Opposition, which is obviously not the result that any of us wanted,” Eby said. “It breaks my heart and I accept full responsibly for that outcome.”
Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson is wasting no time after his Conservatives swept into power last night in British Columbia.
Doerkson was gracious in victory.
He told his supporters that Eby had “given to the province for years,” a remark that was greeted with warm applause.
Doerkson also congratulated BC Green Leader Emily Lowan, who won her bid for a place in the legislature, and said British Columbians could be “grateful for her passion.”

At a party in Brentwood Bay on Vancouver Island, BC Green Party Leader Emily Lowan celebrated her party’s two-seat win, though she told supporters that she was scared of what a Conservative government would mean.

“The Conservative agenda is one of cuts to the programs that we rely on the most. It’s one of culture wars and needless attacks on human rights and the basic tenets of a dignified life. It stands against everything that brought this movement together,” she said.

Doerkson campaigned on his vow to supercharge the economy, pledging to bring down the record deficit with the help of growth his platform forecast to reach 3.2 per cent, a prediction Eby and other critics suggested was optimistic at best.
He promised no tax increases and to raise B.C.’s basic personal income tax exemption from $13,216 to $32,000, resulting in a $1,000 tax cut for most individual workers.
But he said his top priority would be repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, and he also promised to end sexual orientation and gender identity guidelines for schools.

The NDP promised a new tax bracket for those making more than $1 million to help fund health care, price caps on some basic groceries and a training program for international medical graduates already living in B.C.

Eby promised more before- and after-school spaces, but was criticized for having two children in coveted $10-a-day daycare spots. He said he and his wife paid to make up the difference with the previous cost.
Both parties singled out Surrey, B.C.‘s second-largest city, for special attention, pledging new hospitals and a SkyTrain extension for the region.

The Conservatives were the only party to initially field a full slate of 93 candidates this election but tossed two candidates for online remarks, one commenting about Hitler and the other saying the driver of a car that rammed a pro-Palestinian protest should have “reversed too.”
Doerkson acted quickly to disavow them.
VANCOUVER - Voters gave Lorne Doerkson’s B.C. Conservatives a two-thirds majority government on Saturday, now members of his party need to do …

But he stood by Conservative campaign director Katy Merrifield, who Eby said should have been removed over social media posts that included describing Islam as an “abhorrent ideology.” Doerkson defended her as a survivor of sexual assault who commented out of anger.
The legislature at dissolution consisted of 47 New Democrats, 29 Conservatives, two Greens, and 13 Independents, with two vacant seats.

But that did not take into account that most of the nominal Independents were Conservatives who returned to the party after Doerkson became interim leader. They may not all have been reflected in the official numbers, but the Conservatives went into the election holding about 37 seats.
The election win caps a remarkable rise not just for Doerkson but for the B.C. Conservatives, whose last premier, Simon Fraser Tolmie, was elected in 1928.

As recently as the 2020 election, the party received less than two per cent of the vote, but the collapse of BC United, formerly known as the B.C. Liberals, paved the way for its rise to official opposition status and now government.

Questions remain about Doerkson’s status as an interim leader, since the Conservative constitution prohibits interim leaders seeking the position permanently, with constitutional changes requiring the support of a two-thirds majority of members.
The party has said it would “pursue the appropriate means under the party’s constitution and bylaws and the Societies Act” to keep Doerkson on as leader.
The Conservative win ends nine years of NDP government that began under the late John Horgan, before he stepped aside and Eby won the NDP leadership in 2022.
His tenure was not smooth.
He inherited a budget surplus from Horgan but the province is now facing a $14 billion projected deficit this year.

Eby eked out a slim win over the Conservatives in the 2024 election, but faced pressure over health care, law and order, a failed drug decriminalization project, and legal challenges related to Indigenous rights.
In the final week of the campaign, his party trailing in opinion polls, Eby appealed to Green supporters, asking them to consider voting NDP to avoid splitting the vote and helping the Conservatives.
He faced criticism over the early election call, with a campaign period that overlapped with the Oct. 17 municipal elections.
“It’s very clear that they just want to do it before the Conservatives get it all together,” said Queena Li, a student voting on Saturday in Eby’s riding of Vancouver-Point Grey.

Eby said on Friday his biggest regret of the campaign was failing to explain to B.C. that he called the election due to the difficulties of working with a bare majority in a “stalled out” legislature.
He must now be regretting that he called it at all.

stories.title: Beth Lew-Williams wins Cundill History Prize for book on anti-Chinese discrimination
stories.summary: Toronto - Princeton professor Beth Lew-Williams has won this year's Cundill History Prize for "John Doe Chinaman: A Forgotten History of Chinese Life under American Racial Law."
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Princeton professor Beth Lew-Williams has won this year’s Cundill History Prize for “John Doe Chinaman: A Forgotten History of Chinese Life under American Racial Law.”

Lew-Williams received the US$75,000 award during a ceremony in Montreal on Friday for the book that explores the laws that constrained the lives of Chinese immigrants in the 19th century American West.

stories.title: U.S. ambassador offers Canada help almost a week after Wainwright tragedy

stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says the United States has offered to help following the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta.

Four soldiers were killed and 39 injured on Oct. 17 when a fire that began during a training exercise on an anti-grenade launching range was picked up by fierce winds.

stories.title: Son says Canadian died in U.S. after declining hospital care due to deportation fear
stories.summary: The son of a Canadian woman who died after a fall at her home in Point Roberts, Wash., earlier this month says she refused to seek treatment as she feared she would be detained by U.S. authorities or prevented from returning to the country.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The son of a Canadian woman who died after a fall at her home in Point Roberts, Wash., earlier this month said she refused to seek treatment, fearing she would be detained by U.S. authorities or prevented from returning to the country.

Dylan Adamson said his 61-year-old mother, Paige Adamson, was afraid to leave the United States because immigration authorities had recently commenced deportation proceedings, alleging she illicitly voted in a state election in 2018.

Health care is limited in Point Roberts, which is cut off from the rest of the United States and accessible by land only by travelling through British Columbia.

Adamson said his mother refused to be taken to a hospital because she was afraid of what might happen if she crossed the border.

He said he only learned of his mother’s fall after speaking with a firefighter who attended the scene of her death last Sunday, within a week of the accident.

“I’m just at a loss. Just because of a vote, my mom is dead. Just because of a stupid technicality, my mom is dead,” he said in an interview on Friday.

The fall came about a month after Paige Adamson, a permanent resident of the United States who had been living in Point Roberts since 2012, was heading home from a dinner to celebrate her birthday in nearby Tsawwassen, B.C., when U.S. border officials held her for hours and questioned her about voting in the country.

Dylan Adamson said his mother did not recall registering to vote or casting a ballot, and the ensuing deportation proceedings sent her into a “panic.”

On top of that stress, he said dental troubles had been affecting her ability to eat.

“She was very skinny when I saw her. I saw her a couple months ago. So, she was very frail and she tripped.”

Adamson said he understood from speaking with her friends in Point Roberts that she tripped and fell on a vacuum, striking her side, “around her stomach, hip side.”

He said he had also learned that paramedics who saw his mother before her death told her she needed to go to a hospital, but she signed a form declining further care.

“She would have went to the hospital. The only reason she didn’t is out of fear,” said Adamson, who lives in Maple Ridge, B.C.

Had he known about his mother’s fall, he said he would have driven to see her right away.

He said he expects to learn more details about her death from a medical examiner on Saturday.

Immigration lawyer Len Saunders said he first heard from Paige Adamson just after she was put into deportation proceedings over allegations she had illicitly registered to vote and cast a ballot in Washington state.

Saunders provided The Canadian Press with photos he said Adamson shared with him showing a transcript of her questioning by a border officer, along with a notice requiring her to appear before an immigration judge in Seattle on Nov. 4.

The notice alleged Adamson “falsely represented” herself as a U.S. citizen in order to register to vote in Whatcom county, then voted in the Nov. 6, 2018 election.

She was subject to removal from the United States on that basis, it said.

Saunders, who is based in Blaine, Wash., said he told Adamson he hadn’t been taking on deportation cases since the closure of a courtroom in the city some years ago, but he referred her to lawyers in Seattle and they kept in touch.

He said Adamson told him she was “losing sanity” over the ordeal.

Saunders said Adamson told him she hadn’t been feeling well, but she was afraid of travelling to see her doctor in Bellingham, Wash., because of the deportation action.

The lawyer said he was “shocked” to learn of her death.

“Quite frankly, when I first heard that, I thought it was suicide. I thought, you know, she’s just so stressed out,” he said.

Saunders said Adamson’s case is part of a recent U.S. government crackdown on people who aren’t American citizens but who have registered to vote, sometimes unknowingly, or cast a ballot without realizing they were ineligible to do so.

“You go into (the Department of Motor Vehicles) and you get your driver’s licence, and quite often they register you to vote,” he explained.

“People think, ‘Okay, if I can register, I can vote.’ So, a lot of these people did register and did vote, but it wasn’t done maliciously. They were naive.”

In the past, Saunders said U.S. authorities wouldn’t typically seek to deport such people as long as they removed themselves from voter lists and attested to registering or voting without knowing they shouldn’t have.

“I’ve never seen someone put in deportation proceedings at a port of entry as a permanent resident for voting. I’ve never seen it in 25 years.”

But that’s changed, Saunders said, noting the shift follows a U.S. government directive earlier this year to look into voter lists and enforce non-compliance.

Saunders said he’s heard of several cases of Canadians who are permanent residents of the United States travelling to Canada last month, then facing questions about possibly registering to vote and voting as they returned home.

He said border officials advised each of them against leaving the country “because they could be at risk when they come back of being put into custody and taken on a one-way trip” to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centre.

“Like, these officers put the fear of God into all of these Canadians,” he said.

“When you go down to one of these detention centres, it’s not (for) days, it’s weeks, or months,” he added.

The transcript of Adamson’s Sept. 15 questioning shows the U.S. border officer asked her whether she had ever filled out a voter registration form in the country, to which she replied “No,” although she did recall a state-level ballot.

“Did they send you a ballot to vote?” the officer asked.

“Yes. It comes with everybody’s mail. I don’t remember when it was. Ten years ago, maybe,” Adamson replied.

Asked whether she received a ballot at her most recent address in Point Roberts, Adamson said, “No. I don’t know. It’s junk mail. I just threw it away. Right?

“Sorry, I am tired,” the transcript reads.

Saunders said he has helped many Canadians become U.S. citizens by naturalization over the years, including those who’d registered to vote or voted, telling them “as long as we can show that you deregistered,” the process should be successful.

“We’d deregister them, we’d do an affidavit, I would take them to their interview in Seattle when they became an American, and it was a non-issue.”

Now, Saunders said he won’t submit someone’s naturalization application if there’s any indication they may have registered to vote or voted in the United States.

“I don’t want to be liable for someone getting deported.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

Brenna Owen, The Canadian Press

stories.summary: The Braves, Trojans and Merchants all have home games tonight.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Friday, 23 October 2026 at 09:46

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

The Braves, Trojans and Merchants all have home games tonight.

PJHL - It's a two-game weekend for the Tavistock Braves, the Thamesford Trojans, and the Norwich Merchants.

The Braves will battle the Paris Mounties at the Tavistock and District Rec Centre tonight, while the Trojans take on the Petrolia Flyers at the Thamesford Rec Centre, and the Norwich Merchants face the Dorchester Dolphins to Nor-Del Arena. The Tavistock and Thamesford games will get underway at 7:30 p.m. and the Norwich game has an 8:00 p.m. start time.

The Trojans will also visit the North Middlesex Stars at 8:00 p.m. tomorrow. Both Norwich and Tavistock will have the day off on Saturday, but the Merchants will welcome the Braves to Nor-Del Arena for a matinee matchup at 2:30 p.m. on Sunday.

The Braves are on top of the Doherty Division standings with 21 points, ahead of the Wellesley Applejacks with 18 points and the New Hamburg Firebirds with 15 points.

The Merchants are in fourth place with 10 points, and the Mounties and Dolphins are tied for fifth place with eight points each. The Hespeler Shamrocks sit at the bottom of the standings with six points.

The Trojans are in fifth place in the Yeck Division standings with nine points, one point ahead of the sixth place Lucan Irish with eight points and two points ahead of the last place Port Stanley Sailors with seven points.

The Mount Brydges Bulldogs are on top of the standigs with 16 points, followed by the Exeter Hawks and the Stars with 14 points each. The Flyers are in third place with 13 points, and the Aylmer Spitfires are in fourth place with 12 points.

Navy Vets Preview - Oct 23rd to Oct 25th Tonight's pre-game ceremony will celebrate the 60th anniversary of the Woodstock Navy Vets.

Norfolk OPP Briefs - October 23rd, 2026 Briefs include two incidents in Waterford; a break and enter on Green Street and a stolen vehicle on Concession 8 Townsend.

Wolverines to Face WPS in Friday Night Lights Charity Classic The Woodstock Wolverines will face off against members of the Woodstock Police Service in the first annual Friday Night Lights Charity Classic on October 30th.

Blandford-Blenheim Candidate Profile - Nancy Demarest When the ballots are cast, a current councillor in Blandford-Blenheim is seeking re-election. Nancy Demarest is seeking a third term on council.

OPP Respond to Weapons Call in Tillsonburg The Oxford OPP responded to a weapons call, which turned into a teaching moment for 5 people.

Navy Vets Celebrating 60 Years It is the 60th anniversary of the Woodstock Navy Vets, and the Woodstock Museum has an exhibit to help celebrate.

Woodstock Receives Gaming Revenue Payment from OLG The cheque is worth $416,310 and its for hosting Gateway Casinos.

Schedule Released for CPKC Holiday Train The CPKC Holiday Train will be stopping in Woodstock on Saturday, November 21st.

Local History Speaker Series Returns Two events will be held in November that are part of the Local History Speaker Series.

Woodstock Police Briefs - Oct. 21st, 2026 An impaired driver has been taken off the road, and a suspect in a theft was arrested by the Woodstock Police Service.

Advance Voting Numbers High in Woodstock As election day comes closer, the City of Woodstock has released the number of ballots cast between online and advance polling stations.

stories.title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet set to continue
stories.summary: Toronto - A coroner's inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony in the presence of police is set to resume this morning after adjourning early on Thursday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s mother was shown snippets of security footage from the day her daughter died as she resumed her testimony at a coroner’s inquest on Friday after making a new allegation against police involved in the case.

Claudette Beals watched several short clips from a nearly 50-minute video combining silent CCTV footage from the hallway outside their west-end Toronto home with audio from 911 calls and a police microphone. The video was previously played in its entirety at the inquest.

In one clip, Beals and her son are seen going into the apartment, minutes after Korchinski-Paquet went in to use the bathroom.

“What is she doing?” Beals says in the recording. She agreed Friday that she was referring to her daughter.

Another clip shows Beals and two officers leave the apartment, and another soon after shows her knocking on the neighbour’s door, saying her daughter “jumped.”

Inquest counsel Roger Shallow asked her about it on Friday afternoon.

“The police told me that Regis committed suicide, so you know what, why are you asking me this question?” she responded.

“Is that what we heard you say at this point in time on the video?” Shallow asked again.

“That’s exactly what you heard me say,” Beals said.

At various points Friday, Beals was asked if she needed a break from watching the video, but she said she was OK to continue.

Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman, fell from a highrise balcony in the presence of police on May 27, 2020.

Beals testified Thursday that she saw officers push her daughter toward the balcony, prompting the inquest to take a prolonged break as counsel for the parties figured out a way forward.

The presiding coroner, Dr. David Cameron, told jurors Thursday counsel were strategizing on how to best have them hear evidence related to the circumstances of Korchinski-Paquet’s death “in a clear and fair manner.”

As the inquest reconvened Friday morning, Cameron said counsel had worked “very late into the evening to reach a consensus on how to proceed forward” but weren’t “quite there yet.”

He encouraged jurors to review and discuss the evidence until mid-afternoon, which is when Beals continued her testimony.

Right before the proceedings wrapped for the day, Shallow asked Beals if she blamed herself for what happened to her daughter, while stressing it was not her fault.

“Do you feel, even though you shouldn’t — because of course we’ve heard of your challenges and your frustration, and you called the police to have your children removed, and this fateful tragedy unfolded — do you feel a sense, even though you shouldn’t, of guilt because of that?” he said.

“I feel very responsible for my daughter’s death, very responsible,” she replied.

Beals is set to face questions from lawyers representing roughly a dozen parties next week.

On Thursday, she said that the family struggled at times to deal with Korchinski-Paquet’s seizures and would have benefited from support and education regarding epilepsy.

The inquest has heard Korchinski-Paquet experienced seizures from epilepsy and had two on the day she died.

Her seizures were often followed by periods of erratic and aggressive behaviour, the inquest has heard. A neurologist who reviewed her records said she had previously shown symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium, an altered state of mind that can follow seizures.

Beals, her son and Korchinski-Paquet each called 911 in the afternoon of May 27, 2020, to report a fight involving knives. Six officers and two paramedics arrived at the building soon after.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

stories.title: Boon or boondoggle? N.S. weighs $10B data centre's promised economic benefits
stories.summary: Halifax - Living more than 200 kilometres from the site of a major artificial intelligence data centre proposal isn't stopping Michael McCluskey from voicing his opposition to the project.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
HALIFAX - Living more than 200 kilometres from the site of a major artificial intelligence data centre proposal isn’t stopping Michael McCluskey from voicing his opposition to the project.

The retired military veteran and training professional from Dartmouth, N.S., has added his name to a Change.org petition that has already collected more than 18,000 signatures since the project was announced last Friday.

Anthropic, an American AI company, plans to lease the Point Tupper, N.S., site for its first Canadian data centre, the first major AI facility to be publicly proposed in Nova Scotia.

However, McCluskey said he just views it as the latest in a long history of Nova Scotia chasing grand economic development projects that never seem to deliver.

He said the site won’t be able to serve any other purpose if Anthropic walks away, and he’s worried the province will be left holding the bag when economic benefits don’t appear.

“They don’t put (data centres) anywhere that’s prospering,” McCluskey said in an interview.

“They don’t put them in San Francisco. They don’t put them in Los Angeles …. What they’re looking for are disadvantaged, economically desperate areas?”

EverWind plans to build the 18,600-square-metre data centre by late 2027 and lease it for 20 years to Anthropic under undisclosed financial terms. San Francisco-based Anthropic says Canada is the sixth-largest worldwide user of its Claude AI model, which is driving the project.

EverWind calls the data centre the biggest private investment in provincial history. It originally planned to build a wind-powered hydrogen plant exporting energy from its Cape Breton marine terminal. The company said it’s still pursuing this hydrogen project.

The proposal has thrust Nova Scotia into a debate that has exploded across Canada in recent months as massive AI corporations race to build computing capacity in areas with enough electricity and water to feed the resource-gobbling sector.

The facilities can range in size from a micro data centre about the size of a refrigerator to a hyperscale campus that consumes a level of power comparable to a small city.

A recent York University report found that Canada’s existing 194 data centres have a combined capacity to draw 1.6 gigawatts of electricity. More than 14-times that amount — about 22.7 gigawatts — are either under construction or in the announcement stage across 213 sites.

The proposals are supersized. Existing data centres have an average capacity of about 11 megawatts and cover an average of 0.05 square-kilometres, about the size of six Canadian football fields. New proposals average about 122 megawatts spread over more than eight square kilometres, almost 1,000 football fields.

York researchers say a 122-megawatt operation will use the same amount of power annually as 49,000 to 78,000 Canadian homes.

EverWind’s data centre will be 95 megawatts in the first phase, and the company has plans for a 325-megawatt expansion by mid-2028.

Paris Marx, a Newfoundland and Labrador-based tech critic and author of “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” said data centre opposition is forming quickly in Canada because communities have seen U.S. headlines about skyrocketing power rates and water consumption over the last 18 to 24 months.

He said if the EverWind project moves ahead, he expects it will follow a global trend where the costs to communities are higher than first projected.

“The benefits just aren’t there to the degree that we expect,” he said in an interview.

“There are not a lot of jobs that are associated with data centres beyond the construction phase. Obviously, we need to employ people to build them. They don’t employ a ton of people to actually run them.”

EverWind expects to create 2,000 jobs during construction and 215 permanent jobs between the data centre and the four wind farms that will eventually power it.

The salaries for the permanent jobs would range between $135,000 and $185,000 per year, the company said, with about half of those jobs in the data centre and half in the wind farms.

Sean Mullin, with the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, said data centres may not create the same amount of jobs as something like an auto factory, but even a couple hundred positions can make a big difference in a small community.

“We’d rather have that economic activity here than somewhere else. And then that also benefits the country in the sense that we have more compute capacity to serve the rest of the country,” he said in an interview.

Kody Blois, a Nova Scotia MP and parliamentary secretary to the prime minister, said at EverWind’s announcement last week that AI is transforming the global economy and Ottawa wants to seize the opportunity.

“These are really important jobs right here in the region. They matter to families, they matter to communities,” he said.

EverWind CEO Trent Vichie said there were already more than 20 Nova Scotian contractors working on the site and economic spinoffs will multiply the direct benefits.

“More people in restaurants, more people buying from local businesses,” he said last Friday. “It’s really providing an anchor to strengthening the community that’s already here today.”

Marx said he doubts the project will actually proceed, saying data centres are seen as a backup at the moment when other projects, such as hydrogen, fail to gain traction. He noted EverWind has already hit roadblocks a planned hydrogen project in Newfoundland.

EverWind said in an email that it’s participating in an auction to sell hydrogen to Europe and that the data centre adds a major industrial use for its renewable energy portfolio and infrastructure while the international hydrogen market develops.

“The data centre helps maintain investment momentum in wind, transmission and shared infrastructure that can also support hydrogen and ammonia over time,” the company said.

“While these investments complement each other, they are not dependent on one another.”

Anthropic lost more than US$80 billion during the first half of 2026, according to Reuters. That’s up from a US$13-billion loss in the first half of 2025. The company is planning an initial public offering of shares as early as November that could value the company at US$1.5 trillion.

The firm declined an interview request this week but has told investors that its plan to spend $518 billion on AI infrastructure over the next decade is needed because computing power is the key constraint on AI development. It has said future demand for AI systems is expected to exceed available supply, according to Reuters.

CEO Dario Amodei and the company’s five other co-founders established Anthropic as a public benefit corporation, a designation that for-profit companies select to balance financial goals and social impact.

The company has also committed to setting aside five per cent of its shares to a public benefit fund which will grow along with Anthropic’s valuation.

The fund will explore large donations to non-profits or direct distributions to specific populations. The company says it has already committed US$200 million to studying and addressing potential impacts of AI technology on the labour market.

But Marx remains skeptical about whether AI companies have a good business model.

“I think that there are also a lot of market questions as to whether something like this will even be necessary, or if a client like Anthropic will actually show up,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: The 4 soldiers killed in fast-moving fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta
stories.summary: Wainwright - Four Armed Forces members were killed when a fast-moving fire overwhelmed soldiers during a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton, ON Saturday. Dozens of others were injured, with 33 still in hospital on Tuesday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WAINWRIGHT - Four Armed Forces members were killed when a fast-moving fire overwhelmed soldiers during a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton, on Saturday. Dozens of others were injured, with 33 still in hospital on Tuesday.

A huge pile of flowers continues to grow at the cenotaph in Wainwright after four soldiers were killed in a weekend training exercise gone fatally wrong. Strong and sudden winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire across the Prairie landscape at lightning speed, stopping soldiers in their tracks and sending 39 to hospital, 19 critically. Six have since been discharged, says the defence minister. (Oct. 20, 2026)

Here’s a look at the four who died:

Pte. Shaun Farrell

Farrell, a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, was from Prince Albert, Sask.

The 23-year-old wanted to make a career in the forces, Prime Minister Mark Carney said during a tribute in the House of Commons.

“Pte. Farrell was generous and deeply loyal friend, known in his battalion as the grandmaster of chess,” Carney said.

Farrell’s mother said in a social media post that the family is confronting a profound loss.

“We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time,” Patricia Farrell said.

She asked for privacy as she grieves the loss of her “darling child.”

Saskatchewan lowered flags in the province to half-mast in his memory.

“Shaun was a young man full of promise who chose to serve his country,” said Premier Scott Moe.

“His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him,” Moe said in a statement.

The Canadian Armed Forces has identified the four soldiers who died in a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, says the service members were from British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta. (Oct. 18, 2026)

Pte. Aidan Goulding

The 23-year-old of North Vancouver was also a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

His family said he was an exceptional athlete and, after high school, became a mechanic.

He later quit to join the Army.

“Although he was making excellent money and had a good life, he decided he wanted to defend his country. His goal was to work for Special OPs and then onto CSIS,” his mother, Sonia Monk, and older brother, Wylder Goulding, said in a statement.

“He was the guy that kept people’s spirits up, a contagious laugh and a cheeky smile, he took his role in the army seriously, and our family and his dear friends have suffered a great loss.”

They said he loved his adopted army family and was looking forward to peacekeeping in Latvia.

“Before he went to basic training, he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”

He went above and beyond in his service, added Carney.

“Pte. Goulding met every hardship with a joke, and when others struggled, he shouldered more than his share without ever being asked.”

Pte. Hayden Lykkemark

The 19-year-old was from Langley, B.C., and served with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

stories.title: Ottawa tells its diplomats not to meet with U.S. midterm candidates
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canadian diplomats were directed this week not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Canadian diplomats were directed this week not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections.

Glen Linder, assistant deputy minister for the Americas at Global Affairs Canada, sent a memo midday Tuesday to members of the foreign service in the United States.

The memo, which was obtained by The Canadian Press, says if diplomats find themselves “in the same physical space” as a candidate or elected official, they should avoid being photographed or having their name or position appear in any public communications materials.

It says meetings or events with other elected officials who aren’t candidates in the midterms can happen if necessary, but they should be discussed in advance with senior officials.

The memo says these instructions are similar to those in place during election periods in Canada, when public servants are expected to avoid contact with elected officials except in exceptional circumstances.

“Especially in view of heightened sensitivity, we need to take our obligation of non-partisanship extremely seriously and take a very risk-averse approach,” says the memo.

The memo comes as the Trump administration accuses Canadian politicians of interfering in American elections.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both disputed claims of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterms on Wednesday, after the U.S. embassy in Canada released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claimed indicate “plans to influence American politics.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is quoted five times in the list the embassy released Wednesday.

The list includes quotes from Joly offered without context about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states through counter-tariffs. Joly made the comments while addressing Canada’s response to U.S.-imposed tariffs.

In a news conference on Parliament Hill on Wednesday, Carney — flanked by Joly — responded to a question about the America accusations by pointing out it was the United States which initiated trade actions against Canada.

“All of our actions are in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy,” Carney told reporters after announcing a $9 billion aid package in response to U.S. tariffs.

Ford, who is also quoted in the U.S. embassy release, said he has “no interest at all” in interfering in American elections.

“I’ll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability,” Ford said, adding he spent 20 years in the United States and “loves the American people.”

Janice Charette, Canada’s chief trade negotiator to the United States, said during a discussion at the Toronto Global Forum on Thursday that Donald Trump will continue to be president after the midterm elections and his administration will still drive trade policy.

“The role of Congress and the role of the Senate may or may not change through all of that,” she said. “We will remain absolutely focused on what Canada’s objectives are here and pursue them whenever the moment arrives.

“Canada will continue to work to try to put our best foot forward and make the best case for Canada.”

Charette said during the discussion that she doesn’t see Canada going back to a “tariff-free existence.”

“We had tariff-free trade, that was the best,” he said. “I don’t think we’re going back. We are in a transition to a new trading relationship with the United States.”

As that discussion began, vice chair of BMO Financial Group Brian Tobin said he wanted assurance, “mostly for the peace and tranquillity of the ambassador to Canada from the United States,” that she was not engaged in any kind of electoral activity at the event.

“I think we’re good,” Charette said as the audience laughed.

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that could end Republican control of Congress.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said earlier this month American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back last week, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

Wednesday’s post from the embassy ended by saying “Americans decide America’s elections.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray and Catherine Morrison

stories.title: Ottawa tells its diplomats not to meet with U.S. midterm candidates
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canadian diplomats were directed this week not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Canadian diplomats were directed this week not to meet with or attend events with candidates in the U.S. midterm elections.

Glen Linder, assistant deputy minister for the Americas at Global Affairs Canada, sent a memo midday Tuesday to members of the foreign service in the United States.

The memo, which was obtained by The Canadian Press, says if diplomats find themselves “in the same physical space” as a candidate or elected official, they should avoid being photographed or having their name or position appear in any public communications materials.

It says meetings or events with other elected officials who aren’t candidates in the midterms can happen if necessary, but they should be discussed in advance with senior officials.

The memo says these instructions are similar to those in place during election periods in Canada, when public servants are expected to avoid contact with elected officials except in exceptional circumstances.

“Especially in view of heightened sensitivity, we need to take our obligation of non-partisanship extremely seriously and take a very risk-averse approach,” says the memo.

The memo comes as the Trump administration accuses Canadian politicians of interfering in American elections.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford both disputed claims of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterms on Wednesday, after the U.S. embassy in Canada released a list of quotes from Canadian politicians which it claimed indicate “plans to influence American politics.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is quoted five times in the list the embassy released Wednesday.

The list includes quotes from Joly offered without context about pressuring American businesses and targeting U.S. states through counter-tariffs. Joly made the comments while addressing Canada’s response to U.S.-imposed tariffs.

In a news conference on Parliament Hill on Wednesday, Carney — flanked by Joly — responded to a question about the America accusations by pointing out it was the United States which initiated trade actions against Canada.

“All of our actions are in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy,” Carney told reporters after announcing a $9 billion aid package in response to U.S. tariffs.

Ford, who is also quoted in the U.S. embassy release, said he has “no interest at all” in interfering in American elections.

“I’ll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability,” Ford said, adding he spent 20 years in the United States and “loves the American people.”

Janice Charette, Canada’s chief trade negotiator to the United States, said during a discussion at the Toronto Global Forum on Thursday that Donald Trump will continue to be president after the midterm elections and his administration will still drive trade policy.

“The role of Congress and the role of the Senate may or may not change through all of that,” she said. “We will remain absolutely focused on what Canada’s objectives are here and pursue them whenever the moment arrives.

“Canada will continue to work to try to put our best foot forward and make the best case for Canada.”

Charette said during the discussion that she doesn’t see Canada going back to a “tariff-free existence.”

“We had tariff-free trade, that was the best,” he said. “I don’t think we’re going back. We are in a transition to a new trading relationship with the United States.”

As that discussion began, vice chair of BMO Financial Group Brian Tobin said he wanted assurance, “mostly for the peace and tranquillity of the ambassador to Canada from the United States,” that she was not engaged in any kind of electoral activity at the event.

“I think we’re good,” Charette said as the audience laughed.

Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that could end Republican control of Congress.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said earlier this month American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back last week, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

Wednesday’s post from the embassy ended by saying “Americans decide America’s elections.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

— With files from Nick Murray and Catherine Morrison

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Toronto Crime Stoppers temporarily stops accepting tips after data breach
stories.summary: Toronto - Toronto Crime Stoppers has temporarily stopped accepting tips after it says more than 175,000 of them were stolen by hackers earlier this year, alongside nearly 15,000 names.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Toronto Crime Stoppers has temporarily stopped accepting tips after it said more than 175,000 of them were stolen by hackers earlier this year, alongside nearly 15,000 names.

The pause comes after CBC reported that 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years were exposed in a massive data breach.

The Supreme Court of Canada will hear federal arguments about the government’s legal justification for using the Emergencies Act to quell protests in the national capital and at key border points four years ago.

For about three weeks in January and February 2022, downtown Ottawa was filled with protesters, including many in large trucks that blocked streets around Parliament Hill.

While many of the protesters were demonstrating against COVID-19 health restrictions, the protest attracted some with a variety of grievances against then-prime minister Justin Trudeau and his government.

On Feb. 14, 2022, the government invoked the Emergencies Act, which allowed for temporary measures, including regulation and prohibition of public assemblies, the designation of secure places, direction to banks to freeze assets and a ban on support for protest participants.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association and others successfully argued in Federal Court that Ottawa lacked sound statutory grounds to usher in the emergency measures.

In January, a three-judge panel of the Federal Court of Appeal unanimously upheld the ruling, prompting the federal government to seek a hearing at the Supreme Court.

stories.title: B.C. NDP Leader Eby campaigns in Vancouver, while Tories heads to Surrey
stories.summary: Vancouver - British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby campaigns in Vancouver and Richmond today after wrapping his swing through the vote-rich city of Surrey with a rally.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - Interim British Columbia Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson is partly hanging his hopes on the province’s beleaguered forestry sector to carry his election platform’s economic growth forecasts, recalling that the sector had been a “ginormous contributor” to the province’s economy in the past.

“But here’s the thing about that forest industry,” he said in an interview on Thursday, when asked how he would achieve the growth predictions that his party says will bring in $2.6 billion in new revenue over three years.

“That infrastructure is there, it’s in place and we can absolutely get back to business in that sector almost immediately.”

He also flagged the gas sector as a source of growth, as has NDP Leader David Eby, in the provincial election campaign that reaches its climax with final voting day on Saturday.

But the Conservatives’ growth projections that reach 3.2 per cent in 2029 exceed both the NDP’s projections for the province and the Bank of Canada’s national forecasts.

The New Democrats have accused Doerkson of using unrealistic growth projections in its costed platform that says the deficit will be brought down from a forecast $14 billion to $10.8 billion by 2030.

Doerkson had little time for skepticism in a brief call after a campaign stop in Surrey, saying he doesn’t “feel anything but bullish about British Columbia right now.”

The forestry sector has been hit hard in recent years by U.S. lumber duties and fibre shortages, resulting in a series of mill closures and temporary shutdowns.

While no one from the NDP was available to comment on Doerkson’s remarks, a background document shared with media last week said Doerkson could not change U.S. softwood tariffs, now close to 35 per cent, low prices or the exhaustion of the most profitable timber stands.

Kim Haakstad, president and chief executive officer of the B.C. Council of Forest Industries, said she was not economist, when asked about the Conservatives’ growth projections.

And she cautioned that expecting the sector to resume the role it had in B.C. in the 1960s or earlier was not realistic.

But she said increasing the annual allowable cut backup to 45 million cubic metres from just under 30 million cubic metres could generate about $600 million in additional revenue.

She said that would return stability to an industry that had seen more than 20 mill closures in B.C. since 2023.

“We would love to get to a place of growth,” she said. “We absolutely believe that the forestry industry has the ability to contribute to economic growth in British Columbia and continue to support services that British Columbians need.”

The industry, she added, had idle capacity. “We want to go,” she said.

The background document shared by the NDP acknowledged the council’s $600 million estimate, but called it rosy.

Harry Nelson, a professor in the Department of Forest Resources Management at the University of B.C., said “a lot of things would have to break for British Columbia” to hit 3.2 per cent growth.

But while forestry would not likely perform as it did in the early 2000s, it could contribute to future economic growth, he said.

“Managed well, it can be a well-run, sustainable, long-term business that can do a lot of good things in a lot of communities,” Nelson said. “Arguably, we haven’t managed it that way.”

The NDP and others have broadly questioned the Conservatives’ growth figures.

NDP candidate Adrian Dix said last week that “pretending you can fund billions in new promises by ‘flipping a switch’ on resource development just isn’t believable.”

BC Green Leader Emily Lowan said of the forestry sector at the leaders’ debate last week that “we’re out of trees and we’re of runway.”

She has also previously said it is time to rethink the role of the natural resource sector, that she said accounted for only 7.2 per cent of provincial GDP and 3.1 per cent of jobs.

Haakstad has previously said the challenges facing the industry do not just stem from U.S. duties and tariffs, saying there were “also homegrown challenges” stemming from “regulatory burden.”

Doerkson said in his interview Thursday that the gas industry was also a growth opportunity that “hasn’t been capitalized on by the NDP.”

“This is a business that speaks in trillions of dollars when you talk to them,” he said.

“What we need to run our province is billions of dollars. There is a massive opportunity in the north to help us,” he said, calling the LNG sector “a bigger opportunity in British Columbia than we’ve had in a decade.”

Both major parties are betting on LNG, a relatively new industry, as well as mining, a historical industry, to get the provincial economy going again.

Whether forestry will ever resume its historical role is another question.

“I don’t think anyone believes that the forest industry is going to go back to the 1940s, 1950s, and 1960s,” Haakstad said.

“A big part of it is that we have learned a lot, and we continue to improve the ways we manage on the land base for the longer term.”

The industry, she said, is not thinking about the past, but the future.

“We think the future can include all of the mills that we have open in British Columbia today,” she said, saying there were opportunities in secondary manufacturing of modern building materials.

But she is not sure whether the mills that have closed will come back.

“Hard to predict, but I think we really need to focus on improving competitiveness,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

— With files by Nono Shen in Surrey, B.C.

stories.title: Why has B.C.'s snap election caught both main parties unprepared?
stories.summary: When a snap election is called, at least one side would normally be prepared.
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
When a snap election is called, at least one side would normally be prepared.

But that hasn’t been the case in British Columbia, resulting in a provincial election campaign like no other, political watchers say.

The campaign has seen interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson going without media availabilities on several days, including on Tuesday and Wednesday in the home stretch, ahead of Saturday’s final voting day.

The NDP has meanwhile pivoted its messaging from focusing on U.S. President Donald Trump, to affordability, to the need for a stable majority.

And campaigning has also been notably muted with relatively few large-scale rallies, although hundreds attended an event with NDP Leader David Eby in Surrey on Wednesday, the same city where Doerkson has a rally scheduled on Thursday.

Even the NDP campaign bus, which was adorned with Eby’s smiling face in 2024, is an anonymous-looking coach, devoid of slogans.

Hamish Telford, an associate professor of political science at the University of the Fraser Valley, said he had noticed the “lack of preparation.”

“This is especially surprising since the NDP called this election. You would think, if they were going to call a snap election, that they at least would be prepared, and that they would obviously catch the Conservatives off guard,” said Telford.

“This was an election of their making, and they are not entirely ready for it,” he added.

Telford said the NDP had initially been anticipating Eby running against Kerry-Lynne Findlay, a divisive and unpopular leader of the Conservatives. But Findlay resigned and was replaced by Doerkson.

Eby called the snap election anyway.

Telford said he would have advised the NDP not to go through with it.

“They should have called the election off, but evidently things were too late, or they had built up too much momentum and couldn’t stop themselves.” said Telford.

Angelo Isidorou, who is chief strategist for the Conservatives, said snap elections can be messy compared with fixed-date polls.

“In this case, this is what makes this very unique … not only is it a snap election, but it was an election that took place at the same time as municipal elections, which never happens. So, it was all very chaotic,” said Isidorou of the Oct. 17 municipal polls across B.C.

Craig Keating, former BC NDP provincial director, called out the relative lack of media access to Doerkson, including a decision by the Conservatives that he would not be doing interviews on election night if he won.

“It’s bizarre to have such limited accessibility of a leader to the press, and even saying yesterday that he won’t do a postelection scrum on election night. I mean that’s totally bizarre,” said Keating.

The Doerkson campaign has not been allowing reporters to ask him follow-up questions at news conferences.

On Thursday, after The Canadian Press was denied the chance to ask a question at a Doerkson news conference in Surrey, B.C., he granted a telephone interview that lasted less than five minutes and was ended by a Conservative staffer after two questions.

Keating said the Conservatives had placed Doerksen “under wraps,” suggesting this was a tell that he was not the campaign’s decision maker.

He said it was clear that the Conservative leadership issue had not been settled, and “Doerkson’s here for a good time, not a long time.”

Isidorou said the “biggest difference” between a snap election and a fixed-date election is the “predictability.”

“It’s difficult being in Opposition because you don’t know when the election is going to come, and when an election is called, you only have maybe over a week to recruit candidates and get them on the ballot because there’s a deadline. When there’s a fixed election, you can predict all of this,” said Isidorou.

“In this case, it wasn’t, and I think what surprised me the most is really how not prepared the NDP was,” said Isidorou, adding that otherwise, the NDP would have fielded a full slate of 93 candidates in every riding.

Elections BC said the NPD was one short of a full slate, after failing to nominate a representative in Peace River North.

But vetting may have suffered in the rush to field candidates.

While the Conservatives managed to fill their 93-riding slate, two candidates have since been disavowed by the party.

Jordan McIntosh, the 18-year-old former Conservative candidate for Vancouver-Strathcona, was dumped last Thursday over online posts that included saying Hitler killed “lots of Jews” not because he “hated them specifically” but because there were so many of them.

Another candidate, Joachim Agou, was ejected from the party earlier this month for online comments saying the driver of a car that rammed a pro-Palestinian protest group in Switzerland should have “reversed too.”

Political scientist Michael Prince said the election has “elements of some really unusual features.”

He said it was puzzling to see parties still fall into the trap of recruiting inappropriate candidates.

“They haven’t really thoroughly vetted their history of social media posts,” said Prince, the Lansdowne professor emeritus of social policy at the University of Victoria.

“We’ve seen, particularly on the Conservative side, candidates that have been removed by the leader or have stepped down very quickly,” he said. “So, that’s kind of the new unusual, but it’s been something that’s unfortunately pretty typical over the last several elections.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

The campaign has seen interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson going without media availabilities on several days, including on Tuesday and Wednesday in the home stretch, ahead of Saturday’s final voting day.
The NDP has meanwhile pivoted its messaging from focusing on U.S. President Donald Trump, to affordability, to the need for a stable majority.

And campaigning has also been notably muted with relatively few large-scale rallies, although hundreds attended an event with NDP Leader David Eby in Surrey on Wednesday, the same city where Doerkson has a rally scheduled on Thursday.
Even the NDP campaign bus, which was adorned with Eby’s smiling face in 2024, is an anonymous-looking coach, devoid of slogans.
Hamish Telford, an associate professor of political science at the University of the Fraser Valley, said he had noticed the “lack of preparation.”

“This is especially surprising since the NDP called this election. You would think, if they were going to call a snap election, that they at least would be prepared, and that they would obviously catch the Conservatives off guard,” said Telford.
“This was an election of their making, and they are not entirely ready for it,” he added.
Telford said the NDP had initially been anticipating Eby running against Kerry-Lynne Findlay, a divisive and unpopular leader of the Conservatives. But Findlay resigned and was replaced by Doerkson.
Eby called the snap election anyway.
Telford said he would have advised the NDP not to go through with it.
“They should have called the election off, but evidently things were too late, or they had built up too much momentum and couldn’t stop themselves.” said Telford.
Angelo Isidorou, who is chief strategist for the Conservatives, said snap elections can be messy compared with fixed-date polls.

“In this case, this is what makes this very unique … not only is it a snap election, but it was an election that took place at the same time as municipal elections, which never happens. So, it was all very chaotic,” said Isidorou of the Oct. 17 municipal polls across B.C.

Craig Keating, former BC NDP provincial director, called out the relative lack of media access to Doerkson, including a decision by the Conservatives that he would not be doing interviews on election night if he won.

“It’s bizarre to have such limited accessibility of a leader to the press, and even saying yesterday that he won’t do a postelection scrum on election night. I mean that’s totally bizarre,” said Keating.
The Doerkson campaign has not been allowing reporters to ask him follow-up questions at news conferences.

On Thursday, after The Canadian Press was denied the chance to ask a question at a Doerkson news conference in Surrey, B.C., he granted a telephone interview that lasted less than five minutes and was ended by a Conservative staffer after two questions.
Keating said the Conservatives had placed Doerksen “under wraps,” suggesting this was a tell that he was not the campaign’s decision maker.
He said it was clear that the Conservative leadership issue had not been settled, and “Doerkson’s here for a good time, not a long time.”
Isidorou said the “biggest difference” between a snap election and a fixed-date election is the “predictability.”

“It’s difficult being in Opposition because you don’t know when the election is going to come, and when an election is called, you only have maybe over a week to recruit candidates and get them on the ballot because there’s a deadline. When there’s a fixed election, you can predict all of this,” said Isidorou.

“In this case, it wasn’t, and I think what surprised me the most is really how not prepared the NDP was,” said Isidorou, adding that otherwise, the NDP would have fielded a full slate of 93 candidates in every riding.
Elections BC said the NPD was one short of a full slate, after failing to nominate a representative in Peace River North.
But vetting may have suffered in the rush to field candidates.
While the Conservatives managed to fill their 93-riding slate, two candidates have since been disavowed by the party.

Jordan McIntosh, the 18-year-old former Conservative candidate for Vancouver-Strathcona, was dumped last Thursday over online posts that included saying Hitler killed “lots of Jews” not because he “hated them specifically” but because there were so many of them.

Another candidate, Joachim Agou, was ejected from the party earlier this month for online comments saying the driver of a car that rammed a pro-Palestinian protest group in Switzerland should have “reversed too.”
Political scientist Michael Prince said the election has “elements of some really unusual features.”
He said it was puzzling to see parties still fall into the trap of recruiting inappropriate candidates.
“They haven’t really thoroughly vetted their history of social media posts,” said Prince, the Lansdowne professor emeritus of social policy at the University of Victoria.

“We’ve seen, particularly on the Conservative side, candidates that have been removed by the leader or have stepped down very quickly,” he said. “So, that’s kind of the new unusual, but it’s been something that’s unfortunately pretty typical over the last several elections.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge mass shooting conspirator set to enter plea in U.S. court
stories.summary: Seattle - The alleged co-conspirator in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., is expected to enter a plea at an arraignment in a Seattle courthouse today.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
SEATTLE - The alleged co-conspirator in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., has pleaded not guilty in a U.S. court and is set to go on trial in December, accused of aiding one of the deadliest school attacks in Canadian history.

James Bryant entered the plea in a brief arraignment appearance in Seattle on Thursday, after a grand jury last week indicted the 30-year-old Bellingham, Wash., resident for conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

Shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight last February, including five students and an educational assistant at the local secondary school, before she fatally shot herself as police closed in.

The criminal complaint against Bryant, who uses female pronouns and goes by the name Melody, alleges she colluded with Van Rootselaar online, helping set up an attempted livestream of the murders.

Bryant, who appeared in a tan prison jumpsuit and dark-framed glasses with her hair down to her waist, has been denied bail.

Her trial is scheduled to begin before U.S. District Judge Kymberly K. Evanson in Seattle on Dec. 21.

Bryant smiled at two people who sat in the gallery of the courtroom during the arraignment, which lasted only minutes. The pair then walked out of the courthouse with Bryant’s public defender, Greg Murphy, speaking with him briefly before they parted ways.

Bryant also allegedly advised 18-year-old Van Rootselaar on where to carry out the attack and sent the shooter money to buy a lighter for an explosive device.

The accusations against Bryant remain unproven.

Magistrate Judge Michelle Peterson presided over Thursday’s arraignment hearing, where Bryant was told she faces penalties of up to life in prison and US$250,000 in fines.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation’s complaint against Bryant says that on Feb. 10, Van Rootselaar told Bryant she had dressed for the mass shooting.

The document shows a photo of someone from their shoulders down, holding a rifle and wearing black fishnet stockings and a black miniskirt.

“A few moments later, Van Rootselaar told Bryant that she went live with the stream and had just killed her family members at their residence,” the complaint said.

Rootselaar allegedly told Bryant, “I’m going now. (for real). Live. I shot them,” after killing her mother and brother at their home.

Bryant is alleged to have helped Van Rootselaar start the family car — she did not know how to drive — before she headed to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

In arguing against Bryant’s detention last week, Murphy and fellow public defender Dennis Carroll said there was no evidence that their client “has ever communicated with any other person as deeply disturbed as Van Rootselaar.”

They also pointed to the delay between Bryant being interviewed by the FBI in February and March, then arrested on Oct. 6, saying that “if that danger were real, the government would not have left Ms. Bryant in the community for seven months.”

“As horrible as Van Rootselaar’s crimes were, and as cold as many of Ms. Bryant’s chats appear, there is no evidence — much less clear and convincing evidence — that she would pose an unmitigable danger to the community,” they said in a court filing.

The arguments were unsuccessful and Bryant was denied bail.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

stories.title: Officials to provide update on fatal fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta
stories.summary: Edmonton - Officials are set to provide an update today about a devastating fire at a Canadian military base in Alberta that left four soldiers dead and dozens more injured.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
EDMONTON - The decision to hold a live-fire training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright during a high-risk fire month will be part of the investigation into the fire that killed four soldiers and injured dozens.

Military officials said the grass fire broke out Saturday on a grenade range at the base southeast of Edmonton in a permanent danger area, which prevented firefighters from putting it out early on.

The fire was being monitored when, in the afternoon, a strong wind quickly shot flames over to an area where the soldiers were in attack training.

The base’s training-range standing orders document cautions that units firing between August and October should plan early morning shoots when fire risk is lower.

The document says the fire-hazard risk is “normally low enough to permit the firing of most ammunition natures” before about 10 a.m.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland of the 1st Canadian Division told reporters in Edmonton on Thursday the decision to hold it later in the day will be part of the review, but cautioned against reading too much into the document’s recommendations.

“That’s a guideline and commanders on the ground have to assess multiple factors in order to decide whether or not to go ahead with shooting,” he said, including the weather, dryness and the type of munitions involved.

“What needs to be looked at is what were the factors on that day, as opposed to general range guidelines.”

Training resumed on the base, although it is not the same kind of training conducted on Saturday, and the entire battalion will redeploy in the coming days.

Rutland said the military knows it must review its safety regulations, but emphasized Saturday’s devastating fire was an anomaly.

“We’ll be reviewing things like our ammunition and our range and training safety standards. Concurrent and ongoing investigations will examine every aspect of what happened,” he said.

Three investigations into the accident are taking place — two led by the military and one civilian.

Military police are leading a police investigation, while a military-led board of inquiry will look into the broader circumstances and recommend how to prevent this from ever happening again. The province’s chief medical examiner will look into the fatalities.

Rutland had told a Sunday briefing that the investigation could take at least a month. But on Thursday, he said he had “underestimated the scope” of the upcoming review by the military’s board of inquiry.

He said that panel’s fact-finding investigation will take “as long as it takes to examine all facets of the situation.”

Officials said 27 injured soldiers remain in various hospitals, with 13 in critical condition. Twelve others have since been released.

Those who died have been identified as: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

The military helped transport 19 intensive care nurses and five operating room nurses from Toronto that specialize in burn treatment to assist.

Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan said she’s heartbroken by the tragedy that has devastated affected families and the wider military community. She promised the military reviews will take place with transparency.

“There are difficult questions about what happened,” she said. “I am acutely aware of our responsibility to establish the facts, share the findings and act on what we learn.”

Brig.-Gen. Vanessa Hanrahan, head of the military police, said 30 officers are on the ground investigating, but the information they can confirm right now is limited.

“The investigation has confirmed that the fire originated as a result of a training event that was taking place on the anti-grenade launcher range,” she said.

“Every other aspect of what happened, from the time that fire originated on that range to what we have today dealing with the tragic accident on a different range in that area, is still under investigation.”

There remains no indication natural gas infrastructure was a factor in the fire, she added.

Officials said the fire had spread at a rapid pace, bypassing fireguards and flying toward what’s called a pair’s range — where two soldiers work as a team to practise live-fire exercises.

Previously, officials had said the fire had leapt to the section attack range.

The fire continued to burn beyond the training base, but apparently did not deal any lasting damage to base infrastructure.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 22, 2026.

— By Kyle Duggan in Ottawa, with files from Lisa Johnson in Edmonton

stories.title: Canadian convicted in U.S. terror plot gets 50 more years for stabbing prison staff
stories.summary: An Ontario man convicted of plotting a terrorist attack in the U.S. has been handed an additional 50-year sentence for stabbing two American prison staff.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An Ontario man convicted of plotting a terrorist attack in the U.S. has been handed an additional 50-year sentence for stabbing two American prison staff.

The U.S. Department of Justice says Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy was an inmate at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood in Pennsylvania when he stabbed two correctional officers in December 2020.

stories.title: Angine de Poitrine announce 2027 world tour
stories.summary: Angine de Poitrine is taking its alien invasion global.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Angine de Poitrine is taking its alien invasion global.

Quebec’s polka-dotted, self-proclaimed extraterrestrial duo has announced it will embark on a world tour in 2027.

It kicks off March 4 in Melbourne, Australia before touching down in South America, North America and Europe.

Among the eight Canadian dates are stops in Calgary, Ottawa and Winnipeg, as well as a performance at Toronto’s RBC Amphitheatre — marking their largest headlining show in the city so far.

The tour comes to a close in their hometown of Saguenay, Que.

In September, Angine de Poitrine won the $30,000 Polaris Music Prize for their second album, “Vol. II,” and the $10,000 SOCAN Polaris Song Prize for their track “Fabienk.”

They’re the first act to claim both prizes at the ceremony.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.

Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press
